I have heard that when the Gṛdhrakūṭa Peak transmitted the seal [of the Dharma], the wondrous truth was preserved in Zhugan (India); when the Horse Temple transmitted the sūtras, the patriarchal style was inaugurated in Zhendan (China).
All phenomena are quiescent and cannot be fully expressed; yet the Great Matter of the causal conditions is likewise realized through explanation.
To manifest the profound mystery, one transmits the mind of the bright sun; to guide and reach both devas and humans, one utters the tongue of the blue lotus. Otherwise, it would not be so.

Then even the lapis lazuli cases would be equivalent to dregs and lees, and the palm leaves no different from old paper. There must surely be something vast and long that unites both the Exoteric and Esoteric;

the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* was expounded at Gṛdhrakūṭa and later flowed into the Red Land of China. Entering into the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, it delivers boundless beings through its definitive meaning;
opening the faculties of those with superior awakening, it bestows the Perfect Teaching throughout the vast eons, illuminating every place it touches.

Truly, it manifests various auspicious signs, thereby revealing the provisional to disclose the ultimate. Emitting distinct rays of light from its hair-tips, it causes the hundreds of thousands of beings among devas and humans to all turn the wheel of Dharma;
four thousand fascicles of sutras are all surpassed by its wondrous verses. It is indeed the heart-essence of all Buddhas and the guiding principle of a thousand sages.
Its subtle phrasing and secret purport have been clarified through three translations alone; as for conjectural glosses and vulgar explanations, they too—
Among the various schools, none is more refined than this. Were it not for one endowed with the power of great wisdom, who could have dissected the true source?

Thus there was the Dharma Master Banweng, a dragon-elephant within the Dharma-gate and a phoenix among those who have transcended the world. Having traveled extensively to visit famous mountains, he was hailed as a peerless leader like Tandi;
having directly transcended mundane realms, he stilled all external conditions like Huike. In his later years, he took up residence in Chang’an, where he remained deeply absorbed in contemplation.

In a desolate temple, he occasionally ascended the Dharma seat; even the stubborn rocks nodded their heads in approval. He extensively expounded the conditions for awakening, and the flowers of emptiness thereby spread their colors.
He reflected that the wondrous Dharma is the most supreme among the Three Vehicles, and that its ineffable reality is the ultimate destination of the Five Teachings.

Although commentaries and exegeses are numerous, they are discordant and lack unity. Thereupon, he summoned the power of his vows to conduct a thorough investigation and open the treasury of the Buddhas.

It is bound with golden cords and gathers the jade-like essence of true dhyāna. Its characters are as closely set as teeth and its phrases are arranged in harmony; between the lines, it points toward the distant past.
When the meaning is grasped, words are forgotten; one realizes non-duality beyond all forms. Beholding the face of Mount Lu, the lingering mists are suddenly dispelled;
gazing upon the throat of the vast ocean, all tributary streams finally converge. To call this "Great Perfection"—how could it be anything less than a minor contribution? It is truly the Inner Canon.
I am unacquainted with the subject; my writing truly resembles the vulgarity of Yuan Zhen. To have presumed to adorn the head of a Buddha is to court the derision of Mazu Daoyi.
I merely offer these words, striving to the best of my limited capacity, out of admiration for Master Qin’s spiritual conduct.
On the twenty-second day of the third month of spring in the year of Yihai, the thirty-fourth year of the Kangxi reign,

[the following was inscribed for] the former Retoucher of the Imperial Library (Hanlin Jianshi), concurrently Left Assistant in the Left Spring Palace of the Office of the Imperial Secretariat (Zhan-shi-fu Zuochunfang Zuozanshan), who holds the rank of Jinshi (Presented Scholar).
Official of the Daily Lecturers and Keeper of the Court Records;
Compiler for the National Histories of the Three Reigns and the *Da Qing Yitongzhi*; Joint Examiner for the Provincial Examination of the Wuchen (1828) Examination Year.
Presented by Zhang Xiliang of Huangzhou,
former Compiler of the Hanlin Academy and former Graduate of the Hanlin Academy, who was specially appointed as the Chief Examiner for the Zhejiang Provincial Examination during the Gengwu year,
serving as the official in charge of the Palace Examination.
Regarding the editorial process:
Since the year of Jiawu (1854), I underwent tonsure at Jinling and traveled to the gates of various great Chan masters throughout Wuyue.

In the year of Bingwu (1866), carrying incense in my sleeve, I passed through the capital and first entered the chamber of my late father, where I began to investigate and compile the *Huayan Xuantan* (Profound Discourses on the Avatamsaka Sutra).
Having examined the ten gates and five teachings, I have finally come to realize that the Great Holy Canon is vast and expansive, beyond all measure.
On several occasions, I have discussed the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* with my teacher and have privately taken note of it.
First, I studied the *Wenju Yaoyi*, the *Zhiyin Huiyi*, and the *Zhengliang Lun*; subsequently, I read the *Zhengyi Duhui* and the *Dayao Yaozhi*. It is thus.

I have examined and compared the commentaries such as the *Jiebingwenbian*, the *Yijiepinjie*, and the *Kezhu*, as well as other sub-commentaries. Having thoroughly tasted and scrutinized them through various methods of cross-referencing, I have integrated these diverse explanations.
Although my own insights are but a narrow view, this compilation may now be arranged into two fascicles. It was compiled in the year Wushen (1868), during the winter of Jiyou (1869).
I followed my teacher in lecturing on the *Changchun* (Longevity of the Evergreen Tree). During the intervals between my leading the assembly in formal inquiries, I compiled another volume.

In the year Gengxu, I traveled to Mount Pan and compiled another volume. By the year Yimao, while residing at Yanshou Temple in Zhuolu, the final three volumes were completed and the manuscript was finalized.
In the year Bingchen, I traveled again to Jiangxi, where I sought correction from eminent scholars and veteran students; they all said: "This..."

The *Ji* (Collection) represents the great culmination of the *Lotus Sūtra*. In the spring of the Guihai year, when the Great Master returned to the capital for his sixtieth birthday, the Master was to lecture in Tianjin;
he therefore charged me with presiding over the Guanyin Hall to expound this sūtra. In the winter of the Bingyin year, the Master returned and commanded me to expound it once more.

He himself attended the lectures and instructed me to preserve the authentic manuscript, awaiting the right conditions to have it carved into woodblocks for publication. In the spring of the Dingmao year, I...
He retired from Guanyin Monastery and chose to dwell at Dizang. His dilapidated house with broken rafters barely shielded him from wind and rain.
Reflecting upon his own meager merit and thin virtue, he set aside worldly affairs and ceased the practice of social courtesies; thus, he adopted the theme of "living burial amidst the mountains.
He once said to a guest: "To dwell amidst the mountains even at a crossroads, and to cease all攀缘 (pān-yuan—clinging/entanglement) within a heap of red dust—this is not 'living burial'."
In the summer of the *renshen* year, my disciples gathered their funds and requested that I expound [this teaching] once more.

There were also those who wished to solicit donations for its carving into woodblocks, yet I did not grant permission. In the winter of the *guiyou* year, my elder brother Yumu came to the capital and urged me most earnestly;
he was the first to contribute thirty taels of gold. I then consulted with my fellow students, and they all joyfully offered their support. Led by the assembly members Daru and others, they...
This was undertaken through public solicitation. Yun, the Chief Administrator (Jianyuan), also exerted himself to the utmost in his labors; yet, at this moment, there was no choice but to proceed.
It commenced in the third month of spring in the year Jiashu and was completed in the fourth month of summer in the year Yihai. The work consists of ten volumes.
The preface was composed by the protective dharma-lord Zhanglao with his own brush; this "protective dharma-lord" is none other than the present-day Wujin (Wu-xin).

Thus, I have recorded its beginning and end as follows. I humbly reflect that our school’s patriarch Zongmi established the three contemplations (*trivipaśyanā*), Yunhua opened the ten gates, and Xianshou categorized the five teachings.
Qingliang annotated and further commented upon these works, so that the principles of the ultimate, perfect One Vehicle were fully realized. It is like the cook...
Fuxi drew the trigrams; King Wen provided the explanatory lines; and Confucius established the commentaries.

Mencius and Zhongni followed their legacy and modeled themselves upon their principles, thereby clarifying the profound purport of the sage’s spiritual transformations and the waxing and waning of the realms of the hidden and the manifest.

As for the "Hanging Explanation of the Ten Gates," the "Analysis of Principles in the Five Teachings," the "Cultivation and Realization through the Three Contemplations," and the "Perfect Fusion of the Ten Mysteries," these are fully detailed in the *Huayan Xuantan* (Prolegomena to the Avatamsaka) and elsewhere.

On the Buddha’s Birthday, in the fourth month of the summer of the thirty-fourth year of the Great Qing Kangxi era, the year of Yihai, I offer this Contemplation of the Dharma Realm (*dharmadhātu-vipaśyanā*).
In tracing back to the root and exhausting the source, I hold deep expectations for future scholars who study the Xianshou school.
The śramaṇa Dàyì of Jīntái, who transmits the lectures, inscribed this at his "Burial Alive" chamber in Jíshān.

Having realized this Dharma within the Bodhimaṇḍa, he immediately wished to bestow it as a gift upon all sentient beings; yet, alas, how can one reach those whose faculties and capacities [are insufficient]?
It was unbearable. Although he knew their faculties were dull, he nevertheless fulfilled his original intention by expounding the Great Avataṃsaka Sūtra;

however, it reached only those of superior capacity, while those of middling and inferior capacities remained in their seats as if deaf or mute. Having no choice, he then established provisional teachings for their sake by preaching the Four Āgamas and the Lesser Vehicle.
The sons of the Buddha had become fixated on a biased emptiness. Consequently, he first rebuked them with the Vaipulya (fangděng) teachings, and further refined them with the Prajñāpāramitā.
For forty years, he spoke here and there, drawing out the vines and extending the tendrils; he guided them step by step and mediated their differences at every turn.

Only now, when the time has arrived and the faculties have matured, the Great Assembly on Vulture Peak gathers a million beings from the realms of humans and devas, as well as the worthy and holy ones of the Three Vehicles and the eight classes of supernatural beings.
Kāla! It is like the myriad streams flowing toward the capital, or like the multitude of stars bowing to the North Star.

The World-Honored One wished to turn a new chapter and overturn the old case; however, as his preaching had continued for so long, he feared a lack of reverence, and thus manifested various auspicious signs.
A marvel that startled the common mind: first the Sūtra was preached, then the Tathāgata entered meditative absorption. Heaven rained down four kinds of flowers, and the earth shook in six ways.

The great assembly focused their minds as one to contemplate the Buddha. From the space between the Tathāgata’s eyebrows, radiance divided and the white-hair mark (*ūrṇā-kośa*) emitted light, illuminating eighteen thousand worlds in the eastern direction, reaching upward to the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) and downward to the Avīci Hell. As it was in this one direction, so it was in every direction. At that time—
Within a single ray of light, the ten dharma-realms and the beginning and end of the activities of birth and buddhahood are perfectly manifested.

Taking up this one scroll of the ineffable *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, I present it before everyone without opening my lips. Alas, the great assembly knows only that flowers rain from the heavens and the earth trembles;
they refuse to turn their heads or shift their minds. How can they bear to neglect the Tathāgata’s present stirring?

Thus, Maitreya harbored doubts; beholding the auspicious signs within the light, he questioned Mañjuśrī. Mañjuśrī accepted the inquiry and replied, citing the deeds of the Buddha Dīpaṃkara to corroborate the auspicious signs of the present Buddha.
These two Great Beings concealed the manifest and revealed the obscure, singing their praises in indirect yet comprehensive ways.

Before the Buddha had emerged from his meditative absorption and before the Dharma had issued from his mouth, they cited precedents and grasped at branches, intending thereby to establish the very purpose for the Buddha’s appearance in the world.

[The Buddha] harbored [this intention], exhausting it completely without remainder. Now that the Buddha has emerged from meditative absorption, what other distinct teaching could there possibly be to expound?

This chapter serves as the introductory section (*nidāna*). From the "Expedient Means" chapter through the "Never-Despising" chapter, comprising nineteen chapters, constitutes the main body (*samyak-siddhānta*).

However, the original intent for the Tathāgata’s appearance in the world is for the sake of the one great cause and condition (*ekamahā-karaṇīya-hetu-pratyaya*). That which is called the one great cause and condition is: opening, showing, awakening, and entering.
This is because all sentient beings are known and seen by the Buddha. The main body of the text is divided into four chapters:

from the "Expedient Means" chapter to the "Dharma Master," nine chapters in total, serve to open up the Buddha’s knowledge and vision; the two chapters on the "Jeweled Stupa" and "Devadatta" serve to demonstrate the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.

From the "Chapter on Upholding" (Dhāraṇī-parivarta) to the "Chapter on the Lifespan" (Āyuṣ-pramāṇa-parivarta), these four chapters are for the purpose of awakening to the Buddha’s knowledge and vision (*jñāna-darśana*).

From the "Chapter on the Analysis of the Dharma" (Dharmaparyāya-vibhaṅga) to the "Chapter on Never-Disparaging" (Sadāparibhūta), these are for the purpose of entering the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. Within the first [section] that opens the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, the text is divided into three cycles.

Following the preceding entry into meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and the emission of light, the intention was directly to cause the assembly to witness it with their own eyes, to realize it through personal experience, and to intuitively comprehend it beyond the realm of words. However, because the faculties of the listeners were dull...

Deluded, they fail to reach the path that transcends words. Therefore, when our World-Honored One emerged from samādhi, he praised the two wisdoms of the Buddhas—the provisional and the real—and his praise reached its ultimate point when he said:
"Stop, Śāriputra; there is no need to speak further. Why is this?"
The Dharma attained by all Buddhas is profound, subtle, difficult to understand, the foremost rarity, unsurpassed, and peerless.
It is something that no śrāvakas can know; only a Buddha and a Buddha can fully exhaustively realize the true nature of all phenomena (*dharmatā*).
Then, picking up the pivot of the teaching once more, he said: "After a long time, the Buddhas must surely speak."
It is true that there is resonance within words, like bait on the hook of a line. Consequently, the twelve hundred śrāvakas gave rise to doubts and reflections.
On three successive occasions, they made formal requests, and the Tathāgata granted their wish to provide a detailed explanation. Below, he extensively reveals the Three to manifest the One.
Whether it be all Buddhas of the past, future, or present appearing in the world, they do so solely for the sake of this One.
This is a matter of great significance; there is nothing else to it. In truth, it was not that there were three first and one later.

It was simply because of dull faculties that the path of the One Vehicle was explained as being threefold. This was done because those of small intelligence delight in minor teachings and do not believe they can become Buddhas themselves;

therefore, by means of skillful expedients, various fruits were distinguished. This correctly clarifies that the Three Vehicles are provisional. Furthermore, it says: "Now I rejoice in the absence of..."
Out of fear, [the Buddha] directly abandons expedient means and teaches only the Unsurpassed Way. This clearly reveals that the One Vehicle is the reality; the Way of every Buddha is the same.
As it was with the Buddhas of the past, so it is with the present Buddha. To first teach the three and later the one is merely following established precedent.
In terms of persons, he teaches only Bodhisattvas, with no śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas. In terms of principle, this alone is the true reality; the other two are...
If it were otherwise, it would not be true. Regarding the teaching (*śāsana*): "In all the Buddha-lands of the ten directions, there is only the One Vehicle Dharma.

Regarding practice (*pratipatti*): "Whatever is undertaken is always for the sake of this one thing. Having fully expounded this through prose and verse, those whose faculties were suited to the teaching realized their destination upon hearing the words.

They stepped out from the assembly to receive understanding, recounting the doubts and regrets of former years and manifesting the realization of this day. The Tathāgata then confirmed and certified them.

Because their understanding was not in vain, they were granted the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*) of the adornment of future kalpas and lands; this constitutes the first cycle of the Dharma teaching for those of superior faculties.

However, as for those of middling and inferior capacities, their delusions remained unresolved. Although Śāriputra’s own realization was already perfected, out of compassion for others who had not yet awakened, he requested [the Buddha] on their behalf.
Thus, the World-Honored One could not avoid stirring the trees and training the winds, raising his fan to liken it to the moon; hence there is [the second cycle].

This is an allegorical discourse: the worldly householder is compared to the supramundane Tathāgata; the triple world is likened to a house; the teachings and principles of the One Vehicle are likened to the gate;
the sentient beings of the five destinies are likened to five hundred people; the five turbidities and eight sufferings are likened to fire;
and the thirty sons are likened to the three vehicles. When the householder saw the great fire rising from all four sides, he was immediately seized with great terror and agitation.
He deliberated on the means to save his children. First, he attempted to rescue them with his own body, hands, and a small table, but this proved unsuccessful.

Thereupon, he skillfully set out three carts outside the gate to entice the children and lead them out of the burning house. He did not give them the three carts; instead, he bestowed upon each child an equal, single great vehicle.
When one asks what is appropriate for their capacity, it is certain and not false; this perfectly accords with the Tathāgata abiding in the Dharmakāya.
On the ground of principle, the Buddha observes with his Buddha-eye that sentient beings are being scorched and boiled by the five turbidities and the eight sufferings;
they are attached to their playgrounds and do not seek liberation. Facing the gateway of the present age, he manifests transformations throughout the three realms.

First, he employs the subtle and wondrous Great Dharma as a provisional measure, but when their faculties prove incapable of bearing it, he then skillfully expounds the Three Vehicles to suit the timing and circumstances. This continues until the present day.
The Sūtra opens the provisional means of the three vehicles to reveal the reality of the one vehicle, bestowing it equally upon all sons so that no one is left to attain nirvāṇa alone.
This is just like the elder who first offers three carts and subsequently provides the single cart; there is not the slightest fault of falsehood in this.
Yet this parable is the Tathāgata’s exercise of unimpeded eloquence, clarifying the suffering of birth and death within the triple world.
This description causes people to feel profound revulsion and renunciation. The prose and verse sections are now complete.

The four sons, with one voice and different mouths, have related the parable of the impoverished son, beginning from the loss and subsequent meeting of father and son, and ending with the entrustment of the family estate.

This prefaces the Tathāgata’s teachings throughout his lifetime, starting from the *Avataṃsaka* and ending with the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*. The sequence of events is orderly, and the principles presented follow a systematic progression.
At that time, their discursive discourse was exhaustive in its precision and detail; thus, the Tathāgata completed his exposition through the parable of the medicinal herbs.

He first praised the four sons for their skillful explanation, specifically regarding the parable of the impoverished son, which fully elucidates the beginning and end of the Tathāgata’s single transformation of beings—truly a skillful exposition.
However, the merits of the Tathāgata do not end here; they are further immeasurable and boundless. As it says:

The teaching of a single mark and a single flavor is bestowed equally upon the great trichiliocosm; it is universal and without distinction, for differentiation lies only in the capacity of the recipient.

If it were like a single cloud and a single rain, where the three types of grasses and two types of trees would not be separated by their withering or flourishing, how could the parable of the one impoverished son alone exhaust the merits of the Tathāgata?
Nevertheless, you all are also most rare, for you have been able to understand this within forty years.
This is because he teaches the Dharma according to what is appropriate. The four sons receive their predictions; this constitutes one cycle of the parable for those of medium faculties.
Following this, in the "Unasked Discourse" (*Anupṛṣṭa-svayaṃbhāṣita*), within the verses, he first introduces a discourse on past causes and conditions:
"My disciples, endowed with majestic power, number five hundred; they shall all receive their predictions and, in a future age, shall all attain [enlightenment]."

The Buddha said: "I and you all share a karmic affinity from past lives; I shall now explain it. Therefore, there is the 'Parable of the Phantom City' chapter, which explains the causal conditions for those of inferior faculties.
The origin of this formation of a connection dates back to before the *rajas-aṇu* kalpas, when the Great Universal Buddha attained enlightenment.

Princes and various devas gathered like clouds; the Buddha of Wisdom responded to their capacities by preaching the Dharma, after which he entered meditative absorption in tranquil stillness. The King...

The sons intuitively understood the Buddha’s intention; each ascended the Dharma seat and preached the wondrous Dharma once more. Each of them brought across six million billion *gaṅgā*-sands of beings.
From that time onward, those with whom they had established karmic connections have encountered one another life after life.

Among them, some were matured in previous lives, while others were matured in this present life—just as a fisherman catches fish: those caught in the first net are obtained first, and those in the subsequent nets follow.

It was later that he attained it. Only today, forty years later, at this great assembly of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, has he opened up the provisional to reveal the real, and unified the three vehicles into the one, thereby resolving the unsolved case from the time of Mahābhijñājñāna and fulfilling the original intent of this descent of the spirit.
Thus, he spoke of the "phantom city" as being established merely to provide rest for the weary multitude, clarifying that the Three Vehicles are provisional, while the place of the treasure is real.
Drawing near, he caused his sons to joyfully advance, thereby clarifying that the One Vehicle is the reality.
Consequently, the five hundred disciples received their predictions and rejoiced. He then spoke the parable of the tied jewel to repay the instruction regarding the causes and conditions.
The twelve hundred śrāvakas and the two thousand learners and non-learners each received their predictions; this constitutes one cycle of the teaching for those of inferior capacity.

Thus, the three rounds of bestowing predictions have concluded. Yet, fearing that the capacities of beings might not be fully gathered, he further provides extensive and prophetic records in the "Dharma Master" chapter for the fourfold assembly and the eight classes of beings, so that they may rejoice and leap for joy, realizing that their own minds are destined for Buddhahood.

Therefore, these nine grades constitute the opening of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. Second, as for "showing the Buddha’s knowledge and vision": because the various sons previously received their predictions, there was only fear of being defiled by...

Because their attachments to [the notions of] pure birth, cessation, and so forth were not yet eliminated, the Stūpa of Many Jewels and Vows manifested before them. From within the stūpa, a great voice issued forth, praising him, saying:

"Excellent! Śākyamuni has been able to preach for the great assembly the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*—the Dharma for instructing bodhisattvas, which is protected by the Buddhas—by means of his equal great wisdom. It is so, it is so! Because of your joyful desire to explain and inquire..."
The conditions were such that the Tathāgata gathered his emanations from all directions and performed the three transformations of the Pure Land.

He removed the attachments to the defiled and the pure, opened the door of the precious stūpa, and revealed the aspect of ultimate reality. Entering the stūpa, he took his seat, free from any view of coming, going, birth, or cessation.

He announced his passing and sought out those capable of ensuring that these teachings would not fall into ruin. Furthermore, he spoke of the chapter on Devadatta, wherein Daḍa mastered the sūtras, and of Śākyamuni...

Relying on this, one accomplishes the Way; Mañjuśrī propagated the sutra, and the dragon girl thereby attained Buddhahood. This clearly demonstrates the divine efficacy of the Sublime Dharma (Saddharmapuṇḍarīka):
it harbors no enmity and no favoritism, making no distinction between man or woman, human or beast. This Great Equal Wisdom is inherently possessed by every person.

Therefore, these two chapters serve to reveal the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. Third, as for "awakening to the Buddha’s knowledge and vision," it proceeds from the preceding "Chapter on the Jeweled Stupa."
He recruited those who had mastered the sutras, for the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* was entrusted to those who were worthy.
Thus, in the "Dharani" chapter, the Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja and twenty thousand mahāsattvas made a vow to propagate this sutra within this Sahā world.

Furthermore, twelve thousand newly ordained śrāvakas, recognizing that their own powers of the Way were not yet sufficient and fearing the difficulties of the Sahā world—its being hard to discipline and subdue—made a vow to [seek] another [land].
Throughout the worlds, whether in this land or other directions, those who were designated by drawing lots to propagate this sutra did not satisfy the Holy One’s intention.
Therefore, the World-Honored One turned his gaze with eyes like blue lotuses toward eighty trillion nayutas of bodhisattvas and great beings.
These worthies, intuitively grasping the Buddha’s mind, vowed to travel back and forth between this land and other directions to widely propagate this sutra.

Abiding in the stage of patience, even if there are monks in this degenerate age who are sycophantic, dishonest, and falsely claim to dwell in the forest (*araṇya*), yet delight in exposing our faults and repeatedly subject us to expulsion—regarding such contempt and slander, one should endure them by recollecting the Buddha.

However, while it is certainly excellent to endure hardships for the sake of propagating the sutras, it is not as admirable as propagating them without difficulty; thus, one should endure all hardships.
Once a fire has already broken out, it is better to prevent all difficulties before they arise.

This is why Mañjuśrī could not restrain himself from asking the World-Honored One: "In this evil age, how can one preach this sutra? By attaining what dharma can one remain far removed from all such calamities?
The Tathāgata then showed him the four practices of peaceful dwelling (*catur-ārāga-vihāra*), beginning with physical peace.
They delight in dwelling on the ground of patience, remaining far removed from all wicked people. Their speech is peaceful and blissful, never speaking of others' faults, evils, or shortcomings.

Their minds are peaceful and blissful, expounding the Dharma with equanimity to teach and transform sentient beings. With vows that are peaceful and blissful, they abide wherever sentient beings may dwell;
by means of their power of spiritual transformations and power of wisdom, they lead them all to abide within this Single Vehicle.

If a Dharma Master who propagates this sutra is indeed able to sustain himself by the three norms and maintain himself by the four practices, then there will be no situation he enters where he does not find fulfillment.
Below, the text extensively praises the divine and wondrous nature of this sutra, likening it to a bright pearl atop a king’s head, which must not be given away to just anyone.
What was not previously explained is now being taught. Those who seek the Buddha-way and desire to attain peace and security should draw near to these four dharmas.
They transform the three kinds of obstacles and achieve enlightenment through the eight phases; because there are such benefits, Bodhisattvas from other lands [come].
Their number exceeded that of the sands of eight Ganges Rivers. They addressed the Buddha, saying, "We pray that You will remain in this land to extensively expound this sutra.
The Tathāgata declined and did not grant their request, for since they were bodhisattvas from other lands, their karmic connection with this land was shallow;
if they were to dwell here and teach, they would lose their primary benefit. "In our Sahā world, there are already sixty thousand Ganges-sands of bodhisattvas, each of whom..."
There are sixty thousand retinues as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. These individuals shall be able to protect and uphold this sutra and preach it extensively in this land;
that is to say, they are my disciples who should propagate my Way, excellently continuing and transmitting it—just as a son inherits his father’s legacy, which is an inevitable principle.
At the moment the Tathāgata utters this command, the ground of the trichiliocosm will all...
The earth quaked and split open. Immeasurable and innumerable bodhisattvas simultaneously surged forth, each proceeding to the void to pay homage to the two World-Honored Ones.
They praised the Buddhas with various verses extolling the Dharma. The four guides stepped forward from the assembly to inquire after the Tathāgata’s well-being and exclaimed, "Excellent!
You have been able to give rise to a heart of sympathetic joy toward the Tathāgata. Thereupon, Maitreya led eighty thousand [bodhisattvas] as numerous as the sands of the Ganges...
The Bodhisattva Śāriputra, harboring doubts, raised a question: "What path do these bodhisattvas cultivate? By what causes and conditions have they gathered?
Who is their teacher? Whose disciples are they? Among this assembly, I do not recognize a single one. The Buddha told Maitreya:
"These bodhisattvas cultivate the wisdom of the Buddhas; they are all my transformations and my disciples. [At this, Śāriputra] moved downward.
Regarding their attachment to recent events, they say: "I sat beneath the Bodhi tree in the city of Gayā and attained the Way of Buddhahood;
there I taught and transformed them. They also say: "I now speak words of truth; you all should believe with one mind that from long ago I have been teaching and transforming this multitude.
Maitreya again harbored doubts, so [the Buddha] spoke the parable of the father being young and the son being old to refute their attachment to the recent.

Because the distant origin is doubted based on the immediate traces, there is the discourse on the span of the Buddha’s life. This reveals the near traces of the Master’s school and manifests the distant origin of the Buddha-ground.
After issuing three admonitions to ensure attentive listening and receiving three requests with the utmost earnestness, he then addressed them, saying:
"All of you—devas, humans, and asuras—believe that the present Buddha appeared in the palace of the Śākya clan and departed from the city of Gayā."

It is not far; sitting in the place of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), one attains *bodhi*. However, good son, it has actually been an incalculable and boundless number of *kalpas*, like motes of dust, since I first attained Buddhahood.
From that time until now, I have constantly remained in this world, teaching the Dharma and transforming sentient beings.

My names have been different, and I have benefited beings through both my physical form and my voice, teaching and transforming them by manifesting birth when there was no birth and manifesting extinction when there was no extinction.

All that has been spoken is true and not false. Just as a skilled physician may employ skillful means to manifest birth and manifest death for the sake of treating a mad son, [the Tathāgata] does so solely to lead all sentient beings into supreme wisdom and enable them to achieve the Buddha-body.

Thus, through this revelation of the Dharma assembly, the great multitude realized the ocean of Vairocana’s nature. The Buddha-ground is remote from its origin, yet benefits beings throughout the three periods of time;
the Dharmakāya is eternally abiding, without past or present. It was not begun before the void kalpa, nor does it end at the limit of the future.
The Buddha’s knowledge and vision exhaustively reach the ultimate source; therefore, these four chapters constitute the awakening to the Buddha’s knowledge.

It is so. Regarding the fourth [stage], "entering the Buddha’s knowledge and vision": because it was previously stated that his lifespan is long and far-reaching, benefiting sentient beings throughout the three periods of time with an uninterrupted succession of transformations, the great assembly at the Dharma-gathering realizes the truth of the Dharma-body.

Their profound faith and understanding reach their ultimate limit through wondrous awakening, such that each and every one enters the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. However, as there are differences between those who enter through realization and those who enter through understanding, the Tathāgata distinguishes them accordingly.

Other merits: some attain the patience of birth (*janma-kṣānti*); some attain dhāraṇī; some attain unimpeded eloquence (*pratibhāna*) and so forth; some attain faith and understanding for a single thought-moment;

some attain deep-seated faith and understanding. There are those who simply give rise to sympathetic joy (*anumodanā*), those who additionally uphold [the teaching], those who exhort others to uphold it, those who practice the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*) concurrently, and those who fully practice the six perfections. The merits obtained by each and every one of these—
Having completed this evaluation, it was found that its ultimate limit had not yet been reached.

Furthermore, by rejoicing with even a single thought, according to what one has heard, and joyfully explaining it to others so that it is transmitted from one to another until it reaches the fiftieth person—who likewise attains the purification of the six sense faculties—how much more so for those who receive, uphold, read, and recite it?
The more these merits are compared, the more they prove to be inexhaustible. Moreover, by means of the five kinds of Dharma-preachers who uphold...

When this sutra was preached, the essential meaning was realized and deluded thoughts were forgotten; both sense organs and their objects became pure. The five kinds of merit were perfected and the six thousand virtues were fulfilled.
How could the wondrous merit of the six faculties being used interchangeably be measured?

Not slighting even a single grade, the Tathāgata cited his own past deeds to propagate the Way with an open mind and benefit others by forgetting himself. With a single utterance of the Buddha’s name, he universally took note of the fourfold assembly. Thus it was seen...
When people bow to him, he does not feel anger even when encountering wrath; when subjected to beating, abuse, slander, or defamation, he joyfully endures it.

This is impossible for anyone who has not entered the Buddha’s knowledge and vision and deeply penetrated the true reality of the emptiness of both person and phenomena (*pudgala-dharma-ubhaya-śūnyatā*). Therefore, these four chapters constitute the text on entering the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
The main body of the teaching (*śarīra*) is now concluded. The following eight chapters constitute the section on circulation (*pariṇāmanā*). Since the main body is finished, [the original]...
Because his inner resolve was already manifest, the Tathāgata displayed great supernormal powers and extolled the virtues of this sūtra to inspire the minds of all beings.

Taking this single scroll of the wondrous Dharma, he proclaimed it—both openly and secretly—throughout space and throughout the world, in every atom and every buddha-field, before the entire assembly.
Upon seeing, hearing, believing, and understanding, great joy fills the body; hence there is talk of "divine power.
Having finished this praise, it should now be entrusted so that the lineage of the Way may be transmitted and these teachings shall not perish.

One should know that in the age of the final dharma, those who ascend the hall and take their seats to propagate the Great Dharma do so because of the singular compassion of all Buddhas. If the patriarchs and ancestors had not understood this, it would have been a calamity.
This is because it has been transmitted through successive generations from father to son and grandson.
Having completed the entrustment, I fear that those who have newly received this teaching might rely on their own innate nature and become negligent in their cultivation;

therefore, I urge them by means of the ascetic practices of Bhaiṣajyarāja, the extensive proclamation of Gadgadasvara, the universal gate of Avalokiteśvara, the protection against Māra through divine mantras, the turning away of evil by Śūraṅgama, and the four practices of Samantabhadra.
Exhort the great assembly: To uphold the Dharma, you should emulate the asceticism of Bhaiṣajyarāja; to propagate the Dharma, you should emulate the skillful means of Gadgadasvara and Avalokiteśvara;
to protect the Dharma, you should emulate the subduing of demons through divine mantras; to practice the path, you should emulate King Śubhavyūha’s conversion of the heterodox;

and to inspire others, you must emulate the essential prayers of Samantabhadra. If these four practices are accomplished and examined with such diligence, the Wondrous Dharma will flow forth and its transmission shall never end.

Thus it is. From this day forward, who among those who proclaim and expound the Great Dharma is not entrusted with the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*? Now, the Wondrous Dharma is absolute and beyond all comparison; fundamentally, it is devoid of words and images.
Yet, because of differences in wisdom and practice, many commentaries have been composed. Since there are so many commentaries, how can one avoid the pitfalls of selection and rejection?
To harmonize with its essential purport, one must investigate its general outline. I have therefore recorded its essentials here to provide a guiding framework.
Thus, on the eighteenth day of the fourth month of the year Yihai in the Kangxi era, Da Yi of Lok Village in Rongze, Zhongzhou, made this record.
The Great Commentary on the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*:
A Preliminary Discourse by the Junior Scholar Dayi of Jinsui Mountain.

△ Now, in order to explain this sutra, I shall introduce it through ten topical gates: First, the causes and conditions for the arising of the teaching; Second, its classification and inclusion within the Tripitaka and the various teachings.

1. The delimitation of principles and meanings; 2. The capacities of sentient beings reached by the four teachings; 3. The depth of the essence of the teachings; 4. The general and specific purports of the doctrines;
5. The categories of sections and assemblies; 6. The transmission, translation, and spiritual resonance; 7. A general explanation of the title; 8. A detailed interpretation of the textual meaning.
First, regarding the causes and conditions for the arising of the teaching:
Now, when the Sages establish their teachings, there must be a specific cause and condition, just as Mount Sumeru and the vast ocean are only moved by great causes.
To now shake the Tathāgata’s mountain of virtue, refined like gold, and to stir his deep and expansive ocean of wisdom, cannot be due to minor conditions.

These causes and conditions are both general and specific. As for the general causes and conditions, they refer to the entirety of the Buddha’s sacred teachings throughout his lifetime, which collectively serve to repay [the debt of] causes and repay...
Please explain the principle for delivering sentient beings. The principle thus revealed is that which is stated in this very sutra:

the appearance in the world of the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, is solely for the sake of the one great causal condition—to open, show, awaken, and lead all sentient beings to the Buddha-knowledge and Buddha-vision.
This wisdom and insight is possessed equally by all sentient beings; yet, being deluded, they do not know it themselves, and thus they sink into the cycle of birth and death.
The Buddha realized this while still on the path of causes, made a vow to attain Buddhahood to reveal it universally, and has therefore established the teachings throughout the five periods.

Although these teachings are said to have provisional and ultimate aspects, and manifest as having varying degrees of slowness or speed, when one examines his original intent, it is solely for the sake of this one great causal event.

To discuss the causes and conditions separately, there are many types; here, I shall briefly indicate ten meanings. First, this sutra is preached because it is the natural order of things (*dharmatā*).
Now, the Way of Kings is broad and level, following the same standard for a thousand ages; the true reality (*bhūtatathatā*) of the One Vehicle is realized equally by all Buddhas.
Therefore, as the nature of all Buddhas, they constantly turn this inexhaustible, wondrous Dharma throughout infinite worlds.
He teaches and transforms sentient beings without ceasing. Therefore, in the passage below, the assembly of humans and devas gathers; he preaches the sutra and enters meditative concentration;
flowers rain down and the earth trembles; the realm of wisdom is fully revealed in a single ray of light, opening its beginning in perfect fullness.
Two sages sing forth in harmony to assist in unfolding its sequence, citing twenty thousand Buddhas, such as Dīpaṃkara, all of whom preached this sutra, up to Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū Buddha.

Buddha King of Majestic Sound (Bhīṣmagarjitasvararāja) all preached the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*. The Way of Buddha after Buddha is the same; as it was with the Buddhas of antiquity, so it must be for the present Buddha. As the text says:
"I have always been here in this Sahā world, preaching the Dharma and transforming sentient beings," and so forth.

Second, he preached this sutra because he wished to express his original aspiration. Having attained enlightenment at the site of awakening (bodhimaṇḍa), he immediately desired to reveal and instruct [others]; however, alas, their faculties were dull and [they did not understand].
It is capable of being received and upheld. Therefore, for forty years prior to this, I suppressed this wondrous Dharma within my breast;

because the five vehicles were adapted to individual capacities, my original intention was not fully realized. Only now, at this great assembly on Mount Ling, do I finally preach this sutra, and thus my original intention has at last been fulfilled.
As the text says: "My former vows have now been satisfied. And again: "The reason the Tathāgata appeared in the world..."
It was for the sake of expounding the Buddha’s wisdom that he taught this sutra. Third, it was taught in accordance with the timing and conditions of the occasion.

Now, the ultimate Way has neither past nor present; yet responding to capacities requires specific seasons and times. For a long time he remained silent regarding this essential point, not being intent on expounding it hastily.

Thus, the reason he did not teach this sutra during the forty years prior was that the time had not yet arrived and the capacities of beings were not yet ready. As the text says: "The faculties of sentient beings are dull, and they are attached to pleasure."

Blinded by ignorance—how can such as these be delivered? By guiding them gradually and skillfully, when their faculties have matured and the time for the teaching has arrived, they may join the sublime assembly.
As the text says: "Now is precisely that time; I shall definitively expound the Mahāyāna.
Such a wondrous Dharma is taught by the Buddhas only at certain times," and furthermore, as the end of his transformation is near, it is the time of his Nirvāṇa.

Having arrived, [the Buddha] taught in accordance with the time and the capacities of beings; he could not help but speak. It was for the sake of the four assemblies and the provisional vehicles that he preached this sutra.

Forty years ago, he taught the One Vehicle as three vehicles and the one nature as five natures, employing provisional means for those of lesser capacity, like using yellow leaves to stop a child’s crying.

Thus, there were the distinctions of the three vehicles and the divisions of the five natures. Who would have known that the five natures are the one nature, and that the three vehicles [are the one vehicle]?
"This is the One Vehicle! The Tathāgata’s teaching of the Dharma is solely for the purpose of transforming bodhisattvas; there are no śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.

Now, through this sutra, those of the three faculties receive their prediction [of enlightenment], merging the provisional fruits of the two vehicles and fully entrusting them with the family inheritance, thereby abolishing the stagnant attachments of the 'grass hut'."

When Śrāvakas receive their prediction of future Buddhahood, they ultimately all become Bodhisattvas. If they were not to reach this ultimate convergence, then their provisional [status] would remain merely provisional until the end.
Fifth, it is to reveal the reality that he preaches this sutra: "In the Buddha-lands of the ten directions, there is only the Single Vehicle Dharma."

There is neither two nor three; the three vehicles are but skillful means (*upāya*). Because the conditions for receiving and understanding [the teaching] differ, this present sutra opens the gate of skillful means to reveal the true aspect (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).
It points to the pearl in the garment and the pearl in the topknot;

it leads one out of the illusory city and the burning house, so that all may ascend together to the house of the elder and proceed forward to the precious site of Bodhi—all of which are discourses revealing the truth. Sixth, it is because of repaying past conditions (*pūrvapratyaya*).

In expounding this sutra, [the Buddha] said: "When the roots are deep, the branches flourish; when the source is distant, the stream is long. Since my past causes were profound, the arising of this teaching is likewise vast.

Thus the sutra says: 'During the time of the Buddha Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū, I individually taught and transformed immeasurable sentient beings as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, who heard the Dharma from me.
Among these sentient beings, there are those who now abide on the stage of the śrāvaka.'"
I have constantly taught and transformed them for unexcelled bodhi. This great matter of long-standing, which was not yet resolved, I shall now repay.
As explained extensively in the *Parable of the City of Illusion*, this sutra is preached to manifest the Buddha’s wisdom. The text says:
"I see these sons of the Buddha and others who are resolutely seeking the Buddha-way; all with hearts of reverence come to where the Buddha is. I then reflect upon them..."
The reason for his coming forth is to expound the Buddha-wisdom; this Buddha-wisdom is none other than the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).

When the Dharma was completed in three cycles, the Stupa of Prabhūtaratna appeared, which is precisely to manifest the impartial Buddha-wisdom. The text says: "From within the stupa, a great voice issued forth, praising: 'Excellent, Śākyamuni!
You are able to teach and transform sentient beings with the great wisdom of equality. As for what is meant by 'equality'—"

This is because there is no distinction between enemies and kin in the absence of arising and ceasing. Eighth, this sutra is preached to reveal the original and the manifested (honji-suijaku). Regarding the original and manifested aspects of the Teacher:
that which was first attained—the True Body (dharmakāya) and the Responsive Body (nirmāṇakāya)—is designated as the "original.

The subsequent periods, such as the time of Mahāvairocana, the time of King Weyin, and the present manifestation at the royal palace and the attainment of honor under the Bodhi tree, are all considered "manifested" (traces). As the *Brahmajāla Sūtra* states: "Eight thousand..."
Manifesting repeatedly in this Sahā world, the *Mahāratnakūṭa Sūtra* states that he has come to this land eighty trillion times. Now, this sutra reveals his original lifespan:
even before the kalpas marked by the dust-points, there were further dust-point kalpas; though those dust-point kalpas are exhausted, his manifestation does not cease.
He neither truly arises nor truly perishes, yet he constantly dwells here preaching the Dharma and transforming sentient beings. How could he have only become a World-Honored One as a Buddha today?

It is said: "The text states: 'I have in fact attained Buddhahood for a duration as long as this; it is only through skillful means (*upāya*) that I teach and transform sentient beings by speaking thus.
As for the fundamental reality and provisional manifestation of the Disciple, he has already attained Buddhahood long ago and now acts as a harpist to strike the strings."
"Secret within and manifest without—how could they truly be śrāvakas? This sutra is preached because it encompasses both the beginning and the end.
The beginning is the root; the root is the *Avataṃsaka*. Therefore, Jizang establishes the *Avataṃsaka* as the Dharma-wheel of the Root.
The end is the branch; the branch is the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*. Therefore, Jizang establishes the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* as the Dharma-wheel of Gathering the Branches Back to the Root. As it is said:
Without the ocean, there can be no hidden current; without the root, there can be no encompassing of the branches. From beginning to end, it is a single thread;

from root to branch, it is a single matter. Therefore, the subsequent text says: "As soon as they see my body and hear what I teach, they all believe and accept it, entering the wisdom of the Tathāgata."
He then began to preach the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, just as when the sun first rises, its light first illuminates the high mountains. Furthermore, he said:

"Except for those who have previously practiced and studied the Hīnayāna, I shall now also cause them to hear this sūtra and enter the Buddha-wisdom. Thus, at the end, he preached the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*.
It is like the setting sun, which still shines upon high mountains and the like; from the root to the branches, beginning and ending are both fulfilled.

There is no matter that is not exhausted, and no principle that is not fully realized. The original intent of his appearance in the world is hereby brought to completion. For the sake of the ten benefits for the future, he preached this sutra.

He expounded the Dharma in three cycles and bestowed predictions of Buddhahood upon those of the three capacities. Among all who have heard the Dharma, there is not one who will not attain Buddhahood.

The benefit for the present: after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, if one hears even a single phrase or a single verse of this sutra, I shall likewise bestow upon them the prediction of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
The benefit for the future: if one considers the Buddha’s presence as the "present," then what is seen and heard now is the "future";
if one considers what is seen and heard now as the "present," then what is seen and heard later is the "future. In this way, [the Dharma] is propagated.
The transmission is inexhaustible; the benefit is infinite. Like swallowing a diamond, it is never consumed.
This concludes the section on the causes and conditions for the arising of the teaching, whether considered collectively or individually.

△ Section Two: Classification by the Two Baskets (Piṭaka). This is divided into three parts: first, clarifying inclusion within the baskets; second, clarifying inclusion within the teachings; third, clarifying inclusion within the divisions.
Regarding the first, clarifying inclusion within the baskets, there are two sections. First, clarifying the three baskets (*tripiṭaka*).
It is already known that this sutra possesses such a great causal nexus; however, it remains uncertain to which division within the *piṭaka* (collections) of the teachings this sutra belongs.
Therefore, the following section clarifies this point. Generally speaking, the term "piṭaka" refers to that which is able to contain and give rise to all principles and meanings.
Regarding the "Three Piṭakas," the first is the Sūtra-piṭaka, also called Sūtranta, and also called...

*Sūtra*. These are all variations of the Sanskrit sound, like the difference between the "Chu" and "Xia" dialects. In ancient translations, it was rendered as *qijing* (契經). "Qie" (契) means to accord with principle (*li*) and accord with the capacity of beings (*ji*).

"Jing" (經) means to string together, penetrate, and gather/instruct. A *jing* that accords with principle and fits the capacity is thus named by depending on its primary attribute (*yishu shouming*). Thus, the *qijing* is itself the *piṭaka*.
This is a *karmadhāraya* compound. According to the five regions of India, there are four names for it: thread (*sūtra*), matting, rope, and sacred teaching (*āgama*).

These are all alternative designations for *sūtra*. When the ancient masters observed that in this land [China], both the Confucians and the Mohists refer to their texts as "Classics" (*jing*), they borrowed the term "matting" from them to designate the sacred teachings;
thus, it simultaneously encompasses two meanings and accords with both traditions, using a borrowed meaning to assist the name.
Furthermore, the term *sūtra* (契) is added to distinguish it from ordinary texts; thus it is called a *Sūtra*. Moreover, the *Abhidharmahṛdaya-śāstra* states that a *sūtra* possesses five meanings:
first, it is like a "gushing spring," meaning its flow is inexhaustible; second, it is "production," meaning it increases and expands through successive transmission;

third, it is "manifestation," meaning it can reveal both phenomena (*dharma*) and principle (*artha*); fourth, it is a "plumb line," meaning it serves as a standard for correcting what is deviant and establishing what is correct.

Therefore, the fifth is called "binding" (*granthi*), meaning that the thread is able to string together the flowers. These five meanings do not transcend the two senses of "stringing together" (*anugata*) and "gathering" (*saṃgraha*);
for by means of the Buddha’s holy teaching, one strings together and gathers up the meanings that ought to be explained for the sake of those beings to be converted.

Second is the *Vinaya-piṭaka*, also named *Vinī*. This is a contraction of the Sanskrit sound; here it is translated as "Discipline" (*vinaya*). This refers to the training and refining of the three karmas, and the subduing [of the passions].
Faults are eliminated. "Discipline" (*vinaya*) applies to both cessation and action; "restraint" (*saṃvara*) clarifies only the cessation of evil.

When named according to the conduct it explains, it is the "Treasury of Discipline" (*Vinayapiṭaka*), a *tatpuruṣa* compound. Alternatively, the treasury that expresses [the meaning] possesses the capacity for discipline, which is a *bahuvrīhi* compound.
*Vinaya* is also translated as "extinction" (*nirodha*), which has three meanings. First, the extinction of unwholesome karma, such as refraining from killing and so forth.
Second, the cessation of afflictions, which refers to non-attachment and so forth. Third, the attainment of the fruit of cessation, which is the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) fruit.

It is also called *śīla*, which here means "cooling. This name is derived from both cause and fruit, meaning that by abandoning the causes of feverish affliction, one attains the fruit of refreshing coolness.
It is also called *pratimokṣa*, which here means "individual liberation. This name is derived from the cause. There are two [aspects]: first, distinguishing it from others...

The meditative concentrations and the paths are termed "distinct" (*viśeṣa*). Because the three types of action and the seven branches each separately prevent what is non-virtuous, they are also called "distinct.

They are also called "conducive to liberation" (*anuloma-vimukti*), a name established in reference to their fruit; that is, because they are conducive to the two kinds of fruits: the conditioned and the unconditioned.
It is also called "inherently virtuous" because its nature is fundamentally good. Third is the Abhidharma Piṭaka; this is translated as "Dharma-against" (Pāramārthika-dharma).
There are two kinds of Dharma: first, the Ultimate Dharma, which refers to Nirvāṇa itself. It is called "ultimate" because it is both virtuous and eternal.

Second, the Dharma of Characteristics, which encompasses the Four Noble Truths. Furthermore, "against" (prati) has two meanings: first, "directing toward," meaning directed toward Nirvāṇa; second, [the meaning of]...

Regarding "counter-observation" (*pratyavekṣā*): it refers to observing the four noble truths. That which is capable of counter-observing consists of untainted pure wisdom (*anāsrava-viśuddha-prajñā*) along with its associated mental factors (*caitta*).
It is also called *upadeśa*, which here means "treatise" (*lun-yi*); it is also called *mātṛkā*, which here means "matrix" (*benmu*).
This is because the teachings and their meanings serve as the basis and the matrix. These three baskets (*piṭaka*), in terms of what they expound, have two meanings.
First, regarding their essential nature: the Sūtras elucidate the three trainings; the Vinaya elucidates only two trainings—precept and mind; and the Śāstras elucidate only the training in wisdom.

Second, regarding the primary and secondary aspects: the Sūtras primarily elucidate concentration; the Vinaya elucidates precepts; and the Śāstras elucidate wisdom. As for the secondary aspects, each of them encompasses all three.
Now, as for this present Sūtra, among the Three Piṭakas, it is primarily subsumed within the Sūtra Piṭaka alone and is not subsumed by the other two.
This is truly because this sutra is neither a vinaya nor a śāstra. If one were to subsume the meaning of the three piṭakas within this sutra, all three would be contained therein.
Indeed, this sutra possesses the wisdom of discussion and debate, as seen in the cases of the Dragon Girl, Śāriputra, Mañjuśrī, and Jizhi;
it also possesses the precepts for initiating practice, such as the Three Guidelines and the Four Practices.
△ Second, the explanation of the two collections (*piṭaka*):

first, the Śrāvaka-piṭaka; second, the Bodhisattva-piṭaka. These are so named because the former three collections elucidate the principles, practices, and fruits of the Śrāvakas, and thus they are called the Śrāvaka-piṭaka;
while they elucidate the principles, practices, and fruits of the Bodhisattvas, and thus they are called the Bodhisattva-piṭaka. If categorized according to the teachings:
Because the practices differ, they are further divided into the Three Piṭakas.

Since Pratyekabuddhas for the most part do not rely on the teachings and appear in worlds where no Buddha is present, while during the time a Buddha is in the world they are subsumed under the Śrāvaka [Piṭaka], there are thus only two Piṭakas.
Now, this sutra is included within the Bodhisattva Piṭaka among these two. As the text says: "It teaches only Bodhisattvas; there are no Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas. For this reason, this sutra...

It expounds the Mahāyāna for the benefit of oneself and others. Its fundamental tenet is the same as that of the *Avataṃsaka*, yet while the *Avataṃsaka* is the "Root One Vehicle," the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* is the "One Vehicle for Dispelling Doubts.

Furthermore, because it preaches the Mahāyāna sūtra named *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* to the śrāvakas and also includes them by formally bestowing upon the śrāvakas the prophecy of attaining Buddhahood, its inclusion within the Piṭakas is hereby complete.
△ Second, clarifying the inclusion within the teachings.

All that was spoken by the Tathāgata throughout his entire life is collectively termed the "Twelvefold Teachings. Regarding the classification of these teachings, there were eighteen masters in both India and China;
this is detailed in the *Huayan Xuantan* (Prolegomena to the Avatamsaka). Here, I shall briefly cite their names. First, Bodhiruci of the Later Wei dynasty.

The Northern Indian native arrived in Luoyang during the Yongping era of Emperor Xuanwu. He categorized the teaching of the single sound (*ekasvara*), asserting that the Tathāgata’s single sound is manifested simultaneously for both the Great and Small Vehicles;
though the single sound is uniform, it possesses distinct manifestations. Second was Kumārajīva of the Yao Qin dynasty, a native of Kuci.

It is called "Small" because it distinguishes between the one-sided and the differentiated; it discriminates between the heterodox and the orthodox, the ordinary and the noble; it differentiates between what is to be rejoiced in and what is to be loathed; and it clarifies cause and effect.

If categorized by its doctrinal characteristics (*dharmalakṣaṇa*), it consists of only seventy-five dharmas. It speaks only of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*); even when it occasionally mentions the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*), it does so without clarity.

This refers to the second and third periods of the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra*, which both agree that śrāvakas of fixed nature and icchantikas lacking the Buddha-nature will never attain Buddhahood.

Therefore, these are now combined and treated as a single teaching. Since this does not yet fully exhaust the principles of the Mahāyāna Dharma, it is termed "Initial. There are those who do not accept this.

The Buddha, for this reason, is called "the Divider" (*vibhajya-vādin*). He extensively explains the characteristics of phenomena (*dharma-lakṣaṇa*) and briefly explains the nature of phenomena (*dharma-tathatā*). The nature of phenomena he explains is precisely included within the categories of the characteristics of phenomena;
he speaks of one hundred dharmas, which are clearly and definitively resolved, and thus there is little dispute. He speaks of eight consciousnesses, all of which are subject to arising and ceasing.

Based on these consciousnesses that arise and cease, he establishes the causes of birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) and nirvana. Regarding the seeds of the natural order (*dharmatā-bīja*), their existence or non-existence is eternally [established].
They are distinct. Therefore, the five natures are determined to be different. For this reason, it is said that a portion of sentient beings will certainly not attain Buddhahood;

Those of fixed nature among the two vehicles and those of no-nature, the icchantikas, shall all eventually attain Buddhahood; only then is the ultimate pinnacle of the Mahāyāna fully realized.

It is taught; therefore, it is established as the "End. Because it accords with the true principle, it is called "Real. It explains the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*) briefly, but explains the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) extensively.
Even the characteristics of phenomena that are taught ultimately converge back into that nature. The eight consciousnesses (*vijñāna*) thus established are identical with the Tathāgatagarbha;
they are established according to conditions, formed by the union of the perishable and the imperishable, being neither one nor different. All sentient beings are [one].

The nature is equal. It is simply True Suchness (tathatā) established through the following of conditions; the lack of intrinsic nature in the dependent (paratantra) is itself the perfected (pariniṣpanna).
Since this single principle is uniformly level, it is said that the realm of sentient beings and the realm of Buddhas neither increase nor decrease, and so forth.

There are many such categories of meaning. As for the fourth, the Sudden Teaching (dun-jiao): it holds that the mere non-arising of a single thought-moment is what is called "Buddha," without relying on the gradual progression through stages (bhūmi).

It is taught next as such; therefore, it is established as "sudden. As the *Sāgaramati-paripṛcchā* states: "One who attains the true nature (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena does not proceed from one stage to another.
The *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra* says: "The first stage is itself the eighth," and so on, up to "what sequence could there be in the state of non-existence?
It does not explain the characteristics of phenomena (*lakṣaṇa*), but only discerns the true nature. Furthermore, there are no differentiated characteristics of the eight consciousnesses; all that...
There is only delusive conceptualization. The entire dharma-realm is solely beyond words.

The five dharmas and the three natures are both empty; the eight consciousnesses and the two kinds of selflessness are both negated. Reprimanding the teachings and urging detachment, destroying appearances and extinguishing the mind:

the arising of the mind is itself delusion; non-arising is itself Buddhahood. Furthermore, there is neither Buddha nor non-Buddha, neither arising nor non-arising—just as Vimalakīrti remained silent. This is...
This is its meaning. As for the Fivefold Perfect Teaching (Yuánjiào): it clarifies that one stage is all stages, and all stages are one stage.
Therefore, the fulfillment of the mind of the Ten Faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*) immediately encompasses the five stages and achieves Equal and Perfect Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*).

Based upon the *Samantabhadra* Dharma-realm, with its infinitely nested Indra’s net and the complete presence of the principal and its attendants, it is called the Perfect Teaching. What it expounds is exclusively the inexhaustible Dharma-realm, the ocean of nature (*dharmatā-samudra*).
Perfectly interfused, the dependent origination is unimpeded; phenomena are mutually identical and mutually inclusive, like Indra’s net, layered upon layer without limit.
The subtle and minute are mutually accommodated, with principal and satellites inexhaustible, for each of the ten-fold dharma gates individually encompasses the entire Dharma-realm.

This is because the Five Teachings of Xianshou and the Four Teachings of Transformation of Tiantai differ only in their method of classification and synthesis; the latter opens up the former while synthesizing the latter.

This opens what follows and synthesizes what precedes. "Small" refers to the *Āgama* (Tripitaka) teaching and the second, Initial Teaching (*ādikarmika-śāsana*). The latter has two parts: first, the Initial Teaching, which asserts that all phenomena are empty; this corresponds to the Shared Teaching (*sādhāraṇa-śāsana*).
Second, the Distinct Teaching (*viśeṣa-śāsana*), which explains only the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) of all phenomena; this corresponds to the Separate Teaching (*pratyeka-śāsana*).

The third is the Final Teaching (*niṣṭhā-śāsana*), which clarifies that the Tathāgatagarbha accords with conditions to manifest all defiled and pure states, and that dependent origination is devoid of intrinsic nature.
All are suchness; this is the meaning of simultaneous illumination within that Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao). Fourth is the Sudden Teaching (Dunjiao), which distinguishes only true nature;
this is the meaning of simultaneous negation within that Perfect Teaching. Fifth is the Perfect Teaching, which clarifies that nature and characteristics are mutually fused;

this is the meaning of the simultaneity of negation and illumination within that Perfect Teaching. That which is elucidated by these three teachings is solely the One Mind, which is fully endowed with...
"All dharmas" refers precisely to the inconceivable Middle Way of the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*). Therefore, these three [teachings] are all subsumed within the Perfect.

This [classification] combines the General and Distinct [Teachings] into a single Initial Teaching (*shijiao*), while opening up the Perfect Teaching into the three teachings of the Final, Sudden, and Perfect.
He then opens this Initial Teaching into two—the Common and the Distinct—and combines this Final, Sudden, and Perfect [Teachings] into a single Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*).

Although there are differences in how they are opened or combined, the essence of the Dharma remains no different. As for their inclusion, this sutra properly belongs to the category of the Perfect Teaching among the five teachings.
If one considers the teachings as being subsumed by the sutra, it universally encompasses the preceding four, because it is complete and perfect.

Sufficient. This [classification] reveals the provisional to manifest the ultimate; it is the final destination of the entire lifetime of the Buddha’s teaching and the supreme proclamation of the five periods.
△ Third, the explanation of the categories of classification.

Formerly called "sections" (bù), ancient masters observed that this term was confused with the "sections" (bù) used for book volumes, and thus changed it to "twelvefold division" (shī'èr fēn). First, the *sūtra* (qìjīng).

1. Sūtra (Itivṛttaka): This refers to those teachings that begin with "Thus [have I heard]" and conclude with "practicing accordingly. 2. Geya (Verses): These are verses that correspond to and parallel the prose sections. 3. Vyākaraṇa (Prophecy):

This refers to the Buddha’s prediction that a disciple shall attain Buddhahood in the future. 4. Gāthā (Verses): These are isolated verses that do not correspond to prose sections. 5. Nidāna (Causes and Conditions):
These are teachings spoken specifically because of a request or a particular circumstance. 6. Avadāna (Self-Explanations): [These are teachings spoken by the Buddha of his own accord.]

1. Ityuktaka (Thus-spoken): because it is spoken without being requested. 2. Geya (Verses): because it consists of verses that restate the meaning of prose. 3. Vyākaraṇa (Prophecy): because it prophesies the future enlightenment of disciples. 4. Gāthā (Stanzas): because they are composed in metrical verse. 5. Udāna (Inspired Utterances): because they are uttered spontaneously out of joy. 6. Nidāna (Causes and Conditions):

because they explain the causes and conditions for the setting of the teaching. 7. Vṛttaka (Past Occurrences): because they relate the past deeds of the Buddha and his disciples. 8. Jātaka (Birth Stories): because they relate the previous lives in which the Buddha and others took various forms. 9. Vaipulya (Extensive Teachings):

because they are vast, correct, and extensive, being equal to and in accordance with the nature of reality, thus universally benefiting and bringing happiness. 10. Adbhutadharma (Marvelous Events): because they concern the extraordinary excellence of virtues and deeds.
Because the nature of the Dharma is rare and wondrous, there are (11) *avadāna* (parables), which clarify through analogy and induction to lead others toward faith and understanding.
(12) *Upadeśa* (treatises/discussions) refers to profound and subtle principles that cannot be understood through direct statement alone, requiring analytical investigation and clarification.

Regarding their classification among the twelve divisions of the teachings (*dvādaśāṅga-pravacana*), they properly belong to the *sūtra*. If one were to categorize the divisions according to the *sūtra*, the remaining eleven would be subsumed within it. *Sūtra*...
The many verses contained therein are subsumed under *geya* (verses). The formal conferral of the prophecy of Buddhahood upon the śrāvakas is subsumed under *vyākaraṇa* (prophecy).

The praise-verses of the dragon girl are subsumed under *gāthā* (stanzas). The three earnest requests and the threefold exposition are subsumed under *nidāna* (causal narratives). The calling out from within samādhi is subsumed under *udāna* (inspired utterances).
King Śubhavyūha’s conversion from error and Bhaiṣajyarāja’s self-immolation are subsumed under *itivṛttaka* (past deeds). His birth as a king [is likewise included].

When the *Sūtra* (Sūtrānta) speaks of one born as a king, it subsumes the *Jātaka*; when it speaks of the great wisdom of equality shared equally by ordinary beings and sages, it subsumes the *Vaipulya*;

when it speaks of the Dharma being like the *udumbara* flower, with radiant auspicious signs emerging and surging forth, it subsumes the *Adbhutadharma*; when it provides extensive explanations through parables, it subsumes the *Avadāna*;
and when there are questions and answers, it subsumes the *Upadeśa*. The classification of the divisions of the Tripiṭaka is hereby complete.
△ Third, the Delimitation of Meaning and Principle.

It has already been known that this sutra is subsumed within the Perfect Teaching (Eon-gyo). However, it remains unclear what constitutes the delimitation of the meaning and principle of the Perfect Teaching.

Now, "meaning" (*yi*) is the substance of the text; "principle" (*ri*) is the master of phenomena. Furthermore, meaning is the aspect (*xiang*), while principle is the essence (*ti*). For these reasons:

The Sages established their teachings, unifying them through principle and analyzing them through meaning. Although principle reaches a single ultimate point, it appears shallow or profound according to the capacities of those who encounter it;
although meanings may be manifold, they all return to principle, which possesses no distinct essence. Thus, the principles and meanings of the various sutras—
Since there are both shallow and deep levels, if those who elucidate the scriptures do not analyze them, how can one know the boundaries and the destinations [of each teaching]?

First, I shall briefly clarify the boundaries of the five teachings. According to the *Awakening of Faith*, there are five layers of depth; these likewise do not depart from the aforementioned five teachings.
However, this [system] proceeds from the shallow to the deep, whereas that [system] proceeds from the deep toward the shallow; thus, they are not the same.
First, there is the single mind as the fundamental source; this is the One True Dharma-realm (eka-tathatā-dharmadhātu), which encompasses the four dharma-realms.

This is the scope of the Perfect Teaching (yuanjiao). Second, based on the single mind, two gates are opened, which encompass the two teachings. First is the gate of the true suchness of the single mind (*ekacitta-tathatā-mukha*), meaning that the nature of the mind is neither born nor extinguished;
this is the scope of the Sudden Teaching (dunjiao). Second is the gate of the arising and ceasing of the mind (*citta-utpāda-nirodha-mukha*), meaning the Tathāgatagarbha.
Its conjunction with arising and ceasing is termed the *ālayavijñāna*; this constitutes the scope of the Final Teaching (*zhōngjiào*).
Third, based on this consciousness, two meanings are clarified: first, the meaning of awakening (*jue*), which refers to the essence of the mind being free from thought, and so forth;

second, the meaning of non-awakening (*bujue*), which refers to not knowing the Dharma of True Suchness (*tathatā*) as it truly is, and thus the mind moving through non-awakening, and so forth. Fourth, based on the latter meaning, the three subtle states arise. First, based on non-awakening...

Because of awakening, the mind moves; this is called the "characteristic of karma" (karmalakṣaṇa). Second, because it depends on movement, there is the capacity to see; this is called the "characteristic of transformation" (pravṛttilakṣaṇa).

Third, because it depends on seeing, objects falsely appear; this is called the "characteristic of manifestation" (nirbhāsalakṣaṇa). This constitutes the scope of the Initial Teaching (ādikarmika-yāna). Fifth, based on the last [of these], the six coarse [states] arise.
1. The characteristic of wisdom; 2. The characteristic of continuity; 3. The characteristic of grasping; 4. The characteristic of calculating names;
5. The characteristic of initiating karma; 6. The characteristic of suffering bound by karma. The third, fourth, and second characteristics constitute the scope of the Hīnayāna (Small Teaching).

The fifth is the scope of humans and devas. Next, we shall specifically clarify the perfect meaning of this sutra. However, the principles of the Perfect Teaching are as vast and profound as the ocean, capable of encompassing the hundred rivers. One hundred...
