The two characters "Hongchuan" (弘傳) constitute the title of the preface. The Great Master originally composed this preface without these two characters;
it is suspected that they were added during the Song or Yuan dynasties, or perhaps the Master Xiang appended this title.
The intention is that when the Great Master composed the preface, his purpose was to circulate this sutra so as to propagate the wondrous Dharma for all people. "Hong" (弘) means to promote.

"Guang" (Broad) means to transmit and bestow. "Xu" (Preface) means to synthesize and extract. Master Nanshan’s refined affinity with the purport of this sutra allowed him to penetrate the heart of the Tathāgata.
Desiring to repay the grace of the Buddha’s protective mindfulness, he fulfilled the charge of the entrustment; thus, he composed this preface.
To propagate it is to drum forth and exalt the Holy Way, expanding from the narrow to the broad. From this day forward, [may all] equalize the Dharma...
It pervades all realms without exception; it flows through kalpas as vast as the motes of dust without obstruction.
As for its transmission, this Way is passed from self to others and from few to many, being handed down in succession. May all who possess consciousness alike ascend to the chamber of the Elder.
This "Preface to the Propagation" (Hongchuan Xu) upholds the universal endowment (*bǐngyí*) shared by all who receive the jewel of the royal topknot (*wángjì*).

It organizes the intentions behind the appearance of the various Buddhas and enumerates the origins of the translations across the three dynasties. It extracts the essential meaning from extensive learning and extends one’s own sentiments toward the sagely transformation.
Furthermore, the term "Propagation" (*hóngchuán*) is explained through three meanings. First, regarding time: it penetrates both antiquity and the present, reaching to that [other] shore.
First, regarding time: from the vast expanse of kalpas to the briefest instant, it circulates through all periods. Second, regarding place:

from the highest heavens to the lowest depths, across this world and other realms, within dragon palaces and ocean treasuries, and even in narrow alleys and the Qǔlǐ Academy, it circulates throughout every location down to the finest atom.
Third, regarding persons: it encompasses both the ordinary and the sagely, penetrating the noble and the humble, and reaching both humans and spirits. One...
The "Wise and the Foolish" encompasses both good and evil; for as long as one possesses breath and blood, this work may be circulated to bring benefit.

Indeed, while the Sublime Dharma is inexhaustible, the mind that circulates this sutra must be as sparing [of its distribution] as this—only then does it truly accord with the Great Master’s intention for wide propagation.

The two characters "propagation" (弘傳) correspond precisely to the two phrases at the end of the preface: "widely praised and perpetually bequeathed. II. (Note: The character "二" at the end indicates the second section of the text.)
Explanation of the Title.
Narrated by the Śramaṇa Daoxuan of Zhongnan Mountain.
"Zhongnan" is the name of a mountain located eighty *li* south of the city of Chang’an, in Wugong County of Fufeng. It lies to the east...
It connects with Mount Taihua to the east and adjoins Mount Taibai to the west; because its form and ridges originate in the northwest and its momentum culminates in the south, it is named Zhongnan.
The *Guangzhong ji* states: "Its other name is Zhongnan; it stands in the center of heaven and lies to the south of the capital."

Therefore, it is named Zhongnan (Central-South). This land possesses lofty mountains and steep ridges, lush forests, and long bamboo; it produces a hundred kinds of rare delicacies and is far removed from the clamor and dust of the world.

Those who conceal themselves to cultivate their practice and maintain tranquility, or who have cast aside worldly affairs to contemplate the mind, all seek to dwell in seclusion and realize their aspirations here.
The reason for designating this place is that the Great Master resided on this mountain to dwell in truth, demonstrating that he did not forget his origins. Thus says the commentator.
He is a dharma-descendant of Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa. In the Sanskrit language, Śākya means "Capable Benevolence" (Néngrén); it is the clan name of the Buddha.
Since all who leave the household life take the Buddha as their clan name, the Āgamas state:

"Just as the four rivers enter the sea and share the same salty taste, so too do those of the four castes who leave the household life all bear the name Śākya. This was spoken from the Golden Mouth [of the Buddha] and originated with him.
"Encompassing Heaven. The Great Master established this title to demonstrate his role in perpetuating the lineage of the Buddha. Daoxuan recorded the master's name in the preface.
The Master was a native of Changcheng in Huzhou; tracing his ancestral pedigree, he is a distant descendant of Pengzu of ancient times.
Sengji was a former Minister of Personnel during the Sui dynasty and the son of Jian Shen. He was born during the Kaihuang era.

At the time of his birth, his mother dreamed that the solar disc pierced her breast before she conceived. She further dreamed of a Buddhist monk who said, "The one you carry in your womb is the Vinaya Master Sengyou of the Liang dynasty.
By nature he was exceptionally gifted; by the age of nine, he had read through all manner of books, and at twelve, he was proficient in...
He was skilled in writing. At fifteen, he studied under Master Riyán Yūn. At sixteen, he recited the *Lotus Sūtra* and mastered it within twenty days. At seventeen, he shaved his head.
At twenty, he followed Zhǐshǒu Lǜshī, the eighth patriarch of the Vinaya school at Hongfú Monastery, to study the precepts.

His three robes were made only of plain cloth, and he practiced eating only one meal per day. In the seventh year of the Wǔdé era of Emperor Gāozǔ of the Táng dynasty, he moved to reside at Zhōngnán, where he constantly...
While practicing the *Pratyutpanna Samādhi* at the Qinggong Monastery, there were twenty assemblies in total over the course of his stay;

he was constantly moved by the appearance of devas and humans who brought him food and served as his guards. Later, while performing his devotions at Ximing Monastery, he stepped onto the stone steps in the middle of the night and tripped, falling down.
A youth clad in armor appeared to protect him. The Master asked, "Who are you? He replied, "Your disciple is Bo..."
He was also Prince Zhang Qiong of the Heavenly Court. Because of the Master’s virtuous precepts, he came to provide protection; he then presented the Buddha’s tooth relic to the Master.

At night, the Master would hold it while practicing the Way, and during the day, he would conceal it in an underground pit. He also bestowed upon him a prescription for medicinal pellets—namely, the "Tianwang Buxin Dan" (The Heavenly King’s Heart-Replenishing Pill).
When the Master inquired about the events surrounding the World-Honored One’s life and his parinirvāṇa, Zhang Qiong explained them to him one by one, responding to each question as it arose.

Record. One fascicle of the *Biography of the Heavenly Attendants Who Were Moved* exists in the canon. He once accompanied Master Xuanzang in the translation of scriptures and was promoted to the rank of *sthavira*.
Having merit in observing the summer retreat, *zhīcǎo* (mushrooms) grew in the courtyard; at his place of reclusion, white springs gushed forth.

Proficient in the hundred schools of thought externally and penetrating the three studies internally, when he took up the brush to continue the biographies, eminent scholars accepted his teachings with reverence. He built earthen mounds to mark the site.
At the altar, the Indian monks offered praises. He remained dedicated to protecting the city of the Dharma, never ceasing his scholarly compositions;

thus, works such as the *Hongming ji*, the *Sengzhuan*, and the *Neidian lu*—totaling over one hundred fascicles—remain preserved in the canon. He once composed the *Fahua yiyan*, of which only this preface survives.
In the second year of the Qianfeng era, the Master passed away at Ximing Monastery in Chang’an, as heard by the entire assembly.
Devas and humans requested that the Master return to the Maitreya Hall. He was posthumously titled Grand Master Chengzhao (Chen-zhao). Emperor Mu praised him, saying:

"In every generation there have been awakened ones who act as envoys of the Tathāgata; dragons and māras take refuge in them, and mountain deities serve them. Their fame has spread throughout the five regions."
These words shall startle ten thousand ages. As the golden sun sinks in the west, the Buddha-sun rises in the east. I prostrate and take refuge in the Master who founded the Vinaya school.

Regarding the terms "author" (*zuò*) and "compiler" (*shù*): the former refers to the act of initiating a composition; the latter refers to the principle of fundamentally elucidating [the meaning]. Thus, that which begins a work is called "author," while that which explains the underlying principle is called "compiler."
The *Yueji* (Record of Music) states: "Those who know the inner essence of ritual and music can create them; those who recognize the outward forms of ritual and music can transmit them.
These words of the Grand Master [Confucius] express his humility and signify his intent to transmit rather than create.

When I first composed this preface, as the *Lotus Sūtra* is so profoundly venerable that it was not easy to offer a prefatory discourse, I reported my intention to the Buddhas of the ten directions. Those who protect the Dharma commended it as excellent and informed me accordingly.
Thus, Cizhao said: "The Great Master Nanshan is most profound and mysterious; he condensed the essential pivot and placed it before the sutra.
The Vajrapāṇi General personally bestowed his report, and the Buddhas of the ten directions authorized the Master’s words. III. Explanation of the Preface, divided into five parts:

1. Quoting the Sutra and indicating its source. 2. Sequencing the origins of the Sutra. 3. Sequencing the purport of the Sutra’s exposition. 4. Praising and comparing [the teachings]. 5. [The fifth part is implied by the heading.]
Prayer. Preface to the Fivefold Dedication. First, citing the scripture to indicate its essence:
The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* is the fundamental purpose for which all Buddhas descend as spirits into the world.
The Preface to the *Dharmadhātu-vipaśyanā* states: "The Dharmadhātu is the fundamental essence of the body and mind of all sentient beings.

It is a great opening and a total presentation, clarifying the fundamental basis of this present sutra, manifesting the sovereign deeds of all Buddhas, revealing the original intent of transcending the world, and distinguishing it as the capital of all teachings.
The first phrase cites the sutra; the second phrase sets forth [the title].

"Fundamental" (*hon*) means to comprehensively encompass and gather all things so as to leave none remaining; hence it is called "total" (*tō*). The three types of awakening are perfectly luminous, and the myriad phenomena are thoroughly illuminated;
hence it is called "Buddha. Emerging from the true signs of sagehood, one engages with the mundane world to benefit all beings; hence it is called "descent of the spirit" (*kōrei*).

When the aspirations of the mind are identical and the ritual regulations are fixed, this is called the "original intent" (*hontei*). Indeed, regarding this wondrous Dharma, whenever the Buddhas appear in the world, this single matter alone is [the purpose]. Thousand... [text ends]
The Sage’s original intent was that there is no other vehicle. For this reason, every Buddha must inevitably appear;

they are alike in that they cannot fail to appear for this one purpose alone. Just as the twenty thousand lamps of brilliance were magnificently spread throughout past kalpas, so too was this taught for this very reason.
Yet, the wondrous light of Dīpaṃkara has left its lingering fragrance to be compiled in these final ages, thereby assisting this [teaching].

Continuing from this: tracing back and inferring, once the Great Universal Teaching at the end of kalpas as numerous as motes of dust was concluded, and the Princes each proclaimed it in turn until the teaching of the majestic Ābhāsvara at the limit of the past was finished, it was for this reason that the Buddha did not expound it with varying degrees of emphasis.
Therefore, although our Buddha, the World-Honored One, had already differentiated the vehicles according to their respective expressions, he nevertheless opened [the way].
The ultimate convergence is revealed within this very sutra, and its fundamental intent is identical to that of all Buddhas.

Otherwise, why would the Multi-storied Stupa of Prabhūtaratna suddenly appear just as the three assemblies had concluded, enabling the various emanated Buddhas to arrive and perfectly realize the supreme assembly on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa?
Knowing this, one understands that all Buddhas of the past, present, and future preach [this Dharma].
The fundamental intent of this sutra is thus made clear. The sutra states: "Only a Buddha and a Buddha can fully exhaust the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena.
This is because the underlying principle for which these Buddhas reveal the provisional to manifest the real is fundamentally the same. Furthermore, it says:
"The Buddhas [teach] solely for the sake of the one great matter," and so forth; this indicates that the Buddhas are identical in their single purpose.

Furthermore, it says, "The Buddhas of the past, by means of various causes and conditions," and so forth; this indicates that the Buddhas are identical in their fundamental intention to establish provisional teachings based upon the ultimate truth.
Moreover, it says, "Within the Buddha-lands of the ten directions, there is only the One Vehicle Dharma"; this indicates that the Buddhas who appear...

The completion of this undertaking largely accords with the fundamental intent of "opening up the provisional to reveal the real. As the ancients said: "This sutra is the heart-essence of all Buddhas and the guiding principle of a thousand sages.
This truly reveals that the original aim of all Buddhas is entirely identical; one may indeed say that such a person knows how to speak of the Dharma.
II. The Second Section: The Circumstances of the Sutra’s Origin. This is divided into three parts: 1. First, the account of the origins in the two lands. 2. [The second part... 3. [The third part...]
Preface to the Translations of the Three Courts. Among the three systems of knowledge, the Qin translations alone stand supreme. To begin with, this work traces its origins in both lands:
it was first compiled in the Great Xia (India) and emerged there after a thousand years; subsequently, it was transmitted eastward to China over more than three hundred years.
In this preface, since it is stated that this sutra encompasses the fundamental aim of all Buddhas, I have not yet ascertained at what time this sutra was transmitted from the West to the East;
hence these words. The first two lines clarify the place and time. "Accumulated" (yùnjié) means to remain stored or gathered.
"Great Xia" refers to the Western Regions, for this land abounds in learning and liberation, where both ordinary beings and sages are gathered together.
Just as all things flourish and thrive during the ninth month of summer, this phrase indicates the place where this sutra was translated into Tibetan.
The following phrase clarifies the time when this sutra emerged from the West.

The intention of the preface’s author is that, since the assembly of the noble ones, this sutra remained in India, circulating only in one corner, before passing through this region during the periods of the Zhou, Qin, Han, and Jin dynasties.

For over a thousand years, it remained in the Western Regions; hence it is called "a thousand-year [period]. Reaching the time of Emperor Hui, Dharmarakṣa came from the east and first transmitted this sūtra.
Having brought it from those Western Regions to these eastern lands, it is therefore said to have "come forth from there."

The final two lines clarify the time of its appearance. According to the records, more than a thousand years after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, the holy teachings manifested through the power of the sages and were first transmitted to the Eastern Land.
This was on the eighth day of the fourth month in the third year of the Yongping era of the Han dynasty.
Emperor Ming was sleeping in the Southern Palace when he dreamed of a golden man, sixteen feet tall, with a halo encircling his neck, who flew into the hall.
At court, at dawn, he assembled his ministers to interpret his dream. The Attendant-in-Ordinary Fu Yi submitted a memorial, saying:

"I have read the *Zhou Shu Yiji* (Record of Anomalies in the Book of Zhou). In the twenty-fourth year of King Zhao’s reign, the Jia-Yin year, on the eighth day of the fourth month, a sage appeared in the Western Regions.
Auspicious light descended from afar upon the Central Lands, consisting of twelve streams of white light that pierced through—"
In the Taiwei palace, the Grand Historian Suyou investigated the matter. He noted that a thousand years hence, the teachings of the Image would be transmitted to our country;

he erected a stone tablet to record this. When the King Mu entered nirvana in the fifty-second year, the Ren-shen year, a detailed calculation of the chronology showed it was precisely one thousand years later.
"The dream Your Majesty had must surely have been caused by this," [he said]. The Emperor then commanded the Crown Prince’s tutor...
King Zūn, the General of the Household Qín Jǐng, the General of Far-Reaching Penetration Cài Tīn, and eighteen others were commissioned to travel westward in search of the Dharma.
Having traversed distant lands, they reached their destination after five years.
Upon entering the kingdom of South India, they encountered two monks, Mòshèng and Fálán, on the road one day. They questioned them, and Cài Tīn related Emperor Míng’s dream.
He reported the matter to them. The two monks sighed and said, "The circulation of the Buddha-dharma is entirely due to the power of the sages.
Through the convergence of causes and conditions, we have met here. Thereupon, they brought forth a painted image of King Udayana and scriptures such as the *Sūtra of Forty-two Sections*.
Kāśyapa Mātanga transported these on a white horse and arrived in Luoyang on the eighteenth day of the seventh month in the tenth year of Yongping. He then made his formal report.
The Emperor was greatly pleased. He quartered the two monks at the Court of State Ceremonial (Honglu Si) and issued an imperial decree for their sustenance from the inner palace.

Later, he established a monastery outside the Yong Gate; because the scriptures had been carried there on white horses, it was called the Baima Monastery (White Horse Monastery). At that time, the Buddha-dharma first arrived [in China].
This was not yet fully known by others. In the fourteenth year, the Daoist masters of the Five Peaks, including Shu Shanxin and others, deliberated, saying:
"The Emperor honors the Buddha-dharma; he will surely hold our Way in low esteem. The assembly selected Shanxin as the leader of the petition. The text of the memorial is not recorded here.

When the Emperor had finished reading it, he proclaimed to the various Daoist masters: "I have sought the Buddha-dharma from afar to bring blessings to the state and protection to the people. Why do you say it is heterodox?"

The Dharma Master Sengxiu and others petitioned, saying, "We beg Your Majesty to test and verify which is skillful or clumsy, and which is true or false. The Emperor commanded the relevant officials to establish a ritual arena at Baima Monastery.
They selected the fifteenth day of the first month to determine the superiority or inferiority of the two teachings.

The scriptures of the two teachings were placed upon two altars, and the Emperor personally presided over the assembly. The people of the entire realm flocked to the ritual arena to witness the outcome.
[The Emperor] failed [to achieve his purpose]. At that time, the Daoist flew talismans and rushed about with seals, yet the two monks did not perform a single such feat.
The Emperor asked the two monks, "What divine transformations does the Buddha’s school possess? The two monks replied, "When a dragon roars, mist arises;

this is not the work of earthworms. When a tiger howls, wind is born; how could this be within the reach of a lame donkey? We monks uphold the Buddha-dharma and circulate it to save the world. Please..."
They were burned with fire; thus their authenticity could be known. When the fire was raised, the two monks looked toward the west and wept, saying:
"After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, the holy teachings were entrusted to kings and ministers, and subsequently to his disciples. We have carried them here."
Today, he was subjected to the test of being burned in fire. May the majestic spiritual power of the Buddha provide secret protection and sustenance!
At that time, the fierce flames reached to the heavens and drifting smoke obscured the sun; yet while the Daoist scriptures were consumed by the fire, the Buddhist sutras remained unharmed.

The Emperor marveled at this man, and the people offered words of praise. Those of virtuous faith wept until they died. Countless Daoists, officials, commoners, and monastics [were moved] because of this.
These two monks were accustomed to the Chinese language; after a long time, they translated the *Sūtra of Forty-two Sections*, the *Ten Stages*, the *Severing of Bonds*, and other scriptures.
From this point on, the Buddha-dharma first flourished in the world. At that time, this particular sūtra had not yet arrived;

the two phrases currently transmitted from the East clarify the period when this sūtra was first transmitted to the Eastern Land. "Zhendan" (China) is the name for our own country. According to the Eight Trigrams (*bagua*):...

The East belongs to the Trigram Zhen, which is the foremost of all movement; hence it is called "Zhen. Zhen is taken as thunder, because its meaning is that the single Yang line has first begun to move.
As for "Dawn" (Dan), it is the beginning of the sun's rising; this is because this direction is precisely where the sun first emerges.
Therefore, a poem says: "The rising sun begins its dawn. Because these two meanings are harmonized, it is called Zhendan (China). "Eastward transmission" is said in contrast to "stopping in the West.
The first phrase refers to the place where this sutra was transmitted; the second phrase refers to the time after the sutra had already been transmitted to the East.
Various commentaries differ on this point; some state that it was more than two hundred years from Emperor Ming to Emperor Hui.
Some say from the Han to the Qin, over three hundred years; others say from the Jin to the Sui, over three hundred years.
Neither of these accounts accords with the intent of the Preface. The author’s intention is that this sutra was first transmitted to this land during the Western Jin dynasty;
passing through the Southern and Northern Dynasties and reaching the Sui until the early Tang, it underwent three translations in total, spanning slightly more than three hundred years.
"Other dynasties" refers to the period from the Western Jin until the time the preface was composed during the early Tang dynasty.
According to historical records, the Eastern and Western Jin together had fifteen sovereigns over one hundred and fifty-six years. As for the Southern Dynasties, the Song had eight sovereigns.
Sixty years. The Qi dynasty had five rulers for twenty-four years. The Liang dynasty had four rulers for fifty-four years. The Chen dynasty had five rulers for twenty-two years.
As for the Northern Dynasties: the Wei had twelve rulers; the Eastern Wei had one ruler; the Northern Qi had six rulers; and the Western Wei had three rulers.
The Later Zhou had five rulers until it was usurped by Yang Jian, who established the Sui dynasty. Thus the succession continued.
The three rulers [reigned] for thirty-eight years before returning to the Tang. From the Western Jin to the beginning of the Tang, there were a total of three hundred and fifty-four years;
excluding the twenty-five years of Emperor Wu’s reign, there were only three hundred and twenty-nine years.

Thus it is said, "more than three hundred years. *Zai* (載) means year. The terms *zai* and *yu* (虞) were used in the eras of Yao and Shun, derived from the meaning of things reaching their end and beginning anew.

The Meaning. △ Second, the sequence of translations during the three dynasties. This also has three parts: first, the translations of the Western Jin; second, the translations of the Eastern Jin; third, the translations of the Sui dynasty.
Regarding the first, the translations of the Western Jin, there are four sections: first, the time of the translation; second, the location of the translation;
third, the master of the translation; fourth, the original title of the translation. Now, concerning the first, the time of the translation:
During the Yongkang era of Emperor Hui of the Western Jin.
The Western Jin was the designation for the Sima clan’s possession of the empire; its national name was Jin, with its capital at Luoyang, later moving to Chang’an.
It is called the "Western Jin" in contrast to the Eastern Jin, which was established by Emperor Yuan in Jiangdong. Emperor Hui’s personal name was Zhong, and his courtesy name was...
Zhengdu was the second son of Emperor Wu and served as the second emperor. Yongkang was the reign title of Emperor Hui.
Emperor Hui ascended the throne in the fourth month of the Gengxu year and established the reign title Yongxi. After one year, it was changed to Yuanhe; after three years, it was changed to Yongping;
and in the sixth year, it was changed to Yongkang, which lasted for only one year. During the Yongkang era, Dharmarakṣa translated Buddhist scriptures.
This was the time of the first translation. △ Second, the location where the sutra was explained:
Qingmen (Green Gate) in Chang’an.
Chang’an is the capital of Guanzhong; it is here that successive dynasties—Zhou, Qin, Han, and Tang—established their capitals. Ancient...

It was called Xianyang when the Han Gaozu established his capital; it was subsequently renamed Chang'an, signifying that for a thousand autumns and ten thousand generations, descendants might enjoy long-lasting peace and security.
This was because its mountains and rivers formed a natural barrier of "one hundred and two," its terrain was perilous and its military strength formidable, making it the foremost in the world.
The Qingmen (Green Gate) was the eastern embankment city gate of Chang'an; it is popularly known as the Qingmen, named for the far-reaching view of the lush green landscape beyond.
Therefore, this is the very place where Shao Ping grew melons. However, the Master of Translation established a monastery and practiced the Way outside this gate;
thus, the present preface distinguishes between the general and specific locations. This was the site of the first translation. △ Third, the Master of the Translation.
Regarding the Bodhisattva Zhu Fahu of Dunhuang:
Dunhuang is the present-day Suzhou Prefecture in Gansu. It was the ancient land of Liusha (the Flowing Sands), situated within the domain of Yongzhou as described in the *Yugong*.

During the Han dynasty, it was the commandery of Dunhuang. He was called a "Bodhisattva" because his teacher possessed the virtue of seeking the supreme [enlightenment] above while transforming sentient beings below.
Zhú Fǎhù was his name according to the *Tripiṭaka* system. In the Sanskrit language he was called Dharmarakṣa, which here means "Dharma-protector.
He was a native of the Yuezhi. Having become a monk at the age of eight, he took Zhú Gāozuò of the foreign land as his teacher. His name was established based on his place of origin.
Therefore, he was called the "Dunhuang Bodhisattva," taking his place of origin as his title. He was also known as Zhu Fahu;

this Great Master thoroughly investigated the arts and doctrines of thirty-six countries and was proficient in their languages. He could memorize ten thousand words a day and was devoted to his studies.
He traveled ten thousand *li* to seek out his teachers and became profoundly versed in both ancient and modern learning. He never harbored worldly concerns regarding praise or blame.

In the second year of the Taishi era, he arrived at the Yumen Pass from India and settled in Dunhuang, where he assisted his teacher in translating scriptures to propagate the Way and glorify the teachings of the Buddha.
All who encountered him were moved by his sincerity; thus, they celebrated his noble reputation. He was the primary master for the initial translations. △
Fourth, the original title of the translation.
This scripture was first translated as the *Zhengfahua* (Saddharmapuṇḍarīka).
The master translator, possessing profound and deep insight as well as versatile talent, propagated the Way throughout the five regions of India without being confined to any single locality.

Thereupon, during the era of the Western Jin dynasty, he came to convert the people of Luoyang. Later, outside the Qing Gate, he established images and erected a stupa to awaken and enlighten sentient beings.
When he first translated this sutra, it was titled *Zhengfahua* (The Lotus of the True Dharma).

This title was taken because this scripture definitively establishes the provisional and the real, converging all toward the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*) with no other path. It directly points to the exposition of the True Dharma; the text consists of ten fascicles.
Twenty-eight chapters. The mantras and characters therein are all rendered in the language of Jin (Chinese). The entrustment (*parindanā*) appears at the end.

△ Second, the translation during the Eastern Jin dynasty, divided into three parts: first, the time of the translation; second, the master who translated the scripture; third, the names of the two translations.

According to the preceding and following [sections], there should also be four [parts], but here there are only three. The location [of the entrustment] subsumes the meaning [of the fourth]. First, regarding the time of the initial translation:
Regarding the Eastern Jin Emperor An’s Long’an era and the Later Qin Hongshi era:

as for the term "Eastern Jin," it refers to the period when the Five Hu tribes threw China into chaos. During the reigns of the two Western Jin emperors Huai and Min, they were murdered by the Liu clan, resulting in the great upheaval of Luoyang.
Emperor Yuan crossed the Yangtze River and established his capital in Jiangdong; thus, in relation to the former capital of Luoyang, it was called the "Eastern" [Jin].
Eastern Jin. There were eleven sovereigns in total. Emperor An was the tenth sovereign of the Eastern Jin; he was the son of Emperor Xiaowu. His personal name was Dezong.
Long’an was the reign title of Emperor An. He succeeded Emperor Xiaowu to the throne and initially changed the era name to Long’an.
This lasted for five years in total. Master Kumārajīva entered Luoyang in the third year of Hongshi, which corresponded to the fifth year of the Long’an era of the Jin dynasty.
As for Later Qin, it was so called in contrast to Former Qin; its ruler was surnamed Yao and named Chang. Former Qin was ruled by Fu Jian, whose courtesy name was Yonggu.
There was a leader with an army of one hundred thousand who styled himself the King of Qin. Later, he usurped the throne and established his capital at Chang’an, founding Former Qin.
Initially, Yao Chang served Fu Jian as the Governor of Yanzhou; subsequently, he was promoted to General of the Dragon Banner (Longxiang Jiangjun).

While leading troops to suppress慕容泓 (Murong Hong) and others, his army was defeated, and fearing for his life, he fled. At that time, the horse-herders of the north bank of the Wei River incited the Qiang tribes, leading their...
Of the households that returned to Yao Chang, there were more than fifty thousand families. They elevated Chang to the position of盟主 (the leader of the confederation).

Chang proceeded to Shaanxi and entered Chang’an, where he assassinated Fu Jian and usurped the imperial throne; he was also titled the King of Qin. Because he distinguished himself from the earlier Qin dynasty, his regime is called the Later Qin.
Upon Chang’s death, his son Yao Xing ascended the throne. Hongshi was the era name of Yao Xing. While the Jin dynasty occupied the legitimate position, the Qin...
To avoid being a lateral usurper: when Master Kumārajīva translated the scriptures within the territory of Qin, he invariably placed Jin first and then Qin in order to preserve the orthodox lineage.
This concludes the section on the eras of these two translations. △ Second, the translators of the scriptures.
The Kuchean Śramaṇa Kumārajīva. "Kucha" is the name of a country;
it was the native land of Master Jīva, not the place where he translated the scriptures. "Śramaṇa" is translated here as "one who exerts effort and seeks rest.
There are four types: first, the śramaṇa of the Noble Path, namely the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and others; second, the śramaṇa who teaches the Path...
The Gate. Those who preach the True Dharma are the Śramaṇas of the Path of Life. Those who cultivate the category of wholesome qualities are the Śramaṇas of the Path of Purity.
Those who engage in various wrong practices are the Śramaṇas of the Path of Defilement. Kumārajīva is the name of the master-translator;
in full it is Kumārajīva, which means "Child-Longevity," because he possessed the virtues of an elder while still a child. "Ji" (什) signifies depth.
He was skilled in the script and language of this land (China). Because he excelled in both the Chinese and the Indic (Sanskrit), he was named Kumārajīva.
At the age of seven, he accompanied his mother to a monastery; seeing an iron alms bowl, he lifted it up, but suddenly realized its weight.

Finding himself unable to bear its heaviness, he attained realization of the principle that "all phenomena are but mind. For this reason, he left the household life. Upon his father’s death, his mother also became a nun. He... [obtained...]
He realized the third fruit of the path. Initially, he accompanied his teacher to seek the Way in Northern India. A certain Arhat said to him, "This youth is extraordinary.

If he does not violate the precepts after reaching thirty years of age, he will save beings in numbers no fewer than a *kūṭadanta*. However, were he to break the precepts, he would merely be a brilliant Dharma master.
His mother often said to him, "Your learning and understanding are sufficient to serve as a teacher for others; it is only that you yourself—"

"The Way is not yet perfected; what can be done? The Master said, "The practice of a Bodhisattva is to benefit all beings while forgetting one's own body. Once the Great Transformation is carried out, there shall be no regret even in the cauldrons and furnaces.
When his mother was on the verge of death, she delivered a prophecy, saying, "The profound teachings of the Vaipulya (fangdeng) should be propagated in the capital of Qin;

however, it will bring some slight disadvantage to your own person. Regarding the various scriptures, both internal and external, the Master knew nothing he did not understand. [As for] the various [masters] of the Western Regions...
"O King, when you request the Master to preach the Dharma, you must kneel long at the side of his seat and command him to step upon it to ascend.
Later, when Fu Jian of Former Qin was campaigning westward, the Grand Astrologer reported: 'A strange star has appeared in the celestial division corresponding to the Western Regions;
there shall surely be a man of great virtue and wisdom who enters to assist the Central Kingdom. Fu Jian said: 'I have heard that Kumārajīva is in Kucha, and [Senglang] is in Xiangyang.'"
Dao’an thought, "Could it not be these two men? He immediately dispatched General of the Light Cavalry Lü Guang to lead seventy thousand troops to attack Kucha and welcome Master Kumārajīva.
Upon reaching Liangzhou, they heard that Fu Jian had been killed by Yao Chang.
Lü Guang then seized control of Liangzhou and ascended the throne as the Three Rivers King, naming his state Daliang; the Master also settled there. Yao Chang heard of this...
The Master’s name had been requested repeatedly, yet Lü Guang did not grant permission. When Chang died and his son Xing ascended the throne, he requested him again, but was once more refused.
Xing grew enraged and dispatched troops to attack him. At that time, Lü Long was ruling in Liangzhou; he submitted a memorial offering his surrender.
It was only in the third year of Hongshi that the Master was finally welcomed into the capital. The Prince of Qin honored him as State Preceptor. These two were the primary translators.
...and so forth. △ Third, the names of the two translations.
Next, this sutra was translated under the title *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*.
The chief translator, being of noble lineage, became a successor to the Dharma-gate; the star of virtue appeared in foreign lands, and his fame...
His fame overflowed throughout Former Qin. Although there was the stagnation of Xiliang, subsequently his teachings were widely propagated. The ruler of Qin revered him as a Buddha.

In the fourth year of Hongshi, at Caidiang Monastery, he extensively assembled śramaṇas learned in doctrine to translate scriptures and treatises such as the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, totaling more than three hundred and ninety fascicles. This scripture is one of them; next is...

Next is the Western Jin period. As for the name *Saddharma* (Wondrous Dharma), it is because this sutra illuminates the truth wherever it touches; that is, it reveals the ultimate reality through provisional means.
It specifically points to the passage: "Cease, cease! There is no need to speak; my Dharma is wondrous and inconceivable. Therefore, it is called the Wondrous Dharma.
The text consists of seven fascicles and twenty-eight chapters; this is the present sutra. The Master entered nirvana in the fifteenth year of Hongshi.
On the thirteenth day of the fourth month, he made a vow at the time of his death:
"If the sutras I have translated are indeed not in error regarding the Buddha's intent, then after my body is cremated, my tongue shall remain uncorrupted. Later, it was exactly as he had said.

This was because the Master’s tongue and the broad, long tongues of all Buddhas were non-dual in their praise of this sutra. △ III. Translations of the Sui Dynasty. Divided into four parts. First, the initial translations.

First, the time of the translation; second, the place where the sutra was translated; third, the master who translated the sutra; fourth, the names of the three translations. Regarding the first, the time of the translation:
it was during the Renshou era of the Sui dynasty.
"Sui" is the dynastic name established by the Yang clan. The High Ancestor, Emperor Wen, surnamed Yang, had the personal name Jian. He promoted—
Nong was a native of Huayin. His father, Yang Zhong, served the Zhou dynasty with merit and was enfeoffed as the Duke of Sui. Upon Zhong’s death, Jian inherited the title.
He later received the abdication of the Zhou and established his capital at Chang’an, adopting the national name Da Sui (Great Sui).
From the division of the Eastern Jin until Emperor Wen finally achieved unification, there were three sovereigns over a total period of thirty-eight years; thus, the country was named Da Sui.
Therefore, it is said: "The Sui dynasty. "Renshou" was the era name of Emperor Wen. Emperor Wen reigned for twenty-four years and had two era names:
first, Kaifu; second, Renshou. These were the periods during which these three translations were made. △ Second, the locations where the scriptures were translated.
Daxingshan Temple was established by Emperor Wen; it was the place where these scriptures were translated. △ Third, the Master of Translation:
the Śramaṇa Jñānagupta from North India.
Northern India is one of the five regions of India. India as a whole is called *Yintu* (Industhāna), which here is translated as "Moonland" (*Candradvīpa*).
This is because the sages and saints of this land have succeeded one another in transforming others and guiding ordinary beings, just as the moon shines upon all.
*Jñānagupta*: these are the names of two translators. *Jñāna* is a partial transcription of the Sanskrit; its full form is *Jñānakūṭa*. This...
Yunzhide (Cloud-Virtue) was of the Kṣatriya caste. Dharmagupta—herein fully called Damo Jidu (Dharmagupta)—is translated as Fami (Dharma-Secret).
Both masters were natives of Northern India; they were the primary figures for this translation of the scriptures. △ Fourth, the names of the three translators.
Those translated later were also titled *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*.
However, both masters vowed to propagate and disseminate it; they traveled to this land, treading upon frost and snow as their former tracks and braving mist and clouds as they advanced.
Thus, they encountered a time of enlightenment and were granted an audience with the Sagely Sovereign. At that time, they erected pagodas and hoisted banners; truly, it was a moment of sincerity.
This temple was established, and robes were distributed and food bestowed as tokens of imperial favor. Jñānagupta served as the chief translator, while Dharmagupta acted as his assistant;

all matters of refinement and polishing were based on these two masters. Since the latter followed the former, the meaning accords with the Qin edition, with the exception that the characters "Supplementary Chapters" (tiānpǐn) have been added.
There are five instances where additions, combinations, and transpositions have occurred: first, [at the point] between the Qin and Jin...

First, the verses at the end of the "Universal Gateway" chapter were added. Second, the complete text of the "Simile of the Sunlight" was supplemented after the "Bhaiṣajyarāja" chapter of the Qin edition.
Third, the "Devadatta" chapter was merged into the "Jeweled Stūpa" chapter. Fourth, the "Entrustment" chapter was moved to follow the "Samantabhadra" chapter.
Fifth, the "Dhāraṇī" chapter was repositioned to follow the "Spiritual Powers" chapter. Thus, the text was completed in eight fascicles.
The twenty-seven chapters [of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*] have not circulated together with the *Zhengfahua jing*; they remain preserved in the Great Canon.

When questioned by the holy masters of the three dynasties as to why, when translating the same scripture, the titles were taken differently and the number of fascicles and chapters varied, they replied:

"The two Jin dynasties and the Sui dynasty were different eras; the Yuezhi and Kucha regions were separated by their customs and geography; and the translators each followed the circumstances of their respective locations."

Throughout the ages, they have merely served to propagate the holy teachings. As for the differences in titles and the distinctions between chapters and fascicles, they are like the names given to one's own eyes;
what is there to differ about? One should seek the point where the essential doctrines of the three translations coincide.
The translations of the Three Dynasties are hereby concluded. △ Third, clarifying that the Qin translation is uniquely supreme.
The three sutras overlap one another, with their texts and purports presented alternately; those esteemed by the people of the time all propagated the Qin edition.
As for the remaining partial chapters and individual verses, they are not without their own lineages, as detailed in the preface chronicles; therefore, they are not recounted here.
The first phrase clarifies intermixture; the second phrase clarifies abbreviation by inclusion. The second translation uses the term *chóng* (repetition); the third translation uses *tá* (layering).

That the transmission of the Way is not disordered is called "text" (*wén*); that there is a standard for its flavor and interest is called "purport" (*zhǐ*). That things are hidden or manifest in one or the other is called "mutual presentation" (*hùchén*).

This refers to the mutual presentation of both literary expression and purport, such as the "ten suchnesses," which are absent in the Jin version but present in the Qin translation. [The character] *yào* (medicine).
The latter half of the "Grass" (Cao) analogy exists in the two translations from the Jin and Sui dynasties, but it is absent from the Qin version;

thus, it is said that the textual expressions and underlying meanings are presented differently. As for the term *zong* (宗), it refers to venerating and honoring through contact with the words; as for *hong* (弘), it means to expand, propagate, and elucidate.

Therefore, although this sutra has three translations, those venerated and honored throughout ancient and modern times have all widely propagated the version translated by Kumārajīva during the Qin dynasty.

This is the fundamental basis for the translation. There are three reasons for his singular veneration: first, regarding his influence, for Master Kumārajīva was the sole individual to translate sūtras since the time of the seven Buddhas;

second, regarding his adaptation to capacities, for Master Kumārajīva translated the scriptures according to their underlying meaning, thereby harmonizing with the needs and benefiting those of this region;
and third, regarding his spiritual resonance, for Master Kumārajīva’s vow-power in translating the scriptures was exceptionally sublime, [as witnessed by] the Ruler of Qin.
Because the power of faith is transcendent, these three meanings have become as well-known as every household, circulating and being recited throughout both heaven and earth;
thus the true reality (*dharmatā*) remains undiminished. This may be compared to the three luminaries spanning the sky, yet the brilliant sun alone shines forth.
The relationship between the Qin edition and the two other translations is likewise so. The remainder below concludes by not further describing the verses of the "Chapter on the Finger. Above.

The preface sets forth the titles of the three sūtras solely to clarify their essential principles. If the specific items were not briefly indicated, it would remain unclear as to how they differ from one another.
It was for this reason that the Great Master provided such detailed treatment;

his intention was to show that, apart from the titles of these three sūtras, the remaining three sūtras vary in the number of chapters they contain and differ in whether their individual verses are complete or missing.
The verses of this chapter follow the sutras; they all possess the sense of being natural outflows (*niṣyanda*) and are categorized according to their mutual affinities.

They are not the least bit disordered, but are fully present in their proper sequence and are perfectly clear. However, as these do not constitute the primary outline of the sutra, they are not described in detail. Nevertheless, regarding these four lines:
There have been many who harbor doubts. Now I shall resolve them once more. To point precisely to the scriptural text:

"extracting the meaning of the divisions" and "distinctly designating the differences" means that the "chapters and verses" (pīṇḍaka-gāthā) refer specifically to the chapters and verses within the scripture. Regarding the division of chapters:

for example, in the Sui edition, the *Tian-shou* chapter (one chapter) was combined with the *Bao-ta* chapter; however, in the Qin edition, these were divided into two separate chapters. This refers to the division of chapters.

The opening and closing [of chapters] are not fixed. While the entrustment (*parindanā*) is placed at the end of the sutra in other versions, the Qin edition places it after the "Chapter on Supernatural Powers" (*Ṛddhyabhisaṃskāra-parivarta*);
thus, the positioning of these divisions is inconsistent. Regarding the separate verses:

for instance, in the "Chapter on Never Disparaging" (*Sadāparibhūta-parivarta*) of the Jin edition, there are verses stating, "Five hundred laymen (*upāsaka*) and five hundred laywomen (*upāsikā*)," whereas in the Qin edition, these verses are not separated [from the prose].

It stops at the mention of the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, and so forth. For instance, there are verses in the "Universal Gate" (*Samantamukha-parivarta*) chapter of the Sui edition, whereas they were only added later in the Qin edition.
This illustrates the differences in the verse sections among these three sūtras. The section on the introduction to the origins of the sūtra is concluded.

△ Third, the introduction to the purport of the sūtra’s exposition, divided into two parts. First, a general introduction to the beginning and end of the Buddha’s single transformation (*ekavyūha*), in order to clarify the capacity of the audience (*tathatā*).

The differentiation of the teachings. Second, the purport of the introductory text of the sūtra, which reveals the correct principle of the provisional and the real. This consists of two parts: first, the general introduction;
this, in turn, has two parts, the first of which is the exposition of the meaning of the introduction.

Now, when a sacred mountain descends with spiritual power, it cannot be transformed and enlightened except by a Great Sage. As for the reach of such transformation, the minds of beings cannot be guided without the presence of past conditions.
Thus, when the Immortal Garden (the Jetavana) was completed, the capacities of beings were distinguished as small or great; and at the Golden River (the Nirvāṇa), the final testament was given.

The Way distinguishes between the partial and the full teachings; is this not because the instruction is adapted to the capacity and timing of the recipient? There is no need to scrutinize its sublime convergence further.
As for the term "general preface" (*fàn xù*), it is used because the teaching is clarified according to the capacities of beings throughout a single lifetime.

Now, these two characters constitute the very inception of a literary work, serving as its opening point. They are like clouds before rain or smoke before fire, acting as the preceding signs. Therefore—
Master Wufeng said: "The oil-laden clouds know the downpour of rain; the golden lightning awakens to the rushing thunder. This is the natural course of principle and circumstance.

"Numinous Peak" (Ling-yue) refers to Vulture Peak (Gṛdhrakūṭa), which is the Śr̥gālagiri mentioned in the sutras. Because it was the dwelling place of the Buddhas of antiquity and is where the present Buddha preaches the Dharma, it is called the "descent of the numinous" (jiang-ling).
Question: Regarding the phrase "the numinous peak is the descent of the numinous," the ancients maintained that the mountain harbors brilliance.

The refinement of the numinous gives birth to this numinous and enlightened sage; this is precisely the "numinous descent" referred to when it is said that the Buddha was born from the numinous essence of Mount Zhong.
Therefore, citing the meaning of the poem to establish this proof is consistent with reason and free of error.
Now, you attribute this "numinous descent" to the Buddha and not to the mountain. Yet, how can one explain that Shenfu was a hero among men by virtue of relying on the spiritual power of the land?
"Does the Buddha, on the contrary, descend as a spirit without borrowing the numinous power of the earth? Answer: "This also has its道理 (principle). Let us now rectify this explanation.

In the eighth chapter of 'Song Gao' (The Height of Mount Song) from the *Da Ya* (Greater Odes), each chapter consists of eight lines. The first chapter says: 'Song Gao, the mountain alone; its loftiness reaches the heavens.
From that mountain alone descends the spirit, giving birth to Fu and Shen. It is Shen and Fu who are the pillars of Zhou.'"
"Guarding the four states as a bulwark; proclaiming [virtue] throughout the four quarters.

This poem was composed by Yin Jifu to see off the Earl of Shen as he was enfeoffed at Xie during the reign of King Xuan of Zhou, who had restored the dynasty. It was written to praise the Earl of Shen for his auspicious birth.
It is indeed said that he was born from a mountain of concentrated spiritual essence; this is but a common saying regarding a land of numinous spirits and eminent men.
Such an interpretation may apply to the Duke of Shen, but it cannot apply to the Tathāgata.

One should understand that the Buddha’s manifestation of traces is due to the power of his primordial compassionate vows to deliver sentient beings, through the perfection of his cultivation and realization and his sovereign mastery in manifesting transformations. Therefore, the Buddha’s mind is...
The mind of the perfectly luminous Dharma-realm is the body of the Buddha, and the body of the Buddha is likewise the perfectly luminous body of the Dharma-realm;
it is only that they appear or disappear in accordance with the capacities of sentient beings. To claim that this body descended to be born upon a sacred mountain is incorrect.
Furthermore, one should understand that the "spirit" of such a descent refers precisely to the Buddha’s presence here to expound this present sutra; this is what is meant by "descent."
This is spiritual essence. The Great Master borrowed the words but not the intent. The Sun of Wisdom rises high, illuminating the profound depths of the myriad dharmas;
the Ocean of Nature is perfectly tranquil, transcending the four great elements to stand alone as supreme. Thus he is called the Great Sage. His transformation and edification are twofold.
First, manifesting form; second, preaching the Dharma. "Opening" means to strip away the film of ignorance and dissect attachments, decisively severing the dust of worldly passions.

"Transforming" means to point out the ordinary and make them holy, smelting and refining illusions and delusions. Thus, the Buddha is the one who opens and transforms, while the spiritual capacity [of the listener] is that which is opened and transformed.
These two phrases introduce the author's intent: that this mountain is the dwelling place of ancient Buddhas, and that the Tathāgata was present here.

This was not in vain; it was intended to reveal the Buddha’s knowledge and vision (*buddhajñānadarśana*), to bring provisional teachings back to the ultimate reality, and to manifest the Dharma of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*).

Yet, were it not for a Great Sage, how could the three vehicles have been opened and transformed? Furthermore, those who followed in the footsteps at Vulture Peak (*Gṛdhrakūṭa*) were none other than sages and worthies.
Some had accumulated profound and vast cultivation, remaining hidden within while manifesting outwardly, such as Śāriputra and Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra.
...and so forth. Or, there are those whose Way is complete and virtues fully perfected, whose merit borders on the ultimate, such as Mañjuśrī, Maitreya, and others.
If there were not a Great Sage [such as the Buddha], how could such eminent persons be transformed and receive this Dharma?

That they are able to be transformed is because the Tathāgata’s form and mind are preeminent, his principle and measure are transcendent, he discerns capacities without error, and his practice and application are [perfect].

Based on this precedent, the present sutra enables those of the three vehicles to universally resolve their obstructions and dispel ignorance; thus, both are able to eliminate delusion and receive predictions of enlightenment.

Therefore, it is stated by way of contrast that "it is not without the Great Sage that they are opened and transformed. The two phrases "suited" (適) and "transformed" (化) describe the response [of sentient beings] depending upon the convergence of conditions.
"Suited" (適) means to accord with, to reach, or to be appropriate. This implies that if there are no conditions, one will certainly not receive transformation; for when conditions are shallow...

Nor did they change their hearts. Therefore, wherever a divine transformation meets with responsive receptivity, it must be a place where there was once a great affinity, and one where that affinity was profound.
Although the Buddha is a Great Sage, he cannot transform those who lack the necessary affinity.

This is because those whose capacities were transformed at Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa had all, in the past during the time of Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū, listened to the Prince’s re-exposition of the Dharma and had already been brought to the One Vehicle.
Because of the seeds of past conditions, it is conversely revealed that wherever the teaching reaches, there is no way to guide the mind without those former conditions.

That which is called "guiding the mind" means that because their spiritual capacity (*mārga*) is superior and their resonance is profound, they do not merely plant seeds or gain benefit through growth;
rather, each attains perfect clear understanding and ultimately reaches the stage of Buddhahood. This is like the assembly of the Dharma at the time of Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū. Regarding the power...

Regarding the three vehicles of sound: those who were previously transformed by the teachings are now at Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa; some have received predictions of enlightenment, while others have partaken in the benefits.
All of this is because they possessed conditions in the past, and only now do they possess their share. If there had been no past conditions, how could they attain deliverance now? Question:
The Great Sage’s intention in opening the way for transformation was to make it universal; why then is it limited to those with specific conditions? Since [the teaching] is already present...

There are those with whom there is a karmic affinity (*sahagata-pratyaya*). What is meant by "pervading all"? The answer is: the Buddha’s mind pervades all, and it likewise pervades those with whom he has a karmic affinity.

Is this not evident in the case of the nine hundred million households of Śrāvastī? Of these, three hundred million saw the Buddha and heard the Dharma; thus, their past affinities were able to guide their minds.
Another three hundred million merely established the seeds [of future realization]. The remaining three hundred million neither saw nor heard him, as they lacked such affinity.
It obstructs them. The ancients said that fox-furs cannot warm those who have no vital breath, and Bian Que could not cure a disease certain to be fatal.
Rain does not moisten rootless grass, and gold cannot enrich one whose destiny is exhausted.
Knowing this, it is clear that the Buddha-dharma cannot save those who lack the necessary conditions (*pratyaya*). This was based on the principle of past conditions.
"How great it is! These two phrases introduce the period when the Tathāgata first attained Buddhahood;

they show how, though he was without intentionality regarding the provisional (half) or ultimate (full) teachings, the capacities of sentient beings naturally differentiated themselves. Although this refers to the initial period, it actually introduces the capacities to whom the Dharma of the entire lifetime [of the Buddha's teaching] was applied.

Thus, the two characters "so yi" (therefore)承接 (receive and connect) the previous discussion on the depth or shallowness of past conditions, explaining that because of these, the faculties of the present are either great or small.
The Immortal Garden (*Ṛṣivana*) is the place where ancient immortals practiced the Way, becoming defiled by the dust of the world and falling [into error].

Regarding the Buddha’s attainment of perfection at this site, there are generally four intended meanings: first, because he attained the four kinds of fearlessness; second, because he sought to awaken the multitude of deluded beings so that they might understand;

third, because five persons with whom he had a karmic connection were present there and ready to be saved; and fourth, because he spoke directly from his true mind to warn against increasing [delusion].
Regarding "due to overweening pride," this specifically indicates that there are two intended meanings for the term "proclaiming completion" (*kōjō*).

First, when the Wheel of Dharma of the Four Truths was turned three times for the sake of the five bhikṣus, he proclaimed his realization by saying, "This is suffering; it has been known by me," and so forth.

This "proclaiming completion" refers to the sense of exhortation and encouragement, which means raising up the fruit [of the path] to inspire joy. Second, in the present sutra, the *Bhaiṣajyavarga* (Chapter on Medicinal Herbs) states: "I am the Tathāgata."
“Worthy of Offerings” and so forth—this “proclamation of completion” signifies the grand opening of the gate of salvation and the universal awakening of beings.

How could this proclamation of completion possibly imply self-conceit or self-exaltation? Nevertheless, although this proclamation of completion occurs at the final stage of the *Lotus Sūtra*, its intent is actually to sequence the Buddha’s initial sitting at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*) and his proclamation of the work of saving sentient beings;
it reveals the purpose of his appearance in the world. Sentient capacities are divided into [the small and the great].

The "lesser" refers to those such as the followers of the Two Vehicles and the Bodhisattvas of the stage of practice through phenomena (*dharmācāra*), because their knowledge and vision are partial and they do not understand that all things are their own mind.

The "greater" capacity refers to those such as the Bodhisattvas of the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*), because their understanding and practice are perfectly luminous and they have thoroughly awakened to the true source.
Thus, the *Āgama* states: "When the Tathāgata first turned the Dharma wheel of the Four Noble Truths, among those who heard the Dharma, there were some who attained realization."

Regarding the stage of the Mahāyāna: there are those who realize the fruits of the Hīnayāna. Based on this, one knows that while the Truths and their Conditions are one, the capacities [of sentient beings] are inherently diverse;
thus, infinite distinctions arise regarding birth and cessation. This is analogous to how the Six Perfections are one, yet the capacities [of those practicing them] are inherently distinct.

Thus, the practice of phenomena (*dharma*) and the practice of principle (*li*) are two distinct things; the Buddha originally had no such intention. It is like the "medicine that prevents the hands from cracking" mentioned by Zhuangzi:

those who use it each have different purposes. Knowing this, one can infer by analogy the smallness or greatness of the capacities of those to whom the teachings were established across the five periods.
Question: When the Dharma was turned in the Immortal Garden, was it the time when the *Avataṃsaka* was expounded all at once? Was the sixteen-foot body manifested in the Immortal Garden?

The site of enlightenment manifests at a thousand fathoms. It is possible for the two beginnings to be simultaneous and for [the Dharma] to be perfectly pervasive; however, when the two images are suspended side-by-side, their superiority and inferiority are clearly evident.

This refers precisely to the preceding signs of the teaching of the Great and Small Vehicles. Thus, while the application to sentient beings may vary between Great and Small, it would imply that the Buddha possesses a dualistic mind.
How can you say the distinction lies with the capacity of the beings? For the Buddha has no such mind. Answer: A single moon is universally reflected in a thousand rivers.
Manifestation may appear obscured or luminous, yet it is but water; the moon has no dual mind. When a single rain falls, ten thousand plants are equally moistened;

though there may be abundance or scarcity, this pertains to the objects themselves—the rain itself remains without distinction. Whether in the immortal gardens or the sites of enlightenment, the forms of six feet or a thousand feet are merely manifestations according to the capacity of the observer;
they are perceived differently because the perspectives of those who perceive them are not fixed. How could the cloud-like body of the Dharma-realm abide within the realm of conceptual thought?

How true these words are! When the Great Master (Zhiyi) set forth these two phrases, he feared that people might say that prior to the *Lotus Sūtra*, it would have been appropriate for the Buddha to preach the truth directly and thereby conclude the great matter of his mission.

He feared they would fail to reflect that there was a distinction between the provisional and the real, and that the Buddha must now once again employ the revelation and unification to bring all things back to their source. Why is this? The Master of the Preface states that when the Buddha first attained enlightenment...

Having already discerned the capacities [of sentient beings], I was compelled to provisionally distinguish between the provisional and the real. Now that they have become fully matured, I am likewise compelled to reveal and manifest [the truth].

This is solely because the capacities [of beings] have evolved from beginning to end. If I were to speak only of the real, how could I respond to these capacities? This meaning is implicit; let the wise examine it in detail.
The two phrases regarding the Golden River [Nirvana] signify that the first period of transformation has reached its conclusion. Because...
The capacity [of sentient beings] is great or small, and thus the teachings are divided into partial and complete. The first phrase distinguishes the time and place of the teaching;
"the Golden River" indicates the location, and "the final charge" indicates the time. In the Sanskrit language, it is called *Aḷiravati*; here it is translated as "Possessing the Golden River.
This river belongs to the territory emerging from the city of Śrāvastī. Because the flow of the river water is rapid, it symbolizes birth and death.
It is not eternal; the golden sands remain unmoving, symbolizing that the one true reality is eternally constant.
On the riverbank stands a śāla tree, the birthplace of Malla the Worldly Hero, where ancient Buddhas of the past once dwelt.

Its grove consists of four pairs of eight trunks—four flourishing and four withered—marking the place where the Tathāgata entered parinirvāṇa. This signifies that both the fundamental and derivative four inversions have been severed.

Because he has fully realized the four virtues of permanence, bliss, self, and purity. Regarding the term "bequeathed charge" (*guming*): "bequeathing" (*gu*) refers to issuing instructions at the time of death;

it signifies the intention to depart. Just as King Cheng, when nearing his end, issued the "Bequeathed Charge" (*Guming*) edict and testament, so too does the Tathāgata, as his conditions for transformation are about to conclude, preach the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*.
This is the final gathering together of the teachings from the five periods.
The "Bequeathed Testament" (*yīzhù*) represents the ultimate model for posterity. The word "words" (*dào*) in the second line refers to the teachings of a single lifetime.

Because the ninefold canon of the Hīnayāna does not exhaust the full meaning of the Dharma, it is called the "half-character" (*bàn zì*). Because the twelvefold canon of the Mahāyāna perfectly realizes the nature of the mind, it is called the "full-character" (*mǎn zì*).
Thus, in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, the Tathāgata spoke of these two characters, "half" and "full," to distinguish between the two vehicles of the Great and Small.
Therefore, that sutra says: "For example, suppose an elder has an only son.

Fearing he will not achieve success quickly, he diligently teaches him the 'half-syllables' day and night, but does not teach him the *Vyākaraṇa* (grammar), because the child is too young and his strength is insufficient.
This establishes the definition of the characters as being taken from the model. It states that within the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, the Tathāgata uses the "half... [to represent the provisional teaching].
The two characters "fulfilling" (man) establish the definitive framework for the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna throughout the entire dispensation, ensuring they do not become confused.

Nevertheless, regarding the four phrases before and after [the main text], the former refers to the initial stages of the Great and Small Vehicles, while the latter refers to the final stages of the partial and perfect teachings.

Because these two textual passages are interwoven like a brocade pattern, the capacities of the audience (*jì*) and the teachings (*jiào*) are spoken of interchangeably, both encompassing the entirety of the dispensation. Furthermore, the two meanings of the preceding and succeeding sections serve as mutual supports for one another.
The differentiation of capacities leads to the diversity of teachings; the diversity of teachings leads to the differentiation of capacities.

The preface addresses this, referring to the reason why the *Lotus Sūtra* reveals and clarifies the truth. Are these two phrases not intended to follow upon the two preceding meanings, indicating that the time has arrived for the *Lotus Sūtra* to be preached?
Are the two characters "qǐfēi" (豈非) not equivalent to saying "if it were not for"? Regarding the phrase "the teaching covers all equally," it refers to...

Prior to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, the teachings were directed toward the three vehicles; thus, as for the teaching, it has reached its ultimate limit here, and as for the capacity [of the disciples], it has reached full maturity here.

This is the time when they may "mount" [the vehicle]. The phrase "there is no need" (*wú zú*) is not intended as a literal negation, but serves rather to manifest the intention of the author’s humility, whereby he dares not speak directly.
"To investigate" (*hé*) means to examine thoroughly; "to substantiate" (*zhì*) means to clarify; these are used according to their respective meanings.
"To grasp it" refers precisely to the meaning of the conditions for seeing and hearing [the Dharma]. "The sublime assembly" (*gāohuì*) points to the assembly at the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
The intent is that unless the teaching has reached those who ride the vehicle, it is difficult to see or hear this sublime assembly. If one follows the clear explanation, one should say:

"Only when the teaching reaches those who ride the vehicle does one then obtain the opportunity to examine and verify the sublime assembly. This is because the arising of this sublime assembly is fundamentally due to the arrival of the teaching.
The capacity has matured; the time has arrived and the conditions are supreme; the momentum is such that it may be seized.

Had it not been for this moment when the capacity was matured and the teaching had arrived, even after passing through hundreds of thousands of lifetimes, there would have been no opportunity to give rise to this sublime assembly.

How could we have investigated the correct principle of the provisional and the real, or scrutinized the universal track of the revealed truth? Furthermore, how could we have universally received the prediction of enlightenment and attained such excellence?
Is there not benefit in seeing and hearing it? Nevertheless, regarding the fact that the single assembly of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* is particularly exalted, there are briefly ten points.
First, this sutra is spoken by all Buddhas alike, such as Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū, Prabhūtaratna, and Dīpaṃkara. Second, it is spoken at a later time [than other teachings].
Third, it is the authentic seal of both the provisional and the ultimate; these two points constitute the meaning of the first fascicle. Fourth, the bestowal of predictions (vyākaraṇa) is universal.

1. Because it is as in the three cycles of bestowing predictions (*vyākaraṇa*). 2. Because all Buddhas have attained perfect realization (*pariniṣpanna*), as in the case of Prabhūtaratna and his emanations. 3.
Because one requires this to achieve Buddhahood, as in the teaching that through hearing, understanding, and cultivation, one will certainly attain *bodhi*. 4.

Because the power of the Dharma is supreme and wondrous, as in Śākyamuni taking it as the cause for his practice and the Dragon Girl relying upon it to realize the fruit. 5. Because it is the fundamental... [text ends]
Because the traces [of manifestation] are profoundly deep, as in the teaching on the revelation of the fundamental and the trace;
because the nine merits are inexhaustible, as in the merit of sympathetic joy (*anumodanā*) and the merit of recitation and so forth;

and because wisdom and practice are revealed in tandem, as in the main body of the teaching where practice is initiated by wisdom, and the dissemination where practice accords with wisdom—due to these ten meanings, it is called the "Exalted Assembly" (*gāohuì*).

How much more so when it transcends the five teachings and stands far apart from other sutras! Although the *Avataṃsaka* is perfectly consummate, if it were not for the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, then the revelation and manifestation [of the ultimate truth] would not be accomplished;
for the provisional must ultimately conclude in the provisional, and the real must ultimately conclude in the real. △ Second, resolving doubts.

Thus we know that the five thousand who withdrew from their seats were those whose arrogance had increased; the five hundred who received predictions of enlightenment were all those who honored the traces of the esoteric transformation.

One might fear such doubts, for while the aforementioned "high assembly" implies that the time has arrived and the conditions have ripened—just as within a sandalwood forest there is nothing else—[the text continues:]

Regarding those of inferior capacity: according to the present sutra, after Śāriputra had requested three times and the Tathāgata granted his request to preach, why did five thousand people prostrate to the Buddha and withdraw?
Therefore, the commentary explains: one should know that the withdrawal of the five thousand from their seats was a manifestation of great skillful means.

It was born of deep compassion, out of pity for those in the assembly who, not having attained realization, claimed they had attained it, and who remained stuck in the "City of Illusion," abandoning the place of the True Treasure.
This was intended to encourage those whose minds were hesitant and lingering to gain deep faith in the Dharma of the One Vehicle; thus, the Preface Master made this mention.
For the assembly of followers who responded to his influence, this serves to further clarify that the Lotus Sūtra is a supreme gathering. The "five hundred" refers to Pūrṇa and others.

The matter of their receiving predictions (vyākaraṇa) encompasses both causal predictions and resultant predictions, as explained in the subsequent text. As for the previous mention of "retiring from one's seat," it refers to those who withdrew.

This is expedient means (*upāya*); its ultimate realization is unfathomable. To now say that the bestowal of predictions (*vyākaraṇa*) is expedient means further clarifies the preceding principle: it conceals the superior and manifests the inferior, and is thus called "secret transformation.
This applies equally to the five hundred [disciples], which is why it is said they "all revere" [the Buddha]. The underlying meaning is that the cycle of causes and conditions has been completed.

Although it refers to those of inferior faculties when speaking of the matter of bestowing predictions (*vyākaraṇa*), in reality, these five hundred noble ones have all practiced and cultivated for many kalpas;

their original [attainment] was great while their outward traces were small. They manifested through skillful means (*upāya*) to assist in the transformation of beings and to enlighten those who had not yet attained faith.

Therefore, the subsequent text says, "Internally secret, externally manifest," and so forth. The general introduction is concluded above. △ Second, the specific introduction to the meaning of the sutra.
The Essential Meaning: To manifest the correct principle of the provisional and the real, this is divided into two parts. First, a brief introduction to the unfolding of the three cycles of teaching.

[The first cycle] explains why the Buddha emitted light and manifested auspicious signs to open the source of the teachings requested by the assembly; it describes his emergence from meditative concentration to extol his virtues and fully express the grand strategy of the Buddha’s wisdom.

[The second cycle,] "The Burning House," provides the textual framework for entering the Great Vehicle. [The third cycle,] "The City of Transformation," ensures that the karmic conditions of the past do not fall away. [The fourth cycle,] "The Pearl on the Robe,"...
This clarifies that the rational nature is ever-present. By "digging a well," it demonstrates the manifold ways of awakening. Regarding the term "sequential order" (*nidāna*):
herein, it refers to the sequence of scripture, doctrine, and analogy. The two characters "so yi" (therefore) universally承接 (receive and connect) the preceding meaning;

for it is only when the time has arrived and conditions have ripened that the manifestation appears to signify [the truth] and the Dharma assembly is convened. The preceding phrase constitutes the *nidāna*.
The Great Enlightenment manifests its fundamental essence in perfect fullness, for it completely reveals the essence and function of the wondrous Dharma through auspicious radiance.

The Buddha represents the essence of the true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*), while the light represents the function of the true reality. Its manifestation from the white tuft (*ūrṇā-kośa*) between the eyebrows signifies that this principle transcends the two extremes and is endowed with the four virtues.
There are six types of such auspicious signs: namely, preaching the sutras, entering meditative absorption, raining flowers, the shaking of the earth, and [the gathering of] the assembly...
Joy, the emission of light—these six are called auspicious omens (*śubha-nimitta*). In terms of time, they are seen by the world for the first time;

in terms of place, they are rarely encountered even across the dust-motes of all lands (*rajas-kṣetra*); in terms of persons, only those who have realized the ultimate can perceive them. All are rare and marvelous omens.

The following sentence introduces the Bodhisattva’s reception of the [Dharma] stream and his assistance in its manifestation. Through questions and answers and citations, he truly acts as one who "inspires me" (*kṛtānuvāda*), thereby opening the way for others to understand.
That which can open [the teaching] is the auspicious light-omen; that which is opened is the dialogue between the two sages.
