Saccaka was so named because he possessed the wisdom of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*). He was the younger brother of Lady Māyā;
thus, there were two from his maternal clan and three from his paternal clan.

These five—first Āśvajit, second Bhadrika, and third Mahānāman Kauliya—had entered the mountains by royal command to attend upon the Buddha and practice the Way. However, they could not endure the hardships.
They subsequently abandoned the Buddha and went to the Deer Park to practice heterodox paths. After the Buddha attained enlightenment, he went first to deliver them.

Because they initially realized the nature of adventitious defilements (*āgantuka-kleśa*), [the Buddha] went first. Due to past causes, when the Buddha was a large red-eyed fish and the five men were carpenters, it was these men who first took the fish’s flesh.
The *Āgama* states: "In my Buddha-dharma, there is broad benevolence and vast erudition; they were the first to receive the flavor of the Dharma."

As for this, the bhikṣu Kauṇḍinya was foremost. Mahākāśyapa—here translated as "Great Turtle Clan"—was so named because his ancestors practiced the Way and moved a numinous tortoise to carry forth a divine chart in response; thus, the clan took that name.
Formerly, during the Dharma of Vipaśyin Buddha, he was a goldsmith. There was a poor woman who obtained a single golden bead and wished to repair the Buddha [statue] within a stūpa.
A goldsmith, seeking no payment, offered to refine it for him. Thereupon, they vowed to become husband and wife.
From that time forward, for ninety-one kalpas, their bodies were all golden in color, and they enjoyed happiness among gods and humans. Subsequently, he was born in the Brahma Heaven;

when his life there ended, he was reborn in the kingdom of Magadha into the family of the Brahmin Gautama. His body was purple-gold in color, and his family was immensely wealthy and superior [to others].
Regarding King Bimbisāra: the king possessed one thousand golden plows, but in order to avoid him, he kept only one less.
At that time, there was a daughter from a wealthy family of another country whose body was also golden; she was none other than the "Golden Woman" who had previously made offerings.
He took her as his wife, forming a marriage based on no prior karmic connection. Later, the couple left the household life to follow the Buddha and practiced the dhūta austerities.
Finally, before the Many-Sons Stūpa, he held up a flower to show the assembly; the Venerable One broke into a slight smile, whereupon [the Buddha] bestowed upon him the gold-threaded *kāṣāya*.
After the Buddha had entered *parinirvāṇa* and the communal recitation (*saṃgīti*) was completed, he took the robe and entered Mount Kukkuṭapāda.

Entering the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), he awaits the descent of Maitreya; only after handing over the robe will he attain final extinction. The *Āgama* states: "Within my Buddha-dharma..."
Among those who practiced the twelve *dhūta* ascetic virtues and performed difficult and arduous practices, Mahākāśyapa was foremost.
The three Kāśyapas were as previously described. Uruvilvā means "Papaya Grove" (*kapitthavana*);

because he lived near this grove, he is called "Papaya Lump" (*kapittha-ghaṇṭa*), for there was a lump on his chest like a papaya fruit. He is also called "Prayer" (*prārthana*), because he was born after praying to the deity of this grove.
"Gaya" is the name of a mountain, namely Elephant Head Mountain (*Gajapadaka*), because he dwelt on this mountain.

It is also the name of a city, because he was near this city. "Nadi" is the name of a river, because he resided by the river. During the time of Vipaśyin Buddha, these three men together erected a sacrificial pillar for a tree;

due to this [karmic] connection, they became brothers. The elder brother served as the preceptor to King Bimbisāra and previously worshipped a fire-dragon; he ordained five hundred disciples. The second...

Each of his two younger brothers had ordained two hundred and fifty disciples, and they all practiced the teachings of their elder brother. The Buddha performed ten kinds of supernatural transformations (*ṛddhiprātihārya*) to convert them.
Although Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa witnessed these miracles, his false attachments were not yet altered, and he said, "Though Gautama possesses supernatural powers, they do not equal the truth of my own Way.
The Buddha said, "You are not an Arhat, nor have you attained the Way. At this, [Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa] was suddenly enlightened and led five...

One hundred disciples returned to the Buddha. When the two younger brothers saw fire-making implements floating down in the water, they went to investigate and found that their elder brother had already become a śramaṇa;
they too returned to the Buddha, and together they became one thousand arhats.
The Āgamas state that Uruvilvā was foremost in protecting the fourfold assembly and providing them with the four requisites so that they lacked for nothing. Gayā—
The bhikṣu who has clearly contemplated all dharmas and is entirely without attachment, being most skillful in teaching and transforming others, is the foremost.
The bhikṣu Nadi has a mind that is profoundly tranquil; having subdued all fetters, he is the foremost in diligence. Śāriputra.
His full name is Śāriputra; this is translated as "Son of the Body" (Shenzi). Because his mother possessed a beautiful physique, and he was born from her body, he is called "Son of the Body.
In the city of Rājagṛha, there were two nāga kings, Nanda and Upananda, who sent down rain at the proper times, so that the kingdom never suffered years of famine.
Consequently, the king and his great ministers would annually hold a grand assembly, setting up three high seats. The [first] seat for the King...
The Master of Discourse sat upon his seat. When Śāriputra was eight years old, he walked through the assembly and asked, "What are these three seats for?
The people informed him of everything. He immediately bypassed the crowd and ascended the debate platform.

The scholars were all ashamed and refused to engage him in discussion, saying, "If we defeat this child, it will not bring us sufficient renown; yet if we do not defeat him, our humiliation would be great."
He sent his attendants one after another to question him, and Śāriputra answered them all. Those who questioned him were utterly defeated; none dared to stand against him.
The king, along with his ministers and citizens, all said, "It is our national good fortune that a man of great wisdom has appeared. At sixteen, he had extensively studied the past and present;
in debate, he was peerless among the great nations and was acclaimed as the foremost throughout the five regions of India. By means of the Brahmin Śāraṇa...
He served as a teacher. His disciple, Zhì, had mastered all his arts and doctrines. When Zhì was approaching death, he laughed joyfully.
Śāriputra asked him about this, and Zhì said: "The world is blind, being bound by the intimacy of affection. I saw the King of Kāñcanamālā die;
his queen wished to be reborn in the same place as him, so she threw herself into the fire and died. Later, I saw a merchant from Kāñcanamālā and asked him..."
This was indeed so. Śāriputra felt remorse, thinking: "I have not yet perfected my mastery of the teacher's arts;

it is because I am not a fit vessel that the teacher did not transmit this dharma to me, and thus he kept it secret. Realizing his own lack of attainment, he sought an even more excellent dharma, but found no teacher to serve.
Although he did not know this one dharma, he was proficient in all other teachings and was the foremost among the hosts of non-Buddhists.

He was friends with Maudgalyāyana, and they made an agreement: "Whichever of us finds a good teacher shall follow that teacher. On the road, he encountered Aśvajit, whose majestic deportment was composed and orderly.
He asked about the teacher's doctrine, and [Aśvajit] replied: "All phenomena arise from conditions; they likewise cease because of conditions.
My teacher, the Great Śramaṇa, always speaks thus. He then went to the Buddha’s presence and left the household life after seven days.
He was universally proficient in the Buddha-dharma. On the fifteenth day, he realized the fruit of arhatship (*aśaikṣa-phala*).

He served as the preceptor for Rāhula and was his teacher in the Vinaya. The Āgamas state: "Within my Buddha-dharma, Śāriputra is foremost among those whose wisdom is inexhaustible and who resolve all doubts.
Mahāmaudgalyāyana—here translated as "Praise-Chanting"—was his clan name; his personal name was Kauṣṭhila. He was...
The name of the tree: because he was born after praying to this tree, it is so called; alternatively, it is said to mean "mung bean.

In ancient times, sages dwelling in the mountains took beans as their food, and thus his clan was named accordingly. This Venerable One burned the Palace of Victory (Vaijayanta), halted the chariot of Jīvaka, and led the five hundred disciples of Devadatta back to the True Dharma.
He retrieved the five hundred Śākyas of Kapilavastu from the Brahmā realm.
The *Āgama* states: "Among my disciples, Mahāmaudgalyāyana is foremost in the lightness of his supernatural powers for traveling to the ten directions by flight.
Kātyāyana—here translated as "of the Shaving Clan"—lived in ancient times when many immortals resided in the mountains.
No one shaves their hair. There was once a seer who had two sons. They went to visit their father, and the younger son shaved the heads of the other seers;
because of this, they established a clan. The Venerable One belongs to this clan. It is also said that [the name] means "adornment," because he is skilled in debate.
The Āgamas state: "Among those who skillfully discern the meaning and expound the teachings of the Buddha, Kātyāyana is foremost.
Aniruddha—also called Anuruddha or Aniruddhu;
this is translated as "Free from Poverty" or "As One Wishes"—was the son of Śuklodana, the nephew of Śuddhodana, and the cousin of the World-Honored One.
He was the elder brother of Ānanda and the paternal uncle of Rāhula; he was no ordinary man. As the Duke of Zhou said:
"I am the son of King Wen, the younger brother of King Wu, and the uncle of King Cheng; I am no lowly or base person."

This Venerable One, by virtue of offering millet rice, obtained a golden man and thereby attained great wealth. By using an arrow to poke out a dim lamp, he was moved to receive the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*) and realize the fruits of the path.
The *Āgama* states: "Within my Buddha-dharma, Aniruddha is foremost among those who possess the power of clear vision through the divine eye.
Kapphiṇa—here translated as "Housing Star"—was born because his parents prayed to this constellation.
Furthermore, because he had shared a room with the Buddha while staying overnight, when the Venerable first went forth, he went to the Buddha’s presence and encountered rain.
He sought lodging at a potter's house and used grass as his seat. At evening, a bhikṣu entered; it was the Buddha himself.

[The Venerable] pushed his grass mat aside to let him sit and sat on the ground himself. The Buddha preached the Dharma for him, and he realized the fruit of Arhatship. Moreover, he was skilled in knowing the stars.
*Xiù* (Constellations). He was named after his understanding of images and diagrams. The *Āgama* states:
"In my Buddha-dharma, among those who skillfully know the stars, the moon, and the sun, Kapphiṇa is foremost.
Gavāmpati—this is translated as "the one with the cow-chewing ailment"—formerly, when he was a śrāmaṇera, he mocked an elderly bhikṣu by whistling like a cow. From that time onward, for five...
For a hundred lifetimes he was an ox; subsequently, when he emerged as a human, for five hundred lifetimes he constantly suffered from the ailment of ruminating like an ox.
Although he has now attained the Way, these residual habits still remain. Fearing that people might slander him and thereby incur transgression, the Buddha gave him a rosary.

When people saw him merely counting the beads, they would recite the Buddha’s name on his behalf. Furthermore, fearing that others might not recognize him as a holy man, he frequently remains in the heavens to receive offerings.

When the Buddha entered parinirvāṇa, the Venerable One heard of it and said: "Gavāmpati, bowing his head in salutation to the Great Virtuous Saṃgha, the foremost among the wondrous assembly, declares:
'Hearing that the Buddha has passed into extinction, I shall follow him, just as when an elephant king departs, the elephant calf follows.'"
The Āgamas state that among those who delight in the heavens and do not delight in the human realm, the bhikṣu Goṣṭhīputra (Niuji) was foremost;
"Goṣṭhī" means "provisional combination. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: Once, while the Venerable One was staying overnight in an empty pavilion, a ghost arrived carrying a corpse.
Another ghost followed and disputed it, each claiming, "I brought this! They sought a decision together.

The Venerable One thought to himself, "Whether one relies on reason or acts contrary to reason, both cannot avoid harm. It is better to answer truthfully. One ghost grew angry, tore off the Venerable One's hands and feet, and ate them.
Another ghost took the hands and feet of a corpse and replaced [the Venerable One's] with them; thus the two ghosts ate each other and departed.
At dawn, he thought to himself, "I cannot discern whose body this is. If it were my own body, I would have seen it with my own eyes."
He was a ghost who ate [human flesh]. If he encountered another's body, it would follow him wherever he went or stayed; whenever he met someone, he would ask, "Do you see my body?
At that time, the assembly of monks questioned him about the reason for this. Knowing that he was easily deliverable, they said to him, "Your body is merely the remains of another person;
it is not your own. He immediately realized that this body exists only through the temporary conjunction of conditions. Through this, his outflows were exhausted, and he attained [Arhatship].
The *Āgama* says: Among those who sit in meditation and enter *dhyāna*, whose minds are not distracted or confused, Upavāna is foremost;
Piṅgiyāśva—here translated as "residual habit"—in five hundred past lives was a Brahmin and was by nature highly arrogant.
Although he has now attained the Way, these residual habits have not yet been extinguished; every time he passes over the Ganges, he calls out to the river deity, saying, "Little..."
The maidservant stopped the flow of water and caused it to pass me by. The spirit informed the Buddha, who instructed her to repent before the spirit.
She immediately joined her palms and said, "Little maid, do not be angry. The great assembly all laughed. The Buddha said, "There was truly no heart of pride; it was merely a habitual tendency."
The Āgamas state that among those who sat in austerity beneath trees, avoiding neither wind nor rain, the bhikṣu Vatsa was foremost;
"Baku-la" (Bakkula) means "Good Appearance" because his countenance was upright and dignified, and it is also called "Revered Lineage.

The *Dharmaguptaka Vinaya* (or *Dharmarājika-sūtra*) states that in the past, during the Dharma of Vipaśyin Buddha, he offered a single fruit to a sick monk, thereby attaining [the fruit of] ninety... [years].

For one kalpa, he enjoyed blessings among gods and humans. Now born into a brahmin family, he has lived for one hundred and sixty years, free from illness and untimely death, having experienced five rewards of immortality:
first, his stepmother placed him in a fire pit, yet he did not die;
second, at his mother’s request for meat, she placed him in boiling water, yet he did not die; third, following his mother to the riverbank, she pushed him into the water...
He did not die. When the four great fish swallowed him, he did not die. When five fish were caught in a man’s net, they cut him open without harming him;

the man subsequently took him as his son. When the boy’s father heard of this, he went to dispute the matter, but the man would not give him up. Later, it was settled that the child belonged to both families.
Therefore, he is called "Double-Clan" (Gautama). The Āgamas state that among those whose lifespan is extremely long and who never meet an untimely death;
who are dignified and not frivolous; and who always delight in living in seclusion, Bakula is the foremost.

Mahākauṣṭhila—translated here as "Great Thigh"—was the maternal uncle of Śāriputra. From the past, he had always excelled his sister in debate; however, once she became pregnant, he could no longer debate her.
It was excellent. Knowing that this man of wisdom harbored such intent, he entrusted his eloquence to his mother’s mouth; how much more so once he had emerged from the womb?

He immediately left his home and traveled to South India, where he studied eighteen scriptures. The people of the time mocked him, saying, "He has been surpassed by his sister while at home, and now he is held in contempt by others abroad.

Yet he sighed deeply and said, "I have been surpassed by my sister within the household, and I am slighted by others outside it. I vow never to cease my studies; I shall find no leisure even to trim my nails."
The people of the time called him the Brahmin Dīrghanakha (Long-Nail). After eighteen years, having completed his studies, he returned home and asked where his nephew was.

When told that the boy had become a disciple of the Buddha, he became greatly arrogant and thought, "My nephew has been a prodigy since the age of eight, his fame resounding throughout the five regions;
what kind of spiritual arts does that śramaṇa possess to have enticed my sister's son? He then went to the place where the Buddha was and reflected for a long while.
Not a single dharma may enter the mind. The Buddha asked, "What do you take as your fundamental principle?
Zhi replied, "I cannot tolerate any dharma. "Tolerance" has the meaning of "peace. I say that I am able to destroy all dharmas so that they cannot attain peace.
The Buddha asked, "Do you see this as patience? Zhi shook his sleeves and departed. On the way, he suddenly realized the truth and sighed, saying:
"In my interpretation, I have fallen into error on two points. If I saw this as patience, it contradicts what I previously said—that I would not tolerate anything.
If I saw this as non-patience, there was no way for me to surpass the Buddha. This is something unknown to all those of the Two Vehicles; only Buddhas and Bodhisattvas know it."
Thereupon, he returned to the Buddha and left the household life. According to the Āgamas, he attained the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*) and was able to respond to any challenge;
among those who excelled in debate, Kaccāyana was foremost. Nanda—referring here to Gopaka-Nanda, which translates as "Good Joy"—was the son of a cowherd.
When King Bimbisāra urged one hundred thousand people to leave the household life, this was one of them. By nature, he was extremely intelligent and quick-witted.

His voice was peerless; he established his name through his joy in the Path. Sundarananda—the first three characters mean "Good-Love" (Sundara) and are also translated as "Handsome"—was the name of his wife.
The Venerable One was born on the ninth day of the fourth month; he was four finger-widths shorter than the Buddha.
His appearance was so exceptionally distinguished that when he entered a crowd, those who did not recognize him would say, "The Buddha has come. [He] selected...

Gopāla Nanda was thus addressed by his wife’s name as well; he was the Buddha’s own younger brother. Accompanied by his wife at all times for eating and resting, he was unwilling to be separated from her even for a moment.
When the Buddha and Ānanda arrived at his door while begging for alms, Nanda was on the upper floor with his wife, in the midst of eating.
He immediately rose to welcome the Buddha. His wife made an appointment with him, saying, "Wait until you have returned, and then we shall eat together. Upon seeing the Buddha, Nanda [departed].
The Buddha said, "Prince of the Wheel-Turning King, how can you humiliate yourself thus? Take this bowl and fetch some rice. The Buddha then returned to the garden.

Carrying the bowl of rice, he arrived at the garden and offered it to the Buddha. The Buddha ordered a man to shave his hair. Grasping his fist, the Prince said, "Who dares to hold a blade over the crown of the King of Jambudvīpa?
Though pressed and unable to stop him, they nevertheless shaved his hair. The following day, the Buddha accepted an invitation. [The Prince] requested...
While staying at a monastery, he intended to flee. The Buddha ordered him to close the gates and sweep the ground;

though he attempted to escape by hiding behind trees and so forth, the Buddha led him to the celestial palace, where he saw the goddess Chán'é (Cāndrī) and felt joy. He was then made to enter hell, where he beheld the boiling cauldrons and his mind was stilled;
his lustful thoughts ceased, and he attained the path of no-outflows (*anāsrava-mārga*). This was Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra.
Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra is named after his parents. Among the seven Buddhas who appeared among men, he was the foremost in preaching the Dharma.
He possessed the four types of analytical eloquence (*catasraḥ pratisaṃvidaḥ*) and was thoroughly conversant with all the scriptures and histories.

Endowed with great wisdom, the *Āgamas* state that he was the foremost in being able to explain extensively and analyze the principles of meaning; thus, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra is the first. Subhūti means "Emptiness" (*śūnyatā*).
He was born at a time when the family’s treasuries suddenly became empty; this portended the auspicious sign of his realization of emptiness (*śūnyatā*).

He was also named Sudarśana, for while the food vessels were all empty, whatever he desired was fully provided. The diviners declared: "Since it is both excellent and auspicious, [let him be called] Śākyamuni."
He was also named Śāriputra. He constantly delighted in dwelling in the tranquility of mountain forests and stone caves.
The practice he cultivated took emptiness as its foundation; he frequently entered meditative concentration and abided in the *araṇā-samādhi* (the samādhi of non-contention).

Just as one stands out of envy for another who is sitting, or sits out of envy for another who is standing, he did not engage in contention with others because of his virtuous mind. Paramārtha said: "In the east is Śaṅkhapāla."
The Buddha is foremost in the realization of emptiness. Ānanda—here translated as "Joyous Celebration"—was the Buddha’s cousin, the second son of Droṇodana, and the younger brother of Devadatta.
He was born at the very moment the World-Honored One attained enlightenment; thus, he was named "Joyous Celebration.
He is also called "Untainted," for since his ordination, he has never given rise to defiled thoughts upon seeing women. Upon first leaving the household life, he attained...
He had entered the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpanna*). At Laṅkā, he attained the second fruit; it was only at the time of the First Council that he realized the fourth fruit.
Later, upon entering parinirvāṇa, he left behind relics for which stupas were erected in four locations.

When Aśoka (King Yūrwang) pointed to one stupa and said, "In the transmission of the Buddha’s teachings, this venerable one alone is peerless," the King rejoiced and provided him with a hundred thousand coins as an offering. The *Āgama* states: "He knew the proper time."

Regarding those who clarify the nature of things, who encounter no doubt in whatever they reach, who remember without forgetting, who are widely learned and profoundly realized, and who are capable of receiving and upholding [the teachings], Ānanda is foremost.
Rāhula—translated here as "Obstruction"—in a former life blocked a rat's hole and did not look at a Brahmin for six days;
consequently, when the World-Honored One first sought to leave the household life, his father-king would not permit it. [Rāhula] was persistent...
She begged incessantly. The King said, "If you have a son, I shall permit you to leave the household life.

He then pointed to the Queen's belly and said, "In six years' time, you shall give birth to a son. Because he was thus obstructed within the womb for six years, he was called *Pārāśika* (The Obstructed).
After the Buddha had left the household life, Yaśodharā became pregnant. All the Śākyas were enraged; they wished to kill her, and foul rumors spread throughout the road.
Because of the fire pit, he made a great vow: "If I have committed wrong, let mother and son both be consumed by the flames; if these are truly the remains of my body, may the heavens bear witness.
Having finished speaking, he threw himself into the fire, which transformed into a lotus flower that cradled his body. Thus did the king and the people of the land [witness].
Only then did he cease to doubt. At that time, as the Buddha returned to his kingdom, Yaśodharā had Rāhula offer a *modaka* (joyous pellet) to the Buddha.
Because of the natural bond between father and son, Rāhula spontaneously held it up before the great assembly to present it to the Buddha; thus Yaśodharā was cleared of slander.
Because she slandered [the Buddha] due to having a son, it is said that she was obstructed by concealment. The Grandfather King was filled with joy; although he lost his son, he obtained a grandson.
Since the grandson would become a Wheel-Turning King (*cakravartin*), what cause for regret could I have? The Buddha commanded her to leave the household life, but the Father King did not permit it.
When Yaśodharā was about to ascend a high tower, Maudgalyāyana flew through the air and took her away. The Buddha ordained her and placed her under the tutelage of Śāriputra.
The disciple, having already left the household life, had lost his royal status; therefore, it is said that he was "obscured.

He was foremost in the secret practices within the Buddha-dharma. Such a person as this, known by the multitude—summarizing the twenty-one individuals mentioned above—is one whose talent and virtue are both complete, and thus is revered and looked up to by others.
"Known" (zhīshí) is a term for teachers and friends; furthermore, "zhī" refers to hearing their name.
To meet [someone] is called "knowing" (*vijñāna*). Furthermore, "knowing" (*jñā*) takes clear understanding as its meaning, while "cognition" (*vid*) takes decisive realization as its meaning;

this refers to penetrating the principles of phenomena and decisively discerning the core vehicle (*yāna*). Regarding the phrase "the great arhats and so forth": "great" means they have pulled out the multitude of sages; "and so forth" (*ādi*) encompasses their peers.
The two characters "thus" (*evaṃ*) refer to the various venerable ones. "Assembly" (*gaṇa*) refers to the eight classes of gods and humans. This is that which is to be known.
"Those who know" (*vijñā*) is a designation for those bound by fetters (*saṃyojana*). "Arhats" refers to their stage of attainment.

That they number twelve thousand is because they all possess such virtues and the excellence of such names. It should be understood that Ānanda was a person still in training (*śaikṣa*), yet he is included here because he was to be born as a member of the retinue.
Furthermore, these Arhats were not merely acquaintances; they were like ten thousand [others].
The two thousand whose names were not listed are those who are *kalyāṇamitras* (spiritual friends) but not *arhats*. Those such as Ānanda and Rāhula are both *arhats* and *kalyāṇamitras*;
these are the ones whose names were thus listed. Those who are neither *arhats* nor *kalyāṇamitras* are the two thousand mentioned below.
△ Second, the assembly of those still in training (*śaikṣa*).
Furthermore, there were two thousand individuals, both those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
Of these, the upper twelve thousand were those beyond training; these two thousand were those still in training.

Because they had not yet completed what was to be accomplished through vision and cultivation, they were termed "those in training" as they investigated the truth and severed delusions. [The others] were those for whom the realization through wisdom and the severance through cultivation were all complete, having reached the ultimate truth and exhausted all delusions.

All were those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*). The various teachings differ: some state that there are six stages of those beyond training and five stages of those still in training (*śaikṣa*), while others state that the Buddha-stage is beyond training and nine stages are still in training, and so forth. The "two thousand" indicates their number;
these two thousand were karmic-born attendants who had planted the seeds during the time of Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū. This concludes the section on the assembly of bhikṣus. 2. The Assembly of Bhikṣuṇīs.
The bhikṣuṇī Mahāprajāpatī (up to) also came together with her retinue.
Mahāprajāpatī means "Great Path of Love" (Dà Àidào). It is because she possesses wisdom that she is able to love the Path.
She is also called Gautamī, which here means "Leader of the Assembly," as she was the leader of the community of nuns.
"Nun" (bhikṣuṇī) is a general term for women in India; she was the Buddha’s maternal aunt. When she first sought to leave the household life, the Buddha did not grant permission.

Ānanda interceded on her behalf three times, and the Buddha then commanded that she observe the Eight Rules of Respect before he would allow her ordination. As for these Eight Rules of Respect: [the first is that] a nun, even if she has been ordained for a hundred years...
1. One should pay homage at the feet of the *pravāraṇā* (end-of-summer) bhikṣus. 2. One must not revile a bhikṣu. 3. One must not expose the faults of a bhikṣu. 4.
One should seek to receive the full ordination within the Saṃgha. 5. If one commits a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense, one should perform the *mānatva* penance before the Saṃgha for half a month.
6. One should seek an instructor from within the Saṃgha. 7. One should not remain in a place where there are no bhikṣus.

The Buddha resided in retreat during the summer rains. When the eight months had concluded, he went among the Saṃgha to seek those who would grant him the *pravāraṇā* (invitation for criticism); there were six thousand such persons.
Regarding "Rāhula’s mother" and so forth: the mother is designated by her son. She is called "Yashodharā" (*Huase*) because of her beautiful countenance;

she is also called "Yaśasvinī" ("Renowned"), meaning that while she was still a laywoman, she possessed the three obediences and four virtues—gentleness, kindness, respectfulness, and frugality—and her virtue was equal [to that of the Buddha].
The Crown Prince held the rank of a minor sovereign; he was the consort of a Bodhisattva, the mother of Arhats, and the leader of the community of nuns—a person of renown known by gods and men.
How could such a person not have a name? Since the mothers of these two sages were leaders of the nunneries, their names are recorded here to preside over their respective followers.
As for "retinue" (*jùanshǔ*): those who are naturally affectionate toward one another are called "kinsmen" (*juàn*); they further submit to and obey one another.

Therefore, they are called "belonging" (*śeṣa*). The same applies to the "dharma-retinue" (*dharmaparivāra*). By expounding various dharma-gates and entering into the minds of others, one comes to know the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) and attains intimacy through the Dharma;
thus, they are called "retinue" (*parivāra*). Because they are trustworthy and submissive, they are called "belonging. This was explained previously among the monks.

The distinction between listing names and not listing names is determined by the nature of their karmic responses. In this context, the determination of superiority and inferiority is established by whether a number is specified or not;

this is the stylistic technique of Master Kumārajīva. Furthermore, the figures "twelve thousand" and "two thousand" serve as the basis for those who receive predictions (vyākaraṇa) during the three cycles [of the Lotus Sūtra].

The mention of the assembly of nuns serves as the basis for the chapter on bestowing predictions upon those in training (śaikṣa) and those beyond training (aśaikṣa). This concludes the section on the assembly of śrāvakas. △
Second, the assembly of bodhisattvas. The Treatise asks: Since bodhisattvas are already included within the assemblies of the laity and the ordained, why are they listed separately?
Answer: There are bodhisattvas who fall among the fourfold assembly; they manifest in accordance with their respective types.

Conversely, there are those among the fourfold assembly who do not fall into the category of the bodhisattva assembly because they have not resolved to attain Buddhahood through the Great Mind (*mahācitta*). Here, we cite those who share the common resolve to attain Buddhahood.
This refers to the assembly of bodhisattvas. The text is divided into three parts. First, the types are raised and their number indicated:
"eighty thousand bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.
In full, this is *bodhisattva-mahāsattva*. *Bodhi* here is translated as "path" (*mārga*), and *sattva* as "mind" (*citta*).
*Mahā* means "great. Combined, it means "great resolve for the Way" (*bodhicitta mahat*).

It should be called the "Great Resolve for the Way" (*mahā-bodhicitta*), because one possesses great roots, is endowed with great wisdom, believes in the Great Dharma, understands the Great Principle, cultivates the Great Practice, establishes the Great Cause, and achieves the Great Fruit.

It is also called "Awakened Sentient Being" (*bodhisattva*). From the perspective of one's own practice, a *bodhisattva* is a sentient being who possesses the capacity for awakening in a partial sense; it is not [merely a sentient being].

Because other ordinary beings lack self-awareness, [the Bodhisattva] acts for their benefit. Furthermore, regarding the benefit of others, the Bodhisattva is able to awaken sentient beings to the *dharmadhātu*, whereas those of the other two vehicles cannot awaken others.
"Awakening" (*bodhi*) refers to the wisdom of perfect enlightenment on the stage of Buddhahood;

"sentient beings" (*sattva*) refers to those born of various deluded attachments. The Bodhisattva seeks supreme enlightenment above and transforms sentient beings below; this is not the compassion of others.
Wisdom is entirely absent, or [it is so] because it is one. In terms of the teachings, there are five teachings; in terms of stages, there are fifty-five stages.
The subsequent passage, "When Bodhisattvas hear these dharmas," etc., is explained according to the first four teachings. Furthermore, it says:

"If they do not hear this sutra, they do not skillfully practice the bodhisattva path; if they hear this sutra, they then skillfully practice the bodhisattva path"—this is explained according to the Perfect Teaching (the *yuanjiao*).

This was spoken from the perspective of their initial resolve. The original ground of these bodhisattvas is difficult to fathom; some dwell at the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*), while others are equal to the Dharma King.

Such as Avalokiteśvara and Mañjuśrī, they are all great beings who have realized the fruit. They benefit sentient beings through the three wheels [of body, speech, and mind], and in their traces, they assist Śākyamuni.

This can be understood through the meaning. "Eighty thousand" is a numerical designation. In other sutras, the assemblies gathered are extremely numerous; why then are there only eighty thousand in this sutra?
Perhaps it merely refers to a large number, as when it is said that they emerged from the earth and gathered like clouds—how could it have been limited to only eighty thousand?
II. Clarifying their Ranks and Praising Their Virtues.
All [of them] have attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* (the Unsurpassed Perfectly Complete Enlightenment), which is capable of delivering countless hundreds of thousands of sentient beings;
they all abide in the stage of non-retrogression and are clearly positioned therein, all attaining the lower praise of their virtues.

*Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* is here translated as "Unsurpassed Right and Equal Perfect Enlightenment," which corresponds to three of the ten titles of the Tathāgata: Tathāgata, Arhat, and Samyaksaṃbuddha. The remaining seven [titles] are included as well.

"Shou" (Gathering/Receiving): It fully encompasses the ten thousand virtues. Since all Buddhas emerge from within the *tathatā-bhūtakoṭi* (the limit of reality) to manifest the attainment of perfect enlightenment, they are honored as supreme throughout the ten realms;
there is none to equal them and none superior to them, hence it is called "Unsurpassed" (*anuttara*).

Furthermore, because they can accord with and respond to the four truths, the two truths, the Path, and Offerings—nurturing the *dharmakāya* through the Dharma—it is called "Perfectly Equal" (*samyaksambuddha*). Moreover, they skillfully know...
It is the ultimate destination of all dharmas. It illuminates the differences in the mental activities of all sentient beings and does not fall into partiality or deviance;
therefore, it is called "Right Enlightenment" (*samyak-saṃbodhi*). It is also the three bodies, the three virtues, and the three greatnesses—the designation for the fruit of ultimate realization.
All of these are encompassed within these two characters. As for "non-retrogression," it refers to having destroyed the delusions of views and thought.

Not retreating from name and rank means never losing the transcendent status. Not retreating from practice means having shattered the delusions as numerous as grains of sand, thereby never losing the conduct of a bodhisattva.
Not retreating from mindfulness means having shattered the delusions of ignorance, thereby never losing the right mindfulness of the Middle Way.
Furthermore, not retreating from the stage of *prajñā* (wisdom) means being free from the two types of death. This is the practice of liberation.
They do not regress because they are endowed with all practices. They do not regress from mindfulness of the Dharma-body because they have realized the realm of reality.

By means of these eighty thousand [dharmas], their fundamental stage is difficult to fathom; through the path of effortless spontaneity (*anābhoga-mārga*), they flow naturally into the ocean of *sarvajñā* (omniscience).

Therefore, it is called "non-retrogression. All attain the three phrases of the *dharani*; this praises the virtue of the three wheels responding to sentient beings in accordance with the three karmas.
The two characters "all obtain" (皆得) govern the following text. The single phrase "dhāraṇī" praises the wheel of mental karma; it is translated here as "total retention" (總持).
Within a single character, one can penetrate immeasurable dharma-gates; within a single gate, one can encompass immeasurable principles and meanings.

It is like observing a single flower bloom and knowing that spring has come to all under heaven, or seeing a single leaf fall and knowing that autumn has arrived for the whole world. Regarding what is...
This refers to the comprehensive inclusion of all phenomena (*sarvadharma*), upholding immeasurable meanings. Briefly stated, there are three names for the *Samantabhadra-parivarta*;
extensively explained, they are immeasurable, such as the "Ten Thousand Billion Revolving Dhāraṇīs. To delight in speaking even a single phrase is to praise the wheel of verbal action (*vākkarma*).

Delight in speaking is one of the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*); it is the analytical knowledge of phenomena (*dharmapratisaṃvid*), which concerns the teaching of both mundane and supramundane phenomena.

1. Because it is unerring, there is unimpededness regarding meaning (*artha-pratisaṃvid*); for in regard to the meanings of the conditioned, the unconditioned, the provisional, and the ultimate, what is taught exhausts the principle.

2. There is unimpededness regarding expression (*nirukti-pratisaṃvid*); for regarding all literary expressions and meanings, they flow forth in composition like water poured from a jar. 3. There is unimpededness regarding eloquence (*pratibhāna-pratisaṃvid*);

for responding to the capacities of beings through the four *saṃgraha-vastus*, one teaches others without weariness. By means of these four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*), one extensively proclaims the Dharma, ensuring that sentient beings hear it as appropriate to them.
It is like the wind blowing through the myriad pipes of nature. In the ninth stage (*bhūmi*) of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, there are forty kinds of eloquence (*pratibhāna*), which are here abbreviated.
The single phrase "turning back from non-retrogression" praises the wheel of bodily action (*kāyakarma*). As for "wheel," it carries two meanings: revolving and crushing.

This metaphor illustrates how the Great Dharma can enter the minds of others and destroy ignorance. That is to say, one attains the spiritual marks of the ten bodies and manifests within the lands of all dust-motes.
Appearing in forms identical to those of sentient beings, whether through provisional or ultimate teachings, one causes all beings to enter the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*).
Therefore, it is called "turning the irreversible wheel of Dharma. When a Bodhisattva attains this path and dwells therein...
Having [attained this], one employs this Way to benefit others; it is not like the Small Vehicle, which does not preach the Dharma but merely preserves itself.

The three phrases concerning "making offerings to the immeasurable" praise the profound and vast virtues of merit and wisdom by way of causes and conditions. This refers to making offerings to the Buddha.

To be protected by excellent spiritual friends externally constitutes the perfection of conditions (*pratyaya-sampad*). To cultivate the roots of virtue and internally practice the myriad deeds as one's sustenance constitutes the perfection of causes (*hetu-sampad*).
Furthermore, there are two modes—transverse and vertical. Speaking in terms of the vertical: from immeasurable eons, one makes offerings to immeasurable Buddhas.

To cultivate immeasurable virtues is for the merit to be profound; to discuss them crosswise, reaching throughout the worlds of the ten directions in a single moment of thought to make offerings to the Buddhas and practice is for the wisdom to be vast.
Furthermore, profundity means that every single practice accords with the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*);
vastness means that each and every gate subsumes all other gates. These roots of virtue contain both the right path and the auxiliary paths.

Regarding the path of teaching and the path of realization: when a single practice is perfected, one virtue is established; when immeasurable practices are perfected, immeasurable virtues are established.

Therefore, they are called the "roots of virtue. Possessing such profound and vast virtues resulting from these causes and conditions, one is worthy of receiving the empowerment and office, and is thus praised by all Buddhas.
This is not like the Small Vehicle, which dismisses such individuals as "withered sprouts and rotten seeds. For...

The two phrases on "loving-kindness" (*maitrī*) praise the virtue of conforming to appearances while remaining detached from them, as expressed through compassion (*karuṇā*) and wisdom (*prajñā*). Regarding "loving-kindness":

using compassion to guide wisdom constitutes the virtue of conforming to appearances; loving-kindness encompasses the four immeasurables (*catvāry apramāṇāni*), thereby engaging with existence while grounded in emptiness, consisting purely of these four mental states.

Adapting one's transformation to sentient beings, one completes one’s own virtue through the practice of benefiting others; hence it is called "cultivating the person" (*xiushen*). Avalokiteśvara gazes upon sentient beings with eyes of compassion.
In the *Avataṃsaka*, it is said that "great compassion is the gate" and "great compassion is the head," and so forth.

One who enters well guides compassion with wisdom, which is the virtue of being free from marks. Wisdom is precisely *prajñā*; it engages with existence without being hindered by the contemplation of emptiness. This is...
One realizes the true mark (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena through non-attainment; thus, it is called "skillful entry.

This is the meaning of the metaphor in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* of extracting a scripture from within a particle of dust, and the account in the secular classics of the "Formless One" (*Wǎngxiàng*) obtaining a pearl.

The Bodhisattva takes the three realms as his home and the four modes of birth as his children; he borrows the act of delivering sentient beings to enter the Buddha-wisdom, which is unlike the perspective of the Śrāvaka vehicle.

The three realms are like a prison, and the four modes of birth are like hostile robbers. "Thoroughly penetrating" and below refer to the praise of the virtue of the three dots of *Ī*, *Vaṃ*, and *M* from the perspective of the original and the manifested (honji-suijaku).
"Wisdom" refers to the virtue of wisdom; by transforming the eight consciousnesses into the four wisdoms, one realizes great *bodhi*.

Therefore, it is said that one "thoroughly penetrates great wisdom. "The other shore" is a metaphor for the virtue of severance (*prahāṇa*); once the ignorance of the four marks has been extinguished, one realizes [nirvāṇa].

This is the nirvana of non-abiding; therefore, it is said that one has reached the other shore. Having transcended this shore of birth and death and crossed the turbulent current of afflictions, one arrives at the other shore of nirvana.
This is not like the Lesser Vehicle, which attains the wisdom of the emptiness of persons while remaining in the midst of the current.
The former two belong to the fundamental [aspect], while "renown" (*kīrti*) belongs to the latter; that is, the grace and virtue within the provisional manifestation (*traces*).

From the fundamental, the traces are extended downward, so as to accord with the principle of the true aspect (*dharmatā*) and manifest the work of broad propagation. It is like the sun shining across the azure firmament: those with eyes all behold it, while those without eyes hear of it.
Therefore, it is said that "renown is universally heard," and so forth. This is not like the Lesser Vehicle, where one seeks only self-benefit and renown remains confined to oneself.

This is the state of a land. Its Way is that the spirit has no fixed direction and transformation has no fixed form. Like the *maṇi* jewel or the celestial drum, it accomplishes affairs without partiality.
Since it can provide salvation to all without exception, those who undergo transformation must be vast in number; hence the phrase "capable of delivering others" and so forth.

In the "Entry into the Dharma Realm" chapter of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, Mañjuśrī was at the eastern side of Puṣpapurī, preaching the *Sūtra of the Universal Illumination of the Dharma Realm*. First...
At that time, immeasurable dragons from within the ocean cast off their bodies and were reborn among humans and devas; ten thousand dragons attained non-retrogression on the path to Bodhi.
Furthermore, immeasurable sentient beings were each tamed according to the three vehicles.

Within this *Dhāraṇī-parivarta* of the sutra, when Bhaiṣajyarāja recited the mantra, sixty-eight thousand people attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). [Then] Viśuddhagarbha...
When Viśuddhanetra manifested his supernatural powers, his father and eighty-four thousand others all became capable of upholding this sutra.

Observing this, one knows that the magnificence with which these great beings benefit sentient beings is not like the small vehicle (Hīnayāna), where the mind does not find joy in the task of maturing sentient beings.
From here on, the various bodhisattvas realize these manifold merits; cause and effect are fully and thoroughly realized.

The fundamental and the manifested are perfectly interfused; how could they be delimited or judged by stages and positions? The *Dharmapada-śāstra* divides this into the upper branch-gate and the lower branch-gate:

praising through general characteristics and praising through specific characteristics. Initially, the single phrase "Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi" constitutes the general [praise], which is the upper branch-gate.
The remaining phrases constitute the specific [praise], which is the lower branch-gate. There are ten kinds of non-retrogression, the *dhāraṇī*...
A single phrase of *dhāraṇī* demonstrates non-retrogression in hearing the Dharma. A single phrase of "joyful eloquence" (*pratibhāna*) is non-retrogression in joyful eloquence.

A single phrase of "turning back" (*āvartana*) is non-retrogression in preaching the Dharma. "Making offerings to the Buddhas and planting the root" is non-retrogression in relying upon spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*).
"Being praised by all Buddhas" is non-retrogression in severing doubt. By means of loving-kindness...
The single phrase: non-retrogression in entering into phenomena. Skillfully entering the single phrase: non-retrogression in entering all-knowledge like a precious mirror.
Thoroughly penetrating the single phrase: non-retrogression by relying on the two emptinesses of self and dharmas.
Reaching the single phrase: non-retrogression in the realm of reality as it is. The two phrases concerning renown: non-retrogression in performing what ought to be done.
[This marks] the transition. △ Third, listing the names and providing a summary:
Their names were Mañjuśrī (through to) eighty thousand Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas, together with them.

"Whose names are as follows" introduces the enumeration of their names. "Mahāsattva" (Great Being) is a grand title; it may be derived from a dharma-gate, from virtuous conduct, or from original vows.

Although each is a single name, it encompasses immeasurable meanings. Now, relying upon the sūtras and śāstras, I shall explain the names of the eighteen bodhisattvas, each according to its specific significance.
Mañjuśrī: this is translated here as "Wondrous Virtue" (*Miaode*). *The Great Sūtra*... [text continues]
It is said that he clearly perceived the Buddha-nature, just like Samantabhadra;

he is also called Mañjuśrī because at his birth there were auspicious signs of radiant light filling the room. In the *Avataṃsaka*, the Bodhisattva represents wisdom, and furthermore, he presides over the gate of faith.
The *Prajñāpāramitā-naya-sūtra* (Questioning the Light Chapter) serves as the presiding host, while the *Dharmadhātu-paṭala* serves as the teacher for Sudhana.

The present sutra’s One Vehicle (Ekayāna) true reality (*tathatā*) likewise belongs to that same school. Without faith, one does not awaken; without wisdom, one does not realize. Therefore, its name is first set forth:

namely, he who has perfected his transformation throughout the realms of dust and whose activity encompasses the three periods of time, having accomplished the Way in a prior kalpa, was named the Honored King Dragon-Species (*Nāga-jāti-rāja*). He manifested the realization of Bodhi...
Ti was named Maṇiratnasañcaya. In the future, he will attain Buddhahood under the name Puxian (Universally Manifest). While on the path of cause, he served as the teacher to eight kings;
upon reaching the state of fruition, he became a Buddha-ancestor among the seven patriarchs. He discussed the profound essence of Prajñā, repeatedly challenging his original teacher;

he expounded the dual practice of the provisional and the real, frequently startling the lesser sages. Thus, he manifested as an influence for the Great Transformation, appearing in the form of a Bodhisattva.
Avalokiteśvara: In India, he is called Bhavagītīkṣa. His single name has two meanings.
First, "Avalokita" (Contemplation) is the true wisdom that contemplates; "Īśvara" (Sound) refers to the auditory object that is contemplated.

Through hearing, reflection, and cultivation, one enters samādhi, unties the six knots, transcends the three voids, realizes the nature of sensory objects, and thereby attains entry into perfect penetration. Second—
Contemplation (*guan*) is the provisional wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*) that observes; Avalokiteśvara (*Shìyīn*) is the opportune moment for those who look up with compassion.

Through the two functions of compassion and loving-kindness, he rescues from the seven calamities and responds to the two petitions. By means of the nineteen modes of preaching the Dharma, the fourteen fearlessnesses, and so forth, he universally responds through perfect contemplation to those throughout the ten directions who call upon his name.
There is no suffering he does not rescue, and there is no joy he does not bestow. Thus, in the past...
He serves as the illumination of the True Dharma. In the present, he acts as an attendant to Amitābha; in the future, he shall succeed the Buddha Universal Radiance and Merit in the Western Quarter.
As for Mahāsthāmaprāpta, he is indeed Mahāsthāmaprāpta. By means of the *nien-fo* samādhi, he assists in the holy transformation;
he wanders without moving and responds without dividing himself. His transformative activity is unceasing, yet he possesses no sense of having performed such transformation. His...
The power and function [of this practice] reach the ultimate degree of greatness. Those who are constantly diligent give rise to the three minds within and cultivate the myriad practices without;

they feel no insufficiency regarding themselves and never grow weary toward others. As for "never resting," it means that in the causal stage one does not consider oneself perfected, and in the resultant stage one does not consider oneself fulfilled;
one simply remains earnest and tireless. Thus, when the merit is achieved, it is achieved through non-achievement. To the utmost...
It lies precisely in not reaching an ultimate limit. "Treasure-palms" refers to the treasure-position (*ratnāsana*), for it is the great treasure of the sages.
From the cause to the fruit, the forty-two stages are all grounds traversed by the sages;

the Mahāsattvas rely upon these various positions to grasp the mechanism of transformation, thereby connecting with sentient beings and benefiting their lives. Furthermore, treasures emerge from within the palms to universally provide relief to the multitudes.
Because he is born [as such]. As for the "Medicine King," in his causal stage he was a skilled physician of the world;

in his resultant stage, he is able to save sentient beings from the two illnesses of body and mind by means of the medicine of the Dharma. Because he administers medicine according to the illness, there is no ailment that is not healed;

because he preaches the Dharma according to the capacity of the recipient, there is no one with the capacity who is not delivered. As for the "Courageous Giver," he is not stingy regarding the three types of giving (*dāna*), and he acts with bold courage. Furthermore, he gives...
By leading all practices, one destroys all attachments, just as a general with great strength breaks through a heavy siege. As for "Jewel Moon" (Ratnacandra):

just as the moon can wax and wane according to the lunar cycle while remaining itself without loss or gain, so too the path of the Bodhisattva manifests or remains hidden according to the capacities of beings while remaining itself without increase or decrease;
therefore, it is named after this metaphor. As for "Moonlight" (Candraprabha): just as light can dispel darkness, so too does wisdom destroy [ignorance].
"Foolish" refers to those who lack wisdom. "Full moon" refers to the perfection of one's own awakened noble wisdom (*pratyātma-āryajñāna*), as it is like the moon on the fifteenth day.
"Great power" refers to the functional capacity for spiritual transformations (*ṛddhi-prātihārya*);

because it is unimpeded between the one and the many, and because the large and the small can contain one another, it transcends the realm of thought and calculation and surpasses the provisional and the Lesser Vehicle. "Immeasurable power" has two aspects. First:

First, such qualities as the three knowledges (*trividyā*), the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*), and the eighteen unique attributes (*āveṇikadharma*) cannot be illustrated by comparison with the sands of the Ganges;
they cannot be reached even after passing through *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas. Therefore, their numerical measure is unobtainable.

Second, each and every karmic function penetrates the three periods of time without beginning or end, and pervades the ten directions without limit or boundary. Therefore, it possesses no measurable extent.
"Transcending the three realms" means that within the three realms, he neither emerges nor remains, because he has attained great mastery (*mahā-vaśitā*).
"Bhaddālaputra" is translated here as "Good Protector" (*Śubharakṣita*); it refers to his guarding of the three types of action (*trikarma*).

Furthermore, because he is the foremost among the wise, "Maitreya"—the full form being Maitreyī—is translated as "The Compassionate One" (*Maitrīputra*); this is his clan name. Also, "Ajita" is translated here as... [text fragment]
"Cloudless Victory" (Wusheng) is his name. The *Sūtra on Rebirth Above* states that he passed away in the village of Pāṭalī and was reborn above in Tuṣita Heaven;
fifty-six hundred million years of the Jambudvīpa era elapsed before he descended to become a Buddha.

All those within the final dharma age of Śākyamuni who diligently cultivate various merits—such as sweeping stupas, smearing the ground with plaster, and making offerings of fragrant incense and exquisite flowers—[shall attain this].

If one recites the name and prostrates, the sins of ten billion kalpas will be eliminated; at the end of life, one will be reborn in the Inner Court (Abhyantarika-maṇḍala), and in the future, will follow Maitreya’s descent to earth.
Furthermore, one will encounter the thousand Buddhas of the Bhadrakalpa and receive their prediction of enlightenment (vyākaraṇa).

As for "Ratnakūṭa" (Treasure Accumulation): within the Tathāgatagarbha there are merits as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, which are like jewels; because they are realized through the accumulation of causes over vast eons, it is called the "Teacher."
"Guide" means to lead and direct. Entering the marketplace with hands extended, he serves as the teacher of devas and humans;
he establishes a grand model for the three realms and guides the masses who are ignorant and deluded. Thus concludes the section below. "Thus" refers to those with names mentioned above;
"etc. includes those without names. "Eighty thousand" refers to the number of principal disciples, while their retinues exceed this count. The above—

All the Bodhisattvas are great beings who have attained the fruit [of enlightenment]; as their shadows and echoes, they assist in the transformation of others, and thus cannot be confined to fixed positions or sequences.
The assembly of Bodhisattvas concludes. △ Third: The Eight Classes of Beings. The ancients said that among the assembly of ordinary people there are actually sages;

they also said that among the assembly of the laity there are actually practitioners of the Way; and they further said that among the assembly of devas and humans there are actually ghosts and spirits. Furthermore, the eight classes are fewer [in number than the other assemblies].
There are two divisions. Now, following this root sūtra, the eight classes are fully enumerated; hence they are called the "eight classes of assemblies.

Since the yakṣas are subsumed under the retinue of the Four Heavenly Kings, and the mahoragas are subsumed under the retinue of the Eight Dragon Kings, and furthermore, although these eight classes differ in their modes of birth, their principle encompasses both the provisional and the real—especially as the various heavenly kings are mostly bodhisattvas who have taken up these positions as a temporary station.
[Sā. The various lords of the worlds in the Avataṃsaka each realize a single virtue of Vairocana; how could it be otherwise for ordinary beings?

Thus we know that this assembly is likewise the same as those. Now, since the worthy and holy ones of the Three Vehicles have already looked up to his virtue and returned [to him], [how much more so for others].
The eight classes of beings are interwoven; how could they not guard [the Dharma] with sincere hearts? For this reason, following the Bodhisattvas, the eight classes of beings are enumerated.
The text is divided into seven parts; first, the celestial hosts.
At that time, Śakra Devānām Indra (up to) was together with his retinue of twelve thousand devaputras.
In the language of India, *deva* means "heavenly being. A heavenly being is so called because they are natural; they possess both a natural body and supreme bliss.
The various devas become increasingly superior and more excellent as they ascend. Thus, the treatise states: "Pure and luminous, the most excellent and most venerable is the deva.
Śakra Devānām Indra is the Lord of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven. "Śakra" is the name; "Śākya" is his clan name. "Devānām Indra" [means...]
This is called the Lord of Clouds (*Meghadhipati*), because he is able to act as the lord of all the celestial kings. *Trāyastriṃśa* means "thirty-three.

There are eight cities on each of the four sides, with the city of Sudarśana in the center, making thirty-three in total. Residing upon the summit of Mount Sumeru, he is the lord of the heavens of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*);
therefore, he is listed first. The dwelling place of this deva is eighty thousand *yojanas* in length and breadth, with city walls made of the seven precious jewels.
Sudarśana is sixty thousand *yojanas* in circumference. The bodies of its inhabitants are one *yojana* in height; their garments are two *yojanas* long and weigh six *zhu*.

One hundred years in the human realm constitute one day and night for this heaven. As for the physical forms and temporal measures of the various devas, they increase twofold as one ascends and decrease twofold as one descends;
all are expressed in terms of doubling. Only their clothing becomes lighter as one ascends and heavier as one descends.
Regarding Chong’er (Zhòng’ěr): The *Saṃyukta Āgama* states that when he was formerly a human being, he practiced sudden acts of giving (*tun-shi*) and was capable of acting as a leader;
thus, he had a total of one hundred and eight names, which now remain as the single name “Ear” (*Ēr*).

During his causal stage under Kāśyapa Buddha, he was a woman who resolved to build a stūpa for the Buddha, with thirty-two people assisting in its completion; these are now the thirty-two Heavenly Kings.
For the various sovereigns. In the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna), this is said to be a *srotāpanna*. The *Qīngliáng shū* states: "This is provisional (*upāya*) rather than ultimate.
The "twenty thousand" and so forth refer to their subordinate retinues. "Bright Moon" refers to the Moon Deva; in Sanskrit, *Soma*, which here means the Moon Deity.
It is called "Moon" because it wanes; having been full, it returns to deficiency. This [palace] and the Sun Palace belong to the Four Heavenly Kings.
They all dwell on the mid-slope of Mount Sumeru, forty-two thousand yojanas above the earth.
Fifty human years constitute one day and night for these devas. Their bodies are half a yojana in height; their garments weigh twelve zhu and extend one yojana in length.
The *Qishi jing* (Sūtra on the Arising of the World) states: "The moon palace is forty-nine *yojana* in length and breadth.
Its city is adorned with the seven treasures, being composed of two parts of celestial silver and one part of blue lapis lazuli. It possesses a thousand rays of light;
five hundred shine downward and five hundred shine sideways. These rays are clear and cool. From afar it appears round, but in reality it is square. [End of] the Moon Palace.
The "tree-shadow" refers to the Jambū tree of the human realm; its reflection appears in the moon, yet there is no actual cassia tree there.
As for "Universal Fragrance," this is the Star-Constellation Devaputra, who is the Purple Microcosm (Zǐwēi).

He is the lord of the myriad stars, presiding over the twenty-eight lunar mansions, the nine luminaries, and the stellar deities. Depending on the goodness or evil of people's hearts, he manifests signs of fortune or misfortune.
The elephants and the palaces of the various stars differ in size; each has its own presiding domain with distinct administrative jurisdictions.
As for "Jewel Light" (Bǎoguāng), this refers to the Sun Deity (Rìtiānzǐ). In Sanskrit, he is called Sūrya, which translates here as "Sun God. He is the essence of the sun.
The *Qishi jing* (Sutra on the Arising of the World) states: "The solar palace is fifty-one *yojana* in length and breadth;
it is composed of two parts of celestial gold and one part of *sphatika* crystal. Its illumination is as described above. These three [palaces] belong to the inner ministers of Śakra.

Furthermore, at the beginning of the kalpa, beings from the Ābhāsvara Heaven came to the human realm; because they consumed the 'earth-fat,' their bodies lost their radiance, and the world fell into darkness. Then, a Bodhisattva manifested [to bring light]."

They form the Three Luminaries: Ratnaśrī becomes the Moon Deva-son, Ratnaprabha becomes the Star Deva-son (who is also Samantagandha), and Ratnamati becomes the Sun Deva-son (who is also Ratnaprabha).
As for the Four Heavenly Kings, they are the outer ministers;
they dwell upon the four jewel-mountains, which are half the height of Mount Sumeru and twenty-four thousand *li* in breadth. To the east is Dhṛtarāṣṭra, which is translated here as "Holder."
The [deity] Guṇa resides on Mount Golden Hill and leads two classes: first, the gandharvas; second, the piśācas. To the south is Virūḍhaka, translated here as "Increasing";
he resides on Mount Lapis Lazuli and leads two classes: first, the pretas; second, the kumbhāṇḍas.
To the west is Virūpākṣa, translated here as "Broad-Eyed"; he resides on Mount White Silver and likewise leads two classes: first, [the nāgas]; second, [the mahoragas].
The rākṣasas; the two yakṣas; and Vaiśravaṇa of the north—translated as "Much-Hearing"—who dwells on the Crystal Mountain.

These also consist of two groups: first, the poisonous nāgas; second, the piśācas. Because they do not allow people to be troubled and ensure that the winds are harmonious and the rains timely, they are called the Four Heavenly Kings who Protect the World.
Īśvara and Maheśvara are the fifth and sixth heavens of the desire realm; they transform themselves into five... [self-transformed].
*Yu* (Kāmadhātu) refers to the five desires of the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Emanations (*paranirmita-vaśavartin*). *Sahā* is translated here as "Endurance" (*kṣānti*);
because the sentient beings of that land are habituated to the ten non-virtues and are unwilling to renounce them, it is named after their human characteristic and thus called "Endurance.

It is also called "Mixed," because the nine realms of existence dwell together therein. *Brahma* is translated here as "Detachment" (*visaṃyoga*); because one abandons the fetters of the lower realms and ascends to the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*), it is so named.

He is also named Kautūhalaprasāda (High Purity) and Śikhin (Crest), the latter meaning "topknot" in this language. He received his name from his virtue, having practiced the fire-light concentration (*tejodhātu-samādhi*) and thereby destroyed the afflictions of the desire realm.
Although the sūtra mentions both the Brahmā King and Śikhin, which might suggest they are two different persons, the commentary correctly identifies Śikhin as the king;
the mention of the title here is merely to clarify his name. This deity dwells within the First Dhyāna.

Internally there is vitarka (applied thought) and vicāra (sustained thought), and externally there is verbal expression; therefore, one attains mastery and becomes a king. The *Abhidharma-kośa* states:
"From the second dhyāna upward, there is no dharma of speech, and thus one cannot become a king.
"Radiant Light" refers to the Heaven of the Second Dhyāna, as well as the third and fourth dhyanas, along with the eighteen Brahma heavens. II. The Dragon King Elephant.
There were eight dragon kings (up to) each accompanied by several hundreds of thousands of retinues.
In the language of India, *nāga*; here it is translated as "dragon. The dragon is the sovereign among scaly creatures; it can manifest in the hidden or the visible, and can become large or small.
At the spring equinox it ascends to heaven; at the autumn equinox it enters the earth. There are scaly dragons (*jiao-long*), and there are winged *ying-long* dragons. There are...

A *jiaolong* (horned dragon) has horns; a *chilong* (hornless dragon) has none. Before ascending to heaven, it is called a *panlong* (coiled dragon). Nanda means "Joy" in this language, and Upananda means "Virtue.
These two brothers, both dragons, constantly protect the kingdom of Magadha. The winds do not rustle the branches, and the rain does not break the clods of earth.
The five grains ripen in abundance, responding well to the hearts of the people. King Bimbisāra held a festival every year to honor them.
When the common people heard this, they were all filled with joy; it was from this that he gained his name. He is the one whom Maudgalyāyana subdued.
Originally he dwelt on the Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*); in his manifested traces, he causes the world to rejoice. Sāgara—this is translated as "the Salt Sea"—he derives his name from the ocean.
Originally he dwelt in the great ocean of the Perfection of Wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*); in his manifested traces, he resides in the deep waters of the vast sea. Vāsuki—this is translated as...

Bahumukha (Many Heads), also called Ratnābhidhāna (Jewel Renown). He fundamentally dwells in the Samādhi of Universally Manifesting Physical Forms (*sarvarūpasaṃdarśana-samādhi*), yet in his manifested traces he appears with many heads.

Takṣaka, which means "Manifesting Poison" (*viṣadarśin*) and is also called "Many Tongues. He fundamentally dwells in the eloquence of joyful speech (*pratibhāna-pratibhāna*), yet in his manifested traces he appears with many tongues.
Anavatapta, which means "Without Heat. At the summit of the Snowy Mountains there is a lake named Anavatapta.
Within the pond is a hall supported by five pillars, where the Dragon King constantly dwells; the pond is named after him.
The dragons of Jambudvīpa have three afflictions: first, hot winds and hot sands strike their bodies, burning their skin, flesh, bones, and marrow, causing them great suffering;
second, fierce winds suddenly arise and blow away their palaces, causing them to lose their precious ornaments, garments, and the like; third, the dragon's body manifests itself [to others].
They consider these things to be afflictions. Third, when the nāgas are enjoying themselves, a garuḍa enters the sea, seizes a newborn nāga child, and devours it;
they consider this to be an affliction. This lake is free from these three calamities; therefore, it is called "Without Heat" (Anavatapta).
The *mūlapratiṣṭhita* (original abode) is eternal, blissful, self, and pure; its trace-abode is this pond.

*Mānasa*—here translated as "Great Body" or "Great Power"—refers to the asuras who, when they pushed back the ocean waters to submerge the city of Sudarśana, were restrained by this dragon coiling its body to block the sea.
Its original abode is the Boundless Body (*anantakāya*); its trace-abode is the Great Body. *Utpala*—here translated as "dark-colored lotus"—[grows] from this pond.
Regarding their names: by nature they abide in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-samādhi*, while in their manifested traces they dwell by this pond. △ Third, the assembly of *kiṃnaras*:
there were four *kiṃnara* kings (up to) each accompanied by several hundreds of thousands of retinues.
In Sanskrit, they are called *kiṃnara*, also known as *kiṃpuruṣa*; here [in Chinese], they are translated as "doubtful deities. They resemble humans but possess a single horn.
When people see them, they wonder, "Is this a human? Or is it not a human? They are the deities of Dharma-music belonging to Śakra, who dwell upon the Ten Jewel Mountains.
Whenever their bodies manifest extraordinary signs, they ascend to perform celestial music. When the Buddha preaches the Dharma, these various devas play stringed instruments and sing.

The one who recites the Dharma-gate is this very deity. "Dharma" refers to the proclamation of the Four Noble Truths; "Sublime Dharma" refers to the proclamation of the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination;
"Great Dharma" refers to the proclamation of the Six Perfections; and "Upholder of the Dharma" encompasses all three of the preceding.

Abiding fundamentally in the inconceivable, without arising from nor entering the meditative concentration of cessation, they praise the Kings of All Dharmas with ten million verses. Their traces are manifested through stringed instruments and pipes, singing and chanting the Ten [Stages].
[The power. △ Fourth, the assembly of gandharvas.
There were four gandharva kings (up to) each accompanied by several hundreds of thousands of attendants.
In the Sanskrit language, they are called *gandhara*, also known as *gandharva*. This translates as "scent-eater," for they take fragrance as their food. Furthermore—

They are called the Fragrant Aggregate (*gandharva*) because fragrance issues from their bodies. They are the deities of the worldly pleasures of Śakra. "Pleasures" refers to such skills as the acrobatic art of the *dhvaja-viloma* (the inverted banner).
"Musical sounds" refers to the various types of drums, cymbals, strings, and wind instruments. "Beauty" refers to the excellence of the *dhvaja-viloma*;
"beautiful sounds" refers to the excellence of the strings and wind instruments. △ Fifth, the assembly of Asuras.
There are four asura kings (up to) each accompanied by several hundreds of thousands of retinues.

In the language of India, they are called *asura*. They are also called *asura* (阿修羅). This is translated as "not upright" (*wu duanzheng*), because while the males are ugly, the females are beautiful.
They are also called "non-gods" (*feitian*), because they possess the fortune of gods but lack the virtue of gods. They are also called "without wine" (*wujiu*). [They] gather the four...
The fragrant liquors of the world are concentrated within the great ocean; yet by the karmic power of the dragons and fish, their flavor remains unchanged.

Because he vowed to sever anger and jealousy and would not drink, it is said that there is no wine [there]. *Vāli* means "the bound," so called because he was once bound during his battle with the Lord of Devas (*Śakra*).
*Kharaskandha* means "Broad Shoulders. As for the one who dammed the ocean waters to submerge the city, he is Vemacitra.
*Tāta* means "pure mind" (*śuddhacitta*) and is also called "various doubts. He is the father of Śakra.

*Rāhu* means "obstructing-holding" (*āvaraṇa-dhara*), so called because he obstructs and holds the sun and moon. The *Sūtra on the Arising of the World* states: "There are four Asura kings who dwell beneath the great ocean at the four sides of Mount Sumeru.
Because they performed meritorious deeds yet gave rise to anger, they were moved by this [karma] to experience one day and one night for three [kalpas]."
At that time they experience pleasure; at the other three times they experience suffering. △ Sixth, the assembly of *garuḍas*.
There are four *garuḍa* kings (up to) each accompanied by several hundreds of thousands of retinues.
In Sanskrit, *garuḍa*; here it is translated as "Golden-Winged Bird" (*jīngì niǎo*).

Its wings are golden in color, and the distance between its two wings is three million six hundred thousand *li*. It feeds upon dragons. Zhuangzi said, "With wings that reach toward heaven, it strikes the waters for three thousand *li*";
this is what he was referring to. Regarding "of great majesty and virtue": its virtue surpasses all its peers, and its majesty subdues all dragons; hence, "Great."

As for its body, it is called "Body" because its physical form surpasses all other beings. It is called "Greatly Satiated" because the dragons it devours are always fully satisfied according to their own desires.
It is called "Wish-Fulfilling" because there is a wish-fulfilling jewel (*cintāmaṇi*) upon its neck. This bird dies at the end of its life through the karmic power of its habit of eating dragons.
Burned by the fires of karma, he was cast into the depths of the ocean until he reached the Golden Wheel (Kāñcanacakravāḷa).

Emerging again, he went to the Diamond Mountains (Vajraparvata) and stayed atop a tree on the mountain, where he burned. He entered the sea once more; thus it happened seven times. When his strength was exhausted, he died beneath the tree.
On his neck was a wish-fulfilling jewel (cintāmaṇi), which the nāgas protected. They sent down rain, and because various nāgas contended for the jewel, it is called [the "Contending Nāgas"].
