The Assembly: King Ajātaśatru, the son of Vaidehī, together with several hundreds of thousands of retinues.
The mention of Vaidehī illustrates the case of the son; the mention of King Bimbisāra illustrates the case of the subject.

Vaidehī was the consort of King Bimbisāra and the mother of King Ajātaśatru; "Vaidehī" translates as "Contemplation. Because her son had harmed his father, she contemplated a virtuous land and took no pleasure in Jambudvīpa.
The Buddha preached the *Amitāyurdhyāna Sūtra* for her sake, enabling her to attain the patience of the Dharma (*dharmakṣānti*). Her son was King Ajātaśatru; this...

He was called Ajātaśatru, and also Aṅgulimāla. Because it was prophesied through divination while he was still unborn that he would certainly harm his father, and because when he was born his father wished to throw him away but only managed to injure one finger, he was protected within the inner palace and named Sudarśana.
When this king was a crown prince, he believed the schemes of Devadatta regarding the new king and the new Buddha;
consequently, he imprisoned his father in a dungeon and cut off his food. His mother entered carrying parched honey, but King Ajātaśatru learned of it and sealed the door with molten iron.
The mother was unable to enter. From afar, the father gazed toward Vulture Peak (*Gṛdhrakūṭa*) and prostrated before the Buddha, lamenting for her rescue.

The Buddha commanded Maudgalyāyana to come and preach the Dharma to her, so that she would not give rise to thoughts of regression. On the very day he was preaching the Dharma, King Ajātaśatru was eating with his mother.
King Ajātaśatru’s son was playing with a dog; whenever they ate, they shared their food with the dog. Because the king loved his son, he wished for the son to eat [the same].
He ate together with the dog and said to his mother, "I am now the king of a nation; because of my love for you, I have eaten with a dog.
His mother said sorrowfully, "When your father first had a sore on your foot, fearing that you would suffer pain, he held your finger in his mouth;
even though pus flowed from the corners of his lips, he did not disdain its filth. When the king heard this, he was ashamed and said, "I have mistakenly trusted wicked people."
Having committed this crime of immediate retribution, he quickly caused the prison to be opened and requested his father, the King.

At that time, the King was oppressed by hunger and asked Maudgalyāyana about the food and drink of the various devas. Maudgalyāyana first described the food and drink of the Four Heavenly Kings, saying it surpassed that of humans;
the King heard this and conceived a craving for it. Suddenly, he heard from outside the gate a request for the King.
He emerged and cried out in alarm, "My son has taken me; he will surely kill me! Terrified, he died and was reborn in the palace of the Four Heavenly Kings.
Because he had long since realized the first fruit of the path, he was destined to be born in Tuṣita Heaven, but due to his attachment to food, that goal was not achieved.

When the king heard of his father’s death, he regretted it deeply, feeling helpless. Because of the crime of parricide, his body was afflicted by a grave illness. His younger brother urged him to go...
The Buddha requested that Mañjuśrī perform a repentance ritual for him. Having attained the *kṣānti* of docility (*anulomikī-kṣānti*), he passed away and entered the Piṇḍala Hell.
Upon entering, he immediately emerged and was reborn in a buddha-field in the zenith, where he attained the *anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*.
He descended to be born as the Bodhisattva Acala, and after many subsequent kalpas, he became a buddha named Śuddhaloka Tathāgata. Since his traces were thus, [the practitioner should follow suit].

How could the fundamental [nature] ever be measured? The causal relationship between father and son is set forth in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*. One must understand that when the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* was preached, those in the preliminary pure assembly were already present;

yet upon reaching the time of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, their transgressions were brought to light. How is this different from Kāśyapa receiving his prediction at the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* but being deemed unfit for the final entrustment in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*?
One must not be deluded by the traces and thereby confused about the fundamental. The listing of the assembly concludes.

Preface on the Initial Assembly of the Multitude.
At that time, the World-Honored One was surrounded by the fourfold assembly, who made offerings to him, revered, honored, and praised him.
The first two phrases clarify his majestic demeanor; the latter two phrases clarify the offerings. As for "World-Honored One" (*Bhagavān*), it fully encompasses the ten titles [of a Buddha].
He is held in high esteem by all beings, for he is venerated and looked up to alike by those in the heavens and those among humans.

Traditionally, the fourfold assembly (*catuṣpariṣad*) was defined as the two groups of householders and the two groups of renunciants; however, this designation is restrictive and its scope narrow. Now, based on a single assembly, it is further divided into four:

first, the Initiating Assembly (*samutthāpaka-pariṣad*), which possesses skillful means and wisdom, discerns the capacities and the timing [of others], and strikes forth and mobilizes [the effort] to bring matters to completion.
1. Those who benefit [others], such as the two Great Beings (Mahāsattvas). 2. Those in the assembly who are ready for the teaching;

having planted roots of virtue in past lives, when the conditions converged and the time matured, they attained the Way upon hearing the teaching without rising from their seats, such as Śāriputra and others. 3. Those who act as echoes and shadows;

the Buddhas of antiquity and the Mahāsattvas of the Dharma-body conceal their perfect and ultimate nature to assist the Dharma King, such as Avalokiteśvara and others. 4. Those who provide a summary...
Regarding the assembly of the multitude: their power lacks the capacity to lead or stir them, and their virtue does not possess the function of subduing or solemnizing things.

Their past roots were shallow, and they lack understanding in the present; however, they serve as causes and conditions for attaining liberation in the future, such as through the bestowal of predictions (*vyākaraṇa*).
As it is with the bhikṣus, so it is with the other three groups. These four groups of four make sixteen assemblies, representing the intersection of the noble and the ordinary.

Gathering together those of high and low station, they forget their distinctions; yet while their outward manifestations are indeed manifold, when categorized according to their spiritual capacities (*indriya*), they do not exceed these four.
Thus, they are called the "four assemblies" (*catur-vidha-parṣad*). Regarding "surrounding": when the Buddha first appeared in the world, people did not yet know the Dharma.
Devas from the Śuddhāvāsa heavens transformed themselves into human forms, arrived, circumambulated him to the right, paid homage, and sat down to listen. It was because of this...
The heavens revere him; humans take him as their model. Consequently, whenever one sees the Buddha, one must first circumambulate him and only then pay homage.

Indeed, within the ocean-like assembly of the One Vehicle, there are surely no ordinary individuals. Observing the majestic and solemn deportment of the fourfold assembly, they appear like the stars surrounding the North Star.
Thus, it is said that they "circumambulate. As for "making offerings," in general discourse, all three types of action (the three karmas) constitute making offerings.
To discuss these separately: providing what they rely upon is called "offering" (*pūjā*); humble and reverent prostration is called "veneration" (*satkāra*);

focused and attentive mindfulness is called "respect" (*gurukāra*); and speaking words of praise is called "eulogy" (*stuti*). Furthermore, "offering" signifies the presentation of offerings through formal approach;
"veneration" signifies the custom of exalting and emulating [the worthy]. In terms of formal approach, incense and flowers are arrayed, and jade and silk are intermingled.
When expressing reverence, one is respectful and composed; when feeling awe and veneration, one maintains a dignified and solemn demeanor.
When praising, one extols virtues and achievements. A solemn demeanor means that one’s movements are calm and steady, without license or excess.
Praise for virtue means that the rhymes flow smoothly and the metaphors are appropriate, much like the *Avataṃsaka* Sūtra’s eulogies of virtue, each according to its particular gate.
This is summarized here; it is explained in detail in the *Sūtra of Immeasurable Meanings*. "Offering" refers to things such as celestial incense and celestial garments.
"Reverence" refers to acts such as joining the palms and placing the hands together. "Veneration" refers to such things as gazing with single-minded devotion.
"Praise" is as stated in that verse: "How great! O Greatly Awakened One, Great Holy Lord! Stainless, undefiled, and unattached—O Elephant among Gods and Men!"
The Master who Tames Horses: the fragrant breeze of his virtue and realization perfumes all. II. The Preface of Auspicious Omens. As for the origin of these auspicious signs:
since the appearance of the Buddhas in the world is fundamentally for the sake of the Buddha Vehicle, [the Buddha] has suppressed it within his heart for more than forty years.

As the Perfect Sound (Sambhoga-kāya) was about to arise, he feared that it might not be treated with reverence; therefore, he first startled the common people with auspicious signs to inspire in them a longing for the Dharma.

There were six such signs: first, the sign of preaching the Dharma; second, the sign of entering meditative absorption; third, the sign of raining flowers; fourth, the sign of the earth quaking; fifth, the sign of the assembly’s joy; and sixth, the sign of emitting light. These consist of three pairs:

preaching the sutra and entering absorption; [absorption and emerging from it]; and [the quaking and the raining]. Regarding the pair of preaching the sutra and entering absorption: [text continues]... absorption.

The pair of wisdom and its counterpart; celestial flowers and the trembling of the earth; cause and effect as a pair; the arousal of the Mahāyāna potential; and the great light shining everywhere as a pair of response and resonance.
When the Buddha had finished preaching the sutra, the assembly did not disperse; even after the Buddha had entered meditative concentration, they remained waiting for further instruction.

Celestial flowers delighted the eyes, and the shaking of the earth stirred the hearts. The multitude joyfully gazed upon the Buddha, who emitted radiance from the space between his eyebrows—various [manifestations].
These wonders gathered at one time; therefore, they are called auspicious omens (*śakuna*). Furthermore, as for the omen of the initial preaching of the Dharma:
for the sake of the bodhisattvas, he preached a Mahāyāna sūtra titled *The Teaching of Immeasurable Meanings*, which instructs bodhisattvas and is protected by the Buddhas.
The Bodhisattva is the capacity for the Mahāyāna. Both the Mahāyāna and the path of the Bodhisattva—this teaching and this capacity—are like the falling of timely rain;

therefore, it is said, "for the sake of all Bodhisattvas. "Great" (Mahā) has the meaning of distinguishing from the "small" (Hīna); "Vehicle" (Yāna) has the meaning of transporting and carrying. According to the *Śīla-sūtra*, there are seven kinds of greatness:
first, the greatness of the Dharma, which refers to the twelve divisions of the scriptures; second, the greatness of the mind, which seeks bodhi...

First, the greatness of extraction (*uddhāra-mahattva*); second, the greatness of comprehension (*avabodha-mahattva*), which is the comprehension of the Bodhisattva-piṭaka; third, the greatness of purity (*viśuddhi-mahattva*), which is the purity of the mind upon seeing the Path;

fourth, the greatness of adornment (*vyūhana-mahattva*), which consists of merit and wisdom; fifth, the greatness of time (*kāla-mahattva*), which is the practice of the paths over three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*;

sixth, the greatness of fulfillment (*paripūraṇa-mahattva*), which is the attainment of Great Enlightenment through self-adornment with the primary and secondary marks. The first six constitute the greatness of the cause, while the seventh is the greatness of the fruit.
Great causes and great fruits are combined to form the Mahāyāna sūtras. This refers to their general designation;

however, as they are subsumed under the Mahāyāna, their various sections and volumes differ, exhibiting distinctions such as the *Karunāpuṇḍarīka* and the *Saṃpuṣpita*, or the *Laṅkāvatāra* and the *Śūraṅgama*.
The title *Unlimited Meanings* (*Anantārtha*) cites its specific designation to distinguish it clearly from others. Yet, names manifest through meanings, and meanings are revealed by means of names.
It encompasses more than eighty categories concerning the nature of persons and subsumes the one hundred and eight questions of the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*.
Its principles and measures transcend thought, and its scriptural measures contain all manner of wonders; therefore, it is titled *Unlimited Meanings*. Self-awakened...

Since beginningless time, the faculties and dispositions of sentient beings have been diverse; thus, the Tathāgata has preached various teachings to guide them through skillful means, bringing the one into the infinite.
Now, in expounding the "Infinite Meanings," he gathers the infinite back into the one.
One should know that this is an alternative name for the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*. The *Dharmapuṇḍarīka-śāstra* lists seventeen alternative names;

the *Anantamukha-sūtra* (*Wuliangyi jing*) is one of them. Now, to explain the meaning of the treatise: the Buddha directly uttered this name and entered this samādhi; therefore, we know it serves as the introduction to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*.

In the *Pañcaviṃśati-sāhasrikā-prajñāpāramitā*, the *Guanzizai pusa jing* (*Avalokiteśvara-bodhisattva-sūtra*), and the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*, all likewise proclaim these names at the beginning of their introductions. So it is with the present sutra.

The ancient commentary states: "The name of the sutra is *Amitārtha* (Infinite Meanings). It further states: "He shall preach the Mahāyāna sutra named *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* (The Lotus of the Wondrous Dharma).
This chanting of the title within the introduction is identical in intent to that of the treatise. According to that sutra, regarding the explanation of "Infinite Meanings," the scripture says:
"The Bodhisattva Mahāvyūha, together with eighty thousand great beings, addressed the Buddha in unison, saying: 'Bodhisattvas...'"
"If one wishes to swiftly attain Bodhi, what Dharma-gate should one practice? The Buddha said, "There is a Dharma-gate named 'Immeasurable Meanings.
Those who wish to study this Dharma-gate should contemplate that all dharmas, from their very origin,"
The nature and characteristics are quiescent, like empty space; there are no two dharmas.

Even that which is called "immeasurable meaning" arises from a single dharma. This single dharma is called "signlessness. Signlessness and non-signlessness are termed the "true mark" (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).
From this true mark arise immeasurable dharmas, namely: the two dharmas, the three paths, and the four fruits. Now, this is explained as signless.
"Characteristics" refers to the absence of the characteristics of birth and death. "Non-characteristics" refers to the absence of the characteristic of nirvāṇa.

Since even nirvāṇa does not exist, it is called "neither characteristic nor non-characteristic. This points to the Middle Way as the true characteristic (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*). The "two dharmas" refer to the sudden and the gradual.
"Sudden" refers to all dharmas within the *Avataṃsaka* (Huayan) Sudden Teaching. "Gradual" refers to all dharmas within the Tripiṭaka, Prajñā, and Vaipulya teachings.
The "three paths" are the three vehicles (*triyāna*). The "four fruits" are the Arhat, Pratyekabuddha, Bodhisattva, and Buddha.
These various dharmas are termed "immeasurable. Their essential meaning is the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*). From this single meaning, the immeasurable emerges.

The Dharma, because it gathers immeasurable meanings into a single principle. This present sutra’s One Vehicle of the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) reconciles the provisional teachings of the forty years of various sutras;
this is what is meant here. "The teaching for bodhisattvas" means employing immeasurable meanings to instruct all bodhisattvas.
This means that the Great Teaching corresponds to those of great capacity. As the subsequent text says: "May all sentient beings everywhere likewise attain this Way. It further states:
"If I encounter sentient beings, I shall teach them all the Buddha-way. This is precisely that meaning.

That which the Buddha protects and keeps in mind is the *Anantarya-sthāna* (The Place of Infinite Meanings); it is what the Buddha has personally realized. Therefore, it is that which the Tathāgata...
"Protective mindfulness. As the subsequent text states: "The Buddha himself abides in the Great Vehicle. Although he wished to reveal and instruct [the disciples], their faculties were dull;

thus, for a long time he remained silent regarding this essential point, not being intent on expounding it hastily. Therefore, it is called "protective mindfulness. △ Second, the auspicious sign of entering samādhi.
After the Buddha had spoken this sutra, he sat cross-legged and entered the Samādhi of the Station of Immeasurable Meaning. His body and mind were motionless.
As for sitting cross-legged: one presses the left leg over the right, which is half-sitting; then, shifting the right leg to press over the left, it becomes full sitting. It is as follows:

The legs are coiled like a dragon’s coils; hence it is called the "double-lotus posture" (*paryaṅka*). All Buddhas of the past, as well as their assemblies of disciples, have entirely practiced this method.

If even when rising from the *paryaṅka* posture one gives rise to unwholesome thoughts, others still conceive a heart of reverence; how much more so when entering deep states of meditative realization—would that not bring delight to gods and humans?
Furthermore, it is not a practice for worldly enjoyment, nor is it shared with non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*); it is capable of destroying all [afflictions].
Because of the demonic armies, and furthermore, because it possesses the four *siddhāntas*. Regarding "entering immeasurable *samādhis*":

*samādhi* here is translated as "straightening and settling" (*tiáo zhí dìng*) or "right concentration" (*zhèng dìng*). There are many names for *samādhi*, and this term is distinguished by its immeasurable meanings. Now, since a *nāga* is always in a state of concentration, how could there be an "entering"?
It is merely that those who have not yet attained concentration perceive it as if there were an entering; in reality, there is no entering.
One may enter it; yet there is also no non-entry. There is neither entering nor not entering, neither fixed nor unfixed, and no place that is not abided in.

It penetrates deeply to the very source and bottom of all dharmas and fully comprehends the fundamental root of the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*). Abiding in non-abiding, one dwells within the secret treasury.
This is what is called the "Place of Immeasurable Meanings" (*ananta-artha-sthāna*); this place is accessible only to Buddha after Buddha.

To be able to exhaustively investigate [all things] is the very essence of the true reality (dharmatā) of all phenomena. From this essence, function arises; therefore, he preached the *Anantamukha-sūtra*.

To gather function back into the essence, he entered the concentration on the station of infinite meanings (*anantārtha-sthāna-samādhi*). As stated in the subsequent text, he arose from it with serene composure.
From this point it arises. With earnest devotion, he offers praise; he praises this place. He speaks in terms of the Dharma, speaking of this place;

he speaks in terms of parables, illustrating this place; he speaks of past-life causes and conditions, explaining this place. It is not that hearing the Dharma and attaining realization, thereby receiving a prediction of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*), is without merit;
yet, ultimately, one does not know this place. This place is subtle and difficult to fathom. Contemplate it!
It is beyond the reach of the discrimination of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Therefore it is said: "Stop, stop! There is no need to speak; my Dharma is subtle and difficult to conceive.
Being beyond words and beyond thought, one returns to this very place. Thus, one should know that the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* speaks only of this place and not of any other.
For this reason, prior to the preaching of this sutra, he manifested these inconceivable signs as a prelude.
This is the sign of preaching the Dharma; therefore, he enters the Samādhi of the Station of Immeasurable Meanings.

Now, as for his entering meditative concentration after having already preached, it is because concentration and wisdom mutually support one another. There is no wisdom without dhyāna, which is why he first enters concentration; there is no dhyāna without wisdom, which is why he first preaches the Dharma.
Thus, wisdom is itself concentration and concentration is itself wisdom; their sequential entry and exit are without obstruction. He preached.
Having entered meditative concentration, he emerged from it and spoke again: "The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* preceded [the *Śrīmālādevī-siṃhanāda-sūtra*] as its precursor.

If one were to establish a sequential order, one should first enter the *Anantamukha-dhāraṇī-samādhi* (Infinite Meanings Samādhi) and then enter the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-samādhi*. If this were the case, the textual evidence would be clearly manifest.

At that time, the assembly understood for themselves; what need was there to wait for Maitreya’s earnestness or Mañjuśrī’s persistence? Thus we know that the preface was composed so that its meaning might become even clearer.
As for "the body and mind being unmoving," this refers to their correspondence with the object of focus (*ālambana*).
The fundamental source of the body is as profound and still as empty space; the rational nature of the mind is ultimately and eternally quiescent. As the text says: "The body and hands..."
It is sufficient. To be tranquil, peaceful, and unmoving; for the mind to be ever serene and free from distraction—this is it.
Furthermore, the body is like a vajra, incapable of being moved or turned; the mind is like space, devoid of discrimination.

Because one maintains the body and mind through the Samādhi of the Station of Immeasurable Meanings, they do not move. Question: The auspicious signs originally discuss marvelous and extraordinary phenomena.
Question: Preaching the Dharma and entering meditative concentration (*samādhi*) are the constant routines of the Buddha; how can these be considered auspicious omens? Answer:

Although the preaching of the Dharma had concluded, the assembly did not disperse, remaining solemn as they awaited something further. Without vacating the Dharma seat, the Buddha proceeded to enter meditative concentration. This event was extraordinary.
This differs from the case of permanence. For what reason would it not be an auspicious sign? Furthermore, Mañjuśrī cited the six ancient auspicious signs, all of which included this event.

If it were not an auspicious sign in the past, how could it serve as proof for the present? Since the present and the past are identical in this regard, is it not appropriate to call it an auspicious sign?
△ Third, the auspicious sign of the rain of flowers.
At that time, the heavens rained down *māndārava* flowers (extending to... which were scattered over the Buddha and the great assembly.
There were four kinds of flowers: formerly translated as "small white" and "great white," "small red" and "great red," "small pleasing" and "great pleasing."

There is "small flexibility" and "great flexibility. Here, I shall explain this by means of "flexibility that accords with one's intent. Forty years ago, through skillful means and guidance, each attained a small fruit;
because these were small and accorded with their respective intents, they were satisfied. Now, the sutra proclaims the true reality (*tathatā*) of the One Vehicle.
This accords with the fundamental intention of all Buddhas. Because it brings such great satisfaction, the devas manifest this through flowers of small and great satisfaction.
Since this sutra teaches the gentle Dharma for bodhisattvas, it does not compare to those who are rigid and stubborn, nor is it for those lacking gentleness.
Over forty years, each has been tamed; this is "small gentleness. Today, each...
Each was given a prediction [of enlightenment]. Practicing the bodhisattva path, they always accord with sentient beings; they possess great pliancy and gentleness (*mahāmṛdutā*).

Therefore, the various devas used small and large flowers of pliancy and gentleness to symbolize this. Their intent was directed toward the Buddha, as stated in the following passage: "As I have previously vowed..."

"Those who have now fulfilled this are they. 'Gentle and responsive to the occasion' refers to the two thousand disciples, both those still in training and those beyond training, whose minds are gentle, tranquil, and pure.
'Scattering [flowers] over the Buddha' means that their superior realization accords with the Buddha's own intent."
"And the great assembly" refers, below, to the convergence with their receptive capacities (*mārga-citta*). △ Fourth, the auspicious sign of the earthquake:
"The entire Buddha-world shook in six ways.
"The entire Buddha-world" refers to the realm of transformation of a single Buddha; according to the verse in the response below, all Buddha-lands shake.
As for the six kinds: shaking, rising, leaping; quaking, roaring, and striking. The Sūtra briefly indicates two categories.

Swinging and tossing about without stability is called "shaking" (kampa). Rising from below toward a higher level is called "rising" (utthāna). The unevenness of ridges and hollows is called "leaping" (valgana);

these three refer to forms. A deep, rumbling sound is called "quaking" (nirghoṣa). A crashing resonance is called "roaring" (garjita). Causing sentient beings to awaken is called "striking" (abhinirhāra); these three refer to sounds.

Each of these [six stages] contains three movements: movement, pervasive movement, and equal pervasive movement. Movement refers to the shaking of a single world; pervasive movement refers to the shaking of the four continents;
and equal pervasive movement refers to the shaking of a great trichiliocosm. The remaining five stages may be understood accordingly.

These represent the six successive refutations of the ignorance-obscuration (*avidyā-āvaraṇa*) by the Perfect Teaching (*pariniṣpanna-yāna*). This ignorance is vast and solid, never having been invaded or destroyed, just as the characteristics of the earth are firm and stable.
It was about to be destroyed; therefore, the earth shook to manifest this. △ Fifth, the auspicious signs of the assembly’s joy:
At that time, the bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs in the assembly (up to) rejoiced, joined their palms, and with one mind gazed upon the Buddha.
"Devas" refers to the various devas of the three realms. There are four kinds of nāgas: first, those who guard the celestial palaces, maintaining them so that they do not fall;
second, those who raise clouds and bring rain to benefit the human world; third, terrestrial nāgas, who channel rivers and open canals;
and fourth, those who guard hidden treasures, protecting the stores of wheel-turning kings and persons of great merit. Yakṣas are swift-moving spirits.
Gandharvas are deities of worldly music. Asuras are "not-gods. Garuḍas are golden-winged birds. Kiṃnaras are deities of dharma-music.
Mahoragas are great serpent-deities. Humans are the common people. Non-humans are the class of ghosts and spirits.
There are four types of minor kings, known as "scattered-rice" kings. There are four types of wheel-turning kings (cakravartin). Humans...

When the human lifespan is twenty thousand years, an Iron-Wheel-Turning King appears and rules over one world-system. When it is forty thousand years, a Copper-Wheel-Turning King appears and rules over two world-systems.

When it is sixty thousand years, a Silver-Wheel-Turning King appears and rules over three world-systems. When it is eighty thousand years, a Gold-Wheel-Turning King appears and rules over the four world-systems.
As for what is meant by "turning the wheel": when a Gold-Wheel-Turning King appears in the world, he possesses seven treasures.
The wheel appeared before him of its own accord, and as he turned it, he ruled over the four continents; thus he is called a Wheel-Turning Sage King (*cakravartin*).
The fourfold assembly rejoiced in this auspicious omen, and the eight classes of beings gazed upon his holy countenance. What has been attained today was never before experienced since antiquity;
therefore, each one joyfully joined their palms and with single-minded devotion beheld the Buddha. [Question: Joy and anger are human...
Question: How can these ordinary occurrences be considered auspicious omens? Answer: Celestial flowers delight the eyes, and the shaking of the earth stirs the heart.
As the Great Sūtra says: "When it shakes, it causes the hearts of sentient beings to move. This is an extraordinary joy, yet one is not moved by that joy;

furthermore, one is able to contemplate the Buddha with a single mind. How could this not be an auspicious omen? The flowers and the earth are external omens, while the joy in the heart is an internal omen.

Therefore, the great assembly at the Dharma-gathering knew only that the one preaching the sutra and entering samādhi was the Buddha; they took the raining of flowers to be the heavens and the shaking of the earth to be the earth.
Why did they not turn their heads and look back? △ Sixth, the auspicious sign of emitting light.
At that time, the Buddha emitted light from the white tuft of hair between his eyebrows (until: ...and erected stupas made of the seven treasures for the Buddha’s relics).
The *Sūtra on the Ocean-like Samādhi of Contemplating the Buddha* states: "The light from the white tuft of hair was five chi long when the Buddha was first born."
When he was practicing asceticism, it was one zhang and four chi in length; when he attained Buddhahood, it was one zhang and five chi in length.
The interior and exterior of its tuft were both hollow, like a tube of white beryl, pure within and without.
All his merits—from his initial aspiration, through his intermediate practices and various manifestations, up until his entry into nirvana—were all manifested within that tuft.
The space between the two eyebrows represents the Middle Way and constancy. Its appearance being supple signifies bliss. Its ability to contract and expand at will signifies self-mastery.
Its color being pure white signifies purity. This mark was brought about by the accumulation of patience, filial piety, and other virtues over many lifetimes;
it is one of the thirty-two marks of a Great Man. Its radiance symbolizes the wisdom of the One Vehicle Middle Way, which illuminates the eighteen thousand [dharmas].

The "thousand worlds" refer to the objective realm (*viṣaya*). Because the realm and wisdom are perfectly interfused, and because principle (*li*) pervades the ten directions, fundamental wisdom is luminously clear and penetrates everything without exception;
hence it is called "illumination. The eastern direction represents the realm of movement and symbolizes the gate of birth-and-death (*utpāda-nirodha-mukha*).

Since True Suchness (*tathatā*) follows conditions (*pratyaya*), it is able to give rise to all phenomena (*dharmas*) within the ten realms. Although these phenomena are in motion, their essence is quiescent extinction (*śānta-nirvāṇa*). [This] is what one desires to [realize].

To move while realizing the principle of immovability means that there is nothing not universally pervasive. By means of the light of wisdom—which is quiescent yet eternally illuminating—there is nowhere it does not shine and no object it does not illumine.
When extended horizontally, it pervades the vast expanse of the ten directions, reaching eighteen thousand worlds in every quarter without exception.
When traced vertically, it exhausts the realms from the celestial heavens above to the hells below.
It is high and thick, pervading everywhere. "Avīci" is translated here as "Without Interval" (Wújiàn).

The *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* explains that regarding the attainment of the fruit [of rebirth], there are five aspects—suffering, time, life-span, and physical form—in which there is no interval; therefore, it is called Avīci. As for "Hell" (Diyù), the name is established according to its meaning:
a prison beneath the earth is called a "Earth-Hell. The *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "Five hundred yojanas below Jambudvīpa, there exists..."
That hell is the very lowest. Akaniṣṭha—translated here as "the ultimate limit of material obstruction"—is the Heaven of Ultimate Form;
beyond this lie the four heavens of the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu), and thus it is the very highest. Between these two extremes are the realms of ghosts, animals, and humans.
Although the retributions of the primary and secondary worlds differ, and the forms of good and evil vary, all are seen within a single ray of light;

there is nothing that is not encompassed. Regarding the phrase "in this world" and so forth, this clarifies the beginning and end of the Buddha-activities of sentient beings and Buddhas throughout the dharma-realm in other lands—all are seen within a single ray of light. Within this Sahā world, [the Buddha] does not move.
Step. Upon opening his eyes, he saw those eighteen thousand sentient beings of the six realms (*ṣadgati*). "Realm" (*gati*) refers to the direction of movement;

according to causes, fruits are summoned, and as these directions of movement differ, they are divided into six classes. Through the delusions of the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*), there is birth through their conjunction.

Therefore, they are called "sentient beings. This refers to the passage in the following verse concerning how the sentient beings of the six realms receive retributions—whether good or foul—and how [the Bodhisattvas] see them all, see them together, see them again, and see them yet again;
this is a change in the wording of the text. However, there are two meanings. First, the scope of vision for those of the Three Vehicles is limited;
thus, the phrase "see them all" means that they do so by virtue of the power of the light from the Tathāgata’s *ūrṇā-kośa* (white tuft between the eyebrows). Second, [it indicates...]
The great assembly attained what they had never experienced before. With single-mindedness they contemplated the Buddha;

by concentrating their thoughts on a single point, the mountains, rivers, and the great earth were transformed in accordance with their thought into supreme awakening. What limits could there be? Furthermore, they saw that land and others like it.
Thus, the Holy Lord Lion descends to expound the True Dharma; the names of the Buddhas, their modes of transformation, and their lands are diverse and not uniform.
Those who hear his preaching differ according to the capacities and conditions of the various lands, encountering either provisional or ultimate dharma-gates.

There is a distinction in their establishment, yet they do not depart from this very place. One sees the forms and images of the various Buddhas with the eyes, and hears the sounds of them preaching the Dharma with the ears.

Seeing all these together, as stated below regarding "if a person encounters suffering," one practices the conduct of the six perfections and the contemplation of conditions to attain the paths of the Bodhisattva, Pratyekabuddha, and Śrāvaka;
these constitute the three vehicles of the two teachings of the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna) and the Initial [Vehicle] (Śrāvakayāna).
Furthermore, he sees various bodhisattvas; these are the great bodhisattvas of the ultimate, sudden, and perfect [teachings].

Thus, within the subsequent verses, there are thirty-one and a half lines of verse that consist of sequential and non-sequential inquiries regarding various causes and conditions, all of which concern a single continuous matter.
For example, when a person with faith and understanding practices giving, this is the path of a bodhisattva; it is like [the offering of] kingdoms and cities.
Wives, children, and others all joyfully practice giving, for such giving is the causal condition for entering the Path. Internally, there is such a mind of giving;
externally, there is such a sign of joy. To resolve with faith and uphold the pure precepts is the Bodhisattva path.
Thus, one purely receives and maintains the various precepts of the Mahāyāna and so forth; and this upholding of the precepts is the entry [into the Path].
The causal conditions for the Way are as follows: internally, there is such an immovable mind; externally, there are such signs of upholding the precepts.
Faith, understanding, practice, and patience constitute the Bodhisattva path. Thus, when subjected to abusive insults or physical beatings, one remains soft and gentle, enduring them all.
For patience is precisely the causal condition for entering the Way. Internally, there is such a mind of endurance; externally, there is—
This is the mark of gentleness. To practice with faith, understanding, and diligence is the path of the bodhisattva;
thus, regarding both adverse and favorable conditions, one is courageous and resolute. Diligence is the causal condition for entering the path.

Internally possessing such a courageous mind and externally manifesting such a heroic demeanor, to cultivate meditative concentration with faith and understanding is the path of the bodhisattva. Thus...
He practiced profound *dhyāna* and great samādhis without ever flagging; indeed, meditative concentration is the very condition for entering the Way.
Internally, he possessed such a mind of focused attention, while externally, he manifested the appearance of a withered tree.

With faith, understanding, and wisdom—these being the path of the Bodhisattva—he extensively studied the various classics and attained thorough mastery and clarity; thus, wisdom is that which leads to entry [into the Way].
Regarding the causes and conditions of the Way: internally there is such a clear and sharp mind, and externally there are such active manifestations.
Because the characteristics of these causes and conditions and one’s resolute belief (*adhimukti*) are manifold and not uniform, they are called "various.

Furthermore, seeing the various Buddhas enter *parinirvāṇa* and so forth refers to the passage in the following verse concerning making offerings to the *śarīra* and constructing stūpas and temples after the Buddha’s extinction. *Parinirvāṇa*...
"Parinirvāṇa" is an abbreviation of the Sanskrit term; in full, it is *mahāparinirvāṇa*, which is translated here as "Great Extinction and Deliverance" (*dà mièdù*).

"Great" refers to the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*); "extinction" refers to liberation (*vimukti*); and "deliverance" refers to wisdom (*prajñā*). It is thus the secret treasury of the three virtues (*triguṇa*).

It is also called "Perfect Quiescence" (*yuánjì*), because when the conditions for transformation are exhausted and there is no further dharma to be manifested, the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*) consequently becomes hidden. As for "śarīra": [it refers to the relics].

In full, it is called *śarīra*; this is translated as "sacred bone" (*ling-gu*). It possesses five colors because it is formed by the condensation of the three types of untainted learning (*anāsrava-śikṣā*).
In Sanskrit, it is *stūpa*; this is translated as "square mound" (*fang-fen*) or "high and manifest place," referring to the location where sacred bones are enshrined.
Fragmentary-body relics (*śarīra-śarīra*) are the final bequeathed teachings of the Buddha, intended for all sentient beings.
Because he created stupas and cultivated merit out of his sincere devotion, he first saw the six realms of existence;

second, he saw the various Buddhas—this is the pair of the sacred and the mundane; third, he heard the Buddhas preach the Dharma; fourth, he saw the fourfold assembly attaining the Way—this is the pair of persons and dharmas;
fifth, he saw the bodhisattvas performing their practices; sixth, he saw the Buddhas enter parinirvāṇa—this is the pair of beginning and end. These are again a single series of events. Since...
Where there are sentient beings who can be transformed, there is a Buddha capable of transforming them. Where there is a Buddha, there is the teaching of the Dharma.
Where there is the teaching of the Dharma, there are disciples. Disciples are the beginning of practice; practice necessarily leads to its completion. Thus one sees these characters.
One must realize this thoroughly; then one will know that the eighteen thousand lands are all the natural radiance of the original ground, flowing forth from this very source.
An ancient worthy said: "The entire earth is one's own radiance; there is not a single person who does not dwell within this radiance.
This aforementioned light extends horizontally and penetrates vertically—how vast and profound it is!
What is this vastness? Within it, the Dharma-realm gives birth to Buddhas;

the events and characteristics from beginning to end, the good and evil, the beautiful and the ugly—these many diverse realms are all manifested simultaneously by a single ray of light before the fourfold assembly of this land, without the slightest obstruction.
Every person possesses this radiance; it is only that sentient beings do not recognize it themselves. If...
The fundamental luminosity is thoroughly penetrating; fundamental wisdom is manifest before one. The wondrous essence, the true reality (*dharmatā*), is clearly visible within the mind and eyes.

How is this different from the Buddha? Mañjuśrī said: "Now the Buddha emits radiance to assist in bringing forth the meaning of true reality. Thus, this light is the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*—the single fascicle that transcends words.
Alas, the assembly of Dharma followers does not understand it, and so they must further trouble the two Great Beings to provide an auxiliary explanation. Worldly...
The Honored One’s exclamation upon emerging from samādhi, as recorded in the full text of the scripture, reveals this very intent. The section on the Manifestation of Auspicious Omens concludes.
△ Third, the Section on Doubtful Reflections, which is divided into two parts. First, Maitreya’s Doubtful Reflections.
At that time, Maitreya Bodhisattva had this thought (up to: "I shall now ask. Herein there are three thoughts:
first, the correct mindfulness of the six auspicious omens; second, the thought of whom to ask; third, the thought of Mañjuśrī.

When the thought of Mañjuśrī arises, the second thought is eliminated, leaving only the first thought. Thus, it results in a single doubt regarding the six auspicious omens of the first thought. [The text] proceeds: "As..."
These are the three words of reflection. This is the scribe’s imitation of Maitreya silently contemplating within himself without speaking.

What kind of reflection does he make? It means: "Why has the World-Honored One now manifested this sign of supernatural transformation? By what causes and conditions does such an auspicious omen exist?
As for the "sign of supernatural transformation," it refers generally to matters concerning both this land and other lands. Now, when a Sage utters a single word...
As a model for the world, he performs a single act as a standard for all under heaven; his timely measures are always appropriate and never applied in vain.
Now that he has manifested his supernatural powers and transformed the characteristics of this realm, how could he have done so without cause?
Yet we cannot fathom by what causes and conditions such a stirring has occurred, nor do we know why it is so.
That is so. You asked whose thought it was, yet since you cannot fathom the causes and conditions for its occurrence, you ought to seek a definitive resolution from the Buddha.
Alas, the Buddha is currently absorbed in samādhi. Furthermore, this samādhi is the realm of the Buddha’s own self-awakened noble wisdom;
its principle transcends the subtle and the profound, its wondrousness surpasses the path of the emotions, and it is inconceivable. Examine this realm closely.

The signs are not of the ordinary; this must surely be a rare occurrence. If it were an ordinary matter, I, with my wisdom as a Bodhisattva of the Final Birth (*caramabhavika*), would have grasped its intent.
Though I do not know it entirely, I could at least have had a vague sense of two or three aspects of it.
Since I do not know, and the Buddha has entered meditative absorption, whom should I ask to resolve this doubt? If I were to ask, it would certainly be—
One who possesses both wisdom and talent can dispel my doubts. If you cannot resolve my uncertainty, what is the use of asking?

At that time, Maitreya looked left and right, scanning the assembly with his eyes to seek someone among them. He observed the sages and worthies intermingled, the great dragons and elephants standing side by side;
taking myself as an example, there was no one among them who did not harbor doubts. What, then, should I ask?
People explain this matter by saying: "One should ask whom? Who is the person capable of answering? Thus, one should contemplate Mañjuśrī three times.
Furthermore, form two characters that follow immediately after the two characters "Who can" (shé néng), using them to search and examine to the left and right of Maitreya.
With right mindfulness, he wondered who could be the one to answer him. Suddenly, he raised his head and saw Mañjuśrī. He thought again:

"This Mañjuśrī is the eldest son of the Dharma King and the most eminent among the assembly. Having made offerings to the Buddhas for kalpas and upheld the Dharma while practicing the Way, it is as the saying goes:
'If you wish to know the path up the mountain, you must ask those who have already traveled it. Since he has served the Buddha so many times,"
Those who have seen this sutra with their own eyes will surely behold these rare and wondrous signs; therefore, it is said: "I shall now inquire and request a resolution of my doubts.
The term "surely" (*bi ying*) is a word of certainty that has indeed been realized. In the following passage, Mañjuśrī briefly provides an answer based on what he has previously seen, saying:
"In the past, among the various Buddhas, I have already seen such auspicious omens; I shall now ask a single question. (The phrase *fan* here indicates a response.)

Regarding the two phrases "What should be used above? and "By whom can it be done?": here, "by what" and "by whom" are further elaborated as "having already done so" and "must surely be done by me now," etc.;

these are all the subtle manifestations of the characteristics of dharmas (*dharmalakṣaṇa*). Furthermore, "spirit" (*shen*) refers to the internal, while "transformation" (*bian*) refers to the external.

"Spirit" clarifies the mind of Heaven, which is the innate internal wisdom; "transformation" is named for its shifting and changing, which refers to the six auspicious omens (*ṣad-prātihārya*) on the outside.
Zhang remarked: "Maitreya could not fathom his external transformations, nor did he know his internal wisdom; thus he gave rise to doubts and thoughts such as these.

As for those who are mediocre and do not know the arts, those who are scattered and do not know meditative concentration, ordinary people who do not know the sages, lesser sages who do not know Śāriputra, Śāriputra who does not know the Bodhisattvas, and the Bodhisattvas who do not know..."
Regarding the "Successor" (Upapadya): even the Successor does not know the ultimate supremacy; this refers to the ultimate state where even Maitreya does not know it. Question:

Since Maitreya has encountered Buddhas and planted many roots of goodness, how can he possibly fail to have a general understanding? Answer: This is a case of concealing the manifest and revealing the obscure;

it is a skillful means of not knowing. It is precisely because he intends to bring forth the Great Teaching that he gives rise to doubt within what was previously free of doubt, and [doubt] arises within the state of no-thought.
The thought [behind this] was none other than to stir the hearts of people, causing others to give rise to doubt and then to faith. 2.
The Doubts of the Great Assembly.
At that time, the bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs... (up to) ... "Who now should we ask about these signs of the Buddha’s radiance and supernormal powers?"

The great assembly at the Dharma-gathering all had this thought: "The Buddha has emitted a single ray of light that illuminates both that land and this land, revealing such miraculous transformations and such manifestations of the realm of universal change; this is a rare and extraordinary event. We should now ask whom it concerns."
The compiler of the sutra feared prolixity and therefore did not record it. This mindfulness has two aspects.

As for "the fourfold assembly looks up with joy, gazing upon you and me," if there were no third mindfulness, for what purpose would they gaze upon you? One should know that this verse was uttered by Maitreya;
it was because he questioned Mañjuśrī that the great assembly then looked toward Mañjuśrī. Before the question was raised, they did not look.
This literary composition of Mañjuśrī is a source of doubt for this assembly gathered here like the ocean; it is the catalyst for awakening to the One Vehicle (Ekayāna).

Were it intended for those of base and vulgar character, there would certainly be no response of uplifted spirit. Now, with minds constrained and anxieties rampant, those who look upward in search of knowledge may understand the resonance between the peck and the crackle [of the hen and chick].
There is indeed a profound reason for this gathering, like a timely rain. This section was thus arranged by the scribe.
Master Kumārajīva’s skillful brushwork leaves both himself and others with nothing but admiration; it has fully captured the physical appearance and circumstances of that time.
△ Fourth, the introduction to the inquiry, which consists of both prose and verse. First, the prose:

At that time, Maitreya Bodhisattva, wishing to resolve his own doubts—[extending] to "he saw all the adornments of those Buddha-lands"—the phrase "wishing to resolve his own doubts" indicates the state of being about to speak what has not yet been spoken; this matter is rare and extraordinary.

I have doubts, and the great assembly likewise has doubts. If there were someone within the assembly to respond and pose a question, their doubts would be dispelled, and my own doubts would naturally vanish.
As the words reached his lips, he hesitated again and again, unwilling to pose the question.
Furthermore, he observed the minds of the fourfold assembly: some stared fixedly at the radiant signs; some lowered their heads in doubt and were overcome by distress;
others looked back and forth at one another. There was not a single person capable of asking the question; thus, Maitreya restrained his impatience and remained silent.
[The Buddha] prohibited [him]. He requested Mañjuśrī to resolve his own doubts so as to dispel the doubts of the assembly.
"Observing the minds of those gathered" means, "I deliberate upon the hearts of others. For what reason [did he do this]? This is no small matter.
This must be a response to the "Great Matter" (mahā-vastu) that corresponds to the text concerning the six auspicious omens; herein, these twenty-four characters encompass it all.
However, this word "doubt" (*yi*) is the most significant, for it is through doubt that faith and awakening first arise.
Question: Mañjuśrī and Maitreya are equal in virtue and rank; why is there one who asks and one who answers? Answer: Although their ranks are equal, [Mañjuśrī] acts as the guest...

This is because the subjects [of their respective teachings] ought to differ. Furthermore, among the Dharma-gates there are the provisional and the real: the provisional should be questioned, and the real should be answered.

Moreover, regarding the traces [of the Buddha's appearance], there are those that are near and those that are distant: the near should be questioned, and the distant should be answered. Furthermore, this present sutra bestows upon the śrāvakas the prediction of future Buddhahood.
One who has not yet attained Buddhahood in the future cannot ask this question; therefore, Maitreya, out of great compassion, asks it.
One who is a Buddha already perfected in the past cannot answer this; therefore, Mañjuśrī, through his great wisdom, answers it.

Furthermore, Mañjuśrī represents great wisdom (*mahājñāna*), while Maitreya cultivates *vijñaptimātra* (consciousness-only); the intention is to reveal that this realm can be entered only by wisdom, not by consciousness (*vijñāna*).
This can be understood. Because there are many such meanings, Maitreya asks and Mañjuśrī answers.
△ Second, the verses in *gāthā*. "Verse" (*gāthā*) is an abbreviation of the Sanskrit original; it is sometimes called *gāthaka*, which is a corruption of the Sanskrit term.
The Sanskrit word is *āryā-stotra* (or *āryā-stava*), which means "praising recitation. Whether in prose or verse, that which consists of thirty-two syllables constitutes one [unit].
One verse (*gāthā*). *Geya* (repetitional verse): this is translated as "corresponding verse" (*ying song*), because it corresponds to the preceding prose (*gadya*).

*Gāthā*: this is translated as "isolated verse" (*gu qi*), because it does not correspond to prose. *Udāna*: this is translated as "verses of inspired utterance" (*ji shi song*), because they condense many meanings into few words.
Regarding the recitation and upholding for others, as for why verses are spoken after the prose, the *Nāgārjuna-vibhāṣā-śāstra* states there are four reasons:
first, according to the customs of the land; there are teachings on scattering flowers and stringing flowers, just like the inscriptions following the prefaces in this region.
Second, because of differing inclinations and desires; some prefer scattering flowers, while others prefer metrical verses.

Third, because the understandings arising in accordance [with the listeners] differ: some attain understanding through scattered flowers, while others attain understanding through the words and phrases.

Fourth, because of the sharpness or dullness of their faculties: those with sharp faculties understand upon hearing once, whereas those with dull faculties understand only after it is spoken a second time.
Furthermore, this serves to manifest the Buddha’s earnest and compassionate instruction; moreover, it is for the sake of the assembly’s sequence of arrival. Therefore, there is...

This refers to verse (gāthā). Furthermore, regarding prose and verse, there are five pairs or ten items of meaning: existence and non-existence, before and after, hidden and manifest, extensive and concise, and opening and closing.
By understanding these, one will not be confused by the meanings of "transcendent verses" (chāosòng), "retrospective verses" (zuīsòng), and so forth.
The verses consist of sixty-two lines and are divided into two parts: first, fifty-four lines of verse that repeat the questions posed above;
second, eight lines requesting an answer. The first part is further divided into two: the first four lines ask about this land.
Thereupon, Maitreya Bodhisattva, wishing to restate this meaning, asked in verse:
"O Mañjuśrī, Guide, for what reason [have you attained] such joy in body and mind as never before?"
The first line, beginning with "Mañjuśrī," praises the auspicious omen of emitting light; the "Guide" is called a Buddha because he instructs and leads people through the preaching of the Dharma.
The one and a half lines beginning with "rains down maṇi-jewels" praise the falling of flowers. *Candana* is a Sanskrit term;

some say it is not translated here because it does not exist in this land [China], while others translate it according to its meaning as "medicine," because it can eliminate illness. As for "fragrant wind," wind is originally without...

Fragrance. Fragrance is truly extraordinary. Fragrance fundamentally belongs to the flower; the fragrance of a flower is like that of sandalwood. Celestial flowers are most wondrous—how could they have color without fragrance?
The fragrance of the wind arises from the flowers; this refers to the fragrance coming from within the flowers as the wind passes through them.
Celestial flowers fell in profusion and in disarray; fragrant breezes blew gust after gust, assailing the senses and delighting the hearts of all, so that there was no one who did not rejoice.

Thus it is said, "It gladdens the hearts of the multitude. Because the wind carries the fragrance of the flowers, and because of the causal conditions of the falling flowers gathering upon the ground, the earth is adorned by the flowers and purified by the wind.
This symbolizes that if the cause proceeds toward the fruit, [the result will be accordingly].
The fruit, however, is solemn and pure. These two lines [of verse] eulogize the auspicious sign of the earth’s trembling (the first line of the fourth section).
The following one line eulogizes the auspicious sign of the assembly’s joy. In the prose (long passage), there is a general inquiry regarding the six auspicious signs in this land;

yet in the present verse, while there is the addition of "fragrant wind" and "earth purified," the phrases "preaching the Dharma" and "entering meditative concentration" are absent. Although the text appears deficient, in terms of meaning, both are encompassed. △ Second, fifty lines.
The inquiry concerning other lands is divided into six parts. The first three lines inquire about sentient beings in the six realms of existence.

The next four lines inquire about seeing the various Buddhas and hearing them preach the Dharma. The following three lines inquire about the members of the fourfold assembly in those lands attaining the Way. The final one and a half lines [inquire about the adornments of those lands].

This section concludes the preceding matter and introduces the subsequent one. It consists of five sections totaling thirty-one lines and a half: the first six or seven lines inquire about various causes and conditions;
the next three lines inquire about making offerings to the *śarīra* and erecting stupas; and the final three lines inquire about sentient beings in the six destinies.
The light from between his eyebrows shines upon the eastern direction (extending as far as... and all the beauty and ugliness of karmic retribution therein are clearly seen.
Although the land was not originally golden, it is transformed into gold by the Buddha’s radiance. Sentient beings are those who are capable of proceeding [toward enlightenment].
Birth and death are the destination. "Good and evil" constitute the cause for proceeding [to that destination].
"Receiving retribution" constitutes the fruit of that destination. Heaven and the human realm are good and beautiful;
the hells and the three miserable paths are evil and ugly. II. Four lines. Question: Regarding seeing the Buddhas and hearing them preach the Dharma.
Furthermore, [the text] says, "Beholding the Buddhas, the Holy Sovereign Lions" (extending to) "illuminating the Buddha-dharma and awakening sentient beings.

The preceding section merely mentions seeing the Buddha and hearing the Dharma; this passage extensively clarifies the characteristics of the preaching of the Dharma. Regarding the phrase "Holy Sovereign Lions": [it refers to the Buddhas].
The "Sage" (ārya) is the "Lord" (pati). "Lord" refers to the leader among his retinue, for these Bodhisattvas are the leaders within their respective circles of associates.

He is called the "Holy Lord" because he honors the four great elements with the Way and surpasses the ten stages with his virtue; he abides in the holy path himself and bestows holy virtue upon all beings—hence this title.
In the Sanskrit language, he is called Upasaṃha; here it is translated as "Lion," and also as "Śarabha."
The Great Sūtra states: "The lion lets out a roar and bellows with a thunderous sound; this is to destroy counterfeit lions and to test his own power.

This serves as a metaphor for the Buddha’s ability to crush and subdue the armies of Māra and to demonstrate the ten powers (*daśabala*) to the assembly, for his merit transcends all that is tainted (*sāsrava*).
The realization of the Way is infinite. The intoxicated elephant of impermanence cannot pursue its harm;

it is like a lion that is fearless. Yongjia said: "The lion’s roar is spoken without fear; when the hundred beasts hear it, their gallbladders all burst. This is preaching the Dharma with a single sound.

It is called "subtle and wondrous" because it responds perfectly to the capacities of beings. It is called "foremost" because, like a jade wheel turning and a pivot revolving, it encompasses all other doctrines.

It is called "pure" because the kalaviṅka-like voice of the Immortal does not cling to names or characteristics. It is called "gentle" because it reaches all according to their needs without being harsh or confrontational.
It is called "innumerable" because those of great faculties and great potential who receive transformation are vast in number. Thus, it is taught through the four *siddhāntas*.

The Dharma does not adhere to written words; this is called the "Sanskrit Sound. Though the provisional and the ultimate differ, their convergence upon the essential meaning is one; this is called "Profound and Sublime.
Those who hear the Dharma never tire of its speech; this is called "Delightful to Hear. That which all Buddhas govern, each according to a particular region, is the teaching.
Therefore, it is said that "in each world," the Dharma they preach is one where a thousand sages share the same carriage; hence, it is called the "Teaching of the True Dharma.
Sometimes they bring it forth through various causes and conditions, or illustrate it with immeasurable parables.
From the minute they lead to the vast, and from the easy they compare to the difficult; all of this is nothing other than the manifestation of the wondrousness of the Buddha-dharma.
The Way uses skillful means to awaken sentient beings, enabling them to understand and enter it. The two characters "illumination" (zhào míng) serve as a metaphor:

the Buddha-dharma is none other than our own mind. Yet, the Buddha’s treasury of the true Dharma-eye is hidden within the *ālayavijñāna* of sentient beings, like a treasure in a dark room that cannot be seen without a lamp;
only by relying on a lamp can it be seen. Humans possess this ultimate principle, yet...
If one hears the Dharma but does not understand it, one must rely on the Tathāgata’s revelation and instruction for sentient beings to finally awaken.
The "Holy Lord" herein refers to the form of Vairocana; his discourse is supreme, like the sun shining upon a high mountain as he expounds the *Avataṃsaka*.

He instructs the various bodhisattvas across the seven locations and nine assemblies. The two lines beginning with "illuminating" refer to first beholding the Buddha’s body and entering the state of the Tathāgata.
This is wisdom. △ Third, the three practices. Questioning how the fourfold assembly in other lands attains the Way:
"If a person encounters suffering and grows weary of old age, illness, and death... [until] seeking supreme wisdom, for them he preaches the pure path."

If a person follows the single practice of the Śrāvaka-yāna, they fully clarify the Four Noble Truths. "Suffering" encompasses both cause and effect, namely the two truths of Suffering and its Origin (*duḥkha* and *samudaya*).
"Weariness with old age and death" refers to the Truth of the Path (*mārga-satya*), and "speaking of Nirvāṇa" refers to the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*).

Alternatively, two of these phrases may be taken as the Truth of the Origin, and four as the Truth of the Path. If a person of small capacity is oppressed by suffering, they become weary of the cycle of birth and death within the three realms as if it were a shackle.
The character *gù* (梏) refers to explaining the *parinirvāṇa* with remainder within the context of partial emptiness.

One cultivates the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*saptatriṃśad-bodhipakṣa-dharmas*) and exhausts the limits of the suffering caused by the ninety-eight proclivities (*anuśaya*). This causes one to know suffering, abandon its origin, realize cessation, and cultivate the path, thereby attaining the Śrāvaka vehicle.
The character *jì* (際) corresponds to the preceding character *zāo* (遭); colloquially, it means "encounter" (*zāojì*). The character *jìn* (盡) implies the labor of cultivation.
Now, in response to the character "weariness" (厭): although one's circumstances may have limits, it is only through the capacity for weariness that one can begin to exhaustively sever them.
Furthermore, if a person encounters suffering yet creates evil karma, that suffering will not come to an end.

If a person encounters suffering yet creates wholesome karma, that suffering likewise will not come to an end. If a person encounters the teachings of non-Buddhist paths and seeks [liberation therein]...
Liberation [is not attained] merely by increasing views and prolonging error; suffering will likewise never be exhausted.

If a person encounters suffering and further feels weary of birth, old age, sickness, and death, and is moved to seek the Buddha who preaches *nirvāṇa* for them, then they can reach the ultimate limit where all sufferings are exhausted.

There is also a single practice of merit: that of the Pratyekabuddha Vehicle. If one’s offerings to the Buddha are few, one will encounter suffering and fall into distress; if one’s offerings to the Buddha are many, [one will not].
Although they encounter suffering, they possess merit. Thus it is said: "Śrāvakas plant the seeds of merit over three lifetimes; Pratyekabuddhas plant the seeds of merit over a hundred kalpas.

By comparing them to the Śrāvakas, it is said that they possess merit; this refers to their extensive cultivation of dhyāna. Having made offerings to the Buddhas refers to their extensive making of offerings to the Buddhas.
"Possessing merit" is the fruit of the present life, while "making offerings to the Buddhas" is the cause from previous lives. Their aspiration is to seek...
Regarding the "Victorious Dharma" (Śrāvaka): they deeply seek the sublime principle of dependent origination and have heard much of the Dharma;

it is called "victorious" because they look toward the teachings of the Śrāvakas. Regarding the "Pratyekabuddha": because they awaken to the principle of ultimate truth by contemplating the twelve links of dependent origination, they are called Pratyekabuddhas.

The *Bie xing ji* states: "In the practice of the Pratyekabuddhas, they do not establish the fruits of the stages; they deeply contemplate dependent origination and have long cultivated [the roots of virtue]."

Third, regarding "many": since their merit and wisdom are both flourishing, they have already begun to overcome the two habitual tendencies and thus rank above the śrāvakas. As for the "Buddha-sons" who practice the single path, this refers to the Bodhisattva vehicle.
Because they possess true kindness and great compassion and succeed to and flourish the lineage of the Buddhas, they are called "Buddha-sons. They constantly cultivate the six perfections.
Therefore, it is said "of various kinds. Supreme wisdom is the Buddha-wisdom. The "sons of the Buddha" (Buddhaputra) possess great capacity.

The six perfections (ṣaṭpāramitā) are the great cause. Supreme wisdom is the great fruit. Because they seek the great fruit by means of great capacity and a great cause, the Buddha expounds for them the path of the pure six perfections.
When the six perfections are free from the six obscurations, it is like medicine being free from disease. The three wheels—
The essence is empty; because it does not abide in marks, it is called the "Pure Path. △ Fourth, one and a half lines conclude the preceding section and introduce the subsequent one:
"Mañjuśrī, I abide here" (up to) "these many [teachings] shall now be briefly explained."
"In this, all are seen," and so forth, means that they are indeed seen. "The preaching of the sutras and dharmas," and so forth, means that they are indeed heard.
Because the general outline is briefly sufficient, it says, "it is like this," which concludes what preceded. "And the thousand billion matters" opens up what follows.
Since there are so many such things, it refers to what will be presented below and continues the discourse; therefore, it says, "Now I shall briefly explain. (5) Thirty-one lines.
Half [of the chapter]. It extensively inquires into the various causes, conditions, and characteristics of the bodhisattvas in other lands, divided into three parts:
first, one line of general inquiry; second, twenty-five lines of sequential inquiry; third, thirty-five and a half lines of non-sequential inquiry.
For now, the first part is the single line of general inquiry.
I see bodhisattvas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in that land seeking the Buddha-way through various causes and conditions.

Since I have asked all those great beings practicing the Way in that land—whose number is as vast as the sands of the Ganges—I have cited "various causes and conditions" as a single phrase to awaken [the understanding] that the characteristics of their faith and realization are contained therein. "Ganges" refers to the River Gaṅgā.
It is also called the Gaṅgā River; this means "Coming from Heaven. The "sand" refers to the sand within this river.
On the summit of the Snowy Mountains (Himavat) there is a lake named Anavatapta; this means "Free from Heat and Torment.

It is fifty yojanas in length and breadth, and its waters, possessing the eight meritorious qualities, fill it completely. The lake has four outlets, each one yojana wide, and from these four outlets flow four rivers.
Each [stream] circles its respective lake once. The four types of precious colors do not intermingle; they flow as turbulent currents into the ocean.
Each divides into twenty-five thousand great rivers that flow and irrigate the four continents. From the silver ox-mouth in the east issues the Gaṅgā River.
Silver sands flow together into the southeastern sea. From the mouth of the Southern Gold Elephant comes the Sindhu River; golden sands flow together into the southwestern sea.
From the mouth of the Western Vaidūrya Horse comes the Vakṣu River; lapis lazuli sands flow together [into the northwestern sea].
It flows into the northwestern sea, passes through the Lion’s Mouth at Pāriyātra, and emerges as the Sindhu River.
The waters of the Pāriyātra sands flow turbidly into the northeastern sea; this is the source of the Yellow River. Only the sands of the Ganges are as fine as flour;

outsiders consider it a river of merit (*puṇya-nadī*) and believe that bathing in it extinguishes sins. Because the Buddha conformed to worldly conventions, he frequently used it as a metaphor, taking only its [quality of being numerous].
"Many as the sands of the Ganges": this uses the great number of people to serve as a metaphor for the sands of the Ganges.

Because their reliance [on various practices] is not uniform, they are described as "various. That is to say, some seek the Buddha-way through causes and conditions such as giving (*dāna*) and observing the precepts (*śīla*).

[The section on] the twenty-five questions regarding the sequence of practices is divided into six parts: first, six lines asking about giving (*dāna*); second, two lines asking about the precepts (*śīla*); third, one...

1. Inquiry into the practice of *dāna* (generosity); 2. Inquiry into the practice of *śīla* (ethical discipline); 3. Inquiry into the practice of *kṣānti* (patience); 4. Inquiry into the practice of *vīrya* (diligence); 5. Inquiry into the practice of *dhyāna* (meditative concentration);
6. Inquiry into the practice of *prajñā* (wisdom). First, regarding the initial six inquiries concerning *dāna*:
There are those who practice giving gold, silver, and coral (up to the point of) joyfully bestowing them in order to seek the wisdom of a Buddha.
Gold and silver emerge from ore; coral emerges from the sea. It is obtained through various means. Its color is red, resembling deer antlers. An ancient saying goes:
"When a great whale swallows the seawater in a single gulp, the coral branches emerge in dense profusion. Pearls emerge from...
Oysters and clams, etc. *Maṇi* is here translated as "stainless" (*vimala*) and also as "wish-fulfilling. *Śaṅkha* comes from stone; it is so called because its form has channels.
*Musāragalva* comes from stone; it is so called because it resembles agate. These two resemble jade. *Vajra* is that which is most hard and sharp.
A *yan* is what a king rides; a *yu* is what high officials ride. "Four horses" refers to four horses.

This refers to riding together. A poem says, "Four horses at the head," referring to a team of excellent steeds. The horizontal bars are called *lán* (railing), and the vertical ones are called *shǔn* (fender).
The *huágài* (canopy) is a parasol made of colored silk. When the Yellow Emperor fought Chīyóu at Zhuólù, auspicious clouds appeared in the void to cover him;
later generations fashioned the parasol based on this. The *xuān* (lounge) is the carriage interior. The horses...
The *Yuanzhuan* says: "When positioned in front, it does not lean forward; when positioned behind, it does not tilt back. Within this there are three meanings.

Precious treasures and slaves are gifts that both the noble and the lowly can give. Chariots drawn by four horses are what the wealthy and the chivalrous bestow. Hands, feet, body, and life—[these are the gifts of the most eminent].
Only those who have attained realization are capable of this. To give away one's wife, children, treasures, and jewels—things external to the self—is the gift of material wealth (*āmiṣadāna*).

To give away one's own flesh, head, and eyes—things internal to the self—is the gift of fearlessness (*abhayadāna*). The gift of the Dharma (*dharmadāna*) is not mentioned here, as it is reserved for the subsequent *prajñāpāramitā*.

Regarding the giving of a wife and wealth, these are the remnants of the body; regarding the giving of one's life, this is the remainder for the sake of the Path. A Bodhisattva regards gold and silk as if they were excrement.
The earth. One contemplates one’s wife and concubines as being like painted vases; one views the physical frame as being like shackles; the five desires are like honey on the edge of a blade;

and this single life is like a hanging vine above a well. Thus, one accords with the nature of reality (dharmatā) and offers these practices as a gift, in order to destroy the delusions of stinginess and greed and to seek the fruit of wondrous enlightenment.
Indeed, those who cherish their own bodies and lives are [the most numerous] under heaven...
These two—the attachment to the physical body and the will to transcend the world—are as far apart as heaven and earth.

Yet, those who sleep do not perceive the urgency of a boat being secretly carried away at night; therefore, they cherish [the body]. Those who awaken deeply comprehend the principle that when the jar is pierced, the sparrow flies out.

Therefore, he distances himself from them. Some say that one must not dare to damage or injure the physical body inherited from one's parents. Have you not heard of the saying, "Rather abandon the fish and take the bear’s paw"?
To abandon the Way and instead cherish the body is to abandon the Way for the sake of the self. If one departs from the Way to pursue the body, [it is a grave error].
"Can it be said that they cherish their physical remains? The person of realization cherishes the body through the Way; they do not cherish the body for the sake of the body.
2. Question on Precepts:
"Mañjuśrī, I see various kings [who] shave off their hair and beards and don the dharma robes."
He went to where the Buddha was; "went" indicates that he did not go elsewhere, for his intention was solely to come. That which he asked was most supreme, hence it is called "unsurpassed.
He humbled himself before the dignity of the Five Emperors to honor the Way of the One Vehicle; thus it is said he "asked about the Way. He abandoned the treasures of the farthest reaches.
What has been discarded is not treated lightly; thus it is said: "Abandoning the blissful land. Adorned rafters and carved beams are called "palaces";
all the guests of the realm are called "ministers"; consorts and attendants are called "concubines. To depart from both body and mind is called "shaving the hair and beard.

Shaving the hair and beard severs the appearance and decorum of worldly truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*); donning the dharma-robes, one perfects the dignified bearing that transcends the mundane. Thus, one removes the hair.
Dyeing one's robes is the outward appearance of a bhikṣu. Discussing the precepts in relation to a bhikṣu: for those living at home, giving is easy while observing the precepts is difficult;

for those who have left the home life, giving is difficult while observing the precepts is easy. Approaching the Buddha to inquire about the Way constitutes the *śīla* of gathering wholesome dharmas (*kuśala-dharma-saṃgrāhaka-śīla*).

Relinquishing one's ministers and concubines constitutes the *śīla* of gathering sentient beings (*sattva-saṃgrāhaka-śīla*). Shaving the head and dyeing the robes constitutes the *śīla* of restraining oneself (*saṃvara-śīla*). Furthermore, by upholding these three types of precepts—...

To realize the three bodies: that which is discipline (*śīla*) consists in the non-cessation of no evil and the undertaking of the practice of the right path; it is the cause of the virtue of abandonment (*prahāṇa-guṇa*) and, through cultivation, results in the realization of the *dharmakāya*.

That which is wholesome dharma (*kuśala-dharma*) consists in the non-accumulation of no merit and the undertaking of the practice that aids the path; it is the cause of the virtue of wisdom (*jñāna-guṇa*) and, through cultivation, results in the realization of the *saṃbhogakāya*.

Regarding sentient beings, it consists in the non-failing to deliver any being and the undertaking of the practice of non-abiding; it is the cause of the virtue of grace (*anugraha-guṇa*). Through cultivation...
