This constitutes the accomplishment of the nirmāṇakāya (emanation body). Such is the benefit [of this practice], which is why various kings leave the household life to become bhikṣus. The *Pañcarājaka-sūtra* states:
"Long ago, when the Buddha was in the world, there were five kings who frequently feasted together in one place. One day, the Great King prepared a banquet;
as he was about to depart, he escorted the four other kings to the city gate and said to them, 'Why do you not each state your aspirations? One of them replied:"
At this time when the spring scenery is most enchanting, one may find pleasure in galloping horses and testing swords, or in flying hawks and hunting dogs;

first, one may find pleasure in having beautiful women attending on the left and concubines following on the right; second, one may find pleasure in governing the realm and receiving tribute from the four seas;
third, one may find pleasure in one’s parents being in good health and one’s children and grandchildren gathered together—this is the joy of a great king.
He said: "Spring passes and autumn comes; time does not wait for man. This pleasure is not constant; amidst the wind and moon, one moment may be another age. It only increases the root of suffering.
Though one may control the four quarters and be the honored sovereign of an era, there is no certainty as to what path awaits in the next life.
Parents and children are entangled by the bonds of affection, making it difficult to escape for many kalpas. The Four Kings said: "We pray—"
Hearing of the Great King’s aspiration, he said, "I wish for the dharmas of non-arising and non-ceasing. The Four Kings asked, "How may this be attained?
They then led him into the vihāra, where the World-Honored One preached the dharmas of suffering, emptiness, and so forth; the five kings immediately attained awakening.
"Having left the household life to become a bhikṣu. This is an interpretation based on the meaning. △ Third, the inquiry regarding patience in a single practice:
"Or seeing a bodhisattva who has become a bhikṣu dwelling alone in a secluded place, delighting in the recitation of the sūtras."

There are three kinds of patience (*kṣānti*). To endure without anger amidst the seclusion of forests and deep valleys, or in the presence of wicked people and ferocious beasts, is the patience of beings (*sattva-kṣānti*).
To restrain oneself and maintain one’s resolve, wearing clothes of grass and eating from trees while practicing asceticism, is the patience of suffering (*duḥkha-kṣānti*).

To seek the path of the Buddha and take no pleasure in minor fruits is the patience of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-kṣānti*). To become a *bhikṣu* is asceticism; to dwell alone in quiet seclusion is the patience of beings.

Delighting in the recitation of the scriptures is the patience of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-kṣānti*). During the reign of Emperor Huizong of the Song dynasty, Ouyang Xiu was a guest in Luoyang and traveled to Mount Song.
Upon arriving at a temple, he entered the hall and saw a monk reciting a scripture. Ouyang Xiu raised his hand, intending to speak.
Senghao did not look back at all. Xiu was surprised by this. After a short while, when the recitation of the sutra paused, he asked, "What sutra is this?

He replied, "The Lotus Sutra. He asked again, "Have you lived on the mountain for long? He replied, "For a very long time. He asked once more, "The eminent monks of antiquity were self-possessed at the moment of death."

"What path leads to this? He replied, "It is the power of concentration and wisdom. He asked, "Why is it so desolate nowadays? He replied, "The ancients were in a state of concentration and wisdom at every thought-moment;
how could they have been distracted at the moment of death? People today are distracted at every thought-moment; how could they attain mastery at the moment of death?
As he spoke these words, Xiu Bu-que knelt upon the ground. This was his practice while reciting sutras in a quiet place.
Such is the nature of man. △ Fourth, a single line questioning diligence:
Furthermore, one sees Bodhisattvas entering deep mountains with courageous and vigorous diligence to contemplate the Buddha-way.
To withstand toil without cowardice is called "valiant courage" (*vīrya*). To be pure and unmixed is called "diligence" (*vīrya*). Now, deep mountains are fearsome;
they cannot be inhabited by those who are indolent or timid. Only those who are courageous and resolute can do so. As it is said:

"Carrying a staff across one's shoulder, heedless of others, one goes straight into a thousand peaks and ten thousand peaks. Thus, those who contemplate the Buddha-way [seek it] in the depths of ravines and remote valleys.
The mountains are vast and the islands are wide; white clouds linger here. Deer and monkeys have forgotten their artifice as they contemplate the true nature (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).
Moment after moment, without ceasing, they advance in pursuit of the Buddha-fruit of Bodhi. If the mind runs toward the imperial palace, what benefit is there in dwelling in the mountains?
△ Fifth: Two lines questioning meditation.
Furthermore, he saw those who had renounced desire and constantly dwelt in seclusion, [extending] up to those who praised the King of All Dharmas with ten million verses.
Because the five desires are an impediment to the divine feet (ṛddhipāda), one must distance oneself from them. When the rishi saw the king’s daughter, a defiled mind arose within him.
This refers precisely to the loss of the supernormal powers (*ṛddhipāda*). A secluded place is a realm free from desire; therefore, one should dwell there constantly.

Eating parched grain and consuming coarse herbs, as if for the rest of one’s life. Meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) is the very essence of the supernormal powers; therefore, one should cultivate it deeply.

In a single thought-moment, ten thousand years pass like withered wood or dried dung. The *Great Commentary* states: "The self-substance of the supernormal powers is *samādhi*; thus it is said to be 'deep'."
As for "cultivation," it means entering from one dhyāna to another, and from one samādhi to another, progressing through all nine grades until they become increasingly profound.

One attains mastery over these transformations and is able to manifest the various supernormal powers (*abhijñā*); thus, it is said that one "attains the supernatural faculties. The *Śrī-mālā-devī-siṃhanāda-sūtra* states:

"The term 'spirit' (*śen*) refers to the celestial mind (*tianxin*), and 'pervasion' (*tong*) refers to the nature of wisdom (*huixing*). Regarding "the celestial mind," this is the naturally innate mind; as for the "nature of wisdom," [it is the capacity for discernment].

"Penetrating without obstruction" refers to the six [supernormal powers]: namely, the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*), the divine ear (*divyaśrotra*), knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*), recollection of past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti*), the body of sovereign power (*ṛddhivideha*), and the untainted penetration (*anāsravābhijñā*).
One should know that the innate nature of wisdom (*prakṛtiprajñā*) is associated with these six dharmas;

therefore, they are called "supernormal powers" (*abhijñā*). The mention of "five" here is because ultimate exhaustion of the outflows (*āsravakṣaya*) has not yet been attained. The preceding verse concerns mundane dhyāna.
The following verse clarifies the supramundane, supreme meditation. Regarding the one who praises the Buddha with wisdom and eloquence:

because wisdom arises from meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), and eloquence arises from wisdom, he settles into meditative absorption to contemplate the Buddha’s virtues. With palms joined and speech composed, he forms this verse.
He may compose it regarding the fruit by modeling it after the three bodies (*trikāya*), or he may summarize the myriad practices to extol the cause; thus, his metaphors and allegories differ.
Their poetic compositions differ from one another. The holy virtue of the Buddhas is inexhaustible; how could the eulogies of the Bodhisattvas ever reach their end? Therefore it is said:
"One praises the Kings of All Dharmas with ten million gāthās. Question: Since one is established in dhyāna, why speak of praising the Buddha with gāthās?
Answer: This is the dhyāna of the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao); it is not comparable to the eight stages of detachment or the nine successive attainments. Whether in stillness or distraction, it is...
They do not obstruct one another; he does not arise from the samādhi of cessation, yet manifests all modes of deportment. It is like the lute of an asura, which produces melody without being struck.
Without conditions or deliberation, it takes form when there is a stimulus. Thus, while abiding peacefully in dhyāna-samādhi, he can praise the Buddha with millions of gāthās.
This means that when he speaks, he is silent, and when he is silent, he speaks with his intent. △ Six: The Three Practices.
Questioning on Prajñā:
Furthermore, one observes that the Bodhisattva’s wisdom is profound and his resolve firm (extending to) shattering the hosts of Māra and beating the Dharma drum.

He resolves doubts and poses inquiries; his spiritual awakening is eminent and supportive. He exhausts the principles of nature (*svabhāva*) and characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), and discriminates between the provisional and the ultimate within the teachings. Therefore, it is called "wisdom" (*prajñā*).

Profound. He has given rise to the three minds and fulfilled the four vows; he wears the iron wheel without retreating and exhausts the kalpa-stones without weariness—thus it is said his resolve is firm.
He knocks at the gates and strikes the joints, skillfully inquiring into the essentials of the mind; thus he is able to question. As sound enters and the mind penetrates, [the truth is realized].

Because one maintains both the words and their meaning, it is called "receiving and maintaining" (*udgrahaṇa*). Due to the profundity of one's wisdom, one is able to inquire about the wondrous Dharma of the Buddhas;
due to the firmness of one's resolve, one hears and receives all teachings without omission.

Possessing these two adornments—being able to inquire and being able to maintain—is self-benefit. The following two lines concern benefiting others. To have concentration without wisdom is called "delusion."
Concentration. To have wisdom without concentration is called "mad wisdom. Through the profound cultivation of meditative concentration, concentration becomes complete; this is right concentration.
Through the profundity of knowledge and the firmness of resolve, wisdom becomes complete; this is right wisdom. Thus, right concentration is fully perfected.
The school of the intrinsic nature (svabhāva) is the ultimate penetration; it is fully endowed with correct wisdom and has a basis for its transmission.
By means of this self-benefit of concentration and wisdom, one is then able to draw upon proximate analogies and employ immeasurable metaphors to preach the Dharma for the sake of benefiting others.

The phrase "for the sake of the multitude" refers to those of middling and inferior faculties; the phrase "to transform all" refers to those of superior faculties. When encountering those of middling and inferior faculties—

Thus, he guides others skillfully and step by step; hence it is said that he employs "innumerable parables. When encountering those of superior faculties, he directly clarifies the Great Dharma; hence it is said that he "preaches the Dharma.
Observing the capacities of beings and preaching the Dharma to deliver them is his primary task, and thus he delights in it. Regarding "beating the drum to destroy Māra":
using the Right Path to subdue the heterodox is like beating a drum to defeat an enemy. What is called "destroying Māra" refers to the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*).

One destroys the four māras. Through provisional observation (*prajñapti-dṛṣṭi*), one destroys the eight māras; through the Middle Way (*madhyamaka*), one destroys all māras. In the Sanskrit language, *māra* means "life-taker.

Just as the Māra of Death (*mṛtyu-māra*) can truly take life, the other afflictions (*kleśa*), the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), and the Lord of Heaven (*devendra*) can act as the causes and conditions for taking life.
Furthermore, these four māras can seize the life-force of wisdom (*prajñā-jīvita*). Having thus destroyed the māras, one should...
Regarding the turning of the wheel of Dharma, what is meant by "beating the drum of the Dharma"? At the very first stage of generating the bodhicitta, one immediately attains perfect enlightenment.
Throughout a hundred Buddha-worlds, one awakens all sentient beings with the truly wondrous Brahma-voice; this is precisely the complete beating of the Brahma-wheel Dharma-drum.

The sequential questioning is now complete. (35.5 lines) Next is the non-sequential questioning. Question: Previously, you asked about the six *pāramitās* in sequence, which already encompasses all myriad practices (*sāhasra-caryā*).
Why is it necessary to ask further? It would be too cumbersome and disorganized. Answer: Sequential [questioning] follows a single, gradual path.
Non-sequential [questioning] does not restrict itself to a single path. Since these are spoken of as various causes and conditions (*nānā-pratyaya-lakṣaṇa*), they are presented in this manner.
As for the appearance [of the text], how could it be limited to two paths while being so complex?

Examining this verse-text in detail, Maitreya’s excellent questioning is orderly and systematic, and Master Kumārajīva’s skillful translation is as effortless as whirling an axe. Otherwise, the sutra text would have merely mentioned "giving."
Furthermore, regarding the mention of "generosity" (*dāna*) and so forth, it first says "seeing the various bodhisattvas," and then again says "further seeing the sons of the Buddha" (*jinaputra*).

One might perceive this as a mere redundancy of words, confused and inverted. Now, by consulting the prose commentary (*gadya*) and carefully examining the verse (*śloka*), one finally realizes how wondrous the sacred scripture is:
there is not a single superfluous character, nor a single word that is not excellent. One should know that the sequence is not fixed.
This refers to asking questions immediately upon seeing [them]. Since there are countless bodhisattvas within the eighteen thousand lands—some practicing giving here, some practicing giving there;
some sitting in meditative concentration here, and others sitting in meditative concentration there—Maitreya did not have the leisure to proceed sequentially.
He asked as soon as he saw them, in a state of great haste and urgency, only then perceiving them.
The excellence of this sequential arrangement is divided into seven sections: first, two lines inquire about *dhyāna*; second, one line inquires about diligence;
third, one line inquires about precepts; fourth, one and a half lines inquire about patience; fifth, two lines inquire about *dhyāna*; sixth, five lines inquire about giving (*dāna*);
seventh, three lines inquire about wisdom (*prajñā*). For now, we shall consider the first two lines, which inquire about *dhyāna*.
Furthermore, one sees Bodhisattvas in tranquil silence (extending to) rescuing those in the hells from suffering and causing them to enter the Buddha-way.

Initially, they practice the meditative absorption of equanimity (*upekṣā-dhyāna*). This is their own cultivation. "Tranquil" means the mind and its objects do not entangle; "serene" means being free from clamor and confusion; "silent" means cutting off words and mental images.

Sitting until the hemp cushion is worn through, they gaze until the iron wall is pierced. White mold grows upon their lips. [The birds... (Note: The final phrase "百鳥" (hundred birds) appears to be a fragmentary or corrupted ending of the source text.)
There is no place to be found; even if a Buddha were to come and offer praise, he would not so much as look back, let alone be moved in his heart by the veneration of devas and nāgas.
This is like when Śūnyatā-janman entered samādhi among the forest trees and Śakra praised him from mid-air.
Second, entering the meditative concentration of compassion is for the benefit of others; deep within mountain ranges and forest glades, he enters profound samādhi.
Because they are tormented by the sufferings of hell, he emits the radiance of moon-love. Not only does he relieve their distress, but he also causes them to enter the Buddha-way.
This is like the Bodhisattvas of the *Avataṃsaka* emitting light, whereby sentient beings in the eight difficult conditions who touch that light instantly transcend the ten stages (*bhūmi*).
△ Second, a single line of inquiry regarding diligence.
Furthermore, one sees sons of the Buddha who never sleep, walking in meditation groves and diligently seeking the Buddha-way.
Their constant walking without sleep is precisely the *pratyutpanna-samādhi* (the Samādhi of Recollecting the Buddha). Sleep is one of the four indeterminate states;
its nature is to cause the body and mind to lack mastery and to be obscured and dull. Its function is to obstruct contemplation, such that the mind becomes extremely dark and inferior.

It functions solely through the internal door; being dull and lacking discernment while in meditative concentration, it is briefly distinguished from the time of waking. Because the mind and spirit are heavy and obscured, one is unable to cultivate contemplation;
therefore, one should dispel this by means of walking meditation. This is what is meant by the "three periods of day and three periods of night," maintaining a firm resolve without wavering.
As the ancient masters said: "Stay alert! Do not allow yourself to be deceived. △ Third, the inquiry regarding the precepts of walking meditation.
Furthermore, they see those who possess the precepts with unimpaired dignified conduct, pure as a precious jewel, seeking the path of the Buddha.
"Unimpaired" refers to the *vinaya-śīla* (the precepts of discipline). The nature of the precepts is like a precious jewel because it does not admit dust.

To "possess the precepts" means that the various sections (*piṇḍa*) are without deficiency and the observance of restraint is appropriate. As for "dignified conduct," it is characterized by rigorous protection that sweeps away all defiled impurities. Deeply...
A mountain stream is insufficient to match its clarity; flying snow cannot compare with its whiteness.
Thus it is said to be "pure as a precious jewel," such as the *gośīrṣa* (cow-head) pearl or those bound by grass. △ Fourth, one and a half lines inquire about patience (*kṣānti*).
Furthermore, one sees sons of the Buddha abiding in the power of patience (up to the point where it says) they are all able to endure in order to seek the path of the Buddha.

As for patience (*kṣānti*), it means the inner mind is able to find peace because it endures external insults. There are two kinds of patience: patience regarding beings (*sattvakṣānti*) and patience regarding phenomena (*dharmakṣānti*). Regarding patience toward beings, there are two types:
first, being able to endure respectful offerings and worship without attachment, so as not to give rise to arrogance or negligence; second, [enduring] anger.

One can endure being reviled, beaten, or harmed, as well as mosquitoes and gadflies, without giving rise to afflictions (*kleśa*). There are two kinds of patience regarding phenomena (*dharmakṣānti*):
first, those that are not mental factors (*acaitasika*), such as cold, heat, wind, rain, hunger, thirst, old age, and illness;

second, those that are mental factors (*caitasika*), such as anger, sorrow, desire, pride, and various false views. To be able to endure these two types of phenomena without being moved is called patience regarding phenomena.
There are six kinds of power: the crying of a child is its power; the anger of a woman is her power; the arrogance of a king is his power;

the advancement of an Arhat is his power; the compassion of the Buddhas is their power; and the forbearance of a Bhikṣu is his power. To strike with objects in a disordered manner is called *chui* (beating);
to pierce directly with a staff is called *da* (striking). The *Bequeathed Teaching Sūtra* says: "If one cannot endure foul abuse..."
One who regards poison as if drinking nectar cannot be called a person of wisdom who has entered the Way. Monks take forbearance as their highest virtue. As the ancients said:
"If someone strikes this old fellow, the old fellow simply lies down and sleeps. The Confucians say: "Inability to endure small matters leads to the ruin of great plans.
Both within and outside the Buddhist teachings, forbearance is held in high esteem, as was the case with the Bodhisattva Never-Disparaging and the Immortal of Endurance.
...and so forth. △ Fifth: Two lines of inquiry regarding dhyāna.
Furthermore, one sees Bodhisattvas who, free from all frivolous laughter (up to) for billions of years, seek the Buddha-way.
Preventing right action through frivolous laughter increases delusion and afflictions; by drawing near to wisdom, one’s insight becomes vast.

With a single mind free from distracting thoughts, one gathers the mindfulness and places it in a single point. By abandoning frivolity, one removes the hindrances of restlessness and regret from the three karmic actions; by abandoning delusion, one removes the hindrance of ill-will.

Proximity to wisdom removes the hindrance of doubt; single-mindedness removes the hindrance of greed; and gathering the mindfulness removes the hindrance of drowsiness, because all teachings on meditation aim to be free from these five hindrances.
The *Ratnakūṭa* states: "There are four things that one should abandon by running away for a hundred yojanas:
first, gain and offerings; second, evil friends; third, evil assemblies; and fourth, dwelling together with those who engage in strife, laughter, and the like. Furthermore—

When mindfulness is gathered, the mind is immediately tranquil; when the power of concentration is deep, the light of wisdom radiates. When the mountain forest is the object of stillness, clamor is severed and serenity arises.
Amidst violent thunder and fierce winds, one is neither startled nor moved. A single thought lasts ten thousand years; ten thousand years are but a single thought.
Thus it is said that one seeks the Buddha-way for billions of kalpas. 6. The Five Practices: Inquiry on Dāna (Giving).
Or they see Bodhisattvas [providing] delicacies and food (up to) with joyful satisfaction and without weariness, seeking the Unsurpassed Way.
They provide sumptuous meals of a hundred flavors and choice foods to fill their bellies; a hundred kinds of pills and powders and wondrous medicines to cure their ailments;
fine linen for the heat and furs for the cold; garments of priceless fame or those beyond price.
Superior clothing is provided for the adornment of the body to ward off cold and heat; one requires a dwelling for rising and reclining, and a bed for sitting and lying down.

Using a dwelling made of precious sandalwood rather than common materials, and exquisite bedding rather than coarse or inferior ones, one provides for the Buddha and the Sangha so that they may rest and dwell.
When these four requisites are fully prepared, yet if one lacks the garden and pond for playing in samādhi—
Such places do not constitute a gift that accords with one's wishes. Therefore, the Bodhisattva further bestows gardens where flowers and fruits flourish in abundance;
they are lush and verdant, possessing a refined air of leisurely wandering.
There are bathing pools of pure, flowing springs, vast and shimmering, where one might sing the song of washing one’s cap at the Yi River. In all such various ways, his efforts are directed toward...
It is pure and refined; therefore, it is called "subtle and wondrous. It is free from stinginess and is bestowed with joy; therefore, it is called "insatiable.
It does not seek the causes and effects of the human or celestial realms, but seeks only unsurpassed bodhi; therefore, it is called "seeking the unsurpassed path.
△ Seventh: Three lines of inquiry regarding Prajñā.
There may be bodhisattvas who preach the dharma of quiescent extinction (up to: by means of this wondrous wisdom they seek the unsurpassed path.
The ultimate principle of quiescent extinction is fundamentally inexpressible; yet, because there are causes and conditions, it can also be expressed.
Therefore, through various skillful means, they instruct and transform sentient beings. This is the Prajñā that speaks of the inexpressible. The nature of all dharmas...

Emptiness is fundamentally unobservable; yet, by practicing in accordance with its nature, it becomes observable. Here, "observation" is the wisdom that acts as the subject, and "dharma-nature" is the object of observation.
When wisdom is practiced through the threefold contemplation, the object is simultaneously illuminated as the three truths.
By practicing in this manner, one realizes that all phenomena possess a nature devoid of dualistic characteristics, as vast and boundless as empty space.
This is the contemplation of Prajñā through that which cannot be contemplated. When the mind has no attachments, the sphere of mental activity ceases.
Because the mind does not cling, it necessarily transcends verbal expression; this is the severance of the path of language.
Through the cessation of language, one speaks while submerging that which is unspeakable. When mental activity ceases, one contemplates while submerging that which cannot be contemplated. Although...
Thus, both are extinguished; yet, without hindrance, there is speaking and illuminating. In every thought-moment one attains Buddhahood, yet one does not perceive a Buddha to be attained.
At all times regarding all phenomena, one does not perceive any phenomenon to be spoken of. Constantly saving sentient beings, one does not perceive any sentient being to be saved.

Externally, one does not follow conditions; internally, one does not dwell in meditative concentration. Wisdom exhausts the nature of reality (*dharmatā*), and practice is perfected as principle becomes complete. This is called...
"O Subhūti, by means of this sublime wisdom, one will certainly attain Buddhahood. This teaching explains Prajñāpāramitā by way of that which cannot be spoken and that which cannot be observed.

Question: Within the light, the phenomena and characteristics are manifold; yet Maitreya, in posing his questions, specifically takes up the causal characteristics of the Bodhisattva and provides a detailed, extensive enumeration of them, asking about each one in detail. Why is this so? Answer: This is precisely for the sake of the Śrāvakas...
Because it is heard by means of the preaching of the Mahāyāna sūtras, it is called the "Lotus of the Wondrous Dharma" which teaches the Dharma for Bodhisattvas.

Its purpose is to cause ordinary beings and followers of the Small Vehicle to feel shame regarding the Small and to aspire to the Great, thereby guiding those who rely on provisional means into the ultimate reality.

Thus, one should know that the text of the seven fascicles, with its single ray of light manifesting forth, contains no further hidden depths. This concludes the preceding inquiry into the various causes and conditions, etc. (6.7).
Regarding the practice of making offerings to the *śarīra* and erecting stūpas:

Mañjuśrī, furthermore, there are bodhisattvas who—like the king of celestial trees with its flowers in full bloom—after [the Buddha’s] parinirvāṇa, construct stūpa-temples as offerings to the *śarīra*, numbering as many as the sands of countless *gaṅgā* rivers; such is the number of these stūpas. They are high...
Regarding the five thousand *yojanas*: one *yojana* is forty *li*, which amounts to a height of two hundred thousand *li*.

"Vertical" refers to length; "horizontal" refers to width. Being perfectly equal in both horizontal and vertical dimensions, each of the four sides is likewise two thousand *yojanas*, resulting in a vast expanse of eighty thousand *li.
Such is the measure of this stūpa. Each of the stūpas and temples as numerous as the sands of the Ganges likewise possesses a thousand [yojanas]."
The planting of banners and streamers symbolizes the subduing of heterodoxy and the support of the orthodox.

The exposed canopy with its interlacing pearl nets, and the jeweled bells chiming in harmonious rhythm—these are the adornments of this stupa. The musical performances of devas and nāgas—these are the offerings to this stupa.
Mañjuśrī concludes [the section on] the adornment of stūpas and temples; that land is naturally wondrous and excellent.
Regarding the "King of Heavenly Trees," the Great Sūtra states: In the Heaven of the Thirty-three there is a tree named Parṇaśabada (Circle-Born).
Its roots extend fifty yojanas deep, its height is fifty yojanas, its branches and leaves spread for fifty yojanas, its fragrant flowers reach fifty yojanas, and its light illuminates fifty...
It is ten *yojanas* in height. Because this tree was cherished by Śakra, it is called the "King of Heavenly Trees" (*devadrumarāja*).

When its flowers bloom, the devas gather beneath it to enjoy their pastimes; they congregate and surround it there. One should know that within this place, the Buddha’s *śarīra* (relics) perform the work of a Buddha.
Bodhisattvas honor them in order to seek the Buddha-way. Stupas are offered to the *śarīra*, and temples are offered to the Sage.

The Buddhist shrines stand side by side like the teeth of a comb, and the banners and streamers follow one another in succession; thus they are likened to the sands of the Ganges for their vast number.

Carved beams and painted halls display extraordinary craftsmanship and exquisite design, magnificently adorning the realm. Their architectural style is towering and majestic, surpassing all in its ingenious splendor.
Banners soar toward the heavens, and bells chime amidst the clouds; pearls interlace like shimmering stars, while curtains lock in the misty vapors of dawn and dusk.
This is not merely a matter of the excellence of veneration; it is also a grand vision of the universe.
Thus, devas and nāgas rain down flowers, and humans and spirits play music, so that the True Dharma may flourish and virtuous people may increase in abundance—just like the celestial tree.
The flowers bloom with exquisite beauty, causing the celestial palaces to appear bright and pure. A subtle fragrant breeze stirs, bringing joy and delight to the devas and humans.
Thus it is said: "It is like the king of celestial trees when its flowers are in full bloom. The verse answering the preceding question is now complete.
△ Second, eight lines requesting the answer.
"The Buddha emits a single ray of light, and I, along with this assembly (up to) gaze upon you, O Benevolent One; please tell us what it is.
The Buddha emits a single ray of light, which is capable of illuminating. "I and the assembly" refers to those who are able to see by means of the light.
"The realm" refers to the sphere perceived within the Dharma assembly. By means of this single ray of light alone, there are seen such various and extraordinary [manifestations].
An especially wondrous and excellent matter. Question: Those eighteen thousand worlds in the eastern direction are at an unknown distance from Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa;
why does one say "see this" rather than "see that"? Answer:

Because of the illumination of the Buddha’s light, what is distant becomes near, as if it were before one's eyes, such that the distinction between "this" and "that" is forgotten. This is due to the power of his spiritual faculties and wisdom. It is rare.
As for "existence," it refers to the vastness, height, and thickness of the world, numbering eighteen thousand [units].

Through the causes and effects of ordinary beings and sages, the sentient and insentient realms, the duration and proximity of kalpas, and the manifold varieties of causal conditions, appearances, and convictions, they are immeasurable and boundless.
Yet, without departing from this, one perceives that; there is no distance between near and far. Without departing from a single moment, one perceives the many.

Regarding the *kalpa*, there is nothing of the past or present that is not seen—whether the hidden or manifest states of sages and ordinary beings, or the mutual relations of cause and effect—not even by the slightest fraction.
There is not the slightest confusion or disorder. If it were not for the power of the Buddhas’ supernatural penetrations and wisdom, how could it be thus?
Therefore, it is called "rare. That which emits a single pure light is able to illuminate what has limits; that which illuminates immeasurable lands is [able to illuminate the limitless].
The objects illuminated are immeasurable. From the initial verse down to the preceding section, all serve to express the doubts of Maitreya alone;
this corresponds to the prose passage beginning with "At that time, Maitreya had this thought" and ending with "I shall now question him.

From here on, the doubts are expressed for the sake of the great assembly at the Dharma-meeting; this corresponds to the prose passage beginning with "At that time, the bhikṣus... and ending with "all..."
Because he has seen the descriptions of the adornments of that land’s realm, the preceding verse says: "I dwell here; I see that land;
I see the various kings"—all of which use "I" as the subject. This is intended to seek an answer in order to eliminate his doubt;
therefore, including the great assembly, it says, "I and the assembly," meaning "we all see this. It begins with oneself...

Regarding the phrase "surpassing others" (jiānrén) and its subsequent title: at this point, the focus shifts exclusively to the assembly’s request. Thus it is said, "I pray you resolve the doubts of the multitude.

As for the phrase "the fourfold assembly looks up with joy," this refers back to the preceding text; it means that if the manifested auspicious signs were merely events from the past, the people would have no doubt.
It is precisely because they suspect that I, Maitreya, am likewise able to resolve the doubts of the assembly [that they look up with such longing].
Because this had never been seen before and was suddenly seen now, the fourfold assembly was filled with joy and reverence.

Each of them gave rise to doubt as they gazed upon the Benevolent One and looked at my own body, wondering why the World-Honored One had emitted this light from between his eyebrows to illuminate the beginning and end of the phenomena of birth and Buddhahood. Since I am unable to resolve the doubts of the assembly, the assembly [further...]
I did not dare to request this from you, O Benevolent One. Therefore, although I have made this request on behalf of the assembly, it is in truth for my own sake.

If you, O Benevolent One, resolve my doubts, then the doubts of the assembly will be resolved of their own accord. Thus it is said: "The Son of the Buddha answers in a timely manner, resolving doubts and bringing joy.
"Answering in a timely manner" refers to the intention of seeking an immediate response appropriate to the occasion. The phrase "What benefit is there," etc., precisely sets forth his doubt.

It is said that when the Buddha ordinarily preaches the sutras, he does not enter meditative absorption; when he enters absorption, flowers do not rain down; when flowers rain down, the earth does not shake;
when the earth shakes, he does not emit light; and when he emits light, such a multitude of phenomena has never before been seen within it.
Now, the Buddha acts in this manner—what benefit for sentient beings is there in this, that he first expounds it so extensively?
"Is this the radiance? [The question] "The Buddha sat beneath the tree" means: Is the Buddha now expounding this radiance?

Is it to reveal the wondrous Dharma attained by the Buddha when he first sat at the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa)? Or is it to bestow the prediction of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi upon the various bodhisattvas?
"To show the various... and so forth means: If it refers to the wondrous Dharma, it has already been taught in the past. If one says... [text ends].

Regarding the prophecy: it was already bestowed in the past, yet I never saw the light from between the Buddha’s eyebrows reveal eighteen thousand world-systems, adorned with various jewels and utterly pure, nor did I ever see so many Buddhas within those buddha-fields.
Now, as he reveals these lands and manifests these Buddhas, I know for certain that this is no small cause.
The conditions must surely be for the sake of this one great cause and condition (*ekamahākaruṇāhetupratyaya*).
With these two phrases—“preaching the Dharma” and “bestowing the prediction”—Maitreya has already finished expounding the entire *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.

All that follows, where Mañjuśrī extensively cites the World-Honored One’s praise after emerging from samādhi, is nothing other than this. Does Maitreya truly not know? Regarding this, the ancients...
A section establishing four "latent objections" (*vighāta*). As for what is called a "latent objection," Mañjuśrī internally formulates a challenge and does not immediately grant an answer;
his intention is threefold: first, this auspicious omen is rare and extraordinary, and it must not be hastily or lightly adjudicated;

second, the assembly of the wise is like the ocean, and he displays humility by deferring to their excellence; third, by being firm and reticent, he stirs the thirst and yearning of the assembly. Therefore, with these [intentions]...

The difficulties were prostrated and hidden away to be rejected. Maitreya clearly elucidated the resolution of these difficulties, and his intention was threefold: first, the auspicious signs were great and the doubts were great;
if they were not resolved, anxiety would remain in the breast, hindering the hearing of the True Dharma. Second, although the assembly in the ocean was vast...
The initiative rests with you, O Benevolent One. As the three assemblies look up to you, we know that your sincere intent is profound; therefore, you have spoken forth to resolve our difficulties.

We pray that you will answer us now. First, to subdue the objection: because Maitreya said, "O Son of the Buddha, Mañjuśrī, please resolve the doubts of the assembly," Mañjuśrī arose to subdue the objection, saying:
"You say there are doubts in the assembly, yet the assembly has never doubted. If they were in doubt, it should..."
Question: "If the assembly does not question now, it means they have no doubts. Since the assembly has no doubts, what is there for me to resolve? Maitreya explained with a verse:
"The fourfold assembly looks up to you with joy, gazing upon both you and me. They look to me because they wish for me to ask; they gaze upon you because they wish for you to answer.
Mañjuśrī then rose and presented two hidden difficulties, saying: "The assembly collectively possesses doubt; it will not be easy to answer."

"Wait until the Buddha emerges from meditative absorption, and only then resolve your doubts. Maitreya explained this with a verse: "The Son of the Buddha shall answer at the proper time, resolving doubts and bringing joy.
When doubt lingers in the breast, anxiety is as heavy as an elephant; one should therefore answer at the proper time, while also knowing when the Tathāgata will emerge from absorption.
Mañjuśrī then raised three challenges: "I and you, O Benevolent One, both dwell on the stage of training."
Wishing to fathom the Buddha’s intention, we deliberated together briefly; yet for him alone to be asked to answer was, in principle, untenable.
Maitreya explained this in verse, beginning with "The Buddha sat at the site of enlightenment," and so forth. I too had been reflecting with a subtle mind, hesitating between the two pillars:
"Should he preach the wondrous Dharma, or should he bestow a prediction? Then Mañjuśrī raised four implicit challenges, beginning with "If it were as you say..."
[The Buddha] spoke; this was to resolve doubts. Why trouble me with an answer? Maitreya explained in verse:
"To manifest the various Buddha-lands is no small matter; how can one judge the Tathāgata’s single great cause and condition [for appearing in the world] based on my own hesitant mind?
Once Mañjuśrī’s challenge had been exhausted, his humble demeanor also ceased; thus, the final verse concludes the request. Maitreya...
Lèyi thought to himself: "I am like a formless phantom; it is difficult for me to discern the Sage’s intent. You are the preeminent leader of the Dharma-gate;

I pray that you will spread the eloquence of the Three Gorges to sweep away all obstructions and stagnation. I hope you will extend your hand, long as a rainbow, to lift up those hidden like an overturned basin.
Do not fail me, nor the fourfold assembly and the dragon deities, who gaze upon the heart of the Benevolent One. Please preach the Dharma here and bestow [the teachings] upon us."
The record of these events: what was it that was taught? The words of the questions are resonant, and their meaning is profound.

The single assembly on Vulture Peak, with its exchange between host and guest, appears as if right before one’s eyes. The sequence of the introductory questions is concluded. △ Five: The Sequence of the Answers to the Questions.
There are prose passages and verse stanzas. The prose consists of four parts: first, the response by means of contemplation; second, the response by briefly citing what was previously seen;

third, the response by extensively citing what was previously seen; and fourth, the response through clear and definitive judgment. Generally, when using the inferior to fathom the superior, one can only engage in vague conjecture;
when comparing the past with the present, one cannot reach an immediate decision. Therefore, the initial [response] proceeds from the approximate, followed by the citation of brief observations.
My brief observation has not been exhaustive; I shall now further cite extensive observations to corroborate the single point with many proofs, so that the answer may be clearly adjudicated.
First, regarding the response based on contemplation:
"At that time, Mañjuśrī... [until] blew the great dharma-conch, struck the great dharma-drum, and expounded the great dharma-meaning."
"At that time," and so forth, marks the heading. "Speech" refers to addressing one another face-to-face. Facing Maitreya, his voice reached the ears of the assembly.
As for "Mahāsattva" (Great Being), there are three names for a Bodhisattva; he is sometimes called a Mahāsattva because he is a person whose mind is set upon the Great Path.
Some call him "Kaisi" (Bodhisattva), because he opens the faith of sentient beings; others call him "Gaoshi" (Noble Being), because he transcends ordinary people and those of the Lesser Vehicle.
The phrase "As I... and following constitutes a formal deliberation. The single phrase "As I" is Mañjuśrī’s manifestation of the true mechanism of the Buddha-way;
thus, he employs contemplation as a preliminary lead-in, rather than truly being ignorant and merely deliberating.
However, since these two great elders are manifestations of provisional power acting as shadows and echoes, they no longer employ actual practice.
If one does not rely on contemplation to clearly and directly reveal the Way, then the ritual of the "tongue-drum" will not be accomplished.

Therefore, the following text explicitly cites the deeds of Dīpaṃkara while implicitly revealing the strategic methods of Śākyamuni; this subtle tapping and resonant selling is the profound mystery within the reality of provisional power.
The pivot: acting secretly while appearing openly is a clever stratagem within the provisional teachings. In the previous section on doubt, it says, "One should ask whom? Who can answer?
The two characters "who" (*shui*) and "can" (*neng*) carry the implicit meaning of referring to Mañjuśrī.
Since Maitreya possesses this power of implicit indication, how could Mañjuśrī lack the skill of explicit manifestation? Therefore, it is said: "As for me..."
"Contemplate" (*cun*) means that one like me is not equal to them. "Only" (*wei*) refers to contemplation; "contemplate" (*cun*) refers to deliberation.
The meaning is that the profound depths of the Buddhas' treasury are principles not easily fathomed. When both sides are categorized together, who would not harbor doubts?

Nevertheless, observing with the eyes and reflecting with the mind, letting the intent settle and contemplating in silence, one draws upon precedents and traces back the threads to gauge the Sage’s intention; it does not go beyond this.
O Benevolent One, regarding your two questions: as I reflect and deliberate upon them, you intend to preach the Great Dharma and so forth.
"Intend" (yu) means that which is about to be preached but has not yet been preached. "Great Dharma" refers to the Sublime Dharma. My intention is this:

forty years ago, you opened up this Sublime Dharma to establish the teachings of the Three Vehicles, the Five Vehicles, and the Seven Expedient Means—discourses adapted to the capacities of beings, delivered with skillful flexibility.
To speak in accordance with the inclinations of sentient beings, following their intentions and skillfully adapting to the timing and circumstances, is not called the Great Dharma.

Today, by emitting light and manifesting signs, you wish to preach this Great Dharma of the One Vehicle; speaking according to your own intention, you reveal the provisional and the real of your own practice.
Furthermore, "great" (*da*) has the meaning of encompassing. It opens up the three to reveal the one, and brings together the provisional to return to the real.

It encompasses the five, the three, the seven, and so forth. "Rain" (*yu*) has the meaning of moistening. The Dharma taught during the forty years prior was like clouds rising over the eastern mountain and raining upon the eastern mountain, or clouds rising over the western mountain and raining upon the western mountain;
the three types of grasses and two types of trees each received moisture according to their respective capacities. It was not...
It is called the "Great Rain. Today, he intends to moisten and nourish all withered sentient beings with the rain of the Great Dharma of equal, single flavor.
This is the rain of the Great Dharma. Like oil, it forms clouds; like a torrent, it pours down the rain. As the subsequent passage states:
"A single cloud universally covers," and so forth. "Conch" (śaṅkha) signifies a proclamation. Forty years ago, by means of various...

Through causes, conditions, and parables, he guides others with steady and skillful persuasion. It is like sounding a conch shell before the vanguard when the command is given, or sounding a conch shell for the left flank when the command is given;
each follows their respective division to arrange the troops and deploy the formations. This is not yet called the Great Dharma Conch.
Today, I wish to change the commands of the Three Vehicles and return to the perfect path of the Single Reality, by means of this one...

The sound universally proclaims to the great assembly; it is the great Dharma conch. Just as when a conch is blown within the central military tent, commands are issued to those in front, behind, to the left, and to the right.
As the subsequent text states: "If there are any who hear this Dharma, not one shall fail to become a Buddha.
"Drum" carries the meaning of urging forward. Forty years ago, he may have struck the celestial drum to cause people to plant the seeds of wholesome precepts.

It is wrong. To lead the various ignorant ones to practice according to the teachings and attain the minor fruits of the Two Vehicles is like failing to call soldiers forward when using a drum to urge them on;

such a drum is not called the Great Dharma Drum. Today, I wish to strike the Great Poison-Coated Drum to urge on the indolent followers of the Lesser Vehicle, causing them to reach the place of treasure.
This is the Great Dharma Drum, like the great drum atop a general’s command post.
When struck, all the generals and soldiers will advance with valor. The subsequent passage states: "I now declare for you the most ultimate reality;
the assembly of śrāvakas has not attained true parinirvāṇa," and so forth. "To expound" (*yan*) means to proclaim and disseminate. "Meaning" (*yi*) refers to the underlying principle.
Forty years ago, I merely expounded upon birth, abiding, change, and extinction, as well as impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and the distinctions of the six perfections.
The meaning of "distinction" takes the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) as its essence; it is not called the "Great Dharma Meaning.

Today, I wish to expound the principle of the non-duality of the true mark, which is the fundamental root of the differentiation of all phenomena; therefore, it is called "expounding the Great Dharma Meaning.
Furthermore, wishing to proclaim the single phrase of the Great Dharma, I shall preach one complete cycle in accordance with the Dharma, revealing the intent of opening the three to manifest the one.

He rains down the great rain of the Dharma; this corresponds to one cycle of the parable, dousing the parching flames of the burning house so that all the children may attain coolness, such that the three types of grass and two types of trees are not separated by withering or flourishing.
He blows the great conch shell of the Dharma; this corresponds to one cycle of dependent origination.
He swept away the minor teachings of the "City of Manifestation" and discarded the stagnant attachments of the "Thatched Hut. He extensively recorded the present and prophesied the future;

he beat the great Dharma drum, responding to the merit of the Dharma Master. From the "Peaceful and Blissful Conduct" chapter, he recruited others to propagate the sutra and practice the Bodhisattva path—this was his intent to inspire and rouse.
He expounded the great principles of the Dharma from the "Emergence" chapter until the end of the sutra, thereby opening the way for the Master.

The immediate traces of the gateway reveal the remote foundation of the Buddha-ground. Together with all the Bodhisattvas who, by imperial command, transmit the sutra, they bring the Great Practice of Samantabhadra to its conclusion.
Thus, the essential purport of the entire scripture is fully expressed through Mañjuśrī’s single act of contemplation.
△ Second, the brief answer concerning what was previously seen.
"O sons of good family, it is because of [the events] from my time with the Buddhas of the past (up to) 'therefore I manifest this auspicious sign' that I have seen [them] in the past.
This refers to the passage from "I have personally attended upon... up to "...you must surely see them," which addresses Maitreya’s doubts.
How is it known that the Buddha intends to preach the Great Dharma? It is because I have seen the Buddhas of the past.
After preaching the sutra and entering meditative concentration, he then emits light; after emitting light, he immediately preaches the Great Dharma.

What is seen now is as it was in the past, and what was in the past is just as it is now. For this reason, one should know that when the present Buddha manifests light, he likewise intends to preach the Great Dharma.
The two characters "desiring to" (欲令) are the fundamental intention of all Buddhas. This Dharma which is difficult to believe is precisely the true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) of the One Vehicle.
Regarding the statement that it is "difficult for all the world to believe": this does not merely mean it is difficult for those in the evil realms to believe;

even humans and devas likewise harbor doubts about it. It is not merely difficult for ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) to believe; even those of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*) likewise harbor doubts about it.
It is not merely difficult for those of the two vehicles to believe; even bodhisattvas likewise harbor doubts about it. Therefore, it is said to be "difficult for all the world. In the past...
What I have previously taught regarding vehicles refers to these three vehicles; regarding natures, there are five natures. It is easy for people to believe this.
Now, I wish to teach that the three vehicles are one vehicle and that the five natures are one nature. This is difficult for people to believe.
Hitherto, it has only been said that the Buddha alone attains perfect enlightenment; now I say that I do not allow [others] to attain extinction alone, but that all [attain it] through the Tathāgata.
He comes to deliver them through his own extinction. For humans are difficult to trust;

he seeks to reveal, cause to awaken to, and lead them into the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, so that all sentient beings may universally hear and know the principle that "mind itself is Buddha" and that there is neither two nor three.

Therefore, he manifests this auspicious sign. Within this context, the statement "if one wishes to speak, one speaks" regarding the difficulty of belief and so forth, is not [the teaching of] Mañjuśrī.

He was willing to speak the wondrous Dharma directly, yet he employed subtle and elegant phrasing merely to consolidate faith. Thus, while the old doubts of the assembly were dispelled, new doubts arose;
it was only upon reaching the definitive response that he clearly explained and broke through them. Furthermore, the single phrase "difficult to believe" is of the utmost importance.

In the subsequent text, after emerging from meditative concentration, there is a double praise, followed by the raising of doubts by the twelve thousand [bodhisattvas], the opening of the near to reveal the far, and the raising of [doubts] by Maitreya.
Doubtful; all are difficult to believe. △ Third, the detailed response based on what was previously seen. This section is more explicit than the brief account.
Previously, Maitreya saw the eastern direction horizontally due to the light and used this as his question; here, Mañjuśrī cites an ancient precedent of seeing vertically to provide the answer.
The horizontal and vertical perspectives reveal that the Way of all Buddhas is the same. The text is divided into three parts; first, citing the identity of one Buddha.
Second, the similarity with twenty thousand Buddhas; third, the similarity with the final Buddha. Now, first, the similarity with one Buddha:
"O sons of good family, just as in the past, immeasurable and boundless [Buddhas]... attained all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*)."
The section "Past" below clarifies the temporal period. *Saṃkhyeya* in Sanskrit is translated here as "incalculable" (*wúshù*). *Kalpa* is translated as "long duration.
Terms such as "immeasurable" (*wúliàng*) and so forth describe the vastness of the number of *kalpas*, signifying that the Way of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*) transcends all common reckonings.
"Then there was a Buddha... and so forth. This indicates his name; his specific title is Candrasūryapradīpa (Moon-Sun-Lamp Radiance).
The *Xuàn zàn* states: "The sun has two capacities: first, to guide with light; second, to bring to maturity. The moon has two capacities: first, to remove heat; second, to provide coolness.

The lamp has two capacities: first, to dispel darkness; second, to transmit illumination. This reveals that the Buddha guides those who are deluded toward awakening, matures their faculties to become vessels for the Dharma, and removes [afflictions].

The heat of the afflictions (*kleśa*) is cooled by the attainment of *nirvāṇa*. By manifesting through birth-by-transformation (*upapāduka*) to transmit the Dharma, one shatters the darkness of ignorance;
because it possesses this efficacy, this name is established. It is also a designation for the perfection of the three virtues (*triguṇa*).

As for how the specific appellations are identical, they should be explained as having distinct names but identical meanings: the sun is wisdom (*prajñā*), and the moon is meditative concentration (*samādhi*); these represent the practice of concentration and wisdom within oneself. The lamp—

This clarifies the virtue of transforming others. The titles of the Buddhas—such as "Able Sage" (Nengren), "Able in Concentration and Wisdom" (Nengdinghui), and "Able [to benefit] Self and Others" (Neng Zita)—are designated differently according to conditions;
however, their meaning is not distinct. The term "Tathāgata" (Rúlái) below is a general title. "Tathāgata" means one who emulates and accords with the virtues of former worthies.

Now, because the present Buddha emulates the re-coming of the Buddhas of the past, the principle of unshakable original enlightenment (*mūla-bodhi*) is called "Suchness" (*tathā*), and the wisdom of investigative and illuminating initial enlightenment (*ādi-bodhi*) is called "Coming" (*āgata*).

This means that when wisdom arises from the state of an ordinary being to sever delusions, and once delusions are exhausted and wisdom itself vanishes, one wondrously accords with the principle of Suchness;
thus, the initial and the original are non-dual, and this is termed "Tathāgata. Furthermore, there is nowhere from which he comes, nor...
Because there is nowhere to go, he is named Tathāgata. Furthermore, the meaning of the "suchness" (tathatā) of all phenomena is precisely the virtue of the Dharmakāya.

As for "Arhat" (Worthy of Offerings), it is a title signifying one who is worthy of being a field of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*). Possessing both merit and wisdom, having realized the perfect enlightenment of the Way, and being capable of serving as the cause for humans and devas to plant seeds of merit, he is thus called "Arhat.
The subsequent text states: "He is universally worthy of receiving offerings therein," which refers to this.

This is the virtue of liberation (*vimukti-guṇa*). "Perfectly Complete Enlightenment" (*samyak-saṃbuddha*) is a title for the universal knowledge of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). "Perfectly" (*samyak*) distinguishes it from the heterodoxy of external paths;

"completely" (*saṃ*) distinguishes it from the partiality of the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*). Whether it be the upright pines and crooked thorns, or the white crane and black crow, he thoroughly understands their fundamental causes.
Even beyond worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, he knows the number of drops in a single drop of rain. This is the virtue of wisdom (*prajñā-guṇa*).

Furthermore, "One Perfected in Knowledge and Conduct" (Vidyācaraṇasampanna) is a title that reveals the fruit based upon causal virtues. "Knowledge" (vidyā) refers to wisdom; "conduct" (caraṇa) refers to merit.

Because the accomplishment of the qualities of the fruit relies upon both merit and wisdom, one is "perfected in knowledge" by upholding the True Dharma, and "perfected in conduct" by making offerings to all Buddhas.
When merit and wisdom flourish together, they induce ten thousand virtues as the result; thus, one is called "Perfected in Knowledge and Conduct. "Well-Gone" (Sugata) refers to the sublime...
He proceeds to the name "Bodhi" (Awakening). Having exhausted the five stages of dwelling and perfected the practice of the Way, he reaches the ultimate limit of wondrous enlightenment.
Only then does he turn his vessel back, mounting the compassionate boat, to manifest the attainment of perfect awakening at the gateway of the present moment; hence it is called "Wondrous Departure.

As for the title "Knower of the World," it signifies reaching the false and penetrating the true. Within the three worlds, there is not a single phenomenon of form or mind that is not pure; thus, he is...
By means of the two wisdoms of the provisional and the ultimate, one thoroughly realizes that illusions and falsehoods are universally identical with the single reality.

First is the vessel-world (*bhājana-loka*), referring to mountains, forests, and so forth; it is called a "vessel" because it contains sentient beings. Second is the world of sentient beings (*sattva-loka*), referring to the four modes of birth and the six realms of existence, each possessing distinct conscious minds.
Third is the world of the perfectly awakened ones through wisdom (*jñāna-saṃbuddha-loka*), referring to the sages and saints of the three vehicles.
Because he possesses the right path of awakening, the Unsurpassed One (Anuttara), the Tamer of Men (Puruṣadamyasārathi), gathers and transforms beings through the name of following the Path.

Having exhausted the five abodes and forever extinguished the two deaths, his fruit and virtue are perfectly accomplished; transcending both the mundane and supramundane, he alone is called "Unsurpassed.
For all those who have attained awakening among humans, devas, and the three vehicles are termed "surpassed. Thus, he refines and governs [beings].
Because he is able to preach and able to practice, he is called a "great man" (puruṣa). All sentient beings fail to awaken to the Buddha’s knowledge and vision;
they transmigrate through the six realms of existence without rest. Therefore, our World-Honored One employs the teachings of the Three Vehicles to regulate and guide them.

It is so that they may, from the state of ordinary beings to that of the sages, awaken to the Buddha’s vision and knowledge. The title "Teacher of Gods and Humans" refers to the teaching of the Dharma in accordance with capacities;
as a model for gods and humans, he teaches the Dharma according to their faculties, universally benefiting those of the three root-capacities and causing them to return to the single tranquility.

The title "Buddha" refers to the perfection of the three types of awakening: self-awakening distinguishes him from ordinary beings, awakening others distinguishes him from the followers of the two vehicles, and completeness distinguishes him from [those who have not yet reached full realization].

"Bodhisattva" is a title for one who is uniquely honored in the world. Because the Buddha alone is uniquely honored both within and beyond the world, [the text] says "expounds," which clarifies the teaching of the Dharma.
To distinguish it from the scriptures of the four classes of followers and so forth, it is called the "True Dharma.

It is "Great" because it encompasses all dharmas; it is "True" because it is free from all marks; it is "Sublime" because it is neither identical to nor separate from, and neither is nor not is. All of these—

First is the Dharma of the True Mark (lakṣaṇa). This refers to the appearance of the Buddha Candrasūryapradīpa in the world, wherein he proclaimed and expounded the True Dharma for the sake of all sentient beings, causing them all to reach the ground of wisdom.
This phrase serves as a general heading indicating that the teachings throughout his entire lifetime were none other than the True Dharma.
Regarding the section beginning with "excellent in the beginning," the ancient and modern commentaries differ; Tiantai alone provides an interpretation specifically for the *Avataṃsaka*.
To combine the sudden teaching with the sequence of the correct transmission—such as this, every single word would be unskillful.

In discourse that accords with the nature of reality (*dharmatā*), there is truly no such thing as "skillful" language. Wēnlíng’s commentary interprets this opening of the three vehicles as the three virtues.

Because all [teachings] accord with the Dharma at their respective times. Thus, the meaning is profound and far-reaching; otherwise, even a single phrase would be contradictory. Now, to explain the "three excellences":
generally, throughout the various Buddhas' appearances in the world, the temporal teachings (*kāla-śāsana*) taught during their entire lifetimes are divided into three periods.

This is analogous to the three seasons of a year in the Western Regions (India), or the three divisions of a day, the meanings being identical. These three "excellent" characters (*śubha*) extend even to the word "good" (*kuśala*).
This goodness refers to the ultimate principle of the true mark (*lakṣaṇa*) of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*). Regarding the three periods:

in the first period, he taught the Great Teaching of the *Avataṃsaka*, primarily for those of superior faculties and sharp wisdom; in the middle period, he taught the teachings of humans, devas, and the three vehicles, reaching those of the three [lesser] faculties;
and in the final period, he taught the Dharma of the equality of the true mark of the One Vehicle, universally reaching all.

Although the capacities of those of the three vehicles and five natures differ according to the distinct teachings given during the three periods, the principle taught by the Tathāgata originally flows forth from the single true reality (dharmatā) and is fundamentally non-dual; therefore, all are called "excellent."

There is no non-returning to the ground of ultimate goodness. These words are the skillful discourse of Mañjuśrī’s great wisdom. First, he provides a general indication that the principle of the entire dispensation is identical;
below, he explains the distinctions in meaning across the three periods. Regarding the profound and far-reaching significance:

this explains the "initial goodness" mentioned above, which refers to the preaching of the *Avataṃsaka*. This is the path of the Buddha’s own cultivation and realization, cultivated over vast eons and traversed through...
It is realized after three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*, yet it is unknown to humans and devas and cannot be fathomed by those of the two vehicles; therefore, it is called "profound and remote.
Regarding the phrase "its words are skillful," this explains the excellence of the middle [period]: it refers to the teaching of the three vehicles.

The Dharma of the true reality (*dharmatā*) of the one vehicle, in accordance with the dispositions and desires of sentient beings, conceals the ultimate and establishes the provisional, teaching the three [vehicles] through differentiation—namely, the teachings such as the *Āgamas*. These are words spoken according to the intentions of others.

It is called "skillful" (*qiao*). To rely on the provisional (*quan*) to manifest the ultimate reality (*shi*) is called "wondrous" (*miao*). Regarding the phrase "pure, singular, and complete," this explains the "excellent conclusion" (*houshan*) above;
it refers to the teaching of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* and *Nirvāṇa* sūtras. It speaks purely of the principle of true reality (*shixiang*), converging toward the path of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*).
It is called "pure and singular," meaning there is neither a second nor a third; this alone is the one true reality.

It is called "unmixed," meaning that while fully cultivating the six perfections and extensively encompassing myriad practices, one remains unstained by even a single speck of dust, with essence and characteristics mutually integrated. It is called "complete and equal.

The upper phrase refers to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* (Lotus Sūtra), and the lower phrase refers to the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*. The passage beginning with "for the sake of seeking" provides a detailed explanation of the intent behind teaching the three vehicles (*triyāna*), as it accords with the capacities of sentient beings.
It is appropriate to speak of the three vehicles (*triyāna*), yet the Buddha’s intention is solely for the one vehicle (*ekayāna*); fundamentally, there are neither two nor three.

For those who seek the state of a *śrāvaka*, he teaches the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths to respond to them, causing them to sever delusions and cross over birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*), entering the Path and realizing *nirvāṇa*.

Because they hear the Buddha’s voice and teachings, they are called *śrāvakas* (hearers). Because all four are examined with precision and are not false, they are called "Truths" (*satya*). [The first is] Suffering (*duḥkha*).

The causes and effects of the mundane world are gathered [in the Truth of Suffering]; the supramundane causes and effects of cessation and the path [are gathered in the Truths of Cessation and the Path].
As for *nirvāṇa with remainder*, why speak of "ultimate" [nirvāṇa] to cause others to rejoice and take it as their realization? It is because it is taught as a skillful means (*upāya*).

For those who seek the state of a Pratyekabuddha, one teaches the law of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) to respond to them; one responds to their seeking according to their inclinations and desires. First, regarding ignorance (*avidyā*): it is so called because there is no clear understanding.
2. The two types of formations (*saṃskāra*), because they involve volitional construction. 3. The false consciousness that enters the womb is called *vijñāna*. 4.

The mental and physical aggregates within the womb are called *nāmarūpa*. 5. The six sense faculties within the womb; because these faculties have the function of entering toward their objects, they are called "entrances" (*āyatana*).

6. Contact (*sparśa*); this occurs after birth when the faculties encounter their respective objects. 7. The experiencing of the preceding object is called feeling (*vedanā*). 8. Craving for the five desires is called... [craving] (*tṛṣṇā*).

1. Craving (*tṛṣṇā*). 2. The pursuit of sensory objects is called grasping (*upādāna*). 3. The non-disappearance of cause and effect is called becoming (*bhava*). 4. Receiving again the body of the five aggregates is birth (*jāti*). 5.
The maturation and decay of the body is old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*). These arise through successive induction of effects as causes; they mutually depend upon one another as conditions.
By contemplating these twelve links, one awakens to the principle of the True Truth (*satyārtha*); therefore, it is called dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).

For those who have awakened and serve as great roots for bodhisattvas, he teaches the Dharma of the six perfections to correspond to their needs, enabling them to attain the fruit of Buddhahood in its full perfection.
Although the teachings of the three vehicles differ, the World-Honored One’s fundamental intention is no different;
it is none other than to cause them to attain unsurpassed bodhi and achieve all-encompassing wisdom (*sarvākārajñatā*). All-encompassing wisdom means that one is able to—
There is one kind of wisdom that knows the path and dharma of all Buddhas and knows the causal seeds of all sentient beings.

It is able to know and understand the single mark of quiescent extinction and their various types of practices; this is called "all-aspect wisdom" (*sarvākārajñatā*), which is precisely the wisdom of the Buddha.
Mañjuśrī’s skillful discourse caused those of the two vehicles in the assembly to reflect and contemplate for themselves upon what they had rejoiced in forty years prior.

They delight in inferior teachings and cling to a partial emptiness, thereby failing for a long time to fulfill the World-Honored One’s intention to cause all sentient beings to universally attain the knowledge of all modes.
△ Second, citing twenty thousand Buddhas who concur.
Next, there was another Buddha also named Candrasūryapradīpa (Moon-Sun-Lamp Brightness), [and so on] until [the description that] the Dharma he taught was excellent in the beginning, middle, and end.
Twenty thousand Buddhas had names and teachings identical to his. *Phalada* means "swift" or "sharp-facultied" (*tīkṣṇendriya*);
because his faculties were sharp and swift, he did not contradict the sentiments of sentient beings, and thus he is also called "One of Full Speech," for what he says is never... [incomplete].

Second, because they fulfill the hearts of the assembly, they are excellent in the beginning, middle, and end. According to Tiantai, these twenty thousand Buddhas taught only the *Avataṃsaka* and did not teach the Tripitaka or the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*.
According to Wenling, these twenty thousand Buddhas taught only the Tripitaka and lacked the *Avataṃsaka* and the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*.
Therefore, we know that the three excellences mentioned in the preceding section undoubtedly encompass and unify the entirety of the Buddha’s lifetime teachings. It is not so.
However, why does Mañjuśrī’s introduction to twenty thousand Buddhas mention only the "three virtues"?
Furthermore, the beginning and end of these twenty thousand Buddhas are fully described in just over seventy words; this is the marvelous skill of Master Kumārajīva’s translation hand.

△ Third, the final Buddha is the same. This is divided into three parts: first, the events previously witnessed are identical to those of the present; second, the events previously witnessed are [identical] to the present... [text fragment ends].

The same. Third, previously witnessed events are the same as those of the present and the future. "Previously witnessed" refers to the distant past; "already experienced" refers to the recent past; the six auspicious omens refer to the present;
and departing from meditative absorption refers to the future. Now, first, previously witnessed events are the same as those of the present and the already-experienced.
Regarding that last Buddha, before he had left the household life (up to the point where it says): "He had already planted the roots of all wholesome virtues under ten million Buddhas.

According to the *Śāstra*, while Dīpaṃkara was a layman, he was a Wheel-Turning King (*cakravartin*) who actually had eight sons; although the accounts of his having sons are similar [to other cases], they are nonetheless distinct.
In fact, the subsequent passage intends to establish that the eighth son attains Buddhahood, named Dīpaṃkara (Dīpankara).

In terms of the Dharma, the eight sons represent the eight consciousnesses (*vijñāna*), while the Buddha represents the mind-king (*citta-rāja*). The eight sons in their secular state are a metaphor for the mind-king, while still enmeshed in *saṃsāra*, transforming into the eight consciousnesses.
As for the fact that all eight sons are called "mind" (*manas*), the mind is the function of the heart-mind; fundamentally, they are one single mind.
As for its essence (*tattva*): it is divided into the functions of the eight consciousnesses. Although these functions differ, their essence is one.

This is because there is that which perceives—namely, the visual consciousness seeing forms—and there is the capacity for discernment; furthermore, there is the suffering of birth and death, and the bliss of nirvāṇa. As for its goodness (*kuśala*): [it is so called because...]
The ear-consciousness hears sounds; it clearly distinguishes between good and evil, skillfully transcends all states of existence, and skillfully enters the six sense objects.
Regarding "Immeasurable": the nose-consciousness smells fragrances; it is formless and immeasurable, being indestructible and unmixed. Regarding "Jewel": the tongue-consciousness discerns tastes;
it is the jewel that sustains the body and life, and furthermore, it is the jewel of the supramundane Dharma through unimpeded eloquence. Regarding "Increasing": the body-

Consciousness perceives contact. When it increases or decreases within the body, its increase constitutes suffering and its decrease constitutes bliss. "Eliminating doubt" means that the mental consciousness cognizes phenomena;
through this, it eliminates doubt and attains thorough understanding, for it eliminates doubts regarding both facts and principles and thoroughly understands the delusions of birth and death.

"Echo" refers to the four [afflictions], such as self-delusion (*ātma-moha*), which are associated with the seven consciousnesses; they constantly and persistently take the eight [consciousnesses] as their internal self, just like an echo.

"Because it follows sound. Regarding "the dharmas": this refers to the eight consciousnesses containing and storing all dharmas—whether with outflows or without outflows, wholesome or unwholesome, erroneous or correct.

Regarding the two phrases on "majestic power and sovereign mastery": this refers to the spontaneous and autonomous functioning of the eight consciousnesses. Regarding "the eight consciousnesses remaining in bondage":
this means they are constrained by the four great elements. Regarding "the King leaving home to become a Buddha": this refers to the mind-king (*citta-rāja*) being free from delusion.

This is the realization of truth. "Renouncing the royal throne" means to weary of the glory of the outflows (*āsrava*) within the three realms and to rejoice in the unconditioned path of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*).
"Also following [the Buddha] into the homeless life" refers to the transformation of the eight consciousnesses from defilement to purity. This is what is meant by "having this as one's father."

There must surely be these sons. If they are deluded, they are deluded together; if they awaken, they awaken together. The lamp is the essence; the eight sons are the manifestations within the traces.
The father begets the eight sons: this is the descent of the trace from the essence. Their following the father into renunciation is the convergence of the trace back to the essence.
The meaning of the Mahāyāna is simply the equality of the three minds and the four great vows; that which is practiced remains undefiled.
To be fully endowed with purity is called the "Brahma-faring. To have no indolence in the mind and to keep this in constant mindfulness is called "constant cultivation.

Each, having perfected the Way within themselves and established a model for the world, is called a "Dharma Master. Regarding these two phrases, the cause is clarified as profound; now one enters the stage of the sages.
This does not arrive without cause, nor does it arrive through a false cause. It is not a matter of one or two [lifetimes].
The Buddha plants all roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*). Because internal causes and external conditions serve as the foundation for all virtues, they are called "roots of goodness.

Question: In the past, the Buddha had eight sons; now, the Buddha has one son. How can these two cases be the same? Answer: Although the numbers are unequal, the eight and the one each respond to different conditions.
Both emerge from the Land of Common Residence (*sahā-lokadhātu*); the eight represent the Eightfold Noble Path, while the one represents the One [Vehicle].
The Way is pure. Now, taking the matter of having sons as a point of comparison: in the past, the eight sons left the household life and resolved upon the Mahāyāna;

now, the Buddha’s one son abides in the fruit of the Hīnayāna. How can you say they are the same? In the past, the path of transformation was already completed, so his original nature was revealed, and thus it was said that he resolved upon the Mahāyāna.
Now, his true identity has not yet been disclosed, so he is still called an Arhat; this will only be revealed later.
The fundamental nature is itself the Bodhisattva; their meaning is identical. △ Second, the fact that what was seen in the past is the same as now.
This also has two parts. First, the similarity of present appearances.
At that time, the Buddha Candrasūryapradīpa preached a Mahāyāna sūtra (up to) "just as these buddha-fields are seen now.
