There are six auspicious omens, following the sequence as in the text. The two phrases "just as these are seen now" encompass everything from the section below down to the emergence of the seven-jeweled stūpas;
the sūtra compiler likely feared excessive prolixity. △ Second, the shared doubt and reflection.

Maitreya, you should know that at that time, within the assembly—[from "up to" the point where they] wish to know the causes and conditions for which this light was manifested—one should follow the previous [format].
At that time, a certain bodhisattva will have a thought; this section of text [describes] that. Now, the entire assembly of the Dharma is being mentioned collectively.

Therefore, twenty billion beings who desired to hear the Dharma were encompassed by these words. To wish to know the causes and conditions for which this light appeared was precisely the state of doubt and reflection.
Question: Since it is said that signs were manifested and there was doubt and reflection, why is there no mention of an assembly gathering to pose questions or receive answers?
Answer: By logical inference, such an assembly must exist. Since the teaching of the Dharma necessarily involves the gathering of a multitude, and since there was doubt and reflection...

There must have been a question; where there is a question, there must be an answer. If it were said that a certain bodhisattva asked and a certain bodhisattva answered in the past, then there would be no need for Mañjuśrī to expend words.
Since neither the answer is mentioned nor the question is set forth, [the point is established].

Third, the events witnessed in the past are identical to those of the present. This is further divided into six parts: first, the identity of the persons; second, the identity of the dharma taught; third...

The timing is the same; fourth, the proclamation of extinction is the same; fifth, the bestowing of predictions is the same; sixth, the mastery of the sutras is the same. First, regarding the identity of the person:
at that time, there was a bodhisattva named Wonderful Light who had eight hundred disciples.

The Sage has no name; it is through his virtues that he is made manifest. His supernormal powers being unfathomable, they are called "wondrous" (miao); his brilliant illumination of the masses in their darkness is called "light" (guang).

Furthermore, this Bodhisattva profoundly penetrates the provisional and the real, and their integration is "wondrous"; his two wisdoms awaken the multitudes of sentient beings, which constitutes "light.
Formerly, the Buddha’s eight sons were disciples of Miaoguang (Wonderful Light). When the Buddha arose from meditative concentration, he preached the Lotus Sūtra for Miaoguang.

Now, the Buddha’s disciple Rāhula is the teacher of Śāriputra; the Buddha emerged from meditative concentration below to preach this sutra for Śāriputra. This is because their causal origins are the same. Some may ask:
"Miaoguang is a bodhisattva, while Śāriputra is a śrāvaka; how can they be the same? When we compare them at the stage of manifesting their true stations, Śāriputra was also a bodhisattva.
As for Miaoguang, he manifested his traces as a śrāvaka; it is not necessarily the case that he was not one.

Mañjuśrī’s skillful exposition is merely a matter of the concealment or manifestation of skillful means (*upāya*). [The phrase] "There were eight hundred disciples" serves as a pivot for the subsequent text.
Later, when Maitreya emerges, he is indeed one of those eight hundred. The *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-ṭīkā* states:

"The teacher possesses the capacity for creative accomplishment, while the student possesses the virtue of being receptive to instruction. Being receptive means abandoning one's father to follow the teacher, honoring the teacher as one would a father. Regarding the teacher—
He was humble and deferential, treating his supporters as if they were younger brothers. △ Second, the identity of the teaching:
At that time, the Buddha Candrasūryapradīpa arose from samādhi (up to) the Dharma for instructing bodhisattvas, which is protected by the Buddhas.

"Must rely on Wondrous Light" means that the Buddha Dīpaṃkara represents the principle of original enlightenment (*mūla-bodhi*), while Wondrous Light represents the wisdom of initial enlightenment (*ādi-bodhi*).
Since this principle cannot be realized without wisdom, the sutra was preached by relying on Wondrous Light. Furthermore, regarding this Wondrous Light:
It is inherently possessed by all people, constant and eternal from time immemorial. Lamp after lamp continues in succession; light after light is perfectly interfused.
Therefore, in preaching the Lotus Sūtra, one must rely on this wondrous light that is without interruption. The title of the sūtra is "Wondrous Dharma.
As Mañjuśrī stated previously, "I wish to preach the Great Dharma," and again, "the Dharma difficult to believe. Having exhausted every subtle nuance and winding turn, we arrive at this point.
Without concealment or hesitation, he first proclaimed the title of the sutra. △ Third, the time period is the same:
for sixty minor kalpas he did not rise from his seat (until) there was no weariness or fatigue arising in either body or mind.
Sixty minor kalpas are like the duration of a meal; now, fifty minor kalpas have passed like half a day.

This is their commonality. The scriptural text is not false. The sincerity with which one hears the Dharma and the Buddha’s inconceivable majesty mean that one may pass through kalpas while sitting in a single posture, forgetting only the length of time.
It is like the world’s dream of the yellow millet porridge, or the seven days spent in the mountains—these can be inferred by analogy. Furthermore, it is great...

The Awakened One established the teachings, possessing a power of spiritual transformation that is unfathomable. He can extend a single day into an eon (*kalpa*) and condense an eon into a single moment.
It cannot be considered a preposterous claim to say that sixty minor eons (*antara-kalpa*) pass as quickly as eating a meal.
Speaking in terms of the increase and decrease [of lifespan]: when the human life span is ten years, a son’s age is twice that of his father’s; thus it increases until—
Eighty-four thousand years ago, the lifespan decreased by one year every hundred years; thus it decreased until it reached ten years.

One period of increase and decrease constitutes a small kalpa (*antarakalpa*). Twenty such periods of increase and decrease constitute a medium kalpa (*madhyakalpa*), comprising the phases of formation, abiding, destruction, and emptiness.

Twenty such cycles of increase and decrease constitute one great kalpa. Now, the appearance of Śākyamuni in the world occurs precisely during the ninth period of decrease within the twentieth small kalpa.
△ Fourth, the proclamation of his parinirvāṇa is the same.
The Buddha Candrasūryapradīpa [will remain] for sixty intermediate kalpas (until) he enters *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*.
Brahmā is the lord of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*); Māra is the lord of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*). "Brāhmaṇa" means one of pure conduct; it refers to a practitioner living at home.

Midnight symbolizes the state of non-action (*asaṃskṛta*) and the correct position. Formerly, when the Buddha finished preaching the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, he immediately announced his extinction. Now...

The *Ratnakoṭi-parivarta* (Chapter on the Jeweled Stūpa) states: "The Tathāgata shall before long enter parinirvāṇa; his work of transformation is complete. This proclamation of extinction is similar [to other accounts].
*Nirvāṇa* is translated here as "Perfect Quiescence" (*yuánjì*), because all virtues are perfected and all delusions are eternally stilled.

It is also called "Extinction and Deliverance" (*mièdù*), because the two obstacles are extinguished and one is delivered from the two types of death. Furthermore, it is called "Unconditioned" (*wéiwéi*), because it is free from arising and ceasing. Moreover—

It is called "peaceful security" because it is supremely quiescent; in essence, it is the single Truth. Even in the Hīnayāna, there is the distinction between *sopadhiśeṣa* (with remainder) and *nirupadhiśeṣa* (without remainder).

When the bonds of the "son" [the afflictions] are exhausted but the bonds of the "fruit" [the body] still remain, it is *sopadhiśeṣa*; when both body and wisdom have vanished like ashes, it is *nirupadhiśeṣa*.

In the Mahāyāna, one speaks of *nirupadhiśeṣa* when the five stages (*pañcavihāra*) are fully perfected and the two types of death (*dvividhamaraṇa*) are eternally extinguished. This is a brief explanation; a comprehensive discussion [would follow].

There are three [purities]: first, natural purity (*prakṛti-viśuddhi*), which is the equality of ordinary beings and sages; it is the *dharmakāya*. Second, complete purity (*pariśuddhi*), which is the perfect clarity resulting from the removal of hindrances;

it is *prajñā*. Third, purity of skillful means (*upāya-viśuddhi*), which manifests birth and extinction; it is *vimukti*. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* opens this into four: first, *svabhāva-viśuddha-nirvāṇa*, which is the principle of *tathatā*;
it is fundamentally neither born nor extinguished, though it is temporarily obscured by adventitious hindrances.

That which is covered is by nature fundamentally quiescent; the existence of sentient beings is not dependent upon cultivation for its attainment. Second is the *sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* (nirvana with remainder):

although views and afflictions (*kleśa*) have been stilled and true suchness has emerged from the obstacle of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*), there still remains the final body and the basis for the suffering of birth and death through fragmentation (*pariccheda-jāti-maraṇa*);

this is that which is attained when the three vehicles realize the path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa-mārga*). Third is the *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* (nirvana without remainder), by means of which [the afflictions...]
Once [the afflictions] are exhausted, the remaining basis (*upadhi*) also ceases, and all suffering is eternally stilled; there is no further basis remaining.
This is what is realized when the body and wisdom of those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) in the three vehicles are exhausted. It is the fourth [state], the non-abiding [nirvana]:

namely, true thusness (*tathatā*) from which the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) have further emerged, wherein compassion and wisdom are conjoined, abiding neither in saṃsāra nor in nirvāṇa. Until the end of the future, it is quiescent yet ever-illuminating, benefiting [sentient beings].
To benefit sentient beings. Among these four, ordinary persons possess only one; noble ones possess three; and only a Buddha possesses all four.
△ Fifth, the bestowal of prophecy is the same.
At that time, there was a bodhisattva named Guṇakośa (至) who was to become an Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha.

Regarding the term "Treasury of Virtue" (*guṇagañja*): it signifies that there are no *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka-sama* (as many as the sands of the Ganges) virtues that are not fully possessed; this is the meaning of "containing" (*saṃgraha*), which refers to self-benefit.
To universally bestow these virtues upon sentient beings is the meaning of "producing," which refers to the benefit of others. The noble speech of "giving" (*dāna*) is termed "bestowing" (*pradāna*).

The "prediction" (*vyākaraṇa*) is the granting of a fruit in accordance with one's mental aspiration. Regarding the "pure body": it is because the body is adorned with the primary and secondary marks (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*) and its essence is luminously pure; thus, [it is] manifold.
"Tathāgata," "Arhat," and "Samyaksaṃbuddha" are the three titles of the Tathāgata. Question: In the past, the Buddha preached the sūtras and transmitted them to Bodhisattvas;
now, this sūtra is transmitted to Śrāvakas. Why do you say they are the same? Answer: In the past, the task was already accomplished, so he spoke of Bodhisattvas;
now, the ultimate convergence is at hand, so he speaks of Śrāvakas. Question: For what reason did he preach the sūtra for the sake of Prabhāketu and transmit it to him?

This is a record concerning Guṇasaṃbhara. [The author] replies: Miao Guang (Wonderful Light) was the primary recipient of the teaching; there must certainly have been a distant prediction regarding him.

The intention is that past events were not yet fit for orderly narration. Furthermore, one lamp divided into two flames: one transmitted to Miao Guang, who propagated the Dharma and benefited sentient beings, continuing this transformation infinitely so that this Way would not perish;
the other transmitted to Guṇasaṃbhara, who became a refuge for humans and devas. Thus, lamp after lamp continues to shine.

Continuation. △ Sixth, the commonality with other sutras, which has three parts: first, the transmission of the sutra after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa; second, the teaching and transformation of disciples;
third, the correlation between the past and the present. First, the transmission of the sutra after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa.
After the Buddha had bestowed this prophecy, he preached the Dharma for human beings throughout the middle watch of the night until eighty minor kalpas were fulfilled.
Having bestowed the prophecy, he entered parinirvāṇa because this path had been sustained, his original vows had been fully realized, and his work of transforming sentient beings was complete.
Thus, during the middle watch of the night, he entered parinirvāṇa and attained the eternal, quiescent light of the dharmadhātu. Now, in this sutra...

He uttered words of extinction, yet there was no actual event of entering nirvāṇa. One should know that after preaching this sutra, he went immediately to the twin śāla trees to preach on nirvāṇa and entered extinction.
As for the one who upheld the sutra after his extinction, it was Prabhāsa;
since Dīpaṃkara preached the sutra through Prabhāsa, the entrustment rested with Prabhāsa. That Prabhāsa received the final charge and upheld the sutra is...
He performed the duties of a Dharma Master. Thus, he took a single lamp of illumination and divided it into two lamps:

he bestowed one lamp upon De-zang as the Dharma King, and entrusted one lamp to Miao-guang as the Dharma Master. These positions of Dharma King and Dharma Master constitute the transmission of the Tathāgata’s spiritual lineage;
it was precisely for this purpose that his original resolve to appear in the world was formed. As for the term "Dharma King," it refers to the Way...
There was nothing he did not transmit. His virtue was without lack; his achievement was without flaw; his practice was without deficiency; and his rank was without limit.

As for what is called a Dharma Master: he studies the Way of the Dharma King, cultivates the virtue of the Dharma King, practices the conduct of the Dharma King, transmits the Dharma of the Dharma King, observes the precepts of the Dharma King, enters the meditative concentration of the Dharma King, and attains the wisdom of the Dharma King. Thus it continues for immeasurable time.
Only after the kalpas have passed and one’s merit is perfected and practice fulfilled may one succeed to the rank of Dharma King. The Dharma Master is thus the very foundation of the Dharma King.
Therefore, when Miaoguang held this sutra and expounded it, he acted as a great Dharma Master for the benefit of both himself and others.

His disciple spent many more than twenty kalpas propagating the sutra; surpassing his teacher like green emerging from blue, his wisdom exceeded that of his master, thereby manifesting the Buddha’s mirror-like discernment.
The capacities [of the disciples] were without distinction. △ Second, explaining the teaching and transformation of disciples:
The eight sons of the Buddha Candrasūryapradīpa all took the teacher Prabhāsa as their master... (up to) ...making offerings to, revering, honoring, and praising him.

Regarding the eight sons of Dīpaṃkara, they did not take their father as their teacher, but took Prabhāsa as their teacher. This follows the ancient practice of exchanging one's own son for another's to be taught;
thus, Rāhula took Śāriputra as his teacher, thereby honoring the Way of the Teacher. As the saying goes: "The father gives life, which was the case with Dīpaṃkara;
the teacher brings fulfillment, which was the case with Prabhāsa. The eight sons took Prabhāsa as their teacher. Prabhāsa—

The Light transformed and taught them, causing their resolve for Bodhi to become firm. Furthermore, they drew near to the Buddha in great numbers; with causes perfected and fruits fulfilled, they all attained the Way of the Buddha.
Those known as "Firmly Resolute" had already attained Buddhahood long ago. Regarding the Lamp-Lighter (Dīpaṃkara), the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
When the Prince was born, his entire body radiated light like a lamp; therefore, even upon attaining Buddhahood, he was named Dīpaṃkara (The Lamp-Maker).
He was the original teacher who bestowed the prediction of enlightenment upon Śākyamuni during the second asaṃkhyeya-kalpa. Furthermore, the *Ekottarika Āgama* states:
"The eighty-four thousand dharma-gates of all Buddhas throughout the ten directions are identical, with the sole exception that the single gate of diligence differs."
Those who are diligent shall attain Buddhahood early; those who are indolent, though they too have a day of attaining Buddhahood, will be delayed by many kalpas.
Regarding the passage "the eight hundred disciples" and below, this clarifies that the indolent must still await the future.
The previous mention of "eight hundred disciples" refers precisely to this point, revealing that Maitreya is one among those eight hundred. His title is *Qiú* (Seeker).
Regarding "names": this is to suppress the mind's preoccupation with fame and profit, which divides one's resolve and exhausts the spirit.

To speak of planting various roots of goodness and encountering many Buddhas is to extol the profundity of the causes and the excellence of the conditions, through which the fruit of sainthood is finally realized.

As for the citation of the eight hundred and eight sons, it serves to resolve doubts on a proximate level while secretly revealing the [Buddha’s] lifespan. Regarding the resolution of doubts: some may say that Maitreya, as the Regent (Upapadya), is...
"Great. Mañjuśrī is not "small" because he is a candidate for Buddhahood (*caryā-pratipanna*). It would be inappropriate for the "small" to answer and inappropriate for the "great" to question.
Therefore, Maitreya is cited as one of the eight hundred disciples of the former [Buddha] Prabhāsa.
The intention is that Prabhāsa was my Mañjuśrī, while Maitreya was a disciple of Prabhāsa. As a disciple, he should question; as a teacher, [Mañjuśrī] should answer. Thus, now...

This dispels doubts and shows there is no error. Regarding the secret revelation of the lifespan: eight sons succeeded one another in attaining Buddhahood, the last of whom was named Dīpaṃkara (Dīpankara).
Dīpaṃkara was the original teacher from whom Śākyamuni received his prediction of enlightenment. All eight sons took Subhūti (Myōkō) as their teacher;
thus, Subhūti was the great-uncle of Śākyamuni’s ninth-generation ancestor. Now that the ninth-generation descendant has attained Buddhahood, even the ancestral teacher remains [as such].
Disciples and teachers are not fixed; this reveals the meaning that birth is not truly born and cessation is not truly ceased.
Furthermore, Śākyamuni received the wondrous Dharma from Dīpaṃkara, and Dīpaṃkara inherited it from his seven elder brothers.

All eight sons practiced the path of the teachings of Prabhāsa, successively attaining the fruit. Prabhāsa, in turn, received the entrustment from Dīpaṃkara, and twenty thousand [disciples] followed him.
The original lamp of illumination was transmitted solely through this; by holding fast to this, it has continued until now.
Even throughout twenty trillion kalpas of the Bhīṣmagarjitasvaras, those who have compiled its fragrant and fierce flames have done nothing more than manifest this wondrous Dharma.
This wondrous Dharma did not come into existence only today; it has existed for a long time. Thus, one can see that Mañjuśrī received it from Bhīṣmagarjitasvaras in the past.
The Lamp of Illumination. Transmitted down through the eight kings to their descendants, its ancestral origins have a basis for verification; later generations may take it as a standard.
Since its name accords with its reality, it shall resolve the doubts of the multitude. △ Third, concluding by correlating the ancient and the modern.
"Maitreya, you should know that the Bodhisattva Wonderful Light of that time... [down to]... the Bodhisattva Seeking Fame was none other than yourself.
The Mañjuśrī of today is the Wonderful Light of the past; the Seeking Fame of the past is the Maitreya of today.
This concludes the extensive response regarding what was previously seen. △ Fourth, the clear and definitive response.
Now seeing this auspicious omen, it is no different from that of former times (up to: the Dharma for instructing bodhisattvas, which is protected by the Buddhas.
He spoke thus regarding the auspicious signs manifested today: they are no different from the auspicious signs manifested by the Buddha Dīpaṃkara in days of yore.
There is no difference whatsoever. Miaoguang is my Mañjuśrī; Qiuming is you, Maitreya. This has been witnessed by the eyes and heard by the ears of both parties.
What the Kāśyapa Buddha did today is no different from the ancient story of Dīpaṃkara. Therefore, it says, "For this reason, he reflected," and so forth.
Regarding the title of the present sutra: before the Buddha had emerged from samādhi and the Dharma had yet issued from his mouth, Mañjuśrī...
To state it in advance: it can be seen that all that has been spoken by the Buddhas of the three periods of time is named the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.

Examining the above, Maitreya’s excellent questioning and Mañjuśrī’s skillful answering constitute a discourse that, though seemingly scattered, is mastered with perfect ease in its release and gathering.
Its waves are vast and immense, like a great surge capable of swallowing a ship; its transitions from beginning to end are fluid and rhythmic, yet as if a string had snapped.
The [text] continues again. How wonderful is this sutra; there is nothing that surpasses it! △ Second, the verse recitation consists of forty-five lines, divided into two parts.
The first forty-three lines recite the preceding prose section. The final two lines conclude with an exhortation to wait for the teaching.

In the beginning and middle [of this section], no verses are provided; only a brief overview of two answers is presented. Within the detailed exposition, only the first and last parts are versified, while the intermediate twenty thousand Buddhas are not.
This is divided into two parts: first, forty-one lines of verse summarizing the answer regarding what was previously seen;

second, two lines of verse providing a clear and definitive judgment. The first part is further divided into two: the first two lines of verse cite the example of one Buddha as being identical [to the others].
At that time, Mañjuśrī, wishing to reiterate this meaning within the great assembly, spoke these verses:
"I recall past ages, immeasurable and incalculable kalpas... [omitted] ...causing them to enter the Buddha’s wisdom."

"Mindfulness" refers to the supernormal power of recollecting past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti-jñāna*). "The number of kalpas in the past" praises the temporal period. "There was a Buddha," these two lines praise his name and title.
"World-Honored One" and below praise his preaching of the Dharma for the benefit of sentient beings. Regarding "among humans":

it is among humans that the Buddhas manifest their forms, so that one may rectify the mind and thoughts and proceed toward Bodhi; this can only be achieved through the human path. △ This is the second part, thirty-nine lines in praise.
Finally, the Buddhas are the same. Furthermore, there are three [sections]: first, one verse on what was previously seen and is now the same;

second, twenty-five and a half verses on what was previously seen and is now the same; third, twenty-two and a half verses on what was previously seen and will be the same in the future. Regarding the first, it is the verse on what was previously seen and is now the same.
When the Buddha had not yet left home, his eight princes, seeing the Great Sage renounce the world, also followed him to practice the pure life (*brahmacarya*).
[This concludes] twenty-five and a half lines. The verses consist of three parts: first, four lines in verse praise the auspicious signs in this land;
second, twenty lines in verse praise the light illuminating other lands; third, one and a half lines in verse praise the arising of doubt. Now, for the first part:
The four lines of verse describe the auspicious omens of this land in the same manner.
At that time, the Buddha preached a Mahāyāna sūtra titled *Anantārtha* (The Infinite Meanings), up until the manifestation of various rare and wondrous events.

The six types of omens correspond to the text. Furthermore, a celestial drum emerged from its place and sounded of itself, signifying that he spoke spontaneously without being questioned. This drum was located...
Upon the Hall of the Sublime Dharma, at the very time when the various devas were enjoying themselves, the drum sounded of its own accord.

For the sake of the assembly of devas, it preached the dharmas of suffering, emptiness, and impurity. This rare event concludes the six auspicious omens. (20) The twenty lines of verse regarding the light illuminating other lands are the same as above.
This light shines upon eighteen thousand Buddha-lands in the eastern direction (extending to) where they preach the Dharma seeking the Buddha-way.
While the prose version merely states, "These various Buddha-lands are as they are now seen," the text here provides a detailed account.

This corresponds to the phenomena and characteristics of other lands seen within the aforementioned light; the two lines beginning with "manifesting all" describe the sentient beings of the six realms of existence.
"Karma" clarifies the cause of birth and death; "retribution" clarifies the fruit of birth and death. "Abodes" refers to the twenty-five states of existence (*bhava*).
Below the section on "existence," there is an extended passage concerning the adornments of the Buddha-lands, such as crystal and water-jade. *Vaiḍūrya* is fully termed *vaiḍūrya*;
this is translated as "blue-colored jewel" and also as "not far. In the Western Regions, there is a mountain located not far from Vārāṇasī.

The city is not far away; it is named for the fact that this treasure emerges from within the mountains. Upon looking downward, one sees the eight classes of beings constantly emerging to make offerings.
Looking further downward, one sees all Buddhas attaining enlightenment, with the three bodies (trikāya) fully perfected.

Those who attain the Way spontaneously do so because, prior to the seventh stage, they practiced through the path of skillful means (*upāyamārga*) with diligent effort, whereas from the eighth stage upward, they give rise to the true path (*bhūtamārga*) without effort.
"Practice accordingly" means that one naturally and effortlessly flows into the ocean of fruition.

"Exceedingly subtle" refers to the Buddha-body as the primary retribution (正報), which sits upon the light-land of the various jewels as the environmental retribution (依報); it is like a golden image appearing within lapis lazuli—the spontaneously accomplished *dharmakāya*.
The golden mountain is the *saṃbhogakāya* (reward body), and the majestic and serene form is the *nirmāṇakāya* (transformation body).
Furthermore, the World-Honored One being amidst the great assembly clarifies the teaching of the profound meaning of the Dharma;

this uses the Dharma to manifest the person. Since the Dharma is both deep and mysterious, it must accord with the capacities of the great [vehicle]. This refers to seeing the Buddha and hearing the Dharma within the aforementioned light. Each instance of descending uses the person to manifest the Dharma;
since the persons are those of the two vehicles, the Dharma must concern the truths and conditions. This refers to the fourfold assembly practicing within the aforementioned light.
Furthermore, "seeing below" refers to the various forms and so forth within the aforementioned light; this single line generally clarifies the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*).
Furthermore, "seeing deep entry" specifically clarifies meditative concentration (*dhyāna*). Furthermore, "seeing knowledge of phenomena" specifically clarifies wisdom (*prajñā*).
△ Third, one and a half lines of verse clarify the shared state of doubt.
At that time, the fourfold assembly, having seen the manifestations of the Buddha Candrasūryapradīpa (up to the point of...
[wondering] what the causes and conditions for these matters were, questioned one another out of genuine doubt and reflection.

Each person, weighing it within themselves, spoke to themselves and consulted with one another, not knowing what the causes and conditions were for the phenomena manifested by a single ray of light. △ Twenty-three.
Two and a half verses. The verses previously seen shall be treated similarly. They are divided into six parts: first, two and a half verses on the identity of the cause;
second, one verse on the identity of the teaching; third, one verse and one line on the identity of the time; fourth, five verses on the identity of the proclamation of extinction;
fifth, one and a half verses on the identity of the bestowal of prophecy; sixth, twelve verses on the commonality after extinction.
The sūtra is the same. Furthermore, for the first two and a half lines of the verse, the causes and conditions are identical:
"The Honored One, revered by devas and humans, has just arisen from samādhi" (up to) "...causing Miaoguang to rejoice."
When a Sage appears in the world, humans and devas revere, honor, and respect him; thus he is called "the Honored One who is served.
He is the "Eye of the World," the eyes for humans and devas, and the refuge for the seven assemblies of disciples.

This is because he is able to uphold the treasury of the Dharma, causing Subhūti (Wondrous Light) to rejoice, and subsequently, based on this, he preaches the sutra—just as he now emerges from samādhi to address Śāriputra.
No. △ Second, one line of verse states that the scripture is the same:
"When this Lotus Sutra was being preached.
△ Third, one line and one phrase of verse state that the time is the same.
For sixty minor kalpas, he did not rise from this seat (until) he was able to receive and uphold [the teachings] in their entirety.
Wondrous Light received and upheld the Dharma of Lamp-Light, just as Śāriputra received the Buddha’s entrustment. △ Section Four:
The five lines of verse regarding the proclamation of extinction are the same.
After the Buddha had spoken this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* and brought joy to the assembly, [he said: "Do not be anxious or afraid.

With these first two lines, he proclaimed his entry into extinction; the original intention for the appearance of the Lamp-Lightening Buddha has been fully expressed, and the knowledge and vision of sentient beings have been opened.
Each was filled with joy. He then descended and addressed the assembly, proclaiming his passing: "Unify your minds and unify your conduct.
The entrustment of the Buddhas of the past is identical to that of today. As stated in the *Śāriputra-prakaraṇa-sūtra* (The Sutra of the Bequeathed Teaching): "O Bhikṣus, after my parinirvāṇa..."
One should cherish the *Prātimokṣa* as one who encounters light in the darkness, or as a poor person obtains treasure.
From "The World-Honored One descended" onwards, the great assembly of the past, hearing that the Buddha had entered *parinirvāṇa*, gave rise to grief and longing; this was the same as today.
As the *Mahāsūtra* says: "Tears filled their eyes, and blood flowed from their entire bodies like *pārijātaka* flowers"—this refers to the gravity of the Dharma.

This expresses the sincerity with which they admire others. "The sons of the World-Honored One" refers to the various sons of the Three Vehicles within the Dharma assembly of the World-Honored One Dīpaṃkara.
The Holy Lord’s single practice was also identical to that of the present time when the Buddha formerly comforted and exhorted the assembly.

As the *Śāsanāntima-sūtra* (The Sutra of the Final Teachings) says: "O bhikṣus, do not harbor grief or distress. Even if I were to remain in the world for one kalpa or two kalpas, this assembly would still inevitably disperse.
Where there is an assembly, separation is inevitable; it can never be avoided. As for benefiting oneself and others, the Dharma is fully complete.
If I were to remain much longer, it would bring no further benefit. Verse 5, line 1½, bestows a prediction of enlightenment identical [to that of the others].
This Bodhisattva Guṇagañja [from] the untainted true mark (*anāsrava-lakṣaṇa*)... also delivers immeasurable multitudes.
As for the "untainted true mark," it is called the true mark because it is free from the marks of false conceptualization; it is the mark of no-mark (*alakṣaṇa*).
Because he internally realizes the principle of the untainted true mark, he externally manifests a body of radiant purity. Therefore...
The Buddha’s name was Pure Body (Jingshen). △ The sixty-two lines of verse regarding the propagation of the sutra after his parinirvāṇa are the same [as the previous section].

Furthermore, there are three parts: first, the initial three lines of verse on the propagation of the sutra after his parinirvāṇa; second, eight lines of verse on the instruction of disciples; third, one line of verse concluding by correlating the past and present.
For now, the initial three lines are the verse on the propagation of the sutra after his parinirvāṇa.

On this night, the Buddha entered parinirvāṇa, like a fire extinguished when its fuel is exhausted... [until] "extensively proclaiming the Lotus Sūtra. Regarding "the fuel is exhausted and the fire is extinguished":
in the Hīnayāna, the Buddha takes the *vipākakāya* (retribution body) as the fuel and wisdom as the fire.

Since wisdom relies upon the retribution body, when the body perishes, the wisdom vanishes; hence it is said that "the fuel is exhausted and the fire is extinguished. In the Mahāyāna, sentient beings with their spiritual capacities (*indriya*) serve as the fuel.

The "stopping" (dòu) should be understood as fire. When the karmic capacities (*mārga*) of sentient beings are exhausted, the manifested form (*nirmāṇakāya*) also ceases; hence it is said that "when the fuel is exhausted, the fire is extinguished.
Zhuangzi said: "When the finger is spent in serving as fuel, the fire is transmitted; one does not know its exhaustion.

Because the fuel of the karmic capacities of sentient beings is inexhaustible, the Tathāgata’s responding fire is never extinguished. Therefore, those who redouble their diligence should follow the Buddha’s command to avoid negligence.
Each of you must strive diligently to seek the fruit of Buddhahood; only Miaoguang has received this entrustment to extensively expound the wondrous Dharma.
△ Second, eight lines of verse on the teaching and transformation of disciples.
These eight princes were converted by the Radiant Light (Prabhāsa), and their number was immeasurable.
Regarding the "Gods among Gods" (Devātideva), there are four kinds of gods: first, worldly gods, such as various kings;
second, born gods, from the Four Heavenly Kings up to the Heaven of Neither Perception nor Non-perception; third, pure gods, namely the Arhats and Pratyekabuddhas; and fourth, dharma-gods.

This refers to the Bodhisattvas of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), who perceive that all phenomena are empty in meaning. Now, the Buddha transcends the four heavens and is thus called the "God among Gods" (*devātideva*).
A "Seer" (*ṛṣi*) is a Great Awakened Golden Seer; because he possesses the power of spiritual transformation that cannot be fathomed, he is called a "Seer.

The preceding section clarifies that the eight sons have perfected their practice and have long since attained Buddhahood. From this point on, below the passage concerning "Wondrous Light," it clarifies the case of one individual who is currently [on the path].
He has attained realization and now dwells in the stage of the Bodhisattva who is destined for Buddhahood. In this passage, Mañjuśrī adopts the pedagogical strategy of his master;
he employs the style of a great elder to suppress Maitreya’s greed for profit and fame while exalting his profound causal roots that lead to Buddhahood.
He describes him as neither ordinary nor holy, yet both ordinary and holy, leaving people unable to recognize him—what is called "Maitreya, the true Maitreya," a manifestation.
His bodies number in the thousands, tens of thousands, and millions; from time to time he manifests himself to people of the age, yet the people of that age truly do not recognize him.
△ Third, one verse concludes by correlating the past and the present:
"After that Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, you who were the indolent one are now I myself, the Dharma Master Wonderful Light."
△ Two verses in pairs clearly provide the definitive answer:
"I see that the Buddha Dīpaṃkara’s original radiance and auspicious signs were like this" (up to) "...aiding in the revelation of the meaning of the true reality.
In the past, the Buddha Dīpaṃkara emitted light and manifested auspicious signs while preaching the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*. Today, the World-Honored One manifests signs in the same manner.
In the past, there was no difference [between this and what follows]. Thus we know that he intends to preach the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*. He merely emits light and manifests auspicious omens;

these are the skillful means (*upāya*) of all Buddhas to assist in revealing and clarifying the meaning of the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*). △ The final two lines conclude by exhorting [the assembly] to wait for the teaching.
All you people should now know: with palms joined and single-minded attention, wait [until the teaching is] exhausted without remainder.
Mañjuśrī has previously cited extensive scriptural evidence; having thus completed the proof of the present auspicious signs, he concludes by exhorting them to wait for the hearing [of the teaching].
To fully satisfy those seeking the Way means that what was previously incomplete is today made full.
If there are those of the Three Vehicles who harbor doubts or feel regret, today he shall eliminate and sever them until nothing remains.
Furthermore, to "eliminate and sever" a single phrase means that Mañjuśrī took a load of a thousand catties and thrust it onto the Buddha’s body, then entered the sea.
To propagate the sūtra so as to escape the censure of non-retrogression—such is the clarity of the great wisdom of prior vision.

Furthermore, these two lines are Mañjuśrī’s words of exhortation to the followers of the Two Vehicles; their phrasing is exceedingly sharp and incisive, appearing exactly like that of the Teacher of all Buddhas.
From the very sound and breath he utters, he is a master of his own craft. The two characters "adequate" (充足) serve as the basis for Śāriputra’s subsequent response.

Regarding the cases of those who receive the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*), there are two terms: "doubt" (*śaṅkā*) and "regret" (*kaukṛtya*). The term "regret" refers to the case of Śāriputra’s subsequent remorse;
the term "doubt" refers to the case of the doubts held by Kauṇḍinya and others. Regarding this, Tiantai establishes four latent doubts (*catur-avasthita-śaṅkā*).

Following the previous section where Maitreya resolved four hidden difficulties so that Mañjuśrī would provide the answers, this section features Mañjuśrī severing four lingering doubts so that Maitreya no longer needs to ask further questions.
Regarding the first doubt: because Mañjuśrī extensively cited how former Buddhas had previously preached the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, Maitreya secretly harbored a suspicion and wished to inquire:
"The Buddhas respond to conditions; the individuals and the times for each are distinct."

"Although the Buddhas of the past preached the Lotus Sutra, why must the present Buddha do so as well? Mañjuśrī resolved this with a verse, saying: "I see that the Buddha Dīpaṃkara and others likewise [preached it];
since the Buddhas of the past preached the Lotus Sutra, the present Buddha does so as well. This was a question intended to sever doubt.

Maitreya then wished to conceal his two doubts and inquire further; for there are cases where both the name and the meaning are the same, and there are also cases where the name is the same but the meaning differs.

"The meaning is the same, but the names differ. What does this name signify? Mañjuśrī resolved [the doubt] with a verse: "Now, the marks are as they were originally, like the auspicious signs," and so forth.
This was a question regarding the substance that cuts through doubt. Maitreya then suppressed his three doubts and wished to ask:
"Who can realize the true mark which is markless? Mañjuśrī resolved [this] with a verse: "All people should now know," and so forth. This was the resolution.

Regarding Maitreya’s inquiry concerning the doubts of the assembly: Maitreya was about to secretly pose four questions. The Buddha rained down the rain of Dharma, which primarily drenched the Bodhisattvas;
would it also moisten those of the Two Vehicles? Mañjuśrī resolved this with a verse: "All those who seek the Three Vehicles...
This was a question intended to sever doubt. Maitreya successively constructed his doubts, and Mañjuśrī repeatedly provided the resolutions. Since the matter...
Having exhausted the principles and reached their ultimate limit, one obtains them within one's own breast and no longer harbors further doubt. The introductory section is hereby concluded.
*The Great Achievement of the Lotus Sutra*, Volume One;
*The Great Achievement of the Lotus Sutra*, Volume Two.
Compiled by the junior scholar Dayi of Jintai Mountain.
This is the second chapter, "Expedient Means," of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
As for the title of this chapter, "Expedient Means" (*upāya*), within this single chapter there are thirty-three instances of the term "expedient means."
Section. Based on various textual meanings, the compiler of the sutra has accordingly titled this chapter.

Its general purport is that while the three vehicles were formerly expedient means (*upāya*), with the advent of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, these expedients have been opened up and relinquished to reveal and harmonize with the ultimate reality. Thus, it is still simply called "expedient means.
Although the literal term "expedient means" is the same as that used for the provisional and the small [vehicles], its underlying meaning is far beyond what words can express. Question:
The Supreme One Vehicle is ultimately complete and perfect. Why, then, at the very beginning of the section on the True Doctrine, do you speak of "expedient means" (*upāya*)?
How does this differ from the expedient means of the former Three Vehicles? Answer: Does the Sūtra not say: "Directly abandoning expedient means"?
It speaks only of the Unsurpassed Way. Furthermore, it says: "To open the gate of expedient means and reveal the true reality.

Here, the term "expedient means" (upāya) contains two senses, provisional and real, pertaining to both the preceding and subsequent stages. The former, the provisional expedient, refers to the differentiation of the single Buddha-vehicle into three.
The latter, the real expedient, refers to opening up the provisional and revealing the real, thereby bringing the three vehicles back to the one.
This is the first skillful means (*upāya*). Question: Why is this not titled "The Chapter on Reality" (*Tattva-varga*)? Answer:

This sutra’s great meaning lies in its purpose of opening up and revealing [the truth] so that all returns to it. If one were to entirely discard the former skillful means, by what means would one then open up and reveal reality?
Therefore, it still retains the title "Skillful Means. First divided and later unified; provisional and real are simultaneous; they are perfectly interfused and dynamically alive.
Because there is skillful means without [deliberate] application, it is named the "Chapter on Expedient Means" (*Upāya-paṭala*). "Expedient means" refers to the application of the Dharma.

The Dharma possesses both squareness and roundness; its applications possess both divergence and convergence. These are indeed according to the inclinations and desires of sentient beings, and do not represent the Buddha’s original intent. As the text says:

"To cause them to leave behind all attachments and emerge from the suffering of the triple world"—therefore, the Tathāgata’s praise of expedient means is not the intended meaning of this present chapter. For this reason...

The "expedient means external to the essence" refers to the provisional skillful means of transforming sentient beings, which consists of speech that accords with the inclinations of others. Furthermore, "expedient means" (upāya) is a "gate" (mukha).

A gate is so named because it is capable of opening the way to that which is to be opened; all expedient means and skillful strategies are introductory inducements that serve as gates leading to the ultimate reality.

As the text says: "Opening the gate of expedient means, revealing the aspect of ultimate reality. This is not the intended meaning of the present chapter; rather, it is also [the gate of] the essence itself.

"External skillful means" refers to the provisional methods of transforming oneself and others, spoken in accordance with the dispositions of both self and other. Furthermore, "skillful means" (upāya) signifies the profound mystery (*guhyaka*).

To skillfully penetrate the direction [of truth] is itself the true mystery. It is like pointing out the priceless jewel within one's inner garment as being no different from the single jewel atop the king’s crown;
they are non-dual and without distinction. It is like pointing to a hired laborer and saying, "This person is the son of the elder."
Furthermore, there is neither duality nor distinction. Such words as these are secret and wondrous. As the text says: "Only I know this mark;
the Buddhas of the ten directions are likewise so. "Cease, cease! There is no need to speak; my Dharma is wondrous and inconceivable. This is precisely the meaning of the present chapter.
It is the skillful means of the same essence (*ekasvabhāva*), for it is the provisional teaching of one's own practice, spoken according to one's own intention. Thus, by means of oneself...
Mañjuśrī replied to Maitreya: "The present signs are like the original auspicious omens; these are the skillful means (*upāya*) of all Buddhas.
Thus, preaching the sutras, entering meditative concentration (*samādhi*), emitting light, and shaking the earth are all skillful means. As the sutra says:

"Since my attainment of Buddhahood, I have extensively expounded teachings through various causes and conditions, parables, and countless skillful means. Therefore, skillful means do not cease with the present moment.

Following the emission of light and the shaking of the earth, it is understood that from the time of his initial attainment of Buddhahood until now, all various verbal teachings have been skillful means (*upāya*).

As the text states: "Throughout countless kalpas of the past, immeasurable Buddhas who have entered parinirvāṇa have employed various causes, conditions, and parables, as well as innumerable powers of skillful means.
Thus, skillful means do not pertain solely to Śākyamuni Buddha alone; rather, they extend throughout the ten directions and the three periods of time.
The appearance of all Buddhas in the world and their preaching of the Dharma are entirely expedient means (*upāya*). Furthermore, it is said:

"Moreover, by means of various other expedient means, they assist in manifesting the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). Thus, expedient means do not stop at the formal scriptures of the three vehicles, the six perfections, and the myriad practices.
Even such acts as raising a hand or bowing the head, building a stupa from sand, or drawing an image with one's fingernails— whether arising from sincere reverence or from playful amusement—
are none of them other than expedient means for the sake of the One Great Matter. Thus, it includes [the Buddha’s] descent into the royal palace,
his six years of ascetic practice, the plucking of a flower before the Many-Sons Stupa, and his entry into parinirvāṇa within the grove of twin trees.
As for Deshan’s staff and Linji’s shout, there is nothing that is not a skillful means (*upāya*).
By placing these two expressions at the beginning of the "Correct Division" (*zhengzongfen*), one knows that the entire seven-fascicle scripture is nothing but skillful means,
because all sentient beings inherently possess the Buddha-knowledge and Buddha-vision.
△ Second, the Main Body of the Text. It consists of nineteen chapters. Based on the essential outline of this sutra, it is divided into four sections.

From this chapter up to the "Dharma Master" chapter constitutes the opening of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision (*buddhajñānadarśana*). The two chapters, "The Jeweled Stūpa" and "Devadatta," constitute the manifestation of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
The four chapters from the "Encouragement of Devotion" chapter to the "Life Span" chapter constitute the awakening to the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. [This concludes] the analysis of the merit.
The four chapters from "Exalted Virtue" (Dete zhì) to "Never Disparaging" (Cháng bù qīng) serve as the entry into the Buddha’s knowledge and vision (*buddhajñānadarśana*).

First, the opening of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision consists of nine chapters, divided into two parts. The first eight chapters explain the Dharma in three cycles and bestow predictions upon those of the three capacities.

The second, the "Dharma Master" chapter (*Fǎshī pǐn*), praises the person who upholds the sutra and the Dharma that is upheld. This first part is further divided into two: first, the brief opening of the three to reveal the one, which moves [the assembly].
Holding onto this gives rise to doubt. [The section] "Extensively Opening up the Three to Reveal the One" consists of two parts:
first, briefly opening up the three to reveal the one; second, raising doubts and making a request. Within the first part, there are both prose and verse.

The prose is divided into two: first, praising the two wisdoms through words; second, praising the two wisdoms beyond words. Within the first of these, there are further two divisions; the first clarifies...
The provisional and ultimate aspects of all Buddhas. Second, the clarification of the provisional and ultimate aspects of Śākyamuni. This section is further divided into two parts.
First, the introduction by the narrator: At that time, the World-Honored One arose serenely from samādhi and addressed Śāriputra.
"At that time" refers to the moment when Mañjuśrī had finished answering Maitreya. "Tranquil and composed" describes a state of being relaxed, at ease, and self-possessed.
One might ask: since the Buddha is always in meditative concentration (*samādhi*), why is it said that he "arises"? There is a specific meaning intended here.
When the Buddhas of antiquity preached this sutra, they invariably entered the Samādhi of Immeasurable Meanings. The present Buddha is likewise;

having emerged from that samādhi to address the arising of speech, he does so for the sake of the world-siddhānta (worldly standpoint). Thus, emerging from concentration, he traverses the conditions of the Dharma, examining both with thorough scrutiny.

What is spoken will certainly not be erroneous; it increases the faith of sentient beings. Because it is for the sake of the *puruṣa-siddhānta* (the teaching for individuals), he arises from meditative concentration.
The Buddha is quiescent yet ever-illuminating, yet even he must enter concentration before preaching the Dharma; how much more so should one who speaks with a distracted mind and false views?

Because it is for the sake of the *pratipakṣa-siddhānta* (the teaching for remediation), he arises from concentration. Entering concentration, he contemplates principle and settles his mind in the true reality (*bhūtatathatā*); emerging from concentration, he causes others to do the same.
This is the true reality of peace of mind, the *paramārtha-siddhānta*. Therefore, arising from meditative concentration, he addressed Śāriputra.

Since Śāriputra was the primary recipient (*pratipannaka*) for whom the Dharma discourse was preached and who received his prediction of enlightenment, and because he was the foremost in wisdom among those of the Hīnayāna, it was to him that he spoke.
Although the number twelve thousand was initially indicated as the assembly, the fact that he addressed Śāriputra alone must have been for a specific reason. The Dharma...
After [the Buddha] had finished speaking, Śāriputra personally recounted his realization, saying: "In the past, I heard such a Dharma from the Buddha;
I saw various bodhisattvas receive predictions of their future buddhahood, yet we were not included in this matter," and so forth. Then the four great disciples said:
"We occupy the foremost positions among the Saṃgha, and our years are already advanced in age; we have not even given rise to a single thought of aspiration..."

With a heart of joy, Śāriputra aspired to study as a bodhisattva and receive the prediction of his own future buddhahood; he only feared that it would not be long before he attained it. Therefore, [the Buddha] took this opportunity to address him.
He asked whether there were similarities or differences between this and the *Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā* (Mahāprajñāpāramitā) and the *Āgamas*.

The answer was that they differ according to their respective contexts: the *Āgamas* are taught to initiate the Dharma-wheel of arising and ceasing, whereas the *Vaipulya* (Vaipulya-sūtras) employ censure and refutation. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā*...

This is an address [of the Buddha] because this sutra now reveals and clarifies the empowerment of the chapters. The *Śāstra* states: "The reason he addresses Śāriputra and not others is that his wisdom is profound.
There are five reasons why he does not address the bodhisattvas: first, because of the tasks to be performed for the śrāvakas;
second, because of the dedication toward great enlightenment (*mahābodhi*); third, to prevent them from becoming timid or weak; fourth, to inspire virtuous thoughts in other people."

Because of mindfulness. Fifth, it is because it prevents the arising of the thought that "what was to be done has already been accomplished. △ Second, the formal praise of the provisional and the real, divided into three parts:
first, the dual praise; second, the dual explanation; third, the dual conclusion. First, the dual praise of the two wisdoms.
"The wisdom of all Buddhas is profoundly deep and immeasurable" (extending to) "that which cannot be known by any śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.

Regarding "all Buddhas," there are two senses: first, the Buddhas of the ten directions and the three periods of time, which refers to the principle stated below that "the Buddha-way of the Buddhas of the ten directions and the three periods of time is the same"; second, Śākyamuni Buddha alone.

These are none other than the various emanated Buddhas who are currently present and preaching the Dharma. Generally speaking, wisdom (*jñāna*) is identical to insight (*prajñā*), and insight is identical to wisdom.
When divided, wisdom is that which can discern phenomena and principles, while insight is that which can resolve and judge the refined and the coarse. This is the essence of wisdom.
This is precisely the one mind and three wisdoms. It is the realm of the self-awakened noble wisdom of all Buddhas;

for the Buddhas, it is *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, the wondrous mind of *nirvāṇa*, and the treasury of the true Dharma-eye. For sentient beings, it is the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, the eternally abiding true mind, and the primordially profound and wondrous nature.
As this sutra says: "The real mark of the One Vehicle," "the family business," "the treasure place," and so forth—how profound!

"Profoundly immeasurable" (*gambhīrāpramāṇa*) is a term of praise. The true wisdom (*bhūta-jñāna*) of all Buddhas is "profound" because it penetrates vertically to the very bottom of reality (*tathatā*);
it is "immeasurable" because it extends horizontally to the limits of the *dharmadhātu*. Thus, it is immeasurable and profoundly deep; its depth is lofty and its horizontal breadth is vast.

As it is said, "When the roots are deep, the branches flourish; when the source is distant, the stream flows long. Since this is true of real wisdom (*samyag-jñāna*), it is likewise true of provisional wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*).
The single phrase "its wisdom" indicates provisional wisdom. Because there is the power of progress through the skillful means prior to the Way, it is called a "gate.

Entering through the gate, one arrives within the Way; that which is within the Way is termed "real," while that which precedes the Way is termed "provisional. It is difficult to understand and difficult to...
"Entering" (*praveśa*) is a term of praise. Because it is immeasurable, it is difficult to understand; because it is profound, it is difficult to enter.
It is understood without deliberation, and its great functioning is without fixed direction. The seven kinds of skillful means cannot fathom it. Furthermore, regarding the "gate of wisdom":
one possesses skillful means and wisdom as the gate through which one enters the Buddha’s wisdom. As the *Sutra of the Adornment* (*Ratnakūṭa-sūtra*) says:
The two types of contemplation serve as the path of means (*upāyamārga*). This is what it means to enter the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*) of the Middle Way.
Having the Buddha’s own wisdom as the gate, one enters the realm of the Buddha’s wisdom; this is precisely what is praised in the present sutra as the "gate of wisdom.
Furthermore, regarding the designation of "expedient wisdom" (*upāyajñāna*) as a "gate": because true wisdom (*bhūtajñāna*) is quiescent and transcends language, it is inherently ineffable. Now...

Employing skillful means and wisdom (*upāya-prajñā*), he sings in manifold ways and penetrates all sides; he opens the gate of skillful means (*upāya-mukha*) and reveals the true reality (*bhūta-lakṣaṇa*).

Therefore, the "gate" is named after skillful means and wisdom; that is, it is the gate of skillful means. The *Qīngliáng Sù* (Chengguan’s Commentary) states: "There are two aspects to the gate of skillful means. First, to exhaustively investigate it from afar..."

The various dharmas taught forty years ago were skillful means and provisional gateways for this present sutra; therefore it is said: "Though various paths are shown, in reality they are for the Buddha-vehicle.
To speak more proximately, such matters as entering meditative concentration and emitting light are the skillful means and provisional gateways for this assembly;
therefore it is said: "Now the Buddha emits radiance to assist in bringing forth the meaning of the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*). All [of these].

It is that which the followers of the Two Vehicles cannot know; therefore, it is said to be difficult to understand and difficult to enter. The specific mention of the Two Vehicles’ ignorance is because their attachments are so heavy.
When the *Avataṃsaka* illuminates all at once, they are like the deaf or the mute, and thus it is said they do not know.

When the *Vaipulya* (Prajñāpāramitā) rebukes and refutes them, they remain settled in their thatched huts, and thus it is said they do not know. When the *Prajñā* transmits the teaching, they have no mind to aspire toward or grasp it, and thus—
He says he does not know. Now that the great capacity [of the Bodhisattvas] has been awakened, light is emitted and the earth is shaken;
yet, regarding both the present and the past, and the fact that the Way of all Buddhas is the same, he still harbors doubt and thus says he does not know.

Bodhisattvas of sharp faculties can understand it point by point, whereas the Two Vehicles of dull faculties likewise do not know. This is precisely the statement intended to stimulate and challenge the Two Vehicles. II. Dual Explanation.
The two kinds of knowledge. Why is this so?
Because the Buddha formerly drew near to [the Buddhas]... up to... being courageous and diligent, his fame was heard everywhere.

First, he poses a double inquiry regarding the two kinds of knowledge. "The Buddha formerly [associated with them]" and so forth explains the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*). This is truly because of the causes of the Buddhas in their past lives.
Throughout kalpa after kalpa and birth after birth, they have never been separated from the Buddha; taking the Buddha as their teacher, they constantly follow and learn from him.
The Buddhas they have encountered are not merely one or two; they have already served hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of countless Buddhas.
Thus, having encountered many Buddhas externally and received the most essential teachings, their ultimate wisdom is exceedingly profound. If one serves such a teacher...
Not to learn is equivalent to not having a teacher. To learn the Way but not practice it is equivalent to not learning at all.
By serving one Buddha, one fully practices the immeasurable Dharma of that one Buddha; by serving countless Buddhas, one fully practices the immeasurable Dharma of those countless Buddhas.
What is accumulated becomes profound and what is cultivated becomes vast. In this way, one's internal practice becomes pure and substantial.
Through personal practice and realization, true wisdom (*bhūta-jñāna*) becomes immeasurable. "Valiant" (*vīrya*) and so forth explain provisional wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*).
"Valiant" means to advance directly with courage, being able to perform what is difficult to do. "Diligent" (*vīryavat*) means that the will never retreats, remaining tireless throughout long kalpas.
"Renowned" refers to the full possession of the ten titles (*daśa-nāmadheya*), as one acts appropriately in all circumstances. "Universally Heard" indicates its perfect manifestation.
The Dharma-realm. Its name and fame are far-reaching because the Buddhas, through their courageous and diligent exertion, are able to enter gates that are difficult to enter.
Having entered these gates, their grace extends boundlessly; all beings revere their supreme virtue, and thus their renown is heard everywhere.
The phrase "valiant" explains that provisional wisdom is profound; the phrase "renowned" explains that provisional wisdom is vast.
Although provisional wisdom lacks explicit terms for "profound" and "vast," this meaning is established by analogy with real wisdom. △ Third, the dual conclusion of the two wisdoms.
To have accomplished the profound and unprecedented dharmas, whose intended meanings as taught according to what is appropriate are difficult to comprehend;

to be in accord with principle and ultimate, possessing the perfection of the fruit of virtue—this is called "accomplishment. It means to awaken to the very source of the mind and reach the bottom of the other shore.

It is said: "Profound" refers to that which was never previously taught, and is therefore unprecedented; this concludes the wisdom of realization (*jñāna*). "Taught according to capacity" means it is spoken in accordance with the faculties [of beings];
this concludes the wisdom of skillful means (*upāya-jñāna*). Because it is not something known through the seven stages of expedient means, it is called "difficult to understand.

Furthermore, "accomplishment" and so forth conclude the provisional and ultimate aspects of one's own practice (*sva-pratipatti*). "According to capacity" and so forth conclude the provisional and ultimate aspects of transforming others (*para-parivarta*). The provisional aspect of one's own practice...

In truth, both are called "real" (*satya*); in terms of transforming others through skillful means (*upāya*), both are called "expedient. Regarding the two terms "intimate" (*qin*) and "near" (*jin*) herein:

according to the [analogy of] reaching the city of transformation (*tāvatiṃsa*) and Devadatta, in terms of intimacy, the Buddha and the Buddhas of the ten directions are all as close as father and son or brother and brother;
in terms of proximity, Devadatta was the teacher and the Buddha was the disciple, serving him for a thousand years.

Because it is proximate, one practices both types of speech. According to the "Chapter on Never-Disparaging," even when subjected to abuse and physical assault, one still offers salutations and praise;

this is for the sake of practicing them exhaustively. Regarding the single phrase of "renown," according to the "Chapter on the Medicinal Herbs," one proclaims it universally to devas, humans, and others with a great voice.
In the "Chapter on Spiritual Powers," the various devas cry out from the midst of the void: "There is a land named..."
"Saha. The name of the Buddha is Śākyamuni; these are all names by which the Buddha’s renown is universally heard. Furthermore, regarding "accomplishments" and so forth:

from the point in the *Tathāgataguṇajñānācintyaviṣayāvatāranirdeśa-parivarta* (The Chapter on the Emergence of the Precious Stūpa) where the stūpa emerges and the earth is transformed, through the gathering of the emanated bodies and the appearance of the retinue, the discourse on the lifespan, the differentiation of merits, up until the prophecy given to Devadatta and the attainment of Buddhahood by the dragon girl—all of these are the accomplishments of the Buddha.

This is an unprecedented teaching (*adbhuta-dharma*), never before expounded to those of the Two Vehicles; that it is now taught in this sutra is why it is difficult to believe and difficult to understand.
Furthermore, the single phrase "drawing near" refers to the depth of what is studied; the single phrase "practicing to the end" refers to the depth of what is accomplished;
the single phrase "valiant and fierce" refers to the depth of one's resolve; and the single phrase "renown" refers to the accumulation of merit.
The depth of "one phrase of accomplishment" refers to the depth of what has been realized. The depth of "one phrase according to suitability" refers to the depth of skillful means (*upāya*).

One who praises in this manner reveals that for those of the Two Vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*), what they have studied and accomplished, their established resolve and accumulated merit, as well as the skillful means of their realization, are all not profound.
This is intended to inspire the aspiration and longing of the Two Vehicles, so that their inner minds may spontaneously—
Awake! Thus have the Buddhas diligently studied and attained profound realization, until their fame was heard everywhere.
How can we, within the Buddha-dharma, allow our minds to become weary and indolent? If one can reflect in this way, one may hope to enter the One Vehicle (Ekayāna). As it is said:
"If the accumulation of wind is not thick, then there is no power to support great wings; small knowledge cannot reach the Great."
[It is] known. It is only fitting that the followers of the Two Vehicles do not know the wisdom of the Tathāgata.

The preceding section concludes the praise of the two kinds of wisdom—expedient and real—of all Buddhas. II. Praise of the Expedient and Real Wisdom of Śākyamuni. This is divided into three parts: 1. Praising the expedient to explain the expedient;

2. Praising the real to explain the real; 3. Concluding the expedient and concluding the real. In contrast to the preceding section, there are generally three points of significance. First, the former...
The praise of the two wisdoms by all Buddhas is given in combination to clarify that the essence of these two wisdoms is identical.
The praise of the two wisdoms by Śākyamuni is given in separation to indicate that the functions of these two wisdoms differ. Second, it clarifies the basis for manifesting traces;

therefore, all Buddhas first praise the Real (the ultimate), manifesting the capacity of the fundamental source. Therefore, Śākyamuni first praises the Expedient (the provisional). Third, all Buddhas manifest themselves...

Because [the Buddha] practices [the truth], he first establishes the real; because Śākyamuni clarifies the transformation of others, he first establishes the provisional. The initial praise of the provisional explains the provisional. Furthermore, there are two parts: first, the praise of provisional wisdom.
"Śāriputra, since my attaining Buddhahood until now... [I have] guided sentient beings, causing them to leave behind all attachments."
Regarding the time since his attainment of Buddhahood: it refers proximately to the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) and distantly to kalpas as numerous as motes of dust.
By means of three kinds of skillful means for transforming others, he accommodates sentient beings; thus, it is said that there are "various causes and conditions. As for "parables":
in the Hīnayāna, the plantain tree and water bubbles are used as metaphors; in the Mahāyāna, the city of the gandharvas, mirrors, and illusions are used as metaphors. These are expounded in detail.
This refers to the ability to produce immeasurable meanings from a single dharma. "Innumerable skillful means" refers to the seven kinds of skillful means. "Freeing from all attachments" means:
teaching the ten mundane wholesome acts to free one from attachment to the three miserable realms; teaching the ten supramundane wholesome acts to free one from attachment to the desire realm;
teaching the dharmas of the truths and conditions to free one from attachment to views and afflictions; and teaching the bodhisattva dharmas...

He is free from attachment to nirvāṇa. He teaches the Buddha-dharma to cause others to abandon attachment to the dharma of love for the path that accords with it. △ Second, the explanation of provisional wisdom:
Why is this? Because the Tathāgata has already fully perfected the pāramitās of skillful means, knowledge, and vision.

Because of skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*), one is able, through various causes and conditions and so forth, to know that which is the knowledge of the three wisdoms (*tri-jñāna*) and to see that which is the vision of the five eyes (*pañca-cakṣus*).
Since these reach the ultimate limit of both phenomena and principle, they are all termed *pāramitās*.
"Fully endowed" refers to the complete perfection of both the provisional and the real. Herein, knowledge and vision are the real wisdom (*bhūta-jñāna*), by virtue of its realization.
This is true wisdom; therefore, it is able to employ various provisional means (*upāya*). This concludes the praise of the provisional and the explanation of the provisional.
II. Praise of the Real and Explanation of the Real. This also has two parts. First, the praise of true wisdom.
"Śāriputra, the Tathāgata’s knowledge and vision are vast and profound.
The phrase "vast" is a praise; "vast" clarifies the horizontal dimension, which refers to the aforementioned immeasurability. "Profound" clarifies the vertical dimension.
This refers to the aforementioned profound [wisdom]. True wisdom is fundamentally neither horizontal nor vertical; it is praised through words as a provisional means.
When its horizontality and verticality are discussed, its illumination is infinite and boundless, like a large box requiring a large lid. △ Second, the explanation of true wisdom.
"Immeasurable and unimpeded powers and fearlessnesses" (up to) "accomplishing all unprecedented dharmas.

"Immeasurable" refers to the four immeasurable minds (*catur-apramāṇa*). "Unimpeded" refers to the four unhindered analytical knowledges (*catasraḥ pratisaṃvidah*). "Powers" refers to the ten powers (*daśa balāni*).
First is the power of knowing what is possible and what is impossible; second, the power of knowing karma; third, the power of meditative concentration;

fourth, the power of the faculties; fifth, the power of aspiration; sixth, the power of temperament; seventh, the power of knowing the path leading to all destinations; eighth, the power of recollecting past lives; ninth, the power of the divine eye;

tenth, the power of the exhaustion of outflows. The Buddha knows these all-pervasively; they cannot be surpassed and cannot be destroyed, and for this reason they are called "powers. There are four fearlessnesses.
There are four fearlessnesses: first, the fearlessness of possessing all-knowledge; second, the fearlessness of having exhausted all outflows (*āsrava*);
third, the fearlessness of proclaiming the obstacles to the path; and fourth, the fearlessness of proclaiming the path to the exhaustion of suffering.

They are collectively termed "fearlessness" because, when one extensively proclaims one's own and others' knowledge and abandonment before a great assembly, being certain that there is no error, one is free from even the slightest trace of apprehension.
Regarding these characteristics: *dhyāna* (meditation) refers to the meditation of the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*). *Samādhi* (concentration) refers to the Great Samādhi of the Śūraṅgama.
*Vimokṣa* (liberation) refers to the various gates of liberation within the stage of Buddhahood. *Samāpatti* (attainment) refers to the twenty-five royal samādhis.

"Profoundly entering" explains their depth and distance; "boundless" explains their vastness. "Accomplishment," and so forth, collectively subsumes all that is possessed within the stage of Buddhahood. One.

Having concluded the praise and explanation of the reality of all merits, there are three parts; the third is the conclusion regarding the provisional and the real, which is further divided into two. First, the conclusion regarding provisional wisdom:
"Śāriputra, the Tathāgata is able to make various distinctions... [his] speech is gentle and soft, pleasing the hearts of the multitudes."

"Various skillful explanations" refers to the aforementioned various extensive expositions. "Gentle and supple speech" means employing skillful methods to suit the capacities of beings without being harsh or violent.
"Delighting the hearts of the multitude" means conforming to the inclinations and desires of sentient beings.
Because he is fully endowed with skillful means and knowledge-and-vision, he is able to provide various skillful explanations that cause others to be delighted. △ Second, the conclusion.
True wisdom.
Śāriputra, to state the essentials: the Buddha has fully accomplished immeasurable, boundless, and unprecedented dharmas.
"To state the essentials" means to speak in broad outline. "Unprecedented dharmas" refers to the aforementioned accomplishment of all [dharmas] and so forth.
The unique qualities of the Buddha-ground are immeasurable and boundless, penetrating to the very limit of the infinite;

they are all dharmas that have never before existed. One must understand that the skillful means of all Buddhas are precisely the expedients of Śākyamuni, and such is the knowledge and vision of Śākyamuni.

This is precisely the wisdom of all Buddhas. Without expedient means (upāya), there is no way to guide toward the ultimate reality; without ultimate reality, there is no way to reveal expedient means.

If there were reality without expedient means, those of middling and inferior capacities would remain submerged; if there were expedient means without reality, those of great potential would be subjected to distortion.

Only when expedient means and reality proceed together can one skillfully bring to fruition both the small and the great without omission. This is why, upon emerging from samādhi, the Buddha offered a double eulogy; it was for this very reason. (From the *Ji*)

The praise of the three wisdoms is concluded. △ Second, the praise of the two wisdoms through the transcendence of words. This is divided into three parts: first, the direct praise through the transcendence of words;

second, the inquiry and explanation of this transcendence of words; third, the explanation of the characteristics of the provisional and the real. For now, we present the first: the direct praise through the transcendence of words.
"Cease, Śāriputra; there is no need to speak further.

To stop while praising at the precise point of perfection is intended to seal the mouth so that one does not speak. Although the mind is full and desires to speak, it merely demonstrates the cessation of words.
It stops and praises in order to sharpen the faculties and inspire faith. "There is no need to speak further" is said for this reason.

The Dharma is profound and tranquil; it is a gateway that transcends all signs. Words fail when spoken, and mental objects are forgotten when contemplated. Therefore, it is set aside and not explained.

Because it is a realm of self-realization and not something known by others, it is set aside and not explained. Even if one were to preach it out of compassion, those who hear it could not understand it;
fearing this might damage their roots of goodness, it is therefore set aside and not explained. II. Investigation and Explanation of the Transcendence.
It is said:
Why is this so? Because that which the Buddhas have accomplished [up to] enables them to exhaustively fathom the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena.

"Accomplished" means the sense of being perfectly complete and fully endowed. In terms of the fruit corresponding to the cause, it is that which has been realized by all Buddhas, wherein the provisional and the ultimate are not [separate].
Second: This is the foremost dharma because that which is attained is subtle and wondrous; it is a rare dharma because it is like the *udumbara* flower;
it is a dharma difficult to understand because it cannot be known by others. From this point downward, all dharmas realized are neither foremost, nor rare, nor difficult to understand.
"Only the Buddhas" refers exclusively to the Buddha and the Buddhas of the ten directions who have reached ultimate [realization].
Ultimately, the limit and depth of the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) are like the moon on the fifteenth day: its substance is not incomplete, and its light is nowhere not pervasive.

Thus, all phenomena (*dharmas*) are the provisional (*upāya*), and the true mark is the real (*tattva*). All phenomena are the provisional that is identical with the real; the true mark is the real that is identical with the provisional.
Being provisional while being the real, there is no real apart from the provisional; being real while being the provisional, there is no provisional apart from the real.

This constitutes the wondrous provisional and the wondrous real of the same essence. The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* reveals and clarifies them, like smelting iron to produce gold; the wondrousness lies precisely here.
