These four characters are the fundamental basis of the *Lotus Sūtra*, the beginning of all teachings, the key to interpreting their meaning, the refuge for sentient beings, the reliance for generating the resolve for enlightenment, the substance of the application of skillful means, and the distinction between delusion and awakening.

The root source of all things, the fundamental principle of the fruition of virtue, the ultimate consummation of the single transformation, and the final conclusion of the five periods—this is precisely what the Buddha has accomplished.
Only the Buddha has realized the ultimate and exhausted the source; therefore, he ceased and did not speak further.
△ Third, the explanation of the provisional and the real.

Regarding the passage from "The so-called dharmas have such characteristics" up to "such are their beginning, end, and ultimate equality," Master Nanyue read all these phrases as "like" (ru), and thus they are called the "Ten Likenesses" (Shiru). Master Zhizhe, however, read the text according to its meaning, applying it in three ways:

namely, "such characteristics" (rúshì xiàng), "these characteristics are like" (shì xiàng rú), and "characteristics are such" (xiàng rúshì), and so forth. All [the ten aspects] are treated in this manner.
"Dharma" refers generally to all phenomena, both mundane and supramundane. Whenever a single phenomenon is brought forth, it is endowed with the "ten suchnesses.

The term "such as this" (*tathatā*) is an expression used to point to a phenomenon according to its specific instance; that is to say, all phenomena possess such-and-such characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), and so forth.

"Characteristics" (*lakṣaṇa*) refer to the external aspect, which can be distinguished by observation. "Nature" (*svabhāva*) refers to the internal aspect, which maintains its own identity without change. It is the primary substance.
Name is the essence; function is called power (*bala*); structure is called activity (*kriyā*). Habitual causes are the cause; assisting causes are the condition (*pratyaya*).
Habitual fruits are the fruit; retributive fruits are the retribution. Initial characteristics are the root; subsequent retribution is the branch.
The ultimate convergence of all phenomena is equality. It is like a single person who possesses physical form, mental nature, body, functional power, and activities.

Past causes and present conditions constitute the human being as the fruit; the variations of wealth and poverty, the duration of life and its brevity, and the integrity or deficiency of the sense faculties and body constitute retribution.
Birth is the root and death is the branch; investigate their equality. Furthermore, the two characters "Thus" (*tathā*) are words that directly point to the very essence of things.
Since these various phenomena, when their characteristics are examined, are found to be without characteristics, it is said: "Thus."
Regarding its marks: if one speaks of its nature, that wondrous nature is innate; if one speaks of its substance, that substance is itself true and eternal;
if one speaks of its power, its functioning accords with reality; if one speaks of its activity, it acts yet is without action; if one speaks of its cause, birth is fundamentally without birth;
if one speaks of its conditions, emptiness of nature accomplishes phenomena; if one speaks of its fruit, the fruit does not depart from the cause.
If one speaks of its retribution, the nature of karma is manifest; if one speaks of its beginning and end, it is a single limit from start to finish.
Therefore, it is said that suchness is both the beginning and the end. All these aforementioned dharmas are, one by one, this very dharma of suchness;
thus it is said they are ultimately equal, quiescent, and non-dual. This is the true mark (dharmatā) of all dharmas. As for the provisional and the real dharmas... [text ends]
This is inconceivable. It is the realm realized by all Buddhas of the three periods of time; it is that which only a Buddha and a Buddha can fully exhaustively comprehend.
△ Second, the verse commentary consists of twenty-one lines, divided into two parts. First, seventeen and a half lines praise the preceding prose section.
Second, three and a half lines briefly open up the three to reveal the one. The first part is further divided into two.
The first four lines of verse express praise for the two wisdoms through directed speech; the remaining twenty-three and a half lines of verse praise the two wisdoms beyond the reach of words.
The former [section] is further divided into two parts. The first two lines combine the verses to praise the two wisdoms of the two Buddhas.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"The Hero of the World is immeasurable; among all devas and worldlings, there is none who can fathom him."

In the prose section, the provisional and the real are praised separately to indicate that their conditions for transformation differ; in the verse, the two wisdoms are praised together to show that the essence of these two wisdoms is identical.
"Hero of the World" (*lokanātha*) is a title denoting one who is preeminent and valiant throughout the world, for he is able to practice what is difficult to practice.
That which is difficult to sever, they are able to sever; that which is difficult to relinquish, they are able to relinquish; that which is difficult to realize, they are able to realize.

As it was said of old: "Leaving the household life is the concern of a great man; it is not something that generals or ministers can accomplish. Those who are able to realize emerge from their kind, yet the Dharma realized—how could it abide within the realm of thought or speculation?
This verse praises the wisdom of all Buddhas mentioned above. "Immeasurable" praises what was mentioned above.
It is profoundly deep and immeasurable. It also encompasses both provisional and ultimate wisdom; for while ultimate wisdom is immeasurable, provisional wisdom is likewise so.
The next three lines extend the scope of those aforementioned "people who do not know. In this regard, there are three differences from the prose section (*chángxíng*):

first, the prose previously cited the person and further designated the Dharma, thus saying "the wisdom of all Buddhas"; now, however, it merely praises the person, using the person to [represent] the Dharma.

This praises the Dharma; thus it is called the "Hero of the World. Second, the previous section opened with a praise of the person, while this verse combines [the person and the Dharma]. Because the Dharma is distinct, it must be opened up; because the person is universal, it must be combined.
Third, whereas the previous section stated that all those of the two vehicles do not know, this now says that all classes of sentient beings do not know.
Regarding "By the power of the Buddha" and so forth: this verse explains the two types of wisdom of Śākyamuni. "The power of the Buddha" and so on refers to his ultimate wisdom (*bhūta-jñāna*).
All other dharmas are provisional wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*). As for what is meant by "other," it refers to the provisional means for transforming others;

these are merely auxiliary to real wisdom (*bhūta-jñāna*). One employs one's own practice as the means to transform others, deriving from a single dharma an infinite variety of causes and conditions and various parables.
All such skillful means (*upāya*) are such that they are both provisional and real; therefore, they too—
It cannot be measured. △ Second, two lines combined as a verse: the Buddhas praise and conclude the praise.
"Originally following countless Buddhas, I have fully practiced all paths... (until) I have already known and seen them all."
This verse concludes the meaning of the two preceding chapters. As for the variations in its phrasing, one need not strictly correlate each word with its specific counterpart.

Because it is profoundly deep, it is difficult to perceive; because it is subtle and wondrous, it is difficult to comprehend. Having practiced the Way for immeasurable eons signifies the fulfillment of expedient wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*).

Attaining the fruit at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*) signifies the fulfillment of ultimate wisdom (*prajñā-jñāna*). The fruit thus attained is precisely the ocean-like wisdom of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).

This is the fruit realized through causes cultivated over vast eons. It is said that the profound and subtle provisional and ultimate [teachings] are most difficult to see and most difficult to comprehend.

Because I and all Buddhas have, from the time we were with immeasurable Buddhas, fully and exhaustively practiced immeasurable dharma-paths, and having practiced these paths for immeasurable eons, have finally sat at the site of enlightenment and attained [Buddhahood].
Because [the Buddha] has attained the fruit of Buddhahood, he is able to fully know and fully see these provisional and ultimate dharmas. The verse concludes the eulogy by means of words.
△ Twenty-three and a half lines. The eulogy on the ineffable is divided into five parts. First, one and a half lines eulogize the characteristics of the provisional and the ultimate.
1. One and a half verses interrogate and explain the ineffable; 2. One and a half verses formally declare the ineffable and offer praise;
3. Forty and a half verses concern those who do not know; 4. One and a half verses concern the most rarefied Dharma known only by the Buddha.
Now, for the first one and a half verses, they explain the provisional and the ultimate aspects.
Such are the meanings of the various natures and characteristics of the great fruit-retribution.
"Great" (大) means "sublime" (妙). "Various" (種種) refers to the differences among the ten suchnesses (*daśatathatā*). "Meaning" (義) refers to ultimate equality (*samatā*).

First the fruit-retribution is mentioned, then the nature and characteristics; the sequence in between can be understood accordingly. This reveals that the methods of contemplation regarding the inverse and the direct are free from restriction.

Furthermore, "great" being prior to the fruit refers to the principle of "the unchanging following conditions. Its meaning appearing after the characteristics refers to the principle of "following conditions while remaining unchanging.
△ Second, the half-verse in metrical form poses a question and explains the ineffability.
I and the Buddhas of the ten directions alone can know this matter.
This matter is precisely the true mark (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena. Only a Buddha and a Buddha can exhaustively fathom the true mark of all phenomena;
having attained profound realization through self-mastery, they alone can know it. △ Third, the latter half of the verse concludes by praising [the teaching] beyond words.
This Dharma cannot be shown; it is quiescent in its verbal characteristics.
Its true mark (bhūtalakṣaṇa) has no location or direction, and therefore it cannot be shown. It is not the path of language, and therefore verbal expressions are quiescent.
As the ancient masters said: "The Buddha-Dharma is exceedingly abundant; it is simply that the tongue is too short. This is precisely that meaning. Furthermore, as stated previously:
The "great fruition" refers to the realm of self-realization, specifically pointing to the Flower Treasury World (*Kusumatalagarbha-lokadhātu*).

It is a sea of fruition characterized by infinite adornments, where all things are perfectly interfused and mutually penetrating without obstruction; hence it is called the "meaning of various natures and characteristics.
Only Buddhas and Buddhas know this matter. Because the sea of fruition transcends words, speech and expression are extinguished. This path beyond words is not...
The realm of conceptualization and discrimination—how could it be something the followers of the Two Vehicles are capable of enduring?

Therefore, [the Buddha] desisted and did not speak of it, precisely to reveal the ground of ultimate, singular reality as the supreme goal to which we now return. What was not fully exhausted in the prose is clarified here in the verses.
△ Forty and a half lines of verse concerning those who do not know; divided into seven parts. First, one line:
1. One line and a half permits those with the power of faith to understand. 2. One line and a half distinguishes those of the Two Vehicles who do not know.
3. One line distinguishes Śāriputra who does not know. 4. One line and a half distinguishes the great disciples who do not know. 5. Two lines distinguish the Pratyekabuddhas who do not know. 6.
Two lines and a half distinguish the Bodhisattvas who have merely resolved their minds [to attain enlightenment] and do not know. 7. One line distinguishes those who do not... [text ends]
The regressing bodhisattvas do not know this. For now, regarding the first line, it is granted that those with the power of faith can understand it;
however, among all other classes of sentient beings, there is none who is able to comprehend it, except for those among the assembly of bodhisattvas whose power of faith is firm and steadfast.

From here on for ten and a half lines, the text expands upon the fact that no class of sentient beings can know the Buddha, clarifying that the two wisdoms of all Buddhas are profoundly deep, immeasurable, difficult to understand, and difficult to enter.

Nevertheless, the personages advance one level higher than the last, and the meanings follow one after another with increasing precision; this is intended solely to bring forth the realization of all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.

This cannot be known; it is only between Buddha and Buddha that the ultimate meaning can be fully exhausted. The first two phrases generally exclude those of the seven stages of preparation from knowing it.
The following two phrases grant permission for Bodhisattvas of the power of faith to enter it;

these Bodhisattvas are those at the stage of the fulfillment of the ten levels of faith in the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*). Apart from the Buddha, there is ultimately no one else who [can know] this wondrous Dharma.
If one can understand this, what benefit would there be in explaining it? Therefore, I permit entry through faith.
As for those who are "firm," they are Bodhisattvas of the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao), great beings of transcendent capacity. Upon hearing this Dharma once, they directly accept it as their own;

they immediately take the immovable wisdom of their own nature (*svabhāva-acala-jñāna*) as the substance of faith. They believe that their own mind and the Buddha are non-dual, such that mind and object are one.
"Suchness" (tathatā) means to accord with the true mark (bhūtalakṣaṇa). It is like carrying a heavy burden upon one's shoulders and proceeding straight ahead;

it is also like a fragrant elephant crossing a river, cutting through the current. Only in this way can one be said to possess firm and solid power of faith. 2. One and a half lines distinguishing that the Two Vehicles do not know this.
The assembly of disciples of all Buddhas who have made offerings to the Buddhas... [up to] "that which their power cannot endure.

"All outflows" (*āsrava*) refers to the views and afflictions (*kleśa*) within the three realms. "Final body" (*caramabhavika*) refers to the ultimate fruit of the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*). "Cannot endure" means:
This is because those of the Two Vehicles are like people who are cold ashes or withered wood; their strength and capacity are shallow and meager, making them unfit for such a heavy responsibility.
An ancient worthy said: "If you wish to shoulder the Great Dharma, you must be like withered wood sprouting flowers or cold ashes emitting flames;
only then will it be possible. △ Third: A single line distinguishes that Śāriputra did not understand.
Even if the entire world were filled with those like Śāriputra, and they were to exhaust their thoughts to measure it together, they could not fathom the Buddha’s wisdom.
This means that although there are many superior disciples of the Buddha, some may have little wisdom and thus fail to understand.
For instance, take the wisdom of one such person, Śāriputra, whose fame resounded throughout the five regions; even if the people filling the entire world were all like Śāriputra—
As for wisdom, even if one exhausts all thought and deliberation, one cannot fathom it; thus, it is known to be profoundly deep, immeasurable, difficult to understand, and difficult to enter.
△ Four lines and a half: Distinguishing that the Great Disciples do not know this.
Even if those filling the ten directions were all like Śāriputra—up to that point—they still could not know it.
This means that it is not only the people filling the world who are like a single son; even if the people filling the worlds of the ten directions were like him, they still could not know it.

May they all possess wisdom like that of Śāriputra; further, may they possess supernatural powers like Maudgalyāyana, ascetic practice like Mahākāśyapa, skill in preaching the Dharma like Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra, extensive learning like Ānanda, and secret conduct like Rāhula.

Even if one were to exhaust one’s divine thoughts and employ every measure of calculation and estimation throughout the lands of the ten directions, such [a being] would still remain unknown. △ Section Five: Two Verses.
It is distinguished [from] the Pratyekabuddha, who does not know it.
Even the Pratyekabuddha’s sharp, untainted wisdom in his final body cannot know even a small portion of it.

Because he contemplates conditions in both direct and reverse order, it is called "sharp wisdom. His own practice of both the provisional and the real is collectively termed "real"; that is to say, it is not only...

The śrāvakas do not know it; even those of sharp intelligence, such as pratyekabuddhas, who fill the worlds of the ten directions as numerous as the bamboos in a grove—even if such a multitude of people were to become one in mind for a long and protracted time—they would still be unable to know even a small fraction of the Buddha’s wisdom.
Thus, it can be known that these two wisdoms are profoundly deep and immeasurable. △ Sixth, two and a half lines distinguish those who do not know [this]:
Bodhisattvas who have newly resolved their minds (navayānasamprasthita-bodhisattva), though they have made offerings to countless Buddhas, cannot know the Buddha-wisdom.

Some refer to those who, though practicing the six perfections over three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*, have not yet severed their afflictions; others refer to those who have resolved their minds within the Small Vehicle or Initial Teachings.
Within their respective teachings, each is able to thoroughly comprehend the meaning and intent of the Four Noble Truths, and based upon them, they give rise to the four great vows.
Each is able to expound the path and dharmas of their respective teaching; compared to what precedes them, each is called "sublime wisdom. That is to say:

Not only those who are Pratyekabuddhas, but even Bodhisattvas who have newly resolved upon the Mahāyāna—having made offerings to countless Buddhas—possess merit that surpasses that of the two vehicles.
By expounding the definitive meaning of the Dharma for their own benefit and the benefit of others, they possess wisdom that surpasses that of the two vehicles.
Their numbers are not merely like those in a bamboo grove; rather, they are as numerous as rice, hemp, bamboo, and reeds, pervading the ten directions.
As for the Buddha-lands: furthermore, it is not through a distracted mind or limited wisdom, but rather through a single-minded, wondrous wisdom;
nor is it in a short time or a few kalpas, but through as many kalpas as there are grains of sand in the Ganges, contemplating together—yet even then they do not know it.
Thus, one can further understand that the two wisdoms are profoundly deep and immeasurable. △ Seventh: A single line distinguishes that non-retrogressive Bodhisattvas do not know [this].
Even non-retrogressive bodhisattvas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, contemplating together with a single mind, cannot know it.
They do not know the perfect principle—that all dharmas are complete within it and that it is identical to all dharmas; therefore, it is said they do not know.

Furthermore, their view of the Buddha’s bodhi is like looking at the moon through a fine silk gauze; thus, although those who have newly resolved their minds belong to the Mahāyāna, there may still be [limitations].

I withdraw; indeed, it cannot be known. Even by those great Bodhisattvas of the eighth stage and above, who abide in the stage of non-retrogression and are as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, though they seek with single-minded intent, it remains unknown.

Thus, the profound and immeasurable nature of these two wisdoms can be further understood. The verses concerning those who do not know have now concluded. △ Fifth, one and a half verses praise the second [wisdom].
First, this rarity can only be known by a Buddha.
Furthermore, [the Buddha] told Śāriputra: "The outflow-free (*anāsrava*) and inconceivable [Dharma]... (up to) the Buddhas of the ten directions are likewise.
This Dharma is called "outflow-free" because it is the singular, ultimate reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*); outside of this reality, there is no other dharma. It is not...

As for "inconceivable," it means that the provisional is identical to the real, and the real is identical to the provisional; it is free from faults and transcends all negation, for it cuts off both mind and speech.
As for "profound and subtle," it is because it is realized and witnessed only by the Buddha. The two lines beginning with "Only I" can be understood as a verse summarizing the above.
This verse concludes the section on the two wisdoms—the provisional and the ultimate—within the prose commentary. △ Next, two and a half lines briefly open up the three to reveal the one.
This is divided into two parts. First, one and a half lines clarify that all Buddhas manifest the ultimate reality.
Śāriputra, you should know that the words of all Buddhas are not different; (up to: they must speak the truth.
"The words of all Buddhas are not different" reveals that the Buddhas' methods of transformation are identical. The two phrases concerning the Buddha encourage faith;

the two phrases concerning the long duration of the Dharma reveal the reality. Since the truth is spoken only after a long time, it can be seen that everything previously taught was not [the ultimate truth].
This is true. This [passage] refutes former attachments and gives rise to present doubts. The following text will show that it was not Māra who appeared as a Buddha, based on hearing these words.
△ Second, two lines clarify that Śākyamuni opened the three vehicles.
"Addressing the assembly of śrāvakas and those seeking the vehicle of pratyekabuddhas... (up to) "...leading them forth so that they may attain liberation.

The preceding section clearly revealed the ultimate reality (*tattva*); this section now clarifies the opening of the three vehicles. The revelation of reality necessarily involves the opening of the three; the opening of the three necessarily involves the revelation of reality.
The path of all Buddhas is identical; they merely manifest one aspect to one another. "Addressing the assembly of śrāvakas," etc., correctly clarifies the three [vehicles] shown in the past.

The Śrāvaka constitutes the Small Vehicle (Hīnayāna); the Pratyekabuddha constitutes the Middle Vehicle. My two phrases refer to the Bodhisattva of the Six Perfections, that is, the Mahāyāna. How is this known?
By practicing the Six Perfections, one is freed from the bonds of suffering of the four realms of existence, yet has not yet entered parinirvāṇa.
Only after three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* and a hundred *kalpas* does one attain nirvāṇa; the word "reaching" (*dài*) implies that it is attained only after a long interval. Thus says the Buddha.

With two lines, [the text] directly refutes that the three vehicles are all merely expedient means. The first [line] generally negates their reality; the latter two lines reveal the intent for manifesting the One:
they lead [beings] out of attachment by citing the three as a necessity, rather than as the ultimate truth, for they are merely gates of expedient means.
This concludes the brief opening of the Three to reveal the One. △ Second, raising doubts and requesting instruction, divided into [sections].
2. First, the Sūtra-master narrates the doubt:
"At that time, among the great assembly, there were various Śrāvakas... (up to) "...and now they do not know where this meaning leads.

This arises because, having heard that three are false and one is true, they cling to movement and thus doubt is produced. The phrase "There were various... and so forth, narrates the doubt of the twelve hundred [monks].
"Śrāvaka" is a designation based on the cause; "Arhat" is a designation based on the fruit.

The reason Cunda alone is singled out as the foremost of those who doubted is that he was the first to attain liberation upon hearing the Dharma of the Four Truths when the Buddha first achieved enlightenment.

Later, he raised doubts regarding the Buddha’s teaching on the single meaning of liberation. In the first year after his enlightenment, the Buddha ordained five men; in the second year, he ordained Yaśas.

The elder [Mahākāśyapa] had fifty followers; over three years, he led the three Kāśyapas and their one thousand disciples; over five years, he led Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana, each with one hundred followers.
Thus, there were one thousand two hundred and fifty-five people who constituted his constant retinue.

Furthermore, when the text below begins by describing the doubts of the fourfold assembly, these are precisely the assembly of those still in training (śaikṣa). Above, it refutes that all three vehicles are [ultimately valid].

Regarding the "expedient means" (*upāya*): the statement that the expression of doubt pertains only to those of the Two Vehicles (*dviyāna*) is because their attachments are heavy and their doubts are deep;
thus, they are singled out for mention. As the subsequent text states: "The bodhisattvas seeking Buddhahood are very numerous, numbering eighty thousand, and they too all have doubts.

Therefore, we know that those of all three vehicles (*triyāna*) share these doubts, and it is only the Two Vehicles who are specifically mentioned. As for the question of why [the Buddha] is so earnest and diligent, it refers to the present World-Honored One.
For what reason, after emerging from samādhi, do you so earnestly praise skillful means (*upāya*)? Previously, it was said that you guide sentient beings through countless skillful means;
again, it was said that the Buddha, by the power of skillful means, manifests the teachings of the three vehicles (*triyāna*).
If this is so, then were all the teachings spoken during the forty years [of his ministry] merely provisional and expedient? Is even what we have realized merely a skillful means?
This is the skillful means for dispelling doubt regarding the statement that "the Dharma attained by the Buddha is extremely profound and difficult to understand. This refers to the present inquiry:
for what reason does the World-Honored One now say that the Dharma attained by the Buddha is extremely profound and difficult to understand?

Previously, it was stated that the wisdom of all Buddhas is vast, expansive, deep, and far-reaching, and that they have accomplished a rare and difficult-to-understand Dharma. If one were to discuss the Dharma attained by the Buddha, [it pertains to] the Three Vehicles...

Regarding the distinction between the great and the small, you have thoroughly investigated the principle of the beginning and end of the conditions of truth and exhausted the mysteries and profundities;
truly, there is nothing further to be hidden. For what reason, then, do you now speak again of "extreme profundity"?

If this is so, is the dharma difficult to understand today not the same dharma as that of former days? Is the dharma profound today more profound than the profundity of former days? This doubt is indeed...

Regarding the statement, "The underlying intention of what has been spoken is difficult to discern": this refers to why the World-Honored One now says again that the underlying intention of what has been spoken is difficult to discern.
For forty years, we have personally witnessed the excellence of the Tathāgata’s physical, mental, and karmic activities;
we have heard his instructions face-to-face and have already understood whatever he has spoken. Why is it that today...?
It is said that this is difficult to understand and difficult to know. If this is so, then does what was understood in the past still have a deeper meaning yet to be understood?
Does what was known in the past still contain a further intent that remains unknown? This is a doubt regarding provisional wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*).
Why, then, do you say today that it is beyond the reach of all *śrāvakas*, and speak of it exclusively for those of the Three Vehicles?
"We are not equal to this. Since we do not know it, could even a Bodhisattva reach it? Or is it that the Bodhisattva does not know it either?
This is the doubt that they themselves do not know. Furthermore, throughout the Buddha's entire life, what he has taught is solely the meaning of liberation.
Previously, he praised the Three Vehicles as the true path of deliverance; now, the Buddha speaks of this single liberation.
This is the meaning. We have relied upon it and practiced accordingly, thereby attaining this Dharma of liberation and subsequently emerging from birth-and-death to realize nirvana.
Although there is a distinction between teacher and disciple regarding their respective status and rank, they are identical in the path of liberation.
Why is it that we do not know how the Tathāgata achieved this? Is it not because the name "liberation" is the same for both?
Is there a difference in principle? Is that which the Tathāgata has realized something we have not yet realized?
Or is that which we have realized something the Tathāgata has not realized? If this were so, why would we both equally transcend birth and death?
"It is not so. Why do you reject us? This doubt concerns what we ourselves have realized.
Since all three vehicles are expedient means, we do not know which one is the ultimate truth. Your words are extraordinary, and their principle must be profound and mysterious.
Thus, the disciples who had entered the gate were suddenly struck with doubt, and so it is said: "We do not know where this meaning leads. II. The Actual Request of the Audience.

The text contains three requests and two refusals; combined with the preceding [section], this makes three refusals in total. The first refusal is because the principle is profound and difficult to understand. The first request is for the sake of seeking a definitive resolution for oneself and others.
The second refusal is because [the audience] would be startled, doubtful, and lack faith. The second request is because those who have long planted [roots of merit] will certainly understand.

The third refusal is because those who slander [the teaching] will certainly fall into suffering. The third request is for the benefit of those with sharp faculties. Now, regarding the first request, there is...
The prose and the verses. The prose section is further divided into two parts. First, the presentation of doubt:
At that time, Śāriputra knew that the minds of the fourfold assembly were filled with doubt [regarding] this most profound, subtle, and difficult-to-understand Dharma.
"Those whose minds harbor doubt" refers to doubt within the fundamental mind. When the single light appeared perfectly and the two sages engaged in dialogue, their doubt was still mild.

However, when [the Buddha] emerged from samādhi to praise and censure the expedient means of the Three Vehicles, declaring that the Truth would be taught only after a long time, he shook their former attachments and agitated their minds;
thus, their anxiety became acute, as the wild ox was no longer at ease. As for Śāriputra, by means of the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*),...

Knowing that the minds of the fourfold assembly were filled with doubt, and that he himself had not yet attained full clarity, [the Buddha] addressed the doubt regarding the provisional through the passage beginning with "The various Buddhas descend," and the doubt regarding the real through the passage beginning with "Profound.
△ Second, the formal request.
"Since the distant past, I have never before heard from the Buddha such a profound, subtle, and difficult-to-understand Dharma.
Previously, I alone presented my request; now, I present the request of the assembly. For what cause and for what condition should this great matter of causal conditions be set forth?
This was the case where Śāriputra doubted that he had received a prediction based on the preaching of the Dharma, while Ājñātakauṇḍinya and the fourfold assembly likewise harbored doubts.
This serves as the basis for receiving the prediction [of enlightenment] during the latter two weeks. Doubt is the very gateway to awakening. Without doubt, there is no opening of awakening;

without the opening of awakening, one does not receive the prediction. Since doubt has degrees of depth and spiritual capacity has variations of sharpness and dullness, the Dharma is presented in three cycles, and the predictions are received in a sequence of first and last.
△ Second, the verse summary. There are eleven lines of verse, divided into five parts.

The first three and a half verses address doubts concerning the two types of knowledge (*jñāna*). The next two and a half verses summarize the doubts of the fourfold assembly regarding the three vehicles.

The third section, consisting of one and a half verses, specifically addresses the doubts of the speaker himself. The fourth section, consisting of one verse, specifically addresses the doubts of the other three assemblies.

The fifth section, consisting of two verses, generally explains how shared doubts led to the request for instruction. For now, the first three and a half verses concern the doubts regarding the two types of knowledge.
At that time, Śāriputra, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"The Great Holy Honored One, the Sun of Wisdom, has long since proclaimed this Dharma... [which is] what all Buddhas have attained."
The three types of wisdom are perfectly luminous and capable of destroying the darkness of ignorance; therefore, it is called the "Wisdom Sun.

Furthermore, if there were no sun in the sky, one would not perceive the efficacy of the four seasons' cyclical transformations; likewise, if the Buddha lacked wisdom, one would not perceive the path of cultivation and realization of the Three Vehicles.

Thus, wisdom is metaphorically likened to the sun. "For a long time" (*jiǔ*) refers to the duration mentioned above. "This Dharma" (*shì fǎ*) points back to the aforementioned True Reality (*zhēnshí*). "Path" (*dào*)...
"Attained at the site" refers to the provisional and ultimate [truths] of one's own practice; it corresponds to attaining the fruit at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*).
"None can pose a question" corresponds to the assembly of the Buddha’s disciples, up to the non-retrogressive bodhisattvas, being unable to fathom the Buddha’s wisdom.

Regarding "my intention is difficult to fathom," this corresponds to the passage: "Even if one were like Śāriputra, one still could not fathom the Buddha’s wisdom. Furthermore, there is none... [who can].
"Those capable of questioning" refers to non-retrogressive Bodhisattvas and myself, Śāriputra. Since we are unable to question, there would likewise be no one else capable of questioning.
To emerge from samādhi and praise the path practiced is the provisional aspect of one's own practice;
the wisdom attained by the Buddha is the ultimate reality of one's own practice. (The two or three lines) summarize the doubts of the three vehicles and the fourfold assembly.
The various arhats who are free from outflows and those seeking nirvāṇa (up to) "I pray that the Buddha will explain this for me.

Furthermore, those seeking even a single phrase refer to the bodhisattvas of the six perfections. They are likened to the animal called the *śṛgāla* (jackal), whose nature is full of doubt; upon hearing a sound, it immediately climbs a tree.
This matter refers to the ultimate reality after a long time, as well as the provisional skillful means of the Three Vehicles. △ [This concludes] three lines and a half.
A separate verse addresses his own doubt:
"Among all the śrāvaka assembly, the Buddha has declared me to be the foremost" (up to) "...this is the path he has practiced.
[This refers to] the ultimate fruit of the Dharma; the path practiced is the cause. These two lines have a dual application. If considered from the perspective of accomplishment...
Regarding the statement "measuring the Buddha’s wisdom," one might ask: does this refer to the ultimate fruit-dharma of the Buddha, or to the path-dharmas practiced as causes by the Buddha?
If one proceeds from the perspective that the disparagement of the three vehicles is merely provisional, one may doubt whether each of the three vehicles possesses its own cause and fruit.
If it is said that these are provisional and not ultimate reality, then is it the case that the realized fruit is not ultimate reality? Or...
Is that which is practiced not the cause of reality? △ Four: One Verse. A separate verse resolving doubts regarding the Three Vehicles:
"O Son born from the Buddha’s own mouth, with palms joined you gaze up in expectation; we pray that you will utter a subtle and wondrous sound and speak at this time according to reality."
Having heard the Buddha preach the Dharma, the Dharma-body is brought forth; therefore, it is said that [the disciples] were "born from the Buddha’s mouth.
Because those who study the Three Vehicles all look up with sincere devotion, they pray that he will emit a wondrous voice and speak according to reality. △ Fifth, two lines:
a general clarification of how shared doubts lead to a request for instruction.
The devas, nāgas, spirits, and others, numbering as many as the sands of the Ganges, desire to hear the complete path.
Those who seek the Buddha and the bodhisattvas are numerous as the sands of the Ganges; their spiritual faculties are great.
They come from ten trillion lands; their journey is far. They wait with palms joined in reverence; their hearts are sincere. Thus they desire to hear the complete path.
It is said that this great multitude of people of superior capacity have all come from afar;
their sincerity is at its utmost, and they do not seek half a jewel, but desire to obtain the complete gem. It was fitting that I should now have fully attained it.

Because Śāriputra’s seeking of the mind was so earnest and his request so urgent, he attained understanding and received the prediction of enlightenment upon hearing the Dharma explained just once; there was indeed a reason for this. △
"Stop! Stop! [The Buddha said] twice, because they were startled, doubtful, and did not believe.
At that time, the Buddha told Śāriputra (up to the point where he said): "All devas and humans shall likewise be startled and doubtful.

He spoke these words repeatedly, "Stop! Stop! This was not out of disdain for their solemnity. That the devas and humans were startled and doubtful means they were startled by what they perceived as strange and exaggerated, and they doubted it.

They will certainly not believe. If they do not believe, they will inevitably incur the transgression of slandering the Dharma. To speak of it would be of no benefit; to leave it unsaid would cause no harm.
It is better, therefore, to cease. △ Second, the request: "For those who have long planted [the roots of virtue], they will surely understand."
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha again, saying: "Upon hearing what the Buddha has taught, one will be able to revere and believe it.
At that time, Śāriputra, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"O Dharma King, Supreme Honored One, please speak; do not worry that there are none among these immeasurable multitudes who are capable of respectful faith.

To repeat "please" twice is to show that while his efforts to stop [the Buddha] were increasingly strict, his request was increasingly earnest, clearly demonstrating the maturity of his awakened capacity.
Nevertheless, the sun does not hide because there are those without eyes; how could the Buddha-dharma be withheld for the sake of the deluded?

Be silent. Furthermore, there are countless sentient beings within this assembly who have seen various Buddhas in the past; their planting of roots has not been shallow, and their roots of goodness are now mature.
Upon hearing the Great Way once, they will take it upon themselves without timidity. Their wisdom is transcendent; as soon as it enters their ears, they believe.
Do not worry about the alarm or doubt of humans and devas. Those who do not doubt are many, and those who revere and believe are vast. You should act for the sake of faith.
If one speaks thus, those who suffer loss will be few, while those who receive benefit will be many. How could one not speak?

Even if there are those who do not believe, it serves as a condition for them to eventually develop faith and acceptance. This compassion for those who lack compassion is the greatest of compassions. To speak brings benefit to both; to refrain brings injury to both.
How can one allow a few doubts to harm the many who have faith, thereby failing in one’s compassion? △ Third: Refraining.
"One who slanders [the Dharma] will inevitably fall into suffering.
The Buddha again addressed Śāriputra, saying that monks of overweening pride (*adhimāna*) are on the verge of falling into a great abyss.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"Stop, stop! I shall not further proclaim my Dharma, for it is subtle and difficult to conceive; those with overweening pride will surely fail to show respect or faith upon hearing it.
This is the constant custom of the Buddha-Dharma: to speak at once when requested. How much more so now, when he has spoken of his own accord without being asked?

That he would refuse a second request is precisely for the sake of those who possess overweening pride. Above, he declined on the grounds that gods and humans would not believe; here, [he declines] because...
Using overweening pride as a pretext, his words were slow while his intent was urgent; thus, the gravity of the offense gradually reached its full extent.

Herein, the Buddha’s compassion and majesty may both be seen. The great pit is none other than hell; if ordinary people do not believe the Buddha’s words, they will fall into hell. How could one preach the Dharma to cause others to invite suffering?
To be struck with alarm and doubt yet not destroy [the teaching] is still a light obstruction. As for those of the class who harbor overweening pride—[they look toward...]

He departed, looking back. If one were to defile this [teaching], resentment would arise in the mind and slander would issue from the mouth; one would surely fall into the deep pit of hell, where myriad sufferings are irreversible.
Not only would it be of no benefit, but it would even cause harm. For this reason, his parting words were profound and his severance was ultimate.
△ Third, the request: so that those of sharp faculties may gain benefit.
At that time, Śāriputra again addressed the Buddha, saying: “[...until... for a long night they shall be at peace and find great benefit.
Then, wishing to restate this meaning, Śāriputra spoke in verse:
"O Unsurpassed Honored One among Two-legged Beings, we pray that you will preach the foremost Dharma"—up to this point—they will give rise to great joy.

Śāriputra here requests [the teaching] on behalf of those who are like himself and numerous; for them, birth-and-death and ignorance are a long night, while the fruit and virtue of Nirvāṇa are peace and security.
Having received transformation from the Buddha, they will surely be able to revere and believe, forever parting from the long night of birth-and-death.
At night, one attains the joy of great peace and security; the benefit is manifold. Regarding the first four lines of the verse, which express a request for oneself:

"I pray that you speak," and so forth—because the preceding section rejected the three vehicles as being false, and because it was heard that after a long time the truth would be revealed, those in the two vehicles did not yet know that the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* was the reality.
They merely relied on the refutation of the three as untrue, [concluding] that there must necessarily be something else beyond them.
Because it is the Dharma, it is called the "Supreme Dharma" (*agradharma*). The passage beginning with "In this assembly... is for the sake of the eight classes of beings;

the passage where Mañjuśrī says, "Now you all should know," and so forth, is likewise. The passage beginning with "We ourselves... is for the sake of those on the same path, namely those who seek the three vehicles (*triyāna*).
The phrasing is plain while the meaning is profound; the deeper one seeks it, the more comprehensive the words become. Thus, within the assembly...
Even though there may be those who do not believe, the Buddha cannot disregard their difficulties and yet wish to exercise compassion.

The first section, which briefly opens up the three to reveal the one and deals with the movement of attachments and the arising of doubts, is complete. II. Extensively opening up the three to reveal the one, severing doubts and engendering faith.
This text is divided into three cycles: 1. The first cycle, the Dharma-exposition, is for those of superior faculties. 2. The second, the Parable-exposition... [text continues].
It encompasses those of middle capacity through three causes and conditions; it encompasses those of inferior capacity through one. The first, the discourse on the Dharma, is divided into five parts:

first, the formal exposition of the Dharma; second, the understanding and realization of Śāriputra; third, the Tathāgata’s confirmation and praise; fourth, the bestowing of the prediction of enlightenment.

The assembly of five hundred and four rejoiced. First, regarding the preaching of the True Dharma (*saddharma*), there are both prose and verse. The prose is divided into three parts: first, the granting of permission to preach; second, the reception of the mandate; and third, the actual preaching. First, the granting of permission to preach: *The Buddha addressed the Venerable Ānanda:* "Ānanda, you should now recite the *Sūtra of the Great Parinirvāṇa*, which I have previously taught for the sake of all sentient beings. Then the Venerable Ānanda addressed the Buddha: "Bhagavān, what is the name of this *sūtra*, and how should it be upheld? The Buddha told Ānanda: "This *sūtra* is named the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*. You should uphold it as such. Ānanda said to the Buddha: "Bhagavān, what is the purpose of upholding this *sūtra*? The Buddha told Ānanda: "Ānanda, if there are sentient beings who hear this *sūtra* and believe and accept it, they shall not fall into the evil realms for one hundred thousand kalpas. Furthermore, if there are sentient beings who hear this *sūtra* and practice according to its teachings, they shall attain the stage of non-retrogression (*avaivartika*) within this very life.

Therefore, Ānanda, you should diligently uphold this *sūtra*. At that time, the Venerable Ānanda, having received the Buddha’s instruction, bowed his head at the Buddha’s feet and withdrew to one side. He then entered the concentration of the "Lion’s Roar" (*siṃhanāda-samādhi*), and by the power of his supernormal knowledge (*abhijñā*), he ascended into the air to a height of seven *tāla* trees. There, amidst a rain of celestial flowers, he sat upon a lion throne and, with a voice like the roar of a great drum, began to recite the *Sūtra of the Great Parinirvāṇa* for the sake of the assembly. [End of section on the granting of permission to preach.]
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Śāriputra: “Listen well now, and I shall explain it for you.

[The phrase] “you have already [spoken] two lines” is an expression of assent. It is like a great bell suspended on its frame; when struck, there is no response that does not follow. Thus, he made his earnest request three times.
How could one not speak? Though one may wish to remain silent, it is impossible. "Now, you must listen attentively" is a permission to admonish.

"Listen attentively" refers to the wisdom of hearing; "reflect well upon it" refers to the wisdom of reflection; and "keep it in mind" refers to the wisdom of cultivation. The Great Sūtra clarifies that four wholesome dharmas are the causes for *nirvāṇa*:
first, associating with virtuous friends; second, listening to the true Dharma; third, reflecting upon it...
Meaning. Fourth is practicing according to the teaching. These four dharmas alone are the causes for nirvana. The "virtuous friend" is the Tathāgata;
the remaining three are the three types of wisdom (*prajñā*). To analyze and explain these four characters: according to the title of the chapter, they are precisely the skillful means (*upāya*).
Regarding the meaning of the treatise, it constitutes a major pivotal point for the preceding and subsequent sections of this sutra. Initially, the Buddha merely said, "Cease;
there is no need to speak further. Śāriputra then requested, "What is the nature of this matter? We pray that the Buddha will explain it for us."
The third section states: "Stop, stop; there is no need to speak. Śāriputra then requests: "Please deign to explain in detail.

Thus, the four characters "to explain in detail" (*vibhajya vyākhyāhi*) were originally the words of Śāriputra’s request. The Buddha now grants this, merely adding the four characters "I shall for your sake" (*ahaṃ te...
bhāṣiṣye*). This is the subtle excellence of the continuity of the discourse's literary structure. As for the meaning that is expounded:
Previously it was said: "This Dharma cannot be shown; words and their characteristics are quiescent. How could it admit of conceptual discrimination? Furthermore, it was said:
"The untainted, inconceivable, profound, and subtle Dharma. How could it admit of explanation?
Thus we know that the Dharma attained by the Buddha is fundamentally incapable of being discriminated or explained. That he now says, "I shall [teach] equally," refers to Śāriputra.

There is no one capable of understanding it; having no other choice, I employ language as a skillful means to analyze that which the Buddhas know but cannot demonstrate, and to explain that which the Buddhas have realized but is inconceivable.
From the passage "This wondrous Dharma" onwards, the text below is all intended for those of the Two Vehicles.
This is an analytical explanation. When these words were spoken, [the assembly] was selected and permitted. Five thousand people were seated;

although the Tathāgata had previously stopped them three times, he now intends to permit the teaching. Therefore, they prostrated to the Buddha and withdrew. Because the obstacles of the five turbidities are numerous, their transgressions are grave.

Because they cling to the Small Vehicle while obscuring the Great, their roots are deep-seated. They have not attained the three fruits, yet they claim to have attained the three fruits. They have not...

To claim realization of the state beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) when one has not realized it is called "overweening pride" (*adhimāna*). Those who possess such faults—namely, the three faults of having hindrances, attachments, and pride—are like this:
just as yellow liquid does not pour into a clay jar, and blessings do not descend upon the lewd, how could the Mind-Seal of the Buddhas be fit for those of meager virtue?
For this reason, they do not abide [in it]. As for those who do not restrain themselves:
It is the constant custom of the Buddha-dharma to grant assent by remaining silent; this is established as a decree, like the edict issued when a Son of Heaven exercises his sovereign authority.

Regarding the teaching that "the three are opened to reveal the one," the words are concise while the meaning remains hidden; thus, even if slander has not yet arisen, it is sufficient to serve as a cause and condition for the binding of the jewel.

Departing [now] would be beneficial, whereas if you were to hear the extensive explanation, it might conflict with your disposition and give rise to slander, which would be detrimental if you remained. For this reason:
He did not stop them. A question was asked: "There were five thousand people in the assembly who received no benefit; what benefit would there be in letting them go? The answer was:

"These were not those for whom the teaching was intended; they were merely people with whom [the Buddha] formed a karmic connection. Long ago, during the time of Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū, there were also immeasurable sentient beings whose minds were filled with doubt.
They have been born together with their teacher in life after life, and now they have all attained deliverance—even after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa."
They were still not yet exhausted; these five thousand [monks] were likewise so. From the words "At that time" onwards, the Buddha personally describes his intention for not restraining them;
this is his own consolation. The later passage, "Now I am joyful and fearless," refers to this.

As for the branches, leaves, and minor fragments, they are unfit for use as vessels; he rejects the five thousand as not being vessels capable of carrying the Way, for they were merely habituated to mere words.

To apply effort at the highest level yet to ply one's trade within a ghost cave—picking leaves and seeking branches without exhausting the root—is precisely what the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* means when it says:
"To cling to branches and leaves while abandoning the root; such a person is not wise. This is that very meaning.
The "trunk" refers to the fundamental; it is spoken in contrast to the branches and extremities. The "fruit" refers to the reality; it is spoken in contrast to the flowers and leaves.

Generally, for all things, if they possess a trunk and fruit, one need not worry about lacking branches and leaves. However, if there are branches and leaves but no trunk or fruit, what benefit would there be?

This phrase praises the assembly for being great vessels. As for the statement, "To withdraw is also excellent," one should understand that those with overweening pride (*adhimāna*) are not entirely devoid of the Dharma;
rather, they merely consider themselves superior while remaining at a shallow stage—this is called overweening pride.

Since they obscure themselves with their own smallness, they further obstruct the great light of others. Now, by withdrawing, they are free from the fault of slandering the Dharma, nor do they obstruct others.
This was his fault; therefore, it is said that [the text] is excellent. Because the branches of the superior [teaching] have not yet been eliminated, the Tathāgata employed the three "stoppings.

Because [Śāriputra] truly wished to hear [the teaching], Śāriputra offered four "requests" below. Master and disciple discerned the capacities [of the assembly]; it was not merely a matter of being parsimonious or withholding [the teaching].

These five thousand followers of pride were indeed proclaimed by the Golden Mouth [of the Buddha]. Since they are designated as "provisional" (*upāya*) within the Introduction, how can this be reconciled? The Great Master must certainly [have had a specific intention].
This is the place where one penetrates the heart-essence of the Tathāgata. Otherwise, for what reason would all the Buddhas have permitted it?

Now there are three points by which we know this is a provisional manifestation. First, when Dīpaṃkara preached the sutra for sixty minor kalpas, not a single person in the assembly experienced physical or mental fatigue;
thus we know that this sublime assembly was like a sandalwood forest—how could there be any ordinary wood therein? This...

The five thousand [monks] had already realized the principle of the ineffable before entering meditative absorption; now, hearing that the Buddha permitted an explanation, they prostrated to the Buddha and withdrew.
Second, if they were truly arrogant people, they would have departed with disdainful looks; since they now prostrate to the Buddha and withdraw, it is clear they have silently realized this truth.
Because this Dharma is beyond words, yet the Buddha has now permitted its analytical exposition, they [fear] falling into conceptualization.

This is because it is a discourse on the second [category] falling into the third. Thirdly, it is because it honors the Buddha’s words, as stated previously: "If one speaks of these matters," and so forth.
These five thousand people are merely a group of hypocrites and those with arrogant tendencies who have entered this assembly to further increase their pride; otherwise, it would not be so.
The introduction greatly deviates from the scriptural text. From "You now" onwards, it concludes with the granting of permission. "Listen well" is an admonition to listen with meticulous scrutiny;

one must not be reckless or superficial, nor should one become attached to names and forms. If you can truly turn yourself around beneath every phrase and find the meaning within every word, [you will have succeeded].
To realize this through total detachment is what makes one’s words not merely empty talk.
△ Second, receiving the mandate. Śāriputra said, “Yes, World-Honored One; I wish most earnestly to hear it.
“Wei” (唯) signifies assent; “nuo” (諾) signifies agreement. “Wei” is rapid and plain; “nuo” is slow and refined. The *Book of Rites* says: “For a father’s command, use ‘wei’.”

And they arise. The Master’s command is likewise. Those who delight in hearing [the teaching] are like those who, when thirsty, long for a drink. △ Third, the actual exposition, divided into two parts:
first, the chapter on the four Buddhas, which extensively explains the provisional and real wisdoms of the aforementioned Buddhas; second, the chapter on Śākyamuni.
This extensively explains the two wisdoms—expedient and real—of Śākyamuni above. The preceding section contains fewer phrases and is thus brief in its wording;

it states generally that "all Buddhas" is a brevity of person, while "opening the three to reveal the one" is a brevity of meaning. From this point downward, the chapters and phrases are mostly extensive in their wording.
The elucidation of the five Buddhas is the expansion of the person; the elucidation of the six meanings is the expansion of the meaning.

As for the six meanings: first, praising the rarity of the Dharma; second, declaring that it is free from falsehood; third, revealing the provisional means; fourth, demonstrating the ultimate reality;

fifth, citing the five turbidities to explain the provisional; and sixth, rejecting the false to emphasize the real. Praising the Dharma causes respect to arise; declaring it free from falsehood stops slander.
He opens up skillful means so that they do not cling to the Small Vehicle; he reveals the reality so that they may awaken to the Great Vehicle.

He cites the five turbidities to show that the three [vehicles] must necessarily be bestowed; he distinguishes the false and deceptive to emphasize that the true must necessarily be realized. Within these five chapters, each should fully contain the six meanings;
as for the fact that they appear in different sequences or are not exhaustive, this is because the Tathāgata’s skillful teaching does not require prolixity. Now, first:
The Chapter on the Four Buddhas is divided into two parts: first, a general exposition of all Buddhas; second, a specific enumeration of the three periods of time.

Within the initial general exposition of all Buddhas, there should be six points, yet here only four are presented: first, praising the rarity of the Dharma; second, declaring that it is free from falsehood;
third, revealing the provisional means; and fourth, demonstrating the ultimate reality. Two points are omitted as they will be indicated in subsequent passages. Now, first, the praise of the Dharma:
"How rare!
The Buddha told Śāriputra: "Such a wondrous Dharma... appears but once in an age, like the udumbara flower.

Thus, both the teaching and the metaphor are presented together, immediately providing the title of the work. As for the phrase "it is preached at such a time," it means that all Buddhas appear together within the five turbidities.
It is certain that [the Buddha] first revealed three [vehicles], as the World-Honored One does now; it was only after more than forty years that he manifested the ultimate truth.

He long remained silent regarding this essential point because he did not strive for a hasty proclamation. That he did not speak for so long was because people were incapable of receiving it and because the time had not yet arrived.

Because five thousand [people] had not yet been dismissed, people were now capable [of understanding], and the time had arrived; since the five thousand had departed, he definitively expounded the Mahāyāna.
Furthermore, regarding the Unsurpassed One Vehicle (*ekayāna*), the sages "preserve it without discussing" and "discuss it without deliberating."
This is a matter of waiting for the proper time. To speak when it is not the proper time is to fail in one's words; to fail to speak when it is the proper time is to fail in one's person.
When one speaks only after the proper time has come, people will not grow weary of what they say, and the words will not fail in their purpose toward the person addressed.
The opportunity is doubly attained; therefore, it is said that one speaks [of this] only at the proper time.
The *udumbara* flower—here translated as "spiritual omen" (*lingshui*) or also as "auspicious response" (*ruiying*)—appears once every three thousand years.

Its appearance signifies that only after the Three Vehicles have been fully ripened does the King of the Golden Wheel appear, and only then is the wondrous Dharma preached and the prediction of a Dharma-king bestowed. The *Parnirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "Within Jambudvīpa..."
There is a king of trees named Udumbara; it bears fruit but no flowers. If golden flowers were to bloom upon it, then a Buddha would appear in the world;
this is the omen of a Buddha. The *Prakaraṇapāda-śāstra* states that encircling Jambudvīpa is the road of the Wheel-Turning King (*cakravartin*).
It is one *yojana* in width. When there is no Wheel-Turning King (*cakravartin*), it is submerged by the ocean waters such that no one can see it.
When a Wheel-Turning King appears, the ocean waters recede, a path of golden sand manifests, and these flowers arise as an omen of the golden wheel.
Question: Such phenomena appear at specific times when they are spoken of. What is the meaning of the word "time" (*kāla*)?
Answer: One [interpretation] explains the sudden from the gradual, taking the final stage as "one time.
The other explains the sudden by means of the sudden, wherein the three periods are equal; this is the "time of no time," termed "one time.

It is like the lotus flower, which has neither beginning nor end, thereby clarifying the principle of the single characteristic and single flavor. Question: Some discuss the color of the lotus in terms of blue and white; is this not so?

"Do not decide [on this]. Is it possible to understand the meaning? He replied: "Wherever the Buddha was, he used the lotus as an auspicious sign to represent the phase of the full unfolding of perfect practice;
from the beginning, there were no five-colored clouds. If one discusses it in terms of color, then these are seen according to the capacities of beings and the teachings they receive."
Now, regarding the teaching of the *Lotus Sūtra*—of a single characteristic and a single flavor—it merely employs the metaphor of the lotus flower; why then discuss its being blue or white? Question:

Regarding this "single characteristic and single flavor," wherein the provisional and the real mutually penetrate one another, I pray that you will demonstrate this through its meaning. Answer: The provisional [teachings] of the Three Vehicles are the truth of partial realization;
the real [truth] of the One Vehicle is the truth of ultimate correspondence. Both are merely words used for the purpose of guiding and attracting beings. It is simply...

One must allow the provisional and the real to mutually integrate, so that the traces of the Great and Small Vehicles are forgotten; like the great void, there are no signs of inner or outer, and like a single lotus flower, there are no signs of identity or difference.
When both the principle and the metaphor are presented together, the truth is indeed thus. △ Second, the teaching is without falsehood.
Śāriputra, you all should believe what the Buddha has spoken; his words are not false.
When it is said that you should believe, it is because he who speaks is one whose words are not false, and the Dharma he teaches is one that is not false.

This principle is most profound; its principle differs from what was taught in the past. These words are most subtle; these words contradict what was taught in the past. This practice is most universal; this practice...

This differs from what was previously [stated]. This person is most excellent; being superior to the inferior one of former times, I fear that beings might give rise to slander. Therefore, I exhort you to have faith.
△ Third, the opening of the provisional means.
Śāriputra, the Buddhas teach the Dharma according to what is appropriate for each case... (up to) "only the Buddhas are able to know this.

Regarding the phrase "the Buddhas" and below, there are three [sections]. As for "according to what is appropriate," the text follows from what precedes it, while the meaning explains what was stated above.
This means that the Dharma of the Buddhas is subtle; they teach it according to the proper time, just as the udumbara flower appears only at the proper time, and thus it is not false or deceptive.

"What is this dharma? What is its subtlety? As for "dharma," it refers to that which I have praised upon emerging from meditative concentration—the teachings spoken by all Buddhas according to what is appropriate, which are skillful and provisional methods.
As for "subtlety," although these teachings are spoken according to what is appropriate within those contexts, the Buddha’s intention lies in the ultimate reality;
beings are unable to understand it, and thus it is said that "the underlying intent is difficult to comprehend. To explain this further, [the text] cites the present Buddha.
The sovereign power [of this teaching] elucidates the skillful means of all Buddhas; because their skillful wisdom is identical, one may use this to explain that.
That is to say, regarding the fact that the Buddhas preach the Dharma according to what is appropriate and that their underlying intent is difficult to comprehend—why is this so?

Let us set aside for a moment the point that the Buddhas’ preaching according to what is appropriate is subtle and difficult to understand; even since my own attainment of enlightenment, I have expounded all dharmas through various [means]. All...

The Buddha’s skillful means are also like this. This concludes the section on the Dharma. The followers of the Two Vehicles employ the seventh consciousness for deliberation and the sixth consciousness for discrimination;
they do not realize that the subtle meaning of all dharmas is beyond deliberation and discrimination. The Buddha’s intent is difficult to comprehend.
Only Buddhas and Buddhas can fully comprehend this. Those who receive the teaching speak of three [vehicles], yet all Buddhas know only one.

△ Fourth, the demonstration of the ultimate reality, divided into four parts: first, the statement of the purpose for appearing in the world; second, the repeated inquiry into the purpose for appearing in the world; third, the explicit clarification of the purpose for appearing in the world;
fourth, the conclusion regarding the purpose for appearing in the world. Now, first, the statement of the purpose for appearing in the world.
Why is this so? It is because the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, appear in the world solely for the sake of the one great causal matter (*ekamahākaruṇā-hetu-pratyaya*).

"Appearing" (*chi*) is spoken in contrast to "entering" (*chu*); "manifesting" (*xian*) is spoken in contrast to "concealing" (*yin*). The term "one" (*yi*) refers to the single true reality (*eka-tattva-lakṣaṇa*).

It is not the three vehicles, the five natures, or the seven stages of expedient means; therefore, it is called "one. "Great" (*da*) signifies that its nature is vast and expansive, encompassing the three vehicles, the five natures, and the seven stages of expedient means.
It is "great" because it is so; it is called a "matter" (*vastu*) because it is the ritual procedure for the appearance of all Buddhas in the world.

"Condition" (*hetu*) refers to the karmic resonance of sentient beings, while "occasion" (*pratyaya*) refers to the Buddha responding to that resonance. Furthermore, the Buddha’s knowledge and vision constitute the "great matter"; the non-duality between the living being and the Buddha is called "one.
The inherent nature of sentient beings is the "cause," and the development [of that nature] by a virtuous friend is the "condition. For forty years prior, [the teaching was] provisional.
This knowledge and vision has been explained. Now, I shall speak truly of this knowledge and vision:

it is that all Buddhas have realized this mark of suchness (*tathatā-lakṣaṇa*), and having mounted upon this true path, they appear in the world. Their sole purpose is for sentient beings to attain this true mark;
they have never had any other concern. 2. A Second Inquiry into the Intent of Appearing in the World.
Śāriputra, as for what is called "the Buddhas appear in the world for the sake of one great cause and condition," [the text] intends to analyze this;
thus, it raises the matter once more to serve as a thematic introduction. Furthermore, because this "great matter" is that which the Buddha most highly honors, he demonstrates it again.
This is as clarified in the *Śāstra*: when the Father King desired to hear the name of his Crown Prince, he repeated it many times.

He speaks of it without ever feeling weary or satisfied. △ Third, the explicit clarification of the intent for appearing in the world, which is further divided into two parts. First, the clarification of the causal conditions of the Great Matter:
"The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, desire to cause sentient beings [to attain the Buddha-way]... for the sake of the one great causal condition, they appear in the world."
The *Dharmapada-śāstra* (Fa-hua lun) provides a threefold explanation: first, the meaning of "unsurpassed," which means that apart from omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), there is nothing else;

second, the meaning of "sameness," because the nature and dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas are equal; third, the meaning of "not knowing," referring to how those of the two vehicles do not know that ultimately there is only the One Buddha Vehicle;
and fourth, it is for the purpose of causing them to realize non-retrogression.

The turning of the earth manifests equality with immeasurable wisdom and karma. The treatise states that this is sequential: first, the opening of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision is established as unsurpassed;

next, it is shown that the three vehicles equally possess the Buddha-nature and the Dharma-body. Although it clarifies that the Buddha’s wisdom is unsurpassed, there was concern that the Buddha alone might possess it;
therefore, it subsequently clarifies that the three vehicles equally possess it. Although the three vehicles equally possess it, the two vehicles...
Regarding those who do not know, it is shown to them so that they may awaken; regarding those who already know, they must not regress. Thus, the fourth [stage] causes them to attain non-regression.
The two sections concerning Bodhisattvas are explained as above. "Showing" means that for Bodhisattvas who have doubts, it is shown so that they may practice according to reality.
"Awakening" means that those who have not yet resolved upon Bodhicitta should resolve upon it. "Entering" refers to those who have already...

It causes the arousal of bodhicitta so that they may enter the Dharma. Regarding ordinary beings, there are three stages: "Opening" is as explained above; "Showing" means revealing that they possess buddha-nature;
and "Awakening" means causing externalist sentient beings to attain realization; "Entering" means causing them to enter Great Bodhi.
Jiashan said: "Revealing and instructing" refers to the capacity to transform others; "awakening and entering" refers to those who are transformed.
Regarding the capacity to transform, there is both "great revelation" and "detailed instruction. To simply state that there is a nature is "great revelation";

to say, "This is the nature of an ordinary person," or "This is the nature of a sage," along with the principles of cause and effect and the practice of the path, constitutes "detailed instruction. Regarding those who are transformed, there is both initial awakening and final entry.

To understand suddenly and thoroughly is called "awakening" (*wu*). To practice and realize through accord is termed "entry" (*ru*). This signifies beginning from the shallow and culminating in the deep.
The two characters "desire" (*yu*) and "to cause" (*ling*) constitute the Buddha’s fundamental intention. "Sentient beings" (*zhòngshēng*) refers to the beings of the nine realms;

thus, these characters correspond to the preceding [section on] causes and conditions. The two characters "pure" (*qīngjìng*) are manifested from the character "open" (*kāi*). To open what was closed is called "opening. The Buddha knows...

Regarding the three characters [“seeing,” “hearing,” and “knowing”], they should be understood as referring to the knowledge and vision that is inherently and originally possessed by nature. “Buddha is precisely knowledge and vision” is a *karmadhāraya* (attributive) compound.

Qingliang says, “Nature is itself knowledge and vision. Guifeng says, “Knowledge and vision are the numinous source of original enlightenment (*mūla-bodhi*), specifically pointing to the nature within the six sense faculties.
The various sutras explain and manifest this in diverse ways, and the designations used by the ancient masters differ; it is through wisdom that one knows this.
This is the Buddha-nature. Fools call it the "vital spirit" (jīng-hún); all of these refer to this very thing. However, because one is deluded and obstructed by the two hindrances, it is kept closed;
therefore, it is opened so that it may be made manifest and rendered pure. "Manifest" refers to the essence while still entangled [in defilements].
For example, when the eye is stained by forms, or even when the mind is disturbed by dharmas, as long as it is not opened, it is not yet pure. Once opened, it immediately—
Far removed from delusion and obstruction, form is the Buddha’s form; sound is the Buddha’s sound.
Both the internal body and mind and the external world are the Tathāgatagarbha, the wondrous nature of True Suchness (bhūtatathatā); this is what is meant by purity.
To "go forth and announce" means to take that which one possesses and clearly proclaim it to others. The wisdom and vision of the Buddha is that of all Buddhas.
This is a *tatpuruṣa* compound meaning "the knowledge and vision that have already been realized as the fruit of cultivation.

Sentient beings possess the knowledge and vision inherent in their nature (*prakṛti-stha*), yet they have not yet attained it through cultivation and realization. If one were merely to open up this inherent nature without demonstrating its cultivation and realization, it would be like ore or unrefined jade;
there would ultimately be no final perfection. Therefore, he instructs and reveals it based on his own cultivation and realization. He says to himself:

"Awakening" (wu) refers to becoming personally enlightened through the previously revealed teaching that the nature is inherently endowed with knowledge and vision. "Entering" (ru) means to personally arrive [at this state].

"The path of knowledge and vision" (zhijian dao) refers to the gateway to the knowledge and vision attained upon the fruition of cultivation and realization; it is, for example, like the Truth of the Path (mārgasatya).

This follows from the previous announcement regarding the completion of cultivation, which refers to personally reaching the realm of realization through practice. The first two [categories] pertain to the teachings (*śāsana*), while the latter two pertain to the capacity of the practitioner (*yogin*).
Furthermore, one and three belong to the category of inherent nature (*prakṛti*), whereas two and four belong to the category of cultivated accomplishment (*bhāvanā-siddha*).

Moreover, it should be understood that "sentient beings" is a name for the distinct functions of the nine realms, while "Buddha" is a title for the identical essence of the one realm. These are the names for the distinctions among the nine realms.
The knowledge and vision of sentient beings: the ten realms and the ten suchnesses are called the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.

As for the knowledge and vision of sentient beings, because delusion and falsehood exist, they obscure the truth and lose their original nature; there is that which they do not know and that which they do not see.

Encountering conditions, they dwell in attachment; they have knowledge yet crave, and they have vision yet seek. Therefore, it is called false knowledge and vision. The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* says: "To establish knowledge within knowledge..."

This is precisely the root of ignorance. As for the Buddha’s knowledge and vision: he has thoroughly penetrated the source of the myriad streams of the true mark (*dharmatā*) and awakened to the wondrously luminous essence.
There is nothing he does not know and nothing he does not see; it is like the sun illuminating the world or a mirror manifesting forms.
Responding without a mind and appearing without thought, it is therefore called "true knowledge and vision. As this sutra says: "The Tathāgata contemplates and knows."
It is the ultimate destination of all dharmas, and it also knows the mental thoughts of all sentient beings.
This concludes the section on Śāriputra. △ Second, clarifying the convergence of provisional means into the ultimate reality.
The Buddha told Śāriputra: "Up until [the point where he said] there is no other vehicle, whether two or three.
Formerly, as a skillful means to teach and transform beings through the three vehicles, yet speaking according to the ultimate truth, he was only transforming bodhisattvas.
