It is like that impoverished son who considered himself a hired laborer, while the elder regarded him as his true son. The various practices of the three vehicles are merely designated as such."

"For the sake of all" means for the sake of the perfect. "For the sake of all" refers to a single matter. What is this single matter? It is solely to awaken sentient beings through the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.

The teaching of the Perfect and Sudden is called the Single Buddha Vehicle (*ekabuddhayāna*). All that falls below this is termed "teachings with remainder," which are of provisional meaning (*neyārtha*).
When it is now said, "merely by means of the Single Buddha Vehicle," it refers to teaching exclusively [the ultimate truth].
This is the Buddha Vehicle; there are neither two nor three, for two or three are not the original intent.
All Buddhas teach Bodhisattvas through this great matter; they preach the Dharma through this; they perform their activities through this;
and they transform and enlighten sentient beings through this. How could talk of two or three be anything but unreal? △ Fourth, the summary of the intention for appearing in the world.
Śāriputra, the Dharma of all Buddhas in the ten directions is likewise.
While the phrasing and meaning of this section are extensive, in the introduction, by means of the light, he saw horizontally eighteen thousand lands;

citing the past, he elucidated vertically twenty thousand Buddhas, none of whom failed to establish provisional teachings for the sake of bestowing the ultimate reality, and to bring those provisional teachings back to the ultimate reality. This applies to all the ten directions.
The oceans of lands are inexhaustible; the worlds, whether pure or defiled, are infinitely diverse.

Among the Buddhas appearing in the world, there are none who do not first employ skillful means and subsequently reveal the ultimate truth. Such is the nature of the great causal conditions. Therefore, it is said that "the Dharma is also like this.

The above concludes the general explanation of all Buddhas. II. Specifically enumerating the Buddhas of the three periods of time. This section is divided into two parts. First, specifically explaining the three Buddhas.
Revealing the provisional to manifest the real. Second, a general summary of the great event of the appearance of all Buddhas. This section is further divided into three parts:

first, clarifying the Buddhas of the past; second, clarifying the Buddhas of the future; and third, clarifying the Buddhas of the present. While [the Buddha's appearance] should fully possess six meanings, only two are explicitly stated here.
Fourth, by analogy with what precedes and follows, we shall first clarify the Buddhas of the past.
Śāriputra, all past Buddhas (up to) have ultimately attained all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*).

As for the "past Buddhas," these are the Buddhas of the *Vibhūṣaṇakalpa* (Adornment Eon). Tracing them back, there were Candrasūryapradīpa (Sun-Moon-Lamp), Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū (Great Supernatural Power), Ghoṣadatta (Gift of Sound), Meghasvararāja (Cloud-Sovereign), and others.
Through countless skillful means (*upāya*), they first revealed the provisional [teachings]. This refers to the passage beginning with "this Dharma."
The two characters "this dharma" (*shishi*) and the two characters "thus" (*ruciruo*) in the chapter on Śākyamuni both point to the provisional as being the real;
they describe the application of the provisional with the intent of revealing the real.

As for the statement that sentient beings of the past attained the fruit by hearing the Dharma from Buddhas of the past, the continued use of the term "sentient beings" refers to their names. For what Buddha has not been accomplished from among sentient beings?
△ Second, explaining the future Buddhas.
Śāriputra, all future Buddhas (up to) will ultimately attain all-encompassing wisdom (*sarvākārajñatā*).
As for these future Buddhas, they are those such as Maitreya and the other Buddhas of the *Tārakakalpa* (Star Constellation Eon), including Padmaprabha, Sāgarabuddhidharaṇī, and so forth.
Those who are currently treading upon the seven-jeweled lotuses and so forth are all future Buddhas; this can be understood through the revelation [of the teaching].
△ Third, the present Buddhas:
"Śāriputra, those currently in the ten directions... ultimately all attain the knowledge of all modes (sarvākārajñatā)."
The Buddhas currently existing are those of the Bhadrakalpa; they are also the emanated Buddhas gathered through the three transformations.

These include the Buddhas such as Prabhūtaratna from the "Chapter on the Exquisite Sound," Śubhavyūha, and Ratnatejobhyudgatarāja, who were contemporaries of Śākyamuni and are currently teaching the Dharma. The names of their respective lands are each different.

The titles of the Buddhas differ from one another in their dignity; yet in establishing words and instituting teachings—first employing provisional means and subsequently revealing the ultimate reality—they are all without exception the same.
Therefore it is said: "Though hundreds of thousands of billions of countless Dharma-gates are preached, in truth they constitute but the One Vehicle."

First, the intention for appearing in the world is indicated; next, the clarification and revelation [of the Buddha-nature] may be understood. △ Second, the summary of the great matter of the appearance of all Buddhas:
"Śāriputra, these Buddhas... [down to] ...desire to cause sentient beings to enter the Buddha’s knowledge and vision."
The preceding section clarified the chapter on the four Buddhas. Having extensively explained the provisional and real two wisdoms of the Buddhas as requested, it is concluded.
△ Second, the chapter on Śākyamuni clarifies the provisional and real two wisdoms of Śākyamuni as previously set forth. Among the six meanings, there is no expression of the rarity of the Dharma.
This is divided into five parts: first, opening the provisional means; second, revealing the ultimate reality; third, citing the five turbidities to explain the provisional;
fourth, distinguishing the false to encourage faith; and fifth, declaring that there is no falsehood. First, regarding the opening of the provisional means:
Śāriputra, I am now likewise thus (up to) preaching the Dharma for them.

First through expedient means and later through the ultimate truth; this is no different from that of all Buddhas, and is therefore said to be "likewise thus. "Knowing all" and below opens the expedient means.

"Various desires" refers to the faculties, natures, inclinations, and aspirations of the five vehicles. In the past, these were called "faculties" (*indriya*), because they are capable of producing [results].
"To act" means the present, which is called "desire"; its meaning is the grasping of objects. "Future" is called "nature" (dhātu); its meaning is non-alteration.

That which is deeply attached to by the mind is precisely the "root. As for "the power of skillful means," it refers to the provisional teachings of the three vehicles as they are appropriately opened up.
△ Second, revealing the ultimate reality.
"Śāriputra, all these... [up to] "...there is not even the Two Vehicles, let alone three.

These two characters ["all these"] inherit the preceding opening of the provisional means (*upāya*) with the intent of pointing toward the reality (*bhūta*). An ancient master said: "The *bān* (crow) and *chī* (owl) tree."
The "upper weeping" refers to the intention [of the Buddha] being within the hemp fields; it is revealed through the manifestation of reality throughout the ten directions.

Throughout the worlds of the ten directions, there is nothing that is not the wondrous principle of the Dharma-realm and True Suchness (tathatā). It is as profoundly still and uniform as space, such that even the name of the Two Vehicles does not exist, let alone the Three.
Yet, according to the capacities and inclinations of sentient beings, and out of necessity, he concealed the One Truth and manifested it as many.

These are merely the three provisional [teachings]. △ Third, citing the five turbidities to explain the provisional. This is divided into two parts. First, stating the names and manifesting their characteristics:
"Śāriputra, the Buddhas appear in the world of the five turbidities and evil ages... [up to] the turbidity of views and the turbidity of lifespan, and so forth."
The world was originally not evil; it became evil because of the turbidity. Turbidity is like throwing earth into water:

the water loses its clarity, the earth loses its distinct boundaries, and the appearance becomes muddied; this is called turbidity. The five turbidities (*pañca-kaṣāya*) mentioned in this sutra differ from those in the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*.
In the latter, from the onset of obscurity, all nine realms are turbid, and only the Buddha is pure. This [sutra] intends to demonstrate how to clarify the turbid.
The principle of entering *nirvāṇa* instantaneously is the ultimate source. The present sutra is restricted to this defiled land during the aeon of decline (*kaṣāya-kalpa*).

It clarifies that the Buddhas conceal their true reality and manifest the three vehicles because of the five turbidities (*pañca-kaṣāya*) of this evil world; it thus perfectly reveals the inconceivable skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*), which is the cutting off of the stream.
When the human lifespan decreases from eighty thousand years to thirty thousand, it is not yet termed "turbid"; it reaches [the stage of turbidity] when...
Twenty thousand years mark the beginning of the five corruptions (*pañca-kaṣāya*). Śākyamuni appeared in the world precisely during the period when the human lifespan was one hundred years.

The corruption of the eon (*kalpa-kaṣāya*) has no separate essence; it is a provisional designation for the time when the other four corruptions are rampant. The corruption of sentient beings (*sattva-kaṣāya*) likewise has no separate essence;

it is a provisional designation based on the three factors of views, pride, and karmic retribution. The afflictions (*kleśa*) take the five dull fetters (*mūla-kleśa*) as their essence. As for the corruption of views (*dṛṣṭi-kaṣāya*), it takes...

The five views of gain (*pañca-lābha-dṛṣṭi*) constitute its essence. The turbidity of life-span (*āyuḥ-kaṣāya*) consists of the three factors of vitality (*āyuḥ*), warmth (*uṣman*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*), which maintain the continuity of form and mind.
The four turbidities intensify and converge at this time: when hatred increases, weapons and warfare arise;
when greed increases, famine arises; and when delusion increases, epidemics arise. Because these three calamities arise, afflictions (*kleśa*) flourish twofold. All...
Views become increasingly rampant; physical forms and mental states grow coarse and debased; ill repute and foul calumny spread; years are crushed and lifespans diminished;

the various turbidities converge like waters rushing toward a dark abyss, where wind and waves surge and fish and dragons are thrown into turmoil, leaving nothing to rely upon. It is the workings of time that cause this;
such are the signs of the kalpa-turbidity (*kalpa-kaṣāya*). At such a time, the world declines and the Way is lost; human affairs fall into disorder. One seeks...
In antiquity, that era of non-action and purity can no longer be found. Greed is like an ocean that receives all streams yet never knows satiety;

it is this state where one is anxious for what one has not yet attained and fearful of losing what one has already gained. Anger is like a venomous serpent that drinks poison and agitates the entire world;
it is this state where a fox borrows the tiger’s majesty. Ignorance is dark and dull-witted, exceeding the blackness of lacquer or ink; it is this state by which the world creates darkness.
Karma is this. Arrogance is looking down upon others with haughtiness, showing no restraint in one's contemptuous endurance, and relying on talent, power, and cleverness.
Doubt is a web of lack of faith, such that one cannot be told the truth; it is the unreality of the world. When it is thus, the mind is heated by afflictions (*kleśa*);
greed and hatred arise alternately. Like empty flowers clouding the eyes, deceit and guile横行 (run rampant). These are the characteristics of the turbidity of affliction (*kleśa-kaṣāya*).
At this time, if one were to seek throughout the entire world for someone who does not recognize or know, who maintains purity and embraces simplicity, such a person could not be found.
When the mind grasps at sensory forms, it establishes a sovereign master; this is likened to sticky glue, which causes one to become attached to things.
Wandering through the six realms of existence and taking birth in every place—this is the characteristic of the defilement of sentient beings (*sattva-kaṣāya*).
When such various karmic signs arise, one does not rush toward fame and power, but instead hides the mind in wealth and goods; one does not become submerged in forms and sounds.
Thus, one becomes bound by emotional consciousness; seeking only to satisfy the belly and frolic, it is impossible to find those who strike the earthen blocks (jiāng) and sing.

To claim there is a person where there is none, or to claim there is a Way where there is no Way—these sixteen views, the sixty-two [views], and so forth, are like a dense thicket of nets, entangling and distorting one so that one cannot escape. This is the characteristic of the turbidity of views.

Thus, with such perverse knowledge and deluded vision, the pure wind has been eroded, and the Way and its Virtue have become diluted. The apertures of emotion open wider by the day, and the primordial unity (*hundun*) dies daily.
Clinging to annihilation or permanence, calculating causes and effects, one seeks true knowledge and true vision, yet it remains unattainable.
Born in the morning and dying by evening, emerging at dawn and vanishing at dusk, they revolve like waves and swirl like smoke, not pausing for even an instant. This...
This is the characteristic of the turbidity of life (*āyuṣkaṣāya*). In such short years and brief lifespans, sensual desires grow ever deeper while the celestial faculties grow ever shallower;
the vital energy of wind and clouds diminishes, while the worldly sentiments of children and women increase. One who seeks to attain the natural wisdom of liberation cannot be found.
Such is the essential nature of the five turbidities (*pañcakaṣāya*). As for the sequence of the five turbidities, afflictions (*kleśa*) and views (*dṛṣṭi*) constitute...
The root. From these two turbidities, sentient beings arise; from sentient beings, there is the continuity of life.

These four, as they pass through time, constitute the *kalpa-turba* (the age of turbulence). Now, do not mistake the sequence or the meaning. △ Second, during the time of the Two Vehicles, three are opened.
Śāriputra, during the period of the turbidity of the kalpa... [up to] "distinguishing and preaching three within the single Buddha-vehicle.
The Tathāgata appears in the world precisely at such a time of the five turbidities and chaos. This is because the innate goodness of beings has been lost and extinguished.
The world has become so corrupt that human beings fail to fulfill their potential for life and things do not abide by their natural principles; hence it is called a time of chaos.
This refers to the kalpa-turbidity, which encompasses all four turbidities. The defilements of sentient beings are deep and heavy; they indulge in greed, anger, and delusion.
Regarding themselves, they would not pluck out a single hair to benefit the world; yet regarding others, they indulge in avarice without satiety and envy those who—

O worthy one, [such people] envy the abilities of others; they are the root of suffering in the three miserable realms and the foundation of all evils. With the five turbidities acting as heavy obstructions, their wisdom is shallow and their faculties inferior.

Utterly foolish and deluded, they are difficult to discipline and difficult to subdue. If one does not accord with what they prefer and instead cast the Great Dharma upon them, it will be difficult [to lead them].
Therefore, the Buddhas, having no other choice, provisionally distinguish and teach the Three Vehicles within the One Buddha Vehicle. Stop.
Weeping over yellow leaves—how could they truly be gold coins? △ Fourth, Distinguishing the False to Encourage Faith, divided into two parts: First, Distinguishing the True from the False;
Second, Dispelling Doubts through Exceptions. The first part is further divided into two: First, those who have neither heard nor known [the Dharma] are not true disciples.

Śāriputra, if my disciples—whether they be non-Arhat or non-Pratyekabuddha—share a spiritual communion with their teacher and are bound by a shared vital essence, following the teacher’s Dharma and continuing the transmission of the lamp, then whatever they speak should be believed with certainty and without doubt.
An Arhat possesses the capacity for both wisdom and the severance of defilements; a Pratyekabuddha likewise...

The wisdom of awakening—raising this once, repeating it three times—he understood it upon hearing it. Within the Dharma of the Dharma King, although there are names for the two vehicles, there is no reality of the two vehicles.
The Tathāgata’s appearance in the world is solely for the purpose of teaching and transforming bodhisattvas; how could there be two vehicles?
They are merely provisional designations established to lead them [to the truth]. What was formerly the expedient of "three" is now the "one."
The true reality of this is as follows: one who transmits this is a true disciple; one who awakens to this is a true Arhat; one who realizes this is a true Pratyekabuddha.

Yet my disciples today claim for themselves to be Arhats and Pratyekabuddhas, yet they neither hear nor know the essential principle of non-duality and non-triplicity, which concerns only the work of the Bodhisattvas.
Such individuals are not disciples of the Buddha, nor are they Arhats, nor are they Pratyekabuddhas.

The Buddha said: "Śāriputra, as for these bhikṣus [up to] 'if they do not believe this Dharma, it is impossible'—this constitutes the formation of overweening pride through hearing [the teaching] without faith or acceptance."

This was said to urge the assembly to believe and accept [the teaching]. Because the obstructions of the five turbidities are heavy, it is taught that the exhaustion of the afflictions of view and thought (*dṛṣṭi- and bhāvanā-kleśa*) constitutes the name "Arhat";
that one no longer undergoes rebirth constitutes the "final body" (*paścima-deha*);

and that one has emerged from the cycle of suffering within the realm of shared residence (*sahā-loka*) constitutes "Nirvana. Yet, since the distinct delusions of ignorance (*avidyā*) still remain, how can they be called Arhats?
The cycle of birth and death through transformation is vast and boundless; how, then, can it be called the "final body"? A conjured city is not yet the true treasure-land;
how, then, can it be called ultimate *nirvāṇa*? If one considers this sufficient and no longer strives to seek unexcelled *bodhi*, [one has failed].
They are all merely people of overweening pride (adhimāna). This is shown by way of contrast:

if one were truly an Arhat, upon hearing this sutra, they would immediately believe and accept it, advancing toward the pursuit of Bodhi; it has never happened that such a person would not believe in this Dharma.
These individuals have not attained Arhatship yet claim to be Arhats, and have not attained their final body yet claim to have done so.
To claim that one has reached the ultimate goal while still in one's final body and before attaining *nirvāṇa*—is this not indeed *adhimāna* (arrogance)?
△ Second, the removal of exceptions and the resolution of doubts:
"Except for after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa when no Buddha is present... (up to) "...one shall attain decisive understanding within this Dharma."
Continuing from above: if this sutra were preached by the Buddha while he was still in the world, those who do not believe or accept it would constitute a case of *adhimāna* (conceit).
The text then clarifies: "Except for after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, when no Buddha is present before one.

This permits that those of a certain class who are biased toward provisional teachings and do not believe in the perfect Dharma (*pariniṣpanna-dharma*) are not considered to be acting out of conceit; such individuals may indeed be regarded as venerable in places where there is no Buddha. This is permitted.
Why is this? Because although this sutra exists after my parinirvāṇa, those who seek to receive, uphold, and understand its meaning will be difficult to find.
Since such people are rare to encounter, it results in these classes of beings not believing, not accepting, not hearing, and not knowing [it].

Therefore, my granting permission for this is not out of arrogance. If one encounters a person of inferior capacity, one should resolve their doubts, fearing they might say: "If, after the parinirvāṇa, there are no arhats..."

If one encounters this sutra but does not encounter someone who recites and upholds it, then one will remain forever stalled at the level of the lesser fruits and will ultimately never hear [the teaching].

Therefore, the commentary states: "Although such a person conceives the thought that they have attained nirvana, after their life has ended, they will be reborn in a land where there is still a remainder [of conditioned existence] and encounter another Buddha.
Under the single word of this Great Dharma, they shall immediately attain definitive understanding. Furthermore:
Regarding "the other Buddhas": these are the Bodhisattvas of the Four Reliances (*catur-apāśraya*). When an Arhat encounters them, he hears the sutras and attains definitive understanding.

Furthermore, by practicing the *buddhānusmṛti-samādhi* (meditative concentration on the Buddha), he sees the Buddhas of the ten directions expounding the Dharma for him, whereby he also attains definitive understanding. Moreover, when a practitioner reaches the point of extreme sincerity in repentance, he sees the Buddha expound the Dharma for him, and likewise attains definitive understanding.
This concludes the section on "Discerning the False and Reinforcing Faith. 5. Expounding that there is No Falsehood.
"Śāriputra, you all should be single-minded [until] there is no other vehicle, but only the Single Buddha Vehicle.
First, he exhorts them to believe in the true words of Kāśyapa; next, he exhorts them to believe in the sincere words of all Buddhas. This is for the purpose of halting doubt and slander.
However, this exhortation is directed toward those who are ready to receive it, because their three prior requests were so earnest; thus, the World-Honored One’s compassionate heart was moved.

It is vital. One moment conceding, the next seizing; one moment suppressing, the next elevating. Having turned and returned to this point, the unsurpassed, wondrous principle is laid open with eight characters and presented upon the entire platter.
It lacks nothing but a single act of faith and understanding at the opportune moment. Therefore, the concluding exhortation says:
You all should be single-minded and impartial. If you wait for understanding through reflection or for faith to arise after seeing, you will miss the point face-to-face;
you would not have known it even from a distance of thousands of miles. It simply requires that you take responsibility within the words themselves.

If you believe directly and without doubt, your entire being will be revealed and your whole essence fully manifested. The Buddhas speak in accordance with the nature of reality; their words are not false. However—
I have given rise to a sincere resolve; I shall certainly not deceive you. If you do not believe this, there is nothing more I can do for you.
The preceding prose section is concluded. △ Second, the verse recitation consists of one hundred and twenty-one lines, divided into two parts.

The first four lines and one phrase constitute a verse summarizing the aforementioned consent to answer. The second section consists of one hundred and sixteen lines and three phrases, summarizing the aforementioned exposition of the True Dharma.
Specifically, the first four lines and one phrase summarize the aforementioned consent to answer.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:
"Bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs who harbor overweening pride... (until)... Śāriputra, listen well."

The pride of superiority (*adhimāna*), the pride of self (*asmimāna*), and lack of faith are common to all four assemblies. However, because those who have left the household life to practice the Way and attained meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) mistakenly claim it to be the fruit of sainthood, they specifically give rise to the pride of superiority.
Laymen (*upāsaka*), on the other hand, often give rise to the pride of self due to their possession of wealth and power.

Because the wisdom of female lay followers (*upāsikā*) is shallow and biased, they frequently give rise to lack of faith; thus, those who do not recognize their own faults conceal their minds with the three losses.
They hide their blemishes and proclaim their virtues, failing to engage in self-examination; such are shameless persons. If, however, one does recognize one's own faults...

This is a person of wisdom. Regarding "defects and leaks": a lapse in the *vinaya* (discipline) is called a "defect" (*chidra*); the presence of lapses in the meditative absorption (*dhyāna*) and the path (*mārga*) is called a "leak" (*asrava*).
Because there is no path or meditative absorption, evil thoughts arise within, like a jade stone containing internal flaws.

Because there is no discipline, one moves the body and speech externally, like a jade stone showing surface blemishes. "Guarding and cherishing" refers to concealment; one conceals their transgressions out of fear that they will be exposed.
Regarding one's own shortcomings: those who guard and cherish them fear losing material offerings.
Those with meager wisdom lack the knowledge of the learner (*śaikṣa*) and the non-learner (*aśaikṣa*), possessing only worldly, petty intelligence—like the dregs of wine or the husks of rice.

These five thousand [monks] possess only worldly *dhyāna*, lacking the moisture of untainted (*anāsrava*) meditative concentration; they possess only an intellectual understanding of the words, but no...
The substance of intellectual wisdom is like chaff; this metaphor illustrates that within this assembly there is no true wisdom.
They are exclusively empty-bellied and haughty in heart, clinging to the literal teachings as if they were mere dregs and husks mixed among the five grains.

Now the Buddha opens the great capacity and manifests the great function, refusing to make his livelihood within the realm of words and language. He intends precisely to sift out the chaff and husks, so that only the substance remains.
O Benevolent One! Because they beheld such majestic power, they paid homage to the Buddha and withdrew; thus it is said, "They departed because of the Buddha’s majestic power.
Such individuals as these possess meager merit and few virtues, and are therefore incapable of receiving this Great Dharma of the One Vehicle.
These two lines concern the Buddha’s self-consolation, while the single line beginning with "Śāriputra" concerns his granting of permission to answer. Within this [passage]:

One reprimands those who are deficient by comparing them to broken vessels; those with blemishes by comparing them to flaws and diseases; those who are dregs and husks by comparing them to a lack of purity and refinement;
those of small wisdom by comparing them to a lack of great wisdom; and those who are mere branches and leaves by comparing them to a lack of integrity and substance.
Only because of transgressions are there omissions; because of omissions, there is guarding and cherishing. This guarding and cherishing is small wisdom. Small wisdom is meager merit.
Because of meager merit, one is incapable of receiving the Great Dharma. Part Two: One hundred and sixteen lines in three phrases.
A verse on the aforementioned preaching of the True Dharma, divided into two sections. First: seventy-three lines and one phrase.
The verses on the four Buddhas comprise forty-three and a half lines. The verses on the Śākyamuni chapter [follow]. First, the verses on the four Buddhas are divided into four parts:
(1) the first thirty-four lines and three phrases praise all Buddhas; (2) twenty-seven and a half lines praise the Buddhas of the past;
(3) six and a half lines praise the Buddhas of the future; (4) four and a half lines praise the Buddhas of the present. Now...

The first three lines and the fourteenth line consist of three phrases that praise all Buddhas. However, they differ from the prose section in three respects. First, there is mutual exclusion between them:
while the prose praises the Dharma and mentions the absence of the five turbidities (*pañca-kaṣāya*), the present verse mentions the five turbidities but lacks the praise of the Dharma.

Second, regarding the sequence of their appearance: in the prose section, the praise of the Dharma comes first, followed by the statement that it is not in vain to reveal the provisional to manifest the real;

now, in the verse, the revelation of the provisional to manifest the real comes first, followed by the clarification that it is not in vain. Third, regarding the difference in opening and closing: in the prose, the exhortation to believe and the statement that it is not in vain are combined;
here, they are separated, with the exhortation to believe placed before the statement that it is not in vain. Furthermore, in the prose, this is presented as the skillful means of Śākyamuni.

This explains the provisional teachings (*upāya*) of all Buddhas; here, by means of Śākyamuni, it manifests the One. It explains the ultimate reality (*bhūta-artha*) of all Buddhas, precisely because it reveals that the Way of every Buddha is identical.
The text is divided into five parts: first, five lines of three phrases, which eulogize the Buddhas’ opening of the provisional;
twenty-three lines, which eulogize the Buddhas’ manifestation of the real; and three and a half lines, which eulogize the Buddhas’ exhortation.
"Faith. Four [verses] and nine lines and a half: these verses praise the Buddhas' opening of the three vehicles within the five turbidities. Two [verses] and two lines:
these verses praise the non-falsity of the Buddhas. Furthermore, the first five lines and three phrases praise the Buddhas' opening of the provisional.
"The Dharma attained by all Buddhas consists of immeasurable powers of skillful means (upāya) [extending] to the preaching of *nirvāṇa*.

This 'Dharma attained' refers precisely to the provisional and ultimate teachings realized at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*). Because these skillful means are adapted to the capacities of sentient beings, they are called 'immeasurable.

They illuminate the capacities of the nine dharma-realms and preach the seven stages of skillful means (*sapta-upāya-śāsana*). The nine realms are those who are to be reached; the teachings do not exceed the seven."

It is said that by teaching the seven [vehicles] and subsuming them within the nine, one gradually leads [beings] into the reality. According to whatever capacity [a being] possesses, one teaches whatever dharma is appropriate;

meeting with their capacity, one accommodates them, for there is no fixed rule. Therefore, it is said: "By means of the power of immeasurable skillful means, he teaches for the sake of sentient beings.
The arising of aspiration is called *smṛti* (mindfulness); the diversity of the dharma-gates is called "various"; the mental intention abides therein, while its activities manifest outwardly.
Regarding the external: that which was practiced in the past is called "nature" (*prakṛti*); present inclinations are called "desire" (*chanda*).

Because mental thoughts are not uniform and karmic activities are not uniform, it is said they are "various" (*nānā*). As for "good and evil karma," this refers to the people of the seven stages of preparation (*saptavidha-prayoga*), who transmit and discuss good and evil among themselves;
these various distinctions of good and evil from previous lives cannot be exhausted by a single condition, a single metaphor, or a single means.
They are able to deliver [beings]. Only the Buddha’s skillful wisdom illuminates and understands them;
according to their capacities and dispositions, he teaches the ninefold Dharma, catering to their inclinations and desires to cause them to rejoice. *Sūtra* refers to a formal discourse.

*Gāthā*, translated as "isolated verse," refers to verses that are not repeated in prose. *Itivṛttaka* (Past Events) refers to accounts of events from former worlds. *Jātaka* (Birth Stories) refers to accounts of former lives.
This refers to the matter of taking birth. "Unprecedented" means that various supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*) are wonders never before seen by sentient beings.
"Causes and conditions" (*nidāna*) refers to all matters concerning the dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) of the Buddha’s words; these are all termed causes and conditions.

"Parables" (*avadāna*) refer to such examples as comparing the moon hidden behind a heavy mountain to the raising of a fan, or using the ceasing of wind in the great void to instruct on the movement of trees. *Geya* is called "repeated verse."

Upadeśa refers to discursive treatises (*vāda*). As with the aforementioned nine divisions, it is said that "expedient means were previously bestowed" because they were taught for the sake of those at the seven stages of expedient skillful means (*saptopāya-kauśalya*).
If one includes the twelve divisions, one adds Vaipulya (Extensive), Vyākaraṇa (Prophecy), and Avadāna (Spontaneous Utterance).

These are added to address those of dull faculties and inferior dispositions who are granted expedient means; because their faculties were dull in previous lives and they lack the capacity in the present life, they are unable to hear the Great [Vehicle]. Therefore, it is so stated.
Because they did not practice the profound [teachings] in previous lives, their obstacles were heavy; because they are now afflicted by manifold sufferings, they can only hear the Small [Vehicle].
Therefore, it is said that for them he preaches *nirvāṇa*. △ Twenty-three lines. Verses on the Buddhas manifesting the reality.
This section has two parts. The first three lines are verses on the causal conditions of the Great Matter (*mahā-kārya*).
"I have established these skillful means to enable them to enter the Buddha's wisdom" (up to) "for this reason I preach this sutra.

In the prose section, it first clarifies the causal conditions for the great matter of transcending the world—revealing, instructing, awakening, and enabling entry into the Buddha's knowledge and vision.
Next, it clarifies the convergence of provisional means into the ultimate reality: there is only the single Buddha-vehicle, with no other vehicles, whether two or three. Now, the verse [states]:
The meaning of their ultimate convergence is clear. Opening, showing, awakening, and entering are all subsumed under the Buddha-wisdom of the Mahāyāna.
Following the preceding [passage], it is said that this *nirvāṇa* was provisionally established for a time; it is not a definitive teaching, nor is it a teaching of ultimate reality.
In truth, through subtle and skillful means, they were secretly enticed to enter the Buddha’s wisdom; however, it was never said, "You shall yourselves become Buddhas."
Regarding the Buddha-way, the reason it was not previously taught was that their faculties were not yet mature and the time had not yet arrived.

Now that their faculties are mature and the time for teaching has come, he speaks with certainty and speaks the truth; tearing down the barriers, he directly imparts the sublime Dharma of the equality of the true mark of the Mahāyāna.
Therefore, it is said that "he definitively teaches the Mahāyāna. Furthermore, when...
He knew that the ninefold teachings previously expounded were all spoken according to the intentions of others and did not represent his own original intent.
The ninefold teachings were intended to accord with sentient beings so that they might enter the Mahāyāna; this was the Buddha’s original intent.
For this reason, he first preached these ninefold sūtras. (20) The twenty verses of the gāthās bring the provisional back to the real.
"There are sons of the Buddha whose minds are pure, supple, and sharp" (up to) "this matter is impossible.

The section beginning with "There are sons of the Buddha" indicates that the verse teaches only the Bodhisattvas. "Pure mind" means not forming companionship with the myriad dharmas nor entering into opposition with the various sensory objects;
it is not like being greedily attached to the five desires, like a foolish fly stuck in honey that refuses to let go.
They have abandoned [worldly attachments]. Being "pliant" means they are disciplined and gentle, easily transformed and guided;
they are not like those who are stubborn and coarse, as difficult to tame and subdue as a wild elephant. Having "sharp faculties" means they act immediately upon seeing the shadow of the whip;

they are not like those who delight in inferior teachings, as sluggish as a hack that does not move despite being spurred. They draw near to the Buddha to practice the Path, for their causes and conditions are profound.
Excellent. It is not like encountering a Buddha and failing to seek the supreme Dharma, thereby missing the opportunity face-to-face. Only in this way is one of great capacity;

only then is one truly called a son of the Buddha and worthy of receiving the Great Dharma. Not only is the Great Dharma preached for such a person, but they are also granted the prediction of attaining Buddhahood.
A doubt arises: "It is appropriate to preach the Great Dharma for such a son of the Buddha; why, then, is he also granted the prediction?"
"Yes. He replied, "Because of his profound resolve, he delights in cultivating all wholesome dharmas; because he recollects the Buddha, he aspires to seek unsurpassed bodhi;
and because he upholds the precepts, he is fully endowed with pure and white Brahma-conduct. If such a person hears the bestowal of a prediction [of enlightenment] but once,"
Great joy fills his body as he takes up the burden upon one shoulder.

Because his resolve is profound, his mindfulness of the Buddha is earnest, and his observance of the precepts is pure, the Buddha knows his mind and understands his practice; therefore, he preaches the Mahāyāna for him. From the words "The śrāvakas...
below, the text correctly clarifies the ultimate convergence. Now, regarding this Dharma of the equality of the Mahāyāna: it may not be preached, but if it is preached...
This Dharma, regardless of whether one belongs to the three vehicles, the heavens, or the human realm—if one but receives a single verse and it permeates the spirit, all shall attain Buddhahood.
It is like the *gāthā* medicine: if it but touches the lips, no ailment remains unhealed. One must not harbor even a hair’s breadth of doubt within one's breast.
The two characters "no doubt" (*wúyí*) are words intended to awaken [the practitioner]. Question: The path of the Buddha is vast and remote; the scriptures...

Question: Accumulating practices over kalpas, yet attaining Buddhahood with a single verse—how can this be so easy? Answer: The Buddha-nature exists within the entanglements, like a divine jewel hidden in one’s clothing.
Because one previously sought it outwardly, it was extremely difficult to attain. Now, this sutra points directly to the essence itself; thus, it is attained spontaneously without seeking.

Since Buddhahood is achieved with a single verse, what cause for doubt is there? [The section] beginning with "In the ten directions" correctly praises [the principle that] "only by... [is it attained].
"The One Buddha Vehicle is taught for the sake of sentient beings; there is no other vehicle, whether two or three.
From "The Buddhas" onwards, this verse summarizes the preceding statement that "all that they do is always for one purpose.

"Only this one purpose, and not by means of the small [vehicle] to deliver them" expresses the meaning of "always for one purpose. From "The Buddha himself abides" onwards, this explains the preceding phrase "not by means of the small [vehicle] to deliver them."
The principle of equality is common to both sentient beings and Buddhas. To awaken the people with this Way is the responsibility of the Sage.
If one does not awaken them through this Way but through some other way, how could that be equal? Indeed, the Way is not the Way of a single person;
it is the Way of all people under heaven. One desires that all people under heaven share in the Way of the Way of all under heaven.
This means that by making the Way public to all people, one truly accords with the Sage’s mind; how could one merely seek personal perfection while failing to reach others? Therefore it says:

"If one were to transform [beings] by means of the Lesser Vehicle," and so forth. △ The three and four and a half lines following praise the exhortation to faith from the Buddhas, which is divided into two parts.
The first two and a half lines cite the fruit to provide the exhortation.
If a person believes and takes refuge in the Buddha, the Tathāgata does not deceive them (up to: "I shall explain for them the seal of the true mark").
When the faculty of faith is perfected, one takes refuge with reverence in the Buddha; such a person is a superior vessel for carrying the Way. Regarding the two phrases concerning the Tathāgata:
it means that if you believe and take refuge in me, I shall treat you with sincerity; I do not deceive those of inferior capacity, nor do I mislead those who are beginners. I...

He desires the Dharma and its benefits, yet does not envy the excellence of others' possessions. The Buddha’s mind is pure; the defilements of ignorance and stinginess are absent, and all evils have been severed.
He speaks from within this purity, and thus his inner heart is trustworthy. As for being "fearless":

he has perfectly realized the Three Greats, reached the pinnacle of the Four Heavens, and his virtue is venerated by the myriad spirits while the hosts of demons submit to his transformation. What, then, is there to fear? Regarding "adorned with marks" and so forth, it is as follows:
The Body of Enjoyment for Others (*sāmbhogika-kāya*) briefly has ninety-six kinds of marks of a great man (*mahāpuruṣa-lakṣaṇa*).
In detail, it is adorned with as many marks and signs of excellence (*lakṣaṇa-anuvyañjana*) as there are atoms in ten *padma-garbha* worlds, shining radiantly and without obstruction;
that is to say, the worlds of the ten directions manifest simultaneously. The "Venerable Ones" are the various lords of the world within the *Avataṃsaka*, numbering forty.
The two assemblies knelt and prostrated, baring their shoulders in sincerity and paying their respects. Some rained down flowers and played music; incense and canopies filled the sky.
As they extolled his merits and recited his virtues, the flow of their words was like the sea. His physical marks were brilliant and manifest, his radiant features upright and majestic.
Within, he was free from darkness and delusion; without, he possessed luminosity. Honored by the multitude, his outward appearance was truly trustworthy. The *Śāstra* says: "All the small..."
Regarding the Mahāyāna sūtras: if they are sealed with the three seals of impermanence, non-self, and nirvāṇa, they are the word of the Buddha;
practicing them, one attains the Way. If they lack these three dharma-seals, they are the word of Māra. The Mahāyāna possesses only one dharma-seal: the true nature of all phenomena (*dharmatā*).
These are called sūtras of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*); they can lead to the Great Way. If they lack the seal of the true nature, they are the work of Māra.
Furthermore, that which is taught is the Seal of the Mind of the True Reality of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna-tattva-cittamudrā*).

Just as a state seal is transmitted from generation to generation, one who obtains this is recognized as a true son of heaven. Moreover, just as the authority of generals and ministers uses a seal to manage affairs, one who obtains it receives the sovereign’s mandate.

Below, they serve the myriad clans; at that time, there is no partiality, and the Dharma has nothing further to bestow. From the transmission between the thousand Buddhas, only the Mind-Seal has been passed down.
Having attained this mind, one becomes a true son of the Buddha, succeeds to the Buddha’s position, and performs the Buddha’s work, possessing majestic virtue and fearlessness.
They shall not be destroyed by Māra. It is difficult indeed for one who has not yet attained [the Path] not to be destroyed by Māra. △ Second, two lines citing the cause to provide encouragement:
"Śāriputra, you should know that from the time I first established my vow... (until) I shall cause all to enter the Buddha-way."
The "Original Vow" refers to the five hundred great vows made during the time of the Buddha Ratnagarbha.

In the past, I vowed not only for my own attainment of Bodhi, but also vowed that all sentient beings would enter together into the Buddha-wisdom. I now speak this in order to repay that vow; it is therefore worthy of belief.
This cites the former vow, while the passage beginning with "As I... below clarifies the fulfillment of that vow. Question: When the Buddha first established his vow, he vowed...
"To save all beings—yet now sentient beings are still so numerous. How can your vow be fulfilled? Answer: "Benefiting beings throughout the three periods of time is without end.

**4. Nine and a half lines in verse: The Buddhas of the Five Turbidities Open the Three Vehicles.** This is divided into four parts. First, one line generally clarifies the five turbidities.

1. The first section generally explains how the five corruptions (pañcakaṣāya) obstruct the Great [Vehicle]. 2. The second section, consisting of six lines, specifically clarifies the obstruction of the Great by the five corruptions. 3.

The third section, consisting of one line, clarifies that the Lesser [Vehicle] was taught because of the five corruptions. 4. The fourth section, consisting of one and a half lines, clarifies that the Lesser was bestowed for the sake of the Great. First, the initial line generally explains how the five corruptions obstruct the Great.
If I encounter sentient beings, I teach them all the Buddha-way; yet those without wisdom are confused and deluded, and do not accept the teaching. The *Madhyama Āgama* states:
"At the beginning of the kalpa, beings descended from the Ābhāsvara Heaven to be born in the world. There were no distinctions of male or female, nor of noble or humble.

They arose together in the world; therefore they are called 'sentient beings' (*sattva*). This is spoken according to the very beginning. If one gathers the various aggregates (*skandha*) and exists, it is a provisional name."
“Sentient beings” (*sattva*) refers to those who undergo retribution throughout a single lifetime.

If one says they are called “sentient beings” because they take birth in various places, this refers to their circulation through the five destinies by the power of karma. According to the *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna Sūtra*, there are ten kinds of sentient beings, namely:
long, short, square, round, triangular, blue, yellow, red, white, and purple. As for the “long,” it refers to their bodies while in hell.
They undergo boundless suffering and harbor boundless evil thoughts. In their existence as animals, they physically devour one another and mentally torment one another.
In their existence as hungry ghosts, their bodies are like burning mountains and their minds are like boiling cauldrons. In their existence as humans, they perform deeds that bring no benefit.
To harbor thoughts of harm; to indulge in idle play during favorable times; and to fail to hear the True Dharma—these prolong the cycle of birth and death. That which is short is as follows:

if a being in hell can, for even a single thought-moment, attain a tranquil mind and take up the precepts; if an animal can, for a single thought-moment, settle its mind and take refuge in the Triple Gem;
if a hungry ghost can, for a single thought-moment, purify its mind and its faculties; or if a human can cultivate the six perfections and practice filial piety.
"Equal" refers to those who, while still in the celestial realms, renounce heavenly pleasures to practice the holy life (*brahmacarya*); this is called "short.

"Square" refers to those such as the inhabitants of Uttarakuru, who regard all things as being without "I" or "mine," and upon leaving their bodies to ascend to heaven, rise further upward from that heaven, proceeding only toward favorable states;
this is "square" or "rectangular. "Round" refers to those who remain only within the three miserable paths and four realms of existence, revolving in a complete circle like a spinning wheel.
The fire-wheel represents the three natures: wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate; by remaining within the cycle of birth and death, one does not escape them.
Blue signifies being perpetually in the dark hells. Yellow signifies the hungry ghosts, who are emaciated, gaunt, and withered from hunger.
Red signifies animals devouring one another, their blood flowing until they are stained crimson. White signifies the white karma of humans and devas, which is wholesome.
The Way is like this: when a deva dies, other devas say, "You have gone to be born in the human realm. When a human dies, their acquaintances say, "You have ascended to the heavens.
*Zi* refers to the asuras; it means that devas, ghosts, and animals are like the color *zi* (purple).

Sentient beings scorch themselves with the fires of suffering, while the Buddhas deliver all things through great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*). Since compassion stands in contrast to suffering, it is said that they "meet.
Furthermore, the suchness of the Buddha and the suchness of sentient beings are one suchness, not two; because their fundamental nature is mutually related, they encounter one another.

If I encounter sentient beings and teach them the dharmas of humans and devas, the Four Noble Truths, and the Six Perfections, I would then fall into darkness, delusion, stinginess, greed, and partiality;
I would merely avoid the three miserable realms and the cycle of birth and death in its various forms, and I would merely escape the twenty-five states of existence.
It is not that he teaches the Buddha-way to some and not others; rather, he causes all sentient beings to equally attain the wondrous wisdom of the true mark (dharmatā).

This is his fundamental intention for appearing in the world; therefore, it is said that he "teaches the Buddha-way to all. Those who lack wisdom practice in confusion, and those who are deluded do not accept the Great Dharma.
When he encounters them, he teaches the Buddha-way to all; thus, the five turbidities cannot obstruct the Great [Vehicle]. It is only because they lack wisdom that they do not accept it.

Therefore, it is said that they "obstruct the Great. △ Second, the six lines specifically clarify the five turbidities (*pañca kaṣāyāḥ*) as obstructions to the Great. They are divided into pairs. The first two lines clarify the turbidity of sentient beings (*sattva-kaṣāya*).

The second [set of] one line clarifies the turbidity of lifespan (*āyuṣ-kaṣāya*). The third [set of] one line clarifies the turbidity of views (*dṛṣṭi-kaṣāya*). The fourth [set of] one line clarifies the turbidity of afflictions (*kleśa-kaṣāya*).
The fifth [set of] one line clarifies the turbidity of the eon (*kalpa-kaṣāya*). Now, regarding the first two lines, they clarify the turbidity of sentient beings.
I know that these sentient beings have never cultivated the roots of goodness (up to: they have fully experienced all manner of bitter poisons).
"Roots of goodness" refers to True Suchness (*tathatā*) and the true mark (*lakṣaṇa*). Because they do not rely on these seeds of goodness, they do not experience greatness;
their roots of goodness are inferior. As for the five desires: form is like a red-hot iron ball; to grasp it is to be burned. Sound is like poisoned ointment.
The drum: hearing it, one will surely die. The fragrance is like the breath of a suppressed dragon; smelling it, one falls ill. The flavor is like honey smeared on a blade;
licking it, one is wounded. The touch is like lying near a sleeping lion; approaching it, one is bitten. These five can give rise to the practitioner’s mind of desire;
therefore, they are called the "five desires. They are the very root of all evils, for evil karma is powerful. This is delusion.

This is ignorance. Craving is greedy attachment. Because craving arises from delusion, there is suffering and affliction in the present life, and one falls into the three miserable realms in the future.
As for sentient beings submerged in the six destinies, they do not transcend good and evil: those who observe the five precepts become humans; those who practice the ten wholesome deeds become devas;

stinginess and greed lead to hungry ghosts; head-butting and violence lead to animals; the ten unwholesome deeds lead to hell; and anger leads to asuras. Thus they pass through the six paths of existence.
They undergo all manner of bitter poisons; this is the defilement of sentient beings (sattva-kaṣāya). △ Second, one line clarifies the defilement of lifespan (āyuḥ-kaṣāya):
"The subtle form received at conception constantly increases life after life; those of meager virtue and little merit are oppressed by manifold sufferings."

There are two aspects to the subtle form (*sūkṣma-rūpa*): first, because it is composed of the four subtle elements (*catur-aṇu*); second, because one falsely identifies with this wretched physical body.

The *Garbhāvakrānti-sūtra* states that there is growth through five stages: in the first seven days, it is the *kalala*, here translated as "coagulated slime," having the appearance of solidified butter;
in the second seven days, it is the *arbuda*, here translated as "blister," having the appearance of a pustule; in the third seven days, it is the *peśī*... [the text continues].
The clouds coalesce; its appearance is like congealed blood. At the fourth week, it is called *khar-māṃsa* (hard flesh), because it gradually becomes firm and solid.
At the fifth week, it is called *peśī* (the stage of form), because the forms of the various sense organs are fully present. After thirty-eight weeks have passed, it emerges from the womb.
From birth until old age and death, it continues to grow; hence it is said that "in life after life it increases. The two lines concerning "meager merit" [refer to the following].
The clear and the turbid are characteristics of destiny. A person of great merit dwells in the womb as if in a painted palace; fragrant breezes touch them, and they gradually grow.
A person of little merit is touched by foul breezes and is oppressed by manifold sufferings, as described in the *Garbhāvakrānti-sūtra*.
Furthermore, "subtle form" does not refer to a minute form within the womb, but rather to the hidden and subtle form of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*).
Because it projects birth into a womb without interruption, it is said that "it increases life after life. △ Third, one verse clarifies the turbidity of views (*dṛṣṭi-kāṣāya*).
Entering the dense forest of wrong views—whether regarding existence or non-existence—one relies upon these various views which comprise the sixty-two [types].
The five views intermingle like a thick and luxuriant forest: "existence" refers to the view of eternalism, while "non-existence" refers to the view of annihilationism.
Based on these two views, sixty-two [views] arise. For example, non-Buddhists (tīrthika) postulate the self (*ātman*) through four propositions:

that form (*rūpa*) is the self; that the self is apart from form; that form is large and the self is small, with the self being within form; and that the self is large and form is small, with form being within the self.

The same applies to the other four aggregates (*skandha*). These constitute twenty [views]. When multiplied by the three time periods, they become sixty, plus the fundamental [two views], totaling sixty-two.

The views of annihilationism and eternalism, together with the sixty-two views—among the five views, the "false" view is singled out because such views are prevalent in the degenerate age of the final dharma.
Those who today do not pay homage to stupas and monasteries, slander the True Dharma, and repudiate cause and effect are precisely these people.
△ Fourth, the turbidity of afflictions (*kleśa-kaṣāya*).
Deeply attached to false and illusory phenomena, they stubbornly grasp them and cannot let go; with self-conceit and arrogance, their minds are crooked and insincere.

this root [affliction] brings forth craving and pride (*māna*), while the secondary derivative (*anuvyañjana*) brings forth crookedness (*śāṭhya*) to encompass the remainder. Thus, they beat the drum of self-importance and raise the banner of pride.
Therefore, it is said they are "arrogant. They wag their tails to beg for pity; their minds are crooked and insincere—hence, it is said they are "unreal.
△ Fifth, one line clarifies the defilement of the eon (*kalpa-kaṣāya*):
For thousands of millions of billions of eons, such people have not heard the name of the Buddha, nor have they heard the True Dharma; they are difficult to deliver.

For a long time there has been no Buddha-dharma; human affairs are in disorder. This period when the four turbidities (*catur-kaṣāya*) converge is called the *kalpa-kaṣāya*. Regarding those who are difficult to deliver:
because the obstacles of the five turbidities are heavy, they do not believe in the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*), and thus cannot be delivered.

Because the five turbidities obstruct the Great [Vehicle], it is said that the exhaustion of delusions within the three realms constitutes the attainment of nirvana; however, this is merely a provisional means and not true extinction.
Since the distinct delusions of ignorance still persist and the birth-and-death of transformation remains vast and pervasive, how could this be true extinction?

If one realizes that all phenomena, from their very origin, have never moved or been touched by even a hair’s breadth, such that their nature is inherently true and eternal and their essence is inherently quiescent, then this constitutes true extinction (*nirvāṇa*).
Although phenomena are fundamentally quiescent, if one does not cultivate the Path, there is no means by which to realize this union.
Therefore it is said: "When the Buddha-son has practiced the Path, he shall become a Buddha in a future life. The above was taught by the Buddhas for those in the Age of Five Turbidities.

Chapter on the Buddha. This chapter extensively clarifies that even minute causes and minor virtues all lead to the path of Buddhahood.

It correctly reveals that not a single word or phrase fails to serve as a condition for the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*), and not a single incense offering or flower fails to be a true cause for Bodhi. Why do those of the Two Vehicles (*dvayayāna*) not reflect upon this?

This section is divided into two parts. The first three lines briefly summarize the revelation of the [true] teaching.
"Throughout countless kalpas of the past, immeasurable Buddhas who have entered parinirvāṇa (up to) causing [beings] to enter the Buddha-way.
The first two lines open up three aspects; the persons, times, and lineages are each different and unequal.
That which cannot be known through calculation or measurement—this is what the following verses clarify as one. △ Second, twenty-four and a half lines: a detailed verse recitation."
Revealing [the meaning]. This section has two parts. First, one and a half lines generally clarify how skillful means assist in the revelation.
Furthermore, the Great Holy Lords, knowing all worlds... [assist in] revealing the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).

The true cause of Buddha-nature is the primary truth (paramārtha). If one employs the perfect and subtle right contemplation, it is the skillful means of the true mark (dharmatā) and is not called "different.
Now, employing the five vehicles and seven skillful means to assist in its manifestation is called "different skillful means";
these include the six perfections, minor virtues, chanting the name, making offerings to images, and so forth. Since the six perfections are the primary practice, why [is this called different]?

They appear as different because, within the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), it is merely the single word "Buddha" that constitutes their difference. This is truly because the inclinations and desires of sentient beings differ;
thus, the skillful means (*upāya*) of the Buddhas vary. Yet, although these means differ, they are identical in their function of assisting the manifestation of reality.
Once reality has been revealed, this difference is no longer a difference. It is precisely for this reason that [the Buddha] so earnestly praises [this teaching]. △
The second section consists of twenty-three lines, which specifically clarify the characteristics of revelation and manifestation. It is divided into two parts:

first, twenty-two lines, which reveal the merit of the conditional cause (*pratyaya-hetu*) by means of various virtues; second, one line, which reveals the merit of the causal cause of realization (*pariniṣpatti-hetu*) by means of hearing the sutra.

The first section has seven parts. The first two lines clarify the revelation [of the truth] by way of the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*). The second part, one line, clarifies the revelation by way of the mind of compassionate longing.
The third part, three and a half lines, clarifies the revelation by way of making offerings to the *śarīra*. The fourth part, three lines, clarifies the revelation by way of fashioning Buddha images.
The fifth part, three and a half lines, clarifies the revelation by way of painting Buddha images. The sixth and seventh parts, six lines...

The first two lines clarify the manifestation [of the teaching] by means of making offerings to the stūpas and images; the seventh line clarifies the manifestation by means of reciting the Buddha’s name;
and furthermore, the first two lines clarify the manifestation by means of the six pāramitās.
If there are sentient beings who encounter the various Buddhas of the past (up to) all having already attained the Buddha-way, this is due to their true causal Buddha-nature;
the essence of the living being and the Buddha are identical. If illusory obstructions are profound, one will never encounter a Buddha.
Those who do encounter a Buddha possess a strong internal causal power that enables them to evoke supramundane conditions. Nevertheless, as for the desires of their deep mind—

They are different; therefore, the Buddhas’ preaching of the Dharma is also diverse. At one particular time, some may hear the sudden teaching (sudden dharma), while others hear the gradual teaching (gradual dharma).
Some practice giving and so forth, while others cultivate a single dharma or a single practice alone; some cultivate other dharmas and practices concurrently;
some are focused exclusively on one, while others act as an aid. Because there are such various differences, it is said: "Various kinds of cultivation of merit and wisdom. [End of previous section]
Five [of these] constitute merit, while the last one constitutes wisdom. Thus, they are revealed below. Viewed from the present perspective, all have already attained Buddhahood.
Among these, the wisdom derived from hearing the Dharma would seem to belong to the "revealing cause" (*vijñapti-hetu*);

however, because it is preceded by hearing the *Lotus Sūtra*, it belongs solely to the "conditioning cause" (*pratyaya-hetu*). 2. One Practice: Clarifying the Revelation through the Mind of Compassionate Longing.
"After the parinirvāṇa of all Buddhas, if there are people with virtuous and gentle minds—such sentient beings have all already attained the path to Buddhahood.

This follows upon the previous point that it is not only those who encounter a Buddha, hear the Dharma, and practice who attain Buddhahood; even after the extinction of all Buddhas, [those with such qualities do so].
They were able to give rise to a heart of compassionate longing for the Tathāgata; in a single thought-moment, they abandoned evil and followed good, transforming the rigid into the supple.
At that time, they appeared to belong to the realms of humans, devas, or the two vehicles, but viewed from the present perspective, they have already attained Buddhahood.
△ Three and a half lines. This section clarifies the manifestation [of the Buddha-way] by means of making offerings to the *śarīra*.
From "Those who, after the Buddhas have entered parinirvāṇa, make offerings to the *śarīra*" (until) "have all already attained the Buddha-way."
In this text, it is first stated that one constructs stupas made of the seven treasures and eight precious substances. Next, one constructs temples using fragrant wood or ordinary materials.

This implies that not only does one whose mind is filled with sorrowful longing attain Buddhahood, but even after the extinction of the Buddhas, those various individuals who have fragmented their bodies into relics erect stupas to make offerings to these śarīras, and erect temples to make offerings to their likenesses, according to their respective capacities.

They vary in scale, from large to small; their adornments differ in refinement and simplicity, ranging from gold and silver to wood and bamboo, and from rosewood to brick and tile—their distinctions are beyond full description. While the physical works differ, the spirit of reverence remains the same.
This extends even to those who pile up earth to form a shrine or gather sand to build a stupa; though performed by children in play without deliberate intent, the merit is not lacking.
Wasted. At that particular time, one might say that their merit was either great or small, or perhaps it existed or did not exist.

one may scatter a single flower with a distracted mind, or pay homage with profound solemnity, or bow the head in haste and negligence. Although there are degrees of reverence, the aspiration of the mind is one and the same.
Through the conditions of a non-mind, the causes of a mind are accumulated; this is conditioned existence (*saṃskṛta*).
This constitutes the steps leading to the fruit of outflowlessness (*anāsrava-phala*). At that time, it was said that there must be distinctions among their merits;

yet viewed from the present perspective, they have all already attained Buddhahood. Not only have they perfected the path to Buddhahood for themselves, but they are also able to transform and deliver sentient beings, leading them into *nirvāṇa*.

They have passed away. Thus it is said: "When the fuel is exhausted, the fire is extinguished. △ Seventh, a single verse clarifies the revelation by means of reciting the Buddha’s name:
"If a person, with a distracted mind, enters a stupa or temple and recites 'Namo Buddha' even once, they have all already attained the path of Buddhahood."
Continuing from the above, it is not only those who offer the five sensory objects (*pañca-viṣaya*) or the three karmas (*tri-karma*) to stūpas and images who attain Buddhahood;

even those who recite the name with a distracted mind likewise attain Buddhahood. *Namo* is translated here as "taking refuge in life" (*kai-mei*), or "deliver me," and may also be rendered as "reverently following."
In a western land, there was a celestial image with a head made of gold. A thief came intending to take it, but he was unable to do so. He simply called out, "Namo Buddha," and then carried it away.
The next day, the assembly said that the celestial image had lost its head and thus the deity was no longer present. The deity, manifesting through a person, said:
"The thief called out 'Namo Buddha. The various devas were startled and moved; for this reason, the head was lost. The assembly then said, "The deity is not here."

Just as with the Buddha, even if one falsely utters the name of a *sāṃvṛti-buddha* (a worldly Buddha) but once, one still attains rebirth in the heavens; how much more so for a worthy person who invokes the name of the Buddha?
It is like a person holding a single stone and placing it in water—it will surely sink without doubt. Yet, if one holds a hundred stones and places them on a boat, they will certainly not sink.
Likewise, an evil person will inevitably fall into hell after death, just like the stone placed in water; however, if they recollect the Buddha at the moment of death, they shall not.
They attain rebirth in the Western Pure Land. It is like the power of a boat that prevents stones from sinking and carries them to the other shore.

Furthermore, there was once an old man during the Buddha’s lifetime who requested ordination from five hundred senior elders (*sthavira*). They observed that he lacked roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*) in his past lives and did not grant it.

In the distant past, across immeasurable kalpas, a person entered the mountains to gather firewood. Encountering a tiger, he was struck with fear and recited the Buddha’s name once.

Because his roots of goodness had matured, he attained deliverance. Since he possessed no other virtues and had long wandered through birth and death over vast kalpas, this matter is beyond the scope of the śrāvaka’s path of vision.
Having already realized arhatship, he will certainly attain unsurpassed bodhi.
This is clear. If one attains Buddhahood by reciting the Name even with a distracted mind, how much more so when the mind is single-minded and undisturbed!

I have privately received instruction from others; whether hearing the teachings extensively or concisely, whether grasping the words or the meaning, whether with a focused mind or a distracted mind, the circumstances have not been uniform.
