This general explanation includes both monastics and laypeople; however, the commentary and the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* restrict this discussion to the robes of those who have left the household life.
This indicates taking refuge. Offering flowers to the Buddha signifies that the cause is identical to the fruit. The revolving of space symbolizes hearing Śāriputra receive his prediction;
the spontaneous turning of the dharma-nature expresses the intent of turning from the Small Vehicle toward the Great Vehicle.

The performance of hundreds of thousands of celestial music in the sky represents the various provisional wisdoms and skillful means, all of which ultimately return to the ultimate nature of emptiness of true wisdom.
...among them. Although the four groups within this assembly had heard the same teaching as Śāriputra, they did not yet understand it in the same way.
Only upon seeing the Venerable One receive his prediction did they first believe in this principle—that everyone possesses their own share [of Buddhahood].

Unconsciously, a sense of joy and devotion arose within them, and they vied with one another to present sublime offerings, thereby creating the conditions for their future fruition. Therefore, the verse below says: "I, too, am like this; I shall certainly..."
He becomes a Buddha. △ Second, the fourfold assembly’s realization and understanding.
They spoke these words: "The Buddha, in the past at Vārāṇasī... [up to] ...the unsurpassed, greatest wheel of Dharma."

The first two phrases open the provisional (*upāya*), while the subsequent two phrases reveal the real (*tattva*). The word "ultimate" (*zui*) indicates that this present sutra represents the perfect within the perfect.

"Opening the provisional" refers to the teaching of the half-syllables; "revealing the real" refers to the teaching of the full syllables. Furthermore, the distinction between the small and great, the coarse and the subtle, may be understood accordingly.
If one contrasts the teachings of the Vaipulya and Prajñāpāramitā with those of the Deer Park, then the Deer Park teachings are coarse, whereas the two [subsequent] teachings are subtle.
Exquisite. This is because the two teachings incorporate expedient means (*upāya*) to lead toward the principle of fulfillment.

If one compares the present sutra with those two teachings, then the two teachings are coarse while the present sutra is exquisite; for the present sutra directly expounds the unsurpassed path to reveal the principle of fulfillment.
II. The Verse Recitation consists of six and a half lines, divided into two parts. The first two lines recite the preceding prose section on the opening and manifestation [of the truth].
At that time, the sons of the gods, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"In the past at Vārāṇasī, he turned the wheel of the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths... (until) there were few who were able to believe."
The "five aggregates" (pañca-skandha) refers to the five *skandhas*. The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* contains a hymn of praise by the devas which says: "In the world there is no peer;

now you turn the wheel of Dharma, expounding the meaning for men and women regarding that from which the decay of the *skandhas* arises. This refers precisely to the arising and ceasing of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) in this present sutra.
[Section] Two: Four and a half lines; a self-narration of attaining understanding and the dedication [of merit].
"Since of old we have repeatedly heard the World-Honored One teach [up to] 'all is dedicated toward the Buddha-way.
The first line describes how they themselves had not previously heard this wondrous Dharma. From "The World-Honored One" downward, they rejoice that they too shall become Buddhas;

"those who are likewise" refers to how Śāriputra, having received his prediction of attaining Buddhahood, summarizes and confirms it. The two phrases concerning the "Buddha-way" [refer to the dedication].

I take charge of the power of hidden implementation. In the following section on dedication, I clarify that all meritorious deeds throughout the three periods of time are not for the sake of minor fruits as gods or humans, but are dedicated toward unsurpassed bodhi.

Those who dedicate their merit toward the Buddha-way silently grasp the purport of the subtle causes and scattered virtues from the preceding chapter; they do not take the conditioned or the unconditioned as their goal, but rather proceed toward...
The fruit of perfect enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*) is the ultimate goal alone. The first cycle of the teaching on the Dharma for those of superior faculties is hereby concluded.

△ Second, the cycle of the teaching by way of parables for those of middling faculties consists of four chapters. This present chapter is the "Parable" chapter, which opens up the three [vehicles] to reveal the one.
The "Resolute Belief" chapter contains the four sons’ realization of their understanding. The "Herbs" chapter is the Tathāgata’s confirmation of that realization. The "Bestowal" [chapter]...
The "Chapter on Prophecy" clarifies the bestowal of prophecies. As these are all explained by means of parables, it constitutes one cycle of the Parable Section.

According to the preceding section on the Dharma-exposition, this should consist of five parts; however, the section on the Fourfold Assembly’s Celebration is omitted as a matter of course, following the pattern of avoiding redundant text at the beginning and end.

The first part, the actual exposition of the parables, reveals the One Vehicle by opening up the Three Vehicles. It is divided into two sections: first, Śāriputra’s request on behalf of others; second, the Tathāgata’s response.

Answer: This section consists of three parts. First, he personally recounts that he has received the prediction of enlightenment and is free from doubt. Second, he concurrently recounts that his peers still harbor doubts.
Third, he universally petitions on behalf of the fourfold assembly. Now, regarding the first part, his personal recounting of having received the prediction and being free from doubt:
At that time, Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying... [up to] "...the prediction of *samyak-saṃbodhi*.

Doubt is one of the fundamental afflictions; regret is one of the indeterminate states. Previously, his doubt and regret were such that he could not receive a prediction equal to that of a Bodhisattva.
Now that he has received this prediction, all his doubts and regrets are completely resolved. △ Second.
I also relate that my fellow practitioners were confused.
These twelve hundred who had attained mastery over their minds (up to the point where they) heard what they had never heard before, all fell into doubt and confusion.

As for those who have attained mastery over their minds: since their grasping at a self (*ātman*) is already empty, their minds have attained mastery; yet their grasping at phenomena (*dharma*) still remains, and they have not yet attained [mastery over] phenomena.

"Masterful" (*svatantra*) refers to the present fruit. The phrase "formerly dwelling in one [truth]" clarifies the past cause; because one investigates the truth, severs delusions, refines and polishes the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), it is called the "stage of training" (*śaikṣabhūmi*).
The three phrases beginning with "The Buddha constantly" recount the instructions of the former Buddhas. The character "teach" (*jiao*) corresponds to the aforementioned "train" (*xue*);
"teaching" refers to the method for attaining the fruit through the exhaustion of delusions and the ultimate realization of truth. "My Dharma" points to the Lesser Vehicle teachings.

This refers to the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths. "Birth and death" (*saṃsāra*) is the truth of suffering (*duḥkha-satya*). The character "leaving" (*li*) implies the truth of origination (*samudaya-satya*); one must sever origination to leave behind birth and death.

"Nirvāṇa" is the truth of cessation (*nirodha-satya*). "Ultimate" implies the truth of the path (*mārga-satya*); through the cultivation of the path, one realizes nirvāṇa. This is the stage of training (*śaikṣa*).

It clarifies that those who previously received the teachings each realized their respective small fruits. The phrase "each [of them]" is used to encompass the multitude. They were born... [text ends].

The fruit of the suffering of death has the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*) and so forth as its cause. The "view of self" is precisely the view of a body (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*). "Existence and non-existence" refers to the views of eternalism and nihilism.

The word "and so forth" (*ādi*) collectively encompasses the ten proclivities (*anuśaya*), both sharp and dull, as well as the coarse and subtle afflictions of the views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa* and *vitarka-kleśa*).

These serve as the causes of the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*). When the causes of origination are severed, the fruit of suffering does not arise. The assembly should follow the Buddha’s words to abandon them; "abandoning" means...
"It is severed. This refers to those who claim to have attained *nirvāṇa*; such words are merely expressions of their own self-conceit.

What is called "the Buddha’s teaching on the single meaning of liberation—we ourselves have already attained it" refers to the fact that within the Dharma-exposition, there was first the provisional and later the ultimate;
because they had not heard this before, they all fell into doubt and confusion. Previously, they held the three [vehicles] to be the final truth, but now...

Furthermore, there is this matter of truth and reality. If one were to claim that what was ultimate yesterday is false today, or that what is true today is false yesterday, then right and wrong would remain undecided and sameness and difference would not be distinguished.
Like a sheep caught in a fence, one would find it difficult to advance or retreat. △ Third, he universally requests on behalf of the fourfold assembly.
"Excellent, World-Honored One! We pray that you will explain the causes and conditions for the sake of the fourfold assembly, so that they may be freed from doubt and regret.
Those who requested [this] as peers did so out of a sense of old acquaintance; those who requested it as members of the fourfold assembly did so for the sake of transforming their realm.

Now, having received this prediction, you exercise great compassion anew and universally request [this teaching] on our behalf. Thus, though not formally requested, we entreat you to explain the causes and conditions."
There are three [points]. First, the "son of the body" enters the Way through causes and conditions; as soon as he speaks, he says it is "by reason of causes and conditions.

Second, because of the request for the "Great Matter of Causes and Conditions," which clarifies the principle of "first three, then one. Third, the request concerns being within causes and conditions;
below, in the answer through parables, after the analogy, he again explains the causes and conditions of past lives. One question and two answers—this may be so.

This means that purchasing stones brings forth abundant clouds, and moving flowers attracts butterflies. Question: Previously, in the discourse on the Dharma, you spoke of "first three, then one," yet I did not awaken to it upon hearing it.
Now I again request an explanation of "first three, then one. How does this differ from what was said before? Answer:

As for the term "causes and conditions" (*nidāna*), it refers to the fundamental root of the beginning and end—the "first three" and the "then one. It is called "causes and conditions" because of this. The preceding section on the four Buddhas was brief.

The Chapter on Śākyamuni is somewhat extensive; however, it clarifies only the application of the provisional [teachings] regarding the five turbidities, leaving the beginning and end unclear, and thus those of middling and inferior capacities do not understand it.

Now, by means of parables, the characteristics of the saṃsāra of the six realms are explained in detail, the reasons for providing the three carts to exit the house are fully set forth, and the intent behind seeking the three and then the one is related, while extensively demonstrating that the gift is bestowed equally upon all children alike.
The Mind. It is in this way that the request regarding the "Great Cause and Condition" (*mahāntam artham*) is fulfilled.

Within this context, the fourfold assembly, regarding the four preceding [teachings], not only acted as the appropriate recipients (*pratipakṣa*) for forming karmic conditions, speaking in understanding and acceptance; they were also the ones who initiated the "influences and echoes" (*pratyaya*).
II. The Tathāgata’s Response. This is divided into two parts. First, the suppression and exaltation that initiates [the teaching].
At that time, the Buddha addressed Śāriputra... [up to] "...those with wisdom attain understanding through parables.
My previous failure to suppress those who did not yet awaken was for the purpose of using various analogies to point toward and clarify the provisional (upāya).

All of these were intended to point toward and manifest the ultimate reality (bhūta-artha). As for "all are transformed into Bodhisattvas," whether provisional or ultimate, all enter the Buddha-way; this has already been clarified above.
The text says: "How can one grasp the teaching? One is deluded and dark, failing to understand. The preceding phrase, "not having spoken the three words," is a term of censure and reproach.
However, from "Śāriputra" onwards, his intellectual understanding is extolled; the character "ran" (然) should be played upon as it carries a sense of admiration.

Furthermore, this serves the purpose of Subhūti acting as a substitute petitioner. Moreover, it exceeds the natural flow of the text: since the previous censure was so severe, there was a fear that he might become despondent and sink into self-reproach; now—
The allowance for parables serves to manifest one's intellectual understanding. Within the "Expedient Means" chapter, the causes and conditions have already been fully analyzed;
one should simply realize this and not continue to harbor doubts. If doubts still persist, then parables ought to be spoken, rather than further explaining the causes and conditions.
Since the single great matter of the cause and condition remains unclear, it must be resolved through parables alone.
[The meaning is] understood. Therefore, it is said: "Now, I shall again clarify this meaning through further parables.
Those who attain understanding from these parables may still be called wise; yet if they have not yet awakened, I shall recount the matters of their past-life causes and conditions.
This serves as the introductory section for the "Chapter on the Medicinal Herbs of Inferior Faith and Understanding. II. The Actual Exposition of the Parables. There is a long [passage]:
The verses on practice consist of two parts: first, the illustrative parables; second, the application to the Dharma. The initial section on illustrative parables is divided into two:

first, the general parable; second, the specific parables. Regarding the first, the general parable, which illustrates the aforementioned skillful means, the following two lines of verse—"Now I am likewise...
and so forth—are divided into six sections: first, the analogy of the elder; second, the analogy of the house; third, the single gate.

The Similes: (1) the simile of the elder; (2) the simile of the four or five hundred people; (3) the simile of the fire breaking out; (4) the simile of the thirty sons. Now, regarding first, the simile of the elder:
"Śāriputra, suppose there were a country, city, or village... [where] there were many fields, houses, and various servants."
The term "elder" (*śreṣṭhin*) is a metaphor for the aforementioned word "I. In terms of name, conduct, status, title, virtue, and deeds, he is clarified as an elder.

"Country, city, and village" refers to his location; "name" is like reality (*yathābhūta*), and "conduct" is like a master. Conduct has degrees of intimacy or distance, and names have degrees of proximity or remoteness.

Therefore, by citing these locations, he reveals the excellence of his name and conduct. A kingdom is defined by its borders and is the furthest; a town is governed from its center and occupies the middle ground;
a village consists of neighboring hamlets and is the nearest. The Elder’s reputation for noble conduct pervades all three places:

those nearby do not perceive any flaw or meanness in him, while those far away merely admire his lofty character. His speech is free from error, his conduct is beyond reproach, and his mind is... [without fault].
The discernment of dharmas (*dharmapravicaya*) is called the true Great Man who acts in accordance with his realization. The "kingdom" (*rāṣṭra*) is a metaphor for the Land of True Reward Adorned;
the "city" (*nagara*) is a metaphor for the Land of Skillful Means with Remainder; and the "village" (*grāma*) is a metaphor for the Land of Co-residence of Ordinary and Holy Beings.

Internally, these correspond to the Tathāgata’s three karmas proceeding in accordance with wisdom, manifesting as the three lands of the Response Body (*nirmāṇakāya*). Adapting to the capacities of beings to bestow transformation, his fame is heard everywhere, and his virtue...
Throughout the *sāhasra-lokadhātu*, there was a great elder of renowned status and title.

A worldly elder is endowed with ten virtues: first, noble lineage; second, high station; third, great wealth; fourth, majestic power; fifth, profound wisdom; sixth, advanced age; seventh, pure conduct;

eighth, complete etiquette; ninth, receiving respect from those above; and tenth, being sought after by those below. As for his lineage, he was a descendant of the Three Sovereigns and Five Emperors. To the left...

As for his station, he was a counselor and regent, like the "Salt and Plum" ministers or the "Arbiter of Balance"; in wealth, he possessed copper hills and golden valleys, characterized by abundance, extravagance, and luxury;
in majesty, he was as solemn as the severe frost, commanding awe without even being stern; in wisdom, his mind was like a military arsenal, extraordinary and transcendent;

in age, he was hoary and imposing, such that all things bowed before him; and in conduct— (Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly. The translation reflects the full scope of the extant passage.)
His white jade-like virtue was without flaw; his conduct accorded with his words. His ritual propriety was characterized by measured decorum and orderly progression, serving as a model for the world.

Above, he was revered by the Sovereign; below, he was the refuge of the four seas. As a world-transcending elder, his virtues were as vast as the sands of the Ganges, fully embodying the ten types [of excellence].
By lineage, he was born from the true suchness and the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) throughout the three periods of time; by rank, his merit...
He has attained the Way and donned the robe; his ten titles are infinite. In terms of abundance, he is fully endowed with the myriad virtues of Dharma-wealth;

in terms of majesty, his ten powers are fierce and heroic, subduing Māras and externalists; in terms of wisdom, his single mind possesses the three types of knowledge, penetrating all things without exception;
in terms of age, he attained perfect enlightenment early on, yet has been so for an eternity; in terms of conduct, his three karmas follow wisdom, moving without error.
In his ritual conduct, he fully embodies the majestic deportment of a Buddha; his mind is as vast as the ocean. Above, he is praised by all those who have awakened to the ten directions;
below, those of the seven stages of expedient means come to rely upon him. He is called the Great Elder among the great elders.
This refers to me, the Teacher Śākyamuni. The four phrases concerning his age illustrate his virtuous deeds. Virtue is twofold: internal and external. Internally, it consists of wisdom and strategy;
externally, it consists of material resources. Being advanced in years signifies a broad mastery of the past and present, which serves as a metaphor for the Buddha’s wisdom and virtue.

In one’s decline and old age, the faculties and resolve become mature; this is a metaphor for the Buddha’s virtue of abandonment (*prahāṇa-guṇa*). This phrase clarifies the internal virtue. “Wealth” clarifies the external virtue.
The two characters “immeasurable” (*apramāṇa*) serve as a general metaphor for being replete with myriad virtues. The two lines concerning “having much” specifically metaphorize the external virtue.

A field can nourish one’s life, which is a metaphor for how meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) can support wisdom (*prajñā*). A house can provide shelter for the body, which is a metaphor for reality (*bhūtatathatā*).
The objective realm is that which is relied upon by true wisdom. Briefly stated, there are eighteen kinds of emptiness; extensively stated, there are immeasurable gateways to emptiness.
If one discusses his merit, there is no practice he has not cultivated; if one discusses his wisdom, there is no object he does not illumine. Therefore, it is said that he "has many.

As for the "servants," these are attendants and messengers, which metaphorically represent the complete perfection of both skillful means and insight (*jñāna-darśana*). Thus, he blends his light with the six realms of existence.
Adapting to the myriad exigencies of circumstances, provisional wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*) is the servant of ultimate wisdom (*tattva-jñāna*). △ Second, the Analogy of the House:
"His house is vast.
"House" is a metaphor for the aforementioned security as opposed to insecurity; "insecurity" is a metaphor for the three realms (*tridhātu*). Sentient beings...
Crowded and bustling, all dwell within the three realms. The Tathāgata, through his responsive transformations, governs and brings them home; therefore, it is called "vast and great.
△ 3. The Simile of the Single Gate:
There is but one gate.
This metaphor illustrates how various teachings are proclaimed for the sake of revealing the Buddha-way.

It is the Tathāgata’s fundamental intention to benefit sentient beings solely through the Buddha-way of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*). Out of necessity, he first guides them by means of various provisional gates;

however, his original intent is solely the One Vehicle. Therefore, it is said that there is "only one gate. In terms of teaching, there is only the single Buddha-vehicle; in terms of principle, there is only the One.

Regarding "knowledge and vision": Question. The One Vehicle of Buddhism is vast, expansive, and great. Since the single gate is already the Buddha-way, the subsequent text should not describe it as narrow or small.
Answer. It is because there are those without the capacity for transformation who wish to be taught the One Vehicle that it is said to be narrow;

the knowledge and vision of sentient beings is itself the knowledge and vision of the Buddha, yet ordinary and inferior beings do not know this. Due to their lack of capacity and their ignorance, it is described as narrow.
Question: Since the three vehicles mentioned in the following passage are already outside the gate, could it be that the children have instead departed from the realization of the One Vehicle?
Answer: The teaching is that which expresses, while the principle is that which is expressed. The nature of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision is fully possessed by sentient beings.

The Tathāgata has fully realized the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. Knowledge and vision are fundamentally one; there is only the distinction between being enmeshed in afflictions and being free from them.

For forty years prior, he concealed the One Vehicle and taught the Three Vehicles. This was spoken for those who were deluded regarding the principles of the teaching; thus, he provisionally set up three carts outside the gate.
As the subsequent text states, the gates of the Buddha’s teaching lead out of the suffering of the triple world. Today, these distinctions are obliterated.
He teaches the One Vehicle through the three vehicles. Birth-and-death is itself nirvana; afflictions are themselves bodhi;
the true nature of ignorance is itself buddha-nature; the illusory and empty body is itself the dharma-body.

All sons dwell within the Way and teaching of the One Vehicle; how could they be outside of it? If you raise the objection regarding "inside the gate" and "outside the gate," the Tathāgata [responds] in the following passage:
The gate from which he was being burned was safely exited. The impoverished son came and went, standing by the side of the gate, while the elder was inside the gate;
the son did not know what further hardship awaited him. △ Fourth, the Parable of the Five Hundred Men.
Many people—hundreds, two hundred, or even five hundred—dwell therein.
This is a metaphor for the "beings" who are established in supreme peace: one hundred represents the devas; two hundred represents humans;
three hundred represents animals; four hundred represents hungry ghosts; and five hundred represents those in hell. The mention of many beings in the evil realms serves to manifest this point.
Those who cultivate white karma are few, while those who perform black karma are many.

Regarding the phrase "five hundred people," this is a general reference to the sentient beings of the five realms of existence, all of whom dwell together within the three realms. △ Fifth, the Parable of the Arising Fire.
The halls and pavilions are decayed and ancient, and the walls have crumbled (down to where it says) "suddenly a fire breaks out, burning the house.

The description of the house being burned beneath the halls and pavilions is as follows: if discussed in terms of the *pariṇāmanirmita* (the environment), the hall represents the Desire Realm (*kāmadhātu*), and the pavilion represents the two upper realms (*rūpadhātu* and *ārūpyadhātu*).
The four great elements—earth, water, fire, and wind—are the walls. The four wheels of gold, water, wind, and space are the pillars.
It is the foundation, for the world relies upon it for support. The eight factors of subject and object are its beams and rafters.

If discussed in terms of the primary retribution (*sabhāga-vipāka*), the lower part of the body is the hall and the upper part is the pavilion. The internal four great elements—bones, saliva, breath, and warmth—are the walls;
longevity, warmth, and consciousness are the pillars and foundations; and the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) is the beam and rafter. "Decayed and worn out" refers to sentient beings.
"Insentient things," because they all belong to the realm of impermanence. "Collapse" refers to the erosion of mountains and rivers and the decay of skin and flesh.
"Decay" refers to the perilous instability of the roots of heaven and earth, as the source of life is incessantly abandoned.
"Tumbling ruin" refers to the shifting transformations of external objects and the ease with which human life comes to its end. "Pervading below" clarifies that [the fire] can burn.
The "flames" refer to the fires of the five turbidities and the eight sufferings, which pervade the four great elements and the four modes of birth; hence they are said to be "all-encompassing.
Since all are impermanent, they are said to be "simultaneous. "Suddenly" means that what was previously non-existent has abruptly come into being; originally, these sufferings did not exist.
They exist because of ignorance (*avidyā*). If one traces their origin, both the primary and secondary retributions arise suddenly through the non-awakening of ignorance.
One portion of this ignorance, which possesses cognitive awareness, constitutes the world of sentient beings;
the other portion, which lacks cognitive awareness, constitutes the insentient world. Thus, this very ignorance serves as the cause.

Taking objective realms as conditions, one engages in hatred and love, grasping and rejecting; the fierce fires of the three poisons then incinerate the internal faculties, the physical body, and the external world-receptacle.
This expands upon the description of the house’s appearance above, precisely clarifying that the three realms offer no peace, being like a burning house. △ Sixth:
The Parable of the Thirty Children.
The sons of the elder, numbering ten, twenty, or even up to thirty, are within this house;

this is a metaphor for the Buddha’s knowledge of the dispositions and inclinations (*śubha-kṛtsna*) of sentient beings. The Buddha is suchness (*tathatā*), and sentient beings are suchness; suchness is one and not two.
Because their natures are thus interconnected, the meaning of "sons" is established. Since their dispositions and inclinations differ, there are thirty: ten are the sons of Bodhisattvas.

The twenty and thirty are the sons of the two vehicles. "Thirty" refers to the sons; this specifically cites those who have followed through transformation, speaking of those who together emerged from the house.
The general analogy above is now complete. △ Second, the specific analogies, which illustrate the passage from "I, with the Buddha-eye, observe...
down to the forty-one and a half verses. Within these verses, six meanings are fully present; here, there are four analogies, with a brief eulogy at the end.
The Dharma is rare and marvelous; it distinguishes the false and consolidates faith. This is supplemented in the subsequent verses. The text is divided into four sections:

first, the parable of the elder seeing the fire; second, the parable of abandoning the stools and employing the carts; third, the parable of the equal bestowal of the great carts; and fourth, the parable of the elder’s lack of falsehood.
Now, regarding the first, the parable of the elder seeing the fire: this illustrates the passage above, "I, with the Buddha-eye, observe... and so forth.
Verse on Practice. Citing the five corruptions to explain the provisional:
"The elder saw this great fire arising from all four sides... [until] his mind felt no weariness or distress, nor did he have the intent to seek escape."

The verse clarifies that the Tathāgata, abiding on the ground of the Dharmakāya, perceives sentient beings being scorched by the five turbidities and the eight sufferings, and thus gives rise to compassionate response to rescue them.
There are three intentions regarding the seer, the seen, and the arising of compassion; here, the metaphors are likewise threefold.
"The elder sees" means that I, with the Buddha-eye, observe and see; this identifies the eye that performs the seeing. This...
A great fire breaks out from the four directions. What is clearly seen is the sentient beings of the six realms of existence. The fire is a metaphor for the five turbidities and the eight sufferings.
It is called "great" because it pervades all six realms. The four directions are a metaphor for body, sensation, mind, and phenomena (*dharmas*).

Taken together with the preceding [elements], these constitute birth, aging, sickness, and death. Viewing the characters closely, the "great fire" represents the fruit, while the "four directions" represent the causes.

This means that this fire does not exist without a cause. Because sentient beings give rise to the inversion of purity regarding the body, the inversion of pleasure regarding sensation, the inversion of permanence regarding the mind, and the inversion of self regarding phenomena, there are the five turbidities and the eight sufferings, which arise from the four directions like fire.
If one knows that the body is impure, that sensation is suffering, that the mind is impermanent, and that phenomena are [selfless]...

When my afflictions are extinguished, that is the single great phrase. The passage "The wise elder was struck with alarm and fear" serves as a metaphor for the aforementioned two phrases regarding sentient beings:
because the fire is great, their alarm and fear are also great; they are alarmed because they contemplate the regression from the Great Goodness (Mahākuśala).
One fears because one is concerned that various evils will arise; this fear corresponds to loving-kindness (*maitrī*), as it involves reflecting on their lack of joy.

One fears because one is concerned that they possess suffering; this fear corresponds to compassion (*karuṇā*), as it involves sympathetic concern for their suffering. Although I am able to explain the aforementioned fears and terrors, this is the intended meaning of compassionate concern.
While these words may not be exhaustive, even the Tathāgata’s compassion was still inflamed by the fire of anxiety.
Therefore, it says "although. One should pay close attention to the character "able" (néng).
This reveals that the various sons [of the Buddha] were unable, despite the Buddha having emerged from the gates burned by birth and death, to abide in the realm of eternal quiescence and peace.
Unable to bear abandoning sentient beings for their own peace and security, they formed this thought. To be untormented by the five turbidities and the eight sufferings is called "peace" (ān). Not...
To be moved by the violent winds of the four inversions is called "concealment. To be serene and detached from external burdens is called "attaining emergence.

Sentient beings are not at peace because they are burned by a great fire; they do not conceal themselves because they are moved by violent winds; they do not attain emergence because their karmic consciousness is in a state of frantic agitation.
Furthermore, regarding the gates that are burned, these gates consist of both the substantial and the empty. Without the substantial, there is nothing by which [the empty can be realized].
The introductory section: It is not without emptiness (*śūnyatā*) that one can achieve penetration. Individual objects may be burned, but emptiness cannot be burned.

This serves as a metaphor for the teaching, which consists of the expressive medium (*vācaka*) and the expressed content (*vācya*). Without the expressive medium, there would be no teaching; yet without the expressed content, how could one attain liberation?
While the expressive medium may be impermanent, the expressed content is not impermanent. The Tathāgata possesses great wisdom and is able to seek out the correct [truth].
The teaching [is the means]. Because one attains what is signified by the teaching, it is said that "one emerges in safety.
Because the signifier itself is consumed, it is called "the door that is burned. Without departing through the door that is burned, by what means could one emerge in safety?
As the Great Sūtra says: "Because the cause is impermanent, the fruit is permanent. This is precisely what is meant. Furthermore, one first emerges in safety; having emerged, one [returns] again...
"Startled. Although they have now emerged, they must still enter; having entered, they will surely be saved. Thus, "peace and security" is used to explain the removal of alarm and fear.
Alarm and fear are themselves compassion (*karuṇā*). This refers to the arising of the mind of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) for the sake of these sentient beings.
As for the passage beginning with "the sons," because the great fire previously burned the house and the sons within did not seek escape, the elder [acted as follows]... [The elder remained] at ease.

They sit and watch. This refers to the intention to contemplate saving their children. The word "all" (等) includes the five hundred people. Because they are attached to views, they are immersed in the four views;
this is called "sport. Their fame and merit are wasted in vain—this is called "play. Furthermore, because they are attached to craving, they are immersed in the five sensory objects;
this is called "sport. To have nothing gained in the end is called "play. Thus, due to their delight in attachment to views and craving, it is all empty and in vain.
They die yet feel no weariness or detachment, like children at play. Not speaking of the presence of fire is called "lack of awareness";
not understanding that fire is a phenomenon of heat is called "ignorance. Not fearing that fire can burn the body is called "not being startled";

not considering that fire can sever one's life is called "not being terrified. This is a metaphor for sentient beings who are entirely unaware of the five turbidities and the eight sufferings, and do not understand them.
The four inversions and the three poisons do not startle or delude the Dharma-body, nor do they terrify or wound the life-force of wisdom (*prajñā-jīvita*).

Thus, one is unaware of suffering (*duḥkha*) and ignorant of its origin (*samudaya*); one is not startled by the loss of the Path (*mārga*), nor terrified by the loss of cessation (*nirodha*). "Body" refers to the five bodies of consciousness;
because the body is oppressed by the eight sufferings, it is said that "fire comes to oppress the body. To be "pressing upon oneself" means to be beset by affliction.

"Urgent" means immediate. Because each and every suffering arises from the five consciousnesses confronting the five sense objects, corresponding moment by moment, it is said that "suffering and pain press upon oneself.
Regarding "the mind does not feel weary or troubled": this refers to the mind-consciousness (*manovijñāna*).

It means not feeling weary of the suffering of impermanence and not being troubled by the accumulation of afflictions (*kleśa*). Regarding "having no intention to seek liberation": this means not cultivating the factors of the path (*mārgāṅga*).

He proceeds; he does not seek the principle of the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*). Herein, "playing" (*xi*) is a metaphor for the turbidity of views (*dṛṣṭi-kaṣāya*); "sporting" (*xi*) is a metaphor for the turbidity of afflictions (*kleśa-kaṣāya*).

The two lines beginning with "not perceiving" (*bù jué*) refer to the turbidity of sentient beings (*sattva-kaṣāya*). The two lines beginning with "fire comes" (*huǒ lái*) refer to the turbidity of lifespan (*āyuṣ-kaṣāya*).

The two lines beginning with "the mind is not [dual]" (*xīn bù èr*) refer to the turbidity of the eon (*kalpa-kaṣāya*). △ Second, the metaphor of abandoning the small table and using the carriage. This is divided into two parts: first, abandoning the table; second, using the carriage.

The first analogy, that of discarding the couch, corresponds to the passage from "I first sat at the site of enlightenment" up to the six lines and a half of verse that clarify the difficulty of introducing the Great Dharma.
This section is further divided into three parts: first, the elder’s thought to save them; second, the sons’ refusal to listen; and third, their running about playing while looking at their father.
First, regarding the analogy of the elder’s thought to save them, this corresponds to the passage from "I first sat at the site of enlightenment" up to "subtle and wondrous."
The foremost [teacher], clarifying the great Dharma according to what is appropriate, Śāriputra—the elder—reflected thus (up to): "He fully informed his sons, saying: 'All of you, come out quickly!'"
One who reflects in this manner is one who should manifest among humans. Having attained the Way, they reflect upon the excellence of the Dharma thus realized.

The body is a metaphor for supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*) that bear the burden; the hands are a metaphor for wisdom (*prajñā*) that uproots [afflictions]. Based on the virtue of cessation (*śamatha*) through meditative concentration (*samādhi*), there are supernatural powers;
based on the virtue of insight (*vipaśyanā*) through wisdom, there is the preaching of the Dharma. As previously stated, "his years have grown old."
The metaphors for knowledge and abandonment are the hands and body; the *kuci* is a vessel from Western India used for holding flowers; the "incense table" (*xiāngjǐ*) is an incense stand;
the "desk" (*àn*) is a writing desk. According to the method below, it should be stated: "If I were to rely solely on the power of my supernormal knowledges and the power of my wisdom..."

Regarding the praise of the Tathāgata’s power of knowledge and vision and his fearlessnesses: sentient beings cannot be delivered by means of these alone. The garment-bag (*kośa*) is a metaphor for knowledge and vision;
the small table (*mañcaka*) is a metaphor for the four fearlessnesses; and the desk (*phalaka*) is a metaphor for the ten powers. Briefly stated, they are called "knowledge and vision.

The names are concise, yet their meaning is profound, just as a single mouth of a garment-bag contains much. When explained from the perspective of their application, they are called the four fearlessnesses.
Regarding the Four Truths: just as a small table may be narrow in its legal dimensions but wide in its physical base, these are broadly explained as the Ten Powers (*daśabala*).

They encompass all things both horizontally and vertically, like a desk with many legs; thus, they are broad in their application to phenomena (*dharma*) and provide great stability in their application to entities (*vastu*).

This is the great transformative power of contemplative mindfulness (*cintā-manasikāra*), meaning that whether through the manifestation of supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) or the proclamation of wisdom (*prajñā*), one possesses knowledge and vision.

Through the powers, fearlessnesses, and so forth, he causes sentient beings to exit the house of the three realms and the dwelling of the five aggregates; hence it is said, "he leads them out from the house.
Furthermore, below this, it clarifies that while the Dharma is great, the capacity of the audience is small, and thus one gate is narrow and limited.

If one were to discuss the principle and the teaching, they are vast and expansive, and therefore not narrow or limited; however, sentient beings are unable to communicate with these principles and teachings by themselves, and [the Buddha] desires to speak of them...
It is inorganic; therefore, it is said to be narrow and small. If one explains each of the principle, teaching, and practice as being narrow and small within a single gate:
the principle is pure and without admixture, hence it is called "one. Because this principle can provide passage, it is called a "gate. It is subtle and difficult to know.
Therefore, it is called "narrow and small. As for the teaching, there is no other vehicle beyond it; it is solely the One Buddha Vehicle, and thus it is called "one.

This teaching is able to provide access, and thus it is called a "gate. This teaching is subtle and profound; compared to the meager knowledge of the two vehicles, it surpasses them, and even the seven expedient means do not know it.
Since they cannot attain realization through this teaching themselves, and are about to discuss their lack of capacity, it is said:
"Narrow and small" means that while practicing, one acts as a cause for oneself; yet by practicing the great and direct path, there are no obstacles or difficulties, hence it is called "one.
Because one skillfully practices the bodhisattva path and proceeds directly to the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), it is called a "gate.

Because the wondrous practice is difficult to perform and requires skillful means (*upāya*) for those without the capacity, it is called "narrow and small. Regarding the phrase "the children were young," although they were taught by twenty trillion buddhas...
Regarding the Unsurpassed Way: because the roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*) of the Mahāyāna are weak, they are called "infants. This clarifies that their goodness is feeble.

If, upon hearing the Mahāyāna, they are able to give rise to slander, they are called "those who have not yet attained understanding. This clarifies that their evil is powerful. At the time of the cause, they are deeply attached to craving and views;

at the time of the fruit, they are deeply attached to the primary and secondary elements (*āśraya-adhiṣṭhāna*). In the Desire Realm, they are attached to the five sensory objects (*pañca-kāmaguṇa*); in the Form Realm, they are attached to...
They relish meditative absorption and are attached to formless concentrations; thus it is said they "cling to places of play. There are two meanings for their potential "falling":
first, being immature, they fall because they recall their former playgrounds—this is a metaphor for falling into the three miserable realms due to attachment to the five desires.
Second, their evil is so powerful that they are entirely devoid of discernment, and thus they fall—this is a metaphor for falling due to slandering the Mahāyāna.
Regarding the "three miserable realms": if one falls into them, one will inevitably be scorched and boiled by the five turbidities and the eight sufferings; hence it is said, "to be burned by fire.
The phrase "I shall preach for them" below refers precisely to this contemplation. Although he knows their faculties are dull, he acts in accordance with his original intention.
The two phrases beginning with "fully told" refer to directly preaching the perfect and sudden Great Teaching of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* while adapting it to those of inferior capacity.

The single true Dharma-realm unfolds the four unimpeded Dharma-realms and expands the ten mysterious gates. It directly elucidates the discourse on the Middle Way that accords with the nature of reality.
As the Sūtra says: "To know all phenomena as being the very nature of one's own mind is to achieve the body of wisdom, which does not depend on another for awakening.

It further states: "At the very moment of first generating the aspiration for enlightenment, one encompasses the five stages and attains equal and perfect awakening," thereby enabling all sentient beings...
Because they give rise to illness and swiftly attain Bodhi, it is said: "He fully informs his children: 'You all must quickly come out.

The subsequent passage, "He hurriedly seizes them and brings them back," carries the same meaning as "you all must quickly come out. Question: As for the contemplation mentioned in the phrase "fully informing his children," such contemplation concerns matters of fear.
Since "fully informing" has already been explained as referring to the *Avataṃsaka*, why is there no mention of matters of fear in the *Avataṃsaka*?
Answer: The Avataṃsaka Sūtra dispatches the Great Beings of the Dharmakāya to expound the dharma-gate of the fifty-five stages.

Its perfect resonance is vast and far-reaching; its primary and attendant elements are layered and manifold. The perfect fusion and sequential arrangement are such that sentient beings cannot endure them;

like a destitute son who is struck with terror, they cry out in lamentation. How could this be anything other than fear? Question: Why do the explanations through dharmas and the explanations through parables not...

Guangming replied: "The *Avataṃsaka* has already passed; it is the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* that is now being expounded. One represents the beginning and the other the end; since these two sutras share the same essential purpose, I have not explained them extensively.
They are fully encompassed within these two phrases. △ Second, the parable of the children who would not listen.
This serves as an analogy for the aforementioned dullness of the faculties of sentient beings, clarifying that sentient beings lack the necessary capacity (indriya).

Although the father felt compassion and exhorted them with kind words—asking what the house was and what the loss was—the sons, being attached to their pleasures, did not listen to their father’s words; they sought no liberation. How, then, could the three types of wisdom arise?

Because they were not startled, they lacked the wisdom of hearing (*śruta-mayī-prajñā*); because they were not afraid, they lacked the wisdom of reflection (*cintā-mayī-prajñā*). Not knowing the five [aggregates]...

The turbidity of the eight sufferings can burn away one’s roots of goodness; yet they do not know this is fire. They do not know that the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and sense-bases (*āyatana*) are the vessels of all these sufferings;
they do not know this is a house [to be abandoned]. They do not know the cause for the loss of the *dharmakāya*, nor do they know how such a loss occurs.
If this is the case, then even the cultivation of wisdom will not arise. The faculties become dark and dull, and the three types of wisdom do not flourish.
"Born [into this state], there is likewise nothing that can be done for them. These are those of middling and inferior faculties who are incapable of receiving the Great Dharma;
namely, the Bodhisattvas who accumulate practices and the Arhats of superior virtue. 3. The Parable of Racing and Playing While Looking at One’s Father.
This parable illustrates the preceding statement, "I would rather not preach the Dharma," clarifying the intention to cease transformation through teaching.
He merely runs back and forth playing, looking only at his father.
In the Dharma, the cessation of transformation resides in the Buddha; this metaphor illustrates that running and playing reside in the faculty (the mind). These two aspects clarify one another:

turning one's back to light and facing toward darkness constitutes "east and west," while the coming and going of birth and death constitutes "running. Within this state, giving rise to craving and views constitutes [the act of playing].
They frolic about—so-called "going out east and entering west," rising or sinking according to good or evil, galloping south and running north—as if in an endless cycle.
Although they employ grand gestures, they do not follow the Great Teaching; thus it is said that they merely look upon their father.
Setting aside the single section on the "Abandonment of the Stool" (the *Ji*), this metaphor refers to the passage from "I first sat at the site of enlightenment" up to "entering into nirvana. Six.
The first half-verse is explained in the Parable of the Poor Son below: "At that time, the poor son, wandering about in search of work, arrived [at his father's house];
[the father] then sent a bystander to forcibly lead him back. This concludes the preceding section on the Parable of Discarding the Stool. II. The Parable of the Carriages.

The eleven verses beginning with "Analogously, he recalls the Buddhas of the past" and ending with "I always speak thus" describe how, while the Great [Buddha] was subduing the Small [Māra], he simultaneously manifested two forms:
remaining unmoved at the site of tranquility (the Bodhi tree), he manifested his transformation by traveling to the Deer Park.
This is divided into four parts: first, the proposal of the three vehicles; second, knowing the sons' original inclinations; third, praising the three vehicles;

and fourth, granting the sons their wishes. Regarding the first, the parable of proposing the three vehicles, it serves as an analogy for the aforementioned passage beginning with "recalling the Buddhas of the past."
He also employs the transformation and deliverance of the three vehicles.
At that time, the elder immediately had this thought: (omitted) "to cause my sons to escape this calamity.
Previously it was said, "a great fire breaks out on all four sides"; now it is said, "this house has already been consumed by flames. Previously it was said, "suffering and pain."
Cease [this]. It is as if one has not yet died; now, since one must certainly be burned, there is the sense of death.

If I and my sons are inevitably to be burned, it is because the merit of transforming others through the Mahāyāna constitutes the father’s life, and the great goodness of sentient beings constitutes the sons’ lives.
If that great goodness is exhausted, then the sons’ lives are severed. When the sons’ lives are severed, the merit of transformation is also abolished; this is the end of the father.
Their lives will end. Therefore it is said: "If one does not emerge in time, one will surely be burned. Previously it was said that those at the burning gates emerged in safety;
now it is said that if one does not emerge in time, one will surely be burned. How should this meaning be understood?
One must know that the former emergence refers to the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*); what is now said regarding not emerging in time refers to the Response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*).

He manifests as having an illness in common with sentient beings. If sentient beings possess goodness such that they form the capacity to receive transformation, he then appears at times in his response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*).
If the goodness of sentient beings is severed and they lack the capacity to receive [the teaching], he does not appear at times in his response-body;
thus, both are consumed by fire. Regarding the phrase "one should establish skillful means," the single vehicle of the true reality (*bhūtatathatā*) is fundamentally inexpressible.

The "crooked" [method] is for those of middling and inferior capacities. It skillfully demonstrates expedient means (*upāya*) by preaching the provisional teachings of the Three Vehicles, enabling all sons to escape the harms of the five turbidities and the eight sufferings.
△ Second, the Parable of Knowing the Sons' Previous Intentions. This parable corresponds to the aforementioned reflection:
"At that time, the Buddhas of the ten directions all appeared," etc., clarifying the capacity of those who attain liberation through the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*).
The father knows the former inclinations of his sons—that they will surely take pleasure in various rare and wondrous objects—and that they previously practiced what was minor;
thus he knows their former inclinations. He knows that their dispositions and desires differ, and thus he knows each has their own preferences.
Since he knows they practiced what was minor, he meets them with the minor. Since he knows their dispositions and desires differ, he divides the one into three. Furthermore...
Knowing that he had previously practiced the Great [Vehicle] is called "knowing his prior inclination. "The middle" refers to birth and death;

"each having their own preferences" refers to various rare treasures and playthings, which are the dharmas such as the Six Perfections conditioned by the Truths—things that do not exist within the Three Realms, and are therefore called "extraordinary.

"His heart must surely be set on one phrase" means that [the teaching] precisely meets what he enjoys. △ Third, praising the parable of the three carts, which serves as a metaphor for the aforementioned contemplation.

Once this matter was concluded, he proceeded to Vārāṇasī and elsewhere to clearly and correctly bestow the three vehicles. This is further divided into three parts: first, the turning that exhorts practice;
second, the turning that reveals characteristics; and third, the turning that provides realization. Regarding the first, the turning that exhorts practice:
He addressed them, saying: "Regarding those things you hold dear for play and enjoyment... (until) if you do not take [this advice], you will surely feel regret later.
This is an exhortation to practice. It means: "This is suffering; you should know it. Its origin should be abandoned. Its cessation should be realized."
The Way should be cultivated; it is rare and difficult to attain—this refers to precious curiosities and wonders. Speaking in terms of three types of persons:

the two characters "playful enjoyment" (wán-hǎo) correspond to the Path and Cessation of the Two Truths for Śrāvakas, and to the gate of Return and Cessation for Pratyekabuddhas, as well as the Dharma of the Six Perfections for Bodhisattvas.

The two characters "sorrow and regret" (yōu-huì) correspond to Suffering and Origination, the gate of Transmigration, and the Dharma of the Six Obscurations. △ Second, the Manifestation of Characteristics.
"These various kinds of sheep-carts, deer-carts, and ox-carts are now outside the gate for you to play with.

This indicates their appearance; that is to say, this [suffering] is of a nature that oppresses, [origination] is of a nature that invites [suffering], [cessation] is of a nature that can be realized, and [the path] is of a nature that can be cultivated.
The sheep-carts, deer-carts, and ox-carts are metaphors for the three vehicles (*triyāna*). It is permitted that they [exist].
"Outside the gate" means that because the afflictions of view and thought have been exhausted, one has emerged beyond the triple world and only then obtains this vehicle.

Furthermore, the "gate" refers to the gate of the true reality (*bhūtatathatā*) of the One Vehicle; because the Tathāgata’s skillful wisdom provisionally distinguishes and teaches three vehicles outside of the One Vehicle, it is called "outside the gate.
"Capable of playing" means that one may exercise the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*) with ease and play freely.
...and so forth. △ Third, the turning through realization:
"You should all come out quickly from this burning house; whatever you desire, I shall give it to you.
This is an induction of oneself to serve as a witness for others. It means: "I have already known this suffering and shall not need to know it again; its origin has already been severed."
There is no further severing; having been extinguished, it is realized and not to be realized again; the Path having been cultivated, it is not to be cultivated again.
Regarding the phrase "I shall grant all to you," this means that I grant it to you because I have already realized it myself and also cause others to realize it.
As the subsequent passage states: "I guarantee for you that this matter shall never be in vain. This is the sequence for demonstrating and encouraging realization. Now...
Following the sequence of first exhorting and later demonstrating as found in the sutra, there is no loss of meaning. △ Fourth, the parable of acceding to the son's wish.
This parable illustrates the aforementioned single verse on "turning the wheel of Dharma," clarifying the reception, practice, awakening, and entry [into the teaching].
At that time, the sons, having heard what their father said, raced together in competition to escape from the burning house.

The preceding verse was brief; now, through this parable, the cultivation of causes leading to the fruit is explained in detail. "Just as they wished" refers to the faculty and the teaching striking one another, which is the wisdom of hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*).
"Brave and swift" refers to the movement of thought and deliberation, which is the wisdom of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*). These two phrases constitute the three provisions (*sambhāra*).

The stage of external ordinary beings (*bāhyapṛthagjana*) refers to the five *sthāpanā-citta*, the mindfulness of specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇasmṛtyupasthāna*), and the mindfulness of general characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇasmṛtyupasthāna*). "Mutually excluding" (*hu xiāng*) below refers to the wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*);

it involves inferring the principles of the Four Noble Truths and suppressing the delusions of views (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*). Because right and wrong have not yet been definitively resolved, it is called "mutually excluding.

This corresponds to the two stages of "Heat" (*uṣmagata*) and "Summit" (*mūrdhan*) within the four stages of application (*prayoga*). "Competing" (*jìng*) means competing to grasp the superior principle; at first, one universally contemplates the eight [realms] above and below.

The Truths. One traverses the sixteen aspects and competes to advance toward the True Path. Subsequently, one contracts the contemplation down to the level of the Suffering Truth of the Desire Realm and proceeds toward the *duḥkhe-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti*.
This is the stage of *kṣānti* for the inner ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*). "Common" refers to the fourth stage, the Stage of Supreme Mundane Dharma;
because the contemplation of the Suffering Truth of the Desire Realm is not distinct from the stage of *kṣānti*, it is called "common. "Rushing forward" refers to entering [the path].

The fifteen moments of mind in the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*) swiftly grasp the principle; hence it is called "galloping. At this stage, one completely severs the afflictions of views (*dṛṣṭi-heya-kleśa*), partially attains *nirvāṇa*, and enters the rank of the Noble Ones (*ārya*);
this is the First Fruit (*srotāpanna*). "Vying to escape" refers to the Path of Cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*), which constitutes the Second and Third Fruits (*sakṛdāgāmin* and *anāgāmin*).

Having emerged from the burning house and completely severed the afflictions of cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya-kleśa*), one realizes the Path of No-More-Learning (*aśaikṣa-mārga*); this is the Fourth Fruit (*arhat*). If one were to act...
The three types of persons discuss this together. First is the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths. For those of the Śrāvaka vehicle, the Truth of Suffering is the initial gateway;
for those of the Pratyekabuddha vehicle, the Truth of Origination is the initial gateway; for those of the Bodhisattva vehicle, the Truth of the Path is the initial gateway.

These three persons uphold it together, these three persons cultivate it together, and these three persons each realize it individually. Therefore, it is said that their minds each vie with one another to emerge [from saṃsāra].
All of these are explained in terms of the wisdom and abandonment of the three vehicles. According to the principles established below, those who speak specifically are as follows:

the śrāvaka hears the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths, which accords with their aspirations and inclinations; they apply themselves with courageous diligence, investigate the principle of the Four Noble Truths, and eliminate the afflictions of views and thought.
Desiring to quickly escape the triple world and realize nirvāṇa, this is the śrāvaka’s striving to exit the burning house. As for the pratyekabuddha, having heard...

Regarding the Dharma of Dependent Origination: they cast themselves into their aspirations and delight; with courageous diligence, they take the cycle of transmigration and its cessation as their primary focus.
They advance against and eliminate the two types of habitual tendencies, gaining deep insight into the dependent origination of all phenomena, thereby attaining the realization of *nirvāṇa*.

This is how the *pratyekabuddhas* strive to escape the burning house. When Bodhisattvas hear the Dharma of the Six Perfections, it accords with their inclinations; they diligently cultivate and exert themselves, seeking and investigating [the truth].
Truly so. Sweeping away and subduing sands of afflictions, he transforms beings through compassion and delivers all. This is the Bodhisattva whom people strive to rescue from the burning house.
The preceding section on abandoning the small stools and employing the carts is concluded. △ Third, the Parable of Bestowing the Great Carts Equally.
This parable corresponds to the aforementioned "I see my sons," etc., where they aspire to seek the Buddha-way. The six lines of verse reveal the reality; this section is divided into four parts.
First, the father sees his sons escape from danger and rejoices; second, the sons request vehicles; third, he equally bestows great vehicles upon all the sons;

fourth, the sons receive the vehicles and rejoice. Now, regarding the first analogy—of the father seeing his sons escape from danger and rejoicing—it corresponds to the verse in the *Śrīmālādevī-siṃhanāda-sūtra* which states:
"I then had this thought: for what reason has the Tathāgata appeared? This second line of the verse clarifies the Buddha’s joy.
Fearless.
At that time, the elder saw his sons [and so forth], and his mind became serene, joyful, and leaping with delight.
The preceding verse clarified the father’s joy; this one clarifies the sons’ joy. Because the sons are joyful, the father is also joyful. That is to say:

Regarding "rejoicing at being freed from calamity": if a son has not yet escaped danger, his father will be filled with anxiety; once he succeeds in leaving the fire, the father’s mind becomes serene.
Thus, rejoicing at being freed from calamity serves as a single metaphor. The "four crossroads" is a metaphor for the Four Noble Truths.

The three vehicles equally realize the principle of the Four Noble Truths; yet, as they have not yet shattered the "dust-like" afflictions (*rajas*), they remain on the middle path, hence it is called "on the way.
When the afflictions of views and thought within the triple world are exhausted, it is termed the "open space" (*ābhoga*); this is *sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*.
Nirvāṇa is called "open space" because, compared to the burning house, it is cool and spacious; yet, compared to the majesty of the precious chariots, it is still incomplete.
It is entirely non-existent. Therefore, it is called the "partial emptiness" of the small fruit. Because one dwells in the fruit without further progress, it is said that one "sits.

Since the afflictions of views and thought (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) have been exhausted, the principle of the True Truth (*satyārtha*) is revealed; hence, it is said there is "no longer any obstruction. Being no longer constrained by views and thought, it is said to be "serene.
Having already transcended the notion of birth and having attained the notion of peace and security, it is said that one is "joyful. △ Second, the sons.
The Parable of the Request for Chariots illustrates the two verses beginning with "My sons, the sons of the Buddha," which clarify the awakening of the capacity for the Mahāyāna.
At that time, each of the sons addressed their father, saying: "...please grant us at this time the goat-drawn chariots, the deer-drawn chariots, and the ox-drawn chariots."

This clarifies the "requesting of the vehicle. Although the word "request" (suo) does not appear in the text, it is by means of these words of petition that the requesting of the vehicle is clarified. There are three types of "requesting": First, the "requesting of the capacity" (*jī suǒ*).
After the realization of the Small Vehicle at the Deer Park, when [the disciples] reached the Vaipulya period, they secretly received great benefit;

though they were rebuked, they did not slander [the teaching]. In principle, there was the sense of seeking the Great Vehicle—this is called the "requesting of the capacity. Second, the "requesting of the sentiment" (*qíng suǒ*). Upon reaching the assembly of the *Prajñāpāramitā* Sūtra, they understood...

Knowing the Great Dharma, they give rise to the aspiration for the Great Mind. Although they do not yet speak explicitly, their seeking of the meaning becomes increasingly earnest; this is called "seeking through emotion. Third is "seeking through speech":
having reached the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, due to hearing the Buddha’s brief exposition at the beginning of the "Expedient Means" chapter, their long-standing doubts are stirred.
For this reason, they speak three times to request [the teaching]; this is called "seeking through speech. Question: They still seek the three vehicles; how is this the Great Capacity?
[The Buddha] replied: "The names are the same, but the meanings differ; it is simply that the great capacity [of the bodhisattvas] has been activated.
However, those of the two vehicles do not know that apart from the three vehicles there is a separate One Vehicle. Because they requested with such earnestness, 'Please grant us a distinction;

we pray you will speak of the foremost,' it is clear that the capacity for the Mahāyāna has been activated. Furthermore, within the Dharma-exposition, first the activation of the capacity is clarified, followed by the teaching on the removal of hindrances. The Buddha—

Joyful Fearlessness. Herein, the metaphor first clarifies the avoidance of calamity, followed by the clarification of the arousal of the spiritual capacity (*indriya*). A full discussion contains four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*):

first, there are those for whom obstacles are removed first and the great spiritual capacity is subsequently aroused, such as the four great disciples and other *śrāvakas*, who had their obstacles removed within the teachings of the Lesser Vehicle, yet only began to arouse the great spiritual capacity at the beginning of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā* and *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* sūtras. Second, there are those for whom obstacles have not yet been removed and the great spiritual capacity...

First, the awakening of the capacity [to receive the teaching] occurs first, followed by the removal of obstacles, as in the cases of ordinary people who attained the Buddha-wisdom in the *Avataṃsaka* and *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* sūtras, where the three great capacities were activated first and obstacles were subsequently removed, as described in the "Expedient Means" chapter (*Upāyakauśalya-parivarta*). Second, the removal of obstacles occurs first, followed by the awakening of the capacity, as illustrated by the present parable.
Although these two cases—where the activation of the capacity and the removal of obstacles appear alternately—they ultimately converge upon a single intent. △ Third, the equal bestowal upon all sons.

The Simile of the Great Vehicle (*mahāyāna-dṛṣṭānta*). This serves as a metaphor for the three verses above concerning bodhisattvas, which correctly reveal the reality. It is divided into three parts:

first, the simultaneous presentation of the children and so forth, and the vehicles and so forth; second, the detailed explanation of the vehicles and so forth; third, the detailed explanation of the mind and so forth.
First, the simultaneous presentation of the children and so forth, and the vehicles and so forth.
Śāriputra, at that time the elder bestowed upon each of his sons an identical great carriage.
"Bestowed upon each of his sons" clarifies that the sons are equal. All sentient beings equally possess the Buddha-nature; because their Buddha-natures are the same, they are all equally his sons.
"An identical great carriage" clarifies that the carriages are equal. This is because the sons are equal.
Therefore, the mind is equal; because all phenomena (dharmas) are equal, there is nothing that is not the Buddha-dharma. This is illustrated by the fact that all dharmas are the Mahāyāna.

Regarding the phrase "each was given," it means that each [person] was shown the truth according to their own prior habitual practice—whether the Four Noble Truths, the Six Perfections, or the immeasurable dharmas.
Because their former habits were different, it is said "each. Since they are all the Mahāyāna, it is called the "Great Vehicle" (mahāyāna). [This is as stated in] the following passage.
All who hear the Dharma shall without exception attain Buddhahood; such is the intended meaning. △ Second, the detailed explanation of the carts, which has two parts.
First, explaining the essential nature and characteristics of the carts.
That chariot was high and broad, adorned with various jewels (up to the point where it says), and was attended by many servants.
"High and broad" is a metaphor for the Tathāgata’s knowledge and vision, which are vast, profound, and far-reaching, extending horizontally to the very limits of the Dharma-realm.

It penetrates vertically to the very bottom of the abyss of principle. Furthermore, it perfectly encompasses and accords with all things, universally gathering together the capacities and occasions of sentient beings;

how could it be anything other than sublime and vast? The phrase "various jewels" is a metaphor for the adornment of the myriad practices. The phrase "surrounding" is a metaphor for the protection of *dhāraṇī*.
The phrase "four sides" is a metaphor for the four analytical knowledges used to transform sentient beings below. The phrase "spread out" refers to the spreading of the canopy and silk.
The carriage is a metaphor for the four immeasurable minds (*catur-apramāṇa*); among all virtues, compassion and loving-kindness are supreme, as they universally cover all beings.

The phrase "rare and wondrous" is a metaphor for the myriad genuine virtues, which adorn this compassion. The phrase "precious cords" is a metaphor for the four great vows (*catvāri mahāpraṇidhānāni*), which solidify the mind of great compassion.
The phrase "hanging down in various ways" is a metaphor for the four means of integration (*catvāri saṃgrahavastūni*), the supernatural powers (*abhijñā*), and so forth.
"To delight all sentient beings" is a repeated phrase; it signifies elegance and beauty. "Sedan" refers to mats and carpets;

it is a metaphor for the contemplative practices of *vipaśyanā*, *śamatha*, *bhāvanā*, and *vāsanā*, representing the layered softness of all meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*). "To place [the head] upon" is a phrase; a pillow has both an inner and an outer part.
The outer pillow refers to when a carriage is being driven; wherever it goes, this support is required to keep it elevated.

This is a metaphor for movement within stillness and stillness within movement. The inner pillow refers to resting the body and head; it is a metaphor for the *ekavyūha-samādhi* (one-practice samādhi), which brings to rest all wisdom and all practices.
"Dan" refers to the color red, which is a metaphor for the dharma of non-discrimination. It is used as a vehicle.

The white ox is a metaphor for untainted (*anāsrava*) prajñā. It is able to lead the practices of the six perfections and all other deeds that take the truths as their object to the ocean of *sarvajñatā*.
"White" is its original color, signifying its correspondence with fundamental purity and the absence of outflows. Its substance possesses ten thousand virtues, like skin that is full and abundant;
it is unstained by afflictions, like a color that is pure and bright. Its physical form—its skin and color—is exquisite and beautiful.
"Filled and pure"—these two phrases metaphorically represent the essence of the *prajñā* of ultimate reality (*dharmatā-prajñā*).

"Possessing great strength"—these three phrases metaphorically represent the function of the *prajñā* of contemplative insight (*pratyavekṣaṇā-prajñā*). Furthermore, the four foundations of mindfulness are the white ox;

within the four right efforts, the fulfillment of the two kinds of worldly good is like the flesh being filled, and the exhaustion of the two kinds of worldly evil is like the color being pure. The four bases of psychic power are called... [the rest of the sentence].

The practitioner’s mind is like a physical form of beautiful appearance. The sinews are a metaphor for the five faculties (*pañcendriya*), signifying their function of providing a firm foundation and giving rise to [spiritual qualities].

The powers (*bala*) are a metaphor for the five powers, signifying their function of overcoming and subduing [obstacles]. Walking with even and upright steps is a metaphor for the equilibrium of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*), as well as the balanced harmony of the seven factors of enlightenment (*saptabodhyaṅga*).
Its swiftness being like the wind is a metaphor for proceeding upon the eightfold noble path (*āryāṣṭāṅgamārga*), swiftly reaching *sarvajñatā* (all-knowledge).
"Sea" (Sāgara) refers to the servant; it is the *upāya-pāramitā* (perfection of skillful means).

Being able to bend and adapt to others to provide service and carry out commands—namely, that all Māras, non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), and those of the two vehicles with their minor practices—all follow the functional application of the wisdom of skillful means.
Thus, the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* says, "They are all my attendants. "Servants and retinues" means providing service to one's left and right; it is synonymous with "retinue" (*parivāra*). This...

The "middle elder" refers to the person capable of realization; the "chariots" and so forth refer to the dharmas that are realized. The chariot itself represents the greatness of essence (*svabhāva-mahattva*);

the various jewels and so forth represent the greatness of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-mahattva*); and the white oxen and so forth represent the greatness of function (*kāritra-mahattva*). That the sons ride upon them signifies that they will become future elders.
△ Second, explaining the reason for having the chariot.
Why is this so? It is because this great elder possesses immeasurable wealth, and all his various treasuries are completely overflowing.

The abundance of wealth and the overflowing of the treasuries are metaphors for the perfection of merit and wisdom on the stage of fruition. As for the "various treasuries," they refer to the treasury of practice (*caryā-kośa*) and the treasury of principle (*tattva-kośa*).
Furthermore, all dharmas do not transcend *dāna*, *śīla*, *kṣānti*, and so forth; this explains the *tathāgatagarbha* by way of practice (*caryā*).
All dharmas do not transcend the aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*); this explains the *tathāgatagarbha* by way of principle (*tattva*).

Any single dharma taken from among the aggregates, elements, and so forth, is none other than the treasury of principle. By realizing this treasury of principle, the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*) are thereby [perfected].

One accomplishes wondrous conduct. Failing to realize this principle, the myriad practices are cultivated in vain. When one’s own practice of this principle is fulfilled, its transformation of others overflows.
Furthermore, the perfection of true wisdom (*bhūta-jñāna*) is called "fulfillment," while the application of expedient wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*) according to circumstances is called "overflowing.

It is not merely that they are stored in abundance; rather, they are all fully overflowing. There is not a single dharma that is not the Mahāyāna; therefore, it is said that they are manifold and immeasurable.
△ Third, the detailed explanation of the mind and so forth. This is divided into two parts. First, the detailed explanation of the mind and so forth:
one forms this thought: "My wealth and possessions are limitless; I shall give them to each [person] individually and it is not appropriate to make distinctions."
This clarifies the equality of the mind and so forth. Because material wealth is inexhaustible, this son is without partiality;

therefore, the mind is equal. If one were wealthy but not a son, there might be stinginess; if one were a son but poor, one might be unable to provide. In such cases, the mind would not attain equality.
Now, his own practice is perfected and his wealth is immeasurable; the conditions for conversion have already ripened. Therefore—

"Love is without partiality. Regarding the "great carriage of the seven treasures," this is a metaphor for the revelation and clarification of the present sutra; whether in teaching or practice, all are Mahāyāna.

Furthermore, it refers to the Vaipulya and Prajñāpāramitā [teachings], as well as the foundations of mindfulness, right efforts, faculties, powers, factors of enlightenment, and the noble eightfold path.
These various different names all reveal the true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*). It is likewise so throughout all phenomena;
therefore, they are said to be immeasurable. Each pair of phrases reveals the true reality without departing from one's original training:
