Yet, this Sphere of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception is not the fruit of *nirvāṇa*; it is mistakenly conceived as eternal.
It is like one whose throat is constricted and whose life is in peril, yet who still clings to their longevity;

thus it is said that "their throat is like a needle. Because there is no form and only mind remains, it is called a "constricted throat. 5. Two verses as a metaphor for the extreme views (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*).
Furthermore, there are various ghosts with heads like those of oxen (and so on), driven by hunger and thirst, crying out and rushing about.
Regarding their single body, they conceive of annihilation or permanence; they cling to permanence as being non-annihilated, and cling to annihilation as being non-permanent.

Clinging to one extreme is called the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*). Those who calculate permanence hold that while the body is annihilated, the self is permanent. Those who calculate annihilation hold that both the body and the self are annihilated.
The two extremes of annihilationism and eternalism are like the two horns of an ox.

Not understanding that good causes produce good effects and evil causes produce evil effects, they cling with single-minded persistence to either annihilation or eternity—like one who eats human flesh and then devours a dog.

At times they calculate eternity, and at other times they calculate annihilation; they revolve back and forth like disheveled hair. To calculate eternity is to destroy annihilationism, and to calculate...

To sever [the roots of goodness] is to destroy permanence; it is like being cruel and predatory. Lacking wisdom and meditative concentration, they sustain themselves on mere food and drink, as if oppressed by hunger and thirst.
Each proclaims their own views and loudly chants false doctrines, as if wailing. They follow all manner of deviant practices.
Samsara does not cease; it is like a galloping horse. The above clearly concludes the explanation of those who are burned. △ Second, one and a half lines summarize those who are burned:
"Yakṣas, hungry ghosts, various evil birds and beasts... (up to) such calamities and fears are immeasurable."
This summarizes the characteristics of the sharp and dull afflictions (*kleśa*) within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*). The first phrase refers to the sharp; the second phrase refers to the dull.

The two phrases "hunger" and "urgency" collectively summarize the two types of latent tendencies (*anuśaya*). These are all out-flowing minds (*sāsrava-citta*) that lack the craving for the flavor of the Path (*mārga-rasa*);

hence they are called "hungry. Because of this hunger, birth and death proceed with great rapidity; hence they are called "urgent. As for the "four directions," these refer to the four modes of birth within the cycle of saṃsāra.

"Peering" refers to stealing a glance. This means that although one clearly perceives the principle of emptiness through deviant contemplation and yearns for the flavor of the Way, even while contemplating emptiness, the mind remains largely mired in attachment and fails to accord with the correct principle;
it is like peering through a window at the sky—one cannot attain unimpeded vision.
The final two lines provide a summary. First, the types of things burned are clarified, which concludes the analogy for the ten afflictions (*daśa-kleśa*).
Second, one verse clarifies the cause for the fire’s ignition, which serves as an analogy for the cause for the arising of the five turbidities (*pañca-kaṣāya*).
This dilapidated old house belongs to a single person who has been away for no long time.

The three realms are the place where the Buddha manifests his transformative response; since first generating the aspiration for enlightenment, he has vowed to deliver all beings, and thus it is said to "belong to one person.
While the elder was in the house, he was able to cause his sons to be cautious regarding the fire; however, after he had left the house, the sons...
Because of ignorance, fire is ignited. This corresponds internally to the Tathāgata being present in the world, which enables him to subdue the five turbidities (*pañca-kaṣāya*).

Due to the relinquishment of his response-body, sentient beings subsequently give rise to the five turbidities once again. Thus, the World-Honored One repeatedly undergoes birth and extinction within this land.

The statement that he has "recently emerged" refers to his final manifestation within the three realms. As the conditions for this land were exhausted and those for the other land matured, he relinquished this realm to respond to that one.
Question: Why do you say both "belonging" and "emerging"? For if he belongs [to this realm], he does not emerge; and if he emerges, he no longer belongs [to it]. Answer:
If one does not speak of belonging, then he would have no concern with himself, and thus there would be no need for rescue. Therefore, both terms must be used.
Ji: "If one does not speak out, one will simply be burned oneself; how then could one save others?
△ Third, two lines describe the momentum of the fire breaking out, which serves as a metaphor for the actual arising of the five turbidities (*pañca-kaṣāya*).
Thereafter, the house suddenly caught fire (until) the beams were shattered and fell, and the walls collapsed.

Suddenly, as it spread rapidly, there was an immediate response throughout the four quarters—namely, body, sensation, mind, and phenomena. Within this, the four inversions, the five turbidities, the eight sufferings, and so forth all arose together;
hence it is called "at once. As these conditions continued and gradually increased, they became intensely blazing; hence it is called "simultaneously ablaze. [The being] groaned...
The wailing of grief becomes the sound of explosions; the destruction of the sense faculties becomes the cracking of earthquakes.
As the breath ceases and the bones separate, there is crushing and falling; as the four great elements disperse, walls and ramparts collapse.

Mountains crumble, the earth splits, trees break, cliffs shatter, and rivers and mountains overturn—this clearly illustrates how the palace of the three realms and the house of the five aggregates suddenly fall into ruin and decay.
"Ruined": the appearance of being scorched by fire such that it is no longer fit for use; this causes people not to harbor greedy attachment [to the body].
△ Four lines and a half clarify the signs of being burned, which metaphorically represent undergoing the five turbidities and the eight sufferings.
The various ghosts and spirits raised their voices in a great cry (up to: they were so overwhelmed with panic and terror that they could not escape on their own.

Those who calculate according to permanence claim that dharmas are fixed and permanent; yet what has existed returns to non-existence, and because this non-existence is itself permanent, they hold this view.

Those who calculate according to annihilationism claim that dharmas are fixed and subject to cessation; there is only this single death, and nothing further continues. They all proclaim these as definitive teachings regarding those matters.

This has already been explained; thus it says, "raising their voices and crying out. The vultures and eagles represent the dull afflictions (*dauṣthulya*), while the *kumbhāṇḍas* represent the sharp afflictions.

These sentient beings have minds turbid with afflictions; the five views (*pañca-dṛṣṭi*) attack them simultaneously. They do not seek the cultivation of the Right Path, nor do they know the means of transcendence.
Constantly remaining within the three realms, they willingly undergo saṃsāra; hence the words "perplexed and terrified," etc. The above clarifies this.

The analogy for the events on the ground—the arising of fire in the desire realm—is concluded. △ Next, two and a half lines clarify the events within the hole, which serves as an analogy for the arising of fire in the form realm.
This is divided into four parts. First, one line clarifies the types of things being burned.
Malevolent beasts and venomous insects hide within their holes and burrows, and piśāca demons likewise dwell therein.
The concentration of the fourth dhyāna is like these holes; although it does not possess the wide-open expanse of the gateway at night, one can still escape from fierce flames.
This is a metaphor for entering the concentration of the fourth dhyāna: although one has not yet exited the boundaries [of the form realm], one can still escape from the desire realm.
This refers to coarse and evil [actions]. The first two phrases refer to the dull afflictions (dull *kleśas*); the latter two phrases refer to the sharp afflictions (sharp *kleśas*).
*Piśāca* refers to ghosts that devour vital essence. △ Second, one sentence clarifies the cause by which the fire arises.
Because their merit is slight;
because their blessings and virtue are meager, they encounter suffering by drawing near to evil. △ Third, one sentence clarifies the power of the fire that burns them:
being oppressed by the fire.
Within the hollows, although there is no fierce fire, there is still the suffering of heat.

This is a metaphor for how the fourth dhyāna, though lacking the coarse evils of the desire realm, still possesses the subtle suffering of the attachment to the flavors of joy and bliss; therefore, it is oppressed by fire.
△ Fourth, two lines clarify the signs of being burned.
They mutually harm one another, drinking blood and devouring flesh, until foul smoke and blazing flames fill the four directions.

Whether their faculties are sharp or dull, those who attain dhyāna are the same in this regard; yet their calculations differ, and they engage in mutual dispute and contention as if they were harming one another.
Since they give rise to various views within dhyāna, they are unable to produce untainted (*anāsrava*) concentration and wisdom, but merely remain attached.

The flavor of dhyāna is like drinking blood; furthermore, attachment to the five factors such as vitarka and vicāra is like eating meat. The jackal serves as a metaphor for the greed of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
Having cultivated the future state of tranquility (*anāgata-śamatha*) within the desire realm and already severed this greed, it is said that they have both already died previously.

The craving for meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) is like a great predatory beast that can swallow the craving for the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*); therefore, it is said that [the latter] comes vyingly to devour it.
The four inversions and eight sufferings of the desire realm are like fierce flames; the four inversions and eight sufferings of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) are like foul-smelling smoke.

Because smoke surpasses the flames, it serves as a metaphor for the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*). The realm of form also encompasses body, sensation, mind, and phenomena, as well as the four great elements (*mahābhūta*);
because suffering pervades all four directions, it is said to be "pervasive. The above has clarified the matters within the hole, concluding the metaphor for the arising of fire in the realm of form.
△ Third, two and a half lines clarify the matters within the void, serving as a metaphor for the arising of fire in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*). This section has two parts.
The first line clarifies the types of beings that are burned.
Centipedes, millipedes, and venomous snakes, when scorched by fire, scramble to flee their burrows.

In the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), centipedes are used as a metaphor for anger (*dveṣa*); now, in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), they are likewise used as a metaphor for anger. Although this is not explicitly stated for the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), [the same applies].
Regarding centipedes, the term "poisonous insects" includes them as well. The *Abhidharma* states:

"In the higher realms, anger does not function because there is no mutual harm, because there is wholesome desire, because their nature is tranquil, and because their minds are moistened. Nevertheless, it ceases to function there; it is not that [anger] is severed.
In terms of seeds, it exists in all three realms; in terms of active manifestation (*samudācāra*), it exists only in the Desire Realm.

Aversion toward the form realm leads to emergence and orientation toward the formless realm. One feels aversion for the coarse phenomena of the form realm and contemplates the phenomena of the formless realm, like a venomous snake that, when scorched, emerges from its hole.
△ Second, one and a half lines clarify the characteristics of that which is scorched.
The kumbhāṇḍa spirits seize and devour whatever they encounter (up to the point where beings), tormented by hunger, thirst, and feverish distress, wander about in agitation and confusion.

If one attains the formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*), one will necessarily extinguish the conditions pertaining to the lower realms; hence it is said that they "seize and devour whatever they encounter.

Even those dwelling at the summit, in the Sphere of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*), cannot escape the suffering of perversion, which is like a fire burning upon the head. This is also true for the Sphere of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception.
There are the fires of the eight sufferings. When the mind gives rise to divergent thoughts, this is the suffering of birth. When moments of thought do not abide, this is the suffering of old age.

When the active mind is agitated and obstructs concentration, this is the suffering of illness. When concentration declines, this is the suffering of death. When seeking concentration and failing to attain it, this is the suffering of not obtaining what one seeks.

When concentration is not attained, there will inevitably be obstructions; this is the suffering of encountering the hated and disliked. When concentration is lost, [this is the suffering of being separated from the loved].
This is the suffering of separation. The four aggregates of mind constitute the suffering of the five aggregates being in full blaze.

Because they lack the sustenance of untainted food and drink, they are tormented by hunger and thirst; this is still within the cycle of saṃsāra, hence it is said that they "run about in frantic distress.
The above clarifies the events within emptiness, concluding the analogy of the fire breaking out in the formless realm. △ Fourth, one verse summarizes all these hardships.
It is manifold.
His dwelling is thus extremely terrifying, with poison, harm, fires, and various calamities beyond count.
He is scorched by the fire of karma and the afflictions of the ten fetters, undergoing immeasurable suffering within the three realms and five destinies. Therefore, it is said: his—
The house is like this. It is truly terrifying, with calamities so numerous that they cannot be fully described; hence it is said to be "not one. The preceding verse concludes the general metaphor.

△ Next, thirty-two and a half lines constitute the second part, which provides specific metaphors, divided into three sections. The first two and a half lines provide the metaphor for the elder seeing the fire.
The next twenty-three lines provide the metaphor for abandoning the small stools and employing the carts. The final seven [lines]...

[He] proceeds. The verse [now] bestows the great chariots; it is abbreviated and lacks the prose commentary (*bhāṣya*). Furthermore, there are three parts at the beginning. The first three lines of the verse praise the Elder’s ability to see.
At that time, the master of the house was standing outside the gate and heard someone say:
The master of the house is the Tathāgata, who is the one capable of seeing. Those standing outside the gate are those who have safely emerged from the gate that was set ablaze.
As for why they are said to be "standing," it is because the Tathāgata, abiding in the stage of the Dharmakāya, constantly maintains great compassion.
Because he wishes to save sentient beings, he does not remain seated upon the throne of the ultimate emptiness (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*);

therefore, it is said that he "stands. Regarding the statement that someone "spoke": previously it was said "saw," whereas here it says "heard," substituting hearing for seeing. This is because what one hears must necessarily come from another;
thus, the dharma of samādhi is the "other. Entering into samādhi, he looks downward to examine the various capacities of sentient beings. Samādhi...
It enables the Buddhas to see [them]; therefore, it is said, "there are people who say. Furthermore, "people" refers to the compassionate vows (*karuṇā-praṇidhāna*).
If there are those who see or hear [this], it is caused by those compassionate vows. △ Second, one line of verse: a summary of what is seen.
"You sons, because of your former play, you entered this house; being young and ignorant, you took delight in it.

Question: "The sons had not yet come out originally; how can it be said that they entered because of play? Answer: "This refers to the time when the Noble One was in the state of Great Penetration (mahābhijñā)."
Having once resolved upon the Great Mind, it is called "exiting" the triple world (*tridhātu*). Yet, to subsequently regress is called "entering.
It is like a person who lifts their foot intending to exit, but turns back upon reaching the side of the gate; this is both called "exiting" and "entering.

With respect to the fundamental purity of the ordinary person's nature (*dharmatā*), which is not a phenomenon of the triple world, it is called "exiting. Because of obscurity and delusion, one gives rise to conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), and thus...
There is birth and death; this is called "entering. Therefore, it is said that he previously came to enter this house while playing.

Because his past connections were shallow and great goodness had not yet taken root, he is called "young and small. After regressing from the Great Vehicle, he wanders through the three realms, shrouded by ignorance;
this is called "ignorance. His joyful attachment is precisely his delight in play within the burning house mentioned before.
[The section on] "play" and so forth. △ Third, two lines of verse praise the arousal of alarm and fear.
Having heard this, the Elder was startled and entered the burning house.
For the sake of all sentient beings, he gave rise to great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*). This marks the emergence of a true sage and his descent into the mundane world. △ Second.
Thirteen stanzas. Regarding the abandonment of the stool and the employment of the chariot, there are two parts. First, five and a half stanzas praise the abandonment of the stool;
second, seven and a half stanzas praise the employment of the chariot. The first part further has three sections. First, four and a half stanzas praise the elder’s thought of rescue.
"One should now provide relief so that there is no burning harm" (up to) "this place of suffering and difficulty, how much more so the great fire.

"Now is the time for what is appropriate" (*fang yi*) means precisely that the Great Teaching is being applied as a remedy. "To inform and exhort" (*gao yu*) refers to fully informing all the children.

Regarding the section "explaining the various calamities and difficulties" below, it correctly clarifies the layers upon layers of what is being burned, extensively listing the two types of sentient beings who are submerged in [suffering].

They have not transcended the three realms, where the creeping vines of manifold sufferings continue without interruption. Because they lack the mutual support of concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*), they are said to be "hungry and thirsty.
To be hungry and thirsty is already terrifying; how much more so to be scorched and boiled by the great fires of the five turbidities!
△ Verses two and three: The sons do not listen.
Although the sons are ignorant, even upon hearing their father’s instruction, they remain attached to their pleasures.

The preceding verse states that although they hear their father’s instruction, they are unwilling to believe or accept it; this clearly demonstrates their lack of spiritual capacity (*anabhavyatā*). Not accepting [the teaching] is precisely what constitutes ignorance.
That is to say, although he was young and ignorant, he still took pleasure in and remained attached [to worldly things]. Having no great aspirations, he further became attached to the three realms.
△ The third line of the verse describes his frolicking and looking toward his father.

He continued his playful manifestations without ceasing until the time came for him to rest from his transformative work. "Playful manifestations" refers to the delusions of views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*); because these delusions did not cease, it was difficult to introduce the Great Dharma, and thus he rested from his great transformation.
II. Seventeen and a half lines: Verses on the Use of the Chariots. This section is divided into three parts. A. The first three lines: Verses on the Provisional Suitability.
The three carts.
At that time, the elder had this thought (up to) he then contemplated and devised various skillful means.
The first line expresses his intention: [he feared] they would fall into suffering and distress, and thus would not accept the Great [Vehicle]. Furthermore, the long passage says:
"This house has already been consumed by a great fire," and so forth. Because the elder feared that he and his sons would be burned together, his grief and distress increased.
The next line clarifies the reason for providing only the "Small [Vehicle]": because they are attached to views and afflictions (*kleśa*), they are given only the Small [Vehicle].
Their indulgence is extreme; "immersed" means they are submerged and do not emerge. There is not a single thing in the house that can be enjoyed.

The passage "Illuminating that the three realms and five destinies are suffering" means that the sons are immersed in and addicted to play. The passage "Illuminating that sentient beings grasp at suffering as pleasure" refers to the two phrases [of the verse].
The phrase "not accepting" clarifies the intent of employing the Small Vehicle. If the Small Vehicle were not employed, then both the Great and the Small would perish;
therefore it says, "they will be harmed by fire. Because they are harmed, they lose their bodies; because they lose their bodies, they lose their lives. Thus, there are these two [consequences].
[Verse] This refers to the correct contemplation of employing minor gifts, namely the teachings of the Three Vehicles. △ Verses 2–3: These verses praise the rarity of the three carts.
[The Buddha] addresses his sons, saying: "I have various kinds of [carts] (up to: which you may enjoy according to your own inclinations for play."
"Announcing to all the inferiors" refers to the verse on the encouragement to turn [the wheel]. "Wondrous jewels" refers to the wondrous jewels within the teachings of skillful means;

because the joy of the lesser fruits involves leaving behind the suffering of the burning house, they are called "wondrous jewels. "The sheep-cart, etc. refers to the verse on the demonstration of turning.
"Standing outside the gate" is like demonstrating the Four Noble Truths to bring about knowledge of the transcendence of the world. "You all, etc. refers to the verse on the realization of turning.
As for the "creator," since the three vehicles were originally non-existent and are merely produced as illusions, the two characters [of the preceding line] implicitly reject the two vehicles.
Being incapable of bearing the heavy responsibility or reaching the ultimate goal, they can only serve their own benefit through playful diversion.
△ Third, one and a half lines: a verse on fulfilling the wishes of the sons.
When the sons hear it said that such chariots [lead] to an open space free from all suffering and hardship—
"open space" (akāśa) here refers to the principle of partial emptiness realized by the Hīnayāna— this recalls the preceding verse on "rushing and contending to escape," and so forth.

The preceding verse concludes the section on abandoning the small stools and employing the carts. △ Thirty-seven lines. This section provides a verse summary of the parable of the equal distribution of the great carts, divided into four parts.
First, five lines provide a verse summary of the joy at being delivered from danger.
The elder sees his sons emerge from the burning house... (up to) "...therefore, O people, I am now joyful.
"The elder sees them" refers to their deliverance from calamity. "Sitting upon the lion throne" has two meanings: first, it is the seat upon which the sons sit;
because they have emerged from the triple world, they are without fear. Second, it is the seat upon which the elder sits; seeing that his sons have escaped the disaster, he immediately attains [joy].
It is fearlessness. Initially, when he was outside the gate while his sons were still within, the father remained standing. Now that the sons have already left the house, he has taken his seat.
Furthermore, because the great capacity [of sentient beings] had not yet been met, it is said he stood; because the minor transformation [of teaching] was already complete, he took his seat.
Thus we know that "standing" refers to benefit through hidden means, while "sitting" refers to benefit through manifest means. And so, he rejoiced in himself.
This is joy. Having encountered those who are to be transformed, one feels exultant and refreshed. At the abodes of twenty trillion Buddhas, they were taught the Great Cause;

therefore, it is said they were "born. During the intervening period, they matured slightly; therefore, it is said they were "nurtured. Having passed through such a long time, they achieved success repeatedly;
since their upbringing was not easy, it is said it was "extremely difficult. Because their roots of goodness were still slight, they are called "ignorant and small. [Their] delusions...

Because they are shrouded by delusion, they are said to be "without knowledge. Being without knowledge gives rise to turbidity; giving rise to turbidity inevitably invites karmic results, hence the phrase "entering the house.

The two lines beginning with "many" provide a general description of the sharp and dull faculties within the three realms. The two lines beginning with "great fire" provide a general description of the force of the eight sufferings within the three realms.
These two sets of lines clarify that through the arising of views and the arising of craving, one is unable to [liberate oneself].
"Uprooted. These two phrases clarify the cause of their joy; therefore, these two phrases conclude the meaning of their joy.
△ The next two lines verse the sons' request for the vehicle.
At that time, the sons knew their father had taken his seat... "Now is precisely the right time; please deign to grant [us our request].
"Knowing their father had taken his seat" refers to the time they requested the chariots. Examining the two aforementioned seats, the father’s sitting represents the primary one;

this is precisely sitting upon the seat of the *Anantarya-samudgata-sutra*. "All went to where their father was" refers to the ritual of requesting the chariots; it is exactly the same as the present day.
Surrounded by the fourfold assembly, they all came to my presence with deep reverence.

"We pray that you grant us [this]" is a formal request for what is sought, such as the three requests made by Śāriputra and others. As previously stated in the section on "the promise," this is the description of the granting;
now, in the following section, it is the conclusion of the granting. (37 lines and a half) This verse praises the granting of the great chariots.
The elder is immensely wealthy, possessing numerous treasuries (up to the point where he bestows these exquisite chariots and so forth upon his sons).

The first two lines of the verse explain the origin of the chariots. The "elder" is the Buddha who has realized [the truth]; "immensely wealthy" and so forth refer to the dharmas that have been realized.
Because his merits are as vast as the sands of the Ganges and cannot be fathomed by causes, they are called "great. The "house" contains the objects.

It is called a "repository" (*kośa*). This is a metaphor for the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍindriya*) and so forth possessing all phenomena (*sarvadharma*). A "treasury" (*kośa*) refers to the earth containing objects;

this is a metaphor for the various formations (*saṃskāra*) possessing all phenomena, as well as the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and bases (*āyatana*) possessing all phenomena. These are metaphorically termed "treasuries" because, in terms of their underlying principle, they are like the earth.

The factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*), the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*), and so forth comprise all dharmas; they are likened to a treasury (*kośa*). This is because, in terms of cultivation, they are like a house.
In reality, within each individual dharma, all practices and all dharmas are contained; and within each individual practice, all dharmas and all practices are contained.
Therefore, it is called a "treasury" because of its manifoldness and great wealth. The four lines concerning gold and silver clarify this.
The body of the chariot—composed of the four treasures of gold, silver, and so forth—is a metaphor for the one true dharma-realm and the four wisdoms of enlightenment.

The inclusion of all manner of jewels represents the myriad virtues and the inherent presence of all dharmas within the nature; these are collectively termed "treasures. To arise from this nature through cultivation is called "construction.
Because the sons are many and their practices are manifold, the chariots likewise become numerous; hence they are called "various. Each individual chariot-body is without exception lofty and vast.

It is called "Great. Furthermore, it must be demonstrated for one to know it. To initiate cultivation is called "creating"; by means of the nature (dharmatā), cultivation is subsumed, so that what was created returns to its original existence—this is the very substance of the chariot.
Regarding the section on "adornment" below, this clarifies the adornment of the chariot. The first four lines are explained as in the prose commentary.
Pearls and so forth represent the characteristics of the canopy and awning. The gates of compassion are not one, being like the mesh of a net.
Within each and every pore there is a single pearl, just as the various gates of compassion all accord with reality.

The extended passage merely mentions "hanging flower garlands," which serves simply to cause those who see them to rejoice. The present statement that they "hang down everywhere" clarifies that the various capacities of sentient beings are universally gladdened.
The phrase "various colors" is a metaphor for the places where transformations are manifested; though the responses provided may differ, [the underlying principle remains the same].
The phrase "surrounding on all sides" (*zōuzhā*) is a metaphor for the appropriateness of gathering beings, such that nothing is lacking.

The previous mention of "repeatedly spreading a soft mat" is here echoed by the two lines beginning with "soft and supple. The four lines beginning with "exquisite and superior" eulogize the two characters "repeatedly spread" (*chóngfū*).

"Silk cloth" (*zéngbò*) refers to fine fabrics; "cotton batting" (*kuàngxù*) refers to soft stuffing; "mats and rugs" (*yīnǔ*) refers to layered cushions. These serve as metaphors for mastery over the various *dhyānas*.
"Cloud-soft" (*mṛduka*): This means that the sublime transcends the coarse, like being covered by fine cotton cloth.

This indicates that the various *dhyāna*s of phenomena are all the true mark (*dharmatā*), unlike those of ordinary beings or the Lesser Vehicle which are mixed with various afflictions (*kleśa*). Therefore, it is said to be "fresh white, pure, and supremely sublime.

Regarding "possessing greatness," the verse [describes] the long prose as being "yoked with white oxen" and so forth; those who precede are called attendants (*purogama*), while those who follow behind are...
It says: "Following. By means of these two lines, the verses praise the chariots and the minds.

Bestowing magnificent chariots and so forth upon the sons manifests that the Buddha is all-encompassing toward all capacities without partiality, and provides universal salvation through the One Vehicle without self-interest.
(△) Four and a half lines praise the joy of obtaining the chariots.
At that time, the sons of the Buddha leaped for joy and exulted (up to the point of) playing and sporting with ease and without obstruction.

The first two phrases indicate that what they sought was slight, while what they obtained was profound. Previously like scorched sprouts, they had severed their own prospects and deemed themselves without share;
yet now, suddenly receiving this prediction, how could there be anything more joyful? Having attained the wondrous function of the One Vehicle, they do not remain stuck in a single [state].

The corners [of the world] are called "wandering through the four quarters," meaning one is not bound by any phenomena (*dharma*). This is called "joyful play" (*līlā*), characterized by sovereign freedom and unimpededness.
Regarding this playful engagement with things, there is neither preconceived intention nor compulsive necessity; one responds in harmony and meets circumstances as they arise.
There is never a mind of attachment or bondage. Toward all phenomena, one acts as if in playful sport; only then can one be truly free and self-sovereign.

There is no obstruction. The preceding verse concludes the section on analogies. △ The next twenty-four and a half lines constitute the second part, the application of the Dharma (the analogy to the teaching).
This is divided into two sections. The first four lines apply the analogy to the general theme.
"Tell Śāriputra: I am also like this... (up to) "...such fires blaze without ceasing.
The first two lines of the verse correspond to the titles and positions; the following two lines correspond to the names and practices, the meaning of which encompasses virtuous deeds.
The Tathāgata is the most honored among the seven kinds of expedient sages and saints, and the father of the nine kinds of worldly beings; the sense of "son" applies universally.

Therefore, because the worldly [realm] proceeds from the nine [afflictions], the meaning of "forming conditions" (*pratyaya*) is restricted; thus, the skillful means (*upāya*) are only seven. This verse combines the Elder [Vimalakīrti].

From "All those below" onwards, the verse combines the five destinies (*pañca-gati*) along with the thirty sons. The thirty are the "sons of conditions," while sentient beings are the "sons of causes.
Regarding the two lines on "deep attachment": if discussed in terms of the five destinies, it refers to attachment to the objects of the five desires. There is no... [text ends].
The supramundane wisdom-mind, according to the *Triṃśikā-vijñapti*, represents the great flourishing of the teachings during the period of universal penetration;

yet in the intermediate period, there was a decline and regression, such that the true knowledge and true wisdom of the One Vehicle were no longer present. The two lines concerning the "three realms" correspond to the description of the entire household; together with the "one gate," they form the whole.
Below the section on "various sufferings," the verse corresponds to the outbreak of fire: the first two lines provide the heading, the next two lines offer the explanation, and the final two...
Section on the Conclusion of the Verses. △ Second part, thirty and a half lines: Verses combining the individual metaphors. Divided into four sections. The first three lines:
Verses combining the elder’s perception of the fire.
"The Tathāgata has already departed from the burning house of the triple world" (up to) "only I alone am able to provide rescue and protection."
The Tathāgata has already transcended the four propositions; this verse summarizes his capacity for vision. To dwell in tranquil stillness is the state of being serene and free from entanglements.
It is precisely because he dwells in such silent seclusion that he is able to perceive the sons of the five turbidities. These are now the six propositions.
The verse above correlates with what is seen: namely, that all sentient beings are being scorched and boiled by birth, old age, and so forth.
Since the three realms of the past already belonged to the Buddha and the Buddha has already attained liberation, the present three realms belong to sentient beings;
these sentient beings must likewise attain liberation. Those who have already attained liberation ought to serve as fathers for those who have not yet attained it.
This portion should be considered as belonging to the son; hence it says, "among them," and so forth. "Calamity" refers to being burned and boiled by fire.
The two lines beginning with "Only I" summarize the sense of alarm and fear: "I" is the one capable of saving, while "the sons" are those to be saved.
The two characters "able to act" (*néng wéi*) correspond to the two characters "to pull out" (*yìng bá*). Since the three realms are already my possession, [the sentient beings...]
Furthermore, you are my son. How could it be that while the father dwells outside the realm, solitary and free from entanglements, he can bear to see his sons rushing about within the realm?
Since I am already dwelling in tranquil peace, how could I fold my hands and remain indifferent, bearing to see my sons suffer the calamities of burning and boiling?
Therefore, it is said that only this [wisdom] can provide rescue and protection. △ Second, four lines: A verse on the combined relinquishment.
The section on "Using a Couch" is divided into two parts. The first line of verse concerns the relinquishing of the couch.
Although he was instructed and exhorted, he did not accept [the teaching] because his deep attachment to and craving for various sensual desires were profound.
The first line indicates the intended course of action; it is the full disclosure to the sons, expressing his original intention.

The second line states that this was not possible, as indicated by the phrase "still delighting in and attached to [worldly things]," meaning that although the father loves his sons, the sons do not accord with the father's wishes—this refers to the Dharma being great while the capacity of the listeners is small.
The third and fourth lines explain the reasons for their lack of faith, while simultaneously containing the intent to cease his transformative activity. This is the formal verse.

The aforementioned [beings] have not yet escaped birth, old age, sickness, death, and the afflictions of sorrow and distress. △ Second, three lines: The verse describes the application of the vehicles;
by these skillful means, he preaches the Three Vehicles (up to) those who attain the state of a pratyekabuddha or non-retrogressive bodhisattvas.
"By these skillful means" refers to the preceding verse which speaks of employing wisdom and skillful means as appropriate.

"For their sake, he expounds the three vehicles" and below praises the rarity of the three carts and the turning of the Dharma wheel of the Four Truths in its three phases. "Knowing the suffering of the triple world" refers to knowing suffering and severing its origin.
The two lines beginning with "opening and revealing" refer to aspiring for cessation and practicing the path. "These sons" and below summarizes the preceding section.

This accords with what the sons desire. As for "definitive certainty" (*niyāma*), from the stage of the patience regarding the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-kṣānti*) upward is true definitive certainty.

This corresponds to the preceding verse, which describes the three vehicles rushing together to escape the burning house. Regarding the "three knowledges" (*trividyā*), the *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states:

through the knowledge of past lives (*pūrvanivāsajñāna*), one knows the suffering of the past and gives rise to great wearying detachment; through the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*), one knows the suffering of the future and gives rise to great wearying detachment; [through the knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows... the outflows...
One who is able to perform correct contemplation (*samyag-darśana*) and sever all afflictions (*kleśa*) is called "clear-sighted" (*vidyā*).

The [supernormal power of] the body has as its object merely craftsmanship; the divine ear merely hears sounds; and the knowledge of others' minds merely takes others' distinct thoughts as its object.

Because these three are thus, they are not called "clear-sight" but are termed "superknowledges" (*abhijñā*). There are two lines regarding those who have attained them, which praise the three types of persons for leaving their homes and realizing the fruits [of the path]. [The verse concerns] the *pratyekabuddha*.

Regarding "both Śrāvakas and Bodhisattvas" and "why they are called non-retrogressive": because Bodhisattvas of the provisional teaching possess a compassionate mind that seeks to deliver sentient beings, their resolve never falters;
this is not something determined by their formal stages or positions. △ Section 38: Verses on the Bestowal of the Great Chariots in Equal Measure.
This is divided into two parts: first, verses on the equal bestowal; second, verses on the resulting joy. The long prose section includes both the equal bestowal and the joy.
In the *Sūtra*, there is joy and the avoidance of calamity, along with the request for a chariot; whereas in the present verse, there is joy but no mention of avoiding calamity.

Thus, the presence and absence of these elements differ between the earlier and later parts of the scripture. Now, first [considering] the five lines, the verse should accord with the equal bestowal [of the chariot].
"Śāriputra, for the sake of sentient beings... [through] meditative concentration, wisdom, and the other dharmas of a Buddha.
For the sake of sentient beings, I bestow the Great Vehicle equally upon all my children, as expressed in the verse 'all are my sons,' and so forth, even unto their final nirvāṇa.

This refers to the equality of the vehicle, the equality of the mind, and so on. Regarding the phrase "this vehicle," the subsequent verses describe it as having but a single characteristic and a single essence.
It praises the supreme bliss. It unifies the essence of the vehicle. When mind and object are non-dual and phenomena and principle are mutually integrated, it is called "subtle and wondrous.
Because it severs the two kinds of death and purifies the delusions of the five stages of dwelling, it is called "supreme. It transcends the three worlds.
He is honored by the Buddhas of the ten directions; he perfectly accords with the Buddha-mind and delights the holy intention, which is why it is said that he "pleases and satisfies.
The phrase "All [beings]" below refers to causing them to revere the One Vehicle. The phrase "Immeasurable...

below is a retrospective verse praising my own immeasurable, boundless treasury of the Buddha-dharma, such as the powers, wisdoms, and fearlessnesses; this provides the reason for the presence of the chariot. △
The next three lines of verse summarize the joy.

"Attaining such a vehicle" means causing all the sons [of the Buddha] to obtain it; "until there is no other vehicle except for the Buddha’s skillful means" indicates that each has attained the joy of the Mahāyāna Dharma.
"Attaining such as this" and below clarify that they have each attained the joy of the Mahāyāna Dharma. "One's own attainment of the wisdom of the Middle Way is like the sun."
Out of compassion, they enter the cycle of birth and death as if it were night; because they constantly practice two dharmas, they are said to "sport.

These are what are called "constantly wandering alone" and "constantly walking alone. Because they extensively transform those of the three vehicles so that they all attain the One Vehicle, they are said to be "equal to all bodhisattvas.
This vehicle is perfect and sudden; from cause to fruit, it has no circuitous aspects, and thus it is said to be "direct. For these reasons...

The subsequent section concludes and clarifies [the meaning]. Because this taught One Vehicle lacks the three causes and conditions, when sought with careful scrutiny throughout the lands of the ten directions, it is found to be only one and not two;
it is merely called "other vehicles" except for the Buddha’s skillful means.
[Verse 45, line 16] The forty-five lines and a half of verse synthesize the absence of falsehood. This is divided into two parts. The first three lines and a half synthesize the non-falsity.
Section Heading.
[The Buddha] addressed Śāriputra: "You and all others... that which you ought to do now is solely the wisdom of the Buddha.

From "You and all others" onwards, he first establishes the father-son relationship to clarify his original intention to bestow [the Dharma] upon them. Since they are all my sons, it is only right that [the inheritance] be equal.
"...is equivalent to the Great [Vehicle]. 'You have spent many kalpas' below clarifies that the teaching of the three vehicles was intended to remove obstacles.
'Although I previously taught' below clarifies that since the obstacles have now been removed, I return to fulfilling my original intention by bestowing the Mahāyāna Dharma.

'Merely exhausting birth and death' refers only to exhausting the *paricchinna-bhava* (segmented existence); since the *pariṇāmi-bhava* (transformative existence) still remains, it is merely called 'nirvāṇa' as a provisional expression, though in reality there is no extinction."
The preceding statement regarding the removal of obstacles now clarifies that what ought to be done fulfills one's original intention, leading [beings] into the Mahāyāna.

△ Twenty-two lines. The verses confirm that this is not in vain. This section is divided into three parts. The first two lines explain that since all are equally children [of the Buddha], they should logically be treated with equality.

If there are bodhisattvas within this assembly—[extending] to the point where all those beings being transformed are themselves bodhisattvas—it means that if the capacity [of the recipient] is great, then the Dharma is likewise great;
this clarifies that there is no other vehicle. This is because they are situated within the assembly.
Listen with single-minded concentration to the Dharma of the One Vehicle’s true wisdom.

Although the Buddhas employ the provisional wisdom of skillful means to transform sentient beings, all such beings were originally Buddha-sons who formed karmic connections in the past; they likewise all equally possess the *tathāgatagarbha* (Buddha-nature).
Therefore, all are indeed Bodhisattvas. △ Second, seven lines: Explaining that those who cannot receive the Great [Vehicle] are taught the Three Vehicles.
"If a person of small wisdom is deeply attached to craving and desire... (until) merely being free from delusion is called liberation."
This means that the "Dharma of the Small" is originally the capacity for self-reduction. This clarifies the exclusion of the Buddha’s skillful means.

Because those with small faculties have heavy obstructions, they cannot receive the Great Dharma; therefore, as a skillful means, he opens the three vehicles to guide them. Because their wisdom is small, they cling to the profound; "affection" belongs to the mind, while "desire" belongs to the object.
These are the bitter fruits of the world's faculties and objects. For these two phrases, he elucidates the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*).

This means that for those who are attached to desire and take suffering to be pleasure, the Buddha taught the true nature of the One Vehicle as the Truth of Suffering (duḥkha-satya) of the Three Vehicles.
Among the Three Vehicles, the Śrāvaka is the least; furthermore, he takes the Truth of Suffering as his initial gateway.
"Suffering" (*duḥkha*) has the meaning of oppression. "Truth" (*satya*) means being real and not false; it refers to the cycle of birth and death within the six realms.
That sentient beings feel joy in their hearts accords with their original habitual tendencies. Originally they were weary of birth and death and sought *nirvāṇa* for themselves;

now, hearing of transcendence, they immediately accord with their past habits, and for this reason their hearts rejoice. "The Buddha said" and so forth refers to the reason why they have attained what was never before experienced.

Regarding "existence" (*sat*): it is because the Buddha taught that suffering is truly and without exception non-different [from its nature]. Being non-different means it is not contingent. The *Śāsanānuśāsana-sūtra* (The Teaching on the Bequeathed Instructions) says:

"The Buddha taught that the Truth of Suffering is truly suffering and not pleasure. Regarding the passage beginning with "If there are sentient beings," this clarifies the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*).

Its meaning is that which invites and brings about [suffering]; it is the cause of suffering, and is thus called the "root of suffering. This means that even if sentient beings of dull faculties know all...
They delight in this suffering, yet they do not even know the root of suffering; they remain deeply attached to the causes of suffering and cannot abandon them for even a moment.

Clinging to the view of a self (*ātman-dṛṣṭi*), he further explains through these skillful means that the cause of suffering does not have other phenomena as its basis, but rather has craving (*tṛṣṇā*) as its basis.
"If it is extinguished" below clarifies the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*); the two preceding lines [above] clarify the cessation of the origin of suffering (*samudaya-nirodha*).

The function [of this]. The final two lines clarify how the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*) derives its name. "Cessation" (*nirodha*) has the meaning of elimination through discernment (*pratisaṃkhyā*).

Building upon the preceding point that craving is the root of suffering, if there are sentient beings who, relying on the contemplation of the principle of quiescent cessation, eliminate craving through discernment, then the cause of suffering is exhausted and the various fruits of suffering have no basis to rely upon. This is what is meant by: "Once the skin is gone... [the rest follows].
If they remain, to what could the hair be attached? One should know that when it is said there is "no place of reliance," delusion still persists and the remaining fruits have not yet been realized.
Only upon reaching the fourth fruit, when the final three grades of afflictions of thought (*klesha*) are completely severed, does one begin to extinguish all suffering;

this is called the third Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*). By extinguishing the preceding truths of Suffering and its Origin, the partial true principle is revealed; through cessation, one attains realization.

It is "True" (satya), and is therefore called the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*). To explain the two phrases concerning "Cessation," this clarifies the Truth of the Path (*mārga-satya*). Its meaning is that of "penetration," for it is able to penetrate and reach true emptiness and *nirvāṇa*.
Briefly stated, it consists of morality, concentration, and wisdom; extensively, it comprises the seven categories of the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa-dharma*).
Free from all dualistic phrases, he again raises the point of attaining liberation. Accumulation (*saṃudaya*) is that which binds; suffering (*duḥkha*) is that which is bound.

To be free from this suffering and its accumulation is called attaining liberation. The passage "this person" below interrogates and explains the following of names: one attains liberation by contemplating the Truths (*satya*).

As for what kind of liberation this is, the passage "merely free from" below explains it: ignorance (*avidyā*) is already unreal, and the views and afflictions (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) arise further attached to ignorance.
Therefore, it is called "false and delusive. There are those who establish the Four Noble Truths; they merely eliminate these delusions and thus name this "liberation.

However, this refers to the provisional vehicle and its minor fruits, which liberate one from the *pudgala-bheda* (segmented existence) but do not liberate one from the *pariṇāma-śarīra* (transformative existence). Therefore, it is not ultimate mastery.

In terms of the Dharma, one has severed the afflictions of views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*); in terms of metaphor, one has emerged from the burning house and is sitting in the open air. △ Third, the three practices.
If, on the following day, he is capable [of doing so], one may return the large amount to him;
yet in truth, it is for the sake of attaining all-encompassing liberation and bringing peace and security to sentient beings that he appears in the world.

In fact, these two lines clarify the violation of reality. In terms of the Dharma, it means that delusion has not yet been severed regarding ignorance, and the fruit has not yet reached its ultimate limit at the stage of Buddhahood.
In terms of metaphor, it is like being on an open ground, yet not having obtained the great treasure of the white ox-cart.
"All liberated ones" refers to those who have exhausted the five stages of dwelling and forever extinguished the two types of death. Thus spoke the Buddha.

Below: The convergence of the three vehicles into one. This means that when the Buddha says a person has not yet attained *nirvāṇa*, he does not mean that they have failed to realize the Small Vehicle (*hīnayāna*) taught in the past;
rather, it means they have not yet attained the unsurpassed path of attaining Buddhahood through the true reality (*dharmatā*) of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*) as taught today.
If one can practice the "non-path," one will penetrate the Buddha-way and manifest it.
The three poisons do not conflict with the three wholesome roots; while manifesting the six obscurations, they do not lose the six perfections.

Pervading all realms of existence, they sever their causal conditions; manifesting nirvana, they do not sever saṃsāra. Taking what is not the Way to be the Way, it is beyond the reach of the two vehicles;
therefore, it is called the Unsurpassed Way. Even though transformation and rebirth still persist, this is not the minor fruit realized through Great Nirvāṇa.

This was not the Buddha’s original intention. Therefore, he said: "It is not my wish that such persons should attain the extinction of a small fruit, thereby abandoning the unsurpassed, great extinction spoken of today.
From the words "I am the Dharma King" onwards, he concludes that [his teaching] is not false.
As for the "Dharma King," he dwells neither in the world nor in nirvana; among all dharmas, he has attained great self-mastery.
Having realized that all dharmas are themselves the Buddha-dharma, there is no entry into it from which one does not attain realization.
Having attained mastery over the provisional and the ultimate teachings, he opens up the three to reveal the one; how could there be anything false in this?

What is called "mastery over the provisional and the ultimate" means that in the past, because the capacities of beings were small, he provisionally made the great into the small to bring peace and security to sentient beings, ensuring they would not destroy the Dharma or fall into lack of faith.
The insecurity of falling into the evil realms has now reached its point where the conditions for beings have ripened;

thus, the small becomes great, and peace follows sentient beings so that they may be free from the insecurity of self-deception and self-reproach. Therefore it is said: "To bring peace and security to sentient beings, he appears in the world.
The preceding verses on the long prose section are hereby concluded.

△ Second, there are sixty-five lines of verse. These supplementary verses praise the rarity of the Dharma and distinguish between the false and the authentic to encourage faith;

these two meanings were previously categorized as "Exhortation to Believe" and "Circulation. Because the three cycles [of teaching] were not yet concluded and the bestowal of prophecies was incomplete, this has now been revised.

Since these [themes] already exist within the "Chapter on the Buddhas' Exposition of the Dharma," they ought to appear in the "Parable" section as well. As they are absent from the prose, they are included here in the verse.

Supplement: A detailed study of the scriptural text reveals that its meaning is extremely pertinent. It is divided into two parts. The first nine and a half lines are verses praising the rarity of the Dharma.
The second, fifty-five and a half lines, are verses distinguishing the false and exhorting faith. Within the first part, there are five sections.
The first line is a verse summarizing how the Buddhas of the three periods of time have taught the Dharma of non-discrimination.
"Śāriputra, I have proclaimed this Dharma-seal for the sake of benefiting the world.
This Dharma-seal is the true reality (*bhūtatathatā*) of the One Vehicle. It is that which all Buddhas transmit from one to another, passing it mind-to-mind.
One who accords with this mind is, in that very moment, a Buddha. It is like the imperial seal passed down through generations in the world: whoever obtains this seal is a Son of Heaven."
This Dharma-seal is taught to reveal, cause awakening to, and lead all sentient beings into the Buddha-knowledge and Buddha-vision;

is this not indeed the non-conceptual Dharma? △ Second, two lines: A verse on the fact that the appearance of the Buddhas is remote and distant, and that the teaching of this Dharma is likewise difficult.
Wherever you travel, do not recklessly proclaim this Mind-Seal of the One Vehicle.
It is unfit for those who are not vessels to receive it; therefore, I warn you not to proclaim it recklessly.
Like the treasure of a Wheel-Turning King, it does not fall into the hands of others. I entrust you with this: wherever you go, you must not treat all cases as one and the same.
Obscure and indistinct. Do not speak of it at the wrong time; do not transmit it to those who lack the capacity. Is this not to say that preaching this Dharma is even more difficult?
△ Verses thirty-four to thirty-six praise the joy of hearing the Dharma and extolling it as being rarer than the udumbara flower.

"If there are those who hear [this] and rejoice, receive it upon their heads, and so forth... including the community of bhikṣus and all bodhisattvas. Regarding "If there are those who hear" and below:
this clarifies that hearing the Dharma and receiving it upon one's head is certainly not an ordinary teaching; it establishes one in non-retrogression. This is the benefit in the present life.
Regarding "If there are those who have faith" and below: this clarifies making offerings to all Buddhas because they have previously heard [the Dharma] in the past.

This is for the benefit [of others]. If there are those of inferior capacity who, upon hearing a single word of praise, believe what you have said and personally witness one assembly, this will bring them benefit in the future.
Because they hear this wondrous Dharma, are able to praise it, are able to believe and accept it, and are able to make offerings to it, they obtain benefits throughout the three periods of time.
Is this person not more rare than the *tánhuá* (the udumbara flower)? △ Section Four: One Line.
The preceding verse stated that it is difficult to hear the Dharma over many kalpas;
this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* is taught for those of profound wisdom, while those of shallow understanding, upon hearing it, become confused and fail to comprehend it.
This Great Dharma of the One Vehicle can only be believed and accepted by those endowed with profound wisdom. Those of ordinary and inferior faculties possess shallow insight and are deluded.
One’s own mind deludes one regarding the holy teachings; even after passing through incalculable kalpas, it is likewise difficult for anyone to hear this Dharma.

This single line also serves to conclude the preceding section and introduce the subsequent one. If one hears it and makes offerings, praises it, and accepts it with faith, such a person possesses profound wisdom and may be taught this—this concludes the superior case.
As for those of small intelligence who are deluded and fail to understand, they do not...
It may be spoken at an improper time; this opens the section below. △ Five: Three Lines. This verse praises those who can hear this Dharma:
"Such people are likewise rare.
From "All śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas" up to "following this sutra is not within the scope of their own wisdom," [it is shown that] it is not within the domain of their own knowledge.

This reveals that those of upright faith are difficult to find and are beyond the power of the followers of the Two Vehicles (śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas). Even Śāriputra, possessed of great wisdom, entered [the path] through faith;
how much more so for others? One should carefully consider the character "enter" (入); it is a passage intended to lead to understanding.

It is only through the various teachings and demonstrations provided by the Dharma that one can attain entry through faith. All other personal intellectual capacities are insufficient; one must simply trust the Buddha’s words and follow them.
According to this sutra, is it not also difficult for those who listen? Question: Previously it was said that "this Dharma cannot be shown;
its words and signs are quiescent," and it was granted that only Bodhisattvas with firm power of faith can understand it.
Yet here, it is further granted that Śāriputra enters through faith, while others merely follow along through faith. How, then, should one have faith?
Answer: The *Zhuan* says, "Heaven is that which is believed without words. It also says, "To have it within oneself is what constitutes faith (*śraddhā*).

Now, in wishing to explain the dharma of *nirvāṇa*, one should rely on the faith of non-speaking; one simply believes in oneself. This is precisely the beginning of the five stages of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.
That sūtra establishes the substance of faith through the immovable wisdom of self-nature (*svabhāva-acala-jñāna*). Faith...
One realizes that one's own mind is no different from the Buddha. By means of this wisdom, the Buddha is immovable; the myriad dharmas do not shift; cause and effect do not move;
ordinary beings and sages are non-dual; and mind and objects vanish into stillness. This seals and accords with the true mark (bhūtalakṣaṇa), such that all things are in harmony.
This is the "trust beyond words. One who can give rise to this trust suddenly overturns the karmic consciousness of ignorance, and through seeing, hearing, and awareness—
One knows that one shall achieve all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*). This refers to entering by means of faith and following in accordance with faith.
[Section Two: Fifty-five and a half lines. Verses distinguishing the false and exhorting to faith. Divided into two parts: first, thirty-six and a half lines of verses distinguishing the false;
second, nineteen lines of verses exhorting to faith. First, regarding the distinction of the false: this excludes [the counterfeit].
"Not the proper vessel. This means that, regarding the gate of great compassion, one must not preach it to evil persons.

The three lines of verse following "In the world of the five turbidities" are further divided into four parts; the first two lines enjoin that it not be preached to those who are not the proper vessels.
Furthermore, Śāriputra, do not speak to those who are arrogant and indolent (up to) those who cannot understand upon hearing it.
The arrogant are haughty and lack faith; the indolent are negligent and lack vigor; those who calculate a self have no penetration in knowledge and vision;
those attached to desire are addicted to worldly defilements. To such as these, even if they hear [the teaching], they will not realize it and will certainly give rise to...
To slander [the Dharma] will result in evil retribution later on. To explain this to such a person would not be without benefit; rather, it would cause them harm.
Out of great compassion and pity, one must not speak of it to them. (Section Two: Four and a half lines clarify the causes for the sin of slandering and destroying [the Dharma].)
If there are those who do not believe in and slander this sutra—listen now further to the retribution for their sins.
This sutra is the ultimate proclamation of the five periods; it gathers the definitive meanings (*nītārtha*) of the entire dispensation.

It comprehensively explains the seeds of the Buddha-nature of the three causes, opening up the knowledge and vision of sentient beings, which is itself the knowledge and vision of the Buddha. It reveals the seed of the true cause of Buddhahood and contemplates all phenomena.

Regarding the Buddha-seed as the cause of realization (*pariniṣpatti-hetu*): those who act in accordance with the true nature of reality—whether raising their hands or bowing their heads—all shall attain Buddhahood.
Regarding the Buddha-seed as the causal condition (*pratyaya-hetu*): the arrogant, being self-conceited and bound by the view of a self, do not believe in this path;

the shallow-minded, being preoccupied with worldly affairs, are unaware that such a path exists, and thus neither believe nor understand it. If one were to insist on explaining it to them, they would surely claim it is grandiose talk intended to deceive them. Thus they regard it...
Because of groundless rumors, they instead slander [the teaching], obstructing the profound transformation above and hindering others from hearing it below.
Consequently, the Way has no means to proceed, and people have no means to become sages; thus, the three causes for the Buddha-seed are severed and extinguished.
Or, upon hearing this sutra, their sorrow is manifested on their faces; upon seeing this sutra, hesitation sprouts in their hearts. If they do not yet believe—
Having become a malevolent obstacle, they frown and knit their brows; because they do not believe, they slander me.
Thus, harboring doubt and confusion, they seek day and night to extinguish my teaching and to destroy its followers, high and low alike. You should conclude by listening to the report in two parts.
From "If a Buddha" onwards, it further clarifies the causes of their transgressions, such as contempt, hatred, and jealousy—referring to those who see someone upholding this sutra.
They treat [the teaching] as lightly as dregs and as base as rubble; they loathe even hearing of it and envy those who surpass them.
They regard it as if it were thorns piercing their flesh and contemplate it as an enemy. Though they wish to eliminate it, they cannot; thus they harbor resentment in their hearts.
These two lines of this person summarize the heavy retribution for their offenses. △ Third, twenty-eight lines show the retribution for the crime of slandering [the teaching].
This is divided into three parts. The first one and a half lines clarify the retribution of the hells:
"When such a person’s life ends, they enter the Avīci Hell... (until) thus revolving through incalculable kalpas."
Due to the aforementioned causes such as slander and the like, one undergoes retribution in this hell. When this world-system is destroyed, one is reborn in another region;
thus being reborn again and again without end, for hundreds of thousands of kalpas one does not see the light of the sun or moon.

Throughout immeasurable lifetimes, one constantly suffers the agony of cauldrons and boiling pots. It is like a stone cast into water: it sinks easily and is difficult to bring back up; such is its inherent nature.
[End of section]. △ Twenty and a half lines clarify the retribution of animals.
From emerging from hell, one shall fall into the animal realm... (up to) "Because of slandering this sutra, one incurs such offenses."

As for the retribution for slandering the sutras: once the punishment in hell is completed, one will further become five kinds of animals—namely, the *kroṣṭu* (jackal), the wild dog (*śṛgāla*), the camel (*uṣṭra*), the donkey (*gardabha*), and the python (*ajagara*).
[The term *jì* refers to a head that is hairless; *tàn* refers to a mixture of black fur; and *ài* describes an appearance of stupidity and ignorance.
△ Thirty-sixth Section: Clarifying the Retribution for Humans.
If one obtains a human form but possesses dull faculties... [down to] ...because of slandering this sutra, one incurs such offenses.

"Constantly born in difficult circumstances" refers to the eight difficulties (*aṣṭāv akṣaṇāḥ*). One will never see a Buddha; this is the difficulty of being born when no Buddha is present or when a Buddha has already passed away.

One will never hear the Dharma; this is the difficulty of possessing worldly wisdom and eloquence. Being deaf, mute, blind, deaf-mute, or mute is the difficulty of the deaf, mute, blind, deaf-mute, and mute. One will constantly dwell in hell. Hell...
The difficulty of being in hell; the difficulty of being in other evil realms; the difficulty of being among hungry ghosts; the difficulty of being among animals such as donkeys and camels;

the difficulty of not seeing the Buddha or hearing the Dharma; and the difficulty of the Northern Continent (Uttarakuru)—the meaning of "long-lived" implies that such persons constantly dwell in the lower states.

This clarifies that those who slander the sutras always remain within the three miserable paths without respite. Because they emerge and enter [those states] from time to time, it is said they "constantly dwell" there; they do not depart for even a morning.
"Evening" is used as a metaphor for a house. Because one comes and goes from time to time, it is called a "place of activity.

As for the phrase "if one attains human status," this refers to emerging from the three miserable realms and subsequently becoming a human being. Furthermore, regarding those who take blindness, deafness, and so forth as their ornaments, they do not realize their own ugliness.
Regarding those who take dropsy and other such ailments as their clothing, they remain unaware that these afflictions are upon their bodies throughout their entire lives.
Their bodies are constantly debased; they further give rise to the three poisons. Those who slander the sutras originally lacked the causes for seeing the Buddha or hearing the Dharma.
They do not know to repent and reform, yet they remain attached to the view of self (*ātman-dṛṣṭi*) and receive this inferior form.

Others may loathe them, yet they feel no shame or embarrassment, but instead increase their anger. Humans and animals are of different species and ought not to mate in the wild, yet their lustful minds blaze up intensely.
To disregard the clouds and rain is to be possessed by greed; it increases anger and hatred; it inflames desire and delusion.

Possessing these three poisons, one will again fall into the three miserable realms. Thus, at the end of an eon, one is reborn once more, revolving through countless cycles—how could there ever be an end?
Furthermore, this entire category of retribution is experienced solely because of slandering this sutra. For this reason...
This sutra fulfills the world-transcending original intent [of the Buddha] and universally records the attainment of Buddhahood. It is the eye for devas and humans;
those who slander it will experience rebirth as blind animals or become blind and sightless in human form. This sutra can cure the mental illnesses of sentient beings and is a Great Physician King;
those who slander it apply remedies to treat illness only to further increase the disease of others. If one makes offerings to this sutra and so forth...
Then the six sense-faculties become pure; one’s gaze is majestic and resolute, and the entire body is light and clear. Those who slander it possess incomplete faculties;
when they are born as animals, their bodies constantly bear heavy burdens and are perpetually subjected to whips and beatings.

When they are born as humans, their lust is so intense that they do not distinguish between birds and beasts. This sutra is the chamber of compassion, the robe of patience, and the seat of the emptiness of dharmas.
For those who slander it, the evil realms become their garden and home; scabies and leprosy become their clothing; and pigs and dogs are their dwelling place.
Yet, by rejoicing in this sutra for even a single thought-moment, one’s breath will not be foul, the mouth will be free from disease, and the tongue likewise will be free from ailment.

Conversely, those who slander it will have breath that is constantly foul and faculties that are dull and dark. This sutra is the seal of the true reality (*dharmamudrā*) that brings about liberation and understanding.
Those who, in every thought-moment, remain in accord with the true nature (*dharmatā*), immediately attain the vision of the Buddha and the hearing of the Dharma;
whereas those who slander it sever the seeds of the Buddha and shall never again see the Buddha or hear the Dharma.

One should know that for those who praise it, the merit is immeasurable, while for those who revile it, they shall wander through the three miserable realms for kalpas. Whether praising or reviling, these do not arise apart from one's own single mind; for the mind is the source of all things.
The mold for form is the influence of the single mind; the good and evil of the three periods of existence are created solely by this one mind.
Just as objects produced from a mold are invariably similar to it, and just as a shadow follows a form, escaping nowhere regardless of where it may be, so it is with the mind.

Śāriputra habitually harbored doubts, regrets, and self-reproach, and was unwilling to settle for the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*). Yet, upon hearing for the first time that a *śrāvaka* could attain Buddhahood, he was able to accept it with faith.

As for why both chapters address the relationship between father and son: it is because the Buddha acts as a father to his disciples, bringing them to completion and fulfillment.
...the virtue [of the Buddha]. Therefore, he is compared to a father. The disciples have the merit of continuing and transmitting [the Buddha's teachings] to the Buddha;

The meaning is as follows: "Fifty" refers to the five fingers and the five paths of rebirth—first, the heavens; second, humans; third, animals; fourth, hungry ghosts; and fifth, hell-dwellers.

As his years have grown and he is further impoverished, he gradually wanders about until he encounters his way back to his native land.

while internal wisdom has already been awakened, externally one lacks the causal conditions and assistance. This is like galloping on horseback in a frantic rush.
"Appearance" (*mào*) is a metaphor for ordinary and inferior beings who, relying on body, sensation, mind, and phenomena, give rise to the four inverted views.

Furthermore, regarding the Dharma of the Four Truths, they seek the Right Path as if seeking food, and they seek the Path of Assistance as if seeking clothing. Moreover, they run to the four quarters to seek teachers and find the Way;

This serves to sustain the single mind, just as food satisfies hunger. That which is gradual is difficult to realize all at once.

Since realization is not sudden, one lacks fundamental wisdom; it is merely incidental. Therefore, it is said that one "meets" [the Way] by chance. As stated above, he "abandoned his father and fled."

The metaphor of "turning one's back on the true and pursuing the delusive" refers to wandering away from the source; the phrase "meeting [one's way] toward one’s native land" is a metaphor for returning from delusion to the true.

hence it is said, "meeting [one's way] toward one’s native land. This represents a child of delusion whose confusion has lightened and whose wisdom has matured; moved by past causes, they are able to encounter the Buddha.
He went out. △ Second, the father seeks his son and stops midway; this has two parts. First, seeking the son and not finding him:

Since it was said above that "the son abandoned his father and wandered abroad," it is here said that he "encountered [him] while heading toward his native land. Since it is said here that he "sought his son but could not find him," it is stated below that he "stayed overnight at a certain place."

It is accomplished. One movement and one pause create a sense of rhythmic cadence. Furthermore, the first two characters, "previously came" (先來), lead into the passage concerning skillful contemplation (*upāya-cintā*).

A single city.

Gold, silver, and so forth are collectively metaphors for such immeasurable and boundless qualities as the ten powers (*daśabala*), the four fearlessnesses (*caturvaiśāradya*), and other dharmas. To "fill with grain" refers to...
A granary is a vessel for storing things; it is called a "storehouse" (kū). To be full within is called "overflowing" (eō); to flow outward is called "spilling over" (yoku).
This metaphorically takes true wisdom (shochi) as the granary, which is filled with the food of the joy of the Dharma (hōki)—this is fulfillment within, which is self-benefit.

The beginning of the five stages is the stage of the ten faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*). Upon first entering the state of faith, one immediately gives rise to the mind that seeks both self-benefit and the benefit of others;

thus, the ten faiths are like servants. Furthermore, the various world-rulers each embody a single virtue to assist in the unfolding of the profound transformation, acting like those who serve as messengers and attendants.
As for the ministers, aides, officials, and commoners, they are those who support and listen to the teachings.
The "assembly" (zhòng) metaphorically represents the forty stages of the Dharma-body Mahāsattvas who have first entered the realm of the Buddha.

Just as all guests from within the realm are none other than subjects of the King, the ten abodes (daśabhūmi) are like the common people; they cultivate various dharmas and are driven about in manifold ways.

Thus, the ten practices (daśacaryā) are like the officials; their affairs and principles are somewhat deeper, and their offices are closer to the King's side. Thus, the ten dedications (daśapariṇāmanā) are like the assistants, supporting the Buddha’s conduct.

Transformation. Subduing demons and overcoming adversaries. Thus, the Ten Grounds (*daśabhūmi*) are like ministers. As for the countless elephants, horses, and so forth: the Ten Grounds are like the elephant vehicle;
