Riding upon the movement of things: in the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna), it is like a sheep riding upon the movement of things. That the immeasurable returns to the one is called "entry" (praveśa); that the one becomes the immeasurable is called "exit" (niṣkramaṇa).
Furthermore, employing [the power] for the benefit of others is "exit"; employing it for one's own practice is "entry.

The dharma of exiting benefits sentient beings as "tranquility" (śānti); the merit of transformation returning to oneself is "benefit" (artha). As this tranquility and growth extensively pervade the trichiliocosm, it is thus said: "Then..."

Regarding these various shortcomings: as for "regret and resentment," one regrets that former instructions were not profound enough, thereby causing the loss of original understanding;

Furthermore, these two characters [regret and resentment] are merely words of rhetorical embellishment. The Great Sage responds without deliberation, like the moon reflected in a hundred rivers—how could there be any regret?

"Regret exists indeed. From "Self-reflecting" (*jinen*) downward, the meaning of repentance (*ke*) is clarified. "The aged and infirm" (*rōkōsha*) signifies that the period of transformation is nearing its end;

What is called "feeling old" means that one's emotions have become thick and one’s thoughts are fixed on children and grandchildren. The Seal of the Mind is not transmitted;

the work of the ancient Buddhas is nearly extinguished—this is truly a cause for concern. However, this too is a word spoken in response to a specific capacity; in reality, it resides within the minds of sentient beings.

The preceding section concludes the analogy of the father and son losing sight of one another. II. The Analogy of the Father and Son Meeting. This has two parts: first, the son.

The immediate reference is to the elder of the burning house seeing the fire; the remote reference is to the verses on the *upāya* (expedient means) clarifying the five turbidities. [End of Section] First: The Son.
The father sees his son; the son sees his father. Regarding the first of these two encounters, there are four initial points concerning the circumstances of the father being seen.
World-Honored One, at that time, the impoverished son, wandering about in search of employment, happened by chance to arrive at his father’s house.

Continuing from the above, he eventually arrived at the city where his father resided and spoke. To hire oneself by the body is called "wage labor" (*yōng*); to take profit according to one's strength is called "rental" (*zhèn*).

To advance forward is called "extending" (*zhǎn*); to retreat backward is called "turning back" (*zhuǎn*). Through the aversion to suffering and the aspiration for joy, one seeks out the flavor of principle;
through gradual cultivation and accumulation, one ultimately achieves supramundane roots of goodness, just as the impoverished son hired himself out for goods.
This refers to successive transmission. By means of these roots of goodness, one is able to knock upon the gate of the Buddha’s house of compassion;

hence it is said that one “encounters” the father’s house. To meet unexpectedly is called “encountering” (yu). When the capacity (the stimulus) accords with the response (the resonance), it is called “arriving” (dao). The Dharma-body subsequent to the Way is called the “father.”
"Equanimity" (*upekṣā*) refers to unconditional compassion (*maitrī-karuṇā*). A city is a place where a multitude gathers; therefore, it is metaphorically compared to the "supreme assembly.

A house is the dwelling of a single individual; therefore, it is used as a metaphor for compassion. By means of these two types of capacities—the great and the small—beings simultaneously knock upon the house of the Tathāgata’s compassion.
Because there is a capacity of the great type, it is said below that they "see their father from afar. Because there is a capacity of the small type, it is said below... [text fragment].

It is said that he stood by the side of the gate. If there were only the small [body] and no large one, then the son would not have been able to see the Honored One’s special body (*vairocana-kāya*) in the passage below;

nor would the father have been able to say, "I now have something to entrust my wealth to. If there were only the large [body] and no small one, then the son would not have been standing by the side of the gate;
nor would he have been able to say, "This is not a place for me to labor as a hireling. Therefore, we know [that both bodies are present].

Within even minor acts of goodness, one secretly enters the gateway of the causes for the Mahāyāna; as these two capacities strike simultaneously, it is logically appropriate that they be fully present.
The scriptural text describes the journey from the country to the city, and from the city to the house, modeling the gradual progression to its ultimate limit.
△ Second, the place where he sees his father.
Standing by the side of the gate, he saw his father from afar.
"The two gates as a skillful means" refers to the two sides of the gate; the "pivot within the circle" is the correct vision facing the gate.

Because the Two Vehicles perceive only partial truth, they are said to be at the "side of the gate. Although they encounter the Buddha’s compassion, they have not yet entered the Buddha’s correct wisdom; their aspirations remain biased.

"Empty. This refers to those whose minds are set on the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna) and who possess only the eye of wisdom that perceives partial truth; they can only catch a glimpse of the Dharmakāya from the side.

Since the great capacity [for enlightenment] has only just begun to arise, the matter of being summoned by it remains distant; hence, it is said that "he sees him from afar. In the preceding dharma-explanation and parable, both clarify that the father first saw the son.

Here, the fact that the son first sees the father is explained as follows: from the perspective of the Buddha, it is his numinous wisdom that knows first; from the perspective of the sentient being, it is the maturation of their capacity that triggers the response. Thus, the son [sees the father].
The father’s seeing is the son’s seeing; the father’s seeing is the son’s seeing. Neither before nor after, it is inconceivable.
This is merely a mutual illustration. △ Third, the appearance of seeing the father.
Seated upon a lion throne with a jeweled footstool supporting his feet (up to: "adorned with various ornaments, his majestic virtue was exceptionally sublime").

This section correctly describes the time of the *Avataṃsaka*. As for "seated upon a lion throne," this refers to the magnificent Lion Throne of Celestial Radiance within the *Flower Treasury World* (*Ghanavyūha*).
The Buddha is the lion among men; therefore, he dwells upon this seat. Furthermore, the lion...
The lion’s roar is spoken fearlessly, signifying that the Buddha is endowed with the virtue of fearlessness. Regarding the jeweled footstool supporting his feet:

it is a stool of various jewels that supports his two feet. Here, meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) constitute the two feet, while the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) constitutes the stool;

for the meditative concentration and wisdom of non-arising depend upon the realm of true reality. Furthermore, the Buddha dwells as the sovereign of all practices, relying upon meditative concentration and wisdom.

This is the foundation [of all], namely, the adornment of the powers of samādhi and prajñā. Regarding those surrounded by the *brāhmaṇas* and others: *Brāhmaṇa* means one of pure conduct and noble integrity;
these are the Bodhisattvas of Equal Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*). *Kṣatriya* refers to the royal caste and nobility;
these are the Bodhisattvas from the first stage (*bhūmi*) up to the tenth stage. The *gṛhapati* (householder) practices the Way while remaining at home, purifying their...
Cao: "Rich but not noble" refers to the Bodhisattvas of the Thirty Minds. As stated in the Avataṃsaka Sūtra:
"In every flower is a buddha-field; in every leaf is a Śākyamuni.

The "merchants" are also very numerous; this refers to them. Those who adorn their bodies with pearls and the like are those who adorn the Dharma-body with the four kinds of necklaces:

The "officials and commoners" are the great bodhisattvas who practice the perfections of conduct, abiding, and faith for the sake of skillful means (upāya-pāramitā). The "white fly-whisk" is that which sweeps away [defilements].

Because it is neither partial nor stained, it is said that he holds a white whisk and stands in attendance at the left and right. The right side represents entering the wisdom of emptiness (*śūnyatā*), using the whisk to sweep away the dust of the four abidings (*catur-vāsa*).
The left side represents entering the wisdom of the conventional (*upāya*), using the whisk to sweep away the dust of the sands of saṃsāra. These two—

rather, he is one who wanders through birth and death, oppressed by manifold sufferings and pained by Great Compassion, and thus is constantly remembered.
Although I wish to rescue and deliver him, there is no opportunity for salvation, and thus it is said, "there is no way to see him. Now, however, there is one who can be delivered.

Because the capacity [of the recipient] has been activated, when he speaks, [the Dharma] suddenly comes of its own accord. Because his great compassion is profound, when he speaks, it is said that it perfectly accords with my wishes.

Regarding "my old age is greedy and stingy," this explains the reason why [the Dharma] accords with his wishes. "Old age" is the same as before, referring to being decrepit. Throughout kalpas of cultivation, I have realized Great Bodhi;
yet, seeing no one of great capacity, I did not recklessly bestow it upon others. Thus, the Dharma was never entrusted to anyone for the future.
As for such a person, from whom could they obtain liberation? Because there was no one capable of delivering them, it was said that they were "greedy and stingy.

Now, the opportunity has come of its own accord; there is no longer cause for such anxiety. Their long-held aspirations have been fulfilled according to their original intent; all former vows are now satisfied.
This is like a father who, seeing his lost son, recognizes him and desires to lead the impoverished child to wealth and abundance. Thus, the superior father and son meet.

[The previous section] concluded. △ Third, the parable of sending a messenger to pursue and entice. This corresponds to the "near" application of the parable—discarding the stool to use the carriage—and the "far" application of the Dharma—infringing upon the Great [Vehicle] to bestow it upon the Small [Vehicle].
It is divided into two parts: first, immediately dispatching an attendant to pursue; second, secretly dispatching two people to entice.
The first and second [sections] each have three parts. First, he is forcibly pursued and brought back. Regarding the proximate analogy, the elder thinks of rescuing him;
regarding the remote teaching, the Great Dharma is appropriately applied.
He immediately dispatches attendants to pursue him urgently and bring him back. (Up to: the messengers seize him even more urgently and forcibly drag him back.

This means that although their faculties are dull, they may for the time being satisfy their original aspirations; thus, the Buddha commanded the Great Beings to expound the Great Avataṃsaka Sūtra across seven locations and nine assemblies.
Regarding the phrase "sending aside others": if explained according to principle, wisdom is that which sends aside, and the teaching is that which is sent aside.

Principle is primary while the teaching is secondary. From the Buddha emerged the twelve divisions of the Mahāyāna teachings, intended to suit the capacities of sentient beings; yet there are those who lack the necessary capacity.

Because they do not accept [it], it is said that "those on the periphery are sent away. According to the *Śāstra*, the Buddha is the central figure and the bodhisattvas are those on the periphery—just as ministers, assistants, officials, and commoners [surround a sovereign].
This refers to the various great beings (mahāsattvas) expounding the Mahāyāna Dharma-gates:

for instance, Dharmamati expounds the Ten Abodes (*daśabhūmi*), Guṇakūṭa expounds the Ten Practices (*daśacaryā*), Vajradhvaja expounds the Ten Transferences (*daśapariṇāmanā*), and Vajragarbha expounds the Ten Grounds (*daśabhūmi*). All of these...

"By virtue of receiving the Buddha’s majestic power," it is said that "attendants were dispatched. To directly expound the perfect and sudden Great Teaching to those with inferior capacities is what is meant by "pursuing them urgently.
Because they possess the great seeds from the past, it is said they are "about to be brought back.

The Sūtra states, "All sentient beings are endowed with the marks of wisdom and virtue"—this is the meaning of the urgent pursuit. That "the messengers went to seize them" refers to the principle of elucidating the Mahāyāna.
The meaning is manifest and revealed, directly pointing to the one true Dharma-realm (*ekadharmadhātu*), enabling sentient beings to swiftly attain *bodhi*. As the Sūtra says:

"At the very moment of first generating the mind [of enlightenment], one encompasses the five stages and achieves equal and perfect awakening. This conveys the sense of rushing forward to seize [the goal]. It is like a great chariot whose speed is like the wind;
the Bodhisattva possesses innate supernatural power (*ṛddhibala*) and is further empowered by the Buddha. Thus, he is able to...
It causes sentient beings to swiftly enter Bodhi. Those of the Hīnayāna were slow to previously resolve upon the Great Mind; having neglected it for a long time, they no longer remember it.

Suddenly hearing the Great Teaching, they are startled because it contradicts their minds, and they are struck with awe because they do not recognize it; thus it is said that the impoverished son is "startled and awestruck. Regarding the phrase "crying out in lamentation and calling aloud":
within the Perfect and Sudden Teaching, afflictions are themselves Bodhi, and birth-and-death are themselves Nirvāṇa. [The Small Vehicle...]
Taking afflictions as one’s enemies and birth-and-death as the bonds of suffering, if one hears that "afflictions are themselves awakening," one cries out in protest;
if one hears that "birth-and-death is itself nirvana," one cries out in agony.
Their hearts were terrified and their mouths uttered complaints: "I originally did not seek greatness; why use this greatness to transform me?

Thus they said, "I have committed no offense; why am I being seized? As for those who were held with increasing urgency, these were the various Great Beings (Mahāsattvas) who, receiving the Buddha’s power and carrying out his mandate, directly expounded the Great Dharma.
Because there was no internal capacity within them while they were externally pressed by the great transformation, it is said that they were "forcibly dragged along."
As he was about to return, Aśoka demonstrated the punishments of a king to him; Jvalanāmukha demonstrated the torment of fire and so forth;
to those who clung to a self, he taught non-self; and to those who clung to permanence, he taught impermanence and so forth. Furthermore, it says: "If a person wishes to fully understand..."
"All Buddhas of the three periods of time should contemplate the nature of the dharma-realm: all things are created solely by the mind.

This means that [the father] grasped [his children] with urgency and force, pulling them toward him. In the parable, he speaks of matters of terror to fully inform his sons. 2. Grasping with Urgency and Fainting:
This refers proximately to the sons in the parable who would not listen, and distantly to sentient beings in the Dharma who lack the spiritual capacity (*anābhoga*).
At that time, the impoverished son thought to himself, "I am innocent," and so forth, until he became even more terrified, fainted, and fell prostrate on the ground.
Though he was forcibly seized against his will, he could not suddenly understand why; thus he thought to himself, "I am innocent.

For those of the Two Vehicles (śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas), they regard the afflictions of view and thought (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa* and *bhāvanā-kleśa*) as their crime, and the three realms as their place of imprisonment. Entering the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*) constitutes their birth, and emerging from that absorption constitutes their death.

This refers to death, specifically the death of transformation (*pariṇāmi-jarāmaraṇa*). Now, for those whose faculties are suited to severing the afflictions of views and thought (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*), one contemplates the nature of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) and emerges from meditative absorption to deliver sentient beings.
This is like being imprisoned without having committed a crime, yet being certain to die. Furthermore, "crime" refers to karma;
there are differences between mundane and supramundane, as well as good and evil. Sentient beings possess the crimes of the evil karmas of greed and hatred.

However, they possess the fault of lacking the wholesome karma of compassion; thus, they constantly follow the prison of birth and death within the three realms, able only to enter but unable to exit.
Bodhisattvas lack the faults of the unwholesome karma of greed and hatred, yet they possess the fault of the wholesome karma of compassion;
consequently, they manifest within the prison of birth and death in the three realms, being able both to enter and to exit. The followers of the Two Vehicles lack greed...
There is no fault in the karma of hatred and malice, nor any fault in the wholesome karma of compassion.

One who constantly loathes the prison of birth and death within the three realms can only exit it but cannot enter it. However, if one cultivates the Mahāyāna, one will certainly and perpetually enter the prison of birth and death within the three realms;
therefore, it is said that one is "taken captive. Without the great skillful means, one enters into birth and death; this is certain.
They will forever lose the life-force of the wisdom of the Three Vehicles; therefore, it is said that "this one will certainly die.

They form this thought themselves, yet not only do they fail to understand, they further increase their confusion; therefore, it is said that "they become even more terrified. Because those of small intelligence cannot comprehend the Great Teaching when it is forcefully presented, it is said that "they faint.
They immediately give rise to slander and will surely fall into the three miserable realms; therefore, it is said that "they fall prostrate to the ground," as in the following analogy.
When the human mind is feverish and deluded, one does not even know life and death; how then could one perceive forms and sounds?
Consequently, the fish thrash its jaws and hide its scales, closing off sight and hearing so that the eyes see nothing and the ears hear nothing. △ Third, the temporary release and attainment of joy.

This includes both the proximate metaphor of the [son] running and playing while looking for his father, and the remote teaching of the Tathāgata’s cessation of his transformative activity. This is divided into four parts. First, the compassion [of the father].
The life of ignorance is released.
The father saw him from afar and spoke to the messenger, saying: "[... let him attain awakening and do not speak with him again.

Because the Small Vehicle is distant from the Great Vehicle, it is called "far. He is a son established through conditions; therefore, he is called "seen. This refers to his spiritual capacity and aspiration.
This is to be near the small while remaining distant from the great. Regarding those who speak as messengers:

in terms of principle (*li*), since wisdom is the basis for expounding the teaching, when wisdom perceives a lack of spiritual capacity (*mūka*), the Great Teaching should appropriately cease. In terms of phenomena (*shi*), he entrusts the matter to the various Bodhisattvas, saying they need not manifest their honored and wondrous bodies to be seen by those of the Two Vehicles.
As the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* says: "Withdraw your bodily fragrance so that it does not cause those others..."
Sentient beings give rise to delusions and attachments. Furthermore, it is Samantabhadra’s intention to enter the Sahā world and contract his body to make it small.
This means that for those who do not require this person [to appear], he need not insist on preaching the One Vehicle (Ekayāna), which is a teaching difficult to believe.

Since they lack the great capacity (mahā-indriya), if he were to manifest a superior body and preach the Mahāyāna Dharma, he would fear it might damage their roots of goodness; therefore, he says "do not."
To forcibly bring [the practitioner] forward is an act of indulgent compassion for those who are deluded. Sprinkling cold water on the face indicates that one recognizes their limited aspirations;

it is appropriate to use the water of the principle of severance through the "ash" of the Hīnayāna to remove the heat of the afflictions (*kleśa*) from the face of views and thoughts, and to turn away from the cycle of birth and death, which is called "aversion."
"Facing toward Nirvana" means that because there are those whose faculties turn their backs on saṃsāra and face toward Nirvana, one causes them to attain awakening.
To cause them to awaken, the Lesser Teaching (Hīnayāna) is opened up to accommodate those of lesser faculties, enabling them to leave behind their distress and realize the Four Noble Truths.
"Do not speak with them again" means that one must certainly cease the teaching of the Mahāyāna for them. △ Second, the inquiry into the intent of the release.
Why is this? It is because the father knows his son [and so forth], yet he does not speak to others, saying, "This is my son.

This is for the sake of transforming him through the subtle and profound. The resolve of those of the Two Vehicles is inferior; they fear the Great Dharma and are content with their limited aspirations.

Thus, it suppresses the Buddha’s original intention. Therefore, it is said that the father knows the son’s inferiority, while [the son] himself possesses the wealth of the Dharma and the myriad virtues. There is none...
They are not fully endowed. Because the wisdom of those of the Two Vehicles is shallow and their merit is meager, they find it difficult to believe in this Great Dharma;

hence the words "knowing for themselves" and so forth. One has inferior aspirations, while the other is of noble and high status. Knowing themselves and knowing others, [the Buddha] therefore ceases his transformative activity.
"Knowing with certainty that he is my son" means knowing with certainty that he was a son who, in the past, under twenty trillion Buddhas, gave rise to the Great Resolve. And...

By means of skillful means (*upāya*) and so forth, within the former teachings of the Hīnayāna, he spoke according to the intentions of others (*parārtha-vāk*), using skillful means to provide protection;

thus he was called a *śrāvaka*, and it was not said that he spoke according to his own intentions (*svārtha-vāk*) as a *bodhisattva*. Because this was not taught in the former teachings, it is said that "he did not speak to others," and so on.
△ Third, causing them to correctly release [the burden].
The messenger said to him, "I now release you; go wherever you please.

By saying, "I now release you," he knew that the great capacity [of the recipient] was weak. By saying, "go wherever you please," he knew that the small degree of goodness [in the recipient] was strong.
For these two reasons, he ceased his great transformation. △ Fourth, joyfully going to poor neighborhoods.
The impoverished son rejoiced at having attained what he had never experienced before; rising from the ground, he went to a poor neighborhood to seek food and clothing.

This is a metaphor for following the capacities of those with inferior faculties. Desiring to conceal the superior and manifest the inferior, [the Buddha] accords with their preferences and fulfills their original wishes;
thus, he conceals the reality to open up the provisional. Because they are not yet pressed by the Great Teaching, they rejoice as they cast themselves toward their own inclinations.

Because there is no great sin of slander, one may escape the three miserable realms; thus it is said, "from the ground. Because even small goodness can lead to birth [in higher realms], it is said, "to rise.

Furthermore, previously, when one was directed toward the Great Dharma, one became bewildered and unable to understand, lying upon the ground of ignorance (*avidyā*). Now, by being accommodated with the Small [Vehicle], one may attain awakening;
hence it is said, "rising from the ground. Regarding the two phrases "going" and "arriving," they refer only to the principle of emptiness (*śūnyatā*), which does not encompass the myriad phenomena.

Therefore, it is called a "poor neighborhood. Among the Four Noble Truths, because they seek the clothing of the Path of Cultivation and the food of the Path of Seeing, they rely on the dharmas favored by the Two Vehicles as provisions for entering the Path; this is like casting away a bright pearl to seek out fish eyes.
The King immediately dispatched attendants to pursue him to the end. △ Second, he secretly dispatched two men to entice him.

Now, the metaphors of "pursuing" and "enticing" correspond to the analogy of leaving the house on fire, abandoning the small stools and taking up the carts. The skillful means involve encroaching upon the great to bestow the small.

The previous section corresponds to "abandoning the stools," as the Great Dharma was deemed unsuitable for him. This present section should correspond to "taking up the carts," whereby the three vehicles are obtained according to what is appropriate. (Text)
It is divided into four parts. First, the gradual inducement to remove filth; second, leading [the sons] up and presenting the three carts as a provisional means.
At that time, the elder, wishing to entice his sons, [proceeds until] the father sees his sons and pities and marvels at them.
The following section correctly clarifies the period at the Deer Park. Regarding the phrase "intending to": this expresses a state that is imminent but not yet realized.

Since the great transformation has ceased, it would be unacceptable to abandon [beings] in isolation; thus, intending to establish skillful means, he says "intending to. In the analogy, this refers to the point when skillful means are about to be established.
Within the Dharma, he reflects upon the power of the skillful means practiced by the Buddhas of the past; this constitutes the external skillful means.
As for "secretly dispatching two people": the previous dispatching of an attendant represents the One True Truth, the One Great Vehicle, and the one person who is a Bodhisattva.
Now, let us clarify the meaning of "expedient means" (*upāya*). To conceal the ultimate reality is "esoteric" (*guhya*); to point toward the partial truth is "dispelling.

In terms of the teachings, to conceal the *pūrṇa-akṣara* (full syllables) is "esoteric"; to point toward the *ardha-akṣara* (half-syllables) is "dispelling. In terms of persons, when a Bodhisattva manifests birth within the triple world, their internal secrecy is "esoteric," while their external manifestation is "dispelling.
Regarding these two types of persons, the four sons have already attained equal realization and each governs his own domain; they do not involve themselves with Bodhisattvas. As for the Dharma:
Regarding the Four Noble Truths as causes and conditions, in principle there are the conventional and the ultimate; in terms of persons, these refer to the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas.

Within the teachings of the Two Vehicles, one does not cultivate the primary and secondary marks (lakṣaṇa-vyañjana); they speak only of suffering, emptiness, non-self, impurity, and so forth—this refers to the "withered and haggard" form and color.
Internally fearing impermanence is called "withered" (jiao); externally encountering the eight sufferings is called "haggard" (cuì). They lack the ten powers and the fearlessnesses.
For these reasons, it is said that they lack majestic power (*an-īśvaratva*).

This means that while the Bodhisattvas conceal within their own being the power of sovereign spiritual majesty (*vibhūti-prabhāva*), they outwardly manifest the appearance of withered wood and cold ashes. As the subsequent text states:

"Knowing that the multitude delights in inferior dharmas and fears great wisdom, the Bodhisattvas therefore assume the forms of Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and so forth, employing the 'sameness of purpose' (*samāna-kārya*) to gather and transform them; they conceal the ultimate and provisionally manifest the expedient."
Furthermore, you should speak slowly because the principles elucidated by the Mahāyāna are true and real; thus it says, "run swiftly to seize him.

Because the principles elucidated by the Hinayāna are circuitous and obscure, it says, "speak slowly. If one were to confront them with direct words, they would surely react with violence and refuse to accept [the teaching].
This means that one should use gentle words to guide them, ensuring they do not become frightened upon hearing the teaching.
This is an instruction that one should gradually entice them with the "lesser Dharma" (hīnayāna) rather than attempting to draw them back immediately by means of the Mahāyāna Dharma.

Just as when one meets a practitioner today, one must receive them with a gracious countenance and smiling words so that their heart will rejoice and they will accept the transformation; if one were instead to use their true [form], [they would be terrified].

Tongs and hammers must be discarded and attached elsewhere. Within this context, there are phrases such as "secretly dispatched to entice and lead," "speaking slowly," "immediately dispatched to pursue urgently," and "swiftly seize.
Regarding the term "doubling" (*bei*) used here, "doubling" means adding one more time (i.e., doubling).

"Direct" refers to wages. It means that if you go to a poor neighborhood to work for hire in order to seek food and clothing, there is a place where you may labor, and the pay shall be double that of other places.
The Path of Seeing and the Path of Cultivation are the places where one performs the severing of views and afflictions.
Previously, by practicing the five precepts and ten wholesome deeds, one merely escaped the three miserable realms; now, one practices the four... [The text continues].
The Truths and their causal conditions enable one to transcend the triple world; this constitutes the first doubling.

Furthermore, while the six practices of the non-Buddhists can only suppress afflictions, practicing the Four Truths now enables one to sever afflictions and attain Nirvana; this constitutes the second doubling.

If one grants that [the teaching] will be received in the future, there are two possibilities: if there is the capacity (*indriya*), it is granted, and thus the teaching is established for them to practice;

if there is no capacity, it is not granted, and thus the teaching is not established. If one says "desire" and so forth—should they ask what it is they should practice—the Buddha immediately delivers them by means of the Dharma they delight in as poor beings, causing them to eliminate the afflictions of views and thought (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa* and *bhāvanā-kleśa*) and realize the attainment of *nirvāṇa*. One must not [further]...

He informs them by means of [teachings such as] the purification of Buddha-lands. To speak of "removing filth" refers to severing the afflictions (*kleśa*). The delusions and karma of the afflictions defile the ground of the mind;

those of the Two Vehicles employ various contemplations to remove them. Regarding the phrase "the two persons working together": in principle, this refers to wisdom and the Truth mutually supporting one another;

in terms of persons, it refers to the person of provisional means (*upāya*) and the person of reality practicing together, thereby gathering and guiding others through the sameness of purpose (*samānārthatā*).
This refers to human beings. For a bodhisattva, afflictions and nirvana do not obstruct one another; therefore, they may be practiced together.

Once these two messengers have been obtained, one immediately seeks the impoverished son; this is the bodhisattva’s practice of following the teachings with diligence. Having ascertained that there is the capacity [to receive the teaching], [he acts accordingly].
Therefore, it is said that he has already attained [the goal]. "To relate in full" means to inform him with the words of the Tathāgata’s exhortation;
this is to follow the Buddha and propagate his transformation of beings. The aforementioned matter refers to the employment for the task of removing filth.

He first takes up the remover of filth because those of the Two Vehicles (śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha) aspire to the fruit while practicing the cause; thus, they first inquire about the price. Therefore, it is called "taking up first. Within the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths—
"First the fruit, then the cause" means first taking the price for the path and cessation, and only later removing the filth of suffering and its origin.
Regarding "seeing the son and feeling pity and wonder": one feels pity because he has taken up the state of an Arhat, and wonder because he does not seek the Buddha-way;
what he loses is great, while what he gains is meager—therefore, one feels pity and wonder. Question: Since you feel pity and wonder, why do you secretly send someone to instruct him?

He went to fetch the fruit. The answer was: "I have searched for him along the way, but he has not returned; the matter must be handled with secrecy. Although he had been instructed to remove the filth, this was not the Buddha’s original intention.

Desiring to entrust [the teaching] through explicit words, he first showed compassion and then expressed his concern. △ Second, on another day, seeing him from afar, he understood that the elder’s superior mind accorded with his son’s prior intention.
Furthermore, on another day, while [the son] was at the window, he saw the appearance of a dung-removal vessel and felt a sense of dread.
It was in response to the *Avataṃsaka* that he preached the Lesser Teaching; thus it is said, "on another day.

Because the son stood by the gate and beheld his father’s majestic power and body adorned with immeasurable marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*), he conceived a thought of terror. Consequently, he withdrew from the Great Vehicle and turned toward the Lesser. Thus says the Buddha.
To see the child’s body from afar through the window is to employ provisional wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*) to observe the capacities of beings and provide instruction accordingly;

it is not the true wisdom (*tattva-jñāna*) of the direct gate. Because it is distant from the Mahāyāna, it is called "afar. Because one knows that he had previously planted great [seeds], it is called "seeing the child.
That the flavor of the Dharma is insufficient is called "emaciated"; that merit and virtue are incomplete is called "wasted and haggard. It is like excrement and soil.

The "dust" is a metaphor for the afflictions of views (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*); the "fine dust" is a metaphor for the afflictions of thought (*bhāvanā-kleśa*), because views are coarse while thoughts are subtle.
"Removing the upper garment" is a metaphor for concealing the infinite merits of the *saṃbhoga-kāya*, such as the forty-two stages, the precepts, meditative concentration, wisdom, and *dhāraṇīs*.
The "silken upper garment" of the patience of cessation (*śānti-akṣānti*) and the "ornaments" of the major and minor marks and the ocean of signs represent the attire and garments.
If he were to appear in his full splendor, his sons would be struck with fear; thus, the two vehicles are unfit to behold these marks and signs of excellence.

Therefore, he conceals his form as the ten-thousand-fathom Śākyamuni, for such a supreme and extraordinary body would be difficult for his sons to endure. Furthermore, by donning the appearance of an ordinary being, he manifests the form of a six-foot-tall aged bhikṣu.
He wears the patience toward beings and the patience toward dharmas as coarse and tattered garments, and allows dust and dirt to cover his body.

This refers to the existing afflictions (*kleśa*), which are conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and outflowing (*āsrava*). The left hand is a metaphor for the Real (*tattva*), which is "contrary" [to worldly ways].
The right hand is a metaphor for Expedient Means (*upāya*), which is "conforming" [to worldly needs]. The application of Expedient Means conforms to what is appropriate;

by means of these expedient dharmas, one severs the fetters (*saṃyojana*) and attains Buddhahood oneself, and further employs these expedient dharmas to transform others, removing the filth of sentient beings' views and discursive thought (*dṛṣṭi-vikalpa*). Therefore, it is said that the right hand holds [the vessel], and so forth, describing its form.
"Having something to fear" means that his appearance is similar [to theirs]. It demonstrates that he shares with those of the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna) the dread of birth and death (*saṃsāra*).
This is like the retributions of the cold wind, the horse-barley, and so forth. This is the Tathāgata’s act of humbling his dignity to conform to the lowly, manifesting among human beings;

he likewise disparages birth and death while praising *nirvāṇa*. △ Third, personally exhorting them to set their minds at ease. This section takes up the previous praise of the three vehicles and is divided into three parts.
First, the exhortation to practice the turning [of the wheel]:
He spoke to the laborers, saying, "You must work diligently and not be indolent; by this skillful means, you shall draw near to his son.
From this point downward is the threefold turning of the Wheel of the Four Noble Truths, wherein there arise the distinct designations of Dharma and Saṃgha. He spoke...
"O practitioners, these Four Noble Truths are praised by the Sages; they transcend birth and death, leading to mastery and freedom from bondage.
You should diligently cultivate them. Furthermore, he admonished those who were indolent:
"There is not a single dharma that arises from laziness and sloth; there is not a single dharma that arises from self-indulgence and negligence. Previously...
"This refers to the instruction: 'One should diligently cultivate vigor.

As for 'attaining proximity through skillful means,' it means that by employing various skillful expedients, the father and son are finally able to see one another, and the son no longer gives rise to doubt or fear.
△ Second, showing the transformation of signs.
Later, he spoke again, saying: "Ho! Man! (up to: ... I am like your father; do not worry further. The address "Ho! Man!
is intended to demonstrate the characteristics of the Four Noble Truths. First, he calls out sternly;
this Dharma is like a vajra-sword that awakens the spirit and resolve of a great man (*mahāpuruṣa*) and severs the fetters of the twenty-five states of existence. Therefore...
First, "dō" (咄) is not a sound of scolding or shouting; rather, it is a word used for calling out to and consoling someone.
For example, if one has affection for a person, instead of speaking those words of affection in front of others, one might go to a secluded place and say in a low voice, "Dō, man!
Do not leave. Because one wishes for that person to always act [in a certain way], one calls out "dō" to console them. You should always...
"Practice it and do not depart": the first phrase exhorts one to constantly cultivate this Dharma; the second phrase further warns against studying the various non-Buddhist paths (*tīrthika*).
"Increasing the price" refers to advancing from the stage of Stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*) up to the four fruits of enlightenment. "The category of all that is required," and so forth.

This demonstrates the characteristics of the primary and auxiliary practices. The basin and vessels collectively symbolize the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*saptatriṃśad-bodhipākṣika-dharmas*).

The rice and flour specifically symbolize the provisions for the three trainings of the outflows-free path (*anāsrava-śikṣā*). The salt and vinegar that harmonize the flavor represent the virtues of the six points of harmony and the five moral virtues.
Regarding all phenomena, he maintains perfect balance and equanimity. As for the aged attendants, he secretly dispatches them so that they may practice and realize the truth together with him.
He provides whatever is needed to those who require it, meaning that within the auxiliary dharmas of their cultivation, should there be anything unclear, one must not harbor doubts or difficulties;
rather, one should inquire of the elder practitioners among one's peers, who will then provide instruction on each point. This is what is meant by "there being... [the following].
"To inquire with doubt" means to seek counsel. "Those who delight in self-comfort" illustrates the meaning of the Truth of the Path (*mārga-satya*);
it is as if saying, "This is the nature of the path that can be cultivated; you all should settle your minds upon this path and practice it, and you will immediately attain mastery and contentment.
"I am like your father" illustrates the meaning of the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*). This is a single phrase whose wording is echoed [in the following]. As it says:
"It is said that this is the cessation (*nirodha*) which can be realized. You should all settle your minds well and practice this path;

you will certainly realize this cessation. Because I have already realized it, I am like a father; because you shall realize it, you are like sons. Below. Since the three turnings [of the Wheel of Dharma], all those who delight in the Lesser Vehicle have been transformed by this Dharma, just like children born from the Buddha’s own mouth.

Regarding this Dharma-gate, he felt joy and delight, exclaiming, "How fortunate to have met with such a sublime encounter! Yet, although he encountered this Dharma, he lacked the mind that delights in the Great;

thus it is said that he considered himself a mere laborer. If one attains a small fruit and, weary of the small, seeks the Great, and the capacity for the Mahāyāna is awakened, the Buddha immediately bestows the Great Dharma upon them.

[He] set out. Because this [state] is great and without pleasure, the Buddha causes him to eliminate the "excrement" of the ten latent afflictions (*anuśaya*) within the teachings of the Two Vehicles.

Regarding the "twenty years": one unimpeded path (*ānantarya-mārga*) and one liberation path (*vimukti-mārga*) eliminate the afflictions of wrong views; nine unimpeded paths and nine liberation paths eliminate the afflictions of cultivation. Therefore, it is said to be "twenty years.
This phrase "twenty years" is connected to the three subsequent locations where it is mentioned; such is the intended meaning.

The four sons describe their own state—fearing the Great and delighting in the Small, lingering in the provisional while being deluded regarding the ultimate, and refusing the transformation of the Great—with full detail.

This is because their faculties and aspirations are narrow and inferior. The parable of sending messengers to pursue and entice them is hereby concluded. △ Fourth, the Parable of Entrusting the Family Estate.

This encompasses, in the near sense, the granting of the great chariots from within the burning house, and in the remote sense, the manifestation of the ultimate truth within the Dharma. It is divided into two parts: first, the taking over of the family estate;
second, the entrustment of the family estate. Within the first part, there are again two sections: first, the mutual trust based on the initial signs; second, the command to take over.
Regarding the household affairs, there are again two initial points. First, it clarifies mutual trust in essence.
After this point, because their mental states mutually trust one another in essence, they enter and exit [the assembly] without difficulty.

This is precisely the period of receiving the Vaipulya (fangděng) teachings; following the period at the Deer Park, it is indeed the Vaipulya. Their mental states mutually trust one another in essence.

This refers to father and son mutually understanding, trusting, and complying with one another. It means that since the price of *nirvāṇa* was obtained within the teachings of the *Āgamas*, this was not false;

The Great [Vehicle] does not fear; even when retreating, it does not stagnate in the Small, nor is it deluded. It enters and exits the Small and the Great without doubt or difficulty.

Nevertheless, their place of abiding remains as it was before.

Firmly uphold the principle of non-action (*wuwei*). Do not move even a single step from where you practiced in years past.

It is like a destitute son who, though his heart is mutually trusted by both [the father and himself], does not find it difficult to enter or exit [the house]; yet in reality, he has not yet taken up residence in his father's home, but still considers himself a hired laborer.

World-Honored One, at that time the elder was ill and knew for himself that he would not live much longer.

Because it is filled within and overflows without, it is said to be "overflowing. As for the quantity contained therein, this refers to the teaching of Prajñāpāramitā.
There are thus two gates: the extensive and the concise. The concise is brief; the extensive is detailed. One may take [the teaching] for one's own benefit, or give it for the benefit of others.

Lost. Second, regarding the principle: this is precisely your own dharma, which you shall employ at a later time. You all must apply yourselves with focused attention and realize this principle through direct experience;

He summoned his son and assembled his kinsmen, kings, ministers, kṣatriyas, and householders, all of whom had gathered.

As for his sons, Mañjuśrī, Samantabhadra, and other great beings who act as shadows and echoes serve as his kinsmen. His emanations gather like clouds, each presiding over a region as a king.

Bodhisattvas of the ten stages (*bhūmi*), being of the lineage of Dharma-kings, serve as Kṣatriyas. Those on the ten abodes (*vihāra*) and the stages of practice (*caryā-pratipatti*) dwell there, having received transformation from the Buddha.
"Those who have all gathered" refers to the fourfold assembly and the eight classes of beings surrounding the World-Honored One. △ Third, the conclusion of the meeting between father and son:
that is, he himself declared, "Gentlemen, you should know... (up to) this is truly my son, and I am truly his father."

"Self-proclaimed" refers to the spontaneous pronouncements made upon emerging from meditative concentration without being questioned. "You all should know" means that I am now speaking this among the great assembly of devas and humans.
Regarding the previous passage, "In the past, I once taught and transformed you, causing you to be born into my Dharma," this is here expressed as:

"From me you have gained understanding; you are my offspring. As for 'one who abandoned me in such-and-such a city,' this refers to one who left his father and ran away.

Having attained meditative concentration, they later fall back and transmigrate through the six realms; hence the phrase "ling-ping" and so forth. "Ling-ping" describes the manner of walking with an unsteady gait.

This serves to confirm the definitive relationship between father and son. "The Original City" refers to the city situated at the center mentioned previously;
because the *Avataṃsaka* is the fundamental One Vehicle, it is called the "Original City. From the *Āgamas* onward, various skillful means have been employed to guide [beings] gradually and well.
He constantly kept in mind the capacity of his Mahāyāna son; thus it is said that he harbored anxiety while searching for him.

Suddenly, within these two lines, at this very day in the assembly of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, the capacity for the Mahāyāna was awakened and he received the prediction of enlightenment. As for "the true son and the true father": [this refers to the realization of their mutual identity].
Judging by their innate nature determines who is father and son. Father and son transmit the same physical essence; their innate natures are no different.

The śrāvakas become Buddhas; all do so through the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata, just as clarified butter (ghṛta) is extracted from matured cream (sarpis).
Therefore, it is said that Great Nirvāṇa arises from the Mahāprajñāpāramitā; this is the fifth flavor. These four disciples have deeply grasped the Buddha’s intent;
one metaphor fully encompasses the teachings of the three periods and five flavors, exhausting the sequence from beginning to end with ultimate precision.
In detail: this is why the *Praise of the Lower Grades* states, "Excellent, Kāśyapa! You have well explained the merits of the Tathāgata and so forth.
