From beginning to end, he has only expounded the *Avataṃsaka*; even to this day, he still preaches the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*. We must truly believe this and forget [all doubts].
"Speech and silence are realized; the assembly is solemn and unified—this is indeed to be hoped for. △ Second, the correspondence of the Dharma. There were four metaphors previously;
now, taking the meaning from each section, they are briefly correlated. It is not necessary to adhere strictly to the pairings. First, this corresponds to the father and son losing one another.
The World-Honored One, the great wealthy elder, is the Tathāgata; we are all like the sons of the Buddha.
The Tathāgata corresponds to the father; "like" corresponds to the son. There are two meanings to this "likeness": first, taking those of great capacity as sons.

Previously they had not yet fled, but since they do not yet occupy the true stage and still dwell among the external ordinary beings (*bāhyapṛthagjana*), they are said to be "like. Second, taking those of small capacity as...
The "son" has a minor capacity that resembles the nature and faculties of the Mahāyāna; hence he is called a "resembling son.
Since he has turned his back on his father and fled, he is degraded to the status of a "resembling son," a meaning that implies a mutual loss. △ Second, the union of father and son and their meeting.
The Tathāgata has always said that we are his sons.

This accords with the meaning of the elder recognizing his son upon seeing him; this establishes the sense of Śākyamuni becoming our son. This is to be understood as the Buddha’s teaching, and not as our own bold self-assertion.
△ Third, the application of the parable of sending a messenger to pursue and entice [the son]. This is divided into two parts. First, the application of the bystander’s pursuit.
“World-Honored One, because of the three kinds of suffering, we have been deluded and ignorant, taking pleasure in and clinging to the lesser Dharma.

The three kinds of suffering arise from the three types of sensation (*vedanā*). From painful sensation arises the suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*), because the faculties and their objects are discordant and oppressive.

From pleasant sensation arises the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkhatā*), because the transformation of pleasure gives rise to various sorrows and afflictions. From neither-painful-nor-pleasant...”

Birth and existence are the suffering of conditioned formations (*saṃskāra-duḥkha*), for they are characterized by the constant flux and passing away of every moment. Due to these three types of suffering, the five turbidities (*pañca-kaṣāya*) are intensified;
birth and death are boundless, and the feverish afflictions scorch the mind. One is deluded regarding the holy teachings and confused within one's own mind.

Enveloped by the darkness of ignorance (*avidyā*), it is difficult to enter the Great Dharma. This refers to a state of mind that is forcibly pursued with stubborn attachment, characterized by urgent confusion and distress. Since there is no great capacity [for awakening], [the Dharma cannot be received].
They delight in and cling to inferior teachings and are only capable of being transformed by inferior means; this is a temporary attainment of joy and satisfaction.

Furthermore, because suffering is abundant, there is feverish affliction (*paridāha*); because of feverish affliction, there is delusion; because of delusion, there is ignorance (*ajñāna*). This ignorance is precisely nescience (*avidyā*).

Because of the presence of this nescience, they are deluded regarding the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*) of knowledge and vision inherently possessed within themselves. Not becoming non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), they instead cling to the inferior [teachings].
The Dharma: How is this different from a destitute son who, fearing his father, delights in going to the poor quarters? △ Second, the combined inducement of the two persons.
Of the previous four, now only three are combined. First, combining the gradual inducement to remove filth.
Today, the World-Honored One has caused us to contemplate [the path] until we attain nirvana as our daily wage.
"Today" refers to the present life in contrast to the many past lives when one delighted in the Hinayana; it also indicates that even in this life, one remains stuck in the provisional stage.
Furthermore, "today" points to the period of the *āgama*. This means that during the period of the *āgama*, the Buddha knew our capacities.
In former days, the suffering and pleasure experienced were slight; therefore, [the Buddha] taught us to practice contemplation and so forth.

"Contemplation" refers to the six consciousnesses. "Eliminating" has the meaning of cultivation and abandonment. The "manure of conceptual proliferation" (*prapañca*) refers to the accumulation of the afflictions of views and thought (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa* and *saṃskāra-kleśa*).
This describes the Buddhist teaching of knowing suffering and abandoning its origin. "We, etc. refers to cultivating the path and realizing cessation. "The price of a day" means:

The Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna) has a remainder; compared to the Great Vehicle (Mahāyāna), it is without remainder. It is like the wages of a day’s labor compared to the wealth of ten thousand strings of cash:
a laborer who exerts all his strength and effort for a single day can obtain only two or three fen of silver.

Those of the Two Vehicles undergo arduous cultivation to sever delusions, yet they achieve only the state of an Arhat. Their principle is isolated and their practice exhausted; ultimately, they cannot attain the great utility [of Buddhahood].
Thus it is said that they are like "a day’s wage. △ Second, rejoicing in the encounter and dwelling for a long time.
Having obtained this, his heart was filled with great joy; because he applied himself with diligent vigor, what he acquired was vast and much.

Yet, regarding the price of a single day’s labor as sufficient for himself, he claimed that what he had gained was extensive and abundant. Thus, being self-satisfied and complacent, he sat idly guarding his own partiality and deficiency.
This is precisely the malady of the Hīnayāna: it is like the vision of the River Lord (Hé Bó) or the frog in the well.
They consider all that is beautiful in the world to reside entirely within themselves, yet they do not know the vastness of the ocean.
△ Third, [the section on] seeing from afar on another day:
"However, the World-Honored One previously knew that we... shall have a share of the Tathāgata’s treasury of knowledge and vision."

Previously it was said that he saw them from afar; now it is said that he knew of them beforehand. Previously it was said that he was emaciated and haggard; now it is said that his mind was attached to debased desires.
Previously it was said that he had cast off his necklaces and other ornaments; now it is said that he abandoned them freely and did not discriminate between them.

In sum, he concealed the ultimate truth while employing skillful means, catering to their inclinations. He did not say that they possessed the destined portion to attain Buddhahood. △ Fourth, the summary and conclusion.
II. Entrusting the Family Business. First, it was appropriate for them to receive the family business.
The World-Honored One, through the power of skillful means, spoke of the Tathāgata’s wisdom [until: "We did not know that we were truly the sons of the Buddha."
"World-Honored One," etc., joins with the essence of the Vaipulya (fangděng) teachings to express faith.

This follows upon the previous point, which states that although the Buddha did not provide such detailed analysis for us within the *Āgama* teachings, he has now, at the assembly of the Vaipulya sūtras, through the power of his skillful means (*upāya*) and provisional wisdom (*prajñā*), taught that the six sense organs and their objects are all the true reality (*bhūtatathatā*) and the wisdom of the Mahāyāna. Now that we have followed the Buddha from the *Āgama*...
Within the teachings they received, they considered gaining a single day’s worth of value as a great achievement.

Thus, regarding this Vaipulya Mahāyāna, although it is said that they believe one another in their hearts and enter and exit [the teaching] without difficulty, they nonetheless lack the aspiration to seek the Great [Vehicle].
This corresponds to what was previously described as "staying still where one is. The phrase "we, the lower [ones]" corresponds to the *Prajñāpāramitā* being turned into a teaching.
This means that within the Vaipulya teachings, the Buddha perceived that we lacked the aspiration to seek the Great Vehicle, because the provisional and the real resided in the Buddha.
Therefore, at the assembly of the *Prajñāpāramitā*, he caused the provisional and the real to reside within himself, so that we might seek them for ourselves.
Furthermore, through the empowerment of the Tathāgata’s wisdom and power, we were enabled to reveal and expound them for the sake of the great bodhisattvas.
Having received the Buddha’s empowerment, we have spoken according to the Buddha’s mind and further expounded it for the sake of the bodhisattvas;
thus, we thought this was the Dharma of the bodhisattvas, and for that reason, we ourselves had no aspiration for this Mahāyāna, nor did we give rise to a single thought of seeking to attain it.
The following section interrogates and explains the meaning of having no aspiration, stating that the Buddha knew we delighted in the Lesser Vehicle.

These skillful and expedient means were taught in accordance with us; there was nothing therein that did not refine away our inclination toward the Lesser Vehicle and spur on our resolve for the Great.

Yet we were unaware that at the time of the previous transmission of the teaching and the entrustment of the treasury, we were already truly Mahāyāna sons of the Buddha. For this reason, we lacked the aspiration to seek it, just as...
Although the impoverished son received the instructions and took charge of the various goods, he had no intention of taking even a single meal for himself.
△ Second, the entrustment of the family estate:
"Now we, for the first time, know that the World-Honored One... [as it says]... all that a son of the Buddha ought to receive has already been obtained by us."
This corresponds to the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*) given in the present sutra. To follow from the preceding statement: it means that we initially did not know that we were truly the sons of the Buddha.
We suspected that the Buddha was merely using his Tathāgata-wisdom to command us to preach for the sake of bodhisattvas, as if he were deeply withholding [the truth] from us.
Now the Buddha says that through various skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*), all [teachings] are for the sake of Bodhi. These...

All that has been taught was for the sake of transforming bodhisattvas. Today we have finally come to know that regarding the Buddha’s wisdom, the World-Honored One does not possess even a single hair’s breadth of parsimony toward us. To explain this further through questioning:
why is it that we previously suspected he was parsimonious, yet now we know he is not? It is because we have, from the very beginning, truly been the sons of the Buddha.
Yet we merely delighted in the Lesser Dharma; thus, taking the true for the false, we became śrāvakas seeking only minor fruits.

Had we possessed even a single thought of delighting in the Great [Vehicle] in the past, then all the Vaipulya and Prajñāpāramitā teachings of the Mahāyāna that the Buddha expounded over forty years would have been spoken for us. How could they have been intended solely for bodhisattvas?
How is this known to be so? Because within this very sutra, the Buddha repeatedly states that all Buddhas teach only the One Vehicle (ekayāna).
The passage beginning with "And in the past" concludes the meaning established above.

As for those who disparage [the teaching], it is as in the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra*, where before Mahāmati, [the Buddha] moved to equate śrāvakas with outsiders (tīrthika), calling them "fools and donkeys" because they cannot attain the *Laṅkā*.

The *Śrīmālādevī-siṃhanāda-sūtra* likens the Śrāvakas to blind men and withered seeds that will never attain Buddhahood; the *Awakening of Faith* instructs people to make vows not to encounter Śrāvakas or non-Buddhists.

Such statements were all disparagements from former times, referring to how, on the occasion of the Vaipulya assemblies, the Śrāvakas who delighted in inferior teachings were disparaged before the Bodhisattvas. This is now verified by the bestowal of prophecies in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
This was not to disparage us; rather, he truly sought to teach and transform us through the Mahāyāna Dharma.
Because we were ignorant, we all spoke in disparagement when we gathered. For this reason, he has today bestowed upon us the prophecy.
We say that originally our minds had no aspiration or seeking, yet now the great treasure of the Dharma King has arrived spontaneously. Thus it is said to have "arrived spontaneously."
This refers to unfathomable wealth obtained without expectation; it is that which is "done by no one yet done," and "reached by no one yet reached.

As for the phrase "like the sons of the Buddha," it means that what was to be attained by the sons of the Buddha during the assembly of the Vaipulya Prajñāpāramitā in the past, we have now already attained, and shall not [seek it] again.
Furthermore, it is attained through cultivation. This corresponds to the intention of bestowing joy upon those who have attained [realization]. The preceding prose section is concluded.

△ Second, the verse commentary consists of eighty-six and a half lines, divided into two parts. The first seventy-three and a half lines versify the preceding prose; the latter thirteen lines praise the Buddha’s benevolent virtues.
Within the former, there are again two sections. The first two lines versify the abbreviated teaching.
Thus it was said.
At that time, Mahākāśyapa, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"Today we have heard the Buddha’s teaching... [until] this unsurpassed treasury of jewels, which we have obtained without seeking."
Today, regarding what was said forty years ago: "The sounds of the teaching" refers to the sounds of the eight qualities of voice and the four analytical knowledges;
"the teaching for the burning house" refers to the skillful means. "With a heart full of joy" refers to speech; "leaping for joy" refers to bodily action.

From "The Buddha said" below, the text correctly clarifies the attainment of that which has never before been encountered. The phrase "unsurpassed" serves as a metaphor for *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. That which was hopeless forty years ago—
Therefore, it is said that he did not seek it; after forty years, it was bestowed upon him, hence it is said that he obtained it spontaneously.
△ Second, there are seventy-one lines and a half, which are verses explaining the parable. This is divided into two parts: first, forty-one lines of verses explaining the parable;

second, thirty lines and a half of verses applying the teaching to the analogy. The first part is further divided into four sections. First, thirteen lines of verses on the loss of the father and son. Second, seven... [text continues]
In thirty-five and a half verses, father and son meet; in thirty verses, he dispatches a messenger to pursue and entice him;
in forty verses, he takes over the family estate. First, regarding their initial loss of one another, there are four parts.
In the first one and a half verses, the son turns his back on his father and flees.
For example, it is like a young child, immature and without understanding, who wanders through various countries for more than fifty years.
"The bright one in the burning house" refers to the sovereign; "countries, cities, and villages" is used here as a broad term.

Herein, "the impoverished son wandering in saṃsāra" means that the three realms are the various countries and the six destinies are the more than fifty [years]. Having regressed from the Great Vehicle and forgotten his origin, he becomes another.

"Earth. To rise and sink without ceasing is called "constant circulation. This collectively expresses that the ground of turning one's back on the Truth is distant, while the time spent pursuing delusion is abundant.
△ Second, seven lines. A verse on the father seeking his son and stopping midway.
His father, filled with anxiety, searched in all four directions for someone as wealthy and possessed of such great power;

this is different from Changwen’s [search] in the four directions. In the former case, he was at the loom, employing reasoning based on the Four Noble Truths to seek out the means—both primary and auxiliary—for food and clothing.
Here, however, the Buddha is among the living beings, constantly seeking those who are fit vessels for deliverance within the four modes of birth. This is the verse.
Seeking a son, he did not find one. "A single city" refers to the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*). As for "suddenly coming to rest," the *Avataṃsaka* belongs to the Perfect and Sudden Mahāyāna;
it accords with the original intention and directly elucidates the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), hence it is called "suddenly coming to rest. "Building a house" refers to...
The arising of compassion and equanimity relies upon the dwelling of emptiness-nature.

As for "constructing and establishing," according to the "Chapter on the Accomplishment of the Flower Adornment World" and the "Chapter on the Flower Treasury World," the twenty kinds of world-oceans were all proclaimed by Samantabhadra Bodhisattva from within the true position of the One True Dharma-realm;
therefore, it is called "constructing and establishing. That which is expounded therein consists of five cycles.
The four sections clarify the Buddha’s mastery over the primary and secondary realms (*dharmadhātu*) and his enjoyment of cause and effect; thus it says, "he delights himself with the five desires.

The phrase "his household" generally clarifies the accumulation of stores where the bamboo slips are worn through by use and the grain has turned moldy, as well as the treasuries marked with purple and yellow banners;
thus it says, "greatly wealthy," which is a metaphor for possessing myriads of virtues. The section beginning with "many [treasures]" specifically clarifies the seven jewels of great wealth. Great...
The fourfold vehicles of wealth: fields and estates, people—both sentient and insentient; the great wealth of kinship, whether near or distant;

the great wealth of generating profit through other lands, whether far or near; and the great wealth of commerce, whether traveling as a merchant or sitting as a shopkeeper, wherein one disburses capital and reaps its returns.
By exchanging existence for non-existence, he pervades all places and is venerated by all beings. The preceding clarifies great wealth and abundant riches;
"ten thousand, million, billion" refers to the latter, clarifying noble status and great power. "King" refers to the sovereign; "ministers" refers to the governors. As the Record says:

The sovereign cherishes and remembers him; this signifies the heightening of the Sage’s favor. The ministers revere and esteem him; this signifies the honoring of his virtuous nature and his learning.
The Buddhas of the ten directions praise him, exclaiming, "Excellent! You are the foremost guide. Hence it is said that the king cherishes and remembers him.
The fourfold assembly surrounds him with reverence and respect; hence it is said that the ministers revere and esteem him. By these two sets of phrases, he is pleased in the immediate vicinity.
They have come from afar; these great beings (mahāsattvas) come and go to listen to the Dharma. The phrase "wealthy and noble" summarizes the aforementioned riches and benefits.
The phrase "possessing greatness" clarifies the power of majestic spiritual authority (*vīrya*). These points are fully manifested here, just as in the long prose version. △ Third, two lines:
this verse skips over [the previous topic] to address how household affairs are not transmitted because they lack continuity.
Now that I am advanced in years, my anxiety for my son increases (up to the point where he asks), "What shall become of the treasures and goods in the storehouse?
This verse expresses the suffering of losing a son; because there is no one to whom they may be entrusted, he is filled with anxiety. "Early" refers to dawn, and "late" refers to dusk;
it means that from morning until evening, he does not forget [his son] for a single moment. "The time of death" refers to the time of *nirvāṇa*. "Foolishness" (*moha*)...

"Son, come down. These words express the father's heartache for his son. Previously he was called a "child" because of his lack of knowledge; here he is called a "deluded son" because he willingly indulges in dissipation;
and later he is called a "poor son" because of the hardships regarding food and clothing. As for the phrase, "What should be done?"—it refers to this.
The father, mindful of his son with deep longing, felt a sense of restless anxiety. (Section Four: Two and a half lines.
A verse summarizing the search for food and clothing and the gradual return.
At that time, the impoverished son sought food and clothing... (until) gradually traveling on, he arrived at the city where his father resided.

The mutual interaction of the sense faculties (*indriya*) and their objects (*viṣaya*) is like a village; the eighteen realms (*dhātu*) are like a kingdom. Cultivating wholesome states within the three realms is "having something attained";
cultivating the heterodox practices of non-Buddhists is "having nothing attained. Furthermore, practicing from the human realm up to the heavens is "having something attained";
when celestial merit is exhausted and one falls back to the human realm, it is "having nothing attained. To see one's own empty belly during a time of famine is [analogous to this].

Because they have not obtained the food of the Mahāyāna Dharma, they appear emaciated and their forms are ugly; because they lack the merit of great power and function, they appear afflicted with sores and scabs.
This is due to the arising of views and afflictions (*kleśa*) within the realm of outflowing phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*).

The two subsequent phrases refer to the gradual process of refinement and cultivation through which one encounters the Great Assembly of the Buddha. The preceding verse concludes the section on the father and son losing each other.
△ Section Two: Seven and a half lines. Verses on the Meeting of Father and Son. Divided into two parts. First, six and a half lines: verses on the son seeing his father.
[The son] travels from one place of labor to another until he eventually reaches his father’s house (up to) inquiring after a poor neighborhood where he intends to go to seek employment.
The two lines concerning "hired labor" describe the manner in which he saw his father. From the phrase "At that time" onwards, they describe the signs by which he recognized his father.

The previous mention of the "place where he saw his father" refers to the vicinity of the gate; now, stating that "the elder was inside the gate," indicates that the description of the signs encompasses the location as well.
"Inside the gate" is a metaphor for the Buddha dwelling within the *bodhimaṇḍa* of the *araṇya-dharma*. "Bestowing great [wealth]" and so forth...

"Seeing the place where his father is" refers to the two phrases concerning the bestowal of the Great [Dharma]. "The secondary retribution (依報)" refers to being covered by protection and free from fear.

"Retinue" and below refer to the primary retribution (正報) wherein the principal and attendants provide mutual protection. "Notes, records, vouchers, and commentaries" refers to the conferral of predictions (授記), clarifying the practice of cultivation.

Using the extensive to manifest the concise constitutes the notes; it is like clouds arising for two hundred questions or pouring from a jar for two thousand responses. This is the conferral of the prediction.

This serves as the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*). It is a supplementary discussion on entering the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) that provides the prediction. The Four Great Vows serve as the bond, and spiritual practice serves as the commentary (*vṛtti*).
The metaphors represent the vast measure of merit rooted in great capacity. The commentary clarifies the stages of practice and bestows the prediction.

From "The impoverished son sees his father" onwards, it versifies the seeing of the father, the arising of doubt, and the retreat. From "Having reflected thus" onwards, it describes the impoverished son’s dwelling and turning back.
He reflected silently, made up his mind, and resolved upon his course of action, thinking:
"Rather than being constrained by the forced demands of wealth and status, it is better to find peace of mind in the natural ease of poverty and low station. △ Second, one verse in prose:
The father sees his son.
At that time, the elder was upon his lion throne; seeing his son from afar, he recognized him silently. The [original] prose consists of four parts;
here, only the single verse regarding the recognition of the son is presented, while the remaining three are not versified. (30 lines and a half.
This verse section on the parable of sending a messenger to entice [the son] back is divided into two parts. The first three lines verse the immediate dispatching of attendants to pursue him.
He immediately commanded a messenger to pursue and seize him, bringing him back [to the point where he] would not believe my words and would not believe that this was his father.
There are three parts to the long prose; herein, the three phrases "immediately commanded" constitute one section. This verse summarizes the forceful pursuit and bringing back.

The two characters "immediately commanded" (jìchì) refer to the father seeing [his son] from afar and recognizing his facial features silently; the father’s longing for his son was so intense that upon suddenly seeing him, [he was overcome].
He immediately instructed his men to pursue him. Because the pursuit was so urgent, the impoverished son had no place to set his hands; thus he cried out in resentment and alarm.
The five lines following "confused and distressed" (*mí-mèn*) eulogize his being seized violently and falling into a swoon.

The line "confused and distressed" should properly follow "causing me to come here," as this would accord with the long prose version; however, the meaning remains consistent [with the current placement]. The messenger seizes him urgently and drags him by force.

"This is not the situation of hiring someone for labor; rather, it has the appearance of a desire to kill me. How could there be anyone capable of providing me with food and clothing who would cause me to be like this?
Terrified and at a loss for what to do, he was seized by unceasing alarm and fear, and thus fainted upon the ground.
The Elder, knowing his son’s four lines of verse, [spoke them] to grant him the joy of being temporarily released. There were four [verses] above; now, however, [only...]
The verse laments the release of those who are deluded; "delusion" refers to the gravity of their confusion, while "narrow and inferior" refers to the smallness of their capacity.

Because they lack the great potential [to receive the teaching], the transformation [of sentient beings] must cease. This corresponds to the passage where the father, knowing his son's disposition, and so forth.

Now, when biological father and son have been separated for a long time, they may not recognize one another in such a manner. Yet, regarding our own fundamental mind-nature, we have never [been separated from it].
In the blink of an eye, how fleeting is this floating world! Once this body is lost, for thousands of births and ten thousand kalpas, one changes head and face;
looking upon kin as enemies, how many are there who take evil for beauty? △ The second section, spanning seven and a half lines, praises the secret dispatching of two men to entice [the king].
The long prose consists of four parts; here, the first three are praised. The first three lines praise the gradual enticement.
He removes the filth.
By means of skillful means, he further dispatches other people [to] remove the impurities and cleanse the various rooms and dwellings.

Since the great transformation has been brought to rest, he therefore employs skillful means to preach the Dharma of the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna) in order to guide and attract them. These "other people" are—
These are the two individuals. They manifest in the form of śrāvakas and are merely the dregs of the Mahāyāna. "One-eyed" is a metaphor for the one-sided emptiness (*ekānta-śūnyatā*);
because what they perceive is not correct, it is so described. "Dwarfish" refers to being short in height; "ugly" refers to being narrow in breadth.

Those who see one-sided emptiness cannot exhaustively reach the source of the true nature (*dharmatā*) in the vertical dimension, and thus they are like the dwarfish. Horizontally, they lack the adornment of the manifold virtues of the Mahāyāna, and thus they are like the ugly.
"Vile! Their virtue is not the four fearlessnesses, hence they are called 'lacking majesty. They differ from the permanence, bliss, self, and purity, hence they are called 'lacking virtue.
You may speak to them below; strictly command that they be gradually enticed. As for those who rejoice, engage them by appealing to their preferences."
He delights in base matters. The "pure chamber" refers to the house of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*).

Furthermore, the four lines heard by the impoverished son—namely, the prose passage beginning with "If the impoverished son consents," and so forth—are all words of instruction from the elder; these are omitted in the verse.
The verse merely summarizes the matter of the impoverished son receiving his orders and entering service. Each has its own distinct meaning, as determined by the translators.
The Chinese and Sanskrit terms are precise in their meaning; they must be understood in full detail and not treated with negligence. △ Second, two lines:
a verse on seeing [the son] from afar on another day. From "The elder constantly saw his son at the window" (up to) "he took a dustpan and went to where his son was."
Regarding "seeing the son through the window," the *Yi* says: "To present sincerity from the window brings no blame at the end. The commentary states:
"A window is not the primary entrance, yet it is the means by which the room receives light. Though there may be initial difficulties and obstructions, one ultimately attains freedom from blame."
This is a metaphor for the difficulty of introducing the Great Dharma; one first receives the Lesser Dharma and ultimately attains the Great Dharma, like the image of "entering through the window.
When [the father] thinks his son delights in base matters, he knows that the son delights in the small. The passage "The elder...

removed his precious [robes]" and "donned tattered ones" refers to disparaging birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) and praising *nirvāṇa*. As the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* says: "Śākyamuni Buddha conceals his immeasurable [qualities]."
By the power of mastery, he delivers sentient beings by means of the Dharma that accords with their inclinations.
(Three lines and a half) This verse personally exhorts [the Bodhisattva] to set his mind at ease.

He skillfully approaches and speaks to him, urging him to work diligently; furthermore, he uses gentle words, saying, "You are like my own son. By anointing his feet with oil, he is able to walk upon water;

though barefoot, they do not crack, just as one who uses the "medicine for preventing hands from cracking" [does not suffer such injury]. This serves as a metaphor for supernatural powers (*abhijñā*) and wisdom (*prajñā*).

The two phrases concerning food and drink serve as a metaphor for the cultivation through contemplation (*vipaśyanā*) and refinement (*bhāvanā*). The meditative contemplations (*dhyāna*) of the Hīnayāna are like a mat.
A seat that is thick and warm is not equal to the meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) of the Mahāyāna, which is like a soft white woolen mat. You should diligently apply yourself;

this is the sincere and intimate exhortation of the mind. The meaning of the "three turnings" is implicitly contained therein. Furthermore, regarding the use of gentle words such as "like a son," the character *zuò* (作) is used here as *ér* (兒).
Although he is originally one's own biological child, terms such as "ruò" (若) and "rú" (如) refer to the varying conditions of people—whether poor or wealthy, noble or humble.
Only karma is determinate. Though one’s compassion may be like that for a close relative, it cannot, even for a single moment or in the slightest degree, alter the fate of a beloved child.
To realize this, those who do not accept their destiny are either ignorant or deluded. (Forty lines).

The Lotus Sutra, Chapter Five: The Parable of the Medicinal Herbs.
This chapter describes and confirms the realization and understanding of those of middle capacity.

Although the four sons in the preceding chapter understood that the provisional teachings were adapted to their capacities and that they all ultimately converge upon the Truth, they had not yet clarified how the One Sound secretly reveals the profound transformation of true knowledge.

This is the merit. Just as that great cloud rains upon all grasses, trees, thickets, and forests, which receive its moisture according to their respective capacities, this metaphor is taught to reveal the impartial compassion of the Great Sage, which is as selfless as heaven and earth while all things are selfish.
Although the text contains mountains, rivers, clouds, rain, grasses, trees, thickets, and forests, it specifically establishes the analogy using medicinal herbs alone.
Regarding the "names": the land represents that which can produce; the clouds and rain represent that which can moisten; and the medicinal herbs represent that which is produced and moistened.
While all that is produced and moistened has utility, the utility of the medicinal herbs is the most powerful.

This is a metaphor for how tainted wholesome states (*sāsrava-kuśala*) can eliminate evil, yet untainted wholesome states (*anāsrava-kuśala*) are supreme. The four sons used the analogy of the impoverished son to understand the "fire."

The analogy of the dwelling deeply accords with the Sage’s mind; thus he exclaims, "Excellent! He describes their attainment of understanding by using it as a metaphor for these people, hence calling them "medicinal herbs.
This is the benefit to the world: once the medicinal herbs have grown together for a long time, they are all at once moistened by the clouds and rain.
Their power and function become fully saturated within, while branches and stalks emerge externally—just as withered seedlings, upon receiving rain, suddenly spring to life.
This is a metaphor for the śrāvakas who, dwelling in their final existence within *nirvāṇa-with-remainder*, no longer aspire to seek the Buddha-way.
Now, having heard this sutra, they are further transported [to the goal]. As previously stated, these are true śrāvakas who cause all to hear;

because they possess superior utility for both the internal and external, for themselves and others, they are called "medicinal herbs. This is for the benefit of persons. Medicinal herbs can eliminate the four [afflictions].

It cures great illnesses, nourishes the five viscera, restores the complexion, and arrests the aging process. This is analogous to how the various śrāvakas, having now heard this sutra, destroy their ignorance and delusions;

this is the benefit of the remedy. Just as all medicinal herbs, trees, and plants, upon receiving the rain from the clouds, attain a fresh luster and each flourishes in its own way, so too do the various śrāvakas, having now heard this sutra, realize that their minds are destined for Buddhahood and rejoice.
They leaped for joy. Previously it was said: "Today we are truly the sons of the Buddha; this unsurpassed treasury of jewels has come to us of its own accord without being sought.

This is the benefit of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). Furthermore, regarding the two characters "medicinal herbs" (*yàocǎo*): while the words are general, their intended meaning is specific; specifically, they refer only to medicinal herbs.

Because it penetrates the three types of grasses and two types of trees; furthermore, it is said that while the specific meaning is general, it is general across the seven stages of expedient means (*saptopāya*) yet specific to the Śrāvakas alone.
△ Third, the Tathāgata’s confirmation and fulfillment, divided into two parts: first, the brief confirmation and fulfillment; second, the extensive confirmation and fulfillment.
The first part is further divided into two: first, the double praise of "Excellent! (Sādhu).
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Mahākāśyapa... [up to] "...it is truly as you have said.
The double exclamation "Excellent! was used to praise his mastery of both the provisional and the ultimate without error. "Well-spoken" refers to the exquisite skill of his phrasing;
thus, the events are arranged with order, and the principles are presented according to their sequence, such as in the account of the impoverished son who initially abandoned his father.

Thereafter, he went toward his father. Because the king suspected him of being his father, and fearing that the man of noble status might depart from his father, [the son] went to work for his father as a hired laborer.
He obtained his father’s family estate; it was not a different person, nor was it different wealth.

Yet, through immeasurable toil and suffering, he expressed the state of his own ignorance, just as in the sequence of the father: first losing his son, then seeking his son, and finally seeing him from afar outside the gate.

O Son, know that I have released you from your lowly state; having employed skillful means to recover you and entrusted you with my family estate, I have harbored no dualistic mind nor any change of heart.
Yet, I have exercised such vast compassion, clearly manifesting the profound grace of the Tathāgata’s skillful guidance.

This single parable alone exhaustively outlines the doctrinal principles of the five periods of teaching and the beginning and end of the entire dispensation; its phrasing is subtle and elegant, while its underlying meaning is refined and precise.

Detailed examination: Unless one possesses the vast brilliance of Mahākāśyapa, with a mind like brocade and an inner core like embroidery, and a tongue like surging waves and a mouth like the ocean, this could not be achieved.
Truly, as stated in a single phrase, it is definitively established and without error. △ Second, acknowledging what one has not yet attained.
The Tathāgata further possesses immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) merits (up to the point where they) cannot be fully described.
To praise both and extol one, while suppressing the other in this section, means that although the cited parable is skillful, its exposition of the meaning is not exhaustive.

By using the single parable of the impoverished son, it merely limits the benefit gained to those of the Two Vehicles; thus, the principle of "first three, then one" is relegated to a level inferior to that of human beings.
O Celestial One, advancing, you do not equal a Bodhisattva; horizontally, you do not equal the eight dharma-realms; vertically, you do not equal the seven stages of expedient means.
This is a deficiency in your realization. As for what the Tathāgata further possesses that is equal [to yours]:

suppose you had an infinite number of mouths upon a single body, each mouth an infinite number of tongues, and each tongue producing an infinite number of sounds, preaching through every atom and every world-system until infinite billions [of eons].
Even if one were to speak for an eon, one could not exhaustively describe them; for while the void might be measured and the wind might be bound, no one can fully describe the merits of the Buddha.
You should know that when the Tathāgata preaches the Dharma, he utters it with a single voice, which is impartial and inconceivable.
In truth, it is not that there is suddenness first and gradualness later, nor that the first three and the last one differ. The five vehicles each attain understanding according to their kind;

there is no distinction between them. It is like a dragon raising clouds and sending down rain of a single flavor, universally moistening all things and everywhere bestowing cool relief, without discriminating between the withered and the flourishing.
How could the parable of the single impoverished son exhaust the merits of the Tathāgata? As for the passage in the following text where the Buddha speaks... [text continues]
It cannot be fully exhausted, much less by Kāśyapa and the others. △ Second, the detailed exposition for confirmation. This consists of prose and verse. The prose has two parts:
first, the exposition confirming the opening of the three vehicles to reveal the one; second, reaffirming the fundamental tenet and offering praise. The first part is further divided into two:

first, the explanation by way of Dharma; second, the explanation by way of analogy. The explanation by way of Dharma is further divided into two: first, citing the fact that [the teaching] is not in vain to encourage faith.
Kāśyapa, you should know that the Tathāgata is the King of all dharmas; whatever he speaks is never false.
Although the Buddha-dharma is vast, it does not transcend the provisional and the real. Beyond the provisional and the real, there is no other dharma.

As for what was said above regarding its being immeasurable and boundless—this meaning is difficult to believe. Therefore, by citing the Dharma King and his words of truth, [the Buddha] exhorts one to have faith.
... Thus it is. △ Second, the actual exposition of opening the three and revealing the one, divided into two parts. First, clarifying the opening and revelation according to the teachings:
"Regarding all phenomena, by means of wisdom and skillful means... (up to) "...all reach the ground of omniscience."
"Below all" refers to the opening of the provisional (*upāya*). "All dharmas" refers to the seven stages of expedient means (*saptavidha-upāya*).

Although these dharmas are numerous, they are expounded according to the capacities of beings through the *pāramitā* of skillful means; there is nothing that does not accord with their needs. For humans and devas, he teaches precepts and wholesome deeds;
for those of the two vehicles, he teaches the Truths and the Conditions; for the Small Vehicle, he teaches the phenomenal *pāramitās*; and for the Initial Teaching, he teaches principle (*li*).

The passage beginning with "The [ten] degrees, etc. and ending with "that which is spoken below" reveals the reality. The "ground" (*bhūmi*) is the true mark (*lakṣaṇa*). It is called "one" because it is ultimately non-dual.
It is called "universal" (*sarva*) because its nature is vast and expansive. It is called "wisdom" (*jñāna*) because it is quiescent yet constantly illuminating.
It is called "ground" because it serves as the foundation of non-abiding upon which all phenomena are established. Next, the opening and revealing [of this reality] is explained in terms of wisdom.
The Tathāgata contemplates and knows all dharmas (up to) manifesting all wisdom to all sentient beings.
"The Tathāgata" and below clarify the opening of the three [vehicles]. Contemplating all those who seek refuge is the skillful means (*upāya*) that can illuminate the provisional;
knowing all those who seek refuge is the skillful means that can identify the medicine. Knowing the depths of their minds...

Practice. This is the power of skillful means (upāya-jñāna) that knows the diseases. Both medicine and disease are provisional dharmas (*prajñapti-dharma*). Each provisional dharma has its own destination:

precepts, wholesome deeds, and the like lead proximately to the realms of humans and devas; yet, if they serve as distant conditions, even bowing the head or raising a hand leads toward the fruit of Buddhahood.

The factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa-dharmas*) and the like lead proximately to nirvāṇa; yet, if they serve as the adornment of merit, what is practiced becomes the path of a bodhisattva, leading [to the ultimate goal]. Far...

Regarding the destination of the Jewels: the dharmas of the six perfections, their principles, and their phenomena constitute the paths toward which one approaches and returns, though the routes differ.

There are two types of practice based on the profound mind (*adhyāśaya*). If the profound mind is attached to the "reliant" (the body) and the "supported" (the environment), it gives rise to the ten grave evils, obstructing the vehicle of humans and devas.
If the profound mind is attached to the dharmas that are grasped as objects, it gives rise to the four inversions, the three paths, the six obscurations, and the five [hindrances].

Abiding therein, it obstructs the four noble vehicles; one should know that the manifestations of the deep-seated sicknesses of the mind differ. The Tathāgata, through his skillful wisdom, illuminates them and penetrates them without obstruction.
Furthermore, below this, it clarifies the single point: "the thorough and complete understanding of all phenomena."
This is true wisdom (*bhūta-jñāna*), which can illuminate reality. All provisional teachings (*upāya-dharma*) enter into reality;
therefore, it is said to be "thoroughly exhaustive. What is seen by the Buddha-eye is clarity; what is known by true wisdom is realization.

If this wisdom illuminates this medicine and this illness, it does not illuminate that medicine and that illness; if that wisdom illuminates that, it cannot illuminate this. This is the illumination of provisional wisdom.
Furthermore, a single wisdom universally illuminates all medicines and all illnesses; this is the illumination of true wisdom (*bhūta-jñāna*).
Because it can demonstrate such a state of perfect fusion between object and wisdom to sentient beings, it is called "all-encompassing wisdom.

Moreover, the previous statement that it is "unimpeded penetration" explains the real by means of the provisional; whereas the present description of being "clearly aware of all phenomena" explains the provisional by means of the real.
Thus, these two aspects appear interchangeably; they precisely clarify that the real is the provisional-real, and the provisional is the real-provisional.

One should know that, in the ultimate sense, it is neither provisional nor real, neither differentiated nor non-differentiated. Through the skillful means of wisdom, the provisional manifests differentiation.

Upon reaching the ground of all-encompassing wisdom (*sarvajñatā-bhūmi*), there is no distinction. This concludes the explanation of the superior Dharma (*uttara-dharma*). **II. Explanation by Analogy.** This is divided into two parts:

first, the analogies; second, the application to the Dharma. Within the first part, there are again two sections: first, the analogy of having distinctions, which illustrates the provisional teachings and provisional wisdom of the aforementioned [section];

second, the analogy of non-distinction, which illustrates the ultimate teachings and ultimate wisdom of the aforementioned [section]. Regarding the first section, it is further divided into six parts. First, the land.
An analogy:
Kāśyapa, it is as if there were mountains, rivers, valleys, and lands within a trichiliocosm.
The trichiliocosm is a metaphor for the world of sentient beings; the mountains and so forth are metaphors for the world of the five aggregates. This is the world.

There is no separate dharma that constitutes mountains, rivers, and the like; there is no separate dharma that constitutes sentient beings. Sentient beings are constituted by the five aggregates (*skandhas*).

Mountains are a metaphor for the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*); they are manifest and visible. Rivers are a metaphor for the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*); their flow fills and empties. Streams are a metaphor for the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*); they wind and meander through light and dark.

Valleys are a metaphor for the aggregate of mental formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*); they are obscure and difficult to see. The land is a metaphor for the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*); it pervades all.
It serves as the basis. Furthermore, because it is composed of five kinds of deluded thoughts—namely, solidity, emptiness-luminosity, interpenetration, obscurity, and inversion—it is so described.
Moreover, the mountain is a metaphor for the five aggregates (*skandhas*) of a Bodhisattva; the stream, for a Pratyekabuddha; the ravine, for a Śrāvaka; the valley, for a Deva;
and the land, for the five aggregates of a human being. Each and every aggregate possesses both the habitual cause (*vāsanā-hetu*) and the habitual fruit (*vāsanā-phala*).
"Dependence" is like mountains, rivers, and so forth, which serve as the basis for the substance and trunk of seeds and plants. △ Second, the analogy of herbs and trees:
the various species of herbs, trees, groves, and medicinal plants that are produced differ in their names and forms.
"Herbs" (*huì*) is the general name for grasses; "trees" (*mù*) is the collective designation for forest trees. A multitude of grasses forms a thicket; a multitude of trees forms a forest.
Those whose curative power is superior are called medicinal herbs (*yàocǎo*). Just as good laws subdue evil, the meaning of subduing evil through untainted goodness (*anāsrava-kuśala*) is superior;
therefore, they are likened to medicinal herbs. As for the five vehicles and the seven stages of expedient means (*saptopāya*), the seeds of cause and effect are not uniform; hence [the distinction].
Regarding the various types of clouds: such types each have their respective designations, which are "name" (*nāman*);
each has its respective substantial characteristic, which is "form" (*rūpa*). △ Third, the Simile of the Dense Clouds.
Dense clouds spread everywhere, covering the trichiliocosm;

this is a metaphor for the Buddha’s three mysteries (*triguhyaka*). The clouds having form and color is a metaphor for the Buddha’s appearance in the world, which is the mystery of body (*kāyaguhyaka*).

The clouds being able to provide shade and cover is a metaphor for the Buddha’s compassion, which is the mystery of mind (*manoguhyaka*). The subsequent teaching spoken by the Buddha is the mystery of speech (*vāgguhyaka*). Through these, one is perfumed by compassion.
The response body (nirmāṇakāya) preaches the Dharma, pervading the ten dharma realms; therefore, it is said to be "densely spread. △ Fourth, the metaphor of raining down:

"Raining equally at once" is a metaphor for the Buddha’s secret of speech (vākmithyatva). Through the eight tones and four types of eloquence, he proclaims and pours down the rain of Dharma. If the clouds were not dense, they could not rain equally.

If compassion is not secret, it cannot bring extensive benefit. Just as the rain from a single cloud universally saturates the great trichiliocosm, this is a metaphor for how a single voice secretly expounds [the Dharma], so that all sentient beings are equally benefited.
△ Fifth, the metaphor of receiving moisture.
Its moisture universally permeates the herbs, trees, and forests—down to their great roots, great stems, great branches, and great leaves.
The rain of Dharma universally moistens the mental ground of the seven kinds of sentient beings, whereby all seeds of habitual causes immediately sprout;

this is called "universal permeation. The roots, stems, branches, and leaves are metaphors for faith, precepts, concentration, and wisdom, which mutually support one another in succession. As for the small roots...
"Equal" (etc. refers to the faith, precepts, concentration, and wisdom of humans and devas; "medium" (etc. refers to the faith, precepts, concentration, and wisdom of the two vehicles;
and "great" (etc. refers to the faith, precepts, concentration, and wisdom of bodhisattvas. △ Sixth, the metaphor of growth.
All trees, according to their superior, middling, or inferior nature, grow and develop, flowering, bearing fruit, and producing seeds.

This illustrates how grasses and trees receive moisture according to their respective capacities. Likewise, the seven classes of sentient beings receive the moisture of the two causes—habitual tendencies and karmic retribution—and the wholesome dharmas.
Once moistened by the rain of the Dharma, both the fruits of habit-energy (*vāsanā*) and retribution (*vipāka*) each attain growth.

"In accordance with their spiritual capacities" clarifies that the provisional [teachings] accord with the faculties; they do not exceed the small, nor do they fall short of the great. This refers to the two causes—the seven types of habit-energy and the two types of retribution.
"The blossoming and ripening of flowers and fruits" refers to the two fruits—the seven types of habit-energy and the two types of retribution. The flowers are like habit-energy.
Fruit. As with the fruit of retribution (*vipākaphala*), this term "fruit" serves as a counterpart; one should say "the blossoming of flowers and the ripening of fruit.

△ Second, the metaphor of non-differentiation, which illustrates the true teaching and true wisdom mentioned above. This is divided into three parts. First, the metaphor of that which is produced from the first stage (*bhūmi*).
Although they arise from the same ground, the ground of the mind of the five vehicles is undifferentiated in its essential substance; yet it is capable of producing all.
That is, from the single ground of the true reality (*tathatā*), the five vehicles and seven expedient means are distinguished. △ Second, the analogy of being moistened by a single rain.

Moistened by a single rain and proclaimed with a single voice, the Dharma-gate of the One Vehicle develops the roots of goodness of the five vehicles; in the end, it is the teaching of the single voice of equality.
Although the beings to be benefited are fivefold, the intent of the transformation is one. △ Third: The Three Grasses and Two Trees.
For example, among various grasses and trees, each has its own distinction.
Small grasses with weak power represent humans and devas; medium grasses that are slightly superior represent the two vehicles; and superior grasses represent [the bodhisattvas].

The bodhisattvas of the Small Vehicle are like small trees and large trees, which surpass the three types of grass. This is a metaphor for the bodhisattvas who have begun to receive the two teachings;
though they receive different benefits from the three types of grass and two types of trees, they do not realize it themselves.

The roots of goodness of the five vehicles, having received the rain of the Buddha-dharma, grow according to their respective capacities, yet they likewise do not know it themselves. Furthermore, these five kinds of causes all rely upon the single Buddha-nature.
They do not know for themselves that the teachings of the five vehicles are all Mahāyāna, nor do they know for themselves that they all ultimately converge upon the Buddha-wisdom;
only the Tathāgata is able to know this. In sum, although the capacities of sentient beings are manifold, the underlying principle is one and the same, and what is taught is but the One Vehicle.
While the five natures of sentient beings differ in their innate seeds and vary in their resolve, there are those who apply themselves with diligence in their cultivation and progress.

Regarding the distinctions of indolence: there is a difference between shallow and deep levels of realization. It is like the earth, which gives life without partiality, and the rain, which moistens without bias;

yet the grasses and trees receive this moisture according to their own capacities, and thus their flowers and fruits differ naturally. This is because the Creator is without partiality, while things themselves act with self-interest.
The Sage’s mind is beyond comparison, yet sentient beings compare it to their own faculties. The preceding allegorical explanation is concluded. △ Second, the application to the Dharma.
This is divided into two parts: first, the application of the analogies for having distinctions; second, the application of the analogies for lacking distinctions.

Within the first part, there are further two sections: first, the formal application of the six analogies; second, the summary application by citing the analogies. Within the first section (the formal application), there are six sub-sections. The first is the application of the analogy of dense clouds.
Kāśyapa, you should know that the Tathāgata is also like this... [omitted] ...pervading and covering the trichiliocosm.

The sequence of the metaphors is not in the same order as before. In the previous analogy, the five vehicles were explained first because they were taught according to the capacities of sentient beings; thus, the five vehicles were mentioned first.
Here, however, the explanation is from the perspective of the Buddha, and therefore the "dense clouds" are paired first, following the logical sequence. It is just as follows:

He comes into the world and subsequently preaches the Dharma. The Dharma necessarily accords with the capacities [of beings]; thus, while the capacities receive and understand it, the conditions for doing so differ.

His appearance in the world is spoken of in contrast to his entry into concealment; this serves to demonstrate that he has reached the ultimate Dharma-body and eternally dwells in the realm of quiescent light.
To "conceal" is to enter; for the sake of all sentient beings, he turns his vessel of compassion backward and flows against the current to emerge, responding to the world as it manifests.
This emergence is like the rising of a great cloud; the metaphor is applied here: a cloud acts without partiality to accomplish its purpose.

Abiding without fixed location, it is like the Tathāgata who is neither born nor extinguished. Furthermore, it carries the meaning of "sheltering": the Great Compassion manifests a body to shelter and nurture all sentient beings.
Moreover, the Dharma-body is like space and the Response-body is like clouds; this unifies the two secrets of mind and body.
Regarding the phrase "with a great voice," this raises the Buddha’s secret of speech, which corresponds to the clouds having sound, pervading both devas and humans.
...and so forth. This separately cites the three wholesome paths as receiving the benefit of the oral secret (mouth-secrecy), which refers to the root-natures of the three vehicles.
The thirty sons individually receive the benefit of the voice; it is like that single phrase where the clouds, when joined, produce sound.

"Pervadingly covering a single phrase" generally indicates that all are Buddha-sons who together receive the benefit of the oral secret. △ Second, the combined metaphor of raining down, divided into three parts. First:
He proclaims his titles so that they may be known;
amidst the great assembly, he utters these words (up to): "Teacher of Gods and Men, Buddha, World-Honored One.
He first proclaims the ten titles so that the multitude may know where to take refuge. His statement "I am [this]" is not an act of self-exaltation; it is because the Buddha has appeared...
In this world, ninety-six different schools each promote their own heterodox views. Now, by calling out their names among the assembly, I cause people to know whom they should revere and honor.
△ Second, the knowledge and vision of the great vows.
"To cause those who have not yet crossed over to cross over, and to cause those who have not yet been liberated to be liberated" (up to: "the opener of the path and the speaker of the path.
These four great vows for the deliverance of sentient beings ensure that one's knowledge and vision are unerring. The great vows fundamentally perfect compassion;

since compassion takes suffering and pleasure as its objects, the great vows are likewise discussed in terms of the Four Noble Truths. If one perceives the Truth of Suffering as oppressive and tragic, [one generates the vow].
The bitterness and agony of suffering are so intense that one gives rise to a vow based upon them; hence it is said: "Those who have not crossed over suffering, I shall cause to cross over suffering.

This is the vow: "Countless sentient beings, I vow to deliver. If one perceives the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*), seeing how beings revolve through inversion, deluded and bound within the shoreless cycle of birth and death, they are truly pitiable.
Based on this, one gives rise to a vow; hence it is said: "Those who have not untied the origination [of suffering], I shall cause..."
"Understanding the Accumulation" means the vow to sever the boundless afflictions (*kleśa*). As for the path of purity, sentient beings do not recognize it;

yet those who practice this path are able to transcend birth and death and reach the ground of peace and bliss. Desiring to demonstrate this path to sentient beings so that they may be established upon it, it is said:
"Those who have not yet settled in the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*), let them settle in the factors of enlightenment. This refers to the vow to master the immeasurable Dharma-gates.

This is study. The place where afflictions are extinguished is called *nirvāṇa*. When the bonds of the seeds and fruits [of karma] are severed, one attains the two types of *nirvāṇa*. Based on this, one gives rise to a vow; therefore it is said:
"For those who have not yet realized the truth of cessation, cause them to realize the *nirvāṇa* of the truth of cessation. This is precisely the fulfillment of the supreme vow for the Buddha-way.

The two lines concerning the present life refer to the three types of supernormal knowledge (*trividyā*) that penetrate all things. The knowledge of past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti-jñāna*) penetrates the past.

The past is known through the knowledge of former abodes; the future is reached through the divine eye; and the present is reached through the exhaustion of outflows—these are also called the three clear knowledges (*tisro vidyāḥ*).
"One who knows all" means being fully endowed with the three types of knowledge. "One who sees all" means being fully endowed with the five eyes.

"Knowing the path" refers to the three phrases: that the three karmas follow the movement of wisdom. "Knowing the path" refers to the non-guarding of the mind; "opening the path" refers to the non-guarding of the body. Thus it is said.
"Dao" (the Way) refers to not needing to guard one's speech. This is because the Tathāgata’s three karmas are always accompanied by wisdom;

thus, there is no error, and so there is no need for protection. "Dao" points to the One Vehicle. Because [the Buddha] realizes this Way through his mind, he is able to manifest forms and reveal it, as well as proclaim it through language.
△ Third, summoning those with the capacity to listen.
"You, the assembly of devas, humans, and asuras, should all come here for the sake of hearing the Dharma.
Beings of the six realms are all within the scope of my compassionate transformation; I exhort those in the three auspicious paths to come and listen, for it is easier for them to hear the Dharma.
Furthermore, the sound of the voice of attaining the Way pervades the triple world, and the great, pervasive light shines afar across the ten directions."
"Square. This means that all were summoned according to their capacities to listen to the meaning. △ Third, the analogy of the local deities:
At that time, countless thousands of myriads of koṭis of sentient beings came to where the Buddha was to listen to the Dharma.

As for the coming of sentient beings: because their resonance and the Way meet, the Great Beings (Mahāsattvas) from other quarters do not come from afar, and the devas and humans of this land arrive according to conditions, appearing like clouds and dragons or wind and tigers. △ Fourth, the analogy of grasses and trees.
At that time, the Tathāgata observes the sharpness or dullness of the faculties and the diligence or indolence of these sentient beings.

Just as in the preceding analogy there were differences among the herbs and trees in their size, here in the application it is clarified that the faculties of the five vehicles have both sharpness and dullness, and their practice involves both diligence and indolence;
this precisely refers to the depth of the causal conditions for cultivation, which is identical in meaning to the analogy of the herbs and trees.
"At that time" refers to observing the opportune moment (*kāla*). If one discusses the beginning, it refers to the time of preaching the Small Vehicle at the Deer Park.

If one discusses the middle period, "at that time" may be applied to various instances. Regarding "the dull and the sharp": those in the three miserable realms (*apāya*) have evil causes and bitter fruits, and thus cannot receive the Path; they are considered dull.
Those of the seven stages of preparation (*saptavidha-prayoga*) who gain benefit upon hearing the teaching are considered sharp. [In another translation, the three miserable realms...]
To experience retribution until the end of kalpas is dullness (*mṛdu*). For humans and devas to possess clarity, intelligence, and wisdom is sharpness (*tīkṣṇa*).

Humans and devas merely receive karmic fruits and rewards; their refusal to accept the Way constitutes dullness. Those of the three vehicles (*triyāna*) who sever afflictions and transcend the realms constitute sharpness.

Regarding diligence and indolence: the negligence of those in the three miserable paths is indolence; for humans and devas, the observance of the five precepts and ten wholesome actions constitutes diligence. Humans and devas...

Not being weary of suffering is indolence; the fear of impermanence in the Two Vehicles is diligence. The greed of the Two Vehicles for their own realization while not seeking the fruit of Buddhahood is indolence;
the bodhisattva’s resolve to seek the Buddha-way is diligence. △ Fifth, the combined metaphor of receiving moisture.
He preaches the Dharma according to their respective capacities, in ways that are manifold and immeasurable, causing all to rejoice and swiftly obtain wholesome benefits.
"Preaching according to capacity" means preaching in accordance with the specific dispositions of the five vehicles:

for those capable of it, he teaches the precepts and wholesome deeds of humans and devas; for those capable of it, he teaches the truths, dependent origination, and the six perfections of the three vehicles, thereby bringing them joy.
"Beneficial benefit" refers to each of the five vehicles receiving the moisture of the Dharma and attaining its respective gain. △ Sixth, the analogy of growth:
"When these sentient beings have heard this Dharma... they gradually enter the Path according to their individual capacities."
Sentient beings of the five vehicles each hear the Dharma and each attain growth;

those who experience happiness in the present life include those in the three miserable realms who, upon hearing the Dharma, find their suffering stilled and their bitterness halted—this is peace and security in the present life—or those who are reborn among humans or devas.
This refers to being reborn in a favorable realm. Cultivating the Path among humans and devas is what constitutes experiencing happiness through that Path.
When humans and devas hear the Dharma and uphold the precepts, their merit supports their bodies, resulting in peace and security in the present life.

Whether born as devas in the heavens, born as humans in the human realm, or born interchangeably as both devas and humans, this constitutes being reborn in a favorable realm. Being born with the capacity for awakening and understanding [is further excellence].
They experience joy through the Way. Those of the Two Vehicles, upon hearing the Dharma, attain *sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*, thereby finding peace and security in the present life;
they are born in the Land of Expedient Means, which is a favorable rebirth for future lives, where they hear the sutras and likewise experience joy through the Way.
Bodhisattvas in their physical bodies, upon hearing the Dharma preached by Vairocana, attain the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*).

They immediately find peace and security in the present life and are born into the land of true retribution (*vipākabhūmi*), where they immediately give rise to wholesome states and experience bliss. Furthermore, those who attain bliss in the present life do so because the causes of their practice have induced the fruits of that practice.
Being free from all obstacles constitutes peace and security in the present life. As for those who enter the Path according to their capacity, this refers to the subsequent [state].

The world experiences happiness through the Way; this is also the case where a causal retribution elicits a resultant retribution. Furthermore, "experiencing happiness" explains peace and security, while "hearing the Dharma" explains being born in a favorable realm.

Moreover, as concluded below, those of the Two Vehicles are freed from the obstacle of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*), Bodhisattvas are freed from the two obstacles (*dvayāvaraṇa*), and humans and devas are freed from the obstacle of the three evil realms. Thus, these five types of beings each enter their respective paths within their respective teachings.
Thus concludes the six similes. △ Second, the application of the similes:
Just as that great cloud rains upon all [beings] (until) they are fully moistened and each attains growth.
The "Great Cloud" (Mahāmegha) Sūtra combines both form and sound to provide dual benefit, raining down upon all things. "Combining the rain" corresponds to the pouring of rain;
"herbs, trees, medicinal plants, and grasses" corresponds to sentient beings receiving transformation—whether they be of sharp or dull faculties, or indolent or diligent.

Adding these two phrases, "combining the moistening" corresponds to receiving benefit and attaining growth. "Combining the present-life peace and security" and so forth contains the meaning of the "land. △ Second.
The analogy of non-distinction consists of five parts. First, regarding the dharma of non-distinction: sentient beings receive its moisture but do not realize it;
the Tathāgata’s teaching is of a single characteristic and a single flavor (up to: the merit they obtain, they themselves do not perceive).
As for "one characteristic": the minds of sentient beings are identical to True Suchness; this is the "One Ground. As for "one flavor":
the Dharma of the One Vehicle equally elucidates a single principle; this is the "One Rain.

In the past, the One Reality-Characteristic was expediently opened into seven characteristics, and the Dharma of the One Vehicle was expediently taught as seven teachings. The Buddha knows that they ultimately all return to the One.
The marks are of one flavor. This is what is called the "lower" dual explanation. Regarding the mark of liberation: it is the absence of the mark of birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*).
Regarding the mark of detachment: it is the absence of the mark of nirvāṇa. Regarding the mark of cessation: it is the non-existence of even the mark of non-existence.

These are the three marks within the single mark. Furthermore, regarding the mark of liberation: it is the absence of the karmic bonds of the two extremes of *paricchinna-vaiparītya* (segmented change) and *pariṇāma-vaiparītya* (transformative change).

Regarding "characteristics" (*lakṣaṇa*): those who are free from characteristics attain the wisdom of the Middle Way, remaining far removed from the two extremes and having nothing to grasp or cling to. Regarding "the cessation of characteristics":
when the causes of the two extremes cease, one attains *nirvāṇa with remainder*; when the effects of the two extremes cease, one attains *nirvāṇa without remainder*.
These are the three marks within the single flavor. Furthermore, all phenomena (dharmas) are suchness; they share the same mark. Every thing is thoroughly saturated; this is the single flavor.
Sentient beings, having been moistened by the rain of Dharma, transcend their entanglements; this very dharma of one mark and one flavor is called the mark of liberation.
Having been moistened by the rain of Dharma, they depart from causes and conditions; this very one mark and one...
The Dharma of flavor is called "the signless. By being moistened by the rain of Dharma, one attains quiescence; this very single sign and single flavor of the Dharma is called the "sign of cessation.
Although there are three names, they ultimately all lead to the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*).
That is to say, in the end, one attains the fruit of omniscience (*sarvajña*). As the Great Sūtra says: "For example, all waters are of one [nature]."
Taste. Because it varies according to the vessel, water appears different; yet the Dharma taught by the Tathāgata is of but a single flavor.
Because the vessels of the minds of sentient beings differ, there are immeasurable distinctions. This refers to the Tathāgata’s contemplative knowledge of the ultimate destination of all phenomena.
The passage beginning with "Those who... clarifies that sentient beings do not know this, which corresponds precisely to what was stated above.
The distinction between grasses and trees refers to those among sentient beings who do not understand at all. "Dharma" here refers to the Dharma of a single sound.
Passages such as "if one maintains and recites it" clearly illustrate this lack of understanding; for since their maintenance and recitation differ, their practice likewise varies.

Those in the realms of humans and devas form the interpretation of precepts and wholesome deeds, while those of the Three Vehicles form the interpretation of the Truths, the Conditions, and the Six Perfections. Since these interpretations are already different, then...

Regarding the phrase "the merit thus obtained is not self-aware": this clarifies that the five individuals each received the benefit of the teaching, yet they did not know that the Buddha’s teaching was of a single sound without distinction.

This is ignorance of the Real (the *tathatā*). Furthermore, they were unaware that the practitioners of the seven stages of expedient means (*saptavidha-upāya*) each clung to their own understanding as being the truth.
This is ignorance of the Expedient (the *upāya*). Therefore, it is said that "it is not self-aware. △
Only the Tathāgata knows them as they truly are. Why is this?
Because only the Tathāgata perceives them as they truly are, with clarity and without obstruction.

There is only the "lower" [category], which is known by means of four dharmas: past causes are the seed; present appearances are the characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*); the primary substance is called the essence (*ātman*);
and that which does not change within its own category is called the nature (*prakṛti*). These seeds, characteristics, essences, and natures are each discussed according to the five vehicles;
as the five vehicles are each distinct, they constitute differentiation. The Tathāgata is able to know them as being, in truth, of one kind, one characteristic, one essence, and one nature.
Nature is itself without distinction; the Tathāgata is also able to know this. Difference is itself non-difference, and non-difference is itself difference; the Tathāgata is also able to know this.
Regarding the phrase "recalling what object," it refers to knowing by means of the three dharmas: mindfulness (*smṛti*), reflection (*manasikāra*), and cultivation (*bhāvanā*).

These are the three types of wisdom (*prajñā*): that which clearly remembers without forgetting is called mindfulness; that which involves silent mental contemplation is called reflection; and that which consists of earnest practice without indolence is called cultivation. What is the object?
This refers to the teachings one has received: those of small capacity contemplate the matters of humans and devas; those of middling capacity contemplate the matters of the two vehicles;
and those of superior capacity contemplate the matters of Bodhisattvas. The same applies to reflection and cultivation. What is this? It is the merit of diligent practice:
as those of small capacity contemplate by means of the five precepts and the ten wholesome dharmas, so those of middling capacity contemplate by means of the causes of the Four Noble Truths.
One contemplates by means of dharmas. Those of superior faculties contemplate by means of the dharma of the six perfections; the same applies to reflection and cultivation.

As for "by what dharma," this refers to employing which causes and conditions. For example, when contemplating humans and devas, one contemplates by means of the causes and conditions of meritorious retribution.
Those who contemplate the Two Vehicles do so by way of the causes and conditions of fearing suffering and seeking happiness;

those who contemplate Bodhisattvas do so by way of the causes and conditions of self-benefit and benefiting others. It is the same for reflection and cultivation. Regarding the three faculties and the three types of wisdom, there is distinction;
however, upon entering the perfect and subtle threefold wisdom, there is no distinction. By what dharma is one brought down? This is categorized according to two [levels].
Knowledge of dharmas: By what dharma is there a cause, and by what dharma is there a fruit? For example, the cause of precepts and goodness is the fruit of humans and devas;

the causes of the Truths, the Bases of Mindfulness, and the Perfections are the fruits of the Three Vehicles. The causes of the five vehicles each obtain their respective fruits—this is differentiation.
Sentient beings and all Buddhas are one suchness and not two suchnesses—this is non-differentiation. All dharmas abide in the lower [realm].
One knows by means of approximately one dharma. The seven stages of expedient means abide in seven positions; therefore, they are called "various grounds.
This constitutes their differentiation. The Tathāgata perceives them with his Buddha-eye as they truly are, clearly and without obstruction, just as all rivers flow into the ocean.

If the original flavor is lost, there is no distinction. When speaking in accordance with the intentions of others, the Tathāgata can know the distinctions through his wisdom and skillful means (*upāya*).
Yet, because all the teachings he expounds reach the stage of omniscience (*sarvajñatā-bhūmi*), the Tathāgata can also know their lack of distinction.
△ Third, an analogy is raised and applied to show that sentient beings do not understand this.
