In the introduction, Mañjuśrī cited his own past lives, wherein the disciples he transformed through the Way of the Lamp-Transmitting Illuminator have all now attained Buddhahood.
Herein, Śākyamuni cites his own past lives, wherein there were twelve hundred disciples whom he transformed through the Way of the Succession of Wisdom-Victory.

He shall attain Buddhahood. This is because, as it is said, "the Way of each Buddha is the same. It is only due to differences in conditions and circumstances that the titles of master and disciple, and their distances from one another, vary;
yet the causal conditions for their transformative teachings remain the same across past and present. △ Second, explaining the offerings of the various devas.
At that time, the various devas of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven first prepared for that Buddha (up to) his parinirvāṇa; it was likewise so.
"First prepared for them" refers to the period before he sat at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), when they first laid out the seat beneath the Bodhi tree.
"The Buddha at this seat" means that once the seat had been laid out, he further made a vow, saying: "The Buddha shall..."
It was upon this seat that he attained enlightenment. Whenever a Buddha attains enlightenment, the lords of the desire realm always provide the seat; this is the constant rule.

Regarding "as soon as he sat upon this seat," it refers to the various devas of the desire realm who, having merely provided the seat, were joined by the devas of the form realm who, from the moment the Buddha first sat at the site of enlightenment until his parinirvāṇa, rained down flowers as an offering. Furthermore, the Four Great Kings... [text continues]
The gods of the Yāma Heaven and others offered celestial music in worship; he too attained parinirvāṇa. As for "a hundred on each side," it means one hundred *yojanas* on each of the four sides.
△ Third, the formal explanation of the attainment of enlightenment.

The passage from "All the bhikṣus [heard] Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū Buddha" up to "attaining *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*" indicates that the manifestation of the Buddha-dharma is a provisional (*upāya*) teaching.
The subsequent section on "immediately reflecting and contemplating," etc., refers to the manifestation of provisional wisdom. IV.
The Offerings of the Retinue. This consists of both prose and verse. First, the prose explains the offerings of close attendance.
Before that Buddha left the household life, he had sixteen sons (up to: who with single-minded devotion joined their palms and gazed up at the World-Honored One.

The eight sons of Dīpaṃkara and the sixteen of Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū both represent the eight consciousnesses within the bonds of saṃsāra. Because these correspond to those of superior faculties, who are upright and not deviant, there are only eight.
This [case] corresponds to those of inferior faculties, where the deviant and the upright are mixed together; hence it is said there are sixteen. [This refers to] Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū.

The father represents original enlightenment (*prakṛti-awakening*), while the sons represent initial enlightenment (*ādi-awakening*). The relationship between father and son signifies that initial wisdom arises based upon the principle of the fundamental nature.

Furthermore, the fact that the son leaves the household life signifies that one accords with original enlightenment by means of initial enlightenment. Regarding the mention of "the first" among the sixteen, this refers to the eldest to include the younger brothers.
As for "Jñānakūṭa" (Wisdom-Peak), it is so called because true wisdom is endowed with merits as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. Thus it is said.

Furthermore, the father’s name is Jñānavijaya (Wisdom-Victory) and the son’s name is Jñānakūṭa (Wisdom-Peak); these names correspond to the mind of the causal stage and the awakening of the resultant stage, respectively.
As for the various rare treasures, they are the heritage of dragons and phoenixes; their ultimate luxury and desire certainly exceed anything reached by worldly people.
They provide the utmost pleasure for the ears and eyes, satisfy the delights of the mouth and body, and possess the splendor of palatial dwellings.

How magnificent! Among the charms and grace of palace ladies, there is nothing that is not a precious plaything. Yet, we hear that when his father attained the Way, he abandoned these treasures and departed;
this shows that he esteemed honor lightly and valued the Way above all.

Wealth and status are what people desire—this is the common sentiment of the world—but to view them as floating clouds is the resolve of the *sage-poets* (*sāo-ren*). Such individuals transcend worldly affairs with their lofty spirits, their liberated wills directed toward the Great Way.
If one does not cast off body and form like a discarded bundle of books, and regard the world as small like a worn-out sandal, who could act in such a way?
Furthermore, worldly affection is impermanent and the span of a natural life is limited;

to suddenly abandon the path of conditioned existence in order to seek the principle of the unconditioned—to repay one's parents through worldly ways provides benefit for only a single lifetime, whereas to repay one's parents through the Buddha-dharma... [provides benefit for all time].
It will benefit beings for ten thousand kalpas; therefore, he abandoned worldly affection and departed from it.

This was not a lack of filial piety, but rather what is called "excellently continuing his father's will and excellently recounting his deeds"—is this not the ultimate expression of filial piety? As for those who wept as they saw him off, they were his various mothers.
Since she was not born from a single mother, she is called "all" (zhū). Because of the affection of flesh and bone, it is difficult to sever or abandon;
the sentiment of longing causes the innermost organs to collapse in pain, and the traces of this bitterness manifest through all the bodily apertures.
Thus, one weeps and escorts her away. Loving her son, she also draws near to her husband to accomplish the Way. The Royal Ancestor followed her to that place.

As for those who possess the Way, even a father cannot claim them as his own son. That ministers and the people also come to such a state is because the superior acts and the subordinates follow suit.
There was one who, leaning upon this father-king, prostrated himself at his feet;
when the king returned the bow as if he were his parent, Master Lien asked, "What is your name? He replied, "I am not worthy. [The Master said,] "You are about to achieve Perfect Enlightenment."
"No," he replied, "I dare not. Wait until you have attained perfect enlightenment and sat for ten kalpas;
it will not be too late to receive the prostrations of your parents upon your assuming the rank of a Great Universal Buddha. You should know that 'returning' means 'reverting.

This refers to the case where the parents at home do not accept the ritual obeisance of their child who has left the household, but instead return that ritual to them. As for the one who has left the household, they say: 'These are my parents; they are the ones to whom I should pay homage.'"
The parents said, "This is a son of the Buddha; you should return his prostration. Furthermore, this text does not clarify that Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū did not accept the prostration from his father.
According to the current account of the Buddha’s attainment of enlightenment, eight years later he returned to his home country and preached the Dharma for his father king.

King Śuddhodana, leading all the ministers and subjects of the entire kingdom, went out a great distance to welcome and see the Buddha. Unconsciously, they prostrated themselves. The Buddha then leaped into the air.
He vanished from sight. Having paid his respects, he then manifested his form and inquired whether the King was at ease.
△ Second, the verses of praise and celebration consist of eight lines, divided into three parts. The first three and a half lines praise the Buddha’s causes and effects.
It is expressed in verse as follows:

"The World-Honored One of Great Majestic Virtue, for the sake of delivering sentient beings... abides in the untainted Dharma. His majesty is such that he is without anger yet possesses awe-inspiring power;

thus he is called "Great Majestic Virtue" (Mahātejas). His transformative influence is pervasive, vast, and profound; thus he is called "Great Virtue" (Mahāguṇa). He acts to subdue the unruly and to gather in those to be trained.
That upon which all things depend is called the World-Honored One. "To deliver those below" refers to the virtue of causal practice; "fully endowed" signifies the perfection of that causal practice.
"Excellent" (Sādhu) refers to the virtue of the fulfillment of the fruit; because the myriad virtues are purely immaculate, it is called "Excellent.
Because all who behold him obtain benefit, it is called "Supreme Auspiciousness. "Seated alone" explains the aforementioned rarity. [The five faculties...]

Because one does not take external objects as conditions, the body and hands do not move. Because the eight consciousnesses have already departed from internal defilement, the mind is constantly serene and tranquil;
this is the meaning of "peaceful stillness" (*āśvasta*). It is like the clear moon in an autumn sky, its cold radiance boundless.

When principle reaches its ultimate and emotion is exhausted, there is nothing further for study to apply; this is called "ultimate" (*niṣṭhā*). When the seeds and manifestations of the two obstacles are both extinguished, it is called "quiescence" (*śānti*). As for the fruits of the two deaths...
When retribution is exhausted, it is called "extinction. Because one realizes this path once and for all until the end of the future, it is called "eternal.
By transforming the defiled dharmas of the conditioned, they become entirely the merit of inherent purity; thus, it is said that one "abides securely in untainted dharmas.
(The first two lines celebrate what one has encountered.)
Now, seeing that the World-Honored One has attained the Way of Buddhahood in peace and security—up until never again hearing the name of a Buddha—they see the Buddha and hear the Dharma;
therefore, it is said they have obtained "beneficial gain. The single character "good" (śubha) refers to the untainted dharmas of teaching, principle, practice, and fruit:
hearing the teaching and awakening to the principle, practicing in accordance with the principle, and realizing the fruit through practice. These constitute such beneficial gains.

One will certainly be able to achieve success; hence it is said that "one attains" [it]. Sunk within the six realms of existence, one is constantly scorched by the three obstacles and is thus perpetually afflicted with suffering and distress.
To lack the eye of wisdom is called "blindness," and for delusive objects to be like the night is called "darkness. All sentient beings are deluded regarding both phenomena and persons;
since both mind and objects are obscured, they are described as "blind and dark. Because they do not encounter a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) to provide instruction, [they remain in this state].

There is no guide. Consequently, they are filled with confusion and obscurity; though they loathe suffering, they do not know the path to its exhaustion. They endure birth and death and do not seek liberation.
Throughout the long night of the three realms, it is like a dream or a drunken stupor.

Among the six destinies, only those of humans and devas belong to the wholesome; yet among sentient beings who create karma, those who fall into the evil realms are many, while those born into the good paths are few. Thus, [the former] increase.
It is diminished; therefore, it is impaired. Passing from one birth to receive another, they do not escape the evil realms; hence it is said, "from darkness entering into darkness.

Constantly obstructed by the eight difficulties, they do not hear the name of the Buddha. Those who are about to encounter the Buddha but have not yet had the opportunity to see Him are like the flying weasel before the dark.
Those who have already encountered the Buddha but do not wish to hear of Him are like the subsequent existence of Kāśyapa. Thus it is.
To see the Buddha and yet fail to recognize him is like the followers of the six heretical teachers. Such deluded people—how could this be caused by their innate nature?
It is rather driven by the habituation of blindness. △ Third, a summary in one line and a half.
"Now the Buddha has attained the most supreme, peaceful, and untainted path" (up to) "I take refuge in the Unsurpassed Honored One.

The first two lines conclude the Buddha’s realization of the fruit. The next two lines celebrate both oneself and others. The final two lines provide a general conclusion of taking refuge with sincerity.
△ Fifth, the request to turn the Wheel of Dharma.
At that time, after the sixteen princes had praised the Buddha in verse, they spoke these verses once more:
"O Hero among Men, peerless and unequaled, adorned by a hundred merits... [until] you shall turn the unsurpassed wheel."
Having previously recited his virtues, [the petitioner] now requests that he turn the wheel of Dharma, desiring to hear the teaching in order to attain the fruit of sainthood.
Regarding the "wheel of Dharma" (*dharmacakra*): both the term and its metaphor are presented here. A "wheel" refers to a chariot wheel, which possesses the functions of transporting and crushing.

The teachings of the Tathāgata can transport sentient beings from the state of ordinary beings to that of the sages, and can crush and subdue all the afflictive obscurations of sentient beings. Furthermore,
Where a carriage passes, even a praying mantis cannot block its tracks. This is a metaphor for when the Great Teaching is proclaimed, demons and heretics cannot obstruct it.
Furthermore, thirty spokes converge in a single hub; it is in the emptiness at the center that the utility of the carriage lies.

The Buddha’s preaching of the Dharma is like wind in the sky or a painting on air—though preached, there is no preaching—and thus it possesses the utility of benefiting all beings. Exquisitely outstanding.
He stands beyond the six directions; thus he is called the World Hero (*loka-vīra*). "Peerless" means that among the four heavens there is none whose merit can equal his;

"matchless" means that among the ten sages (*daśārya*) there is none whose wisdom can reach his. "A hundred merits" refers, in terms of the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*), to the thirty-two marks (*dvātriṃśan-lakṣaṇa*).

In terms of the *saṃbhogakāya*, this refers to the ninety-six marks of a great man (*mahāpuruṣa*). "To deliver myself and others" expresses the intent that self and others may realize [enlightenment] together.

"For the sake of discernment," etc., means that one vows to manifest and reveal [the Dharma] according to the four *siddhārtha* (purposes) to suit the capacities of beings, so that we may hear, understand, contemplate, and practice it, thereby also attaining this wisdom.
Wisdom is precisely the *prajñāpāramitā*. [This concludes] the cultivation of merit.

This includes the five perfections. The two phrases of the World-Honored One constitute the request for him to preach the Dharma according to the capacity of the listeners. That which is contemplated and practiced is the capacity for the Way;
the power of wisdom and the power of merit are the substance for receiving the Way; and past-life karma is the cause for attaining the Way.
Each [being] has their own varying degrees of capacity—great or small, shallow or deep—and the Buddha knows them all. He shall preach the Dharma in accordance with these capacities.
Once the Greatly Penetrating Wisdom Buddha had completed his attainment of the Way: △ Next, the explanation of the invitation by the Brahma Kings of the ten directions is divided into two parts.
First, the majestic light shines forth and moves all.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus: "From the time the Buddha Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū [attained enlightenment] until his light filled the world, surpassing the radiance of all the devas...
one returns to Bodhi through non-attainment. What is now called 'attainment' is merely the attainment of non-attainment.
This world is a common manifestation produced by the collective karma of sentient beings; it is obstructed and not permeable, solid and difficult to move, blocking one's own true nature."

This is the wisdom of the original source. Therefore, when the Buddhas attain enlightenment, they first move the ground of sentient beings that is difficult to move, manifesting the breaking of darkness to reveal the light of wisdom.
As for "the middle," it refers to the space between the Iron Ring Mountains (*Cakravāḍa*).

That "the sun and moon cannot illuminate it" means it is shrouded by the obstructions of evil karma. That "it all becomes greatly bright" means it becomes luminous because of the Buddha’s attainment of enlightenment.
Sentient beings have long dwelt in darkness, each unaware of the others. Once they were graced by the Buddha’s light, they were all able to see one another;
thus, they marveled, saying, "How is it that sentient beings have suddenly appeared here? The *Sutra on Cause and Effect* states:

"When Siddhārtha was dwelling in the womb, the three thousandfold world-system was filled with a brilliant, vast radiance. Where the sun and moon do not shine, all became brilliantly illuminated. Within this...
Sentient beings were each able to see one another; it was the same when [the Buddha] first attained the Way.

This light extended horizontally across five hundred myriads of koṭis of lands, and vertically from the peak of existence above each land down to the Avīci Hell below—identical to the present single ray of light shining to the east.
That Buddha represents the beginning, and the present Buddha represents the end; through this mutual manifestation, the primordially inherent nature is revealed.
This is the Greatly Penetrating Wisdom-Victor (Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū). Furthermore, once sentient beings have received the Buddha’s light, there are none who do not obtain benefit.
As the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states: "The Bodhisattva emits light from the soles of his feet, illuminating the hells;

sentient beings who receive this light are all reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, where they hear the Dharma being preached by celestial drums and immediately realize the ten stages (*bhūmi*). The present sutra is likewise: wherever the Buddha’s light shines, it must be...

Those who have planted the seeds of affinity in past lives and once receive this light will surely be freed from suffering if they have not yet left it, and will surely escape from calamity if they have not yet been delivered from it.

One should know that where this light shines, its grace is never bestowed in vain. Furthermore, below this, it clarifies the trembling of the Brahma palaces, wherein the light surpasses that of the heavens.
△ Section Twenty: The Invitation by the Brahmas of the Ten Directions, divided into two parts; first, the clarification of the nine directions.

Next, the upper direction is clarified. This "Invitation by the Brahmās of the Ten Directions" is an expansion of the section on the Expedient Means (*upāya*) in the preceding chapter, concerning the request for the Dharma by the various devas.

Furthermore, the statement that they arrive from the ten directions in succession implies that their presence was not manifested instantaneously. To speak according to ultimate reality (*tattva*), the light of the ten directions shines simultaneously;
they see one another at the same time, deliberate together at the same time, and seek out the light at the same time.

They pay homage to the Buddha; there is no sequence of before or after. Furthermore, within the nine directions, they are divided into four parts. First, the gathering of clouds in the eastern direction is further divided into seven sections.
First, the Wisdom Buddha manifests auspicious omens.
At that time, five hundred *koṭis* in the eastern direction [up to] were illuminated by a radiance twice as bright as the usual light.

This "usual light" refers to the light of the heavens. As for the term "twice as bright," it means that the Buddha’s light is the functioning of the outflow-free (*anāsrava*), and thus it is twice as bright as the outflow-bound (*sāsrava*) bodily light of the heavens.
△ Second, the astonishment of the Brahma hosts.
Each of the Brahma Kings had this thought: (up to) "By what cause and condition has this sign appeared?
△ Third, mutual inquiry and resolution.
At that time, the various Brahma Kings (up to) spoke these verses for the sake of the assembly of Brahmas.
"The radiance of our various palaces is such as has never been seen before, illuminating the ten directions.
As for the one called "the Great Virtuous One born in heaven," he is a Bodhisattva in his final birth who, being about to dwell in the world, was first born in Tuṣita.
A great radiance was emitted. Because of this extraordinary omen, there must surely be an extraordinary person appearing. △ Fourth, seeking the light, he beholds the Buddha.
At that time, [the light reached] five million billion lands... and he also saw the sixteen princes entreating the Buddha to turn the wheel of the Dharma.
Seeing the Buddha at the site of enlightenment, he finally realized that the light he had previously seen was not from the Great Virtuous Deva, but was the light of a Buddha appearing in the world.
Brahmā then reflected upon this, consulted with his peers, and sought him out; seeing the Buddha, he requested the Dharma.

Compared to the sentient beings in the dark realms mentioned before, this was a sudden and startling transformation—a true chasm between clouds and mud. △ Fifth, the extensive presentation of offerings.
Immediately, the Brahma Kings prostrated themselves with their heads at the Buddha’s feet (up to: with single-mindedness and in unison, they praised him in verse, saying:
"The World-Honored One is most rare and difficult to encounter (up to: we only pray that you will compassionately accept [our offerings]."
Regarding "making offerings both to the Buddha and to the tree": the tree is that upon which the Buddha relies; to revere the tree is truly to revere the person.

It is like the sentiment of the people who could not bear to cut down the sweet-tangerine trees (*gan-tang*). The tree is ten *yojanas* in height, the seat is one *yojana*, and the flowers are like Mount Sumeru.
What are their characteristics? One should know them to be inconceivable matters, where this and that do not obstruct one another. Furthermore, it is like...

"Mountain" (*śaila*) signifies "most abundant"; it does not mean that [the compassion] is actually like a mountain. Just as one uses "deep" to describe the ocean and "high" to describe a mountain, these are all terms used to express the ultimate degree of manifestation.
"Receptacle" (*ādhāra*) means "to retain. The first four lines of the verse praise the compassionate mind. "Attainment of the Way" is called "virtue" (*guṇa*);
"benefiting both [self and others]" is called "merit" (*puṇya*). "Incalculable" means its number cannot be known; it accords with the principle of the *dharmadhātu* and is without limit.
"Without deficiency. It is said: "Complete. His compassionate salvation is vast and far-reaching; there is no being that does not receive his transformation. It is said: "Saving all.

The four lines beginning with "Heavenly and Human" praise his compassionate mind. He encompasses the five vehicles without missing their essential timing (*ji*), and he brings the six realms to completion through subtle perfection without leaving anyone behind.
His words possess the Dharma, and his actions possess the rule. It is said: "Teacher of Gods and Humans. [The suffering of] the three evil karmas is the cause...
When light gathers them, they immediately find rest; those of the five natures who drift in the deep current borrow the oar of wisdom to reach the shore.

Thus it is said, "Universally Beneficial. Regarding the passage from "The place from which he comes" downward: this clarifies the sincerity of his purpose in coming. From afar he hastened toward the Dharma, not sparing his own toil.
His heavenly fortune was extraordinary, such that he abandoned the bliss of the four dhyānas and humbled himself to come, for the sake of making offerings to the Buddha.
In previous lives, [the donor] sought to have their sincerity reflected upon so that their offerings might be accepted.

Thus, the palaces—produced by their own past merits and originally for their own enjoyment—are now offered to the Buddha. By means of these fruits of out-flowing existence (*sāsrava*), they create the causes for the out-flow-free (*anāsrava*).
△ Sixth, the request to turn the Wheel of Dharma.
At that time, after the Brahma kings had praised the Buddha with verses, they spoke these verses with one mind and a single voice:
"O Hero among Men, Honored One among the Two-legged, we pray that you will expound the Dharma; by means of your great compassion and power, deliver all suffering beings."
△ 7. Silent Acceptance.
At that time, the Tathāgata Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū silently granted his consent.
This silent acceptance is the ritual for Buddhas when receiving an invitation; such is the natural law (*dharmatā*). There are four meanings [to this]: first, compliance...

First, because it follows the rules established by previous Buddhas; second, because it causes people to respect and yearn for it with thirsting devotion; third, because it differs from that of ordinary people and non-Buddhists;
fourth, because it enables one to perceive the Way through direct observation—these are the benefits of the four *siddhāntas*.
△ Second, the gathering of clouds from the southeast, which has seven parts. First, the manifestation of auspicious signs by the Wisdom Buddha.
Furthermore, the light from the palaces of five million billion [Brahma-kings] in the southeast shone brilliantly.
△ Second, the assembly of Brahmās was struck with awe;
they were filled with unprecedented joy and leaped for gladness, giving rise to a sense of wonder.
As before, each of the Brahmās should form such thoughts; the following sections are all to be treated accordingly. △ Third, mutual inquiry and resolution:
they each went to one another’s abodes to deliberate on this matter (up to) speaking these verses for the assembly of Brahmās.
For what cause and condition do these signs appear in such a manner? (Up to: To deliver sentient beings from suffering, there must necessarily be an extraordinary person;
only then can there be such extraordinary portents. Judging by this, it is certainly not born of heaven, but is most likely the appearance of a Buddha.
[The passage] "passing through thousands of myriads of koṭis" states that this light does not belong to this land.

One should seek it by passing through thousands of myriads of koṭis of lands; yet one must know that although one passes through thousands of myriads of lands, it fundamentally does not depart from its original location.
△ Fourth, seeing the Buddha by following the light.
At that time, five million billion Brahma Kings (up to) requested the Buddha to turn the wheel of Dharma.
△ Fifth, the extensive presentation of offerings:
At that time, the Brahma Kings bowed their heads at the Buddha’s feet (up to) with single-mindedness and one voice, they praised him in verse, saying:
The Holy Lord, King among Gods, with a voice like that of the kalaviṅka (until: Now we have encountered the World-Honored One.
"Holy Lord" (*ārya-svāmin*) refers to one revered by the multitude of sages; "King" (*rāja*) refers to one honored by the Four Heavenly Kings.

Because he governs and rules over the ten realms as a sage of the ultimate fruit, his Brahma-voice is resonant and majestic; thus he is compared to the *kalaviṅka*, here called the "Bird of Wondrous Sound."
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "While the kalaviṅka bird is still within its shell and has not yet emerged, the sound it produces is subtle and exquisite, surpassing that of all other birds.
The *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna-sūtra* says: "Such beautiful voices cannot be matched by either gods or humans, except for the voice of the Tathāgata.
In the three evil realms and elsewhere, evil beings are many while virtuous beings are few; this is according to the fruits they have induced through their respective causes.
Sentient beings are blind and obscured; they have lost right view and do not know the essential way out. The Buddha points it out for them and leads them forth.
Therefore, it is said that he acts as the eye for sentient beings. He does not initiate holy works on their behalf, but nurtures living beings like a parent:
those who have already entered the evil paths, he rescues and brings out; those who have not yet entered the evil paths, he protects so that they do not enter. Thus, he is called "compassionate."
This is for the benefit [of all beings]. △ Sixth, the request to turn the Wheel of Dharma.
At that time, after the Brahma Kings had praised the Buddha in verse, they spoke these verses with one mind and a single voice:
The Great Sage turns the wheel of Dharma to reveal the characteristics of all phenomena (up to: for those who are well-established in patience, there is increase).
The Great Sage is the one who preaches the Dharma; the wheel of Dharma is the Dharma that is preached. The Dharma possesses both sudden and gradual aspects regarding its nature and characteristics;

it is expounded according to the capacities of beings to deliver suffering sentient beings, so that they may leave suffering behind and attain happiness. Those who attain the Way are the three vehicles.
The "worthy and noble ones" (āryas) are those who receive blessings, namely the various devas of the three realms; therefore, those in the evil paths are few while those who are virtuous are many.
As for "those who endure and do good," it means that they are able to hear the Buddha-dharma and exert themselves in performing wholesome deeds. △ Seventh: Silent Acceptance.
At that time, the Tathāgata Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū silently granted his consent.
△ Third, the gathering from the south. This section also has seven parts; first, the manifestation of auspicious signs by the Buddhas of Wisdom.
Furthermore, the bhikṣus [of the south]—five million billion [in number]... each saw their own palaces illuminated with brilliant light.
△ 2. The assembly of Brahmās was struck with amazement;
they experienced unprecedented joy and exultation, giving rise to a sense of wonder.
△ 3. They questioned one another to resolve their doubts.
They immediately went to one another and deliberated on this matter (until) they spoke these verses for the sake of the assembly of Brahmās:
"The radiance of our various palaces is exceedingly majestic and brilliant... (until) it is because a Buddha has appeared in the world."
△ 4. Seeking Light and Seeing the Buddha.
At that time, five million billion Brahma Kings (up to) entreated the Buddha to turn the wheel of Dharma.
△ 5. Extensively Presenting Offerings.
Then the Brahma Kings prostrated themselves with their heads at the Buddha’s feet (until: with one mind and in unison, they praised him in verse, saying:
“The World-Honored One is most difficult to behold, he who has shattered all afflictions (until: we only pray that you will graciously accept [our offering].”
He preaches the Dharma to shatter the delusive obstructions of sentient beings, enabling them to attain the unsurpassed fruit.

Furthermore, because he uses samādhi to destroy afflictions, he appears but once every one hundred and thirty kalpas; thus it is said that he is "extremely difficult to see. This implies that vast ages have passed since his last appearance.
Now, at last, we have been able to see it once. Sentient beings do not partake of the flavor of the Dharma; they are like those who suffer from hunger and thirst.

When the Tathāgata preaches the Dharma, sentient beings who hear it are like those who find food when hungry or drink when thirsty; their long-standing hunger and emptiness from kalpas past are instantly dispelled.
Sentient beings do not receive the holy moisture; they are like withered grass and trees.

Upon hearing the wondrous Dharma even once, they are able to resolve their minds toward enlightenment and cultivate the causes to achieve the fruit—like grass and trees that encounter rain, which wither no more but flourish and bear flowers and fruit, arriving without being expected.

In the former phrase there is the capacity [to respond] but no teaching; in the latter phrase there is the teaching but no capacity. What was stated previously was an exclamation on the difficulty of encountering a Buddha.
[We] encounter [this opportunity]. We pray that you will graciously accept it. △ Sixth, Requesting the Turning of the Wheel of Dharma.
At that time, after the Brahma Kings had praised the Buddha in verse (up to), they with one mind and in unison recited these verses:
"I only pray that the Honored One among Gods and Humans will turn the unsurpassed Wheel of Dharma" (up to) "you shall now proclaim the profound and far-reaching sound.

The first two phrases constitute the request for the Dharma; the striking [of the instruments] in the third phrase is a metaphor. The drum takes the sense of inciting and stimulating; the conch takes the sense of issuing commands;
the rain takes the sense of moistening and nourishing. The power of the teaching is able to cause sentient beings to shatter delusions and repel Māra.
Breaking through the heavy encirclement is like the drum urging on the warriors. The proclamation of the Dharma-sound causes those afar to rejoice and those nearby to assemble;
they gather in great numbers to receive the Way, as if hearing the conch and gathering to listen to the command. Thus, he preaches the Dharma with a single voice.

Each according to their kind attains understanding; there is none who does not enter the Way. It is like the single rain from the *Bhagavat*, which, though falling as one, is received differently by each terrain, each obtaining its own nourishment.

When the Tathāgata preaches the Dharma, there are two benefits: those pertaining to form and those pertaining to sound. Like a wish-fulfilling jewel or the king of medicinal trees, the benefit conferred is vast and manifold;
therefore, it is said that he delivers immeasurable sentient beings. In the speech of the Sages, what is valued lies in meeting the needs of others.
The "trigger" (ji) refers to something near that points toward something distant; there is flavor within the plainness. Hence it is called the "profound and far-reaching sound.
△ Seventh, silent assent:
At that time, the Tathāgata Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū silently granted his permission.
△ Fourth, a general explanation of the gathering from the six directions.
It is the same for the southwest, and so on, down to the nadir.
The southwest, west, northwest, north, northeast, and nadir—these six directions follow the preceding example. All seven sections are thus.
The same. △ Next, the gathering from the upper direction is explained, divided into six parts. First, the manifestation of auspicious signs by the Wisdom Buddhas:
At that time, in five million billion lands of the upper direction... (up to) ...the palaces where they reside were radiantly illuminated with majestic light.
△ 2. The assembly of Brahmās was struck with awe;
they experienced unprecedented joy and exultation, giving rise to a sense of wonder.
△ 3. They questioned one another to resolve their doubts.
They immediately went to one another and deliberated on this matter (until) they spoke these verses for the assembly of Brahmās:
"By what cause and condition have all our palaces [appeared]... because a Buddha has appeared in the world."
△ 4. Seeking Light and Seeing the Buddha.
At that time, five million billion Brahma Kings (through) requested the Buddha to turn the wheel of Dharma.
△ 5. Extensively Presenting Offerings.
Then the Brahma Kings bowed their heads at the Buddha’s feet (and so forth), and with one mind and in unison, they praised him in verse:
"Excellent is the sight of all Buddhas, the Holy Honored Ones who save the world (and so forth), until all together attain the Way of the Buddha."
The final two lines, beginning with "Excellent! (*sādhu*), praise the Buddha’s grace and virtue. "Excellent" is a term expressing one's own good fortune.

Because he delivers sentient beings through boundless Dharma-gates, he is called the "Savior of the World. Sentient beings are submerged in birth and death, revolving within it without finding an exit.
Therefore, it is likened to a prison. Within a prison, one does not forcibly detain those who are innocent; likewise, the three realms are entirely composed of those who are self-deluded.

By means of the two gates of exhortation and admonition, one causes them to exit the three realms; hence, it is said, "exerting oneself to exit. The two wisdoms illuminate all phenomena without omission, which is called "universal wisdom" (*samantabhadra-jñāna*).
As for "the multitude of sprouts": although sentient beings may be wicked, they do not sever their inherent goodness. This is likened to grasses and trees.
Sprouts: Although they may be damaged and destroyed, it is not that no new shoots will grow. Ambrosia (*amṛta*) is the medicine for eternal life;
it serves as a metaphor for how the Buddha-dharma inevitably realizes the fruit of true permanence. The *Zongjing* (Mirror of the Source) says: "There is a tree of ambrosia.

On the fifteenth day of the eighth month, dew drips onto its leaves. People gather it to use as the medicine for eternal life. If it enters the earth, it transforms into pearls. As it is said: [The text continues with the analogy of the pearl].

When people hear the Dharma and it enters their consciousness, it is transformed into the seed of Bodhi. In the four and a half lines following "In the past," the bitter fruits of the three realms are clarified.
Within the verses of the various devas, it is said that there were one hundred and eighty kalpas, one hundred and thirty kalpas, and again, immeasurable kalpas.
From this, one may truly know that the Buddha-body is omnipresent and manifests at all times.
It is merely due to what is evoked by conditions that there arise perceptions of prolongation or brevity, and of birth or extinction.

When physical strength and vitality diminish, the form becomes inferior, wretched, and ugly, and no longer possesses noble marks. When wisdom decreases, the mind becomes defiled by false dharmas, and right wisdom no longer exists.
All this is brought about by their own sinful karma. They fail to obtain the blessings of humans and devas and lose their happiness.
Taking suffering to be pleasure, they do not know to cultivate the causes for future bliss; thus, they lose the perception of happiness.

Dwelling in the heterodox and false teachings of external paths, they do not recognize the protocols of the sages nor receive the transformative guidance of the Buddhas. Consequently, they wander through birth and death, constantly falling into evil realms.
The Way. The Buddha, for the sake of those in the three lower realms, rejoices in their auspicious encounter. With the vow that follows, he dedicates [the merit] to all sentient beings.
All the Brahmā deities follow this pattern; each contains a passage regarding such dedication. △ Sixth, the Request to Turn the Wheel of Dharma.
At that time, five million billion Brahma Kings (up to) then the Brahma Kings spoke these verses:
"The World-Honored One turns the Wheel of Dharma and beats the drum of the nectar-like Dharma... [up to] having practiced the Dharma for immeasurable kalpas."
The Dharma drum of ambrosia causes those who are about to die to hear its sound and not die, and those already dead to be restored to life.
Those "about to die" are ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*); those "already dead" are those who have abandoned all roots of goodness (*icchantika*).

One who has practiced the Dharma for immeasurable eons refers to the Buddha’s own realization through cultivation over long kalpas; may he speak according to that which he has realized. O Brahma Kings of the ten directions!
There were various kinds of Buddha-activities. Their intention was focused solely on seeking the light to see the Buddha.
Since every person possesses this light and each individual possesses this Buddha, it is only because they do not know the origin of the light that they are unable to see the Buddha.
If one knows where the light comes from, then seeing the Buddha is not far off. Therefore, the devas formed this thought, all saying: "By what cause..."
Due to these conditions, this manifestation appeared. Looking west from the east, or looking north from the south, one was merely tracing this single segment of light;
it was neither here nor there, having no fixed location. Looking west, it was in the east; looking north, it was in the south.
It seemed to be before one’s eyes, yet suddenly was behind one. In truth, it did not depart from the side of the Buddha of Great Pervasion. In truth...
It does not depart from the single thought-moment of the person present. This is why all the Brahma Kings, upon seeing the Buddha for the first time, immediately rejoiced and offered praise.
The preceding section on the distant causes for establishing karmic connections is concluded. △ Second, explaining the proximate causes for establishing karmic connections.

This is divided into two parts: first, the turning of the *ardhākṣara* (half-syllable) teaching; second, the turning of the *pūrṇākṣara* (full-syllable) teaching. The first part is further divided into three sections. First, the Wisdom-Buddha accepts the invitation.
At that time, the Tathāgata Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū [accepted the invitation] up until the request made by the sixteen princes;

this is the proximate cause for establishing the karmic connection. Because the Buddha accepted their invitation and preached the Dharma, the princes were later able to provide a detailed exposition of it.

He was then performing the formal establishment of karmic affinity. △ Second, the actual turning of the teaching, which is further divided into two parts. First, he preached the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths.
At that moment, he turned the Wheel of Dharma in its three revolutions and twelve aspects (extending from) "This is suffering" up to "This is the path to the cessation of suffering."
This was the initial turning of the Wheel of the Half-Syllables (*ardhākṣara*). As for the "three turnings," they consist of demonstrating, exhorting, and realizing.

"Demonstrating" means showing its characteristics, such as saying, "This is suffering, characterized by oppression, and so forth. "Exhorting" means urging one to practice, such as saying, "This is suffering; you should know it, and so forth.
"Realizing" means citing one's own realization as proof for the other, such as saying, "This is suffering; I have already known it."

Furthermore, regarding "knowing and so forth": for those of dull faculties, the Śrāvakas, there are three turnings; for those of middling faculties, the Pratyekabuddhas, there are two turnings; and for those of sharp faculties, the Bodhisattvas, there is one turning.
Regarding the "three turnings and twelve aspects," there are two perspectives: First, in terms of teaching (*śāsana*):

this refers to each of the Four Noble Truths having its characteristics demonstrated, its practice exhorted, and its realization enjoined. These constitute the twelvefold Wheel of the Dharma-teachings. Second, in terms of practice (*caryā*): this refers to the three turnings applied to each of the Four Noble Truths.

In all cases, there arise eye, knowledge, clarity, and awakening; this is the Wheel of Dharma with twelve aspects. These consist of the receptivity to the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-kṣānti*), the knowledge of the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna*), the subsequent receptivity to the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-anvaya-kṣānti*), and the subsequent knowledge of the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-anvaya-jñāna*). Thus, for each of the [four] truths, there are four [moments], making sixteen.

Each of the three types of persons attains these sixteen moments of mind, resulting in forty-eight aspects. Here, we discuss the twelve aspects based on a single truth. I, the fool, call this the "three turnings."
These are the Four Truths. The twelve modes of activity are the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination. Herein, they are first indicated;

below, the Dharma of the Four Truths is explained first, followed by the Dharma of the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination. Let the wise examine this: the teaching and practice follow one another in succession to jointly destroy the obstacles of delusion—this is called "turning.
To turn these Dharmas so as to enter into the minds of others and cause them to attain awakening is called "turning."
The Wheel of the Dharma. If śramaṇas and others are incapable, then as śramaṇas they have not even heard it, let alone know it; how much less could they turn it?
Although brahmins have heard it, they do not understand its principle and likewise cannot turn it. Devas are attached to pleasure, Māras destroy the Dharma, and Brahmās are savoring dhyāna;
therefore, none of them can turn it. Only the Buddha can turn it, just as [only a sovereign] presides over ritual, music, and military expeditions.

The execution of punishment originates from the Son of Heaven; no other person may arrogantly exercise such authority on their own. This refers to the "suffering of the lower realms," which denotes the initial turning of the Wheel of the Four Noble Truths for the sake of the Śrāvakas.

These Four Noble Truths encompass both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna, as well as the partial and the perfect, including the truths of arising-and-ceasing, non-arising-and-non-ceasing, the immeasurable, and the unconditioned.
What is presented here is the Four Noble Truths of arising-and-ceasing. "Suffering" (duḥkha) has the meaning of being oppressed.
All conditioned mental activities are constantly oppressed and afflicted by the calamities of impermanence; therefore, they are called "suffering" (*duḥkha*).

This refers to the three types of suffering, the eight types of suffering, and so forth. "Origination" (*samudaya*) has the meaning of "invoking and eliciting"; it refers to the afflictions of views and thought.
These afflictions coexist with karma and are able to invoke birth and death; therefore, it is called "origination. Origination is the cause, and suffering is the fruit. The fruit must necessarily...
Because it is the cause, it is called the "accumulation of suffering. This refers to the causality of this world. "Cessation" has the meaning of extinguishing the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).

Once delusions and karma are exhausted, there is no longer the burden of birth and death; therefore, it is called the "cessation of suffering. The essence of the Truth of Cessation consists of the two types of *nirvāṇa*.
"Path" has the meaning of being able to lead [to liberation]. The Right Path and the Aids to the Path support one another, thereby being able to lead [the way].

Because it leads to *nirvāṇa*, it is called the "Path. Because the Path can extinguish suffering, it is said to be "the Path leading to the cessation of suffering. Briefly stated, this consists of morality (*śīla*), concentration (*samādhi*), and wisdom (*prajñā*);

extensively stated, it consists of the seven categories of the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*). The Path is the cause, and cessation is the fruit; this is the supramundane cause and effect.

The accumulation that gives rise to suffering is called the "origin of suffering" (*duḥkhasamudaya*); the extinction that exhausts suffering is called the "cessation of suffering" (*duḥkhanirodha*). Cessation of suffering...
The path to this [cessation] is called the "path to the cessation of suffering.

It cannot be called simply the "path of suffering," because the path does not produce suffering and is thus unlike the origin (samudaya), nor does it extinguish suffering and is thus unlike cessation (nirodha). Because it is able to realize the cessation of suffering, it is named the "path to the cessation of suffering."

△ Next, the Dharma of Dependent Origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) is explained, as well as the detailed exposition of the twelve links of dependent origination, up to: "With the cessation of birth, old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and affliction cease.

This constitutes the Pratyekabuddha’s turning of the twelve links of dependent origination. It expands upon the previous [explanation of] Suffering and its Accumulation as the gate of forward progression (*pravṛtti-mukha*).

The preceding explanation of the cessation of the path is expanded here as the gateway of reversal (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha). Regarding the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*), the terminology used in the sūtras and śāstras is not uniform.

They are variously termed "factors of existence" (*bhavāṅga*), "the fortified city," "the thorny enclosure," "the interconnected," or "the matter of suffering. Some speak of them as spanning three lifetimes, two lifetimes, or a single moment.
Those who speak of three lifetimes do so to refute the views of nihilism and eternalism. Those who speak of two lifetimes do so to refute attachment to a self. As for the single moment...
Because its nature is substantial and real, it is now explained by means of the two layers of cause and effect across the three periods of time.

They function as causes by successively inducing results, and they function as conditions by mutually depending upon one another. As for "ignorance" (*avidyā*): all afflictions of the past are ignorance;
their essence is delusion (*moha*). Because of this folly and delusion, one is confused and lacks clear understanding; therefore, it is called ignorance. That is to say:
"Delusion" (moha). "Volitional formations" (saṃskāra): they are called volitional formations because they universally involve the world's performance of various karmas.
Since karma is created by delusion, it is said that "ignorance conditions volitional formations. These two belong to the past causes. "Consciousness" (vijñāna) has the meaning of discernment;

because it is brought about by karma, it draws one into birth within the three realms. Through the deluded thoughts of the mental consciousness, one is entrusted to parents. Therefore, it is said that "volitional formations condition consciousness."

Once consciousness has entered the mother’s womb, it undergoes a transformation every seven days, forming mind and form (*nāmarūpa*). "Mind" refers to the mental faculty, and "form" refers to the physical substance;
thus, it is said that "consciousness conditions name-and-form. As for the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), after five weeks have passed, the six faculties are formed within this womb.

The sixth and seventh weeks are termed the stage of hair, body hair, nails, and teeth; the seventh week is termed the stage of the possession of faculties (*indriya*), because the five faculties are fully perfected.

Since the faculties have the sense of "entering" into their objects, they are called "entrances" (*āyatana*). Because the physical form and mind have achieved the six faculties, it is said that "name-and-form conditions the six [entrances]."
"Entering" refers to the period after birth, during the third or fourth year, when one has not yet attained cognitive clarity through the interaction of the sense faculties with their objects;
this is "contact" (*sparśa*). Therefore, it is said that the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) are the condition for contact. "Feeling" (*vedanā*) has the meaning of experiencing.

From the age of five or six until twelve or thirteen, due to the contact of the six sense objects with the six sense faculties, one experiences the qualities of the preceding objects, such as being pleasant or unpleasant.
Although one is able to discern, one has not yet been able to give rise to a mind of craving; therefore, it is said that "contact conditions feeling.
These five [aggregates] belong to the present fruit. "Craving" (tṛṣṇā) means the sense of greedy attachment.

From the fourteenth to the twentieth [moment], one craves various excellent requisites and objects such as sensual desires, though one has not yet extensively or universally pursued them. This is because of the experience of reception (vedanā). That is to say:
Craving arises; therefore, it is said that "feeling conditions craving. Grasping (*upādāna*) means the sense of pursuing and clinging.

From the twenty-first moment onward, whenever one perceives any object, a mind of grasping and attachment arises. Since attachment is produced from craving, it is said that "craving conditions grasping.
These two are afflictions (*kleśa*), identical in nature to the ignorance (*avidyā*) of the past. Existence (*bhava*) means that cause and effect do not perish. Having already clung to various...

Regarding the object (*viṣaya*): one initiates wholesome and unwholesome karma, which accumulates and draws forth rebirth within the three realms; thus it is said that "clinging conditions becoming" (*upādāna-pratyaya-bhava*). This [becoming] is itself karma and is identical to past formations (*saṃskāra*).
The aforementioned three [links] belong to present causes. As for "birth" (*jāti*): it refers to taking birth through the four modes of birth and the six destinies.
From "becoming," one again undergoes the birth of the five aggregates in a future life; thus it is said that "becoming conditions birth" (*bhava-pratyaya-jāti*).

"Old age and death" refers to the maturation and decay of the body that has undergone birth; these two belong to the future fruit, as sorrow, lamentation, and so forth, all pertain to old age and death.
This is the gate of forward progression (*pravṭti*). Below the phrase "the extinction of ignorance" is the gate of reversal (*nivṛtti*).

With respect to suffering and its origin (*duḥkha-samudaya*), there is ignorance up to old age and death; with respect to the path and its cessation (*mārga-nirodha*), there is the extinction of ignorance up to [the extinction of] old age and death.

The cessation of old age, death, and so forth is observed both in direct and reverse order. Since all these are rooted in ignorance (*avidyā*), when ignorance alone ceases, then volitional formations (*saṃskāra*) cease, and so on, up to the cessation of birth and the cessation of old age and death. In reality, one begins with old age and death and observes them in reverse order.
As the *Pratītyasamutpāda-sūtra* states: "Due to the existence of what does old age and death exist? Thus, regarding this old age and death..."
For what reason? The first phrase is the knowledge that investigates the cause; the second phrase is the knowledge that examines the cause.

Regarding these twelve factors, with the exception of the single factor of ignorance (*avidyā*), each possesses seven types of knowledge. This is because ignorance has no cause that can be investigated or examined.
First, one investigates old age and death: from what cause do they arise? Knowing that they arise from the cause of birth is the knowledge that investigates the cause. Next, regarding this old age...
Death. Furthermore, by what conditions [is this known]? This is the knowledge of the analytical cause (*nidāna-jñāna*), for it is subtler than mere inference.

There are two types of knowledge for each of the three times, making six; the seventh is the knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-jñāna*). Thus, there are seven knowledges for one branch, and seventy-seven knowledges for the eleven branches combined.
Question: All Buddhas teach the Three Vehicles; why is it not stated here that they teach the Six Perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*)? Answer: It is because now...

Because this discourse on the causes for establishing karmic connections is intended for those of inferior faculties, it does not reach the level of the Bodhisattvas. △ Third, attaining the Way through hearing the Dharma:
The Buddha was amidst a great assembly of devas and humans (up to) immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable in number.
One who does not accept any phenomena awakens to the truth that conditions are empty, exhausts all fetters of existence, and brings the consciousness to cessation;

thus, they realize there is nothing to which they are attached. For the mind is fundamentally liberated; it is burdened by the presence of reception (*vedanā*). Its nature is fundamentally luminous and pure, yet it becomes obscured by the presence of attachment.
By neither accepting nor attaching to any phenomena, one attains the fruit of liberation. Furthermore, one does not accept even a single [phenomenon].

"All dharmas" refers to the stage of the Path of Vision (*darśana-mārga*) of the first fruit, wherein one severs the eighty-eight proclivities (*anuśaya*). "All outflows" (*āsrava*) refers to the afflictions of both vision and cultivation (*dṛṣṭi- and bhāvanā-kleśa*).

"Liberation of mind" means being freed from the two bonds of the seeds and their fruits; having completely severed the afflictions of cultivation, one attains the stage of the fruit of No-more-learning (*aśaikṣa-phala*).

Through the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*), one severs delusion; through the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*), one realizes the principle. With cause extinguished and fruit lost, one realizes and enters the principle of emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
Because the mind has attained mastery, it is called liberation. Regarding "profound and wondrous meditative concentration":

for the followers of the Two Vehicles, the cultivation and refinement through the nine successive stages of concentration (navānupūrvavihārasamāpatti) are termed profound and wondrous. When the Dharma of the Truths and Conditions was first taught, six hundred trillion nayutas attained the Way;
when this Dharma was taught during the second, third, and fourth assemblies, those who attained realization became even more numerous.
First: The Turning of the Half-Character Teaching is concluded. △ Second: The Turning of the Full-Character Teaching, divided into seven parts. First: The Prince’s Renunciation of Home.
At that time, the sixteen princes... [until] ...sought *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

*Śrāmaṇera* is translated here as "Cessation and Compassion" (*xīcí*). From the age of seven to thirteen, one is a *qū'wū* (crow-chaser), so called because of the manifest conduct [of driving away crows].

From fourteen to nineteen, one is an *yìngfǎ* (one who accords with the Dharma), because one is close to receiving full ordination (*yuán*). At twenty and above, one is a *míngzì* (named one), because the precepts have not yet been fully received.
Furthermore, regarding the *śrāmaṇera* who has received full ordination, they observe the ritual protocols of the twenty-four gates. Now, this is the Bodhi... [text ends]
The śrāmaṇera Saśa, because he has resolved upon the Great Mind, possesses the two phrases regarding the faculties, which signify the purification of the six sense organs.

In terms of his universal scope, he does not stagnate in the Lesser Vehicle; in terms of his benefit, he does not delight in provisional vehicles; in terms of his clarity, he does not dwell within the aggregates and realms;

and in terms of his realization, he does not remain stuck midway. These are all internal causes. As for "making offerings to the Buddha" and so forth, these are external conditions. Having already extensively planted blessings and deeply cultivated virtue.
This means they aspire to seek the fruit of Buddhahood. △ Second, the request to turn the wheel of Dharma.
They all addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One... (up to)... that which is contemplated by their profound minds, the Buddha himself knows and witnesses."

"All have already attained accomplishment" means that the turbid obstacles have been cleared away and the capacity for the Mahāyāna has been activated. All the sons are fully endowed with the merits of the Mahāyāna;

yet, out of compassion for the Śrāvakas who have not yet reached the ultimate goal, they again entreat [the Buddha] to reveal and clarify [the truth], setting aside the "half" to manifest the "full," which is identical to the present *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*.
"What is contemplated by their profound mind" refers to the delight of the profound mind.
Because he gathers all wholesome dharmas, he maintains a straightforward mind and right mindfulness of *tathatā*, thereby seeking bodhi.

With a heart of great compassion, he delivers all sentient beings, encompassing them within his vow. This aspiration to seek enlightenment above and transform others below is personally realized and known by the Buddha.
△ Third, the assembly of people he leads forth to leave the household life.
At that time, among the multitude led by the Wheel-Turning Sage King, [those who] also sought to leave the household life were immediately granted permission by the King.
These eighty trillion people, the subjects led by the Wheel-Turning King, having seen the Prince leave the household life, suddenly gave rise to the aspiration to emulate him.
Thus, they deeply yearned for the Noble Path, departing from the house of worldly entanglements and entering the house of the Dharma-nature. The Sage King—
He transformed the world through the ten wholesome deeds. For this reason, when the servant requested to leave the household life, he granted it immediately.
Question: Why was this sequence [of events] established regarding the servant’s renunciation? Answer: It was precisely for the sake of providing a teaching opportunity for the younger prince;

it was because of the assembly of those who were confused by the Buddha of Wisdom (Jñānabuddha), and thus it served as the means for establishing a karmic connection with the prince. 4. Accepting the Invitation and Preaching the Sūtra.
At that time, that Buddha accepted the request of the śrāmaṇeras (up to the point where they all together received, upheld, recited, and mastered [the teachings]).

Regarding the "twenty thousand kalpas": previously, he had already taught the Dharma of the Truths, the Conditions, and so forth for the sake of those of the Two Vehicles; subsequently, he accepted the requests of his sons.
Furthermore, since he preached the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, we know that there was no silence during the intervening period; he must have preached the Vaipulya and Prajñāpāramitā sūtras.
The following verse states: "He preached the six pāramitās and various matters of supernatural powers (*abhijñā*).

Since the Vaipulya teachings predominantly clarify inconceivable matters of supernatural power, we know he preached the Vaipulya. Because the six perfections are the affairs of bodhisattvas, we know [this].
He preached the Prajñāpāramitā. To "receive and uphold" it and so forth means to be earnest and never lose its intent; all those above should together practice and study this.
△ At that time, among the assembly, some understood while others did not.
When this sutra was being preached, sixteen bodhisattva śrāmaṇeras (up to) ten million billion kinds all gave rise to doubt and confusion.

Regarding what is called a "bodhisattva śrāmaṇera": because they had heard the Vaipulya Prajñāpāramitā and had practiced the six perfections for twenty thousand kalpas, the śrāmaṇeras of the two vehicles—namely, those of the assembly who believe and understand—gave rise to doubt and confusion; that is, the assembly who do not yet understand.
This refers to the occasion when these [beings] formed a karmic connection by listening to the sutras from the sixteen princes.

Those of superior capacity, upon hearing the Way, practice it with diligence; the princes were such as these. Those of middling capacity, upon hearing the Way, are sometimes present and sometimes absent;
among the śrāvakas, there are those who have faith and those who do not. Those of inferior capacity merely laugh loudly upon hearing the Way; the masses who do not understand give rise to doubt.
This is a delusion. △ Sixth, the duration of the preaching of the sutra:
The Buddha preached this sutra for eight thousand kalpas without ever ceasing or resting.
This reveals the extreme length of the time the sutra was preached, such as when the Buddha of Lamps and Brightness did not rise from his seat for sixty minor kalpas.
△ Having finished the seventh discourse, he entered meditative absorption.
After preaching this sutra, he immediately entered his private chamber and dwelt in dhyāna-concentration for eighty-four thousand kalpas.

As for the location where he entered concentration in his private chamber, the duration of time he remained in concentration—eighty-four thousand [kalpas]—it was when the Buddha of Wisdom entered meditative absorption.

This is the proximate cause for establishing the karmic connection (*kṣetra-bandha*). Because [the Buddha] entered meditative absorption and did not emerge, the multitudes of hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis who were filled with doubt and confusion had no one to consult.
Therefore, the sixteen śrāmaṇeras acted as his proxy preachers (*pōu-jiang*) of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. The section on the causes for establishing the karmic connection above is concluded.

II. The actual explanation of establishing the karmic connection. This is divided into two parts: first, establishing the karmic connection through the Dharma-exposition; second, establishing the karmic connection through the parable-exposition.
The conditions. This section also has three parts: first, clarifying the shared formation of karmic conditions in the past; second, clarifying the encounters during the interim;
third, clarifying that [the Buddha] now returns to preach for them. The first of these also has three parts; first, the prince’s secret lecture.
At that time, the sixteen bodhisattva śrāmaṇeras [up to] extensively expounded and analyzed the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
They knew that the character "wisdom" (*jñāna*) is the most important. That the Buddha entered meditative absorption was not without cause.

Throughout the beginning and end of my Śākyamuni’s single transformation, everything has been brought about by the Buddha entering meditative absorption through wisdom. This is because the capacities of those currently being transformed are all...

This is the causal seed for the occasion of reciting [the teachings] on behalf of the Buddha Jñāna. Because that Buddha entered meditative absorption after preaching the Dharma, the assembly had no one to consult with regarding their doubts;
therefore, the Prince recited them on their behalf. From that time onward, he has constantly served as a vessel for their transformation.
Had they not known the intent behind Jñāna Buddha’s entry into absorption, the conditions of the past would not have been established, and today—
What is it that is brought to maturity? It is that which is reached through appropriate transformation; for there is no way to guide the mind without past conditions.

When the Buddha of Wisdom entered meditative absorption, he already knew that among the doubting multitude, this prince possessed the spiritual capacity (*indriya*) and would surely attain ultimate liberation through him.
Therefore, he remained in absorption for eighty-four thousand *kalpas*. The prince then delivered a secondary exposition, excellently continuing and faithfully transmitting [the teaching].

Thus it was. Once the Great Master Xuanzang had initiated this teaching, he temporarily demonstrated the transcendence of words; therefore, Jiran entered into meditative concentration to continue and transmit his work.
Desiring to disseminate what he had heard, each ascended the Dharma seat. The subsequent "metaphor of the string of pearls" precisely refers to this.
△ Second, the benefits obtained by the assembly.
Each and every one of them was led across [to liberation], up to the mind of *samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Because they gave rise to the bodhicitta, it is said that they "attained crossing. The six hundred and so forth sentient beings are precisely those aforementioned multitudes who did not understand.
"Showing" means pointing out; "teaching" means instructing. To cause others to obtain benefit is "benefit"; to rejoice in others obtaining benefit is "joy.
That is to say, it reveals the Buddha’s knowledge and vision to sentient beings, enabling them to awaken and enter [the path], thereby attaining benefit.
△ Third, the praise upon emerging from meditative absorption. This section also has two parts. First, the formal praise for its rarity:
"The Buddha Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū... [omitted] ...reveals and instructs sentient beings, causing them to enter therein."
Possessing both internal causes and external conditions, as well as the virtues of benefiting oneself and others, it is therefore exceedingly rare.
Those who enter therein will immediately deliver all sentient beings, causing them all to enter the Buddha-wisdom. △ Second, exhorting others to draw near.
"You all should repeatedly draw near [to the Buddha] until you attain the wisdom of the Tathāgata, Samyaksaṃbodhi.
Those who are able to believe and not disparage [this teaching], I fear there may be those who do not believe and instead disparage it; therefore, I first extol their virtues."
The subsequent exhortation to draw near [to the teaching]. The reason for this is to explain and clarify the intent behind the exhortation to draw near.
Those of the three vehicles who can believe what is taught, uphold it, and do not disparage it, shall attain the same ultimate destination as the One Vehicle and enter the wisdom of the Tathāgata.
△ Second, clarifying the encounter during the intermediate period.

The Buddha told the bhikṣus: "...[up to] those who have encountered forty trillion Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, and have not yet finished [their encounters], being born together with Bodhisattvas in every successive life.
Where there is no affinity (*pratyaya*), they will certainly not gather; where there is affinity, they will certainly not be separated.
As for the forty trillion Buddhas whom they have encountered and not yet finished [encountering]: Śāriputra, possessing sharp faculties, has encountered two [thousand]."
Regarding the ten thousand billion Buddhas: those of inferior capacity encounter forty thousand billion Buddhas; these are the Buddhas who repeatedly manifest birth, extinction, and so forth.

Those whose roots were first matured are the first to receive deliverance, while those whose roots were matured later are the last to receive deliverance—just as a fisherman catches those in the front net first and those in the back net later. If they encounter them in the interim, they shall constantly receive the Mahāyāna.
Among these groups, all have already attained accomplishment and have not remained so until the present.

If, in the interim, they encountered [teachings] and their great resolve receded, they were nevertheless received with the Small Vehicle; thus, among these groups, there are still some who remain unexhausted.

Now that they have been able to hear the teachings of the Mahāyāna once again—whereas previously one would only speak of encountering the Small and not the Great—it follows that those in the interim had not yet been delivered.
Even now it is not yet exhausted; it is only from today that he has begun to receive the Great [Vehicle], culminating in his attainment of the Way after the Parinirvāṇa.

Question: Having passed through many Buddhas over such a vast period of time, he has only now attained Arhatship. How can such a stage of the *anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti* (patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena) be so easily reached?

Answer: The Great Sage employs skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*) to teach the Dharma according to the capacities of sentient beings, for the purpose of causing them to weary of the [prolonged] path of Buddhahood.
Those who speak of the long as short—those who conceive of the Buddha-way with thoughts of ease and say that one attains arhatship after such-and-such kalpas—are practicing expedient means (*upāya*).
This is to lead those of true practice and cause them to enter the Way.

△ Third, explaining the present return, which is divided into two parts: first, reconciling and concluding the ancient and the modern; second, correctly expounding the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*. The first part is further divided into two.
The first assembly brings together the masters of past and present.
"O bhikṣus, I now tell you" (up to) "attaining *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
First, this indicates the attainment of the Way and the preaching of the Dharma. Second, below that, it lists the names of the Buddhas of the eight directions. *Akṣobhya* means "Imperturbable."
Movement: The east is the foremost of all movements. "Joy" carries the meaning of movement; it signifies that while manifesting movement, one realizes the principle of immovability.
The Buddha possesses myriad virtues and stands loftily above all things; thus he is likened to the summit of Mount Sumeru.
The characteristics of his voice provide two kinds of benefit—form and sound. His speech is fearless, and his form is majestic without being wrathful; therefore, he is likened [to the mountain].
O Siṃha, the principle realized by the Buddha encompasses all beings; its nature is truly eternal, abiding like empty space.
Its substance was not produced in the past, does not move in the future, and does not arise in the present. Being without birth and without cessation, it is called "eternally extinguished.
As the Teacher of the World, the Buddha nurtures all living beings, just as a worldly sovereign brings his transformation and influence to pervade the myriad regions. Therefore...
He is named "Emperor" (Bhagavān). His holy life (*brahmacarya*) is pure; he traverses existence without being defiled, and is thus called the "Brahma-mark.
He possesses immeasurable longevity; his *dharmakāya* is eternally abiding, and his teaching is inexhaustible. As for those who deliver others from the sufferings of the world:

he delivers himself through wisdom and delivers others through compassion, so that both self and others emerge from the suffering of outflows (*āsrava*). *Tamasa*, etc., refers to the nature being stainless (*vimala-svabhāva*). Thus is the Tathāgata.
Supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) are able to rescue sentient beings from the defilements of affliction so that they may attain pure wisdom.

Mount Sumeru is the king of all mountain peaks, serving as a metaphor for the Buddha as the sovereign of all dharmas. Clouds unfold and retract at will, impartially providing shade without conscious intent.
The analogy illustrates that the Sage’s mind is without partiality, for his essence and function are unimpeded. The King’s benevolent virtue is vast and great, rectifying the four seas;
this illustrates how the Sage’s virtue flows forth, moistening and nourishing the ten directions. His virtuous function is inconceivable, subduing demons and restraining the heterodox.
Because sentient beings are freed from fear and attain peace and happiness, Śākyamuni is called "The Capable One" (Nengren). Muni means "Silent One";

one who realizes the principle through the wisdom of ultimate truth is called "Silent," while one who benefits living beings through the wisdom of skillful means is called "Capable. This has two meanings: first, the meaning of contrast.
"Capable" refers to excellent skillful means that adapt flexibly to the capacities and circumstances of beings; "Benevolent" (Ren) refers to supreme virtue and vast grace that extend universally.
To embrace all categories of beings is the meaning of Great Compassion benefiting others. To be tranquil is to be limpid and unmoving, suddenly ceasing all conditions;
to be silent is to be indifferent and forgetful of words, forever departing from conceptual proliferation. This is the meaning of Great Wisdom merging with principle.

Through the sense of the two being perfectly fused—because compassion is itself wisdom—one spends all day saving sentient beings, yet there are no beings to be saved; this is movement within stillness. Wisdom...
It is because of compassion (*karuṇā*). One does not fail to give rise to even a single thought of constantly delivering sentient beings; this is stillness amidst movement.

These two characters, "compassion" and "wisdom" (*prajñā*), encompass the Buddha’s complete virtues without exception. The Land of Endurance (*Sahā-lokadhātu*) is a great trichiliocosm, the transformation realm of a single Buddha.
The *Karunāpuṇḍarīka Sūtra* states: "These sentient beings endure the three poisons as well as all afflictions (*kleśa*)."

Because they are able to endure these evils, it is named the "Land of Endurance" (Sahā). △ Second, reconciling the disciples of the past and present. This is divided into two parts: first, the actual reconciliation;
second, the resolution of doubts. The first part is further divided into two: first, those who received the Great [Vehicle] and later regressed; [second, those who did not].
"O Bhikṣus, when we were śrāmaṇeras... [the wisdom of the Tathāgata is difficult to believe and difficult to understand].
From "When we were śrāmaṇeras" downward, it clarifies that they received the Great [Vehicle] and did not regress, abiding in the Unsurpassed Way.

From "At present" downward, it shows that after planting the seeds of the Great [Vehicle], they subsequently regressed from the Great toward the Small, abiding in the stage of the Śrāvaka. Although the Buddha constantly taught and transformed them through the Mahāyāna, [they remained in this state].
All people should enter the Buddha-way gradually by means of the Mahāyāna Dharma. The reason for this is to investigate and explain the meaning of their regression and remaining behind.
Although they have planted the great seeds, because the Buddha’s wisdom is difficult to understand, they regress from the Great Vehicle and turn toward the Small.
Judging by this present moment, it is fortunate that we have heard the Great Dharma; surely there must have been causes from past lives.

Who knows that we, his disciples, might not be the lingering dust of Jñānavijaya? If we can exert ourselves with diligence, we may come close to attaining it. △ Second, correctly correlating the ancient and the modern.
Those immeasurable sentient beings, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, who were transformed at that time [up to] the śrāvaka disciples, are these very people.
Those sentient beings who were transformed during the Great Pervasive [Dharma-assembly] when he preached the Dharma in secret to establish karmic conditions are you, the bhikṣus, here today.
This bond manifests before me; furthermore, [the phrase] "and my future disciples" refers to those who will follow after my parinirvāṇa. △ Second, resolving doubts:
"After my parinirvāṇa, there will again be disciples" (up to) "...except for the skillful means of the Tathāgatas' preaching of the Dharma."
