One might fear that doubt will arise, saying: "Those who hear the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* in the present and enter the One Vehicle may indeed be those with whom [the Buddha] has established a karmic connection;
however, as for those in future ages who enter parinirvāṇa without hearing the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, how could such people abandon the Lesser Vehicle to enter the One Vehicle?
Answer: After my parinirvāṇa, although the disciples in this land do not hear this sutra, they will not—by their own accord—[fall back into the Lesser Vehicle].

To realize that one's own practice is the bodhisattva path, and for those who conceive the thought of having attained nirvana upon their own realization and enter parinirvāṇa—I shall become a buddha in another land so that they will ultimately hear this sutra.
As for "another land," it means that while the spiritual capacity (*indriya*) in this realm has been exhausted, the conditions (*pratyaya*) have ripened in another realm.
Although [the Buddha] passes away in this land, he appears again and the sutra is heard again in other lands. As the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* says:

The names of the Tathāgata accord with the minds of sentient beings and are each different; from within a single four-continent world system up to the ten directions, there are ten thousand distinct names for each.
When the Tathāgata appears in the world, there is no other vehicle by which to attain extinction.

The single Buddha-vehicle; through skillful means, it is taught as three. △ Second, the formal exposition of the Lotus Sūtra, which also has three parts. First, the purification of the assembly: "When the bhikṣus...
[if] the Tathāgata himself knows... [up to]... having thoroughly mastered the dharma of emptiness, he enters deeply into meditative concentration."

Regarding "the time for *nirvāṇa* has arrived": this refers to when the Buddhas appear in the world and their work of transforming beings through the Path is about to conclude; it is precisely the time for preaching the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*.
For example, Kāśyapa appeared in a pure land, and having finished preaching the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, he immediately entered *nirvāṇa*.

Śākyamuni appeared in a defiled land; having preached the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, he immediately announced his imminent extinction and further preached the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*. [The assembly] was pure.
Those who have already obtained the benefit of the minor teachings on the Four Noble Truths are spared from the calamities of the five turbidities and the eight sufferings.
Those with firm faith and understanding hear the initial teachings of the Vaipulya Mahāyāna and believe in its essence with their minds.

Those who have thoroughly realized the dharma of emptiness hear the final, ultimate teachings of the Prajñāpāramitā; they attain thorough realization within the dharma of emptiness, and thus transform.
This is the intended meaning of the teaching. "Entering deeply into meditative concentration" refers specifically to the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi*.
This section subsumes five passages of scripture concerning the Parable of the Poor Son. △ Second, the formal preaching of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*.
He then assembled the bodhisattvas and the assembly of śrāvakas (until the point where it says): "Only through the single Buddha-vehicle can one attain extinction.
"Assembling the bodhisattvas" refers to gathering his kinsmen. "And the śrāvakas" is a single phrase that refers to commanding his sons.
"To preach this sutra" is precisely the entrustment of the family estate. From the words "In the world," below, it is because the two vehicles cannot be spoken of [in this manner].
Nirvāṇa. Those who attain nirvāṇa do so solely through the Single Buddha Vehicle. This precisely clarifies the intent of revealing the ultimate reality by opening up the provisional means.
△ Third, resolving doubts:
"Bhikṣus, you should know that the Tathāgata’s skillful means... (up to) "...if such persons hear this, they will immediately believe and accept it."
If there were no followers of the two vehicles who could attain extinction (nirvāṇa), for what reason would the Tathāgata establish three? The explanation says:

"Bhikṣus, you should know that the Tathāgata, through his skillful means and provisional wisdom, deeply understands that sentient beings have small dispositions and desires; they are attached to the five sensory objects and defiled by the five turbidities.
Therefore, he first speaks of the two types of nirvāṇa. Upon hearing this, they will surely believe and accept it, which causes them to break through their defilements."
They shall be spared from calamity; later, they will surely reunite and return to the Great [Vehicle]. The explanation of forming karmic connections through the Dharma is concluded.

△ Second, the explanation of forming karmic connections through parables. This is divided into two parts: first, the explanation by way of parable; second, the application to the Dharma. The first part is further divided into two: first, clarifying the analogy of the Guide; second, clarifying the analogy of the Leader.
The first of these is further divided into five sections. First, the analogy of the five hundred *yojanas*.

For example, "five hundred yojanas" is a metaphor for the multitude of beings above who have not yet crossed over, who delight in and are attached to the various realms of existence—the places of saṃsāra. This corresponds to the general metaphor of the burning house.
That house is vast and great; the triple world offers no peace. This is a brief verse on skillful means, wherein "peace and security" is contrasted with [the state of suffering].

Regarding the meaning of "peaceful security" (*kṣema*), according to the stages of the lands (*bhūmi*): the Land of Common Abode for Ordinary Beings and Sages is three hundred; the Land of Skillful Means with Remainder is four hundred;
and the Land of True Reward Adornment is five hundred. According to the afflictions (*kleśa*): the delusions of views (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) constitute one hundred;

the five lower grades [of delusions] constitute two hundred; the five upper grades constitute three hundred; the dust-like delusions (*rajas-sama-kleśa*) constitute four hundred; and ignorance (*avidyā*) constitutes five hundred. According to...
The contemplation of emptiness can surpass three hundred; the contemplation of the provisional can surpass four hundred; the contemplation of the Middle Way can surpass five hundred.
△ Second, the analogy of dangerous difficulties and evil paths.

This perilous and evil path, vast and desolate, devoid of people and filled with terrors, is a metaphor for the multitude of those above who have not yet crossed over, whose afflictions and defilements are heavy; it corresponds to the fire breaking out within the burning house.

Within the realm of skillful means, there are the five turbidities and the eight sufferings that lack peace and security; the two types of birth and death—segmented and transformative—are the perils of the result.
The afflictions of views and thoughts, the dust-like afflictions, and ignorance are the perils of the cause. It is by virtue of these causes and results [that beings wander].
Therefore, they are called the "evil realms. The three realms are places of terror; because they are perilous and difficult to traverse, they are called "terrifying.
The three realms are boundless, vast and expansive; therefore, they are called "desolate and remote.

If nirvāṇa and bodhi were present within the afflictions of birth and death, then even though this path is desolate and remote, there would still be something for people to rely upon. If, however, within the afflictions of birth and death...
Within affliction there is no nirvāṇa or bodhi, just as there is no medicine within illness; thus this path would be desolate and cut off, leaving no one upon whom one could rely.
△ Third, the Parable of the Great Multitude.
If there is a great multitude—
comparable to the hundreds of thousands of millions of beings transformed by the Prince above, all of whom have given rise to doubt and are a crowd that does not understand—
this corresponds to the thirty sons and five hundred people within the burning house. Within the skillful means, [the Buddha] knows the dispositions and inclinations of sentient beings.
[The character for] "intention" (yi). △ Fourth, the analogy of desiring to pass beyond a perilous road.
One desires to pass this road to reach a place of precious treasures.

The Two Vehicles sever the afflictions of views and thought (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa* and *bhāvanā-kleśa*) to exit the triple world; therefore, it is said they "desire to pass this road. Furthermore, they must sever the [afflictions] as numerous as motes of dust and sand (*rajas*).

"Enlightened. Because they seek to attain the fruit of Buddhahood, it is said they reach the place of supreme treasure. This place is precisely the "one-flavor rain" in the parable of the medicinal herbs.
Within the burning house there is but a single gate; this represents the intention of proclaiming the Buddha-way through skillful means.
△ Fifth, the Parable of the Single Guide.
There was a guide who was wise, intelligent, and profoundly discerning, well-acquainted with the characteristics of the treacherous paths and the signs of their passability or obstruction.

This guide is none other than the sixteen princes; he corresponds to the elder within the burning house, to the "I" in the discourse on skillful means, and to the dense cloud in the discourse on the medicinal herbs.
To have keen hearing is called "wisdom"; to have clarity in the mind is called "discernment. This represents the threefold wisdoms integrated within a single mind.
It is said that wisdom is the "eye," and being fully endowed with the five eyes is called "clarity. Taken collectively, this refers to the purification of the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍ-indriya*).
Regarding "obstruction" and "penetration": suffering, its origin, the twelve links of dependent origination, the six obscurations, the sands of afflictions, and ignorance constitute obstruction.

The path, cessation, the wisdom that extinguishes dependent origination, the six perfections, single-mindedness, and the three contemplations constitute penetration. Question: Why does he not depict the scene of father and son losing each other and entering a fire in terror?
Question: Does the meaning of "house" not imply that they do not fail each other? Answer: Generally, metaphors are employed according to what best serves the intended purpose.

Above, we took up the presence or absence of the response to the capacity [of sentient beings], and thus spoke of "failing each other" and "seeing each other. If we take it as the beginning of the response reaching the capacity, we speak of "startled entry into the burning house.

Here, the primary intent is to clarify how the Tathāgata guides sentient beings so that they meet one another life after life; how then can you say they fail each other? Over a long period, they form karmic conditions.
Those words were finally appropriate. For this reason, there was no loss of the characteristics [of the provisional teachings], nor was there any alarm at entering into the ultimate meaning.

Thus far, through three cycles and twenty-two instances, the provisional has been opened up to reveal the real; the intent is now manifest. It was not in vain that I originally intended to exhort you toward faith.
For those of inferior faculties, faith will arise before long; therefore, there is no need for it to be otherwise. The analogy of the Guide is concluded.
II. The Analogy of Leading the Caravan. This is divided into three parts: first, the analogy of the multitude of people to be led; second, the analogy of weariness and retreat on the way;
third, the analogy of destroying the conjured city to reach the place of treasure. First, the analogy of the multitude of people to be led.
He leads the multitude, intending to pass through this peril.
This is a metaphor for those who originally formed karmic connections but have not yet attained liberation; because their original connection has not been lost, they are led by the Teacher.

Thus it is said: "To lead and guide the multitude" refers to the analogy of the burning house, where one is startled and terrified by seeing the fire; likewise, through skillful means (*upāya*), one gives rise to compassion upon seeing the five turbidities (*pañca-kaṣāya*).
II. The Analogy of Laziness and Retreat on the Way. This is divided into two parts: first, the retreat from the Great [Vehicle]; second, the reception into the Small [Vehicle].

This corresponds to the passage within the burning house where, without using one's own body or strength, one praises the rarity of the three vehicles; in the context of skillful means, this represents a temporary cessation of the Great Transformation.

This refers to the application of the three vehicles. First, there is the initial retreat from the Great [Vehicle]. Furthermore, there are three types. First, those who become weary and retreat midway;
these are the people being led who become weary and retreat midway.
"The people being led" is a metaphor for those who encounter [the teaching] midway and retreat from the Great to take up the Small. "Midway" does not refer to...
This is the middle way. It begins with the initial arousal of the mind (*cittotpāda*) and ends with the attainment of Buddhahood;

because one gives rise to the intention to retreat from the Great Vehicle within these two pillars, it is called the "middle road. This refers to those who lack the great capacity (*indriya*) for the supreme [Mahāyāna].
△ Second, addressing the Guide:
They addressed the Guide, saying: "We are utterly exhausted and filled with fear.
There are four kinds of guides: first, the guide of universal compassion who leads all others; this refers to the one guide in the text who leads the multitude.
Second, there is the guide with whom one has established a karmic connection, being restricted to one's own teacher.
The multitude of people mentioned in the text say to their guide, "It is so. There is a guide who possesses provisional wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*);
this refers to the fact that he takes what is small because it was given. The guide in the text who possesses many skillful means (*upāya*) is one who possesses actual wisdom (*bhūta-jñāna*).

This is because it reveals the provisional means (*upāya*). Within the text, the "Teacher" refers to this very assembly of people. Fourth, there is a difference in time, though the person remains the same;
both were princes. The one who is now white is precisely the Teacher who established the conditions for affinity (*karmabandha*).

Because their regression from the Great [Vehicle] results in the extinction of the Great, while their engagement with the Small [Vehicle] gives rise to the Small; this cycle of one arising and one ceasing affects the Dharma-body. This is called "white.

The Prince knows that their regression from the Great is precisely what they have heard described as "white. Because their roots of goodness are feeble and obscured by ignorance, he says they are "exhausted.
Their weariness with birth and death constitutes fear; it is because of this fear— [Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly. The translation reflects the portion available.]
Therefore, it is most appropriate to receive only a small portion [of the teaching]. This implies that he will not accept the Great Teaching. △ Third, he does not advance further.
Being unable to proceed any further, and with the path ahead still long, he now wishes to turn back.

"Furthermore, the path ahead is still long" means that the afflictions of views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*), the *pāṃśu* (dust-like) afflictions, and the ignorance of *asaṃkhyeya-saṃsāra* are difficult to sever abruptly.

Nevertheless, one employs the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*) to receive them, so as not to cause them to return suddenly to their original state; this also carries the sense of "progressing," which refers to the preparatory stage for the cessation of transformation (*upasaṃhāra*).
△ Second, Receiving the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna-upasaṃhāra*). This also has four parts. First, the many skillful means (*upāya*).
The Teacher possesses many skillful means (*upāya*).

These are modeled after the three vehicles within the burning house; within these skillful means, the three [vehicles] are opened up. Because the four intentions (*catur-abhiprāya*) are fully present, there are many skillful means.
△ Second, lamenting the loss of the treasure.
He then thought: "These people are to be pitied; how can they wish to turn back and abandon such great treasures?

He grieved that they were abandoning the treasure, which serves as a metaphor for knowing that they possess the capacity for the Small Vehicle (hīnayāna) but lack the capacity for the Great Vehicle (mahāyāna). △ Third, he magically creates a city.
Having formed this thought, by the power of skillful means (upāya), [he thought: "If one can proceed forward to the place of treasure, it is possible to go there.
From the point where he formed this thought, he manifested a city as a transformation; this refers to the provisional teaching of the Lesser Fruit (*hīnaphala*).

This employs the teaching of skillful means to transform and guide those of the Two Vehicles (*dvayayāna*), enabling them to sever the afflictions of views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa* and *bhava-kleśa*) and emerge from the suffering of the triple world (*tridhātu*). Therefore, it is said that they pass through the perilous path.
[The Buddha] causes them to provisionally realize a small fruit [of the path] over a distance of three hundred *yojanas*; therefore, it is said that he "created a city.

From the passage "he addressed the multitude" onwards, he leads them into the conjured city, which is the "three turnings of the wheel of Dharma. The two lines beginning with "You all" constitute the "turning through exhortation," urging them to advance forward and enter the city.
These current three lines constitute the "turning through demonstration," demonstrating that the city is a place where they may dwell. "May" (*kě*) means:
"Merely to cease" means to rest for a time. "Acting according to one's will" refers to the exercise of the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*) and so forth.
If one enters the second line, it signifies attaining the turning [of the wheel] and reaching the city of peace and security. If one can fulfill the second line, it simply means entering the city;
furthermore, it speaks of proceeding forward. Before the gates have opened, this phrase cannot be made explicit. Now, the three turnings are nearly complete.
The exposition being complete, it may now be explained. △ Fourth, the joyful entry into the city.
At that time, the exhausted multitude felt great joy (until) they conceived the thought that they had already crossed over and the thought of security.
This is like the burning house analogy, wherein [the Buddha] accords with the sons' wishes as a skillful means for them to accept, practice, and realize [the teaching].

Because he accommodates their inclination toward the "lesser" [vehicle], they joyfully exclaim: "We two," etc., which explains the "unprecedented. To escape the evil realms is to be free from suffering;

to attain peace and security is to obtain happiness. The preceding phrase, "entering," refers to accepting, practicing, and realizing [the teaching]. This is the thought that they have already crossed over.

Attaining the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) is the stage of "peaceful attainment" (*anupādāyāśaya*), which is the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*). This is because one is then fully endowed with the two virtues of wisdom and abandonment (*jñānaprahāṇa*).

Herein, "rejoicing" refers to the wisdom derived from hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*). "Not yet having [attained]" refers to the stage of "heat" (*uṣmagata*). "Avoiding evil" refers to the stage of "summit" (*mūrdhan*). "Peaceful attainment" refers to the stage of "patience" (*kṣānti*).

"Entering the city" refers to the stage of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*). "Having already crossed over" refers to the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣamārga*). "Laxity on the middle path" refers to the stage above that.
The section on "Retreating" concludes. △ Third, the parable of extinguishing the illusory city and proceeding to the place of treasure.
At that time, the guide, knowing this multitude of people... (up to)... "What I have manifested as a transformation is merely for the sake of providing rest."
This is the correct teaching of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*. It is the "burning house" and so forth; within the provisional means (*upāya*), it teaches the Unsurpassed Way.
Once they have ceased [their wandering] and are free from weariness, this is a metaphor for the time of the ultimate *nirvāṇa* having arrived.

The assembly is further purified, and having escaped the calamity, their great capacity (*mahā-indriya*) shall be awakened. "Then he extinguished... refers to leading them toward the treasure place. "He extinguished the phantom city" refers to its abolition.
This is the principle of expedient means (*upāya*). "Coming and going" refers to spatial terminology; the character for "coming" implies speech.

From the perspective of ultimate principle, it is said that sentient beings do not come and do not go, while the Lesser Sages go and do not come—neither of these accords with the Buddha’s intention. Now, one should understand that coming and going are simultaneous:

returning to the triple world to benefit sentient beings and engage with all things. Do not emulate those of inferior capacity who remain stationary and seek only their own private perfection. [The section] "The Precious Place" below clarifies this.
This is truly for the purpose of abolishing the provisional. Question: In the preceding chapters, the three vehicles were opened up to reveal the One;

what is the difference between these two? Answer: From a general perspective, there is no difference; from a specific perspective, they are not the same. Regarding the teaching of the *Upāya* (Expedient Means) chapter, the text says:

"I preach the Dharma to sentient beings using only the Single Buddha Vehicle; there is neither a second nor a third. Regarding the *Fire House* chapter, which concerns practice, the text says: "Each [child] mounts a great..."

The carriage travels through the four directions; there is joy and play. Regarding the person who binds by means of faith: within the text, the one who joins together through hired labor is the son of this elder.
Regarding medicinal herbs, there are distinctions and non-distinctions, which clarify the provisional and the real. The seven kinds of distinctions are the provisional;
their common reliance on a single principle without difference is the real. Regarding the provisional and the real of one's own practice, it follows one's own intention.

[The Buddha] spoke. Therefore, while the Buddha is able to know [this], sentient beings do not. Now, regarding the "transformed city" (parinirmita-nagara) in terms of principle (*li*): the transformed city and the treasure place represent the two principles of the Great and Small Vehicles. By eliminating the transformative principle of the Two Vehicles, the single principle of the treasure place is revealed. Within the text, this is expressed as "the transformed city has been extinguished" and "the treasure place is near," and so forth. The preceding allegory is concluded. II. Second: First, the actual application; second, citing a simile to apply it. The first [section] has two parts. First, the application of the simile of the guide:
"O bhikṣus, the Tathāgata is also like this" (up to) "the perilous and long journey that must be traversed and crossed."
The metaphors above number five; now three are combined. The "Tathāgata" is combined with the "guide" from above to form a single phrase.
The "multitude of people" is combined with the "ability to lead," thereby manifesting the multitude of people being led. Regarding the passage beginning with "knows all":

this combines the "perilous and evil paths" with the two kinds of birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) and the afflictions (*kleśa*) of the five stages of dwelling. Because the Buddha knows them all, it says "knows all."

"Long and distant" refers to its being five hundred *yojanas* away; therefore, one must go and cross over. This implies that one should properly understand the characteristics of the perilous path, as well as how to pass beyond it to reach the place of treasure.
"Should go" means that having already entered the illusory city, one no longer proceeds further, and thus should depart.
"Should cross over" means that those who have not yet entered the illusory city and have been submerged for many eons should be delivered by means of the illusory [city].

He builds a city and ferries them across. △ Second, the combined application of the analogy of the guide. This is divided into two parts. First, the application regarding the withdrawal from the Great Vehicle and the reception into the Small Vehicle:
"If sentient beings were to hear only the Single Buddha Vehicle... (up to) "...it is for the sake of providing rest that I speak of two nirvāṇas."
"Sentient beings" refers to the multitude of people being led. The One Vehicle was originally intended for those of great capacity;

yet now, those who delight in the Lesser [Vehicle], upon hearing this, do not wish to see it nor draw near to it. This runs contrary to their inclinations and causes them to falter and retreat midway.

There is no sense of a great capacity [for the Dharma]. Their faculties are shallow and inferior; they would rather remove filth for a wage and settle into the life of a hired laborer seeking a livelihood through manual toil than desire to see or approach [the Great Vehicle].
As for the Great Dharma of the One Vehicle, it is like a lone horse and a single blade.
Traversing ten thousand *li* alone, his words failed to strike the right chord; considering them mere idle talk, they did not wish to see him or draw near to him.
The phrase "the Buddha-way descends" corresponds to the meaning of being unable to advance further and ceasing one's transformative activity.

As for "long and far-reaching," it refers to the cultivation of practice throughout three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* and the refinement of causes over a hundred *kalpas*; just as a great ocean is not exhausted by a single scoop, how could a multi-storied tower be completed in a single day?

And thus it is accomplished; hence the phrase "having long endured," etc. "The Buddha knows" below corresponds to the aforementioned intermediate stage of withdrawing from the Great [Vehicle] and subsequently receiving others through the Small [Vehicle];

"inferior beings" refers to those with small capacities. "Expedient means" (*upāya*) refers to the many various skillful methods. The two *nirvāṇas* correspond to the aforementioned manifestation of a single city.
Regarding the teaching of the "Middle Way" as twofold: while the delusions of the three realms are exhausted, the *censha* (dust-like) afflictions have not yet been eliminated.
[This section] refutes [the opposing views]. Between these two pillars, it distinguishes between the two fruits of *sopadhiśeṣa* (with remainder) and *nirupadhiśeṣa* (without remainder).

Furthermore, between the two types of death—wherein *pariccheda-maraṇa* (segmented death) has been exhausted but *pariṇāma-maraḥa* (death through transformation) has not yet been eliminated—it distinguishes between the two fruits of existence and non-existence. Therefore, it is called the "Middle Way.
△ Next, merging the destruction of the city with the arrival at the treasure place.
If sentient beings abide in the two stages (up to) the One Buddha Vehicle, [the Buddha] differentiates and teaches three vehicles.

The "two stages" refer to the latter two fruits. Regarding those who have not yet completed their practice: from the perspective of cultivation, the four abidings (*vihāra*) are already exhausted, while the fifth abiding still remains;

the grasping at a personal self (*pudgala-grāha*) has been discarded, yet the grasping at phenomena (*dharma-grāha*) still persists. From the perspective of realization, although they have attained [realization], it is with remainder.
There still remains the Great Nirvana without remainder; for although the stage of segmented birth has been transcended, one has not yet transcended the transformational birth (*parināmika-jāti*).

Since the proximate [stage] has already passed by three hundred *yojanas*, one should observe what lies below, causing them to examine themselves: that this "below" is merely the provisional means employed within the ultimate reality.
△ Second, citing a metaphor to apply it to the teaching.
Just as that guide, for the sake of providing rest, [created] this city—which is not real, but was manifested by me as a transformation—so too should one fix one's gaze upon the single phrase:
"The place of jewels is near. What is called a "transformed city" (nirmāṇa-pura) refers not only to the Two Vehicles, but even the wondrous stages such as the Ten Bhūmis;
all are provisional establishments for the purpose of guidance and are thus transformed cities. The "place of jewels," however, is the true mind.
The Original Buddha is the treasure of self-nature. This treasure does not belong to the realm of conceptual cognition; it cannot be established. There is neither Buddha nor sentient being;
there is neither subject nor object. Where, then, is there a city? If one asks, "Since this is a conjured city, where is the place of the treasure?
the answer is: The place of the treasure cannot be pointed out. To point it out would be to have a specific location, and that is not the true place of the treasure.

Therefore, it is simply said that [the Buddha] is "nearby," and one must not speak of this with fixed measurements. Rather, one should transcend words and realize it through silent testimony; its very essence is suchness itself.
△ Second, the verse commentary consists of forty-nine and a half lines, divided into two parts.

First, twenty-two and a half lines praise the reasons for establishing karmic connections. Second, twenty-seven lines correctly praise the establishment of those connections. The first part is further divided into two.
The first twelve lines praise the distant causes; the twenty and a half lines praise the proximate causes. Within the former, there are two parts;
the first six lines praise the Great Penetration and Attainment of Enlightenment.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke these verses:
“The Buddha Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū sat at the site of enlightenment for ten kalpas... (until) filling all of me.”

The three lines following "Greatly Penetrating" (Dàtōng) eulogize the events prior to his attainment of the Way. The line following "Passing ten [kalpas]" (Guò shí xià) eulogizes the actual attainment of the Way.
The two lines beginning with "That Buddha" (Pǐfó) eulogize the request to turn the wheel of Dharma, as well as the offerings made by his retinue.
△ Second, six lines eulogize the requests from the Brahmās of the ten directions.
The World-Honored One is extremely difficult to encounter; appearing but once in a vast period of time, he turns the unsurpassed wheel of Dharma.

The first line of the verse praises the majestic light that shines forth and moves all beings. The next three lines praise the Brahma King of the eastern direction, who, seeking the light, gathers like clouds.
The following section praises the remaining nine directions. Twenty and a half lines praise the proximity [of the assembly].
This is divided into two parts. The first five lines of verse transform the teaching of the "half-syllables.
The World-Honored One of Immeasurable Wisdom accepts the request of those people (up to: "one cannot reach its limit."

The two lines beginning with "Immeasurable" (*apramāṇa*) praise the acceptance of the invitation. The following one and a half lines praise the proclamation of the teaching. The three lines below praise the thorough exposition of the Dharma.

The ten thousand beings attaining the Way praises the realization of the path upon hearing the Dharma. Ten myriads make one hundred million (*koṭi*); ten hundred million make one billion (*nayuta*); ten billion make one ten-billion (*prabhedaka*); ten ten-billion make one hundred-billion (*kamkara*);
ten hundred-billion make one trillion (*bimbara*). Regarding "not receiving any dharmas": this refers to the ability to subdue and sever [false] views.
This is the section on reflection. △ Second, five lines and a half: a verse on the transformation of the full-syllable teaching.
From "At that time, the sixteen princes left home to become śrāmaṇeras" (up to) "eighty-four thousand kalpas."
The first two lines praise the prince’s renunciation. The following one and a half lines praise the request for the turning of the wheel of Dharma.

The two lines beginning with "The Buddha knew" praise the period of twenty thousand kalpas during which he taught the Vaipulya Prajñāpāramitā—the practice of Prajñā and the matters of supernatural power (*abhijñā*).
The Vaipulya sutras primarily clarify the inconceivable matters of supernatural power; these two [lines] refer to that.
This verse praises the acceptance of the invitation to preach the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*. In that Buddha’s *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, there were verses as numerous as the sands of the Ganges;
now, this Buddha’s version consists of seven fascicles. One should know that even with the ink of the ocean, the single-character Dharma-gate could not be exhausted.

This verse records one line from when the previous Buddha, having finished preaching the sutra, entered meditative concentration in a quiet chamber to await the prince’s subsequent exposition for the sake of establishing karmic connections. This verse concerns the establishment of such connections.

The conclusion [of the previous section]. △ Next, twenty-seven lines of verse summarize the formal formation of karmic conditions (*saṃbandha*). This is divided into two parts: first, eight lines summarizing the formation of conditions through the Dharma-exposition;

second, twenty-nine lines summarizing the formation of conditions through the parable-exposition. The first part is further divided into three sections. The first three lines summarize the formation of conditions in the past.
These śrāmaṇeras knew that the Buddha had not yet emerged from dhyāna (up to the point where he was surrounded by a multitude as numerous as the sands of the Ganges).

These two lines indicate that they knew the Buddha had entered meditative absorption. [The following] one line and a half is omitted; it was a re-exposition for the purpose of establishing karmic connections.
Each subsequent line brought benefit to the assembly. △ Second, one line of verse describes encountering [the Buddha] in the interim.
After that Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, these who have heard the Dharma will always be born together with their teacher in various Buddha-lands wherever they may be.
△ Now, the following four lines of verse shall be recited once more.
"These sixteen śrāmaṇeras have fully practiced the Buddha-way" (up to) "be careful not to harbor fear or dread.
This section on the "sixteen [śrāmaṇeras]" concludes by correlating the present master and disciples. Previously, the "eight directions" were mentioned; now, the "ten directions" are mentioned.
By means of the general encompassing the particular, the mutual concealment and manifestation [of the teachings] is shown.

From "For this reason" onwards, the verse explains that he is currently preaching the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and concludes the original causal conditions from the time of the Great Penetration; therefore, he exhorts them not to be alarmed or afraid.

Having finished the verses on the conclusion of the conditions through the "Teaching by Dharma," there are twenty-nine lines of verse for the conclusion of the conditions through the "Teaching by Parable. This section is further divided into two parts; the first eleven and a half lines are as follows: the verse...

The allegorical explanation consists of two sections and seven and a half lines. The application to the Dharma follows; the first part further divides into two, with the initial three lines providing the verse on the analogy of the Guide:
"For example, a perilous and evil path, remote and desolate, abounding in many venomous beasts... [omitted] ...rescues the multitude from their hardships while in the wilderness."
For example, the verse below describes a perilous and difficult evil path. The "poisonous beasts" are a metaphor for the afflictions (*kleśa*) of birth and death (*saṃsāra*).
"Lacking water and grass" is a metaphor for not cultivating the path to enlightenment (*bodhimārga*). The two lines concerning "countless" refer to the great multitude of people.
The two lines concerning "that road" refer to five hundred *yojanas*. The single line concerning "at that time" refers to the presence of a guide who possesses strong discernment.
"Below. This refers to being intelligent, wise, and far-reaching in understanding. △ Second, eight lines and a half: Verses on the metaphor of the guide. This also has two parts. First, six lines:
Verses on the provisional establishment of the transformation-city along the way.
All the people were weary and said to the Guide: "[They] claimed for themselves that they had already attained deliverance.

The passage on "the multitude descending" expresses their exhaustion and retreat. The passage on "the Guide descending" laments their loss of the treasure. The passage beginning with "immediately" describes his transformation into a city.
"The various houses and dwellings" refers to the objects of the various contemplations of emptiness (*śūnyatā*). "The gardens and groves" refers to the [teachings] of the Two Vehicles in general.

It is a forest of untainted dharmas (*anāsrava-dharma*). The nine successive attainments (*navānupūrvavihārasamāpatti*) are its channels; the eight liberations (*aṣṭavimokṣa*) are its bathing pools; the triple gate of emptiness (*trīṇi śūnyatāmukhāni*) are its double gates;
the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*) are its pavilions; and male and female are its concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*).

"Various people descend. This verse praises the joyful entry into the city. △ Two and a half lines follow. This verse praises the extinguishing of the city and leading [the caravan] to the place of treasure.
The Guide, knowing they were rested, gathered the assembly and addressed them, saying: "[... you should all go together to the place of treasure."
Abolishing the provisional authorities of the past and establishing the reality of the present, it causes [beings] to give rise to the Great Mind and seek the fruit of Buddhahood.

△ Second, seven lines and a half: Verses on the Application of the Dharma (dharmasama). This is divided into two parts: first, six lines and a half, which are the main verses on the application of the dharma;
second, one line, which is the verse on citing the analogy and applying it. The first part is further divided into two: the first two lines are verses on the application of the analogy of the Guide.
I, likewise, am thus the guide for all. △ Second, six lines.
These verses combine the analogy of leading and guiding. This section has two parts. The first two lines provide the verse-commentary on indolence and retreat.
"Seeing those who seek the Way falter and desist midway" (up to) "all that was to be done has already been accomplished.

The phrase "seeing those who are inferior" below corresponds to "faltering and retreating midway" in the verse; thus, the following section connects to the "lesser" [vehicle]. As for the expression "already accomplished":
Realizing the state of an Arhat beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) is the ultimate fruit of the provisional teaching. △ Second, four lines:
Verses on reaching the City of Extinction and arriving at the Treasure Place. "Having known that reaching Nirvana means all have attained Arhatship" (up to) "this is the true extinction."

Having already understood the two phrases and knowing that [the path] has been brought to rest, the following verse describes the convergence of cessation and transformation at the place of the treasure.
Thus, it says "the two": this refers to the two types of *nirvāṇa* mentioned above as being brought to rest. "You have realized," etc. [follows].
The treasury of the three virtues is complete. All-knowledge is *prajñā*; the thirty-two marks are the *dharmakāya*;
true cessation is liberation (*vimukti*). When these three virtues are neither vertical nor horizontal, one directly perceives the Buddha-nature.
One should arouse diligence; it is fitting to strive and seek this. △ Second, one verse: a stanza that presents a simile and applies it to the teaching.
The Guides of all Buddhas preach Nirvāṇa for the sake of rest; once they know that [the beings] have found rest, they lead them into the Buddha-wisdom.
The first two lines refer to the manifestation of the great city as a place of rest. The following two lines refer to the precious destination being near.
This chapter, which correctly explains the causes and conditions, is now concluded.

The Lotus Sutra, Chapter Eight: The Chapter on the Prophecy for the Five Hundred Disciples.

Although this chapter records the prophecies for all twelve hundred śrāvakas, the title of the chapter mentions only five hundred because these five hundred received their prophecies with identical names, eons, buddha-fields, and adornments. Furthermore, these five hundred spoke in unison.

This is because they serve as examples for those who understand and accept [the teaching]. As for the five types of retinues, these five hundred were born accordingly; the others were all practitioners of true conduct (*satyācāra*).
These five hundred may have been teachers of seven hundred, which is why only five hundred are specified. Furthermore, according to the preceding text, it says:
"Their number is five hundred, and all shall receive a prediction of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*). According to the subsequent text, it says: "Those who were not present in this assembly..."

"You should proclaim it for them," [the Buddha said], because the other seven hundred were not present in the assembly. The previous bestowal of predictions was named after the Buddha, hence it is called "bestowing" (*shou*).
The present one is named after the disciples, hence it is called "receiving" (*shou*), meaning they receive the prediction from the Tathāgata.

II. The latter two chapters correctly clarify the bestowal of predictions. This is divided into two parts: first, the bestowal of predictions upon the twelve hundred; second, the bestowal upon the two... [the text continues].

The Prediction for the Thousand Disciples. This section also has two parts: first, the prediction granted to Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra; second, the prediction granted to the twelve hundred disciples. The first part also has two sections:
first, the sūtra narrator describes his silent contemplation and realization; second, the Tathāgata confirms this and grants him the prediction.
The first section is further divided into four parts. First is the introduction explaining the cause for attaining understanding:
"At that time, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra... [up to] ...possessed the power of great sovereign supernormal abilities."
Hearing this wisdom, he understands that the two aspects of dharma and parable reveal the reality, as well as the skillful means and so forth.
Furthermore, hearing what follows, he points to the predictions of the five elders. Again, hearing what follows, he hears of the matter of the "burnt-out city" in a past life.
Again, hearing what follows, he perceives that the Tathāgata’s three types of supernormal knowledge are unimpeded; he observes that which is remote and distant as if it were today. That is to say:
This is the great sovereign power of supernatural penetrations. △ Second, the sequence of attaining understanding and rejoicing:
"Attaining what was never before attained, the mind becomes pure and leaps with joy" (up to) "gazing up at the Honored Countenance, not for a moment averting the eyes."
Because in the past one had not heard the revelation of the provisional to manifest the real, but now one has heard it, it is called "unprecedented.
As with the aforementioned bestowal of predictions, mastery over causes and conditions, and so forth, all are unprecedented, except for the attachment to the assurance of nirvana.
Having severed ignorance and its derivative afflictions, it is said that "the mind is pure. Having opened the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, he therefore leaps for joy;
this belongs to the joy of internal realization. From here below, he manifests outward respect. Although he has attained silent resonance within his heart, he has not yet heard the command;
though he wishes to present his understanding through speech, he finds his words difficult to express. He merely bows deeply while listening.
"No. Therefore, our eyes do not for a moment cease gazing up at the World-Honored One. △ Third, the sequence of silent contemplation and realization:
they then formed this thought: "The World-Honored One is most extraordinary... (up to) we cannot fully proclaim the Buddha’s merits with words."
In the first two cycles, Śāriputra and the others attained awakening and all spoke words to express their understanding. Why is it that here they remain silent?

It is because in the previous instances, Śāriputra and the others were of inferior faculties and had not yet awakened; thus, it was necessary to use explicit words to exhort and stir them. Now that those of inferior faculties have already awakened, there is nothing further to exhort or stir them;
therefore, they remain silent and do not speak, but merely praise [the Buddha] as marvelous and rare. Furthermore, they reflect silently:
This is true realization. The realm of self-enjoyment transcends verbal expression; thus, Vimalakīrti remained silent, for he had truly entered the gate of non-duality.
Furthermore, the provisional and the ultimate are inconceivable; they are beyond speech and thought, yet they are expressed through thought and speech.
To speak when there is nothing to say; thus, Śāriputra and others received understanding through verbal expression. To contemplate when there is nothing to contemplate;

thus, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra and others received understanding through silent reflection. This means speaking when it is silent and remaining silent when it is spoken. To "accord with the world" means to cater to people's inclinations and preferences.
If one does not accord with them, slander will inevitably arise. Sentient beings are not uniform; their dispositions and natures differ.

It is distinct. The expedient means follow the faculties [of beings], teaching seven kinds of dharmas. The Tathāgata’s various teachings are intended solely to uproot the attachments of sentient beings to their respective states.
For those attached to existence, he leads them out and introduces them to emptiness; for those attached to emptiness, he leads them out and introduces them to the Middle Way;

for those attached to the Middle Way, he leads them out and introduces them to the Buddha-wisdom. The merits of the Buddha are immeasurable and boundless, beyond what can be exhausted by words or discourse. As stated previously:
"It is said that even after immeasurable kalpas, one could not exhaustively describe it. How then could we possibly proclaim it?
Furthermore, the four sons’ metaphors were exquisitely skillful in their analogies and thorough in their descriptions; even they could not exhaustively describe it for immeasurable kalpas.
Are we any superior to these four? 4. The Four Remembrances: Revealing Their Origins and Requesting Prophecies.
Only the Buddha, the World-Honored One, can know our deep-seated original vows.
By "we," it is meant that all those who have been called forth and transformed are included.

Since we were already transformed during the time of the Great Universal [Dharma-Cloud] Samādhi, and have passed through kalpas until now, the duration has been long and the journey far; how could we not possess deep-seated original vows? It is only that we feel ashamed...

One's past lives are shallow and near; one cannot possess wisdom that reaches far back. Furthermore, there is the obscuration caused by the interval between deaths, which inevitably brings the affliction of forgetfulness.
To illuminate the details of antiquity and to mirror the karmic conditions of all sentient beings—who else could it be but the Buddha?
Therefore, it is said that only the Buddha can know this. The profound mind is the root; what is now manifested is its trace. This is the original vow.

This refers to seeking [enlightenment] above and transforming [beings] below. Seeking above is to seek the prediction of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*); transforming below is to seek the manifestation of one's original station.

Furthermore, because it proceeds from the profound mind, it clarifies how [the bodhisattvas] assist in proclaiming the Buddha’s transformation throughout the three periods of time; because it proceeds from their fundamental vows, they are granted the prediction. Question:
Question: Why did [the Buddha] not previously seek to reveal his true origin for those of the two higher capacities? Answer: It was because those of inferior capacity had not yet attained awakening.

Now that those of inferior capacity have understood, the purpose of expedient transformation is fulfilled. To guide the faculties of sentient beings, he demonstrated the existence of three capacities.

If the trace of the inferior capacity were once revealed, then the traces of the superior and middle capacities would be clearly manifest without further effort. II. The Tathāgata’s Confirmation and Fulfillment.

The Prediction (Vyākaraṇa). It consists of prose and verse. The prose section is divided into two parts: first, the description of the manifest and the fundamental; second, the bestowing of the prediction. The first part is further divided into three sections:
first, revealing the origin by means of Śākyamuni’s practice of causes in the present world; second, manifesting his fundamental practices through past lives;
third, describing his cultivation of causes as recounted by the Buddhas of the three periods. The first of these is further divided into two: first, presenting and indicating it...
"O monks, at that time the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus: 'Do you see this Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra? Do you see him or not?
There are two meanings [to this]: first, seeing his outward traces as those of the Hīnayāna; second, seeing his fundamental nature."
"Is this not a matter of merit? The multitude saw only his outward traces as those of a śrāvaka; they did not know that he was originally a bodhisattva.
Therefore, he asked the great assembly whether they had seen him. △ Second, revealing the traces to manifest the original nature.
"I have always praised him as being among those who preach the Dharma (up to: one whose eloquence in debate can never be exhausted.
"Always praised" means that for forty years he has been extolled everywhere; it is not only from today that this begins.

By preaching with such *pratibhāna* (eloquence), his heroic prose and beautiful verses are able to cause the deluded to attain awakening, the doubtful to give rise to faith, and those with divergent views [to be transformed].

He was so influential that even those who were haughty and defiant became compliant. Thus, he is said to be foremost in preaching the Dharma. If it were not for his wondrous fundamental nature (*mūla*), how could there be such superior traces (*vyañjana*)?
This passage cites the traces to reveal the fundamental nature. Furthermore, the phrase "also constantly extolling" and so forth reveals the merit and wisdom of his fundamental stage (*bhūmi*).

This is the gateway of the myriad practices; hence it is called "various merits. Since there are already various gateways of the Dharma in the fundamental stage (*mūla-bhūmi*), why would the provisional traces (*traces-stage*) consist of only those for the two vehicles?
This cites the fundamental to clarify the traces. From "Diligently" onwards, the meaning of the "various" is set forth.
Those who assist in proclaiming my Dharma—whose traces were at the Deer Park and whose traces received censure and rebuke—are now turning the teaching.
Having attained awakening through the sutras, for forty years there was not a single assembly in which he did not protect, uphold, and assist in proclaiming my Dharma.
He inherently possesses both provisional and ultimate merits, yet manifests his traces across the five periods of teaching to assist the Buddha in maturing sentient beings of true practice.

Is this not precisely his diligent protection, upholding, and assistance in proclaiming my Dharma? He is able to extract even a single phrase to propagate the transformative teachings for the fourfold assembly.
This refers to receiving benefit. "Complete in a single phrase" means that having realized it within oneself, one bestows it upon others.
"Great in a single phrase" means assisting the Buddha in bringing abundant benefit to fellow-practicing sentient beings. Regarding "those who have abandoned themselves" and so forth:

from those below the Buddha down to the practitioners of the seven stages of expedient means, they do not know the eloquence of the discourse on the Original Ground. With their talent for vertical and horizontal mastery, they wield the power of killing and enlivening.
The Buddha’s intent was to exhaust Pūrṇa’s eloquence; for none but a Buddha could fully know it.
Although he used the Buddha’s wisdom to suppress Pūrṇa, he was in fact extolling Pūrṇa’s manifold merits.
Thus we know that the worthiness of Pūrṇa cannot be compared to the worthiness of ordinary sages. △ Second, revealing his past practices.
"You all must not think that Pūrṇa (up to the point where it says) 'constantly performs the work of a Buddha to transform sentient beings'—do not take these words as a mere prohibition.
If one views Pūrṇa merely through the lens of Pūrṇa, then one loses sight of what makes him Pūrṇa.
Now, I reveal his profound and far-reaching foundation, so that my fellow students may not view him by means of his superficial traces."

Furthermore, it is said that Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra has not only assisted in my own transformation of beings; he has also assisted in proclaiming the Buddha’s transformation at the sites of Buddhas of the distant past.

His assistance in proclaiming it today constitutes his trace (*traces*), while his assistance in proclaiming it in the past constitutes his root (*basis*). As for these roots, there are those that are distant and those that are near.
The distant origin is profound and remote; it is truly difficult to believe. For now, we shall simply cite the more recent origin spanning ninety billion years to inspire faith.
As for that first [period], by virtue of his profound eloquence, he did not merely excel as an outstanding figure of his time alone.

Truly, he alone shines throughout the ages. Although there are ninety billion Buddhas—such a vast number as this—and their retinues are not lacking in breadth, could there not be others of noble capability?
Yet even Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra was called the foremost among them; thus, the depth of his internal realization may be known.
As for the two phrases he spoke, they clarify that all the dharmas taught by the Buddhas are ranked [according to their profundity].

Regarding the "unimpededness of one meaning" (*ekārthā-pratibhāna*): Pūrṇa understood it clearly and without doubt. To see with precision is called "clarity" (*vidyā*); to penetrate thoroughly is called "comprehension" (*prativedha*);

to be without obstruction is called "penetration" (*vyūha*); to reach the depths is called "mastery" (*prāpti*). These terms describe one who has entered deeply into the Way and seen the Dharma with precise penetration. How could such profound internal realization be easily attained?

Having obtained the four [unimpeded knowledges], the first is the unimpededness of meaning (*artha-pratisaṃvid*), for wisdom is itself eloquence. Thus, there is unimpededness regarding a single meaning.
1. Knowledge of phenomena (*dharmapratisaṃvid*): This refers to knowing the meanings and principles of all phenomena, because one understands them clearly and penetrates them without obstruction.
2. Knowledge of the dharma (*dharmapratisaṃvid*): This refers to knowing the names of all phenomena, because one distinguishes them without error. 3. Knowledge of expression (*niruktipratisaṃvid*):
This refers to the unimpeded eloquence in speaking all the diverse languages of different regions, so that all who hear may fully understand their words.
Fourth is the unimpeded knowledge of eloquence (*pratibhāna-pratisaṃvid*). Within a single syllable, one can expound all syllables;

with a single word and a single dharma, one instructs others without weariness. Because one does not seek profit or fame, one’s speech is pure. Because one carefully examines the capacities and suitability of others, there is no doubt or confusion.
By virtue of possessing the power of supernormal knowledges (*abhijñā*), one is able to constantly cultivate pure brahma-conduct throughout the duration of one’s lifespan.
The body is in the Way, and the Way is in the body. Diligent and tireless, whether merit is accomplished or not, whether one reaches the ultimate or not, it is therefore called "constant cultivation.
As for those Buddhas and others, they have not only been unrecognized by people in the present age; this has been so since ancient times, throughout the long course of the world.
Those with knowledge are many; yet one still compares them to śrāvakas. To judge a person by their appearance is to fail at Ziyu.
The reason for this is that when a sage exists among people, they wear the heavens above and tread upon the earth just like any other human being.
Yet, there exists something within that wearing and treading which distinguishes them from others—something that cannot be discerned by those of shallow understanding.
Therefore, both ancient and modern authorities have all referred to him as a *śrāvaka*, rather than calling him a bodhisattva.

Nevertheless, the way to benefit sentient beings cannot be accomplished without skillful means (*upāya*). Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra employs these skillful means to cultivate Buddha-works for the great benefit of living beings.
Furthermore, those whom he transforms and establishes cause them to stand out with self-reliance and firm resolve in the path to enlightenment, like a mountain of silver.
This is the "Iron Wall" [section]. It constitutes three phrases concerning purification: by borrowing the practice of benefiting others, one adorns and purifies one's own Buddha-land.
If one does not establish karmic connections with sentient beings, there will be no receptive capacity (*indriya*) to be saved when the Bodhisattva attains Buddhahood.
△ Third, the cultivation of causes as described by the Buddhas of the three periods of time.
The various bhikṣus, including Pūrṇa, constantly and diligently exerted themselves in vigor to teach and transform sentient beings.
As for the seven Buddhas, according to what appears in various texts, they are:
Vipaśyin Buddha, Śikhin Buddha, Viśvabhū Buddha, Krakucchanda Buddha, Kanakamuni Buddha, Kāśyapa Buddha, and Śākyamuni Buddha. These...
The three Buddhas of the subsequent *bhadrakalpa* (Fortunate Aeon) and the first four Buddhas of the present *bhadrakalpa* constitute the Seven Buddhas.

According to the current text, the Buddha himself states: "Among the teachers of the Dharma among the seven Buddhas, and now among the teachers of the Dharma under my own dispensation"—from this it is known that the seven Buddhas are considered past, Śākyamuni is present, and Maitreya and others are future.

One should understand that these refer to the four Buddhas following the *Vyūha-kalpa* (Adorned Kalpa) and the first three Buddhas of the *Bhadrakalpa* (Auspicious Kalpa), who together constitute the Seven Buddhas.

The preceding section on the "Original and Traces" [of the Buddha] is concluded. II. Bestowing the Prophecy. This is divided into three parts: 1. Explaining the perfection of causes and the fulfillment of the fruit;

2. Explaining the adornment and purity of the land; 3. Explaining the kalpa, lifespan, Dharma, and stupa. First, explaining the perfection of causes and the fulfillment of the fruit: [The text continues with the specific details of the prophecy.]
"Gradually fulfilling the Bodhisattva path (up to) the Teacher of Gods and Humans, the Buddha, the World-Honored One.
"Gradually descending" refers to the perfection of the cause. "Passing through immeasurable [eons]" refers to the fulfillment of the fruit. This land symbolizes the principle of the Dharma-realm.
Those who attain the fruit therein manifest the Way of the Sages and Worthies; there are none who do not take their beginning from this and return to it.

This reaches its ultimate limit. He expounds the Dharma to shatter the ignorance and delusion of the world, like the bright sun appearing in the sky; therefore, his alternative name is Faming (Dharma-Clarification).
△ Second, explaining the majesty and purity of the land, divided into four parts. First, the majesty and purity of the land.
That Buddha [is as numerous as] the sands of the Ganges River... (up to)... humans and devas meet and are able to see one another.
Their palms are like the hands of a Buddha; they are not the same as the palms of worldly people. It is said that beneath the ocean there is a stone called "Palm Stone" (Zhangshi).
There is not even a single mote of dust that is uneven or unequal; this is the meaning of "emerging from the earth" (*dibhūmi*).

It is all that which is evoked by a mind of universal equality (*samatā-citta*). The "seven treasures" and so forth are evoked by the adornment of the minds of sentient beings with the various jewels of the Dharma (*dharmaratna*).
As for "the human and celestial realms interfacing," it is because the human path completes the celestial path; man has never been anything other than this.
Heavenly beings—before they were heaven, they were not originally non-human. Because they correspond with the Way, humans and heavenly beings are close to one another;
it is not that a difference as vast as the sky and the earth serves as their limit. △ Second, these are purely paths of goodness.
There are no evil realms, nor are there women. (Up to: "The first is the food of Dharma-joy; the second is the food of dhyāna-delight.

As for "no evils," this means there are no three miserable paths. Because Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra expounds the Dharma, those who hear it practice according to the teachings and do not create the causes for the three evil destinies or the eight difficulties.
Therefore, at the time of his Buddhahood, he possesses this Pure Land. As the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* says:
The straightforward mind is the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*). When a bodhisattva attains buddhahood, sentient beings who are free from flattery will come to be born in that land.
The profound mind is the pure land. When one attains buddhahood, sentient beings endowed with merit will come to be born in that land.

By inferring the cause from the fruit, the causes for Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra can be known. As for those born by transformation (*upapāduka*), it is as in the Land of Ultimate Bliss, where there are no women.
They are human beings. Since they are all born by transformation (*upapāduka*) and are free from all defilements of desire, they possess bodies of radiant light and golden forms.
Such a wondrous body is inherently possessed by humans; it is only because they are obscured and covered by the turbidity of desire that [this state is not manifest]. Thus, Ānanda said:

The vital energies of desire are coarse and turbid; if one were to sever sexual desire and not undergo birth from a womb, then the original essence and form would no longer be obscured by defilement, and the adornments of pervasive light would naturally manifest.
Examining this through worldly analogies, it is like inhaling and exhaling the refined essence.
It is therefore not at all surprising that [the body] can still rise lightly, its wondrous form being refined and brilliant, and its flight being unimpeded.
The *Candragarbha-sūtra* speaks of "food of Dharma," "food of joy," and "food of dhyāna. This present sutra speaks of "Dharma-joy and dhyāna-delight. "Food of Dharma" refers to hearing the Dharma.
It is like being born within a lotus flower in the Land of Ultimate Bliss, where one constantly hears the Dharma preached by Amitābha and Avalokiteśvara.

Regarding "joy-food" (*prīty-āhāra*): hearing the Dharma itself constitutes the food of the Dharma; having heard it, it becomes joy-food. Regarding "meditation-food" (*dhyānāhāra*): one sustains oneself through meditative concentration (*samādhi*) without depending on solid food (*kavaḍīkārāhāra*).
Such are the merit and wisdom of sentient beings with virtuous karma. △ Third, the multitude of the Three Vehicles.
There are immeasurable, asaṃkhyeya, thousands of myriads of koṭis [of beings] who possess the six supernormal powers, the three clarities, and the eight liberations,
and who transform the various classes of sentient beings, each transforming them according to their respective categories.
△ Fourth, the summary of the adornments.
That Buddha-land was thus accomplished with such immeasurable merits and adornments.
Possessing such virtues, its land was as vast as previously described; its environment was thus pure and bright;
its humans and devas were thus exquisite and refined; and its assembly of noble ones was thus eminent and distinguished—all of which resulted from...
When the nature of humanity flows forth, there is not a single dharma apart from the mind.

△ Third, the Dharma-tower of the lifespan during the *kalpa* named Precious Radiance (*Ratnaprabhāsa*) in the land named Well-Purified (*Suvimala*). [From] the arising of stupas made of the seven treasures until they fill that entire land.
Good people flourish and increase; their bodies are all golden in color, hence it is called "Treasury of Radiance" (Bǎomíng).

There is no lust or evil in the land, and all are born by transformation, hence it is called "Virtuous Purity" (Shànjìng). The section beginning with "That Buddha" clarifies the lifespan of the Buddha and the duration of the Dharma. The section beginning with "After the Buddha's extinction" clarifies the construction of stupas and offerings.
△ Second, the verse summary consists of twenty-one and a half lines, divided into two parts. The first fourteen lines summarize [the preceding prose].

The revelation of the manifest traces and the manifestation of the fundamental source occupies two sections of seven lines and a half, followed by the bestowal of predictions upon them. This first part further divides into two:

first, seven lines that generally reveal the fundamental and manifest traces of all the śrāvakas; second, seven lines in verse that reveal the fundamental and manifest traces of Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra. The first of these further divides into five parts.
The first line provides a general heading, stating that his conduct is inconceivable.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"O Bhikṣus, listen attentively! The path traversed by the Son of the Buddha is such that, because he has skillfully studied expedient means, it cannot be conceived."
He blends with the multitudes without being aware of it, and enters into the realm of worldly toil (*saṃsāra*) without being defiled by it; therefore, he is said to be "one who learns well.
To benefit sentient beings, one must rely on skillful means (*upāya*); his practice is inconceivable, for he has already attained the method of manifesting traces.
If one does not learn skillful means well, one cannot achieve this. △ Second, a single verse clarifies the reason for manifesting traces.
Knowing that the multitude delights in minor dharmas and fears great wisdom, the Bodhisattvas manifest as Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas.
Only through great wisdom can one shoulder the Great Dharma; this is the task of a Bodhisattva. Minor dharmas are easy to practice; these are the tasks of Śrāvakas.
Because the Bodhisattvas know that the multitude delights in the minor, they conceal their perfect and ultimate nature and hasten toward [the realization of] the Lesser Vehicle.
Realizing that the masses fear the Great [Vehicle], he likewise appears as a śrāvaka and does not give rise to a fondness for the Dharma of the bodhisattvas.
△ Third, the two lines describe the manifestation of traces for the benefit of others.
By means of countless skillful expedients, he transforms all classes of sentient beings (up to) gradually causing them to become Buddhas.
"Those with small desires" refers to those shown to seek the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*). "The indolent" refers to those shown to regress from the Great Vehicle (*mahāyāna*).

Through the skillful and expedient means of the great disciples, they secretly communicate and subtly entice, transforming sentient beings and causing them to enter the Buddha-wisdom, as in the case of Kātyāyana.
Having heard of the Bodhisattva’s inconceivable Dharma-gate of liberation, Yaśas said to Śāriputra:
"It is like showing forms and images to a blind person; they are not seen by that person. When Śrāvakas hear this Dharma-gate, their inability to understand it is just like that.
(Section Four: Two Verses Clarifying Inner Secrecy and Outer Manifestation.)
Internally they keep secret the practices of a bodhisattva, while externally they manifest as śrāvakas (up to: using skillful means to deliver sentient beings).
"Having few desires" means being free from the defilement of greed. "Disgusted with birth and death" means desiring to transcend the triple world.
Although these are the activities of a śrāvaka, they actually purify their own buddha-field. They do not merely manifest as śrāvakas; they also act as followers of external paths.
Ordinary beings possess three poisons, which are the five dull afflictions; wrong views are the five sharp afflictions.
Sentient beings have these maladies, and the sages treat them accordingly. By using poison to counteract poison, they cause those ailments to heal themselves.
Greed is like Nanda’s attachment to his wife; hatred is like Śāriputra’s dispute with Rādha over who was superior; delusion is like Devadatta’s attempt to harm the Buddha; and wrong views...
It is like the case of the three Kāśyapas who served fire;

or when Sunakṣatra slandered the Buddha, and the group of six and Pāpīyas—there were in each instance Great Beings of the Dharma-body practicing the means of conversion through "sameness-in-action. At the beginning, they were different yet the same;
at the end, they were the same yet different. One cannot achieve sameness by means of their difference; one cannot achieve [difference] by means of their sameness.
They are different. The power of synthesizing these [teachings] is so fluid and transformative. My disciples who skillfully learn these expedient means perform deeds that are inconceivable.
△ Fifth: A single practice concludes the brief exposition while suppressing the extensive.
If I were to fully explain all the various manifestations and transformations, sentient beings who heard them would harbor doubts and suspicions.
Fearing that sentient beings might doubt and lack faith, I have therefore spoken briefly and not at length.
Next, seven lines of verse reveal the original and manifested traces of Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra.

Now, this Pūrṇa, from the time of the thousand billion Buddhas of the past (until) the accomplishment of all-knowledge—these five lines below praise the depth of his original practice in the past. He diligently cultivated, proclaimed, and protected [the Dharma], seeking the fruit of Buddhahood above.
That which is spoken by wisdom is for the purpose of transforming sentient beings below;

according to whether their faculties are sharp or dull, one constantly expounds the pure meaning of the Dharma, causing them to abide in the Mahāyāna and truly purifying one’s own Buddha-field. The next two lines concerning the future describe the causes for future conduct.

△ Second, seven and a half lines. This verse grants him a prediction of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*). It is divided into three parts. First, one line: it praises the perfection of causes and the fulfillment of fruits;
having made offerings to all Tathāgatas and protected the treasury of the Dharma-jewel, he will later attain Buddhahood under the name Dharmaprabhāsa (Light of the Dharma).
△ Two to three lines of verse [describe] the name of the eon and the land.
That land is named "Excellently Pure," composed of the seven treasures; the eon is named "Jewel Radiance.
△ Three to five lines of verse [describe] the adornment and purity of the buddha-field.
The assembly of Bodhisattvas is exceedingly vast, their number being immeasurable billions (up to: "I now shall briefly explain").

Having finished bestowing the prophecy upon Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra. △ Second, the bestowal of prophecies upon the twelve hundred [disciples]. This is divided into three parts. First, the silent contemplation and request for prophecy.
Second, the Tathāgata grants the prediction; third, five hundred [disciples] attain understanding. Regarding the first, the silent contemplation and request for a prediction:
at that time, the twelve hundred arhats [thought], "Would it not be likewise wonderful for others such as the great disciples?"
The twelve hundred [disciples] had already attained the minor fruits and were no longer afflicted by the delusions of views and thoughts; thus, it is said that their minds were "self-mastery.

Having heard the Dharma preached during the three turnings of the wheel and having seen the bestowal of predictions upon the sons, they experienced an unprecedented joy and desired to request their own predictions.
To "form a thought" means that while the mind has attained realization, one is as yet unable to speak; one merely remains silent and contemplates the prediction. If one discusses this...

Through the mysterious convergence of causes and conditions, he is no less than Śūnyatā-ja (Maudgalyāyana) in his birth from emptiness; in his sincere faith in attaining Buddhahood, he is no inferior to Śāriputra.
Yet, because his talent is lofty and his wisdom vast, his words flow like polished compositions; thus I venture to present these phrases before him in person.

Others among us may possess internal substance yet lack sufficient eloquence, stammering and faltering as they find it difficult to express what they mean; therefore, I have silently set forth my heart’s aspiration.
"Is it not indeed a joy? refers to the Buddha’s statement that twelve hundred [disciples] would become buddhas;

why then have they not yet received their predictions (*vyākaraṇa*)? If they were to receive such predictions, we would feel a profound sense of joy and fulfillment. Furthermore, we share the same doubts:
since he has already granted them predictions, we too shall surely receive them. II. The Tathāgata Grants Predictions. This section contains both prose and verse. Prose:
The section on practice is divided into three parts. First, the granting of predictions for twelve hundred [disciples].
The Buddha, knowing the thoughts in the minds of these [disciples], grants them the prediction of *samyak-saṃbodhi*.

He addresses Kāśyapa because, as will be seen in the subsequent text, seven hundred [disciples] were not present at this assembly; he therefore commands Kāśyapa to proclaim [the prediction] on their behalf.
Therefore. △ Second, the specific bestowal of the prediction upon Cunda.
Among this assembly, my great disciple [from "Cunda was the first to attain awakening" until] "the Buddha, the World-Honored One, Teacher of Gods and Men," [is described].
Because Cunda was the first to awaken and occupies the position of the foremost elder, he is specifically granted this prediction. Question: If he occupies the foremost position...

A Separate Record. Question: Why is the Dharma not recorded here? Answer: If we consider actual practice (*sakyācaryā*), the conditions for the Great and Small Vehicles differ, as their initial stages are distinct.

Śāriputra first established a Great Vehicle connection; therefore, he attained awakening first during the first week. Cunda (Kātyāyana) first established a Small Vehicle connection; therefore, he attained awakening first at the Deer Park.
If we consider expedient practice (*upāyakauśalya-ācaryā*), it is for the purpose of guiding sentient beings toward aspiration. This is a manifestation of great skillful means.
The method of manifesting traces cannot be fixed. This is explained by the verse following the name of the Buddha. △ Third, the separate record of the five hundred [disciples]:
those five hundred arhats (up to) all share the same name, called Puming (Universal Radiance).
Kālodāyin: This is translated as "Black Radiance" (Heiguang) or also as "Coarse Black" (Cūhe). His complexion was black yet radiant. Udāyin:
This is translated as "Appearance" (Chuxian), because he was born at the time of sunrise. Cunda is also called Cūḍapanthaka; this is translated as "By the Side of the Great Road.
Śāṇavāsika is also called Paṇṭaka; this is translated as "By the Side of the Small Road. [From the] *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya-kṣudraka-vastu* (Benxing jing).
It is said that her mother followed her husband to another country. After some time, she became pregnant; as her delivery drew near, she longed to return home.
Upon reaching the halfway point, she gave birth to her son. This occurred twice, resulting in two sons; thus, they were distinguished as the elder and the younger.

Furthermore, it is said that according to the customs of the West (India), when the day of childbirth arrives, a woman must return to her mother’s home. Because she gave birth twice while on the road, [the sons were so named]. Question: The Buddha permitted...

[Question: Previously, one thousand two hundred were granted predictions in succession, yet now there are only five hundred; we do not see those one thousand two hundred receiving their predictions. [Answer:

These five hundred are precisely the number of the one thousand two hundred. This is because, in the one and a half lines following the verse, the remaining seven hundred are collectively granted predictions.
△ Second, the verses in praise consist of eleven lines, divided into two parts. First, nine and a half lines praise the five hundred names of Cunda.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:
The bhikṣu Kauṇḍinya shall see immeasurable Buddhas (up to) all as described above.
