Therefore, in benefiting sentient beings, one takes compassion as the foremost; in engaging with the phenomenal world, one takes patience as the foundation; in preaching the Dharma, one takes non-self as the basis.
One who can practice these three dharmas so that the Great Teaching is widely proclaimed is therefore named a Dharma Master. This is according to the facts.
Discussing it: one must ascend the hall, adjust one’s robes, and take one’s seat before one may expound upon it. △ Third, the exhortation to practice:
"Abiding therein, and then with a mind free from indolence... extensively proclaim this Lotus Sūtra."
There are five kinds of Dharma masters. Because they take these three dharmas as their own standard of conduct, it is said that they "dwell securely therein.

Because they employ these to transform others, it is said that they "preach the Dharma with a tireless mind. Therefore, the Buddha taught that [such a master] enters my room, puts on my robes, and sits upon my seat.
If one lacks these three dharmas, how could one be considered a Dharma master who propagates the sutra? II. Clarifying the Benefits.
"O Bhaiṣajyarāja, I dispatch emanated persons to other lands... when I return, I shall explain [the Dharma] for them so that they may attain fulfillment.

In the passage "I dispatch emanated persons," the emphasis lies on the character *ji* (集), which refers to the assembly of those who have been inspired; this is the response elicited by the Dharma-preacher entering the chamber of compassion.
Furthermore, in the passage "I also dispatch... refers to the dispatching of the fourfold assembly, with the emphasis lying on the two characters *wenfa* (聞法), meaning "hearing the Dharma."
The phrase "this assembly" refers to those who are directly responsive to the teaching and influenced by it; this is the response to donning the robe of patience.

"If [he] speaks below," he dispatches the eight classes of supernatural beings (*aṣṭau mahānāgarājānaḥ*); since there are no people in the mountain forests, these eight classes act as the audience for the Dharma. This is the assembly that forms karmic connections;

this is the response to sitting upon the seat of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharmasūnyatā*). "Although I... and so forth: the Buddha manifests his body and preaches the Dharma to cause them to achieve accomplishment.
This is the result of being inspired by tireless diligence. To behold the Buddha’s body, one possesses the potential to attain Buddhahood;
to hear the Buddha’s teaching, one becomes fully endowed with *dhāraṇī*. How could the benefits of propagating this sutra be fully described?

△ Second, the verse recitation consists of eighteen and a half lines, divided into three parts: first, one line of general exhortation; second, twenty-six and a half lines of verse corresponding to the long prose section; third...
A single line of verse serves as an exhortation; first, this initial line provides a general exhortation.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:
"Those who wish to abandon all indolence should listen to this sutra. This sutra is difficult to encounter, and those who can hear it and accept it with faith are likewise rare."
△ Twenty-six lines and a half. A verse summarizing the long prose. Divided into four parts. First, one line and a half summarizes the parable:
"Just as a person thirsty for water digs in high ground... [until] they know for certain that water is near."
△ Two lines and a half [of verse]. The verse and its application:
"O Bhaiṣajyarāja, you should know that such persons as these... are close to the Buddha’s wisdom.

This sutra records the three vehicles in general and extensively encompasses the five teachings; therefore, it says, "The definitive resolution of the Śrāvaka Dharma," by means of which [the Śrāvakas] are opened [to the Mahāyāna].
The Buddha’s knowledge and vision: because one enters directly into the Buddha-wisdom. △ Third, three lines and a half: the verse shows the method and practice.
"If a person preaches this sutra, they should enter the Tathāgata’s chamber" (up to) "...because they mindfully recollect the Buddha, they should exercise patience."

"If a person... and below, the verse establishes the headings. "Great compassion... and below, the verse provides the explanation. Compassion gives rise to all that is wholesome; gentleness wards off all that is evil;
the emptiness of dharmas sweeps away all marks. "If one speaks... and below, it exhorts practice. Furthermore, regarding those who are encouraged by the power of patience:
in the Dharma-ending age, when propagating the sutras, patience is a matter of urgent necessity. △ Four: Nine lines; the verse on benefits.
Furthermore, throughout my thousands of millions of billions of lands, I manifest a pure and firm body (up to: able to cause the great assembly to rejoice.

This constitutes the first line. Manifesting the body necessarily involves preaching the Dharma; preaching the Dharma necessarily involves manifesting the body. These two benefits—form and sound—extend across all directions.

"Vertical" means distant. The following eight lines are as can be understood from the preceding prose. The protection provided by the emanated beings is implicit in the long prose (*dīrgha-pada*) and explicit in the verse (*gāthā*).
△ Third, one line concludes with an exhortation.

If one draws near to a Dharma Master, one will swiftly attain the Bodhisattva path; by following and learning from this teacher, one attains the vision of Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
To "draw near" means to remain by their side without departing, like a shadow following a form. If one draws near but does not receive the teachings, such proximity is of no benefit.
One who draws near, follows, and attains the path and the vision of the Buddhas does so through the causal practices of a Bodhisattva and the resultant virtues of all Buddhas.
This is because one does not depart from this wondrous Dharma. The first major chapter, "Opening the Buddha’s Knowledge and Vision," is hereby completed.
*The Lotus Sutra*, Chapter Eleven: "The Appearance of the Jeweled Stupa.
This chapter reveals that the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body is eternally abiding, and directly points to the true realm of the Pure Land of Real Reward. [Desiring...]
To cause sentient beings to know this and see this is precisely the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.

Yet, this true realm of the Dharma-body first began with a single ray of light shining eastward, perfectly manifesting the beginning and end of both the living and the Buddhas, thereby universally demonstrating the subtlety of the mind and environment of sentient beings.
Because those present had not yet attained awakening, the two sages provided supplementary guidance; since emerging from meditative concentration, they have employed various means to open [the way].

Having shown that all sons [of the Buddha] have already believed that their own minds create Buddhas, yet their emotional perceptions of birth-and-death and purity-and-impurity have not been forgotten, he now directly reveals the eternally abiding Dharma-body.

Thus, a wondrous stupa of the seven treasures emerges from the earth, containing the entire body of the Tathāgata Prabhūtaratna undissipated, in order to eliminate views of birth-and-death; immediately, this defiled land is transformed into a pure land.

The earth serves to eliminate attachments to impurity. When the emanated bodies gather like clouds and fill its expanse, it manifests that within every atom and every land of the *dharmadhātu*, everything encountered by the eye is the true realm of reality (*bhūtatathatā*).
This true realm is the dwelling place of the *dharmakāya*, for the *saṃbhogakāya* and *nirmāṇakāya* arise in dependence upon it; thus, all Buddhas realize it as the totality of all things.
The Body of Universal Wisdom (Sambhogakāya) dwells upon it as the Flower Treasury Adornment; the Transformation Body (Nirmāṇakāya) employs it as its wondrous supernatural powers.
Sentient beings, deluded by it, mistake it for the five aggregates of body and mind and the eighty thousand afflictions.

If practitioners who cultivate the mind do not penetrate and see this clearly, they remain merely lodging outside the gate and do not achieve true realization. Therefore, the precious stupa appears to serve as...
This demonstrates the manifestation of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. "The assembly" refers to the capacity of those who can see;
"the jeweled stūpa" refers to the realm of the true reality (*dharmatā*) that is seen. In Sanskrit, it is called *stūpa* or *caitya*, which here means a square mound or a high and prominent place.
Stūpas were erected in four locations; this is the stūpa where the previous Buddha entered parinirvāṇa, for the previous Buddha had already resided there.
Now the Buddhas sit side by side; it is likewise for the Buddha [Śākyamuni]. Therefore, this is designated as the "Chapter on the Appearance of the Jeweled Stūpa.

Furthermore, the emergence of this stūpa serves to authenticate what precedes and to initiate what follows. It authenticates that the three cycles of preaching of the Dharma previously given were all true and real. As for initiating what follows:
if one wishes to open the stūpa, it is necessary to assemble the emanated bodies (nirmāṇakāya), clarify the profound entrustment, summon the original disciples, and discuss [the matter].
The lifespan [of the Buddha] was witnessed by all fourfold assemblies; therefore, it is called the "Chapter on Seeing the Jeweled Stūpa.
△ The second major section, "Revealing the Buddha’s Knowledge and Vision," is divided into two parts: first, the appearance of the jeweled stūpa to manifest the true reality (*dharmatā*);

second, the equality of the Dharma as evidenced by the attainment of the fruit through both difficult and easy paths. The first part contains both prose and verse. The prose is further divided into...
Three. First, the precious stupa emerges from the earth; second, the emanations gather from afar; third, Śākyamuni issues the call for offerings. Regarding the first [section], there are six parts.
First, the appearance of the stupa’s emergence.
At that time, before the Buddha, there was a stupa made of the seven treasures, reaching as high as the palaces of the Four Heavenly Kings.

The seven treasures represent the seven factors of enlightenment and the seven noble riches. The stupa represents the realm of true reality (*dharmatā*), serving as the locus upon which the Dharma-body relies.
Its height of five hundred [yojanas]—equivalent to twenty thousand *li*—vertically symbolizes the myriad practices within the causal stage and the [myriad virtues] within the resultant stage.

The "ten thousand virtues" represent the cause looking toward the fruit; this is the meaning of "high. The "two hundred [yojanas] and so forth," totaling ten thousand *li*, represent the horizontal manifestation of the adornment of the ten thousand good deeds;
this is the meaning of "broad. The "ground" refers to the ground of the mind of ignorance (*avidyā*).

That which "surges forth" reveals the equality of the birth of Buddhas, the eternal abiding of the Dharma-body, and its inseparability from the ground of one's own mind. It is only that it is shrouded by the covering of ignorance.
Because the mind-ground had not yet opened, this stupa did not emerge. That it now wells up from the earth symbolizes the shattering of ignorance to reveal the true mark (*dharmatā*).
To "dwell in emptiness" means to dwell in the emptiness of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*). By having nothing to be shattered, one shatters ignorance;
by having nothing to dwell upon, one dwells in the emptiness of the ultimate truth. This is what is meant by "ultimately returning to emptiness. [The planting of] seeds...
The "seeds" are adorned with manifold concentration and wisdom. The "balustrades" signify the meaning of dhāraṇī.
The "chambers" are the chambers of immeasurable compassion. The "banners and pennants" are the supreme marks of supernormal powers (*abhijñā*). As for the "hanging jeweled necklaces":

This represents the merits of the forty stages (*bhūmi*): above, it adorns the Dharma-body; below, it covers sentient beings. The jeweled bells represent the eightfold voice and the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*).
As for the fragrance emanating from the four sides, it is the wind of the Path of the Four Truths blowing forth the fragrance of the four virtues.

The banners and canopies symbolize the virtue of bestowing gifts upon all things; there is nothing they do not cover. Their height reaching the four celestial palaces symbolizes that their manifold virtues are most honored and supreme.
△ Second, the offerings of the various devas.
The gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven rained down *mandārava* flowers (up to) paying homage, showing respect, and offering praise.
△ Third, the praise by Prabhūtaratna:
At that time, a great voice issued forth from within the jeweled stupa (up to) "those who have spoken thus are all speaking the truth."

This proof demonstrates that the previous revelation of the provisional to manifest the real is not in vain. "Great Wisdom" (Mahāmati) is that which is attained at the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa).
As for what is called "equality": "level" means there is no high or low; "equal" means there is no distinction. This principle is inherently present in every person;

all sentient beings possess it equally. This is what is meant by the famous exclamation: "How marvelous! All sentient beings are equal. "In this way" means in accordance with the true nature of phenomena (dharmalakṣaṇa). This is...

They praise what the Buddha has taught because it accords with reality. Second, they praise it as being according to the capacities of the faculties, for this praises the Buddha’s teaching at five distinct stages, as he never errs regarding the spiritual aptitude of his audience.
△ Fourth, the assembly is struck with wonder and astonishment.
At that time, the fourfold assembly saw the Great Jewel Stūpa [rise]... they stood to one side with palms joined in reverence.
When the great multitude beheld this stūpa surging upward into the vault of heaven, with wind-blown banners manifesting auspiciousness, there were portents that startled the world;
the bells and music resonated in harmony, performing the beauty of the celestial orchestra. Furthermore, they heard voices praising it, whereby all attained the joy of the Dharma.
There were three wonders: the stupa emerged from the earth, it remained suspended in mid-air, and there was a voice within the stupa.

These three matters were so extraordinary that how could one not harbor doubts? Hence, it is called "a marvelous occurrence. As for "stepping back to one side," this was to await what they might hear.
△ Fifth: Inquiry with Joyful Eloquence.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva (up to) further uttered these sounds therein.
The great assembly marveled at this unprecedented occurrence; with palms joined, they stood still, each harboring doubts and awaiting his revelation.
This Bodhisattva could no longer restrain his impatience and spoke forth to inquire, desiring to quickly resolve their doubts. Furthermore, this Bodhisattva...
This belongs to the same category as the "Medicine King" [Chapter]. It transmits the supreme method for propagating the sutra throughout the three periods of time;
one who has not rendered service to this literature is insufficient to rely upon it. This chapter convenes the Buddhas of the ten directions to entrust [the teaching];
one who does not possess unimpeded eloquence is insufficient to inquire about it. There are three points in the intent of the inquiry: by what cause...
Because this stupa exists, for what reason does it emerge from the earth? For what reason does a great sound issue forth from within the stupa?
By what causal condition is a single phrase clearly revealed as the one great matter (ekamahākaruṇā-kāraṇa)? In the following text, the emanated bodies gather from all directions.

The proclamation of entering *nirvāṇa*, the solicitation of a person for the entrustment, the emergence of his original retinue, and the revelation of his original lifespan were all implicitly contained therein.
Immediately following this, the Tathāgata reveals the power of the vow of Prabhūtaratna, desiring to manifest his own body to the fourfold assembly;
he then addresses the question of Mahāpratibhāna regarding the desire to see the emanated bodies of that Buddha gathered in one place. Thereafter—
This is the sequential exposition. △ Sixth, the Tathāgata’s response, divided into three parts. First, the answer to the second question:
At that time, the Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Mahāsukhavighuṣṭa (至), [granting him] witness and praising him, saying, "Excellent! (善哉).
The land named Ratnaviśuddha is so called because it is composed of the seven treasures and is free from all defilement.
The Buddha is named Prabhūtaratna because he bestows the inexhaustible wealth of merit and Dharma. [The interlocutor] asks: for what reason has he emerged from the earth?
Now the answer states: It is because the Buddha has a vow that serves as the proof for the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* that he emerges from the earth.
△ Second, the answer to the first question:
"After that Buddha had attained enlightenment and was approaching the time of his parinirvāṇa... [until] one great stūpa should be erected."
The Emperor asked by what causes and conditions this stupa exists. The current response states:
"It was because that Buddha, when approaching his parinirvāṇa, left a final injunction ordering the construction of this stupa. △ Third, the answer to the third question.
That Buddha, by the power of his supernatural faculties and vows, [emerges] from the earth and praises [the speaker], saying, "Excellent, excellent!
Śāriputra asks why he has uttered such a sound, and the answer is given: that Buddha utters this great voice because he acts as a personal witness.
Below the section on Mahāpratibhāna, the conclusion provides the answer. The *Śāstra* clarifies that the Buddha Prabhūtaratna cannot [be seen].
He preached the Lotus Sūtra and then entered parinirvāṇa. For this reason, whenever the Lotus Sūtra is preached, one should rejoice and bear witness.
[The author] privately comments: This is solely due to the power of the causal vows of the Buddha Prabhūtaratna. When he was practicing the bodhisattva path in former lives, he made a great vow:
"If I should attain Buddhahood... and so forth. Thus concludes the section on the emergence of the jeweled stupa. (Part Two)
The assembly gathers from afar. The text is divided into seven sections. First, the request for the joyful exposition and the desire to see Prabhūtaratna:
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāpratibhāna... [we] wish to behold the body of this Buddha.

Regarding "by the Buddha’s supernatural power": when one wishes to open the stupa, it is necessary to assemble the emanated bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*). Once the emanated bodies have assembled, the entrustment is made clear;
this entrustment immediately summons those from the lower regions, whereupon the disciples of the lower regions surge forth.

Thus, the near is opened to reveal the far—this is the reason for this great matter. Is this not indeed the empowerment of the Buddha’s power? Although those who delight in eloquent speech have heard these words, they have not yet seen [it].
Because their physical appearance and deportment were such, they requested to see the Buddha’s body, desiring to resolve the doubts of all sentient beings and inspire faith in them.
△ Second, the Buddha tells his emanations to assemble.
The Buddha addressed Mahāpratibhāna: "Those who are currently preaching the Dharma throughout the worlds of the ten directions should now assemble.
If I were to appear in person, it would be because of the vow and words of Prabhūtaratna. Regarding his vow to assemble the emanated bodies that have appeared, there are three meanings.
First, it signifies the perfect assembly and perfect realization; for since Prabhūtaratna’s entire body resides within the stupa, it must be his complete body [that appears]."
Seeing the entire body is the gathering of function back into the essence; it is a single characteristic throughout all time, past and present.

This is why, when the jeweled stupa once opens, Prabhūtaratna and Śākyamuni sit together upon a single seat. Second, it is intended to show that while the Dharma-body is without birth or extinction, there must necessarily be the response-bodies that come and go.
From the Dharma, the response arises; the response is gathered back into the Dharma. The one becomes the immeasurable.
To take the immeasurable as one causes one to forget the views of arising and ceasing, as well as the marks of coming and going.

Only when there is no obstruction between the one and the many does one attain the vision of the fundamental substance of the Dharmakāya. Third, if one wishes to assemble the emanations from the ten directions, one must necessarily transform this defiled Sahā world.

One must cast away the mind that discriminates between the defiled and the pure, the consciousness that imposes limitations, and the attachments regarding self and other; only then can one attain the vision [of the Buddha].
The true realm of the ultimate reality possesses these three meanings; therefore, the assembly manifests. Regarding "Great Bliss" below:
since that Buddha has made such a vow, my emanations should now likewise assemble. There are two ways in which they should assemble:
first, the stupa of Prabhūtaratna appears perfectly throughout the ten directions, while Śākyamuni alone emanates throughout the *dharmadhātu*. Now...
The "Collection" (Ji) is intended to demonstrate that the Way is the same across ancient and modern times. Second, it is for those of provisional capacity who are small-minded;

they know only that the Buddha’s transformation and guidance are limited to this Sahā world, and do not realize that his emanations are boundless. This present Collection is intended to reveal the profound depth and vast breadth of the Buddha’s wisdom.
As the *Buddhanusmṛtisamādhisāgara Sūtra* states: "The lands, clans, and methods of transformation manifested by Śākyamuni in the eastern direction are [identical to those in other directions]."
Regarding those who resemble Śākyamuni: even if one were to grind the dust of a great trichiliocosm into fragments, it could not be counted;
if this is so for a single direction, how much more so for the ten directions? △ Third, the request to joyfully proclaim the gathering of the emanated bodies.
Mahāpratibhāna addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One... [and so forth] "...to pay homage and make offerings.
△ Fourth, the Tathāgata emits light to summon from afar:
At that time, the Buddha emitted a single ray of light from his white tuft of hair... [and so forth] "...the places where it shines are likewise thus."
First, the adornments of the *parinirmita-vipāka* (retributive environment) are clarified; next, the preaching of the Dharma by the *sambhoga-kāya* (the primary retribution) is clarified.
In each of the four cardinal directions, the four intermediate directions, and above and below, there are Buddhas in five hundred *koṭi-nayuta* Ganges-sand-like lands.
Each Buddha has countless thousands of millions of *koṭis* of bodhisattvas. Thus, the lands are immeasurable, the Buddhas are immeasurable, and their retinues are immeasurable.

The measures are such that the principal and its attendants are layered upon one another. He preaches the Dharma for the assembly; wherever his radiant marks shine, the great multitude receives that light and beholds him without obstruction.
△ Fifth, all Buddhas inform the assembly to come together.
At that time, the Buddhas of the ten directions (up to) together with the offering to the precious stupa of the Tathāgata Prabhūtaratna were of one essence;

fundamentally, there was no distinction between self and other. To address those who had gathered, he manifested provisional responses according to their capacities, merely establishing the roles of host and guest as a skillful means.
It is truly laughable that these venerable elders would perform such blind Buddhist rituals. △ Six: Adornment.
Purifying the realm of endurance (*sahā-lokadhātu*) is divided into three parts. First, the transformation of the single realm of Sahā:
at that time, the Sahā world was immediately transformed into purity... [until] the emanated bodies distributed throughout the various directions were still not yet exhausted.

"Great marshes" are called "reeds. Phrases such as "the ground is made of lapis lazuli" reveal the pure realm of the Flower Treasury (*Kusumatalagarbha*), while "there are no villages or settlements" conceals the sordid impurities of this Sahā world.
When the conditions for the assembly are ripe, he remains; when humans and devas are not yet fit vessels, he departs.
Thus, amidst defilement, there is immediate purity: jewel trees and golden cords appear as if from nowhere, and so do the cities and towns.

Mountains and rivers—how could one know from where they have ceased to exist? If one happens to perceive purity while failing to perceive impurity, it is because purity and impurity are merely the perceptions of the collective mind.
When the mind and its objects are as one, how can there be any discussion of existence or non-existence? This is what follows below.

The manifested bodies gather like clouds, pervading the great trichiliocosm. That even one region cannot contain all these manifested bodies fully is sufficient evidence of the vastness of his responsive transformations.
The manifested bodies of Śākyamuni are like a single lamp that kindles hundreds of thousands of lamps;
the true and the manifested are inexhaustible, yet the vessel-worlds have their limits. Therefore, even the great trichiliocosm cannot accommodate them all. II. Further Transformations into Eight.
Throughout the world-systems, at that time, Śākyamuni Buddha [reached] such that celestial jewel-flowers were spread across the ground.

Within the transformative realm of a single Buddha, the emanated bodies of that single direction had not yet finished taking their seats; the emanated bodies from the ten directions stood in dense array.
"Forests and clouds arrive; one cannot help but undergo transformation. "The eight directions" refers to the eight directions outside of the Sahā world.
"Mucilinda and so forth" refers to the small and large stone mountains. "The Small and Great Iron Ring Mountains" encircle the Small Thousandfold and Great Thousandfold World Systems.
"Sumeru," meaning "Wondrously High," is composed of the four precious substances. "Together constituting a single Buddha-land" refers to sixteen hundred [worlds].
Ten trillion nayuta lands are unified into a single land; it is transformed from defilement to purity, adorned as previously described.
△ At the third watch, he transforms the worlds of the eight directions.
Śākyamuni Buddha [transforms] for the sake of all Buddhas... until... all the Tathāgatas fill the space within.
This is because the emanations from the ten directions are to come and sit there. Furthermore, he again transforms each of the eight directions.
At that time, "the lower part of the eastern direction" clarifies the arrival of the emanations from the eastern direction; the emanations from the ten directions gradually arrive. These various...
The Buddha pervades its entirety, appearing like a solemn scroll of the Flower Treasury (Avataṃsaka) world-system. As the Great Sūtra says:
"The inexhaustible ocean of all dharma-gates converges within the single dharma-site of the Way. This refers to this very point. Furthermore, it says:
"In a single thought-moment, the Buddhas manifest immeasurable worlds and unspeakably diverse Buddha-bodies. This is the proof.
He is an emanation. Within a single thought-moment, he manifests the various adornments of immeasurable worlds;

thus he realizes this Pure Land. Question: The chamber of Vimalakīrti was vast enough to accommodate many seats, yet why could Śākyamuni’s transformed lands not be contained by his emanations, necessitating three successive transformations?
Answer: This is to reveal the principle through specific events, using the wondrous realm of the Pure Land as a means.
Buddhahood is inherently possessed by all beings. As the transformation-body of the Dharmakāya, there is no deficiency in either object or self.

It is only because sentient beings are obscured by the delusions of their own consciousness and are confined by the dust of false perceptions that the Buddha manifests through his divided bodies specifically to provide them with instruction and revelation.

The first transformation symbolizes the turning back of the third transformative consciousness, the six *vijñapti*-consciousnesses; the second transformation symbolizes the turning back of the second transformative consciousness.
This also refers to the manas-vijñāna. Regarding the "three transformations," these represent the transformation of the first evolving consciousness, the ālaya-vijñāna.

Furthermore, the first signifies the destruction of the afflictions of views and thoughts (dṛṣṭi- and kleśa-āvaraṇa), emerging from the burning house; the second signifies the destruction of the afflictions of the sands (rajas-āvaraṇa), emerging from the illusory city;

and the third signifies the destruction of the afflictions of ignorance (avidyā-āvaraṇa), reaching the place of treasure. To speak of the ultimate reality, this is precisely the Flower Treasury World (Puṣpaka-dhātu). One.
This is the realm of true non-delusion, which eliminates the dualistic attachments of the two vehicles regarding defilement and purity.

Initially, one enters the Flower Treasury World (Huazang) from the Sahā world to preach the *Avataṃsaka*; now, one enters the Sahā world from the Flower Treasury World to preach the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*.

Having completed the three cycles of teaching and reached the fulfillment of the record, the proclamation of extinction is not far off. Upon reaching this point, there is not the slightest bit of concealment; the six characteristics and ten...
Xuan: "The ten thousand practices of the Dharma-gate, their essential nature and characteristics, their ultimate fruition and retribution, and the great wisdom of equality—all are thus.
Question: Since all three transformations involved the relocation of devas and humans, how is it that there are still celestial jewel-flowers spread across the ground?
Answer: Does the Sūtra not say, "Only this assembly was left behind"? How could it be that this assembly contains no devas?

[The assembly consists of] the eight classes of beings, including the nāgas. Question: In the *Lotus Sūtra*, which is characterized by the great wisdom of equality, why are the devas and humans moved elsewhere? Answer:
To speak in terms of the facts, the devas and humans of other lands may not yet have reached the proper time to enter this assembly;

they would not hear the three turnings of the wheel, nor would they hear the bestowal of predictions. How could they be shown the true realm of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision? They are like those of the two vehicles [who cannot perceive it].
Although they hear of the Flower Treasury World (*Huāzàng*), they do not see Śākyamuni; thus, for the time being, they are temporarily relocated.

Upon reaching the "Chapter on Supernatural Powers" (*Shénlì pǐn*), they are again made to hear that the name of the land is Sahā, the name of the Buddha is Śākyamuni, and the name of the sutra is the *Saddharma*.

This causes them to plant the causal roots of merit (*kuśalamūla*) as conditions, so as not to lose the spirit of equality. Analyzing this according to principle: when "heavenly beings" are relocated, it is not their physical forms (*rūpa*) that are moved.

He then shifts their knowledge and vision so that they may attain the Buddha’s knowledge and the Buddha’s vision; thus they behold the entire body of the Dharma-body and the pure marks of the Buddha-land.
△ Seven: Granting the Consent to Open This Jewel Stūpa. Divided into five parts. First: The Buddhas inquire after his health and express their consent.
At that time, each of the Buddhas was beneath a jeweled tree... (up to) "the Buddhas dispatched messengers in the same manner. Regarding those who each held jeweled flowers:
in terms of principle (*li*), they are one person—Śākyamuni in his divided manifestations; yet in terms of traces (*ji*), they are distinguished as this and that.
Since host and guest have been established, there is no lack of human ceremony; thus, each dispatched an attendant to hold flowers and express their reverence.

To use illness as an excuse is in accordance with worldly etiquette. As for "that certain Buddha," it refers to the fact that the various emanation Buddhas each instruct their attendants to speak on their behalf using their own names;
thus one should know that emanation Buddhas do not necessarily all bear the name Śākyamuni.
This is what is meant by the statement: "I am in another land and have yet another name. The vow of Prabhūtaratna has already been fulfilled, and he delights in preaching.
Their request has not yet been fulfilled; therefore, all Buddhas equally desire to open this precious stūpa. "Desire" (yù) here carries the meaning of aspiration or necessity.

It is intended to clarify that when the Saṃgha performs ritual acts, their intention must be resolved through collective assembly. However, due to the divergence of conditions, their wishes have not been realized.

Have them deliver the *yūyu* (consent) to the Saṃgha so that it may be known there is no opposition. Their formula for expressing the consent is as follows: "Venerable Sirs, please attend to me with one mind.
That bhikṣu so-and-so, regarding the Dharma-compliant business of the Saṃgha, grants his *yūyu* and purity. Now all the Buddhas together desire to open the stūpa."
Just as in the Saṃgha the formal act (*karmavācanā*) and the intention to grant consent (*chanda*) are identical, so too, by the power of the Vow of Prabhūtaratna, all Buddhas were summoned;

furthermore, this was intended to let the assembly know the great number of their emanations (*nirmāṇakāya*). Thus, one knows that the Buddhas came to assemble for the purpose of opening the stupa. Yet, having assembled, they did not arrive themselves;

instead, each dispatched an attendant to convey inquiries and the like, in a manner similar to expressing consent. Therefore, the attendants were sent to present the questions, though there was no verbal discourse [from the Buddhas].

This is intended as a refutation. Question: When the emanated bodies wish to open the jeweled stupa, they must wait for Śākyamuni. Is it that their supernatural power (*ṛddhi*) is not equal to his? Answer:
Śākyamuni is the original Buddha of the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*). The emanated bodies from the ten directions are transformations within a transformation.

Many Treasures (Prabhūtaratna) is the original Buddha of the complete body (*dharmakāya*). Only when the complete body is present can the complete body be seen; therefore, opening the stupa necessarily requires waiting for Śākyamuni.
[This is] the text. It is not that his spiritual power is inferior [to theirs]. △ Second, Śākyamuni opens the stupa with his right finger.
At that time, Śākyamuni Buddha... (up to)... as if removing the bolt and opening the great city gate.
The stūpa is in mid-air, and Śākyamuni likewise dwells in mid-air; this signifies that all Buddhas ultimately return to emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
Opening the stūpa symbolizes the disclosure of the provisional (*upāya*); beholding the Buddha symbolizes the revelation of the real (*tattva*). "Qu" (却) means to remove.

A "guān" (關) is a horizontal beam used to secure a gate; a "yào" (鑰) is a lock. These signify the removal of obstructions that cling to the traces [of phenomena] and the manifestation of the fundamental [reality].
This refers to the manifestation of spiritual capacity. △ The fourfold assembly saw and heard it together.
Immediately, all those in the assembly [extended their vision] up to Śākyamuni Buddha.

The entire assembly saw the presence of Prabhūtaratna. Just as Maitreya snapped his fingers and the gates of the pavilion opened—with Maitreya appearing at every gate—so now the Tathāgata presses his finger and the Stūpa of Prabhūtaratna opens, such that everyone beholds Prabhūtaratna.
Each person has their own seat within the stūpa; each person has their own Buddha Prabhūtaratna. It is simply that the present Buddha lacks the spiritual power to press [the finger] himself.

[The Buddha] pointed [toward the stupa], but the door of the stupa did not open, nor did the Buddha Prabhūtaratna appear. Regarding the phrase "to speak joyfully": first, it serves as a testimony for the preceding intention to express one's heart's content;
second, it opens the way for the subsequent intention to speak quickly. From the words "At that time" onwards, there is a praise of the marvelous offering.
Fourth, the two Buddhas divide the seat and sit together.
At that time, the Buddha Prabhūtaratna, from within the jeweled stupa, sat upon half of the seat in the full lotus posture.
Since the stupa remained open in mid-air, Prabhūtaratna shared his seat to yield it to him. Thus, the Buddha entered the stupa.
The two bodies being in harmony signifies that wisdom accords with its object; this represents the *saṃbhogakāya*. The emanated bodies gathering together represents the *nirmāṇakāya*.
The entire body of Prabhūtaratna represents the *dharmakāya*. Emerging from the earth demonstrates that [the Buddha] is not subject to extinction.

Sharing his seat and sitting upon it demonstrates that he is not subject to birth. Entering the stupa demonstrates that he is not eternal. Manifesting the stupa demonstrates that he is not discontinuous. [The division...]
The manifestation of the body shows that it is not one; the manifestation of the entire body shows that it is not different. The offering of a seat by Prabhūtaratna shows that he does not come;
the Buddha’s sitting upon half the seat shows that he does not go. By means of these eight "nots," all are the reality.
What was previously called "manifesting the mark of reality" refers to this. △ Fourth: The fourfold assembly silently requests the addition of their presence.
At that time, the great assembly saw the two Tathāgatas [up to] receiving the great assembly, all of whom were in the void.

This reveals that the three vehicles and the eight classes of beings, having received their predictions, all abide in the emptiness of meaning. The section on the distant gathering of the divided bodies is concluded.
△ Third, Śākyamuni’s call for volunteers.
With a great voice, he universally announces to the fourfold assembly (down to): "The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* has been entrusted to those who possess [the capacity].
From "universally announces" downward, it concerns those who seek the Dharma. Who among these is capable?

This Sahā world is the native land where the World-Honored One attained his resolve for enlightenment and realized the fruit; furthermore, it is the fundamental place where this great assembly heard the Dharma and received their predictions of enlightenment.
Furthermore, because the faculties of the sentient beings in this land are sharper than those in other lands, they will enter parinirvāṇa before long; thus, the time for entrustment has arrived.
As for those who remain: while the Buddha was in the world, he benefited beings according to their capacities and taught the True Dharma himself without depending on others.
Now that his transformative conditions have come to an end, he wishes to ensure that this Dharma brings benefit without limit; therefore, it must be entrusted.
To have attained the person [of the Dharma]: first, to ensure its presence nearby, it is entrusted to eighty thousand and twenty thousand [beings] to propagate the sutra here in this Sahā world.
Second, to ensure its presence afar, it is entrusted to my original disciples—the bodhisattvas as numerous as the atoms of the lower realms—to proclaim it everywhere.
Furthermore, examine these two characters repeatedly; do not mistake white paper and black ink for the *Lotus Sūtra*.
This very Dharma of this one school is utterly complete and perfectly round; it is majestic and transcendent, beyond words and beyond thought.
It is suddenly placed before the great assembly, yet no one dares to look through it or is willing to circulate it.

Therefore, from the appearance of the Buddhas of the ten directions in the world until the present day, their manifestation of the *stūpa* of vows and the gathering of their emanations have been nothing more than this.
This wondrous Dharma has been pointed out face-to-face and entrusted to others, to be transmitted from one to another so that the flame shall not be extinguished and the smoke shall not cease.
Thus it is said, "The entrustment has its place. II. Verse Recitation. There are forty-eight lines, divided into three parts: 1.
The first three and a half lines recite the appearance of the jeweled stupa. 2. The next eight and a half lines recite the distant gathering of the emanations.
In thirty-six verses, Śākyamuni proclaims this exhortation. For the first three and a half verses, he describes the manifestation of the jeweled stūpa.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
Although the Holy Lord, the World-Honored One, has long since entered parinirvāṇa, he constantly goes wherever he may be to listen to the Dharma.

How can you not be diligent for the sake of the Dharma? This means that even though the Buddhas of the past have already realized this Dharma and have entered parinirvāṇa, they do not forget their original vows and still come for the sake of the Dharma. You people, although you have heard the sutras, have not yet attained realization.
Why is it that some are unwilling to make the vow? It is because the arrival of Prabhūtaratna urges the assembly of that time to diligently practice this Dharma.

Since the Dharma is like the udumbara flower, it is said to be difficult to encounter. From the passage "That Buddha" [downward], it clarifies how, through the power of his vows, he listens to the sutra everywhere.
[The second section] consists of eight and a half lines, which versify the distant gathering of the emanated bodies.
Furthermore, my emanations—the immeasurable Buddhas—[from] "by these skillful means" [until] "causing the Dharma to abide for a long time.
This long passage consists of seven sections; now it is summarized in verse. That the Buddhas of the ten directions have gathered here is not without cause;
it is because they wish to ensure that the lineage of the Buddhas is not severed in the final age and that it abides long in the world that they have come together. For the sake of sitting.

Below, the verse describes the threefold transformation and purification of the land. The two lines concerning "all Buddhas" eulogize the complete gathering of the emanated bodies. The two lines beginning with "like the clear...
mean that when the Buddha is beneath the jewel trees, like a lotus in a pond, his physical marks and signs are adorned and most lovely.
When he is beneath those jewel trees, it is like lighting a torch in the darkness; his radiance and adornments are so brilliant that they are utterly delightful.

"From the body issues forth [fragrance] below. This clarifies that sentient beings, being perfumed by the fragrance of the Buddha’s body, fall prostrate in joy as if small branches blown by a great wind, all of them bending low;
thus, perfumed by the fragrance of the fivefold Dharma-body, they cannot contain their own joy.
These two lines serve as the concluding summary. △ Third, thirty-six lines of verse explain Śākyamuni’s call for volunteers. This section is divided into two parts:

first, eight and a half lines, which cite three Buddhas to encourage the upholding of the sutra; second, twenty-seven and a half lines, which cite the difficulty of upholding it to strengthen one's vows.
The first part is further divided into three sections. First, one and a half lines, which seek out those who will volunteer.
He addressed the great assembly: "After my parinirvāṇa... [until] now, before the Buddha, I have personally uttered this vow.

This establishes both the gates of upholding and expounding, encompassing both self-benefit and the benefit of others, and containing all five aspects. It is for the purpose of propagating the sutra in the final age.
Since nothing can be accomplished without a vow, he causes [the Buddha] to proclaim a vow. II.2–3. He exhorts by citing three Buddhas;
although the Buddha Prabhūtaratna has long since entered parinirvāṇa, [he says that one] should make a great vow so that [the Dharma-body] may abide for a long time.
The ancient Buddhas made vows upon hearing this sutra; I have expounded this sutra through my great vows.

Now that our emanations have gathered from afar and we wish to open the jeweled stupa, you should know the intent of the three Buddhas and not fail them. From the words "O sons of the Buddha" onwards, [the text] intends to ensure that these teachings do not fall into decline;
therefore, you should give rise to great vows. (Section 34) These four lines explain the meaning of the exhortation above.
Whoever is able to protect this Dharma of the sutra— up to and including the Tathāgata Prabhūtaratna and all the manifested Buddhas—
if one can protect, uphold, and expound this sutra, that is equivalent to making offerings to the three Buddhas and beholding the three Buddhas.
The Buddhas take the salvation of sentient beings as their primary concern. If one preaches this sutra, one will truly succeed to the Way of the Sages and not fail the charge of the final testament.
When one’s mind accords with the Buddha-mind and their spirits commune, this constitutes personally beholding the three Buddhas.
Part Two: Twenty-seven lines and a half, raising the difficulty of upholding [the teaching] to strengthen the vow. This is divided into two sections. First, twenty lines.

This section correctly exhorts and encourages the upholding [of the teaching]. The second part, consisting of two and a half lines, provides a general explanation of the intent behind the exhortation. This is divided into three sections. First, one line of admonition and exhortation:
"O sons of good family, each of you should reflect deeply upon this difficult task and resolve to make great vows."
To uphold this sutra in the final age is truly a difficult task; only one endowed with the power of great vows is capable of undertaking it.
Wherever the vow resides, there the Buddha resides. Thus, while Vairocana’s vows pervade the entire dharma-realm, Śākyamuni originally established his own vows.
The *Prabhūtaratna-vow-stūpa* that validates the sutra does not, in any case, depart from the vow. △ Twenty-seven lines of the main exhortation, divided into six parts.
First, five lines on the difficulty of preaching without a vow.

While other various sūtras are as numerous as the sands of the Ganges [up to] being able to preach them is difficult, to speak of the multitude of sūtras with one’s tongue, to grasp Mount Sumeru with one’s hand, to shake the great trichiliocosm with one foot, or to stand at the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) while transmitting the sūtra—though these four are difficult, they do not equal the difficulty of preaching the Dharma.
Why is this? Because it concerns the upholding and preaching of the multitude of sūtras.
To be fearless when amidst the multitude is possible for one who possesses the eloquence of Pūrṇa;
to grasp Mount Sumeru as if it were an autumn hair, or to hurl the trichiliocosm like a tiny mustard seed, is the task for one who has attained the supernormal powers of Maudgalyāyana.

To stand with majestic dignity in the heavens of the Form Realm and to let the resonant echoes of other sutras flow forth is sufficient to subdue the multitudes through debate for one who bears the wisdom of Śāriputra.
Virtuous One, if even the Three Sages made vows to go to other lands, one can know how difficult that was.
Yet, in this world of turbid evil, the two attachments are as lofty as Mount Sumeru; ignorance is as solid and thick as a great trichiliocosm;
and the arrogance of the mind is as high as the Peak of Existence. If this sutra is preached, it can shatter these two attachments and sever ignorance.
One must be able to extinguish the mind of pride. When those who lack faith see this, they may feel resentment, jealousy, or revile one;
if one lacks a great vow, one will then give rise to despondency and retreat—this is what makes it difficult. △ Second, two lines: the difficulty of writing without a vow.
Suppose there were a person who could grasp empty space with their hands (and so forth), even if one were to cause such a person to write it down, that would be difficult.
For while the great void is signless (*animitta*) and might still be grasped and traversed, it is difficult to inscribe the sublime meaning upon paper and brush.
This is because in the final age, strange traces are easily esteemed, whereas the eternal Way is difficult to practice. Nevertheless, although this sublime Dharma...
Words are quiescent; their principle truly accords with the nature of reality. Thus, words can be used to practice, yet apart from words, there is nothing to be realized.

To take the written scriptures as the very words [they express], one thereby realizes the path that transcends words. Because people find this difficult to believe and easily harbor resentment and jealousy, it is indeed a hardship.
△ Third, the two lines: "It is difficult to read without aspiration."
If one were to place the great earth upon the tip of a toenail (up to the point that) briefly reading this sutra is considered difficult—
whereas the vast expanse of the earth could be placed upon the heavens by one possessing supernatural powers—

it is because the secret treasury of the One Vehicle is difficult for those of inferior faculties to read in this degenerate age; it is so for those whose four elements are stubbornly grasping and whose ignorance is thick and heavy.
It is difficult for even one who turns their light back for a single thought-moment to read this sutra for a brief instant. △ Fourth, two lines on the difficulty of maintaining it without aspiration:
"Even if the kalpa-fire burns and one carries dry grass upon one's back... to preach this for the sake of a single person—this is what is truly difficult."
When the kalpa-fire blazes forth and the great trichiliocosm is utterly destroyed, one who carries grass does not burn; this arises from supernatural power and sincere faith.

To uphold this sutra in an evil age depends upon the capacity of the individual being free from indolence. If one lacks the power of aspiration, one will ultimately succumb to retreat and discouragement;
this, then, is what is difficult. △ Fifth, three lines: the difficulty of listening without aspiration.
If one upholds the eighty-four thousand treasuries of the Dharma (up to) inquiring into their underlying meaning, that indeed is difficult.

Yet the eighty thousand treasuries of the Dharma do not equal the perfection and immediacy of the One Vehicle. How could the six supernormal powers compare to the ultimate realization of the Three Bodies?
In this degenerate age, to be able to hear the words of the wondrous Dharma with one’s ears and to have one’s spirit endowed with the true reality—this is truly rare.
As for the flavor [of the teaching]: one is able to inquire into the tenet of the cause and effect of the One Vehicle and the four kinds of practices for peace and happiness.
Yet, if one lacks the great vow, although the ears may hear, the mind will not receive it; although the mouth may ask, the body will not practice it. This, then, is the difficulty.
△ Six: The Three Practices. It is difficult to offer [this teaching].
If one preaches the Dharma—[even] for thousands of myriads of koṭis—as found in a sūtra such as this, that is indeed difficult.
To transform people as numerous as the sands of the Ganges so that they attain the fruits of the Lesser Vehicle is not equal to upholding this sutra—namely, making offerings to the wondrous Dharma.
Even a single color or a single fragrance all become the path to Bodhi; by upholding, reciting, and revering it, joining one’s palms and bowing the head, one shall all attain Buddhahood.
If one lacks great vows, one cannot make such offerings. To cultivate both merit and wisdom simultaneously is what is truly difficult. Alas!
"Ha! To lift it up into the air and cast it to the ground—such a thing does not exist in the human world. Yet this Dharma of the sutra exists right here and now.
It is only those who are perverse and eccentric who seek the marvelous and loathe the ordinary path; as the melody is high, those who can harmonize with it are few, and those who find it are rare.
Therefore, the Buddha uses the non-analogous as analogy and repeatedly exhorts you to uphold it. △ Third, the conclusion and exhortation in two lines.
For the sake of the Buddha-way, throughout immeasurable lands... if there is anyone who can uphold this, they uphold the body of the Buddha.
Among all sutras, it is the foremost; it is the key to the multitude of scriptures and the life-gate of the thousand sages.
One who can uphold it upholds the body of the Buddha, because the entire bodies of all Buddhas do not depart from this sutra. If one upholds it...

Hearing, contemplation, and cultivation are the fundamentally wondrous and numinous faculty; when realized in their true essence, they are fully manifest. Wherever one encounters them, this is itself Bodhi—how could it be easily grasped?
△ Next, seven lines and a half provide a general explanation of the intent of the exhortation.
"O sons of good family, after my parinirvāṇa... (until) all devas and humans should make offerings to them.

[The passage from] "O sons of good family" downward recruits those who uphold this sutra. [The passage from] "This sutra" downward clarifies that it is difficult to uphold, yet those who can uphold it bring joy to all Buddhas.
Regarding "temporarily holding": this means that when inhaling, one does not dwell within the aggregates or realms; when exhaling, one does not involve oneself with manifold conditions.

Needless to say for those who constantly turn this sutra, even if one turns the light inward for a single thought-moment and temporarily holds and recites it in accordance with the Buddha’s words, [the merit is immeasurable].
All Buddhas likewise rejoice and praise this. This section below clarifies that praising the upholder and the capacity to uphold constitutes the accomplishment of supreme practice.
By means of this path, one inwardly maintains self-restraint and attains the power of fearlessness; this is valor.

When the mind does not retreat or succumb, exhausting all the methods of the Path, this is diligence. Being inwardly and outwardly upright, one rationally encompasses the three clusters [of pure precepts].
This is the upholding of precepts. To be free from defilement in one's very essence, with the power of sensory dust naturally purified, is *dhūta*.
One who swiftly attains the Buddha-way realizes the self-nature of the mind, accomplishing the body of wisdom (*prajñā-kāya*) without depending on the awakening of another.

To transform an age of decadence, one must rely on a pure wind; to abide in ultimate goodness, one is born through transformation by the Dharma, realizing the principle of the *dharmakāya*. [The text] opens—
The Eye of Humans and Gods truly relies upon the understanding of its meaning; therefore, those who are able to understand and explain it should be venerated by all humans and gods.
The appearance and manifestation of the supreme jeweled stūpa, revealing the true reality (*tathatā*), is hereby concluded.
The Lotus Sutra, Chapter Twelve: Devadatta.
This chapter reveals that the great wisdom of equality is one and the same, yet there are differences in the ease or difficulty of awakening to it.

Because the śrāvakas have long harbored fear regarding the distant nature of the Buddha-way, they have failed to give rise to joy; now that they have received their predictions of enlightenment, they shall attain it only after many kalpas.
Regarding the realization of the fruit: fearing that he might not be willing to seek it with diligence, the Buddha himself cited a past life story.

Formerly, as a king—the most honored among men—he did not spare his own body or life, becoming a slave to seek the Dharma. Among the noble ones, he was one of the greatest wisdom and the easiest to instruct.
It was only by reaching the present that he attained Bodhi; this demonstrates the difficulty within what is easy.

Fearing that they might not progress because of the perceived difficulty, it is further said that Mañjuśrī taught in the Dragon Palace, where a dragon girl offered a pearl and, in that very instant, attained Equal and Perfect Enlightenment.
The ocean is a place of drowning in birth and death; the dragon is one of the three poisons; and the female represents turbid defilement.
Among these classes, those who are most difficult to transform can realize the truth through direct perception at that very moment; this demonstrates the ease found within difficulty.
Devadatta—meaning "Heavenly Heat" in Chinese—was so named because when he was first born, the minds of humans, devas, and other beings were all struck with alarm and feverish distress.
He is also called "Heaven-Conferred" (*Devānāmpriya*), as he was obtained through prayers to the heavens. He was the son of King Droṇodana (斛飯王). Ānanda...
Regarding his own elder brother, the *Mahāyānasaṃparigraha-śāstra* asks: "Pūtimukta was an enemy of the Buddha in life after life; how can he be called a bodhisattva? The answer is:
"If he were an enemy, how could they encounter one another in every lifetime? It is like two people walking who turn further and further apart toward the east and west;
how could they be companions? The *Baoen jing* (Sutra on Requiting Kindness) states: "If one says that Pūtimukta was truly an evil person..."
It is impossible for such a person to fall into hell. The *Mahāmegha Sūtra* states:
"The deeds practiced by Sudatta are inconceivable and equal to those of the Tathāgata; yet he himself committed the crime of a heinous offense and instructed King Ajātaśatru to harm his father."
Matters such as these are all manifestations of great skillful means (*mahopāya*). By practicing what is not the Way, one penetrates the Buddha-way.
Since the faculties and natures of sentient beings differ, their entry into the Way varies—some through opposition and others through compliance—to propagate the Way and benefit all things.
Thus, we know that those who manifest acts of opposition do so out of fear for evil people, merely to prevent them from giving rise to evil. Furthermore, this chapter title identifies the person.
To manifest through practice: the practices of a bodhisattva transcend the sands of Ganges. Now, taking the meritorious deeds of the four types of noble ones, we clarify the five practices.

Devadatta practiced on what is not the Way yet attained penetration into the Buddha-way; this is the practice of heaven (*deva-caryā*). The dragon girl realized the principle and attained fruition in an instant;
this is the practice of heaven. The Buddha cultivated the six perfections and attained bodhi; this is the noble practice (*ārya-caryā*). Mañjuśrī entered...
The ocean is great compassion, untainted; it is the Brahma-conduct (*brahmacarya*). The four modes of conduct are applied according to the capacities of beings to bestow transformation:

they are the infant-like conduct. Without the celestial conduct (*deva-caryā*), one cannot realize the principle; without the Brahma-conduct, one cannot traverse the realm of existence (*bhava*). One’s own cultivation rests solely upon the holy conduct (*ārya-caryā*).
Benefiting sentient beings requires the two practices of [the infant-like] and [the sick-like]. △ Second, the equality of the dharmas that realize the fruits of ease and difficulty.
This is divided into two parts: first, explaining how Maitreya transmits the sutra and Śākyamuni relies upon it to achieve enlightenment; second, explaining how Mañjuśrī propagates the sutra.
The Dragon Girl thereby attained Buddhahood. This section has three initial parts: first, the origins of the master and disciple; second, a synthesis of ancient and modern accounts;

third, an exhortation to faith for the cultivation of goodness. The first part contains both prose and verse. The prose is divided into four sections; the first clarifies the timing of the quest for the Dharma.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the bodhisattvas (up to the point where he says): "In seeking the Lotus Sūtra, there is no weariness.
He recounted how, throughout many past kalpas, he had diligently sought the wondrous Dharma to exhort and inspire the people, asking: "How can you not seek it with such diligence?"
△ Second, the explicit explanation of seeking the Dharma. This also has two parts. First, the explanation of making vows:
throughout many kalpas, he constantly served as a king and made a vow to seek unsurpassed bodhicitta so that it would never regress.
△ Second, the explanation of practice. This also has two parts. First, the explanation of the fulfillment of the six perfections:
"Desiring to fulfill the six *pāramitās*... [omitting intermediate text] ...not sparing even one's own body, flesh, hands, or feet, nor begrudging one’s life."

First comes the vow, followed by the practice; when practice and vow support one another, one attains the Buddha-way. The first is the degree of phenomena (*dharma*) in the Hīnayāna; the second is the degree of principle (*tattva*) in the initial teaching;

the third is the degree of sequential classification; and the final three are the degrees of perfect interfusion. Giving up both the physical basis and its contents is called the perfection of giving (*dāna-pāramitā*).

Preventing the seven types of misconduct is called the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*). Not responding to beating or abuse is called the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*). Carrying out an undertaking from beginning to end is called the perfection of vigor (*vīrya-pāramitā*).
"Crossing over": meditative concentration is called the dhyāna-pāramitā; wisdom is called the prajñā-pāramitā.

As for the six pāramitās, it means that by practicing these six dharmas, one leaves the near shore of birth and death, crosses the turbulent middle current of afflictions, and reaches the further shore of nirvāṇa.

Regarding those who fulfilled [the perfections]: King Śibi fulfilled generosity (*dāna*) by substituting himself for a dove; King Samantaprabha fulfilled ethical discipline (*śīla*) by renouncing his kingdom;

the Rishi fulfilled patience (*kṣānti*) by having his limbs cut off while serving as king; Prince Mahādatta fulfilled diligence (*vīrya*) by draining the ocean and standing on one foot for seven days;
Śāṇakavāsin fulfilled meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) by having a nest of sparrows upon his head; and the minister Gopaka fulfilled wisdom (*prajñā*) by dividing the land to settle a dispute.
The wisdom is fulfilled. Diligently practicing below, one offers support for both the primary and secondary [requisites]. △ Next, to clarify the seeking of the sublime Dharma:
At that time, the lifespan of the people of the world was immeasurable... (up to)... "I shall serve as an attendant and provide for them for the rest of my life."
△ Third, seeking out a Dharma Master.
At that time, a rishi came and addressed the king, saying: “[... If you do not oppose me, I shall proclaim the teaching for you.
The rishi said to the king: “It is through the mutual resonance of the Way that this occurs; were it not for this king, the rishi would have had no means to receive [the transmission].”
He became his friend. Had it not been for this immortal, the King would have had no means to honor him as a teacher. The King was truly seeking a teacher, and the immortal arrived;
the relationship between master and disciple was perfectly harmonious—a rare encounter in the history of the world.

Yet, regarding this wondrous scripture, the five branches of knowledge (*pañcavidyā*) cannot obstruct its axle, and the four Vedas find it difficult to equal its chariot. Its principles transcend the four Āgamas; therefore, it is named Mahāyāna.
Its meaning governs the One Vehicle; therefore, it is named "Wondrous Dharma" (Saddharma).

To not oppose me means that when a teacher guides others through the Way, they must have their words heard and their deeds followed, rather than merely assuming a name to purchase favor. Furthermore, one must test whether they harbor any ulterior motives;
if they rely on noble status or power, they are insufficient for discussing the Way. That a common man becomes a teacher for a hundred generations—this is the Immortal.
He was a human being. △ Fourth, receiving the Dharma and practicing it:
Upon hearing the words of the seer, the king was filled with joy and leaped for gladness (until: ... he served him with diligent devotion so that [the seer] had no need to go elsewhere).
His body never grew weary; he labored tirelessly. His mind never grew weary; he applied himself earnestly to the sublime Dharma.
He renounced the wealth of the four seas and suddenly forgot his dragon-and-phoenix-like bearing. He humbled himself to the toil of a servant. How fervent was his resolve to reach this state!
For a thousand years he did not grow weary; he studied without satiety. His service and provisions were never lacking, and his constant heart never faltered. Thus it was.

The immortal holds his conduct in high esteem; he is able to humble the mind of a sovereign. A man of the Way does not serve as a minister to the Son of Heaven, nor does he form friendships with kings and lords.
When the immortal reaches this state, he knows that he has a teacher, yet he does not know his own body;
he knows that he possesses the Way, yet he does not know the world. Thus, when the sovereign reaches this state, he too is perfected. II. Verse Recitation. There are seven [verses].
The practice is divided into five parts. The first two lines of the verse summarize the timing for seeking the Dharma.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
I recall that in past kalpas, for the sake of seeking the Great Dharma, [I underwent such hardships].
(Two lines and a half. This verse clearly explains the seeking of the Dharma:
"Though acting as a king of the world, I did not crave the pleasures of the five desires... [until] my body would even become a slave."
△ Section Three, Verse 1.5. Seeking a Dharma Master:
At that time, the Rishi Asita came and addressed the Great King (up to) "I shall expound it for you."
Asita: this means "Incomparable" (Wubi). Both his physical form and his Dharma were incomparable; this was his former name, Jñānada.
