At that time, upon hearing the words of the seer, the king’s heart was filled with great joy (up to the point where) his body and mind were free from weariness.
Fruits produced by trees are called *phala*, such as peaches and plums; fruits produced by vines are called *lōha*, such as melons and gourds. △ Section Five:
Two lines concluding the testimony and exhorting faith.
"For the sake of all sentient beings, I have diligently sought the Great Dharma (until now), and therefore I speak it for you.

This concludes the account of the origins of master and disciple. II. Concluding by correlating the ancient and the modern. This is divided into two parts. First, the formal correlation of the ancient and the modern.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus: "The seer of that time was none other than Devadatta today.
Śākyamuni today was once a king; the seer of the past is now Devadatta. Though their forms have changed,"
There exists that which does not undergo transition. Although the spirit (*shen*) does not change, there are those who change as they pass one another in succession.
That which neither transitions nor changes is the spirit of the two sages. That which undergoes transition and change is the physical form of the two sages.

This is what is meant by the saying: "I am still the man of old, yet I am not the man of old. △ Second, clarifying that the master and disciple have fulfilled their merit. This is divided into two parts. First, the clarification.
The disciples' merit and retribution were brought to fulfillment;
it was due to the spiritual friend Devadatta (up to) all being because of the spiritual friend Devadatta.
Regarding the section on "Causes": Causes are fulfilled through three types of spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*).

First, the external protector (*bāhya-pālaka*), who makes no distinction between the virtuous and the non-virtuous, but is simply able to provide for one's needs, like a mother nourishing her child, managing affairs so that they are properly attended to; this refers to those who solicit offerings for established practitioners.

Second, the fellow practitioner (*sahāya*), who mutually encourages and inspires one another so as not to fall into dullness or distraction, ensuring daily progress through mutual refinement and inquiry.
"Polishing and refining. This refers to those who share the same heart and align their wills, as if riding in a single boat, and who mutually respect one another.
"The Three Teachers": that which proclaims the sacred words is called "Teaching" (*śāsana*); that which instructs and exhorts me is called "Imparting" (*avavāda*).

These are those who can decisively resolve all internal and external skillful means, as well as obstructions and hindrances, and who skillfully expound the Dharma to instruct, benefit, and gladden others. *Ekottarika Āgama*.
It says: "Do not associate with evil companions or engage in affairs with the foolish; you should instead cultivate intimacy with virtuous friends and the wise.
If a person is originally without evil yet draws near to an evil person, they will inevitably become an evil person later, and their ill repute will spread throughout the world.
The virtuous are the opposite of this. Regarding the phrase "causing me to be fully endowed," this clarifies his former vows. Formerly, [he was] Ratnagarbha (寶藏).
At that time, when the Buddha was the brahmin Ratnasāgara, he made five hundred great vows. At that moment,
there was a naked ascetic named Vikṣiptamati-bhairava who said, "O noble son, during the immeasurable kalpas of the future while you practice the bodhisattva path,
I shall beg from you for kingdoms, cities, head, eyes, and so forth, to assist you in fulfilling the six perfections."
"May I attain the fruit of Buddhahood early. May you become my disciple and grant me a prophecy. Precious Ocean said:
"Truly, you are my spiritual friend and peerless companion on the Path. The names 'compassion,' 'joy,' and 'equanimity' are derived from their objects;

because the objects—the sentient beings who are the focal points—are immeasurable, the mind that takes them as its object is likewise immeasurable. It is able to bestow happiness upon others and is able to extract [them from suffering]."

He suffers. He rejoices that others are free from suffering and attain happiness. Being free from both hatred and attachment toward others is also called the four immeasurable concentrations (*catur-apramāṇa-samādhi*).
Below this, in thirty-two sections, the perfection of the fruits is clarified. Beginning from the level soles of the feet up to the *uṣṇīṣa* on the crown of the head, there are thirty-two types.
Beginning from the invisible crown of the head down to the marks of excellence on the hands and feet, there are...

Eighty. As for the ten powers (*daśabala*): they begin with the power of knowing what is possible and impossible (*sthānāsthāna-jñānabala*), and extend up to the power of the destruction of the outflows (*āsravakṣaya-jñānabala*).

As for the four fearlessnesses (*caturvaiśāradya*): fearlessness regarding omniscience (*sarvajñatā-vaiśāradya*), fearlessness regarding the destruction of the outflows (*āsravakṣaya-vaiśāradya*), and fearlessness regarding the teaching of the obstacles to the path (*antarāyika-dharma-vaiśāradya*).
He speaks with fearlessness regarding the path to the exhaustion of suffering. As for the four means of integration (*saṃgrahavastu*): first is integration through giving (*dāna*).

For those beings who delight in material wealth, one gives material gifts; for those beings who delight in the Dharma, one gives the gift of the Dharma. Second is integration through kind speech (*priyavādita*).
With a virtuous and gentle mind, one accords with all beings, comforting and instructing them so that all beings conceive a sense of kinship.

1. Loving-kindness (*maitrī*): Adhering to and following the Path. 2. Beneficial conduct (*arthacaryā*): Encompassing all through the actions of body, speech, and mind as they arise, enabling all sentient beings to each receive benefit.
3. Common purpose (*samānārthatā*): Clearly perceiving sentient beings and manifesting various forms and reflections [to guide them].
He universally harmonizes his light and aligns his activities with theirs, so that each may receive benefit. As for what is meant by "gathering":

among all that sentient beings cherish in their hearts, there are only these four methods. By employing these four methods, he responds to their sentiments and guides them, leading them through the correct path of the Mahāyāna to deliver them across.
This is what is called "first using desire to entice them, then causing them to enter the Buddha-way. (The eighteen [unshared dharmas]...)
Regarding "together": it begins with one's own body, speech, and mind being without fault, and culminates in the knowledge of the past, present, and future;
all of this results from the final summary. Using the extraordinary standard of the *ṛṣi*, one molds and casts the extraordinary virtues and deeds of Śākyamuni;

therefore, it says "all resulting from," and so forth. △ Second, explaining that the wondrous fruit of the Dharma Master shall be attained. This also has three parts. First, the actual explanation of what is attained.
The Fruit:
[The Buddha] addressed the fourfold assembly: "Devadatta... [in the world named] Heavenly Path (*devamārga*).
Within the teachings of humans and devas, he cultivated by following his innate nature; thus, through human affairs, he attained the principles of Heaven, and thereby perfected the Heavenly Path."
In the Mahāyāna school, one cultivates the myriad practices by following the Buddha-nature and realizes the true mark (*dharmatā*) through all phenomena, thereby perfecting the primordial principle.
Thus, the world is likened to the celestial realm, and the Buddha is titled the Heavenly King (*Devarāja*). Question:

When Devadatta committed a transgression and entered prison, the Buddha had not yet delivered the Dharma teachings there; how, then, could he have conferred upon him a prediction of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*)? Answer: Devadatta... [text fragment]
While he was in prison, Ānanda went to visit him and asked about him. Dānta said, "It is as if one were experiencing the bliss of the third dhyāna.
These words alone were sufficient to establish him as the Tathāgata Heavenly King; what need was there for a formal prediction (vyākaraṇa)?

The reason a prediction is now granted is so that it may be known that Dānta’s current state of hatred is no different from his former mastery of the sublime Dharma, and that Śākyamuni’s enemy today is no different from [his former self].

This differs from the understanding of former times; it is only through such [realization] that the true mark (*dharmatā*) of the One Vehicle is revealed—the great wisdom of equality, which is without enmity and without favoritism.
△ Second, clarifying the transformation and guidance after attaining the fruit.

At that time, the Buddha Devendra dwelt in the world for twenty intermediate kalpas, [until] sentient beings attained the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) and reached the stage of non-retrogression.
While the Buddha Devendra dwelt in the world preaching the Dharma, all sentient beings who heard the teaching attained the fruits [of the path].
△ Third, the benefits after his parinirvāṇa.
At that time, after the Parinirvāṇa of the Buddha Devendra, [the beings] generated the bodhicitta and reached the stage of non-retrogression.

After his passing, they erected stupas and made offerings, thereby attaining the fruit. This concludes the correlation between the past and the present. △ Third, exhorting faith to give rise to wholesome roots.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus: "In future ages... [up to] if one is born by transformation upon a lotus flower in the presence of a Buddha, hearing this sūtra will give rise to faith;
they shall not fall into the three miserable realms, but shall be reborn in the three happy states. That which exists not but suddenly comes into being is called "transformation" (*nirmāṇa*).

To speak of "transformation" regarding that which is not [ordinary] transformation is like being born by transformation upon a lotus flower as one's parents. Question: By what means does one have faith?
Only then can one attain pure faith and be free from doubt. The answer is: there are three [aspects]. First, to believe that the true mark (*dharmatā*) is equal and non-different;

by this, one avoids rebirth as a hungry ghost (*preta*), is born before the Buddhas of the ten directions, and constantly hears the sutras. Second, to believe that those who are unwholesome are the resources for those who are wholesome;
by this, one avoids rebirth as an animal (*tiryagyoni*), is born among humans or devas, and experiences supreme and wondrous bliss. Third, to believe in the Buddha-mind within enemies.
By personally committing the immediate transgressions (*ānantarya*), one is immediately liberated from hell and born through transformation within a lotus in the Pure Land.

Furthermore, regarding the intent behind this exhortation to believe: since Devadatta’s evil reputation was long established, yet he has now attained such a sublime fruit, the vast disparity between cause and effect would lead those who cling rigidly to the teachings to harbor doubts.
If one can revere and believe without doubt, one will accord with the realm of self-awakening of the sages and worthies.

It is certain that one will experience the fruits of both the mundane and supramundane realms. Upatiṣya was widely proficient in the sutras; Śākyamuni relied upon him to complete his realization of the Way.
II. Mañjuśrī’s Propagation of the Sutra. Because of this, the Dragon Girl attained Buddhahood. This section is divided into two parts: first, explaining Mañjuśrī’s mastery of the sutra;
second, explaining the benefits of such mastery. The first part is further divided into five sections. First: Zhiji (Jñānakūṭa) requests to withdraw.
At that time, the World-Honored One Many Treasures from the region below [said]... (until) he addressed the Buddha Many Treasures, saying, "I shall now return to my own land.
His intention was that the appearance of Many Treasures was for the purpose of witnessing this sutra; since the witnessing of the sutra was completed, he requested to withdraw.
△ Second, Śākyamuni stops him.
Śākyamuni Buddha told Zhijī: [omitted] "...you may return to your native land to discourse upon the wondrous Dharma.
The intent behind this injunction is that although the matters of the *jitemon* (trace gate) have been concluded, the *honmon* (essential gate) has not yet been revealed;
therefore, he entrusts Mañjuśrī with the task of retaining Prabhūtaratna. The Buddha’s secret intention is not something known by the bodhisattvas. △ Thirdly, Mañjuśrī immediately arrives.
At that time, Mañjuśrī [arrived] and, having exchanged greetings with one another, withdrew to stand to one side.
"Flower" (Hua) symbolizes the causal practice; "Wheel" (Lun) symbolizes the perfection of the fruit. Sāgara means "Salt Water. This refers to the Ocean of Fragrant Water outside Mount Sumeru.
Outside the Ocean of Fragrant Water are the Seven Golden Mountains, and outside the Seven Golden Mountains lies the Salt Water Sea.
Question: In the introduction, Mañjuśrī was present in the assembly; it was not mentioned that he had departed. Why, then, does he come from the ocean? Answer:
The Dragon Palace is within the Sahā world; its distance from Vulture Peak is not far. Since it is as if he were on his own mountain, it is not said that he has "departed."
Furthermore, the Sages alternate between movement and stillness, manifesting the Dharma according to the capacities of beings.

Now, by borrowing the events of the transformation at the Dragon Palace, the principle of the original enlightenment of the ocean of nature is revealed; thus, [Mañjuśrī] came from the ocean. Moreover, Mañjuśrī possesses great wisdom and supernatural powers;
how could he be measured by ordinary sentiments? It is likewise logical that he did not remain in this assembly but went to the ocean to transform sentient beings.
As stated in the "Chapter on the Ten Supernatural Powers": "The Bodhisattva has no intrinsic nature and no movement;

yet he goes to all Buddha-fields to pay homage and seek the Dharma, never stirring from his original place. How much less could there be any phenomenon of coming and going in the Dragon Palace of this Sahā world?
Therefore, although Zhiji did not come in the manner of coming, he requested to return to his own land, while Mañjuśrī—

Because they depart without the mark of departing, they proceeded to Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa. Question: Beyond the three thousandfold world-system, there are each four hundred trillion nayutas of lands where there are no longer great oceans.
Since the devas and humans have been relocated there, why do the dragon hosts now transformed by Mañjuśrī still emerge from the sea?
Answer: There are three reasons. First, although they have already been relocated to the heavens...
1. Regarding humans: when the great ocean is transformed, those of great wisdom and supernormal powers come from a place that has been moved yet remains unchanged.
Although the two oceans have shifted, the Dragon Palace does not move; yet, though the palace does not move, the dwelling place has already been transformed.

Those of great wisdom and supernormal powers come from a place that is transformed yet remains unchanged. 2. Regarding those without karmic connection: Śākyamuni has moved them away. Regarding those with karmic connection:
From the moment Mañjuśrī arrived, this inconceivable mountain and sea appeared vividly; yet, through the Buddha’s supernatural power, the assembled multitude did not see it.
Since Mañjuśrī had not physically departed, that land likewise shifted from being defiled to being pure. As stated in the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*:
"He transfers gods and humans to other lands without causing anyone to perceive the act of coming or going. This refers to that very point. △ Fourth: Wisdom.
Jizhi asked. Bodhisattva Jizhi questioned Mañjuśrī (up to the point where he asked): "How many sentient beings have been transformed?
[His] thought was that the Dragon Palace is low and damp, not a place for preaching the Dharma; and that the nature of dragons is arrogant, not fit for carrying the Way."
As for those who are to be transformed, it is feared that they will be difficult to reach in great numbers; therefore, he asks, "How many are there?
△ Fifth, Mañjuśrī provides the answer:
Mañjuśrī said, "Their number is immeasurable... [up to] the manner in which he transforms beings throughout the ocean is such as this."
The meaning is this: those who skillfully expound the Dharma do not select their location; those who skillfully deliver sentient beings do not select their faculties.

The lower the ground, the more extensive the transformation through the Dharma becomes; the more arrogant the faculties, the more swiftly they attain the Way. Hence it is said, "their number is immeasurable," and so forth.

The phrase "those of lower [status]" refers to those who have gathered and realized the teaching through transformation. The phrase "originally [as] voice[-hearers]" refers to those who first adhered to the provisional teachings and remained therein.

The "Lesser Path" merely spoke of matters such as suffering and its origin. Now [all] descend; now, having heard the true reality (*tattva*), they all abide in the meaning of the Great Vehicle’s emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
"Mañjuśrī descends" concludes the benefits, stating that those who traverse the sea to propagate the teaching have saved beings in such a manner.
II. Clarifying the Benefits of Penetrating the Sutra, divided into ten parts. First, the verse inquiry of Jñatikauṇḍinya.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Jñānakośa praised him in verse, saying:
"With great wisdom, virtue, and heroic vigor, you transform and deliver immeasurable multitudes... [leading them] to swiftly achieve Bodhi."
The first line praises the person; the second line praises the Dharma. The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states: "The wisdom of the Supreme Person is immeasurable;
he transforms countless multitudes like an ocean. He reveals only the holy intent and explains its meaning through analysis.

The first two phrases praise the person, and the latter two phrases praise the Dharma. "Revealing the holy intent" refers to speech according to one's own realization, teaching only the true nature (*dharmatā*).
Regarding those who teach through analysis: these are words spoken in accordance with the intentions of others, taught as a skillful means by way of the three vehicles.
In that sūtra, the meaning of the question is explicit; in this sūtra, it is implicit. It asks:

"Do you transform the vast multitude of beings you guide by expounding the meaning of the true reality (*dharmatā*), or do you reveal various provisional gateways through the true reality of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*) to lead sentient beings?"
"Ultimately they all return to the One Vehicle, causing them to swiftly achieve Bodhi. There must be an underlying intention behind this question for it to correspond with the following text.
△ Second, Mañjuśrī’s brief response.
Mañjuśrī said: "In the midst of the ocean, I have always expounded only the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
Following the legacy of Dīpaṃkara and emulating the statutes of Śākyamuni, I transmit the essential tenets of the 'Mind-Only' and unfold the volumes of the Perfect and Sudden teachings;
hence it is said, 'I have always expounded [only this],' and so forth. △ Third, the question regarding the attainment of the fruit."
Zhijie asked Mañjuśrī, saying: "By practicing this sutra, can one quickly attain Buddhahood?
[Mañjuśrī] spoke of it as the ultimate treasury of a thousand Buddhas, calling it "profound"; he exhausted the subtle principles of essence and characteristics, calling it "sublime.
Its expanded meanings are inexhaustible, like a mani jewel; it is a rare wonder of the age that no other scripture can equal. This is a praise of the sutra.

This is the essential point. Are there any who, relying on this, practice with diligence and realize sudden enlightenment in a single lifetime? This question concerns those with the capacity for transformation.
△ Fourth, the answer: there are such people.
Mañjuśrī said: [The passage] from "his will was harmonious and elegant" up to "able to reach Bodhi" contains one phrase, *sa*, which indicates his clan and identifies the person.
The phrase "in his early years" reveals that although he was of a tender age, he possessed far-reaching wisdom.
The phrase "wisdom" (below) clarifies that his sharp intelligence observed the capacities of others. The phrase "attained the *dhāraṇī*" (below) clarifies that he held the treasury of the Dharma.

The two phrases following "profoundly enter" clarify the perfection of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*). The section below "at the moment of a *kṣaṇa*" clarifies the swift realization of complete virtue.

To say it is "subtle and wondrous" means that the four *siddhāntas* (purposes) respond to the capacities of beings; to say it is "vast and great" means that all return to the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*). With compassion one rescues all things, and with benevolence and humility one masters oneself.
Being harmonious, one dwells among things without discord; being refined, one rectifies oneself without frivolity. Possessing such a character, one stands firmly in this very place.

One attains Buddhahood; hence it is said that one "is able to reach Bodhi. Herein, within a single *kṣaṇa*, the Dragon Girl should descend and attain Buddhahood, which indicates the brevity of the time and the swiftness of the realization.
The initial arousal of the mind (*cittotpāda*) occurs at the beginning of the stage of abiding (*vihāra*). Non-retrogression corresponds to the eighth stage (*bhūmi*).
Eloquence corresponds to the ninth stage. The nurturing of compassion and the completion of the merit of great compassion correspond to the tenth stage.
The merit is fully perfected and the cultivation and realization are complete. This state of Vajra-like Equal Enlightenment is the fruit realized through this arousal of the bodhicitta;
it does not transcend a single kṣaṇa. As it is said: "In one cultivation, all are cultivated; in one abandonment, all are abandoned; in one realization, all are realized.
Just as when cutting silk or dyeing it, in the space of a single kṣaṇa, one can reach Bodhi—how could there be any sequence?
Chapter Five: The Questions of Jñānākūṭa.
The Bodhisattva Jñānākūṭa said: "I have seen that Śākyamuni Tathāgata [attained] perfect enlightenment in a mere moment."

"Those capable of performing difficult practices" refers to the relinquishing of one's head, eyes, and so forth. "Accumulating merit and virtue" means that by accumulating a thousand good deeds, one perfects the thousand marks and signs of a Buddha;
by accumulating ten thousand virtues, one achieves the adornment of ten thousand merits.

The section beginning with "The three thousand [worlds]" summarizes these difficult practices and ascetic austerities, extensively demonstrating the vastness of Śākyamuni’s self-sacrifices—there is not even a space the size of a mustard seed where he did not give himself away. Not... [the text ends].

Regarding the phrase "those who believe in this girl" and so forth: the intention of Jñatikauṇḍinya was that because the wondrous Dharma is so rare, one may attain its excellent exposition and be able to practice it;
thus, one ought certainly to give rise to faith in the attainment of Buddhahood.

However, when comparing the Muni, who has accumulated merit and virtue over many eons, with the Dragon Girl of eight years at the start of her resolve, there could not but be doubt concerning the difference in speed. If one believes in [her] swiftness, then such doubt is dispelled.

Kāśyapa is one of dull faculties and lacks wisdom; if he were slow to believe, he would surely doubt that a dragon girl could resolve her mind on enlightenment in a single instant and suddenly transcend the many kalpas it takes Śākyamuni [to reach Buddhahood]. Therefore, it says, "He did not believe," and so forth. △ Sixth: The Dragon Girl Resolves Doubts.
Before his speech had concluded, the Dragon King’s Daughter approached and stood to one side, praising him with these verses:
"Thoroughly penetrating the nature of sin and merit, You illuminate the ten directions, Liberating sentient beings from suffering."
[The section on] Discourse follows. The narrator introduces the present expression of reverence.

In the verse, after the Dragon Girl has praised the Buddha and offered her testimony, the two lines beginning with "Deeply penetrating" clarify that true wisdom shines forth clearly without omission. This means that because the Tathāgata deeply penetrates both transgression and merit, he will naturally testify and know for himself that I shall attain Buddhahood in an instant.
To speak of it in general terms, the three miserable realms constitute transgression, while the human and heavenly realms...

Regarding merit: to speak analytically, nine realms constitute demerit, while only the Buddha-realm constitutes merit. From the perspective of ordinary sentiment, one perceives the characteristics of demerit in the nine realms and the characteristics of merit in the Buddha-realm.
Since these characteristics of demerit and merit can be apprehended, this is not called profound, far-reaching, or clear realization.
However, when the Tathāgata contemplates them with inconceivable, wondrous wisdom, he does not perceive them as [existent].
One does not perceive the marks of transgression in the nine realms, nor does one perceive the marks of merit in the Buddha-realm.
One thoroughly realizes that all phenomena possess only a single true reality (*dharmatā*), such that no marks of transgression or merit can be found.

Yet, the reason the dragon girl praises the Buddha by virtue of her profound mastery over transgression and merit is because Zhizhi did not believe she could attain *bodhi*, given her status as a dragon...
A female being among the animal species is a sentient being burdened by suffering and transgression. Yet, upon seeing the Tathāgata, she perceives him as one adorned with merit and virtue.

If one can profoundly penetrate the nature of both transgression and merit, then one will not see the dragon girl as a being of suffering and transgression, nor the Tathāgata as one adorned with merit.

One will then have self-confidence that the dragon girl will undoubtedly attain Buddhahood in an instant. "The ten directions" refers to the ten realms; having thus deeply penetrated this, [she realizes her own potential].
Regarding sin and merit: one does not perceive the characteristics of the nine realms or the Buddha-realm as obtainable, and thus the ten realms are extinguished.
Although the ten realms are extinguished, this does not prevent the ten realms from remaining manifest. This is because the inconceivable, wondrous wisdom universally illumines the ten directions;
while the ten realms remain manifest, sin and merit are not lost. "Subtle and wondrous" and below clarify the purity of the Dharma-body.

"Pure and perfect. "The devas and humans below" clarifies that the eight classes of beings revere and follow him with respect. "Furthermore, having heard [the Dharma] below" proves that he has already attained Buddhahood and saves sentient beings;
by citing the Buddha as testimony, it shows that one can reach Bodhi, thereby dispelling the doubts of Zhijizhang.
"I shall expound... (two phrases) corresponds to what follows: "He immediately went to the south to attain Buddhahood and preached the wondrous Dharma," etc. △ Seven: The Interlude.
Māṇava (or Śāriputra) raised an objection.
At that time, Śāriputra said to the dragon girl: "[... up to "How can a female body so quickly attain Buddhahood?
[The phrase] "You say" below serves as a general summary of the point of the objection; it recounts what she has said and sets forth his own doubts. His intention is to say: "I..."

Those who possess the endowment of a true man and bear the excellence of one who transcends the mundane have fortunately heard this Dharma throughout their lives, yet they still await many kalpas to achieve the Way.

How much more so for you, a woman of a different species—seeing the fruit of Buddhahood as so easily attained, I fear your grand claims may wound the reality of things, making it difficult to inspire confidence.
Therefore, I shall examine the matter below to resolve these difficulties of faith. First, the impure body is difficult [to purify].
First, faith. Second, it is difficult to believe because it is causeless. Third, it is difficult to believe because of obstacles. What are the five obstacles?
The Brahma King practices pure conduct, whereas women are prone to defilement. Śakra has few desires, whereas women have many desires. Māra is firm and resolute, whereas women are soft and weak.
A Wheel-Turning King is benevolent and compassionate, whereas women are envious and harmful. The Buddha possesses ten thousand virtues, whereas women possess afflictions.
Therefore, the *Chao Riyue Sanmei Jing* (Sūtra on the Samādhi that Transcends the Sun and Moon) says: "By purely cultivating the four dhyānas, one becomes a Brahmā King;

by being licentious and unrestrained, one receives a female body. By being courageous and having few desires, one becomes Śakra; by having a coquettish air and many affectations, one receives a female body.

By fully possessing the ten wholesome dharmas and reverently serving the Triple Gem, one becomes a Māra King; by being arrogant, disrespectful, and disobeying, and by destroying and losing the true teaching, one receives a female body."
One who possesses a female body practices the bodhisattva path and has compassion for sentient beings, yet acts as a wheel-turning monarch (*cakravartin*).

One must undergo pure conduct while in a female body and fulfill the bodhisattva practices before one can become a Buddha. Since women do not possess these practices, they do not become Buddhas. Having heard of such obstacles:
One should loathe the female body and cultivate the conduct of a man; only then can one become a Buddha. △ Eighth, Offering Jewels to Remove Doubts.
This also has two parts. First, offering jewels to symbolize perfect understanding.
At that time, the dragon girl had a precious jewel... [until] "...my attainment of Buddhahood shall be even swifter than this.
The dragon girl thought to herself: "Zhijí (Jñānakūṭa) is the excellent successor of Prabhūtaratna, while Śāriputra is the foremost disciple of Śākyamuni.
Yet Zhijí’s doubts remain somewhat cursory, whereas Śāriputra’s refutations are increasingly detailed. If these two worthies are such as this, how much more so must the multitude of worthies [be]?"

This can be understood. If one were to further employ words to argue the point, it would ultimately be deemed mere flattery; therefore, the precious jewel is used as a metaphor to demonstrate the swiftness of realization.
The jewel symbolizes wisdom (*jñāna*), and the Buddha symbolizes principle (*tattva*). By harmonizing wisdom with principle, one proceeds from cause toward fruition.
Her "receiving [the prediction] quickly" signifies the swiftness with which the dragon girl attains fruition. Next, the fulfillment of the fruit correctly dispels the doubts of the assembly.
At that time, the entire assembly saw the dragon girl—[and so on]—preaching the sublime Dharma to all sentient beings.
That she suddenly became a male is because the myriad dharmas are like illusions and possess no fixed characteristics; how could they possibly undergo transformation?

It is not by changing that she transforms, but rather, being female, she is male. Her "possessing the bodhisattva practices" signifies the perfection of the causes, while her "sitting upon the lotus" and so forth signify the fulfillment of the fruits.

It is also for the sake of those below. This is the preaching of the Dharma. The South is a land of emptiness and luminosity; proceeding from the North to the South, one enters from delusion into awakening and achieves the Knowledge of All Modes (*sarvākārajñatā*).
A single jewel is the bestowal that accords with the nature of reality; its meaning encompasses all practices, making them perfectly complete.

Not abiding in the gift of the Dharma requires little effort yet yields great merit; how could it ever require the sacrifice of a thousand-fold world-system of body and life? Much more so... [the rest of the sentence is incomplete in the source].
Is it that six kalpas are equivalent [to a single day]? This refers to the meaning of the saying: "A bird of a thousand years cannot equal a phoenix born this morning.
The distinction between those with complete faculties and those without complete faculties, as well as the comparison of days and kalpas, is precisely this point. △ Ninth: The Assembly Gains Benefit.
At that time, the bodhisattvas and śrāvakas of the Sahā world (up to) having resolved their minds toward enlightenment and received their predictions.
At that time, the assembly below rejoiced and paid homage. "Immeasurable multitudes of beings below" refers to those in that land who received benefit.
Below the description of the Sahā world is the section on how this land receives benefit. The conditions for the two lands are not equal in their depth;

there is a distinction between the many and the few regarding the capacity for entering the Way. Since it is said that all sentient beings are ordinary folk who suddenly realize the truth and abide in the stage of non-retrogression, the assembly at the tenth assembly remained silent.
The Bodhisattva Jñānakūṭa, Śāriputra, and the entire assembly accepted this in silence.

Jñānakūṭa had not yet believed and remained in doubt; Śāriputra, employing his skillful means, raised objections. Only upon reaching this point did they realize that the dragon girl had practiced according to the perfect [teachings] and swiftly attained Buddhahood.
Witnessing the reality with their own eyes, their hearts were convinced by her words; their arguments were rendered powerless by her eloquence.

The grasping at the preservation of life naturally vanished, and the difficulties of the five obstacles were resolved like ice melting away. Therefore, together with the entire assembly, they silently accepted it with faith.
The first two chapters, demonstrating the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, are hereby concluded.
The Thirteenth Chapter of the Lotus Sutra, "The Encouragement of Devotion.

From this chapter up to the "Life Span" chapter, the purpose is to awaken one to the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. This is because the preceding two chapters have revealed the great wisdom of equality.
There is neither birth nor extinction; neither enemy nor friend. The divine efficacy of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* is inconceivable.
Therefore, the Tathāgata proclaimed his parinirvāṇa and sought out people so that this Way might endure forever and these teachings not fall into ruin.

To propagate this sutra in the final age requires nothing less than the power of a vow. For this reason, this chapter includes various bodhisattvas as well as newly ordained śrāvakas who have resolved [to uphold it].
I vow to propagate this sutra. While it is virtuous to endure hardships, it is not as excellent as being free from them altogether.

If one can indeed maintain oneself through the three guidelines and preserve oneself through the four practices, thereby blocking all hardships before they arise, what need is there to endure hardships after they have already occurred?
For this reason, great bodhisattvas from other lands, numbering more than eight times the sands of the Ganges, have made vows for this land.

When [Śāriputra] requested that the Tathāgata propagate the sutra, the Tathāgata declined, waiting instead for the disciples of the "Original Gate" (honmon) to emerge from the earth in immeasurable numbers.

Maitreya raised questions regarding this, whereby the Buddha revealed his long life-span (jūryō). This opened up the recent traces of the Master’s gate and manifested the remote origin of the Buddha-ground.
The great assembly at the dharma-congregation realized the nature-ocean of Vairocana; thus, the remote origin of the Buddha-ground is threefold.
The world benefits from it; the Dharma-body is eternally abiding, its transformations infinite and inexhaustible.
Without past or present, it was not first in the void kalpa, nor does it end at the limit of the future.

Reaching the ultimate and exhausting the source, these four chapters constitute the text for awakening to the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. This chapter is titled with the character "Holding" (持) because twenty thousand bodhisattvas...
Because he was commissioned to propagate the sutra, it is called "upholding by mandate.
If one gazes with blue-lotus eyes upon eighty trillion nayutas and so forth, causing them to make vows, this should be called "exhorting to uphold.

Since the number of twenty thousand bodhisattvas is specifically designated as the count for the separate commission in the "Dharma-Teacher" chapter, whereas there was no such separate commission prior to the figure of eighty trillion and so forth, [the present instance] involves gazing with the eyes.
Exhort the mind. Because it encompasses both and maintains them through exhortation and maintenance, it is called the "Chapter on Maintenance.
△ The third major section: Awakening to the Buddha’s Knowledge and Vision. This is divided into two parts. First: The disciples’ thorough understanding of the Sūtra through the Trace Gate.
Mañjuśrī requests instruction; the Tathāgata reveals the four practices as the proper method. Second, the disciples from the original gate set forth to propagate the sutra;

Maitreya raises doubts, and the Tathāgata elucidates his original lifespan. This section has two parts: first, clarifying the upholding of the sutra; second, demonstrating the proper method. The first part also has two sections:
first, clarifying the receiving and upholding; second, clarifying the exhortation to uphold. The first of these also has three sections: first, the bodhisattvas' offering...
He commanded him to propagate this sutra in this land.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Bhaiṣajyarāja (up to) made various offerings, not sparing even his own body or life.
Bhaiṣajyarāja and the twenty thousand others were the persons to whom the "Dharma-preacher" chapter was addressed as its basis; they were also those who delighted in preaching.

Regarding the *Ratnakoṭi-parivarta*, as the appropriate recipients had already heard the Tathāgata proclaim his entry into extinction and seek those who would propagate the sutra, the various Great Beings immediately accepted this command and made their vows.

"I pray that you do not worry" means that while the Holy Path is recorded in the scriptures, the power to expand and propagate it rests with the wise; if such a person is not found, these subtle words will perish.

If these teachings were not clarified for those capable of receiving them, and could not be put into practice in this world, such that the common people fell into the eight great ravines, it would truly be a cause for concern to Your Holiness’s sacred mind.
Now that you have been able to undertake this task, I pray that Your Holiness’s mind may be free from anxiety.
That the roots of goodness are meager is the defilement of sentient beings; that of overweening pride is the defilement of views; and that of greed...

Gain and offerings are the turbidity of afflictions (*kleśa-kaṣāya*). The increase of unwholesome states is the turbidity of lifespan (*āyuḥ-kaṣāya*). To be far removed from even a single phrase is the turbidity of the eon (*kalpa-kaṣāya*).

When the worldly path has fallen into ruin and heterodox views compete for dominance, in such an age of the five turbidities (*pañca-kaṣāya*), those with right faith are few while those with false views are many.
People strive only to pursue profit to nourish their four limbs; how could they possibly maintain their minds to repel the five desires and the ten non-virtues?
As one nourishes oneself, the three voids gradually distance themselves; even in the way of human relations, there are still lapses in the fundamental constants of conduct.
How much less can those who have escaped to the realm beyond the world enter into divine transformation? Thus it is said they are difficult to teach and transform.

Those who give rise to the power of great patience are not bodhisattvas of the deep stages; unless the power of patience is perfected, one cannot recite [this scripture]. Enduring all evils while maintaining outward form—
Hài: One must traverse hardships to practice this path; hence it is said that one does not spare body or life. This is not the case for those with bodies of earth or wood;
those who have not awakened from the dream of birth and death cannot achieve such a resolve. △ Second, the śrāvakas make vows to propagate the sutra in other lands.
At that time, among the assembly, five hundred arhats—[up to] because their minds were turbid with anger, crooked with flattery, and insincere—their power of the Path was not yet sufficient.

They were unable to endure the evil age; thus they made vows to propagate the Dharma and benefit sentient beings in other lands and different realms, fearing the difficulty of taming and subduing those in the Sahā world. To explain this further: "the corrupt and evil" refers to...
They are persons who destroy virtuous qualities and accumulate evil karma. Those who harbor overweening pride claim to have attained what they have not attained;

by mentioning one, they imply all seven. Those of meager merit possess even a small amount of goodness, yet it is entirely tainted (*sāsrava*) and not a cause that accords with the nature of reality (*dharmatā*).
Hatred contains greed and delusion, which turbidly cloud the nature of wisdom (*prajñā*). Deceit and crookedness consist of clever speech and a contrived countenance.
Those who are sycophantic and fawning—among these, anger and pride are the two roots, while flattery is the foremost of the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*).

By combining the two roots with the four tendencies, and by having the foremost govern the rest, the full complement of roots and tendencies constitutes the meaning of the aforementioned "corrupt and evil.
Possessing all these evils, one is hypocritical, deceitful, and lacks faith; thus it is said, "because the mind is not real. Because it is not real...
It is difficult to speak of the Way; therefore, I vow to go to other lands and distant realms to expound this sutra extensively.

This is truly because those of the Two Vehicles have a biased and withered view of the ground, failing to understand the transformation from "raising the waves" to "drinking the dregs. It is difficult to transform an age mired in turbidity and intoxication; thus, it could not be otherwise.
△ Third, the six thousand bhikṣuṇīs request a prediction [of their future enlightenment]. This section is divided into three parts.
First, Mahāprajāpatī requested a prediction [of her future enlightenment]. There were two [parts to this]: first, she requested the prediction.
At that time, the Buddha’s maternal aunt, Mahāprajāpatī—[omitted]—gazed upon the Honored One’s countenance, never for a moment averting her eyes.
Kauṇḍinya was the leader of the assembly of nuns; therefore, she presided over six thousand [nuns] and requested a prediction of enlightenment.

When the assembly of nuns saw that the śrāvakas had received their predictions and that the dragon girl would attain Buddhahood, their resolve was inspired. They thought: "If even a śrāvaka [can attain it]..."
"He is a śrāvaka, and I too am a śrāvaka. Since we have heard the Dharma together, it stands to reason that there should be no difference between us;
why then is the prediction of enlightenment not granted to us? As for being female: she is a dragon girl, and we too are women."
Since we share the same status, we must surely share the same path. How could we, the dragon girls, be inferior?

For this reason, though our hearts were already resolved, we hesitated and remained undecided; thus, with a sense of pent-up longing, our mouths desired to speak yet found it difficult to find the words.
We merely turned our heads and gazed at you, awaiting your command. △ Next, [the Buddha] bestows the prediction.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Gautamī (up to the point where she) shall attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
This was what I previously stated in summary; it refers to the end of the chapter on the five hundred disciples, specifically the one and a half verses beginning with "Kāśyapa, you already know.
From the words "Now you" onwards is the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*); from "shall attain" onwards is the name of the fruit: Sarvasukhasaṃdarśana.

Because the Dharma Master gladdens people with the joy of the Dharma, the fruit is likewise named after him. From the phrase "All these" below, he sequentially bestows predictions of enlightenment upon them.
Furthermore, the term "bodhisattvas" refers to the six thousand who will in the future possess the path of a bodhisattva.
II. Yaśodharā’s Request for a Prediction, which also has two parts. First, the request for a prediction.
At that time, Rāhula’s mother [thought]: "The World-Honored One has not mentioned my name alone among those receiving the prediction.
Having heard this general prediction, how could I not know that I too have a share?

Yet, seeing that the Noble Mother received her prediction face-to-face, I also requested that my name be mentioned, desiring thereby to manifest my own virtue and to satisfy the expectations of the multitude. △ Next, the bestowal of the prediction.
The Buddha told Yaśodharā [and so forth], up until: "The Buddha’s lifespan shall be immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas.
Yaśodharā manifested these traces to represent Great Compassion; her joy in the Dharma accords with Great Wisdom.

Only after wisdom and compassion are practiced in tandem are the ten thousand virtues fully perfected and the thousand marks adorned with light. Therefore, the fruit is named "Endowed with Ten Million Radiant Marks. Thus it is taken.
Adorned with the primary and secondary marks (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*), his bodily radiance was inexhaustible, and his lifespan was immeasurable.
Since it is called a "Land of Virtue," benevolent people succeed one another, and their allotted lifespans are long; thus, according to their capacities, their stay in the world is also eternal.

The *Karunāpuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states that the maternal aunt was originally a water deity who made a vow in birth after birth to become the Buddha’s maternal aunt. Yaśodharā was originally a... [text fragment] ...śū.

The goddess of Mount Mīna has made a vow in life after life to become the Buddha’s wife; she now seeks the Buddha’s permission to leave the household life, attain the Way, and receive a prediction of enlightenment.
The present bestowal of this prediction fulfills her long-cherished wish. △ Third, the assembly of nuns understands and makes a vow.
At that time, Mahāprajāpatī [approached] and spoke these verses before the Buddha:
"O World-Honored One, Guide who brings peace to devas and humans, having heard this prediction, our minds are fully satisfied."
After the bhikṣuṇīs had spoken these verses, they widely proclaimed this sutra in other lands.
They joyfully praised it with verses and made vows to propagate the scripture; the text is clear and easy to understand. This concludes the section on receiving and upholding [the teaching].
II. Explaining the Exhortation to Uphold. This consists of both prose and verse. The prose is divided into two parts; first, the Tathāgata gazes upon them.
At that time, the World-Honored One gazed upon eight hundred trillion nayutas of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.
By looking at them with his eyes, he observed these great beings whose rank was second only to the sages and whose realization surpassed that of the lesser worthies;

their talent was sufficient to shoulder the Great Way, and their character was sufficient to sustain the degenerate age. He remained silent, sending them forth in his mind, so that they might present themselves of their own accord. Furthermore—

To divide the counting sticks between this land and other lands to determine the final tally does not accord with the Sage’s intention; therefore, he looks upon the various bodhisattvas and causes them to make vows.

These bodhisattvas are all *avaivartika* (non-retrogressive); dwelling in other directions, they behold and protect [the assembly] from afar.

However, as their physical forms are already present while their words have not yet reached him, they thus formulate a thought to request his instruction. Furthermore, the following section refers to the present.
The Buddha remained silent. His intention must surely have been present; we had not yet heard his command, so what plan should we devise?
We did not dare to act on our own initiative, for we respectfully followed the Buddha’s intent in two ways: first, his gaze was itself a dispatch of messengers, requiring no words;
second, he wished for people to shoulder this Dharma, upholding and expounding it so that it would not perish. Thus, we continued his resolve and recounted his deeds.
This is to reverently uphold the Sage’s intent. Why wait for a formal command before making this vow? My original vow is the Way of the One Vehicle:
having awakened to it myself, I shall further awaken others. Above, I shall cause the Dharma drum to ring constantly;

below, I shall startle the masses of the deluded so they never rest. This is my original vow. To achieve both goals with a single effort—this is what is meant by "reverently following [the intent] so that it is spontaneously fulfilled. Thus he hesitated.
Having stepped forward with firm resolve, he approached and proclaimed his vow, undertaking this difficult task with fearless speech; hence it is called the "Lion’s Roar.

Regarding "pacing throughout the ten directions": although the various worthies each preside over a single direction, establishing boundaries and demarcating territories, there is in fact no person in the world who cannot be transformed, nor any place where the Path cannot be practiced. When the time is ripe...
When the Way flourishes, what further need is there for the Sage to act?

Therefore, he speaks without discriminating between good and evil, pervading all places so that all sentient beings may benefit others by copying and explaining these teachings, and benefit themselves by practicing with right mindfulness.
This Bodhisattva differs from the previous two; whereas the former merely upheld [the teaching] for themselves, this one receives the intent of the Tathāgata’s entrustment and acts universally.

"Causing others to uphold it" means that all [this] is due to the Buddha's power; this attributes the merit to the Buddha, for it is through the empowerment of the Buddha’s three wheels (*trimaṇḍala*) that this occurs.

"May you, etc. refers to the fact that this Dharma is the wisdom-life of all Buddhas and cannot be achieved by anyone else. Although one's original vow is thus, it cannot be fulfilled without the Buddha's power;
therefore, one relies upon his protective mindfulness so that the divine chariot may arrive at the Peak of Spirituality (*Liṅfēng*).

Traversing perilous paths and driving straight ahead, it carries the sentient beings of this turbid world across to liberation from suffering. △ Second, the verse summary consists of twenty lines, divided into three parts.

From within the mind of right concentration, he gives rise to the wisdom of contemplative observation (*vipaśyanā-prajñā*) and observes all things—both mundane and supramundane—within the three aggregates (*skandha*), seven elements (*dhātu*), and four bases (*āyatana*), as well as birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) and nirvāṇa.
He perceives that the very substance of these various phenomena is truly pure; not even a single speck of dust can be received. Therefore, they are called "empty.
This is precisely the emptiness of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*). As for "the true mark" (*yathābhūta-lakṣaṇa*), it refers to the mental states and objects of all sentient beings...
The Dharma is identical to the true reality (*dharmatā*) realized by all Buddhas; it is the equality of the ten suchnesses (*daśa-tathatā*), immovable and indestructible.
Because it is free from delusive conditions, that which is non-perverted immediately transcends all suffering and peril. To remain far removed from perversion is the function of true reality.
As for being "immovable," it is like observing the rushing currents of rivers and yet seeing no flow; one understands that perception follows conditions.
"Unchanging" is the essence of the true mark (*dharmatā*). "Non-retrogressive" means that, from the perspective of sentient beings, there has never been any retrogression;
True Suchness does not diminish as it accords with conditions. "Non-transforming" means that, from the perspective of the Buddhas, there has never been any transformation;
True Suchness does not increase as it accords with purity. "Non-perverted" is right view. "Immovable and non-transforming" is true knowledge. This is seeing.
Without inversion, they do not discriminate between the existence or non-existence of phenomena. Their minds are without fluctuation;
they gather their minds so that they are as immovable as Mount Sumeru. Because Bodhisattvas possess right knowledge and right view, they contemplate all phenomena in this manner.
The phrase "like space" is an illustration. It establishes that space is without intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*) and is beyond the reach of verbal expression.
The subsequent passage explains that space lacks the characteristics of arising, production, and origination; thus, it cannot be indicated by linguistic designations.
One observes that space has no nature of arising in the past, and therefore it does not arise. One examines that space has nothing [of the nature of arising] in the present...
Because it arises from the nature of existence, it does not emerge. Because one investigates the arising-nature of the void, the future, and non-existence, it does not originate.
It is absent throughout the three periods of time; only the One Emptiness remains. This emptiness has no fixed name:

when obstructed, it becomes form; when unobstructed, it becomes space. It also has no fixed characteristics: in a square vessel it is square, and in a round vessel it is round. In reality, there is nothing at all.
That which possesses a fixed nature is beyond the reach of verbal expression; therefore, the path of language is cut off.
The realm of the principle of the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) should also be viewed in this way. Within the essence of the true mark, there is likewise no nature of "non-existence";

thus, these dharmas cannot be demonstrated, and the characteristics of speech are quiescent. This is because they were not produced in the past, do not emerge in the present, and will not [arise] in the future.
It arises because the three periods of time do not shift. One examines that the true mark (dharmatā) is nameless; the Buddha is a provisional name for that which is without arising.
One investigates that the true mark is signless; it possesses no signs such as birth-and-death or nirvana. Therefore, it is said that "in reality, there is nothing at all."
"Immeasurable and boundless" means that space cannot be exhausted; this is the vastness of the true mark (*dharmatā*).
"Unobstructed and unimpeded" means that space cannot be differentiated; this is the penetration of the true mark.
Space is thus, and the true mark is thus. Since the nature of all phenomena is inherently quiescent, what words can there be to express it?
How profound! All that can be spoken arises only from causes and conditions and is produced through inversion; thus there exist all verbal expressions.
One should know that which does not arise from conditions and is not produced from inversion is ultimately inexpressible;

hence it is said that "all paths of language are cut off. For the essence of the mind is fundamentally quiescent; it is through mutual dependence that it becomes agitated, arising from the perception of inversion.
Inversion means that dharmas have birth and arising; therefore, the mind has movement and transformation, like the shifting of the shore when a boat moves.
If one can contemplate according to the true mark (*yathābhūtalakṣaṇa*), the mind neither moves nor transforms, and dharmas neither arise nor appear.
If the wind ceases, the waves become tranquil; the nature of mind is one and the same. When viewed with a perverted mind, delusory objects appear in chaotic confusion;
when viewed through the lens of true reality (*dharmatā*), the true state of things is naturally quiescent.
One who practices the path of peace and bliss and constantly delights in viewing all phenomena as they truly are in their true reality is said to be a bodhisattva’s second station of intimacy.
...as well. △ Second, the verse summary (*gāthā-paṭala*). It consists of twenty-eight lines and three phrases, divided into two parts. First, twenty-three lines summarize the preceding prose section.
Second, five lines and three phrases conclude by clarifying the accomplishment of practice. The first part is further divided into two.
First, fifteen lines summarize the practices regarding the two locations.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:
"If there are bodhisattvas in the evil world of the future... (up to)... by means of these two bases, they will be able to preach with peace and joy."
A mind free from fear means that one abides in the stage of patience (*kṣānti-bhūmi*) and the mind is not startled.
"Superiority" (*adhimāna*) refers to conceit regarding the qualities of superior persons, such as claiming to have attained what one has not yet attained. Regarding the "Three Baskets" (*Tripiṭaka*):
when the Buddha was at Vārāṇasī, he first taught the Sūtra Piṭaka to Kauṇḍinya and others; furthermore, when he was at Rājagṛha, he first...
He expounded the Vinaya Piṭaka for Sunakṣatra. Furthermore, while at the Markaṭahrada Lake in Vaiśālī, he first expounded the Abhidharma Piṭaka for the son of the Vṛji clan;
this refers to the Tripiṭaka of the Hīnayāna. He was one who practiced and adhered to the Hīnayāna.

This hinders the propagation of the Great Dharma; therefore, one must distance oneself from such people. As for those who bear the name, they are called "Arhats" by way of a provisional designation, yet they have not attained actual realization.
Those who seek manifest parinirvāṇa desire to quickly attain realization and are not vessels for the Great Dharma; thus, one who propagates the Great Dharma [should avoid them].

One must not associate with them. To have "no expectations" means that in the past, there were those who never spoke a single word of Dharma for the sake of profit, nor ever accepted so much as a hair’s breadth of wealth on account of the Dharma; only such a person may be said to have no expectations.
Regarding "butchering": to slaughter is called *tu*; to mince meat finely is called *huai*. A "peddler" (*fan*) is one who buys at a low price and sells at a high price. To "display" (*xuan*)...
This refers to selling [goods]. All such practices are not pure conduct; therefore, one should distance oneself from them. Regarding entering a village to beg for food, the *Saṃyukta Āgama* states:
There was once a sheep that went to a dung heap, ate its fill, and returned to the flock, behaving with arrogance and self-importance.
It is the same with the bhikṣu. Having received the four kinds of offerings, he gives rise to thoughts of attachment and does not know the way of transcendence;
he disparages others, thinking, "I have obtained this, while they have not. This is the sheep-like bhikṣu who goes for alms.
As for the lion king, when it encounters a large beast, it devours it without savoring or attachment; when it obtains a small beast, it devours it without contempt or disdain.
So it is with the bhikṣu: having received the four kinds of offerings, he does not give rise to a mind of defiled attachment;

he knows for himself the way of transcendence, and his mind is free from increase or decrease. This is called the lion-like bhikṣu begging for alms. Furthermore, before the bhikṣu has obtained food...

One should maintain mindfulness for the sake of cultivating the Path and for the purpose of mending the wounds of hunger. Once food has been obtained, one should not cease mindfulness of the Path in order to repay the kindness of the donor.
The *Ratnamegha Sūtra* states: "When begging for food, one should divide it into four portions; one portion should be offered to fellow practitioners of the holy life."
One part is given to beggars; one part is offered to spirits and deities; one part is eaten by oneself. △ Second, the eight lines of verse praise the practice of benefiting others.
This is divided into two parts. First, two and a half lines praise the practice of benefiting others.
Furthermore, not practicing the superior, middling, or inferior dharmas—this is what is called the bodhisattva’s sphere of practice.

[The "superior, middling, and inferior" refers to the three vehicles. Question: Since the middling and inferior [vehicles] should not be practiced, and the superior is the One Vehicle (Ekayāna), which is precisely what a bodhisattva ought to practice, why do you now say they should not be practiced?
What other dharma should one then practice? Answer: This very One Vehicle is nothing other than that; there is no separate [dharma].

Regarding the Dharma, what is called "non-practice" does not mean that one ultimately fails to cultivate the intent of the One Vehicle. It means cultivating without cultivation and practicing without practice.
If there were truly a dharma being practiced that accorded with one's emotions, then there would be a person who practices existing within the mind;
subject and object would be established, right and wrong would arise, suffering and difficulty would emerge, and peace and happiness would be lost. This pertains to the conditioned world.

Because it is a conditioned dharma, it is unreal; because it is an unconditioned, supramundane dharma, it is real. Its true mark is fundamentally beyond words and cannot be differentiated, and so forth.
This verse further concerns the non-engagement with dharmas and so on. [This concludes] the two lines regarding "not obtaining."
This means that one should not give rise to false knowledge or views regarding all phenomena; rather, one should give rise to right knowledge and views.
To integrate this through principle, there are no marks of any differentiation or equality, for every phenomenon is identical to the single Dharma.
△ Next, five lines and a half of verse praise the practice of proximity.
All dharmas are empty and non-existent (up to: eternally abiding in a single characteristic; this is called the proximate station.
This corresponds to the preceding verse on contemplating the emptiness of all dharmas and so forth. There are no two [separate] phrases; it is precisely the true mark of suchness (*tathatā*).
Following conditions, it is not permanent; remaining unchanging, it is not annihilated. Being neither annihilated nor permanent, when the fruit arises, the cause ceases. All dharmas...

The Dharma is fundamentally neither of annihilation nor permanence, neither existence nor non-existence, and so forth. It is only through inverted, deluded conceptualization that one discriminates between "existence" and "non-existence.
Ultimately, one fails to know that it is neither existent nor non-existent, neither real nor unreal, neither arising nor ceasing—it is ultimately equal.
[The following section] clarifies placing the mind in a single location so that it does not wander into the weeds, like Mount Sumeru.

Abiding immovably, one contemplates all phenomena according to the principle of their true suchness (*tathatā*). Like space, they are eternally abiding in a single mark, without marks of differentiation.
△ Second, the three phrases on the five practices, concluding with the clarification of the perfection of practice.

If there are bhikṣus who, after my parinirvāṇa, are able to preach the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* in future ages, they will achieve success through the practice of phenomena (*dharmatā*), whereby their external deportment will be without fault;
and they will achieve success through the practice of principle (*tattva*), whereby their inner mind will be without obstruction.

Therefore, it is said that they shall have no timidity when preaching the sūtra. At times, the Bodhisattva descends to explain the causes of peace and bliss, entering stillness by means of these causes.

By practicing meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) within the chamber, one ceases transgressions and evils. By attaining the selflessness of persons (*pudgala-nairātmya*), one is not harmed from without.
By cultivating wisdom through correct mindfulness, one becomes free from all attachments and grasping. By attaining the selflessness of phenomena (*dharma-nairātmya*), there is no inversion within;
the mind is peaceful and undaunted, and thus there is bliss. The first method is precisely the rectification of the body. The practice of physical ease and bliss is concluded. △
Second is the practice of peaceful conduct through speech (*vāk-sukha-vihāra*). This consists of both prose and verse. The prose section is divided into two parts:
first, the presentation of the chapter headings. Furthermore: "Moreover, Mañjuśrī, after the Tathāgata has passed into extinction... [one] should abide in peaceful conduct."
The heading indicates "Peace and Bliss. △ Next, the explanation of the practice of cultivation is divided into two parts. First, the clarification of the practice of *śamatha* (calm abiding):
"Whether speaking aloud or reading the scriptures... [omitted] ...nor does one give rise to a mind of resentment or aversion."
If one does not speak of faults regarding the words below, [the interlocutor] asks: "What fault is there in the person? What fault is there in the scripture? The answer is:

"The scriptures comprise both Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna; persons possess both great and small capacities. When the vehicle is matched against the capacity, it is difficult to understand according to what is appropriate.

Furthermore, the scriptures have the fault of revealing the nature while setting aside the provisional to establish the real, and the fault of destroying appearances while concealing the real to open up the provisional. Persons, moreover, have attachments."
The fault lies in the principle that one does not believe in gradual cultivation; the fault lies in the practice that one does not believe in sudden enlightenment.
If essence and phenomena are mutually integrated, what fault is there in the sutras? If principle and phenomenon are unimpeded, what fault is there in the person?

To say there is a fault would only disturb those who hear and receive the teaching, bringing no peace to their speech; therefore, it is forbidden. Furthermore, do not belittle them, nor treat them with contempt.
Those who propagate the sutras must not rely on the perfection of the *Lotus Sūtra* to despise teachers of partial and expedient teachings.

Even the Buddha employed diverse expedient means to assist the true path of perfect reality; how much more so should those propagating the sutras in later ages refrain from slighting or disparaging the provisional and the lesser?
One must accord with the Buddha’s intent and protect the capacities of sentient beings; therefore, this is cautioned against. "Do not speak [of them] as inferior," and so forth.

Do not praise or disparage. First, do not speak of all people. It is a fact that those who receive the substance of the two polarities possess a natural disposition that is never incomplete, yet their physical and emotional natures are never without partiality.
Since people loathe hearing of their own failings, one does not speak of others' shortcomings.
Since those who love praise inevitably excel at disparagement, one does not extol others' virtues. This is how one who is skilled at harmonizing things with things acts.

That which is not uniform is brought to uniformity; thus, there is nothing that is not uniform. Next, [the text] separately addresses the śrāvakas. These individuals possess indeterminate faculties (*indriya*);
if one praises the excellence of the two vehicles (śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha), it may cause them to regress from the Great Vehicle and adopt the Lesser.

If one disparages the faults of the two vehicles, it may cause them to lose both the Lesser and the Great. Therefore, neither disparagement nor praise is appropriate. As the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
Self-praise, self-deprecation, praising others, and disparaging others—these four things are not practiced by the wise.
Why is this? One who praises themselves is a person of arrogance; one who deprecates themselves is a person of delusive deception; one who praises others is a person of sycophancy;
and one who disparages others is a person of slanderous treachery. If even one of these exists, there is no peace in the mouth. Furthermore:

Furthermore, one must not harbor resentment or aversion. To think that the person from whom one has received [the teaching], or the Dharma they uphold, obstructs one’s own path is a mind of resentment.
To think that such a person or their Dharma is base and inferior is a mind of aversion.

One who practices for peace and happiness, in order to propagate the Great Canon and to protect those of lesser practice, must abandon both resentment and aversion; only then can it be called right practice. Mind.

As soon as the faculty moves, speech and explanation immediately issue forth; thus, by blocking the source of transgression, the mind does not arise. △ Second, the explanation of contemplative practice:
Because one skillfully cultivates such a mind of peace and bliss... (up to)... causing one to attain all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*).
Cultivate this well in such a manner. Following what was stated above, do not speak harshly, nor harbor resentment or malice.

Let the mind be free from attachment; never insist on being great while disparaging the small. Rather, act in accordance with the sentiments of others and do not oppose their intentions. Should there be difficult questions or inquiries, [respond accordingly].
One does not deliver beings by means of the Hīnayāna, but instructs and guides them solely through the Mahāyāna. There are two intentions here:
if one perceives that a person lacks the capacity for the Great Vehicle and teaches them the Small Vehicle, it merely allows them to obtain the provisional benefits of the Small.

If one does not perceive that they lack the capacity for the Great Vehicle and yet teaches them the Small Vehicle, this obstructs their connection with the Great. Therefore, one teaches only the Great; thus, there is no fault of duality. Furthermore:
The followers of the Hīnayāna understand only the sequential unfolding of practice (*khyāpana*) and do not recognize its perfect interfusion (*yuanrong*).

Although difficult questions are many, the phenomena of ordinary beings and sages, as well as the primary and secondary realms, do not exceed ten pairs of oppositions: first, the difficulty of the divergence between delusion and awakening; second, the difficulty of the contradiction between phenomena and principle;

third, the difficulty of the lack of clarity regarding the provisional and the real; fourth, the difficulty of the non-convergence of essence and function; fifth, the difficulty of the obstruction between natures; sixth, the mind and objects...

The difficulty of conceptual differentiation; the difficulty of the divergent modes of the seven wisdoms; the difficulty of the varying depths of cultivation and realization; the difficulty of the distinctness of cause and effect;
and the difficulty of the hierarchy between sentient beings and Buddhas. If one has not clarified these ten pairs as returning to the single reality-mark (dharmatā), [one cannot attain liberation].
All these are of the Hīnayāna. Should such an objection arise, one guides them by appealing to what is easily understood by their minds;

perhaps answering one question may resolve ten difficulties, causing them to awaken through a single word, turning from the Small Vehicle toward the Great, and hastening toward the cultivation of the seed-wisdom of Bodhi.
△ Second, the verse commentary consists of sixteen and a half lines, divided into two parts. First, eleven [lines].

The first part consists of seven and a half lines, which are verses summarizing the practice of *śamatha* (calm abiding). This is followed by five lines that conclude by clarifying the accomplishment of the practice. The initial section [of the commentary] is further divided into two parts;
first, the seven and a half lines are verses on the practice of *śamatha*.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"The Bodhisattva always delights in teaching the Dharma with peace and security... [omitted] ...teaching the Dharma with a compassionate heart, free from all sorrow and affliction."
If you desire peace and happiness in speech, you must preach the Dharma. If you wish to preach the Dharma, you must first select an appropriate place.

Ascend the seat, bathe, and don your robes; let your inner state and outer appearance be one and the same. Only then, according to the questions asked, do you preach, and according to the principles involved, do you answer, so that all may resolve to enter the Way.
Laziness hinders valor; indolence hinders diligence; and anxiety and affliction hinder peace and happiness. Thus it is with the Bodhisattva.

Only by preaching the Dharma with a mind of loving-kindness can one truly be free from all obstacles. The preceding section was based on *śamatha* (calm abiding); the present section is based on *vipaśyanā* (insight).
Therefore, it does not correspond in detail to the text above. Next, four lines of verse describe the practice of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*).
Day and night they constantly preach the unsurpassed Way of the Buddha (up to: this is indeed a great benefit, peace, and blissful offering.
They preach the unsurpassed Way; their verses explain it solely through the Mahāyāna. They contemplate only the attainment of Buddhahood and cause all beings to attain Buddhahood.

The verse praises the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*); this constitutes a great benefit. There are five such benefits: first, teaching without interruption day and night, which manifests the benefit of the eternal nature of the Dharma-body;
second, teaching through immeasurable causes and analogies, which manifests the benefit of inexhaustible sublime function;

third, teaching so as to cause all to rejoice, which manifests the benefit of vast compassion; fourth, teaching without expectation of the four requisites, which manifests the [benefit of] accomplishment...
Regarding the benefit of the four virtues, the fifth [chapter] explains the attainment of Buddhahood by oneself and others, manifesting the benefit of the equality of the Buddha’s wisdom.
△ Second, the conclusion of the five practices clarifies the perfection of practice:
"After my parinirvāṇa, if there should be bhikṣus... (up to) ...it cannot be fully described even by means of calculation or analogy."
The mind is peerless. When there is no fault or evil within, external difficulties—such as being reviled and so forth—will not arise.

(For details, see the verses of the "Chapter on Guarding. "The wise person," and so on: because there are wholesome dharmas within, one's practice is perfected. "That person," and so on: this concludes the "Peaceful Practice of Speech.
△ Third, the Peaceful Practice of Mind. This consists of prose and verse. The prose is divided into two parts; first, the heading:
Chapter.
Furthermore, from "Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva Mahāsattva" up to "those who receive, uphold, read, and recite this sutra," it indicates that their intention is for peace and happiness.
△ Next, the explanation of the method of practice is divided into three parts. First, the explanation of the practice of cessation (*śamatha*).
One should not harbor a mind of jealousy, flattery, or deception (up to: nor should one engage in frivolous speculation regarding phenomena or contend with others).

"Not harboring" means being without jealousy or flattery. Jealousy (*īrṣyā*) has the nature of envying the prosperity of others and being unable to endure their success, while being preoccupied with one's own fame and profit.
Flattery (*śāṭhya*) has the nature of being crooked and devious, assuming a false appearance and deportment for the sake of deceiving others. Deception (*māyā*) is for the purpose of gaining...
Making offerings while feigning virtue; having deceit as one’s nature—these three minor derivative afflictions. Envy violates the mind of compassion;
flattery and deception run counter to the path of wisdom. These are not the methods for one's own practice; if wisdom is thus obstructed.
If compassion were an obstacle, with what would one seek the Buddha-way above? If it were an impediment, with what would one transform sentient beings below?

A Bodhisattva practicing the path of mental peace and bliss must guard against this. One must not disparage or revile others; specifically, one should not rely on the practice of the Perfect [Teaching] to criticize the provisional practice, which is why it is called "disparaging.
Nor should one rely on the strengths of the Perfect Teaching to seek out the shortcomings of the provisional teaching.
This is because it causes those who have retreated from the path of training in the Buddha-way to lose their roots of goodness; therefore, it is forbidden.

"If a bhikṣu," and so forth, means not to cause distress or confusion, nor to harbor doubt or regret. Doubt refers to questioning whether what one has attained is incorrect; regret refers to lamenting over the magnitude of what one has lost. Thus, it says "below."

Explanation of the terms: To depart from the Way and lose the wisdom [of it], and to feel weary of birth and death while being indolent toward transforming and guiding others, is called *kausīdya* (laziness).

The *Karunāpuṇḍarīka Sūtra* states: "Those of the Two Vehicles are people of laziness. Furthermore, below this, not engaging in contention and making inverted discriminations regarding the existence or non-existence of all phenomena is called frivolous proliferation (*prapañca*) and contention.
All of the above constitute subtle, unwholesome conduct of the mental ground (*manobhūmi*).
Therefore, one must cease them. The *Śrīmālā-sūtra* (Yijing jing) says: "Various frivolous discourses cause the mind to become distracted;
