even though one has left the household life, one still cannot attain liberation. For this reason, bhikṣus must abandon them. II. Explaining Contemplative Practice.
Toward all sentient beings—even those who deeply love the Dharma—I do not speak at great length.
The twelve classes of living beings are all encompassed within my heart of compassion; pitying their delusion and infatuation, I employ thoughts of pity to rescue them.
If I were to abandon them, who else would? As for the "Compassionate Father," all of my forty-two stages of merit are fully contained therein.
Within the sphere of the Tathāgata, all is summarized and rectified. If one were to set aside the Tathāgata, who else could there be?
As for the Great Master: the path of the Bodhisattva is entirely my perfected dharma. Mañjuśrī perfects my wisdom; Samantabhadra perfects my practice.
Without Avalokiteśvara, my virtue of the Universal Gate would not be perfected. If one were to set aside Viśuddhagarbha, who else could turn the wheel for me?
How could this not be a benefit to those who are heterodox? One should, with a profound heart, pay respectful homage.

Gathering the teachings of the multitude of sages from the ten directions to perfect the Way of one's own person—what else could they be but teachers? "Equanimity" means the absence of partiality and private bias;

"conforming to the Dharma" refers to discourse that accords with principle. That there is neither too much nor too little is because the capacity of the recipient—whether sharp or dull—is measured. It is not done for [selfish ends].

Regarding those who speak much: it is valued that one neither loses the person nor loses the words. To love the Dharma and speak much while the mind is not equanimous—how could the intention be at peace?
△ Third, the conclusion on the accomplishment of practice.
Mañjuśrī, when this bodhisattva-mahāsattva—up to the point of being revered, honored, and praised—their mind is at peace and blissful.
When they preach this sutra, how could any obstacles or difficulties possibly afflict them? Therefore, it is said that "none can disturb or confuse them.
As for obtaining good companions in study, I shall be their virtuous associate, and others likewise shall be my virtuous associates.
This is what is meant by "friends come from afar. When one gains the ear of the multitude, their inner virtue naturally becomes full;
they will surely be verified as trustworthy by others, and all people will follow them. This is what is meant by "virtue is not solitary.
To listen is to study the Way I uphold; to uphold it is to chant the virtue I recite; to recite it is to contemplate the meaning I explain; and to explain it is...
To transmit my Way, one records it in writing; from the time of the first scribe until now, through offerings and praises, the practice has been perfected and its retribution manifested.
Thus it is. △ Second, the verse in praise consists of six lines, divided into three parts. The first two lines praise the practice of *śamatha* (calm abiding).
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"If one wishes to preach this sutra, one should abandon jealousy, anger, and pride... [until] saying, 'You shall not attain Buddhahood.'"
Substance implies simplicity. Uprightness means not being partial. If one can practice this, then one’s words and deeds will not be crooked; how could there be any flattery or deception?

Uprightness is the foundation for entering the Way, therefore one should constantly cultivate it. Do not look down upon others lightly. The preceding verse regarding this can be understood accordingly.
△ The second and third lines of the verse describe contemplative practice.
These sons of the Buddha preach the Dharma with constant gentleness and the ability to endure [up to] preaching the Dharma without obstruction.
Patience is the fundamental principle of the four practices; therefore, it is mentioned repeatedly in the text.

By cultivating compassion and practicing the conduct of honoring those above and treating those below with equality, one can destroy arrogance. By practicing the path of integrity, gentleness, and patience, there is thus no obstruction.
Difficult indeed. △ Third, the accomplishment of practice through one verse:
"The wise person should thus protect this Dharma; dwelling in the blissful practice of single-mindedness, they will be revered by immeasurable multitudes."
The wise person guards their speech as one protects a jar, defends their mind as one guards a city, protects their faculties as one protects a child, and honors the Buddha as one honors a father.
With a single mind, they dwell in peace and joy; their three karmas are pure. Who would not love and revere one who can practice this path?
This concludes the "Peaceful Practice of Mental Tranquility. △ Fourth, the Peaceful Practice of Vows. This consists of both prose and verse. The prose section is divided into two parts. First:
The section on elucidating the Dharma of practice. Second, the praise of the sutra-Dharma. This first part is further divided into three. First, the heading of the chapter:
Furthermore, Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva Mahāsattva... (up to) those who uphold this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*.
This indicates the practice of peaceful conduct based on vows. The four practices constitute the headings; the five kinds of Dharma-preachers are cited alternately.
△ Second, the explanation of the methods of practice:
[from] "among householders and renunciants" (to) "leading them so that they may abide in this Dharma."

"Laypeople and monastics" refers to the fourfold assembly. Although these four assemblies are distinguished by the categories of clergy and laity, they all dwell within the triple world (*tridhātu*) and alike take suffering to be pleasure.
A Bodhisattva practicing the *sukhavihāra* (blissful conduct) should give rise to a mind of great compassion (*mahāmaitrī*) toward this assembly;

first, he should pull them out from the suffering of the segmented existence (*bhavāgra-pratibaddha-duḥkha*) within the triple world and bestow upon them that which is realized by the sages of the Three Vehicles.
Regarding the joy of praise: those who are not bodhisattvas do not give rise to the Great Mind.

Although there is a distinction between the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas of the Two Vehicles, they both transcend the triple world and regard pleasure as suffering. Among these two vehicles, the bodhisattva...

One should give rise to a heart of great compassion, pull others out from the suffering of the cycle of birth and death characterized by transformation, and bestow upon them the bliss of the wisdom of the Buddhas of the One Vehicle.
This is how one should form firm and resolute vows; otherwise, it would be a great loss.
For sentient beings possess the marks of wisdom and virtue, yet the lesser sages are satisfied with their meager wisdom, despite the fact that they harbor the precious treasury of the Tathāgata.
Yet they cannot attain it; though they possess vast majestic power (*mahā-prabhāva*), they are unable to employ it, and thus it is said there is a "great loss.

This sentence provides the general heading; the following explains the three losses. The Tathāgata’s preaching of the Dharma according to what is appropriate refers to his skillful wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*);

that is, he expounds the teachings of the Three Vehicles out of necessity to suit the capacities of beings, yet this is not his ultimate intention. Those of the Two Vehicles do not understand this and cling to [the teachings] as...

To have realized the truth yet not seek further advancement is the first great loss. Those who do not hear, do not know, and are not awakened do not understand the true reality (*dharmatā*) of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*).
This wondrous Dharma of the One Vehicle was indeed taught for the sake of those of the Two Vehicles;
because they have not heard this sutra, which definitively resolves the teaching for *śrāvakas*, they do not know that the Tathāgata’s purpose was solely to instruct the bodhisattvas. Furthermore...
Not realizing that what one has personally realized is not the ultimate cessation is the second great loss.
Not inquiring, not believing, and not understanding refers to being ignorant of the ritual of the teaching—first three [vehicles] and later one [vehicle].

Because one does not inquire into these three vehicles as skillful means taught according to the capacities of beings, one consequently fails to believe that this One Vehicle teaching is the level [of truth].

All those who possess the wisdom equal to that of a Buddha have the potential [for enlightenment], yet they fail to understand the great matter of the Tathāgata’s appearance in the world—the revealing, awakening, and entering into the Buddha’s knowledge and vision;
this is the third great loss. Regarding the phrase "those people": this refers to those who have committed the three losses.
Although they do not inquire whether the Three Vehicles are the skillful means of all Buddhas, they do not believe that the One Vehicle is for sentient beings.
There are those who do not understand this sutra as being spoken for their sake. Although they are thus, I shall give rise to great compassion to deliver and liberate them.
"Attaining Bodhi" refers to seeking the supreme [enlightenment] above; "wherever they may be" refers to transforming those below.
This means that although they have no intention of seeking the wondrous Dharma, wherever they may be situated—whether among humans or devas—I shall cause them to emerge from the triple world.
The two vehicles are led into the One Vehicle. All this is by means of the Tathāgata’s sovereign spiritual power and the power of immeasurable wisdom;
he guides them so that they may dwell within the sublime Dharma of the equality of this One Vehicle, ultimately attaining the fruit of all-encompassing knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*).
△ Third, the conclusion on the fulfillment of practice. This also has two parts: first, clarifying that the fulfillment of practice is free from fault.
Mañjuśrī, when this bodhisattva mahāsattva preaches this Dharma, there is no fault whatsoever.
Because he abides in peace and happiness through his vow, he is free from all faults such as envy, anger, indolence, and deceit.
Next, the benefits resulting from the accomplishment of practice are explained.
Because he is constantly protected by the spiritual power of the Buddhas of the present—from the bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs down to all current Buddhas—he is always endowed with great compassion;
thus the great assembly is pleased and submits to him, providing the four kinds of offerings.

Because his practice and the Dharma are superior, from the realm of empty space downward, all devas turn toward him, honoring the Dharma and respecting the person. Whenever there are questions or challenges, [he remains unshaken].
There will inevitably be setbacks; yet, by obtaining their protection, one’s right mindfulness will not be lost, one’s speech will surely hit the mark, and all will attain joy.
This is why the subsequent passage provides an explanation, manifesting that the Buddhas of the three periods of time all protect this sutra, and not merely the various devas who attend and guard it.
II. Praising the Dharma of the Sutra. This section is divided into two parts. First, the explanation through Dharma (dharmadeśanā).
Mañjuśrī, regarding this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*—let alone seeing, receiving, upholding, reading, and reciting it—it was not previously proclaimed;
therefore, it was not heard in the past. As for "in immeasurable lands," in terms of place, this refers to remote borderlands and humble villages where it was neither heard nor seen.
In terms of time, during the forty years prior [to the preaching of this sūtra], within those immeasurable lands, [the Buddha] had long remained silent on this matter.

It is essential. How much more so for those below [the rank of the Bodhisattvas]. This reveals that they have now obtained the opportunity to hear it. △ Second, the explanation by way of analogy, divided into two parts:

first, the analogy of not giving the jewel, which symbolizes that it was not previously revealed; second, the analogy of giving the jewel, which symbolizes that it is now heard. The first part is further divided into two.
First, the explanation by way of analogy.
Mañjuśrī, it is as if, for example, [a powerful king] (up to) his retinue would surely be greatly astonished.
There are six analogies, as follows: the analogy of subduing all kingdoms by one's majesty. The *Abhidharmakośa* states: "The lifespan of humans in Jambudvīpa is eight..."
When the human lifespan reaches ten thousand years, a Wheel-Turning King (Cakravartin) appears. As the human lifespan diminishes and all manner of evils gradually increase, the Buddha appears.
A golden wheel rotates to guide and lead him, its majesty subduing all; thus he is called a Wheel-Turning King. It is fully explained that there are four such types.
If one of the Kṣatriya caste receives the consecration of the royal throne, on the fifteenth day during the time of fasting and purification, suddenly from the east—
The precious gold wheel appears; its wheel has a thousand spokes, complete with hub and rim, radiating wondrous light as it comes to attend the king.

This king is certainly a Gold Wheel-turning King (Cakravartin); the other three types are to be understood by analogy. These four kings bring peace and stability to all directions through their majesty.

There are also distinctions among them. Ci'en says: "The Golden Wheel King brings transformation by the mere sound of his reputation; the Silver Wheel King brings submission only after dispatching envoys;

the Copper Wheel King achieves submission through the intimidation of his majesty; and the Iron Wheel King establishes order only when he brandishes his spear. Now, the Universal Monarch (Cakravartin) is used as a metaphor for the Tathāgata.
Possessing both meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) and wisdom (*prajñā*), he is thus called "one of powerful strength.

As a Wheel-Turning King (*cakravartin*) and sovereign of the orthodox lineage, he grasps the six dragons to embody the *Qian* hexagram and receives the cauldron amidst the seven phoenixes. With the imperial heart’s selection upon him, he serves as the teacher of kings for a hundred generations.
The One Man under the four seas is the parent of the myriad people; therefore, he is called a Sage-King (*śāstṛ-rāja*).

That his majesty subdues all nations is a metaphor for the realms of the sense-fields (*āyatana*) and elements (*dhātu*). Whether through civil or martial means, he greatly manifests a brilliant and majestic influence.

All come to offer tribute and submit as vassals, sitting in receipt of offerings of jade and silk; this is the subduing power of a Wheel-Turning King (*cakravartin-rāja*). Thus he attains the kingdom and rules over the land.
To preach the Dharma and transform sentient beings within the triple world, and to subdue afflictions and all demons, is the majestic subduing power of the Tathāgata.
As for the phrase "the various petty kings below," this is a metaphor: the petty kings represent those who are rebellious and usurping;

they defy the imperial mandate and oppress the people, which is a metaphor for the various afflictions, the five aggregates, and other demons. Not having attained the subduing power of untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*), they are called "unsubdued."

In obedience to the command, the army gradually descended. They raised troops and marched to attack the city of *Yù* (喻), beating drums and proclaiming their crimes as they launched the punitive expedition.

As for those who rang the bells and marshaled the troops: the methods cultivated by the Seven Sages served as the vanguard; the methods cultivated by those in the first two fruits [of the path] served as the middle army;
and the methods cultivated by those in the third and fourth fruits served as the rear guard. Those to be destroyed were the three poisons and other such afflictions.
The eighty-four thousand enemies represent the eighty-four thousand afflictions. Those capable of defeating them are the officers and soldiers of the eighty-four thousand Dharma-gates.

The passage "The King sees below" refers to the analogy of the King’s joyful appreciation for merit; it illustrates that when the Buddha sees sentient beings cultivating progress and severing delusions, he likewise experiences great joy.
The passage "According to merit below" refers to the analogy of bestowing rewards according to merit; "field" refers to samādhi, and "dwelling" refers to... [the text continues].
This is wisdom. The villages and cities are metaphors for the four fruits [of the śramaṇa]. Clothing is a metaphor for the wholesome dharmas of shame and patience.
Adornments for the body are metaphors for the wholesome dharmas that assist the path. The various kinds of seven treasures are the seven factors of enlightenment.

The elephants, horses, and carriages are the knowledge of exhaustion and the knowledge of non-arising. Servants and slaves are the supernormal powers. Possessing impure wholesome dharmas is like having subjects. This is...

These are the seven stages of the worthy ones (*saptakulaputra*). Although those of the Lesser Vehicle have made slight progress in destroying the afflictions of views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi-āsrava* and *bhāvanā-āsrava*), the Buddha, according to their capacity for diligence and merit, bestows upon them various meditative concentrations (*dhyāna-samādhi*) and so forth;
yet he does not grant them the jewel from beneath his topknot. The topknot symbolizes the provisional (*upāya*), while the jewel symbolizes the real (*tattva*).
It is said that the bright pearl within the topknot exists, yet it is concealed by expedient means. That which is situated upon the crown is what the ultimate fruit venerates.

For those with the capacity to transcend birth-and-death within the realm of segmented existence, it constitutes a minor achievement; for those with the capacity to transcend birth-and-death through transformation, it constitutes a great achievement.
When the topknot pearl was suddenly bestowed upon one who had not yet attained such great achievement, his kinsmen were struck with wonder and alarm.

This is an analogy for when the great capacity of sentient beings has not yet been stirred, yet this sutra is suddenly preached; consequently, those of the two vehicles harbor doubts and perplexity, while the bodhisattvas are struck with wonder and astonishment.
It is as the saying goes: "The treasure of a wheel-turning monarch does not fall into the hands of others. △ Second, the application to the Dharma.
Mañjuśrī, the Tathāgata is also like this... [up to] ...yet he does not preach this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* for them.

"Successively" corresponds to the six preceding metaphors. "The Tathāgata" below corresponds to the metaphor of subduing all the kingdoms through majesty. "But those" below corresponds to the metaphor of the minor kings being disobedient.
"The Tathāgata" below corresponds to the metaphor of raising an army to go and attack. "The king has elephants, horses, and chariots."

They advance with various kinds of troops. The Buddha has noble and holy generals: those of the first fruit of the Small Vehicle (Hīnayāna) are the "noble" (bhadra), while those of the second, third, and fourth fruits are the "holy" (ārya).

Furthermore, regarding the first fruit as "holy," this is to distinguish it from the preceding stage of ordinary beings (pṛthagjana). In the Great Vehicle (Mahāyāna), those in the stages of abiding, practice, and orientation (marga-sthiti-pratipatti-mukha) are the "noble," while those in the ten stages (daśabhūmi) are the "holy.
Below these [stages], there is a combined analogy of joy for those who have achieved merit; this applies to the four lower [stages].
The analogy of rewards according to merit: the faculties and powers refer to the faculties and powers within the seven categories of practice.
By cultivating these faculties and powers, one does not fall into the cycle of birth and death within the six realms; therefore, they are called "outflow-free" (*anāsrava*).

Nirvāṇa refers to the true emptiness of the Lesser Fruit, which can prevent the errors of view and thought and repel the enemy of birth and death; therefore, it is called a "city. Because [the practitioner] does not descend, he does not receive the pearl.
The Parable. △ Second, the parable of giving the jewel, illustrating what has been heard today. This is divided into two parts. First, the illustrative explanation:
"Mañjuśrī, it is like a Wheel-Turning King... [omitted] ...who does not give it to others recklessly, yet now gives it to him."

As it turns out below, there are great meritorious achievements: in serving the king, there is the labor of mending the state's robes; in military expeditions, there are strategies for quelling chaos.
This is analogous to the merit of wisdom and severance (*jñāna-prahāṇa*) in extinguishing delusions, and the capacity for the Mahāyāna in advancing one’s cultivation.
Therefore, the mind is filled with great joy. From "By this" onwards, [the pearl] is given; for over forty years, it has been covered by the provisional [teachings]. Hence, it is said:

"Long ago" refers to the opening of the provisional (*upāya*) by untying the topknot; "giving the jewel" refers to the manifestation of the real (*tattva*). This serves as a metaphor for the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*’s opening and manifestation.
Having long kept this essential point silent and not spoken of it in secret, it is said that he did not give it to others recklessly. △ Next, the application to the Dharma.
The Tathāgata is likewise thus (up to) "and shall expound it for you. From the passage "The Tathāgata" downward, this summarizes the great meritorious achievements.

The *Mahāsannipāta Sūtra* states: "By knowing suffering, one destroys the demon of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha-māra*). By severing the origin [of suffering], one leaves behind the demon of afflictions (*kleśa-māra*).

By realizing cessation, one leaves behind the demon of death (*mṛtyu-māra*). By cultivating the path, one destroys the demon of the Lord of Heaven (*devaputra-māra*), who is the ruler of the desire realm."
Those who delight in and cling to false views, and who harbor hatred and envy toward all the noble and holy paths of the Dharma, are called the Māras, Lords of the Heavens.

As for those of great merit, when the Tathāgata beholds these noble and holy ones, he sees that they have already eliminated the afflictions within their realms and are no longer ensnared by the net of Māra.
It extinguishes the suffering of the three poisons; it emerges from the causal suffering of the triple world to transcend its resultant suffering; it shatters the malicious net of the various māras;
it attains one's own *dharmatā* and realizes one's own *nirvāṇa*. Therefore, there is great joy.

Below this teaching, [the Buddha] should bestow the jewel upon those who possess all-knowledge—that is, those capable of knowing and understanding all phenomena. As for "those with many enemies," it is like the five thousand who withdrew from their seats; they were still numerous.

It is characterized by resentment and envy. Regarding those who find it difficult to believe: they are like those of middling or inferior capacity, who only begin to achieve faith and understanding through parables and causes and conditions.
"Among all teachings" means that it is the foremost among what has been taught, what is being taught, and what is yet to be taught.
As stated below, this provides an illustration. "The secret" refers to the heart-essence of all Buddhas, like a jewel within a topknot. It is the most supreme.

This is like being upon the crown of a king’s head. Having waited for this opportune moment throughout the long night of birth and death for forty years, it is called "guarding through the long night.
△ Second, the verse recitation consists of thirty-seven and a half lines, divided into two parts.
First, fourteen and a half lines are a verse summary of the preceding prose. Second, twenty-three lines provide a general conclusion on the accomplishment of practice. Regarding the first part:
2. First, the four practices. The verse explains the method of practice.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"Always practicing patience and compassion for all [beings]... (omitted)... he preaches this Dharma for them so that they may abide therein."
The first line clarifies that it is through patience and compassion that one is able to propagate the sutra; the subsequent verses correspond to this, as can be understood.
Next, ten and a half lines praise the Dharma of the sutra, which is divided into two parts: first, four lines praise the parable; second, six and a half lines praise the application to the Dharma.
The first part is further divided into two: first, three lines praise the parable of not giving the jewel.
For example, it is like a powerful Wheel-Turning King (up to the point where he) joyfully bestows his servants and wealth.
In the preceding [prose] there were six similes; here, in the verse, the rewards are granted according to merit. The rest all contain the meaning in sequence. △ One line of verse:
the simile of the jewel.
Just as a king who possesses courage and strength capable of performing difficult tasks unties the bright pearl from his topknot and bestows it upon him;

because his power enables him to attain the truth, he is called "courageous and strong. Because he relies on principle to initiate the practice of diligence, he is said to be "capable of performing difficult tasks.
Now, the Buddha unties the provisional and bestows the real, just as the king untied his topknot to give away the pearl. △ Second, the six lines.
Half [of a verse]. This section, consisting of two parts, with the first three and a half lines, provides the verse-commentary on the analogy of not giving the jewel.
It states: "The Tathāgata is likewise the King of all Dharmas... [up to] ...preaches these various sūtras through great skillful means."
Although he is the Dharma King, possessing mastery over the Dharma, he first employs patience as the great power for engaging with the world and wisdom as the treasure-trove for his own benefit.
Next, with a heart of great compassion, he observes the capacities of beings to provide them with appropriate teachings.
To receive even a single phrase is the worldly cause and effect; to seek even a single phrase is the supramundane peace and happiness. [He] bestows these five...

He battles the Māra of the aggregates (*skandhamāra*) to destroy worldly fruits and not undergo various sufferings; he battles the Māra of afflictions (*kleśamāra*) to extinguish worldly causes and not undergo various vexations.

For the sake of these sentient beings, he preaches the various dharmas of the Truths and Dependent Origination, as well as the sūtras of the Three Vehicles and nine divisions, so that they may transcend the triple world and attain liberation. (The second and third lines of the verse summarize this.)
The Parable of the Jewel:
Having already known that sentient beings have obtained its power, [the Buddha says: "Now is the very time for me to speak it for you.
As for that power, it is the power of diligence (*vīrya-bala*). That he did not reveal it falsely was because their great capacity had not yet matured. Now is the very time.
"Time" refers to the time of revelation and manifestation; this can be understood by contrast with the long prose version.
△ Second, twenty-three lines summarizing the completion of practice, divided into three parts. First, one and a half lines summarize and exhort regarding the four practices.
After my parinirvāṇa, those who seek the Buddha-way (up to) should draw near to these four dharmas.
△ Second, twenty and a half lines: The fulfillment of practice and its resulting portents. This is divided into two parts. First, four and a half lines:

Clarifying the retributions for the three obstacles. Second, twenty-six lines: Clarifying the portentous signs within dream-states. The first part is further divided into three. First, one line: The obstacle of retribution.
Pure. Those who read this sutra will always be free from sorrow and affliction, as well as free from illness, and their complexions will be bright and radiant.

This is the transformation of present retribution (*dṛṣṭadharmavipāka*). Regarding the transformation of karmic obstacles: it is because one eliminates the decline and distress that would otherwise follow in the present life. One should maintain the dhāraṇī and mudrā in mind.
His gaze is majestic and resolute; from within, it reaches outward. This principle is indeed true. △ Second, two phrases:
his karmic obstacles are purified, and he is not born into poverty, low status, or ugliness.
This refers to the transformation of retribution for future births. Regarding the transformation of karmic obstacles:

because the evil karma conducive to future birth is extinguished, the causes of evil karma—which would otherwise result in evil fruits—are transformed through the power of upholding this sutra; thus, one attains excellent fruits instead.
One does not create the karma of poverty in the present, nor will one be born in lowly or inferior states in the future. △ Third, the three practices: the purification of afflictions.
Sentient beings delight in seeing [the Buddha] as they long for sages and saints... (up to) the light of wisdom shines like the sun. This is the transformation of subsequent retribution.
As for the transformation of the obstacle of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*): it is because one extinguishes the coarse retributions that follow [this life]. "The sentient beings" and so forth—
This clarifies the transformation of the obstacle of greed. Those with excessive desire are treated with contempt by others; this is an obstacle to rebirth in the Brahma Heaven.
Now that the obstacle of greed has been transformed, everyone delights in seeing him and does not dare to treat him with contempt; everyone looks up to him as they admire the sages and saints.
The "Heavenly Youth Bestowing Messengers" does not obstruct rebirth in the Brahma Heaven. Under the section on "Swords and Staves," it clarifies the transformation of the obstacle of anger.
Anger is like a sword or arrow; anger is like a poisonous drug. Anger can lead to harsh speech. When the internal obstacle of anger is transformed, the internal swords and staves are abandoned;
once the internal poison is removed, external weapons will not wound and external poisons will not harm. Internally...
Since anger is absent, one does not offend others. Even if they should wish to revile one with abuse or unjustly inflict harm, the mouth remains closed and one is unable to utter insults.
Since one is neither harmed nor insulted by others, wherever one travels—
Without fear or apprehension, having forever abandoned the obstacles of dread, he wanders with sovereign ease; thus he is like a lion king. Regarding "wisdom below":
this clarifies the transformation of the obstacle of delusion. Delusion can obstruct wisdom;
now that delusion has been transformed, wisdom blazes forth, its radiance like the shining of the sun. (26) Twenty-six lines clarify the signs of the dream-state.
This is divided into six parts. The first one and a half lines concern dreaming of the Buddhas preaching the Dharma:
"If, within a dream, one sees only wondrous things... [until] the Buddhas surrounded by a multitude of bhikṣus preaching the Dharma."

Through the fulfillment of the merits of the preceding four practices, combined with the power of propagating the sutra, the transformative merit was attributed to himself, and the signs of fruition first manifested.
Therefore, within his dreams, he beheld various wondrous events; these were all signs of future retribution in subsequent lives.
△ Second, one practice: dreaming of being surrounded by the eight classes of beings.
Furthermore, one sees nāgas, devas, asuras, and others, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, reverently joining their palms.
(Three lines, two sentences. Dreaming of preaching the Dharma oneself:
one sees one's own body preaching the Dharma.
△ Four pages and six lines and a half. Dreaming of hearing the Dharma and receiving a prediction of enlightenment;
furthermore, seeing the bodies of various Buddhas with golden complexions (up to) there being also the fourfold assembly with palms joined listening to the Dharma.

Furthermore, [the text] speaks of "seeing below. This refers to seeing the Buddha emitting light and preaching the Dharma; seeing one's own body below; hearing the Dharma with joy, making offerings, and attaining realization;

and the Buddha knowing [the practitioner], as indicated by "knowing below," whereby they receive a prediction of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*). △ Five lines and a half: dreaming of practicing dhyāna and seeing the Buddha.
Furthermore, one sees oneself in mountain forests (up to) entering deeply into meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*) and beholding the Buddhas of the ten directions.
△ Six: The Five Practices. Dreaming of the accomplishment of the Way through the Eight Phases.
"The bodies of all Buddhas are golden in color, adorned with the marks of a hundred blessings" (up to) "like a lamp extinguished when the oil is spent.

The first four lines conclude the preceding section and introduce the subsequent one. Furthermore, from "dreaming" onwards, it describes the successive vision of the conduct from the beginning of cultivation and progress until the attainment of Buddhahood.
The fruit of all Buddhas is reached through such practice; thus, those who practice for peace and happiness first perceive these signs. They shall surely [attain it].
The fruition is certain. [The sequence includes: dreaming of becoming a king; descending from Tuṣita; entering the womb; birth; the three signs; leaving the palace and the five desires;
proceeding to the tree of enlightenment—these are the signs of renunciation. Attaining enlightenment and subduing Māra—these are the two signs of attaining enlightenment and subduing Māra.
Turning the wheel of Dharma and entering Nirvāṇa—these two signs are as described in the text. When the field is exhausted, the lamp is extinguished.
This is a metaphor for the fact that when the karmic conditions are exhausted, one should likewise cease [existence].

Yet, all these things are explained by means of dreams because it is intended to cause the practitioner to contemplate how all dharmas are empty and non-existent, arising only through the inversion of causes and conditions; thus, even though one personally sees the Buddha and hears the Dharma, [it is all like a dream].
Up until the ultimate attainment of Buddhahood, all are but dream-like events; they are utterly ungraspable, lacking any permanent abiding, and are without arising or ceasing.
Constantly contemplating these characteristics, one will thereafter attain true and real practice of peace and bliss in all places.
△ Third: A single verse summarizing the benefits.
If, in a future evil age, one preaches this supreme Dharma, that person shall obtain great benefit, including all the aforementioned merits.

Thus concludes the section on the disciples' mastery of the sutra following the "Trace Gate" (Jikimon), wherein Mañjuśrī’s inquiry and the Tathāgata’s demonstration of the four practices have been completed.
The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, Chapter Fifteen: "The Emergence from the Earth.
Because of the four practices of the aforementioned *Anraku* (Peaceful Dwelling), practitioners are able to transform their obstacles in the present life and attain Buddhahood in the future;
such are its benefits. Fearing that people might hear this Dharma and yet lack evidence for it, [the Buddha] thus employs the Bodhisattvas from other directions as witnesses.
Regarding the excellence of the four practices, [the Bodhisattvas] requested that the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* be propagated in this Sahā world.

The Buddha immediately forbade it, intending to demonstrate that within this land there are naturally those capable of cultivating these practices; thus, from the earth, a multitude such as these emerged.

These leaders of the assembly were named after the four practices to certify that the Buddha’s words are not empty and his undertakings are not false, so as to cause them to be realized in the present.
Thereafter, one may believe with certainty and without doubt, having a basis for further cultivation. The teacher is revered and the Way is honored; one bows deeply and serves with devotion.
At the single command of the Tathāgata, people from all quarters rushed forth; thus it is said they "surged forth from the earth. Furthermore, the person manifests the Dharma.

By means of phenomena, one clarifies principles; thus its name is established. That which is called "ground" (bhūmi) is the ground where the wisdom of Bodhisattvas dwells, the source from which all Buddhas originally arise, and the ground of ultimate reality (bhūtakoṭi), wherein all dharmas are quiescent and unconditioned (asaṃskṛta).
As for "surging forth," it refers to the fact that all worthy ones and sages manifest distinctions through unconditioned dharmas; they transform while remaining unmoving.
It is accomplished without effort, perfectly manifesting the transformation of beings through instruction.

Furthermore, while the four practices previously explained take abiding on the ground of patience as their primary principle, the various assemblies of practitioners who can now cultivate these practices all emerge from that ground of patience.
Therefore, the text does not permit those from other regions; for one who enters through the gate is not a treasure of the house, whereas those who emerge from the ground are.
As for "emerging," it flows forth from within one's own breast, only then covering heaven and earth.

Although this chapter summarizes the essentials of the wondrous practices mentioned previously, it actually serves to refute the near and reveal the far, providing the causal basis for opening up the original lifespan.
△ Second, the disciples of the Original Gate set forth to master the sutra. Maitreya raises doubts, and the Tathāgata reveals his original lifespan.

This section is divided into three parts: first, the emergence from the earth; second, Maitreya’s inquiry; third, the Tathāgata’s detailed response. Within the first part, there are again three sub-sections:
first, the bodhisattvas from other lands request permission; second, the Tathāgata stops them and summons these [bodhisattvas]; third, those from the lower regions.
The Bodhisattvas emerged from the earth. First, the Bodhisattvas of the soil requested their leave.
At that time, the Bodhisattvas who had come from other lands [until] they shall extensively expound it in this land.
Bodhisattvas from other lands, having heard the merits of these four practices, have made vows to dwell here and propagate them; for this reason, they are invited.
△ Second, the Tathāgata restrains others and summons these [bodhisattvas].
At that time, the Buddha addressed the assembly of Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas... [up to] "...to protect, uphold, read, recite, and extensively expound the true sutras.
There are three reasons why the Tathāgata restrains others: first, the Bodhisattvas of other lands each have their own assigned duties;

if they were to remain here to propagate the sutras, it would neglect their own benefit. Furthermore, the Bodhisattvas of those lands have shallow karmic connections with this land; although they may wish to...

If one were to propagate the sutra [without such a mandate], there would certainly be no great benefit. Furthermore, if it were permitted that those from other directions could not summon those from the lower direction, then the Bodhisattvas of the lower direction would not emerge;
their recent traces could not be broken through, and their distant origin could not be revealed. Because these principles exist, [the Buddha] desisted and did not permit it.
There are also three reasons for summoning the Bodhisattvas of the lower direction: first, because they are my disciples, they ought to propagate my Dharma; and furthermore—
The karmic connection is profound and vast; one will certainly obtain immense benefit. Furthermore, it serves to reveal the near and manifest the distant;

for this reason, those there cease and these are summoned. △ Third, the emergence of the Bodhisattvas from the lower regions. This section has two parts: first, the narrative by the scribe regarding their appearance;
second, their praise and inquiry. The first part is further divided into five sections. First, the earth cracks open and they emerge.
When the Buddha spoke these words, [the assembly from] the Sahā world up to the Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas simultaneously surged forth.

As for the cracking of the earth: beneath the earth lies the original retinue, like footprints hidden by the ground. Now, wishing to reveal the traces (*traces*) to manifest the fundamental reality (*the fundamental*), the earth cracks to signify this.
Indeed, the way of the sages and worthies has its proper times for emergence and withdrawal; before the earth had cracked, [they remained concealed].

"First" represents the image of the hidden dragon; thus, the Way of the multitude of worthies was suppressed and remained concealed. After the [silk] was torn apart, it represents the image of the appearing dragon;
the Way of the multitude of worthies should then be extended and made manifest. This is "concealment used to dwell within oneself."

This manifests the benefiting of sentient beings; it is the simultaneous provision of both compassion and wisdom. Responding to the summons, they arrive like the rising of mist when a dragon roars or the blowing of wind when a tiger howls;
hence it is said that they "emerge simultaneously. △ Second, the physical characteristics of the bodhisattvas.
The bodies of these bodhisattvas are all golden in color, endowed with the thirty-two marks and immeasurable radiance.
△ Third, the dwelling places of the bodhisattvas:
they all previously resided beneath this Sahā world, dwelling in the space of this realm.

The *Tianwen* (Heavenly Questions) of Qu Yuan asks: "Why does it close and become dark? Why does it open and become bright? When the constellation Jue has not yet dawned, where does the numinous luminary hide?
Zhou Gongchen remarked: "'Where does it hide? means hiding in what place? The *Shanhaijing* says:
"Mount Changyang is where the sun and moon enter. The *Qiongtian lun* says: "The sun revolves around the celestial pole; it sets in the west and returns."

To the east, the sun neither enters nor exits the earth. According to the theory of mountains and seas, the sun is hidden within the earth; according to the theory of the vaulted heavens, the sun is hidden within space.
How could I possibly soar above the inverted reflections [of the sun], ride upon the sun and moon, traverse heaven and earth, and reach out to touch it?
The *Tianwen Zhi* (Treatise on Astronomy) in the *Book of Jin* states: "During the day, the sun travels above the earth; at night, it travels beneath the earth. If this is indeed so...
If the earth were not empty, how could the sun move? These [objections] all stem from ignorance that the sun and moon revolve around Mount Sumeru.
According to our internal teachings (Buddhism), the sun and moon are situated at the midpoint of Mount Sumeru and rotate to illuminate the four continents.
Because this Sahā world is a tilted universe, the sun and moon appear to have upper and lower positions. In the Flower Treasury World (Huāzàng shìjiè), there are immeasurable banners; each banner...
There are twenty tiers of worlds. The present Sahā world is situated within a single banner of the Flower Treasury World (Kusumatalagarbha-lokadhātu), on the thirteenth tier.
The multitude that has emerged dwells in the void of space, below the thirteenth tier and above the twelfth tier.
Although the Book of Jin states that the earth is empty, it does not recognize that there are worlds beneath the earth. Furthermore, "the lower direction" refers to the Dharma-nature (dharmatā).
The bottomless abyss of the Profound Mystery (*xuanzong*) is its ultimate ground. It does not belong to this world below, nor does it belong to that space above.
Being neither that nor this, it abides in the Middle Way. Emerging from here, it is not in the heights above, nor is it in the depths below.
Neither above nor below, it dwells in the midst of space; this too is the Middle Way. When asking about the person capable of cultivation, one does not say they belong to a separate world.
Question: Why is this world-realm called Sahā? Answer: "Sahā" means Endurance.
Because the Practice of Peaceful Dwelling takes endurance as its place of abiding. Question: Why does it reside here in this realm, rather than above, below, or in the empty space?
Answer: The four practices take patience as their primary principle; one cultivates patience by means of humility.
As for "originally dwelling in the space below": this refers to being humble and self-effacing, because non-abiding is itself emptiness.
△ Fourth, "coming because they heard the summons":
these bodhisattvas, having heard the sound spoken by Śākyamuni Buddha, came forth from below.
The intention for coming forth: I have come because I have heard your command; I have come to propagate the Dharma; I have come to shatter attachments; I have come to reveal the fundamental source.
△ Fifth, the multitude of attendants.
Each and every bodhisattva is a leader of a great assembly, beyond what can be known through calculation or analogy.
They are the masters who lead and guide; each brings with them sixty thousand Ganges-sands of followers.
These sixty thousand Ganges-sands of followers have each of these as their master. Thus, each single master has sixty thousand Ganges-sands [of disciples].
The disciples of the sands of six myriad *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka* teachers—their total number is beyond calculation.
This is the "analogue" (*upamāna*). What follows below is the "analogized" (*upameya*).

There are eight layers of text, all of which, within this section where the former halts and the latter is summoned, emerge from within the phrase "six myriad *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka* etc. via the word "etc. (*ādi*).
Regarding the assembly now being illustrated: beyond these sixty thousand leaders as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, there are further leaders;
beyond these followers, there are further followers. Therefore, the Buddha subsumes them with the term "etc.
(*ādi*), while the compilers of the sutra represent them through figures such as fifty thousand, forty thousand, down to one thousand, one hundred, ten, and even one disciple, and so forth.
Furthermore, as for the leaders and the followers they have brought with them, each is different.

There are those who lead retinues as numerous as the sands of fifty thousand *gaṅgā* rivers, forty thousand, thirty thousand, twenty thousand, ten thousand, or even one *gaṅgā* river’s worth of retinues. This constitutes one layer.

When the disciples are few and the teachers many, one surpasses the superior grade. How much more so when it reaches even as many as one *gaṅgā-vāluka* [sands of the Ganges], or even a fraction of a *nayuta*.
These two tiers likewise surpass the superior grade because the teachers are many and the disciples are few;
how much more so when there are hundreds of thousands of millions of *nayutas* of followers? In these three cases, the number of disciples is reduced while the number of teachers is increased.
Furthermore, regarding those with hundreds of thousands or tens of millions of followers: in these four tiers, the disciples decrease while the teachers increase.
Furthermore, regarding those with ten million, down to ten thousand: in these five tiers, the disciples are few and the teachers are many.
Furthermore, regarding those with one thousand, down to ten: in these six tiers, the disciples are few and the teachers are many. Furthermore, regarding those with five, four, or three...

Regarding "three, two, one disciples": this refers to the seventh layer, where the followers are few and the masters are many. How much more so for those who are alone? This refers to the eighth layer;
those who do not lead a retinue are, conversely, more numerous than the number of those above who lead followers and kin.
As it becomes increasingly so, it further reveals their infinity and inexhaustibility; thus, the character "furthermore" (況復) is used to illustrate the seventh layer.
He emerges alone, delighting in solitude. Above, there is no Buddha-way to be accomplished; below, there are no sentient beings to be saved.
Both self and other are forgotten, and all emotional consciousness is utterly dispelled. Sentient beings and Buddhas are equal, without duality or distinction;
thus he is called "alone. As for "solitude," it means being detached from the practices of the two kinds of birth-and-death and the two kinds of nirvana, delighting only in—
It is the state of constant quiescence, ultimately returning to emptiness; therefore, it is said above that [the Buddha] dwells in empty space.
From the perspective of human sentiment, those who lead sixty thousand or fifty thousand are considered many, while those who lead three, two, or one are considered few.
"Single individuals" (*ekavihārin*) refers to those who dwell alone. If one investigates based on the text, sixty thousand or fifty thousand is few, while single individuals are many.
As the following verse states: "Those who dwell alone and solitary, their number exceeds even that [of the former]. At first glance, this is so.

There exists a distinction between teacher and disciple, as well as a gradation of degree. If one examines these individuals closely, each subsequent figure exceeds the number of those preceding them;
if one scrutinizes their conduct, each subsequent figure surpasses the virtue of those preceding them.
Thus, the manner in which they emerge is most wondrous, and the literary composition of the sūtra-writer is even more skillful. Such a multitude as this...
They descended from below. In solemn and reverent order, they surged like water and rushed like clouds, filling the void so completely that they could not be numbered;
thus it is said, "such as these cannot be known. II. The Section on Praise and Inquiry, which has five parts.
First, the Oceanic Assembly offers praise.
After these bodhisattvas had emerged from the earth, they filled the voids of hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of lands.
Regarding their various praises of the Dharma: some praised the vast and profound power of the vows of Prabhūtaratna, who hears the Dharma everywhere;

some praised the Original Teacher for expounding the teachings according to the capacities of beings without ever becoming weary; and some praised the wondrous efficacy of the supernatural powers of the emanated bodies, which inspire sentient beings.
Because he was sovereign, his sitting in silence encompassed the entirety of the present moment and fully returned to the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*).
That the fourfold assembly also remained silent signifies that the way of teacher and disciple had merged, without the slightest movement.
That fifty minor eons passed like half a day clarifies the matter of inconceivable extension and contraction—the power of sovereign supernatural faculties (*abhijñā*)—which caused the assembly...
Regarding the phrase "like half a day": this means shortening those long kalpas so that they appear brief. Question:
From his descent into the royal palace until his parinirvāṇa in the twin śāla trees, from beginning to end, it was merely eighty years.

Now, the Bodhisattva praises the Buddha for fifty intermediate kalpas, and the Tathāgata remains silent for fifty intermediate kalpas as well, yet causes the great assembly to perceive it as only half a day. Is this not [contradictory]?

"Is this not utterly absurd? [The Master] replied: "This is the inconceivable realm of the Buddha. A single thought-moment (*citta-kṣaṇa*) is immeasurable eons (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*), and immeasurable eons are a single thought-moment.
Extension and contraction are sovereign; thought-moments and eons are perfectly interfused. One cannot fathom their length or brevity with the mind. As the Great Sūtra says:
'Immeasurable past eons are placed within the present and future; immeasurable future [eons are likewise placed therein]. "

As for the kalpas: when placed within the past, they are both long and short; why, then, should one have any doubt? At that time, from the passage "the fourfold assembly" downwards, what was narrow appears as vast.
The two eyes of ordinary beings—the fleshly eye and the celestial eye—differ in their capacity to penetrate or be obstructed.

The two eyes of the sages—the Dharma-eye and the Wisdom-eye—are distinct in their superior or inferior qualities. Relying on their own power, what they perceive does not extend far; yet now, suddenly, they see afar.
"This refers to the supernatural power (*ṛddhi*) of the Tathāgata. 'Pervading the void' reveals that which the Bodhisattvas have realized:
the ultimate truth that fills the entire Dharma-realm. △ Second, the inquiry of the leaders.
Within this assembly of bodhisattvas, there were four leaders (up to: at that time, the four great bodhisattvas spoke these verses:
"O World-Honored One, are you at ease, with little illness and little affliction? (Up to: Do you not cause the World-Honored One to experience fatigue?"
The body is that which practices; thus, the myriad deeds depend upon cultivation. Therefore, rectifying the body is called "superior practice.

The mouth is able to proclaim boundless, wondrous meanings; therefore, rectifying speech is called "boundless practice. The mind is free from envy and flattery, preaching the Dharma with equanimity; therefore, rectifying the mind is called "pure practice.
Through the power of great compassion and vows, one causes all beings to abide within this Dharma; therefore, it is called "great compassion."
To establish practice is called "chanting" (shāng); to guide sentient beings according to their capacities is called "leading" (dǎo).
These four Bodhisattvas are the leaders among the sixty thousand teachers as numerous as the sands of the Ganges; therefore, they are called "the teachers who chant and lead.

Regarding the two phrases "few illnesses and few afflictions," [they] inquire after the Tathāgata’s well-being, noting that he has already departed from the worldly outflows (*āsrava*) of the five [aggregates].
[The Buddha asked: "Are you suffering from any illness? It is merely that I wish to manifest the manner of a fellow human being and accord with the constant etiquette of this land;
therefore, I must inquire about your illness. Regarding the phrase 'those to be delivered,' [the Buddha] asks whether sentient beings are easy to deliver.

The body is the vessel for carrying the Way; as matters of fortune and misfortune, joy and sorrow, are related to daily life, he asks about them first. Sentient beings are the material through which the Way is received. The Way—
Success or failure depends upon this; therefore, he asks about it next. The two questions in the verse and prose can be understood accordingly.
△ Third, the Buddha’s answer regarding peace and bliss:
At that time, the World-Honored One, amidst the great assembly of bodhisattvas... (until) they shall hear this sutra and enter the Buddha-wisdom.
First, he answers regarding peace and bliss; next, he answers regarding ease of deliverance (*sukha-vinaya*). The following section interrogates and explains the meaning of "ease of deliverance.

The passage beginning with "There are two kinds" clarifies those whose faculties are sharp and whose virtues are profound—those who, throughout successive lifetimes, have constantly received the Great Transformation (*mahā-pariṇāma*), as they are precisely the ones transformed by the teaching of the Original Gate concerning the Lifespan (*āyus-pramāṇa*).
Upon first beholding my body, they immediately uphold the *Avataṃsaka* and enter the wisdom of the Tathāgata.
When fruit ripens, it falls easily; this class of beings is likewise easy to deliver.

With the exception of those who have previously fallen away—those of dull faculties and meager virtue who, from lifetime to lifetime, have not received the Great Transformation, delighting instead in the small and seeking only its realization—for such people as these, it is necessary to open the way for the Sudden teaching and explain the Gradual.
Having led them through the preceding various teachings to bring them under discipline, one also causes these individuals to hear [the truth] now.
The Lotus Sūtra: Entering the Buddha’s Wisdom. That is to say, whatever one does is always for a single purpose;
whether going, coming, sitting, or standing, there is never any other business. △ Fourth, the verses in praise of sympathetic joy.
At that time, the great Bodhisattvas spoke in verse:
"Excellent, excellent, Great Hero, World-Honored One! Having heard [this], we shall practice with faith; we rejoice in accordance with it."
The repeated exclamation "Excellent! praises the Buddha’s dual employment of skillful means and ultimate reality, as well as his equal benefit for those of the Great and Small Vehicles.

"The questioner" refers to Śāriputra and others who made their three requests. "Profound wisdom" refers to the revelation of the true nature of all phenomena (*dharmatā*) throughout the three stages of the discourse.
"Faith and practice" refers to the essence of faith and understanding, as well as the conviction that one will become a Buddha and the practice of the bodhisattva path. Furthermore...
The ability to inquire about the four propositions initiates the subsequent request from Maitreya, which opens up the original discourse on the lifespan. We rejoice in this.
△ Fifth, the Tathāgata’s description and praise.
At that time, the World-Honored One praised the leaders [up to the point where he said], "You are all able to give rise to a mind of sympathetic joy toward the Tathāgata.
Because he commended their ability to give rise to sympathetic joy, he spoke again, saying, "Excellent!

This clearly demonstrates their ability to protect, uphold, recite, and widely expound this sutra after his parinirvāṇa. The section on those who emerged from the earth concludes here. △ Second, Maitreya’s inquiry.

This section is divided into two parts: first, the doubts of the bodhisattvas of this land; second, the doubts of the bodhisattvas of other lands. The first part is further divided into two: first, the prose expression of doubt;
[it begins with] "At that time, Maitreya Bodhisattva... (up to) "...joining his palms toward the Buddha, he asked in verse:"

As for why Maitreya and the various bodhisattvas raise this inquiry: from the time at the site of initial enlightenment until now at Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa, although the great beings from the ten directions who have gathered here are beyond measure, I—by the power of my wisdom as one in the position of succession—know and see them all;
yet among this assembly, I do not recognize a single person. Nevertheless, I have traveled and transformed beings throughout the ten directions.
He had personally attended upon all the Buddhas and was thoroughly acquainted with their entire assemblies; yet, when one infers from his own current experience, he does not recognize them either.
Furthermore, as that Great Being proceeded forward, Maitreya, being but a junior student, could not know those who were ahead.
Therefore, he did not recognize him. Furthermore, that Great Being is fundamentally grounded in the ultimate reality (*dharmatā*), manifesting throughout the ten directions;

all such true and responsive manifestations (*nirmāṇa*) are beyond the sphere of Maitreya’s perception, and for this reason, he did not recognize him. Moreover, the Buddha, entrusting the propagation of the sutra, summoned the various bodhisattvas.
The secret revelation of the lifespan was not something known by the assembly at that time; therefore, it was initiated through the feigned doubts of Maitreya and others.
When Maitreya descended, the intention was that the multitude of sages had already emerged from below, startling the minds of the assembly, such that many kalpas were perceived as half a day.
Who could not find it strange? Eight thousand bodhisattvas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, were already perplexed by the traces of what had already occurred.

Maitreya, with the wisdom of one in his final birth before Buddhahood, wished to investigate the reasons why this was so; thus, he composed verses based on those traces to request an explanation, thereby resolving the doubts of both himself and others.
△ Second, the verses of the formal inquiry consist of nineteen and a half lines, divided into five parts. First:
A single line and a single phrase ask from where [the assembly] has come.
"Immeasurable thousands of myriads of kotis of great assemblies and bodhisattvas" (and so on) asks from where they have come;

it asks for the place from which they set out. The meaning is that although the Yellow River has nine bends, it originates from Kunlun; when a person travels ten thousand *li*, [they must first know their starting point].
Village. How could there not be a place of origin? The provisional and the real depend upon one another; where did you originally reside? △ Second, one line in three phrases:
Asking for what reason he has come.
By what causes and conditions has he gathered this massive body and great supernormal powers (up to) "from where have you come"?

The question concerns the origin of those who emerged from the earth. Generally, the movement and transformation of all things are linked to fortune or misfortune; how then could the conduct of human beings be considered insignificant?
Therefore, it is said: "By what causes and conditions did they assemble? Following the words "of great bodies," this refers to the multitude that emerged from the earth.
His appearance and demeanor were exceptionally distinguished, and his intellectual power was extraordinary; he was a joy for all to behold, and thus he moved the multitude to inquire after him.
△ Third, nine lines describing the immeasurable number [of attendants].
Even the retinues brought by each of these bodhisattvas cannot be fully known.
△ Fourth, two lines ask who their teachers are:
"This assembly of bodhisattvas of great majesty and vigor... (until) what Buddha-way do they practice?"
Who is it that provides the Dharma teachings and instruction? It is the benefit derived from hearing and reflection; there is no such thing as being without a teacher.

Who is it that clears away the reed-thicket of ignorance? Who is it that inspires the aspiration for enlightenment? It is like the bird heading south for ninety thousand *li*; what is precious is the first step. And who is it that points the way?
It is through the proclamation of the Buddha-Dharma to benefit others, and the upholding and recitation of the sutras to benefit oneself. Thus one cultivates...
We have practiced this and cultivated this; it was not without a transmission from teacher to student. May I venture to ask: who is the master you take as your primary lineage?
Furthermore, whose song does your teacher sing? Whose ancestral style (zongfeng) do you succeed? △ Five lines and a half: requesting an answer regarding the origins and details.
"Thus, the supernatural powers and great power of wisdom of these bodhisattvas... [up to] "...I pray that you will resolve the doubts of the assembly.
The first two phrases praise their virtues. "Abiding in mid-air" refers to their supernormal power (*ṛddhi*). "Various praises of the Dharma" refers to their power of wisdom (*jñāna-bala*).
[The Buddha] asked from below: "Please tell me where you have come from. Thus, this multitude has emerged from no great distance; from what place must they have come?
I pray that you will describe their land—what shall it be named? [The Buddha] asked from below regarding the causes and conditions:
"The lands I have traversed are many, and the assemblies of my teachers and friends have not been few. Such a multitude as this..."
"I do not understand this first point. How did they suddenly surge forth from the earth? It cannot be without cause; I pray that you will explain it.
Now, the great assembly below longs to hear the origins and details of these bodhisattvas; they cannot have arisen without a source. May the Holy One speak at once."
This is to resolve the doubts of the assembly. △ Second, the doubts of the bodhisattvas from other lands.
At that time, [the passage] from "The various Buddhas who are emanations of Śākyamuni" to "you yourselves shall, by means of this, come to hear it."
The attendants of that Buddha are bodhisattvas from other lands; they are members of his retinue who have come from the eight directions.
Like Maitreya, they share the same doubt, for none of them know that the Tathāgata attained Buddhahood in his original ground long ago.
Thereupon, each presented their doubts to their own Buddha, and every Buddha suppressed them and waited for Maitreya. Therefore, it is said: "You yourselves shall [know]..."
Because of this question from the Bodhisattva of the Stage of Succession (*abhiṣikta*), we have been able to hear the reason why [the Buddhas] emerge from the earth.

The intent behind the question of the attendants from the eight directions was to require the manifestation of emanated bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*) in order to authenticate the traces of transformation and to initiate the meaning of the Lifespan (*āyus-pramāṇa*).

The emanated bodies did not answer, intending that this matter is not trivial; throughout the single dispensation of the World-Honored One, it had never been explicitly taught. It is because of this one question [that it is now revealed].
The lifespan is extensively revealed; the profound mysteries of this entire dispensation shall be opened by the Buddha himself. Thus ends Maitreya’s inquiry.
△ Third, the Tathāgata’s detailed response, divided into two parts: first, the admonition to listen; second, the actual response. The first part is further divided into two: first, the prose section.
At that time, Śākyamuni Buddha [throughout] by the majestic and powerful might of all Buddhas—this is the name A-yi-duo (Ajita), which here means "Invincible.
Such a great matter is precisely the opening of the proximate traces to reveal the distant origin;

it is the great matter of benefiting sentient beings throughout the three periods of time, a process of transformation and further transformation that never ceases. Maitreya serves as the successor...
The Lord of the Abode did not recognize the assembly emerging from the earth; therefore, he posed this single question to reveal and develop the profound wisdom of all Buddhas.
Thus, he praised them twice with "Excellent! to commend them. He then exhorted them as follows: "Exhort yourselves to one-pointedness of mind so as not to be distracted;
exhort yourselves to don the armor so as not to be indolent; exhort yourselves to diligence so as not to retreat or be timid; exhort yourselves to firmness so as not to harbor doubt."
The reason for issuing this admonition prior to the teaching is to cause them to listen with courageous diligence, so that having heard it, they may practice with faith;
lest, because the meaning is profound and subtle, they should give rise to doubt and retreat. From the words "The Tathāgata" onwards, the fruit-wisdom is clarified:

the wisdom of all Buddhas is exceedingly deep and immeasurable, such that ordinary people cannot know it; now, by means of the assembly emerging from the earth, the duration of the Buddha's life is revealed.
This is to manifest the profound wisdom of the Tathāgata; hence it says "to reveal," and so forth.

Beginning with a single ray of light, which perfectly manifests from beginning to end, up until the emergence of the seven-jeweled stūpas and the threefold transformation of the clouds gathering together—this is the Buddha-work performed by the Tathāgata in this present assembly, termed "sovereign spiritual power.
Now, innumerable bodhisattvas emerge and praise [the Buddha] for fifty minor kalpas.

An *kalpa* refers to what is like half a day. This precisely reveals that since attaining Buddhahood, [the Buddha] has manifested the causes and conditions of his transformations throughout successive *kalpas*.

Because he possesses mastery over recollection, it is said: "Now, wishing to manifest the power of sovereign spiritual penetrations (*abhijñā*), beginning with the *Avataṃsaka* and ending with the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, he opened the three vehicles in the interim and now enters the one vehicle.
One should simply know that this is the original intent of his appearance in the world during this single lifetime.
It is solely for one purpose. This is the "Lion’s Vigorous Display. The multitude now surging forth from the earth consists entirely of bodhisattvas who have all attained omniscience;
this clearly reveals that the Tathāgata’s fundamental intention in appearing in the world over many kalpas was solely for this one purpose.
Therefore, it is said: "Now, wishing to manifest the power of the Lion’s Vigorous Display, he comes to bestow predictions upon the śrāvakas," and there are [many] such instances.
It is limited; yet, observing that over forty years he has served others without weariness, this is the power of his fierce and great majesty (*vīrya-mahāvega*).

Now, those who spring forth from the earth are immeasurable and boundless, inexhaustible in accordance with the nature of reality (*dharmatā*). This clearly demonstrates that the Tathāgata’s ceaseless salvation of sentient beings is like the fierce majesty of a great general.
Therefore, it is said: "Now, wishing to manifest the power of fierce and great majesty. If one were to manifest [this] below...
The meaning of this chapter is as follows: "Mastery of spiritual power" refers to manifesting nirvana through skillful means while, in reality, not passing into extinction;
thus, causing deluded sentient beings not to see it even when they are near. This was his past benefit for beings.
"The Lion’s Vigorous Stride" refers to his constant reflection: "By what means can I cause sentient beings to enter unsurpassed wisdom quickly?"
He has attained the body of a Buddha; this is his benefit for beings in the present.

As for his majestic and powerful might, throughout billions of asaṃkhyeya kalpas, he constantly preaches the Dharma to teach and transform countless billions of sentient beings, causing them to enter the path of the Buddha;
this is his benefit for beings in the future. Now, wishing to proclaim such a great matter, he has emerged from the earth in incalculable numbers.
[He is] also a Bodhisattva. △ Second, the verse summary:
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:
"One should be diligent and single-minded; I wish to speak of this matter... (until) you all listen with a single mind."
"Exert yourself with diligence" below is an exhortation. "The Buddha’s wisdom" below praises the resultant wisdom. Faith is the source of the Way; by giving rise to it, one may enter the Way.

Goodness is the provision for the Way; by practicing patience, one may accomplish the fruit. Those who harbor doubt and fear do so because they doubt the traces of his transformation and fear the magnitude of what he has accomplished.
"The Buddha has no... below is an exhortation to listen to these sincere words. Regarding "what he has accomplished":
This means that even if the sun and moon were to fall, or Mount Sumeru were to tilt and shake, the true words of the Buddhas would not differ from them at all.

△ Second, the direct answer, divided into two parts: first, briefly opening up the near to reveal the far; second, extensively opening up the near to reveal the far. The first part is further divided into two:
first, opening up the near to reveal the far; second, further inquiry due to doubt. The first [section] contains both prose and verse. Within the prose, there is again...
2. First, the answer regarding the teacher and disciple:
At that time, when the World-Honored One had spoken these verses (up to the point where it says) "he tamed his mind and caused him to resolve upon the Way," [the text asks:
"By my teaching, he tamed his mind; by my guidance, he caused him to resolve upon the Way. To whom does this refer?

"From that time until now, I have constantly remained here (extending to) incalculable lands (*asaṃkhyeya-kṣetra*), guiding and benefiting sentient beings.
Since it was stated in the preceding analogy that he attained Buddhahood a very long time ago, it is not yet clear where he has resided for so long;
therefore, it says "constantly remaining in this land" as well as in other lands. Now, this Sahā world is precisely the land inhabited by his original response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*).
Today, the traces [of the Buddha] remain no different from their original state; it is only that the times of then and now differ.

That which perceives the burning is said to be near, while that which illuminates the source reaches the far. Therefore, the text below says: "When the great fire burns, this land of mine remains peaceful and secure;
I am always on Vulture Peak and at other dwelling places. How could one seek the eternal tranquility apart from Gayā? It is not something transient.
Outside of this state of quiescence, there is another Sahā world; it is also shown below that the places where he benefits sentient beings are vast and numerous.
△ Second, the doubt regarding the Buddha’s traces:
"O sons of good family, within this interval" (up to) "...all these are distinguished through skillful means."

In the past, I observed that the various teachings describe different causes for practice in various places; thus, I doubted the cause. Furthermore, I observed that the predictions of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*) received in various places were inconsistent;
thus, I doubted the result. Since such practices and the attainment of predictions were all not understood as skillful means (*upāya*) subsequent to the result, doubt arose.
As for the "intermediate" period, it begins from the kalpa prior to the *rajas-bindu* (dust-point) kalpa and extends until the end of the future.

The future limit constitutes the end; that which lies between these two pillars is entirely termed the "middle. Now, by pointing to the causal practices performed during the time of Dīpaṃkara Buddha, one immediately dispels doubts regarding the cause.
Furthermore, by pointing to the prediction of enlightenment (vyākaraṇa) received from Dīpaṃkara and his entry into nirvāṇa, one immediately dispels doubts regarding the fruit.
Such causes and effects are not merely a single path; they all constitute skillful means and are not spoken as ultimate reality.

Therefore, this is called "dispelling doubt. The first three phrases cite specific instances, while the final phrase serves to dispel [doubt]. Furthermore, one phrase describes the intermediate manifestations and parinirvāṇa.
Thus, this one phrase, regarding what was taught in the former teachings, results from practicing the cause.
The fruits [of these practices] are all merely provisional expedients and conceptual distinctions; therefore, this single phrase serves to dispel doubts.
Furthermore, since the Buddha Dīpaṃkara and others are mentioned, the matter of practicing the causes and receiving the prediction of enlightenment is included within the word "etc.

Moreover, another point is that even the present teaching of extinction in this sutra is entirely an expedient. △ Third, the actual clarification of benefiting sentient beings. This also has two parts. First—
This clarifies the principle of resonance.
Good sons, if there are sentient beings— from those with sharp faculties to those with dull faculties— who come to me according to their respective needs for deliverance,
these are precisely the two types of capacities, sudden and gradual, of past sentient beings who have silently struck against my Dharma-body.

Regarding the "observation with the Buddha-eye": this refers to one who has already attained Buddhahood long ago. The Buddha-eye illuminates the capacities of sentient beings without error, manifesting two types of responses—superior and inferior—to benefit them.
Faith and the others are the five faculties (*pañcendriya*). Wisdom is the "revealing cause" (*vijñapti-hetu*), while the others are the "contributing cause" (*pratyaya-hetu*).

These two types of goodness each possess degrees of sharpness and dullness. Accordingly, the five vehicles are manifested through forms and sounds to deliver beings according to their individual capacities.
This is the second benefit. △ Next, the manifestation of transformation is explained:
[The Buddha] himself declares his names differently in various places (up to) being able to cause sentient beings to give rise to a heart of joy.
"Everywhere" (處處) below refers to the manifestation of form (*rūpa*). Discussed horizontally, it refers to the lands of the ten directions of the past;

discussed vertically, it refers to the lands where causes were practiced throughout the various stages of the past and the intermediate periods. Regarding the difference in names: once form has manifested, there are names;
names are used to summon the essence. Since capacities vary in magnitude, forms vary in excellence or inferiority. "Inferior" refers to...
The "inferior response" (hīna-nirmāṇa) is for those of lesser capacity; the "superior" (viśiṣṭa) refers to the superior response, which is for those of great capacity.

This distinction concerns the different names used for the manifestation of the Buddha’s Dharma-realm body (*dharmadhātu-kāya*). As for the manifestation of bodies belonging to the nine realms of existence (*navadhātu*), they are immeasurable and boundless, and can be understood through the power of the mind.
Regarding the size of their age, this clarifies the length of their lifespan: the "great" refers to the superior response, while the "small" refers to the inferior.

The "Corresponding" [Buddha] manifests a lifespan that is limited; the "Superior Corresponding" [Buddha] manifests a lifespan that is limitless. Their lifespans differ, their names differ, and the bodies they manifest are also distinct.
All of these serve to benefit beings according to what is appropriate for their deliverance.

Furthermore, they are "equal" in that while the Buddha is in the world, he does not cause beings to conceive the thought that he is difficult to encounter; rather, by declaring his entry into nirvana, he causes them to feel longing and devotion.
Through yearning and aspiration, they attain liberation. For those who have been invited and for whom parinirvāṇa is appropriate, he immediately manifests parinirvāṇa.
