Furthermore, "below" refers to the benefit of voice. For those with small bodies and short lifespans, he teaches the gradual teaching; thus it is said, "by various skillful means. For those with large bodies and long lifespans, he teaches the sudden teaching;
thus it is said, "he preaches the subtle and wondrous Dharma. Moreover, the Great Dharma of the One Vehicle [is for the assembly...]
He gives rise to the insentient through various expositions; this refers to the principle of first employing provisional means and subsequently revealing the ultimate truth.

"Able to cause... and so forth, refers to the bestowal of transformation through the four *siddhāntas*. The two benefits adapt to capacities, being directed toward what each finds pleasing; thus, they obtain benefit and give rise to a heart of joy.

Having concluded the section on benefiting beings in the past, △ second, clarifying the benefit of beings in the present, which is divided into two parts. First, clarifying the resonance of capacities.

"Good sons, when the Tathāgata sees sentient beings who delight in inferior teachings (*hīna-dharma*), whose merit is meager and whose defilements are heavy—this 'seeing' by the Tathāgata is the illumination of the Buddha-eye.
'Delighting in inferior teachings' refers to those with the capacity (*indriya*) for such views.
'Craving the twenty-five realms of existence' refers to those with the capacity of humans and devas. 'Clinging to nirvāṇa and seeking self-liberation' refers to those of the two vehicles."
Those whose faculties delight in gradual progression and take a circuitous route toward the Buddha-way are the faculties of bodhisattvas; these are all termed "delighting in the small.

Those of meager virtue are those for whom the two types of goodness—the conditional (*pratyaya*) and the consummate (*pariniṣpanna*)—are weak in their functional efficacy. Those with heavy defilements are those who have not yet been able to subdue or sever the two delusions of views and thought (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa* and *bhāva-kleśa*).

This discussion of delighting in the small is based on their provisional traces (*traces of manifestation*). If discussed in terms of their fundamental nature (*the root*), they delight in hearing [the account] of departing from the royal palace and approaching [enlightenment].
They achieve only the small; they do not delight in hearing of the greatness of long-term and far-reaching accomplishment. Such narrow-mindedness is not something that begins today.

Had they previously delighted in the Great [Vehicle], the Buddha would not have spoken of "initial accomplishment. That he speaks of initial accomplishment is solely because they delight in the Lesser Dharma.

II. Clarifying the Manifestation of Response and Transformation. This is divided into two parts: first, manifesting birth where there is no birth; second, manifesting extinction where there is no extinction.
[The section on] Extinction. Furthermore, there are two parts to the first. The first clarifies that what is not born appears as born;
for the sake of such people, [the Buddha] said, "I left home at a young age" (up to) "causing them to enter the Buddha-way," and spoke in this manner.
For those who delight in the minor [vehicle], I manifest traces in birth and speak of leaving home at a young age and attaining the fruit through ascetic practices. However, from the words "But I...
onwards, it clarifies that the fundamental reality is non-arising. If this is so, as in the preceding analogy, it has been a very long time since I attained Buddhahood;
how could it be that I have only now been born and only now attained enlightenment? Question: Since there is no actual birth, for what reason do you manifest birth? Answer:

It is solely for the sake of those who delight in the small [vehicle] and whose defilements are heavy that he enables them to attain the Buddha-way; therefore, he speaks thus: "I left home at a young age," and so forth.
△ Second, clarifying the benefits manifested in this life, which is further divided into two parts. First, clarifying that benefiting sentient beings is not in vain.
"Good sons, all the sūtras expounded by the Tathāgata, and all that he has spoken, are entirely true and not false.

'Speaking' refers to the benefit of sound; 'showing' refers to the benefit of form. When he speaks of his own body, it is as when he said that the prince of the past, the king, and Aśoka were all his own bodies.
When he speaks of the bodies of others, it is as when he said that the past Āṣāḍha was [himself]."
Much. Those who saw him with joy are the Medicine King; those sentient beings who heard the Dharma in the past and the present śrāvaka disciples are all his other bodies.
As for manifesting both his own body and other bodies, it is like the gathering of emanated bodies and the multitude of those who emerged from the earth.

"Manifesting one's own affairs and the affairs of others" refers to manifesting the matter of one's own practice and attaining Buddhahood, the matter of disciples' practice and attaining Buddhahood, the matter of one's own preaching of the Dharma to save sentient beings, and the matter of disciples' preaching of the Dharma to save sentient beings.
These two phrases in total conclude that the spoken words are not false; although they are cited here primarily for the benefit of sound, sound necessarily encompasses form as well. △ Second.
The explanation of "not being in vain" is twofold. First, it is not in vain because it illuminates the principle.
Why is this so? Because the Tathāgata knows and sees according to reality... [up to] ...the Tathāgata perceives clearly without error.
"One who knows and sees according to reality" refers to true wisdom that illuminates the reality of the three realms (tridhātu) in accordance with the principle;
there is truly no causal characteristic of the three realms. "There is no birth-and-death" means there is no suffering of the two kinds of results of birth-and-death.
Regarding "if one withdraws": there are five abodes of accumulation called "withdrawal," and there are two results of death called "emergence. [End of] section.

The first two lines concern cause and effect. "Nor abiding in the world," and so forth, means that there is neither abiding in the world of birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) nor entering the extinction of *nirvāṇa*.
Since both of these have ceased, it is said that they "do not exist.
"Neither real nor empty" means it is not the reality of extinction, nor is it the emptiness of birth-and-death. "Not like something different" means it is not... [the state of] emergence.

The True Suchness (*tathatā*) of the world is not something separate from or distinct from the world. Because sentient beings of the six realms perceive the three realms as being different, "difference" is existence.
Because those of the Three Vehicles perceive the three realms as being suchness, "suchness" is emptiness. The Buddha perceives the three realms as neither suchness nor difference;
he simultaneously illuminates both suchness and difference—this is the Middle Way. It is not like the [perceptions of] the three realms.

"Is the same as. The Buddha possesses both provisional and ultimate wisdom; he is certainly not the same as those two kinds of threefold world perceived by ordinary beings and followers of the Lesser Vehicle.
This single phrase summarizes all the preceding phrases. It is that which only the Buddha’s ultimate wisdom illuminates;
it is also speech according to his own intention, and it is a disclosure of the matters concerning his own person. That is to say:
There is no cause and effect; no birth and death; no exiting; no arising and ceasing; no reality or unreality; no suchness or difference.

Within the principle of the ultimate reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), not a single dharma can be apprehended. As the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* says: "In the primary truth (*paramārtha*), there is nothing to be discriminated. This refers to that very point.
Although the Tathāgata’s true wisdom is without discrimination, it does not hinder his provisional wisdom from being identical with the triple world.
I see that although there are no two deaths, I speak of two deaths in accordance with others; although there is no exiting [the world], I speak of exiting in accordance with others;
although there is no arising or ceasing, I speak of those who exist in the world and those who attain extinction in accordance with others;
although there is no reality, I speak of the reality of nirvana; although there is no falsehood, I speak of the falsity of the triple world; although there is no ultimate truth...
It is as if there were [a distinction], yet it is said that there is [such a distinction]. Although there is no difference regarding the three realms, it is said that there is a difference;
to view the three realms as identical with the three realms—all such instances are speech according to the intentions of others (*parārtha-vāk*), spoken to demonstrate the affairs of another’s body.

Within these texts, only true wisdom (*tattva-jñāna*) illuminates the reality; now, provisional wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*) manifesting the provisional is further clarified, thereby revealing the thorough and precise nature of the Tathāgata’s two wisdoms.

The benefits of both form and sound are entirely real and not empty; there is no error, which is precisely what is meant by "not empty. △ Second, [the teaching] is not empty because it accords with the capacities [of beings].
From "All sentient beings possess various natures" (up to) "the Buddha-work performed has never for a moment been abandoned."

"Nature" (*xing*) refers to the nature of the faculties (*indriya*). Since the natures of the faculties are not uniform, he teaches according to their capacities; this is for the benefit of individuals. "Desire" (*yu*) refers to inclinations and aspirations.
Since inclinations and aspirations are not uniform, he establishes transformations according to those desires; this is for the benefit of the world. "Practice" (*xingzhe*) refers to cultivation.

Regarding the practices cultivated, there are obstacles that must be removed; this is for the benefit of remediation. "Recollection and thought" (*yixiang*) refer to conceptual understanding based on resemblance. Because of the presence of goodness...

Because of the faculties (*indriya*), there is aspiration (*chanda*). Because of aspiration, there is practice (*pratipatti*). Because of practice, one attains a corresponding understanding (*anurūpa-adhimukti*).

According to that understanding born of recollection and conceptualization, the Dharma is further taught for them, enabling them to enter into the principle; this is the benefit of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).

When [the practice] has become habitual and formed into a nature (*prakṛti*), how could the nature come first and the aspiration later? It is because there exists the fundamental nature of the faculties from previous lives that one is able to give rise to aspiration in the present day.

Desire is like the afflictions; because there are afflictions, there are the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*). Furthermore, based on the five aggregates, further afflictions arise. The nature of desire is also like this.
The various differences among the natures and desires of sentient beings cause them to give rise to roots of goodness; therefore, [the Buddha] employs various means and so forth.
Regarding the two phrases concerning "what is done": he preaches the Dharma according to their faculties, causing all to enter the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, and not for the sake of others.

The two vehicles and the heavens are minor matters; therefore, they are called "Buddha-works" (*buddhakārya*). If only one person alone were to attain *nirvāṇa* while others did not, then Buddha-works would be subject to abandonment.
How could it then be said that [the teaching] is truly real and not false?

Now, since those of the seven stages of expedient means all enter into the single reality, it can be said that all are real and not false. Thus, Buddha-works are never for a moment abandoned. The above is not...

The section on the manifestation of birth as birth is concluded. △ Second, the non-extinction of what is not extinguished, manifested as extinction. This is divided into two parts. First, the non-extinction manifested as extinction;
second, the benefit of the manifestation of extinction. The first part is further divided into two. First, the fundamental reality does not undergo extinction.
"Thus, since I attained Buddhahood (up to) even now it is not yet exhausted; furthermore, it is double the number mentioned above.
Thus [the text] below clarifies that the state of fruition is eternally abiding. Attaining Buddhahood is the fruition; being exceedingly great and remote is "eternal.
Because it is eternal, it does not perish. Since it does not perish, its benefits extend into the future; therefore, these four characters are used to clarify the benefits for the future.
This is a matter of things. "All those who practiced the bodhisattva path below" refers to citing causes to illustrate effects in order to clarify permanence.
If one takes Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū, Prabhūtaratna, Dīpaṃkara, and others as the "origin," these are all origins within the realm of traces (*traces-of-trace*).
One must, however, take the atoms of five hundred thousand million billion *nayuta* *asaṃkhyeya* triple-thousand great thousandfold world systems [as the true origin].
Passing beyond five hundred thousand million billion nayuta asaṃkhyeya lands, one places a single mote of dust.
When all such lands have been covered with motes of dust, these are further reduced to fine particles. One mote of dust represents one kalpa.

Since his attainment of Buddhahood has exceeded even this duration, if one traces back to its source, the fundamental basis is the practice of the bodhisattva path at the very moment of first generating the aspiration for enlightenment. This original practice of the bodhi...
When he was on the path of practice, the lifespan induced by his causes had not yet been exhausted, already exceeding the aforementioned immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* number;
how much more so, then, his resultant lifespan! Thus we know that by means of this unexhausted causal lifespan, one may infer his unexhausted resultant lifespan.
This is to clarify that both cause and effect are eternal. △ Second, the manifestation of passing into extinction within the traces.
However, this is not an actual parinirvāṇa (until: "The Tathāgata uses these skillful means to teach and transform sentient beings").

Regarding the three bodies within the traces (*traces* = *yǐ*), each possesses the meaning of "proclaiming extinction" despite being non-extinguished. As for the Dharma-body being non-extinguished yet proclaiming extinction:
as the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* states, "The Dharma is fundamentally unborn; therefore, there is nothing that can be extinguished. This is the intent of the Dharma-body’s non-extinction.

Furthermore, it says, "This is the meaning of quiescent extinction (*śānta-nirodha*)," which is the proclamation of extinction. Regarding the Reward-body (*saṃbhoga-kāya*) being non-extinguished yet proclaiming extinction: who possesses wisdom... [text fragment ends]
Wisdom. Who possesses afflictions such that one could say wisdom can destroy them? This refers to the *saṃbhogakāya*, which is not subject to extinction;

yet sentient beings, failing to understand this, hear of it and immediately claim it is the Buddha, thereby giving rise to arrogance and self-indulgence, no longer practicing the Way. Therefore, [the teaching] further proclaims:
"The Way can extinguish delusions. This is the proclamation of extinction. As for the *nirmāṇakāya* not being extinct yet proclaiming extinction—this is the Dharma.

Regarding the function of the retribution-body: since its essence is indestructible, how could its function ever be exhausted? Thus, the intent is that the response-body (nirmāṇakāya) does not perish;
it is only because sentient beings are habitually arrogant and self-indulgent that [the Buddha] proclaims, "At midnight, I shall enter parinirvāṇa. This is the proclamation of extinction.

The passage beginning with "The Tathāgata" concludes this by showing that while there is no actual extinction, he manifests extinction as a skillful means for teaching and transforming others. △ Second, the benefit of manifesting extinction.
Furthermore, there are two points. First, not extinguishing sentient beings causes harm; second, proclaiming their extinction is beneficial for things. Regarding the first, there are again two parts:
first, the harm caused by not extinguishing [existence].
Why is this? If the Buddha were to remain in the world for a long time, [the people] would fall into the net of conceptualization and false views.
Like those of meager virtue who delight in the small, they would see the Buddha as eternally abiding;

they would not plant roots of goodness, remaining poor and lowly, failing to produce the two kinds of good and failing to sever the two kinds of evil. They would not extinguish that which is constant, resulting in no benefit but only harm. (5)

"Desire" refers to the afflictions of the realm of thought (*bhāvanā-heya-kleśa*); "recollection and imagination" refer to the afflictions of the realm of views (*dṛṣṭi-heya-kleśa*). Because these defilements are heavy, it is necessary to proclaim [the Buddha's] extinction.
2. Explanation of the meaning of "being subject to loss":
If one sees the Tathāgata as eternally present and never extinguished, one will be unable to give rise to the thought that he is difficult to encounter or a mind of reverence.

If one perceives the Buddha as always remaining in the world, arrogance and indolence arise; thus there is harm. Because one does not give rise to the reverence that [the Buddha] is difficult to encounter, there is no benefit.
Arrogance and self-indulgence increase the delusions of views (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*). Indolence gives rise to the delusions of thought (*bhāvanā-kleśa*).

If one does not give rise to the perception [of the Buddha's rarity], one cannot produce the understanding of the realization of the truths (*satyābhisamaya*); therefore, one cannot sever the delusions of views. Without reverence, one cannot produce the wisdom of contemplation (*bhāvanā-mayī-prajñā*).

Because one has not yet severed discursive thought (*vitarka*), for this reason, it is appropriate that [the Buddha] manifest extinction. Furthermore, hearing that the three Buddhas do not enter extinction carries the implication of pride and self-indulgence.
Hearing that the Dharma-body does not enter extinction leads one to claim that there is only one suchness and no second suchness;
from this, arrogance arises in the mind, leading one to say that all afflictions were originally unarisen and are so now.
Furthermore, since there is no cessation, what need is there to cultivate the Path? They then indulge in their passions and become dissolute, proclaiming:

"The Dharma-body has the meaning of quiescent extinction. Upon hearing that the Reward-body does not cease, they claim that all sentient beings are themselves the mark of *nirvāṇa*, and that the mark of *nirvāṇa* is identical to the mark of afflictions (*kleśa*).
Consequently, they give rise once more to arrogance and indulgence, no longer cultivating goodness, and falling into indolence.
Being indolent and negligent, they proclaim: "The wisdom of the *saṃbhogakāya* can extinguish afflictions.

Upon hearing that the *nirmāṇakāya* does not do so, they claim, "The Buddha’s great compassion constantly protects and covers me. Because of this, they again give rise to arrogance and self-indulgence;
they become greedily attached to base desires and harbor a mind of weariness and indolence, failing to plant roots of goodness. For this reason, they proclaim: "I shall now enter [parinirvāṇa]."

Nirvana. When sentient beings hear this proclamation of extinction, they immediately conceive the thought that the Three Buddhas are difficult to encounter and develop a heart of reverence toward them.
△ Second, the benefit of proclaiming extinction for all things. This also has two parts. First, praising the difficulty of encountering a Buddha.
Therefore, the Tathāgata speaks through skillful means, saying: "Bhikṣus, you should know that the appearance of the Buddhas in the world is difficult to encounter.
As for the difficulty of encountering the Buddhas: sentient beings delight in inferior teachings (*hīna-dharma*), and their afflictions of views and thought (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) are heavy.

Upon hearing that the three bodies (*tri-kāya*) are imperishable, they do not cultivate the Path; thus, it is difficult to achieve union with the Buddha. △ Second, the interrogation and explanation of the difficulty of encountering [the Buddha].
Why is this? Because those people of meager merit (up to) speak of "extinction" (nirvāṇa) even though there is no actual extinction.
If they were to see the three Buddhas, such people would have much goodness and little evil; for them, I do not proclaim extinction. Such people see the Buddha as always dwelling on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa.
As for those who do not see the Buddha, their obstructions are heavy and their goodness is slight; for them, I preach [the teaching of extinction].
The three Buddhas are difficult to encounter. When sentient beings hear this, they immediately think:

"Although the three Buddhas are neither born nor extinguished, one must produce goodness and eliminate evil in order to realize and behold them. This matter is not easy; therefore, it is said they are 'difficult to meet.

From "the mind harbors" downward, it shows that although they manifest extinction, there is no loss but rather benefit. From "for this reason" downward, it concludes by showing that they do not truly perish when they manifest.
Extinction. The benefit of beings throughout the three periods of time has now been concluded. II. Second, the summary that [the teaching] is not in vain:
Furthermore, good sons, the dharmas of all Buddhas and Tathāgatas are thus; for the sake of delivering sentient beings, they are entirely real and not false.

When the Buddhas appear in the world, they first employ three [vehicles] and subsequently one; they reveal the near to manifest the far, benefiting sentient beings throughout the three periods of time. All such dharmas are like this.

To deliver sentient beings, they preach that [the Buddha-nature] has been eternally abiding from the beginning, and yet they further manifest parinirvāṇa—none of these fail to use the Buddha’s lifespan to instruct and awaken sentient beings;
all is real and not false. The explanation by way of the Dharma is concluded. II. The Parable.
The explanation is divided into two parts: first, the explanation by way of analogy; second, the application to the Dharma. The first part is further divided into two:

first, the analogy of the skilled physician treating his son, which illustrates what is appropriate for the manifestations and transformations throughout the three periods of time; second, the analogy of the actual benefit derived from treating the son, which illustrates that the benefiting of sentient beings throughout the three periods of time is not in vain.

The first section is further divided into three parts. First, the analogy of the physician traveling far away, which illustrates benefiting beings in the past. Second, the analogy of returning and then departing again, which illustrates responding to and transforming beings in the present.
Third, the analogy of seeking them out and subsequently returning home, which illustrates responding to and transforming beings in the future.

The first of these [three] is further divided into two: first, the analogy for responding to and transforming beings; second, the analogy for manifesting extinction. The first of these [two] is further divided into two: first, the analogy for responding to and transforming beings.
For example, it is like a skilled physician who is wise, discerning, and proficient in prescriptions and medicines, capable of effectively treating all manner of illnesses.
This is a metaphor for my use of the Buddha-eye (*buddhacakṣus*) to observe; there is the wisdom that corresponds to this, which is excellent.

There are distinctions between an ordinary physician and one called "skilled" or "excellent. Before the Buddha appeared in the world, the non-Buddhist practitioners engaged in various forms of suffering and were unable to attain meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*).

They cannot sever the fetters; they are like the common physicians of the world. The practitioners of the Two Vehicles sever the afflictions of views and thoughts and realize the state of *sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*, treating only one or two types of sentient beings with whom they have a connection; they are like the physicians of their time.

The Bodhisattvas of the gradual teaching, though able to treat illnesses, cannot simultaneously treat all illnesses everywhere; they are like the renowned physicians of the world. Although these three...
Although they can treat illnesses, their treatment is not universal; thus, they cannot be compared to the Tathāgata.

Only a skilled physician can properly prescribe medicine according to the disease, treating all ailments simultaneously and universally—this is a metaphor for the Tathāgata preaching the Dharma according to the capacities of beings to extensively deliver all sentient beings.
"One whose wisdom is sharp and penetrating" is a metaphor for the Buddha’s true wisdom, which is profoundly deep and immeasurable. This clarifies [the meaning].

The practitioner of medicinal formulas is a metaphor for the Buddha’s provisional wisdom, which is difficult to understand and difficult to enter. The teaching is like a medical prescription; the principle is like a wondrous medicine.

Internally, the Tathāgata possesses the three types of supernormal knowledge (*trividyā*) and a penetrating illumination, and his five eyes (*pañcacakṣus*) are perfectly clear; thus he has skillfully mastered the nature of the medicine.

Externally, he recognizes the root causes of the illnesses arising in all sentient beings and proclaims the twelvefold division of the teachings as the prescriptions for their medicines throughout [the world].
This cures the various diseases of sentient beings—namely, their diverse inclinations, natures, behaviors, perceptions, discriminations, and afflictions.

The Tathāgata’s preaching of the Dharma is fundamentally for the purpose of treating these diseases; if sentient beings were without disease, the Tathāgata would likewise not preach the Dharma. △ Next, an analogy for the resonance between the capacity and the stimulus.
That person has many sons, numbering ten, twenty, or even up to a hundred.
That person is a metaphor for the Buddha. The "many sons" and so forth refer to the ten as bodhisattvas and the twenty as those of the two vehicles (śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas).
The "hundreds" serve as a metaphor for the ten classes of sentient beings; it means that those who receive transformation are few, while those who do not receive transformation are many.
There are three meanings of "son" (*putra*): first, the "direct cause" (*zhengyin*). Since all sentient beings possess the Buddha-nature of the direct cause, they are all sons of the Buddha;
thus it is said, "All sentient beings therein are my sons. This refers to the passage in the current text stating, "There are many sons."
Second is the causal condition (*pratyaya-hetu*). This is like a prince giving a lecture in secret;

by hearing the Dharma, one gives rise to understanding and initiates practice, which assists the understanding of the decisive cause (*nirvedha-hetu*) and develops the nature of the true cause (*dharmatā-hetu*). Past connections for establishing affinity all belong to the causal condition. Third is the decisive cause (*nirvedha-hetu*).
This refers to the present *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. Abiding within true wisdom, [one realizes]: "I shall certainly become a Buddha," from the mouth of the Buddha.
Those such as Śāriputra are called true sons. △ Second, the metaphor for manifesting extinction:
"Because of certain affairs, he travels far to another land.

This metaphor illustrates the manifestation of extinction within the past responsive transformations, as the spiritual capacity (*indriya*) of those in this land was exhausted and the conditions (*pratyaya*) in that other region had matured.
In this land one should pass away, while in that land one manifests birth; thus it is said that "due to the arrival of circumstances, one goes to another country.

The analogy of the physician traveling far illustrates the completion of benefiting beings in the past. △ Second, the analogy of returning and then departing again illustrates the responsive transformation in the present.
This also has two parts: first, the analogy for the stirring of spiritual capacity.
Later, the sons drank another person’s poisonous medicine; when the medicine took effect, they became dazed and disoriented, writhing upon the ground.

This is a metaphor for the correspondence between the capacity [of the recipient] and the response [of the teaching]. Seeing that sentient beings have meager virtue and heavy defilements, and that after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa they delight in and cling to the teachings of false teachers, it is said:
"Later, they drink another’s poisonous medicine. They do not know the essentials of transcending the world.

Because one follows the Way, it is said that one is "confused and disordered. Because one falls into the three realms and revolves through the various destinies, it is said that one "tumbles and turns upon the ground.

Part Two: The Metaphor for Responsive Transformation. This has two sections: first, not being born yet manifesting birth; second, not being extinguished yet manifesting extinction. The first section has two parts:
first, the metaphor for the two benefits of form and sound; second, the metaphor for how these benefits are not in vain. The first of these has two parts; first, explaining the benefit of form.
Furthermore, at that time, his father returns home and wishes to be saved and healed, so that he may be granted further life.
"Returns home" is a metaphor for the Buddha returning to be born in this land; this is precisely the benefit of the physical form (*rūpakāya*), not the manifestation of birth.
This refers to being born. To say one "receives false teachings" is called "drinking poison. Regarding "losing what was not lost":

it means that by being greedily attached to the five desires of the triple world, one loses the roots of goodness of the three vehicles previously planted, and thus fails to manifest the responsive capacity for either the Great or Small Vehicles.

For such people, the Buddha proclaims extinction even though he has not actually entered extinction. Furthermore, although one may be attached to the five desires, if one does not lose the roots of goodness of the three vehicles, there is still great [potential].

Regarding "the small capacity experiences": for such persons, the Buddha manifests birth though he is not subject to birth. Regarding "seeing from afar": when the Buddha appears in the world, sentient beings also see the Buddha’s body;
however, because they are obstructed by the five parts [of the faculties] due to the hindrances of views and afflictions (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*), they are unable to behold the Dharma-body.
Therefore, it is called "seeing from afar. Because seeing and hearing of the Buddha’s appearance all involve matters of joy and reverence, it is called "rejoicing."

Prostrating and kneeling. [The passage from] "Śubhānkuśa" downward consists of words seeking salvation, following the pattern of the verses of the Brahmā-kings. △ Next, the benefit of the sound is clarified:
"The father saw his sons' suffering and distress thus... (up to) "...may their suffering and distress be swiftly removed, and they no longer have manifold afflictions."

The "various sūtras and prescriptions" refer to the teachings of the twelve divisions (*dvādaśāṅga-pravacana*). The "medicinal herbs" are the eighty thousand dharma-gates expounded within those teachings.

That which issues forth from the Buddha as the twelve divisions represents the sudden medicinal herbs; that which issues forth as the nine divisions represents the gradual medicinal herbs. Color is a metaphor for ethical discipline (*śīla*);
because it guards the body and speech, its phenomenal characteristics are coarse and manifest. Fragrance is a metaphor for meditative concentration (*samādhi*); [it represents] spiritual merit...
"Exquisite fragrance" refers to its pervading all things. "Flavor" is a metaphor for wisdom (*prajñā*), because it enables one to attain the flavor of principle.

The *śūnyatā-samādhi* (emptiness samādhi) is like pounding; the *animitta-samādhi* (signless samādhi) is like sifting; the *apraṇihita-samādhi* (wishless samādhi) is like mixing. Each of these samādhis is endowed with morality, concentration, and wisdom.
Because one preaches this Dharma to sentient beings so that they may practice it, it is said: "giving to the children to cause them to take it. The following passage explains this.
I exhort you to take the medicine of the Dharma; yet by taking the poison of others, your suffering and affliction will increase day by day.
By taking this medicine of the Dharma, however, your suffering and affliction will be swiftly eliminated. △ Second, the analogy showing that the benefit is not in vain.
Among those sons, those who did not lose their minds (up to) immediately took [the medicine], and their illnesses were entirely cured.
Since they did not lose their minds, there were three types of karmic capacities for the Three Vehicles; each took up the medicinal dharma, and all their illnesses were cured.
How could such benefit be in vain? [The section on] "Manifesting Birth within Non-Birth" concludes. △ Second, "Manifesting Extinction within Non-Extinction," divided into two parts. First:
The analogy of the imminent death, and second, the analogy of the sons’ awakening. The first [section] further has two parts: first, clarifying the reason for proclaiming his passing;
the remainder concerns those who have lost their senses, who see their father coming [and yet], despite such excellent medicine, refuse to take it.

This explains the reason for manifesting parinirvāṇa: because sentient beings have meager merit, seeing the Buddha constantly remaining in the world only increases their arrogance and self-indulgence, such that they do not practice;
it is as if they are unwilling to take medicine. The following section provides a critical inquiry and explanation. "The father acts... and so forth.
He takes pity on those who are deluded and do not seek the True Dharma. △ Next, he formally utters the parable of the impending death:
"I shall now employ skillful means... [and] dispatch a messenger to inform your father that he has already died."

My present two lines serve as a metaphor for the fact that while the Buddha remains in the world there is loss, whereas his manifest extinction brings benefit. "Then he acts below" serves as a metaphor for his manifest extinction.
Because the period of transformation is nearing its end, it is said he is "aged and weary. "The time of death has arrived" means he is about to enter *nirvāṇa*.

Although the Buddha has passed into extinction, he leaves behind the scriptural teachings to remain in the world; therefore, it is said, "The excellent medicine is here. Furthermore, he proceeds to another...
“Nation” refers to the manifestation of extinction in this world and the manifestation of birth in another realm. Regarding “sending messengers” and so forth:

the four reliances (catvāri pratisaraṇāni) are bodhisattvas who speak to sentient beings, saying, “The Buddha has already entered parinirvāṇa; he has left behind only this Dharma. I shall now proclaim it for you; you should receive and practice it.
If, in future generations, there were no four reliances to transmit and explain the scriptures and the Dharma, how could sentient beings know it for themselves?
Therefore, the four reliances for bodhisattvas are the messengers dispatched by the Tathāgata. △ Second, the parable of the sons being awakened, which has two parts.
First, the benefit of manifesting extinction.
At that time, the sons heard that their father had passed away (up to the point where he) now abandons them and has gone far away to another land.
It was only through knowing of their father’s death that the sons were finally able to awaken.
This is a metaphor for how, when the Tathāgata manifests his parinirvāṇa, sentient beings only then begin to feel grief and longing. △. Second, the response of future capacities.
Reflecting upon myself, I am orphaned and exposed, with no one left to rely upon... (up to)... I immediately took [the medicine] and wore it, and my grievous illness was entirely cured.

This is truly because, after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, sentient beings have awakened; by taking the medicine and practicing cultivation, they create the causes and conditions that can evoke the response and transformation of the future.
As the *Śālistamba-sūtra* (Teaching Left Behind) says: "Those who have not yet been delivered, all shall now attain deliverance."
The causal conditions. The preceding section on "returning and then departing again" serves as a metaphor for the completion of benefiting sentient beings in the present.
△ Third, the metaphor of "seeking out and returning later" serves as a metaphor for the future manifestation of transformation.
When the father heard that his sons had all recovered, he immediately returned and allowed them all to see him.
This is a metaphor for benefiting sentient beings in the future. The father hearing of their recovery constitutes the "responsive capacity" (*nenggan zhi ji*) that can evoke a response;
his appearing before them is the arising of the "response" (*ying*) in the future. Thus, both physical form and voice will bring about benefit. Within this context, "recovering" refers to—

These words do not mean that delusions are completely severed; rather, there are those with the capacities for the Three Vehicles, and whether their delusions are severed or not, they are all said to have recovered.
The preceding analogy of the excellent physician treating his sons concludes the section on the appropriate manifestations of response throughout the three periods of time. II.
The Analogy of the Actual Benefit to the Sons. This illustrates that the benefiting of sentient beings throughout the three periods of time is not in vain.
"What do you think, sons of good family? [up to] "Is it not a false and deceptive offense? "No, World-Honored One.

Just as a skilled physician, in order to treat his mad son, speaks of death when he is actually alive, so too does the Tathāgata, in order to deliver sentient beings, manifest extinction when there is no extinction.
Although the matter appears to be false and deceptive, its benefit is vast and profound; therefore, it is said, "Is there perhaps... and so forth. The single phrase "No" is direct.
The answer is that it is not false. To feign death in order to save those on the verge of being poisoned is a temporary expedient;
how truly a skilled physician! The mind of the Sage takes the people as his own heart. In the Way of benefiting beings, there are both the definitive (nītārtha) and the expedient (upāya).
There is nothing that cannot be done, provided it is of benefit to sentient beings. What dharma could not be employed? Thus we know that he manifested birth.
The great skillful means of manifesting extinction are all instances of conforming indirectly to the timing [of beings]. How could they be false? The preceding analogy is concluded.
Next, the application to the Dharma:
The Buddha said, "I am also like this" (up to) "and there is no one who can rightfully charge me with the fault of being false."
Since attaining Buddhahood, an immeasurable number of kalpas have already passed. For the sake of all sentient beings, he employs skillful means to say that he has entered extinction;
yet in reality, he was never born, though he manifests birth everywhere. In reality, he never perishes, though he manifests extinction everywhere.

He benefits beings throughout the three periods of time, his transformations continuing without end. Because this is true and not false, it is said: "There is none who can equal him. The prose section concludes. II. Verses:
The verse consists of twenty-five and a half lines and is divided into two parts. The first twenty and a half lines versify the teaching by way of the Dharma;

the second five lines versify the teaching by way of parable. The first part is further divided into two. The first nineteen and a half lines versify the benefiting of beings throughout the three periods of time;
the second single line versifies that all is real and not false. The first of these is further divided into three. The first four lines versify the benefiting of beings in the past. The second...
The first five lines praise the benefit of sentient beings in the present. The thirty-five and a half lines praise the benefit of sentient beings in the future.
Furthermore, the initial four lines praise the benefit of sentient beings in the past.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"Since I attained Buddhahood, the number of kalpas that have passed—[until now]—though close at hand, I have not seen [the end]."

From "I myself" downwards, the verses describe how since attaining enlightenment, [the number of lifetimes] has long been established: one hundred births become one thousand; one thousand births become ten thousand; ten thousand births become one hundred million (*billion*); one hundred million births become one trillion (*zhào*);

one trillion births become ten quadrillion (*jīng*); ten quadrillion births become one quintillion (*zǐ*); one quintillion births become ten sextillion (*hài*); ten sextillion births become one septillion (*rǎng*); and one septillion births become ten octillion (*gōu*). [Supplementary Note: One hundred births become one thousand; one thousand births become ten thousand; ten thousand births become one hundred million; one hundred million births become one trillion; one trillion births become ten quadrillion; ten quadrillion births become one quintillion; one quintillion births become ten sextillion; ten sextillion births become one septillion; one septillion births become ten octillion.

From the ravines arise the streams; from the streams arises the source; from the source arises the vessel. "Constantly preaching" refers to the lower [verse]. The verse’s middle section concerns benefiting sentient beings.

From that time onward, he has constantly preached the Dharma to transform and teach others. Since it is said "constantly preaching," how could it be merely like the flowing of water or the movement of wind?

It extends even to the end of the future limit—preaching in every dust mote and in every world-system. "In order to deliver" refers to the lower [verse], which praises his dwelling place. In the past, at Śā...
"Vipaśyin, this very day, the defiled land of sentient beings in this Sahā world is itself the pure realm of all Buddhas.

There is neither past nor present; therefore, it is said that [the Buddha] eternally abides here. Although he eternally abides here, the reason sentient beings do not see him is due to the obstruction of their inverted views.
**Part Two: The Five Verses on Benefiting Beings in the Present.** This section is divided into two parts. The first three verses praise the non-... (text continues).
He manifests birth after birth.
The multitude perceives my parinirvāṇa and makes extensive offerings to my relics (up to: yet I am always here and do not perish).

"The multitude perceives [me] below" clarifies the response of the spiritual capacity; through their offerings and yearning, their minds become supple, and they apply themselves with rigorous diligence.
"I wish to see the Tathāgata. At that time, I descended and manifested my birth, causing him to see that the assembly on Vulture Peak had not yet dispersed.
I then told him: "I am constantly here preaching the Dharma; I truly do not pass into extinction. (△ Second, two lines:
Versifying the non-extinction while manifesting extinction.)
By the power of skillful means, he manifests both extinction and non-extinction (up to: yet merely says, "I have entered parinirvāṇa.

Because sentient beings thirst for him with longing, he manifests birth; because they become arrogant, self-indulgent, and negligent, he again manifests extinction—all of this is through skillful means.

There is extinction and non-extinction. Fundamentally, what is there to arise and extinguish? It may be that in other lands I have not yet entered extinction, while in this land I manifest extinction;
I preach the Dharma there, yet you do not hear it nor know of it, thinking instead that I have truly passed into parinirvāṇa. (30½ lines)

The verse describes the future benefit of sentient beings. While the preceding long prose merely alluded to the four characters "permanently abiding and not extinguished," the present verse elaborates upon this in detail, divided into four parts.
First, one and a half lines concern the future awakening of responsive conditions.
I see all sentient beings submerged in suffering and affliction... (until) I therefore appear in the world to preach the Dharma for them.
Because sentient beings look up to me with longing, I manifest my body in the world; because they are to be delivered from suffering and affliction, I further preach the Dharma for them.
△ Second, four lines clarify that [the Buddha] abides eternally and does not perish.
Such is his supernormal power that, throughout incalculable eons (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*), he scatters [flowers] upon the Buddha and the great assembly.

"Gṛdhrakūṭa" (Vulture Peak) refers to the Land of True Reward (*vipāka-bhūmi*). "Other dwelling places" refers to the Land of Expedient Means with Remainder (*upāya-śeṣa-bhūmi*), which is the aforementioned "other lands.

The Land of Reward is the Land of Enjoyment for Others (*para-sambhogakāya-bhūmi*). If one relies on the expression "always abiding," it refers to the Land of Self-Enjoyment (*sva-sambhogakāya-bhūmi*).

According to the words of Ratnavyūha, this refers to the *parasaṃbhogakāya* land during the original time. As for the "other-enjoyment" (*parasaṃbhoga*), it is the land inhabited by the other *saṃbhogakāya*;
it is called the Land of True Reward (*saphala-vipāka-bhūmi*) and pertains to the phenomenal realm (*vastu*).

This "other-retribution" (*para-vipāka*) is the supreme *nirmāṇakāya*, so named because it is perceived according to the karmic conditions of sentient beings; thus it is called "other-retribution. As for the "self-enjoyment" (*svasaṃbhoga*), it is the locus of self-enjoyment.
The land where it resides is named the Land of Constant Quiescent Light; this pertains to principle (*li*). The other [land], retribution, is wisdom. As the text says:

"That which is obtained through long-cultivated practice; the light of wisdom shines immeasurably. When the kalpa-fire blazes forth and the great trichiliocosm is utterly destroyed, that is the land of sentient beings.
This land, peaceful and indestructible, is the land of the Buddhas. "Constant quiescence" is the Great Nirvana.
This is the realm of great peace and bliss; therefore, it is said that this land is secure and tranquil. Regarding the passage "Gods and humans" and below:

the ten stages of sages and three stages of worthies maintain dharani and meditative contemplation. One should reflect upon the self-proclamation of the celestial drum without being questioned, and the causal practices of the worthy sages through celestial flowers.
△ Third, two lines clarify the non-perception of causes and conditions.
My pure land is not destroyed, yet the multitudes see it as being consumed by fire (up to: they do not hear the names of the Triple Gem). The transformations of the pure land are as described above;
[the experiences of] sorrow and fear are like those in the mountains and forests of the three miserable realms.

As for the "Triple Gem," they are the leaders of the four modes of birth and the ships that ferry one across the six destinies; thus, there are six [aspects]. First, the original Triple Gem, namely the Tathāgata, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha. The fourth...

The Truths. There are five types of persons. Second, the Three Jewels of the Hīnayāna: these refer to the Buddha of sixteen feet, the Dharma of the Truths and Conditions, and the Saṃgha of those on the paths of fruition and application.

Third, the Three Jewels of the Mahāyāna: these refer to the Buddha of the three bodies and ten bodies, the Dharma of the principle of the two emptinesses and so forth, and the Saṃgha of the three stages of worthies and ten stages of sages.
Fourth, the Three Jewels of Institutional Maintenance: these refer to the Buddha represented by carvings, paintings, and images, and the Dharma in the form of palm leaves and yellow scrolls.

The Dharma refers to the monastic community who have shaved their hair and donned dyed robes. The Three Jewels of Distinct Characteristics consist of the Buddha as Dharma-body, Reward-body, and Transformation-body;

the Dharma as teaching, principle, wisdom, and cessation; and the Sangha as the successive stages of the three vehicles. The Three Jewels of the Single Essence consist of the Buddha as the awakening to True Suchness;
the Dharma as the totality of the sustaining norm; and the Sangha as the harmony of phenomena and principle. The *Mahā-upāya-sūtra* states: "Three..."
The Three Jewels are that to which one returns; their essential purpose is to provide rescue and protection. It is like a criminal who flees toward a foreign land seeking rescue and protection.
The king of that foreign land says: "Come here without fear; do not leave my realm, and do not disobey my instructions;
I shall certainly protect you. Sentient beings are likewise: bound by Māra and possessing the transgressions of birth and death, they take refuge in the Three Jewels.

One seeks their instruction and protection. If one sincerely takes refuge in the Triple Gem with no other direction, and does not contravene the Buddha’s teachings, then even the evil Māra King can do nothing against such a person.
(Section Four: Three Verses on Attaining the Conditions for Vision.)
Those who cultivate merit and are gentle, upright, and straightforward—up to those who have attained this through long-term cultivation of practice—are those who cultivate merit.

Because they are fully endowed with both the objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) and the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*), they are able to see the True Reward Land (*samyak-vipāka-kṣetra*) and the Other-Response Body (*para-nirmāṇa-kāya*).

For these individuals, it is said that the lifespan is immeasurable. For those whose defilements are heavy due to the five turbidities (*pañca-kaṣāya*), it is said that [the Buddha] is difficult to encounter after a long time.
It was only after a long time that I saw [the truth]. My wisdom is inferior; my fetters are bound. My wisdom and lifespan are immeasurable and innumerable;

all are obtained as the retribution for having cultivated various karmic practices over a vast period of time. The preceding verse concludes the section on benefiting sentient beings throughout the three periods of time.
Next, one line of verse praises how all is real and not false.
"You who possess wisdom, do not harbor doubts regarding this; you should sever them so they are forever exhausted. The words of the Buddha are truly not false.
Old doubts should be severed, and new doubts should not arise. The Tathāgata’s words of truth and reality are all without falsehood.
Part Two: Five Verses. A Verse on the Parable. This has two sections. First, one verse: a verse on the parable.
Just as a skilled physician, for the sake of treating a mad son, may say he is dead while actually being alive, yet cannot be accused of speaking falsehood;
since the prose exposition is extensive, I shall now briefly indicate it in verse. II. Four lines: Verses on the application of the Dharma.
"I, too, am the Father of the World, rescuing all who suffer from their ailments" (up to) "...may they quickly accomplish the Buddha-body.

"I, too," follows below. This verse summarizes the benefit of beings throughout the three periods of time. Each subsequent line completes the meaning of the preceding one, meaning that one should constantly maintain this intention:
"By what Dharma may all sentient beings attain supreme wisdom and quickly accomplish the Buddha-body?"
The third major chapter, "Awakening to the Buddha’s Knowledge and Vision," is hereby concluded.

In the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, from the seventeenth chapter, "Distinguishing Merits," up to the chapter on "Never-Disparaging"—these four chapters constitute the entry into the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. This follows from the preceding discourse by the Buddha on his lifespan.

It is long-lasting, benefiting sentient beings throughout the three periods of time, with transformation following transformation without end. The great assembly at this Dharma gathering has already realized that the Dharmakāya is eternally abiding, neither arising nor ceasing.

Furthermore, they have heard that the Pure Land is indestructible; yet, when the world perceives the exhaustion of an eon, it realizes through the principle that the triple realm is mind-only, not departing from its present location.
Reaching this state, the sentiments of birth and death are forgotten, and the dualistic views of purity and defilement are extinguished. With deep resolve, they believe.

[The Buddha] explained: "Their wondrous awakening has reached its ultimate limit; each has entered the Buddha’s knowledge and vision (*buddhajñānadarśana*). There are distinctions between those who have realized entry and those who have entered through understanding;
therefore, the Tathāgata distinguishes them accordingly. The following chapter on 'Rejoicing' (*anumodanā*) is also a continuation of this entry through understanding.
The merit obtained therein is incomparably superior. This is true even for rejoicing for a single thought-moment, let alone for the five kinds of Dharma-preachers."
Following this, the merit of the Dharma Master is further elucidated: the purification of the six sense faculties and adornment both internally and externally.

This section clarifies the method of realization and entry; it does not slight even a single grade [of practice]. By citing his own past deeds, it specifically reveals the person capable of realizing and entering [the truth], thereby exhorting those of the future to advance in their cultivation.
Thus, these four chapters constitute the discernment for entering the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.

The stage of separate practice (*pṛthag-caryā*) clarifies the distinctions between hearing, realization, and testimony; this is termed "division. The differences in depth regarding the cultivation of the path and the realization of the nature are termed "separate.
This refers to the past disciples who emerged from the earth and the present disciples on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa, upon hearing that the lifespan is long and far-reaching.
To obtain various benefits is called "merit" (*guṇa*). When the multitude of sages heard the Dharma, they understood it silently and their minds were harmonized;

yet, as dragons and snakes could not be distinguished, both parties remained in mutual delusion. When the Buddha analyzed and extolled them for them, the characteristics of things became self-evident—like cleaving a jade ore to reveal the gem, or like Bodhisattva Pāṃśupradāna seeing gold.
Because there are such persons and such teachings, both the capacity of the recipient and the instruction are sublime; thus, [the heavens...]
People raise offerings; they celebrate the Dharma and celebrate people.
△ The Fourth Major Chapter: Entering the Buddha’s Knowledge and Vision. This text consists of four sections, divided into three parts: first, clarifying the merit of realization and understanding;

second, clarifying the purity of the faculties of those who uphold the sutra; third, revealing the person capable of such realization. The first part further has two sub-sections; first, clarifying realization.

[The Buddha] enters [the exposition]. Next, the "Entrance through Understanding" (*prativedhapraveśa*) is explained. This consists first of a prose section followed by verses. The prose section is divided into three parts. First, the narrator describes the benefits:
at that time, the great assembly heard the Buddha speak of his lifespan (up to the point where) incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) sentient beings attained great benefit.

"Life span is thus. This refers to the preceding chapter. "Benefiting beings throughout the three periods of time," "neither arising yet manifesting as arising, neither ceasing yet manifesting as ceasing," "truly real and not false," and so forth.
Under "immeasurable," there is a general indication of the assembly that attains benefit. II. The Tathāgata’s Detailed Analysis. This is divided into three parts:
first, the merit of entering the Path; second, the merit of attaining the fruit; third, the merit of generating the resolve [for enlightenment].
Furthermore, regarding the merit of those who have first entered the Path, at that time the World-Honored One addressed Maitreya Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva [up to] "able to turn the pure wheel of Dharma.
Within this group, the number of people varies and is not uniform; their realizations differ in being either shallow or deep. Thus it is with the Tathāgata’s three...
It is thoroughly penetrating and illuminating; all is truly so and not false. In each section, the number of people is first cited, followed by an explanation of what they realized.

Having heard the Buddha’s lifespan, they understood it to be devoid of arising and ceasing; they suddenly awakened to their own minds and immediately attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).

This patience is not the same as the patience attained after the three gradual stages in the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*. The latter belongs to the stages of sequential cultivation and advancement within the definitive teaching (*nītārtha*).

This is the awakening of entering the holy path instantaneously according to the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao). It corresponds to the fourth stage, the Patience of Non-arising (Anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti), among the five patiences of the *Renyō-kyō* (*Benevolent Kings Sūtra*).
When one realizes this principle, one understands that all phenomena are empty and quiescent, and perceives not even the slightest arising or ceasing of any dharma.
Because one accepts [the truth] within the mind, it is called the "patience toward the non-arising of dharmas" (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). This attains the merits of the seventh and eighth stages.
The subsequent verse, "Or abiding in the stage of non-retrogression," praises this very patience. By maintaining both the words and their meaning, one attains the great *dhāraṇī*.
All other *dhāraṇīs* emerge from this; therefore, it is called a "gate. This attainment of *dhāraṇī* is the merit of the fifth stage, the Difficult to Conquer (*sudurjayā*).

To delight in eloquent exposition, to encounter the source from every side, and to teach others without weariness—possessing the fourfold analytical knowledges of dharma, meaning, phrasing, and eloquence—is the attainment of unimpeded eloquence (*pratisaṃvid*);
this is the merit of the ninth stage, the Good Intelligence (*sādhumatī*). To turn...

Having shattered ignorance and manifested the inherent virtues, one returns to the source within all phenomena and employs skillful means to deliver sentient beings, attaining mastery over both the inverse and the direct order of reality;
thus it is said that through "hundreds of thousands" [of practices], one attains the merit of the tenth stage, the Cloud of Dharma (*dharmameghā bhūmi*).
He turns toward the Dharma of non-retrogression, far surpassing the two vehicles. Through skillful means he benefits sentient beings, never again falling back;

this is also the merit of the eighth stage (*bhūmi*). His cultivation and realization are not absent, yet defilements cannot stain him; thus he is free from the impurities of the mind and suddenly perfects pure precepts.
Therefore, one is able to turn the pure wheel of Dharma; this is the merit of attaining the second stage, the Stainless (*vimalā-bhūmi*).
△ Second, the merit of attaining the fruit:
Furthermore, [as for] a small chiliocosm [up to] one shall attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

Regarding the statement that one shall attain *bodhi* after eight births: this refers to transcending into the stage of the noble ones (*ārya*). It is a birth like being born into the family of the Buddhas, not a birth characterized by the emergence and submergence within *saṃsāra*.
As for the expression "eight births," it means that upon hearing the Dharma of the Buddha’s lifespan, one immediately transcends into the merits of the fourth stage (*bhūmi*).
There are eight such instances of attaining the state of *samyak-saṃbodhi*; thus, the following verse says: "The remainder are each eight."

"Attaining Buddhahood in one birth" refers to this. "Those who shall attain it in four births" refers to the merit of directly transcending into the eighth stage (*bhūmi*), wherein there are four births remaining until the attainment of the rank of *samyak-saṃbuddha*.

"Those who shall attain it in three births" refers to the merit of directly transcending into the ninth stage, wherein there are three births remaining until the attainment of the rank of *samyak-saṃbuddha*.
"Those who shall attain it in two births" refers to... [the merit of directly transcending into the tenth stage].
Regarding the merit of transcending into the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), there are two types of attaining the rank of *samyak-saṃbodhi*.

One type is "attaining it in one more birth," which means transcending into the stage of *samyag-avabodha* (Equal Enlightenment) and attaining the rank of *samyak-saṃbodhi* in a single lifetime; this is direct entry. Therefore, it is said:
"With one birth remaining, he shall accomplish all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*). The lifespan of the Tathāgata is the indestructible Original Enlightenment (*mūla-bodhi*).
The true reality (*dharmatā*)—that aforementioned great fruit of retribution consisting of various natures and characteristics—is something that only I and the Buddhas of the ten directions can know.
Having reached this point, he has laid it out on a platter and turned it over completely, leaving no further residue.
Thus, these various multitudes have awakened to and entered the true reality, each realizing it according to their own faculties; and so the Tathāgata...
He distinguished them for him. Question: In the past, the stages of faith, abiding, practice, and penetration were used as a sequential framework for interpretation.

Why is this not employed now? Answer: First, this sutra is a perfect and sudden (yuantun) Great Teaching; fundamentally, it has no fixed sequence of stages. Second, it is a direct entry that transcends all, regardless of whether one’s faculties are sharp or dull.
Upon hearing it, one realizes and attains enlightenment. Although there may be degrees of depth, these are all cases of sudden transcendence, not gradual cultivation.

First, because they have made progress; second, because at the Great Assembly on Mount Ling, there were no ordinary beings who, upon hearing this wondrous Dharma, immediately received predictions of enlightenment and transcended into the ranks of the sages;

third, because those who gained benefit were the multitude who emerged from the earth, all of whom had been transformed and cultivated during the *rajas-bindu* kalpas prior—how could there be any among them belonging to the categories of the three stages of worthiness or the ten levels of faith? As the text says: "the bodies of bodhisattvas."
Golden in color and endowed with the thirty-two marks, he had already perfected the virtues of a Buddha. △ Third, the merit of generating the resolve:
Furthermore, there were beings from eight worlds (up to) who all generated the resolve for *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
For such sentient beings, the Sahā world is revealed as the Flower Treasury (Kusumatalagarbha) World; by means of the "Endurance" [world], the Pure Land is elucidated.
The present time is revealed as the remote origin; by means of the three bodies (trikāya), the lifespan is elucidated.
Therefore, each gives rise to the mind of the true cause and together seeks the fruit of perfect enlightenment. The Tathāgata’s detailed exposition is complete. △ Third, the assembly’s offering.
When the Buddha had spoken thus, these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas sang immeasurable verses in praise of the Buddhas.
At that time, the assembly, having heard this profound and far-reaching Dharma, attained great benefit and therefore presented various kinds of offerings. This is the *Vastusaṃgrahaṇī*.
When the Buddha had finished his exposition, the void rained down incense and flowers as an offering to the three Buddhas and the great assembly.
The sound of celestial drums resonated deeply and far, while celestial garments and necklaces hung down; canopies reached to the limits of the sky, and sublime voices praised the Buddha.
It is like the majestic Flower Treasury World (Avataṃsaka-lokadhātu), with principal and satellites arrayed in successive layers. This, too, is a case of using phenomena to manifest principle:

from within the emptiness of intrinsic nature (prakṛti-śūnyatā), one gives rise to the four kinds of causal practice; above, these accord with the Buddha of the three bodies (trikāya) as the fruition, and below, they pervade all those on the path within the nine realms of existence.

"Banner" (*dhvaja*) signifies the meaning of turning; "canopy" (*vitāna*) signifies the meaning of covering. This represents how wisdom and abandonment turn progressively, and how compassion covers progressively.

Its heights and depths, its shallow and deep levels, do not lose their proper sequence. That it reaches as far as the Brahma Heaven represents the Bodhisattva’s sudden realization upon hearing the Dharma, being adjacent to the ultimate fruit.
II. Verse Summary. There are nineteen lines, divided into two parts. First, eleven [lines].
The Tathāgata analyzed this in verse.
At that time, Maitreya Bodhisattva rose from his seat (and so forth), joined his palms toward the Buddha, and spoke these verses:
"The Buddha has preached a marvelous Dharma, never heard before... like space, it is boundless."
The World-Honored One spoke in prose; Maitreya spoke in verse. This is because the World-Honored One is the Buddha of the present fruit, while Maitreya is the Buddha of the future cause.
As a son inherits his father’s legacy, the father acts and the son recounts; they share the same root and follow the same thread, joining their efforts to complete the task.

Thus, through the realization of the teacher and disciple, benefit is accomplished. Regarding "The Buddha spoke," etc., this verse praises the great assembly for receiving benefit. There is no [further text].
The first section praises the merit of entering the Path; the second, the merit of attaining the fruit. Regarding those who attain Buddhahood according to their number of births:
this refers to attaining Buddhahood upon entering the stage of Subtle Enlightenment (Miaojue) after four, four, three, three, two, or two births, respectively.
In this way, this single practice brings together those who have attained sudden enlightenment and those who realize it gradually.

Upon hearing the wondrous Dharma of the Buddha’s long-lasting life span and the retribution of the purity of the three bodies, each attains entry into the immeasurable and boundless pure *dharmakāya*.
They shall attain the cultivation and realization of the untainted (*anāsrava*) and unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) perfect *saṃbhogakāya*, and also attain the application of the... [nirmāṇakāya].

The arising [of the mind] is not subject to extinction, for it manifests thousands of times more emanations; hence it is said that one "attains the immeasurable and so forth. Furthermore, the following verses praise the merit of generating the bodhicitta.
The single line beginning with "World-Honored One" summarizes how the benefit is vast and extensive. Next, eight lines of verse describe the offerings made by the assembly at that time.
"Raining down *māndārava* and *mahāmāndārava* [flowers]... to assist the unsurpassed mind.

This "single phrase of the bird" describes the manner in which superior incense and flowers fall in profusion. Thus, by bestowing these various [offerings], the assembly at that time was benefited, and they fully developed the virtuous aspiration for enlightenment (*bodhicitta*).
The section on "Realization through Practice" (*shōnyū*) is concluded. △ Second, explaining "Entry through Understanding" (*kai nyū*). This is divided into two parts. First:

The clarification of principle pertains to the entry through understanding (*prativedha-praveśa*). Second is the clarification of future entry through understanding. This first section is further divided into four parts: first, faith and understanding in a single thought-moment;

second, a brief explanation of the approach to the words; third, explaining extensively for others; and fourth, the characteristics of profound faith and understanding. Regarding the first, there are both prose and verse.
The prose is divided into three sections; the first identifies the person.
At that time, the Buddha addressed Maitreya Bodhisattva... [omitted] ...up to "being able to give rise to even a single thought of faith and understanding.

To have no doubt is called "faith" (*śraddhā*); faith fundamentally establishes the measure of one's lifespan. To understand clearly is called "understanding" (*adhimukti*); it means realizing that the *dharmakāya* is eternally abiding.
This refers to the sudden and clear illumination upon hearing the teaching wherever it may be, such that there is no further obstruction. △ Second, the evaluation of the merit.
Furthermore, there are three parts. First, the title indicates that his virtues are immeasurable;
the merits he has attained are without limit.
Second, the standard for comparison is presented.
"If there be sons or daughters of good family... [up to] "...excluding the *prajñāpāramitā*.
Taking the preceding five perfections as the basis for comparison, *prajñā* is wisdom; it is precisely the single-moment of faith and understanding (*ekakṣaṇa-adhimukti*).
Therefore, these are excluded. *Dāna* means giving; *śīla* means precept; *kṣānti* means patience; *vīrya* means diligence;

*dhyāna* means meditative concentration. These five are not themselves the "other shore" (*pāramitā*); however, because one diligently seeks unexcelled bodhi through them, they are also called the "other shore.
△ Third, the evaluation of their relative magnitude.
Compared to these merits, the former merits—even those known through calculation, analogy, or metaphor—cannot be fathomed.
When the merit of a single moment of faithful understanding is compared to the merit of practicing the five perfections over a long period, the latter does not equal even a fraction of the former.
This is because the blessings of the five perfections are limited, whereas the wisdom of faithful understanding is immeasurable. △ Three.
The seal of illumination is non-retrogressive.
If a son or daughter of good family were to retrogress from *samyak-saṃbodhi*, such a thing is impossible.
Hearing of the merit of the lifespan provides sustenance from without; a single thought of faith and understanding provides internal perfuming. Therefore...
One does not regress from the *bodhi* of the Buddha-fruit. △ Second, the verse summary consists of nineteen and a half lines, divided into three parts.
The first fourteen lines summarize the measurement of merit.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke in verse:
"If a person seeks the Buddha’s wisdom for eighty myriads of koṭis of nayutas of kalpas... their merit shall be such as this."

"If a person" and below: the verse explains that for the sake of seeking the fruit of Buddhahood, one practices the first five perfections (*pāramitās*). "In this regard" and below: clarifies the perfection of giving (*dāna-pāramitā*). "If again" and below:

clarifies the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*). "If again" and below: clarifies the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*). "If again" and below: clarifies the perfection of vigor (*vīrya-pāramitā*).

"Furthermore, in" and below: clarifies the perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-pāramitā*). "This person" and below: concludes upon the merit of the aforementioned five perfections. "There being good" and below: provides a comparative evaluation.
To what extent? △ Second, four lines. A verse concluding the explanation of non-retrogression:
"There are bodhisattvas who have practiced the Way for immeasurable kalpas... (up to) the teaching of their lifespan is likewise."

"One who has practiced the Way for immeasurable kalpas" refers to one who has long cultivated the various perfections (pāramitās). "May I... and so forth expresses the arousal of the vow of compassion.
Having heard [the teaching on] longevity, one attains faith and understanding in a single thought-moment; may my lifespan be equal to that of the Tathāgata’s life when preaching the Dharma.
Regarding the Bodhi of the Buddha-fruit, how could there be any regression? △ Third, one and a half lines concerning deep-seated faith and understanding.
If there are those with a profound mind who are pure and upright, they will have no doubt regarding this.

"Profound mind" means exhausting the principle of non-duality; "uprightness" means being consistent from beginning to end. Having developed faith through extensive learning, one expounds the teaching according to its meaning.
A single moment of faithful understanding is equal in merit to long-term practice. How could one with such profound faith and understanding harbor any doubt?
△ Second, a brief explanation of the meaning of the words. This is divided into two parts. First, identifying the person:
Furthermore, Ajita, if there are those who hear that the Buddha’s lifespan is long and far-reaching, they will understand the meaning of these words.
Previously, there was only a single thought of faith and understanding, yet one could not expound it for others;
now, because of the meaning and purpose heard, one explains it slightly for others. △ Second, the measurement of merit.
The merit obtained by such a person is limitless and can give rise to the unsurpassed wisdom of a Tathāgata.

Having heard of the original lifespan, they speak of it to others even slightly; the power of their preaching the Dharma can give rise to the unsurpassed wisdom of a Tathāgata—how could their merit possibly have a limit?
△ Third, extensively preaching for others. This also has two parts. First, providing an illustration by citing a person.
How much more so for one who extensively hears this sutra (up to) making offerings of fragrant oil and ghee lamps to the scroll of the sutra, hearing it extensively,
understanding it extensively, explaining it extensively to others, practicing extensive offerings, and causing others to do likewise. △ Section Two.
As for the measure of their merit:
the merit of such persons is immeasurable and boundless, capable of giving rise to all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*).
By means of a single kind of knowledge, they can know the path and teachings of all Buddhas, and they can know the causal seeds of all sentient beings.
To explain this extensively for others is impossible without possessing the Buddha’s wisdom. △ Fourth, the characteristics of profound faith and understanding. This also has two parts.
First, identifying such a person:
"Ajita, if a son of good family (up to) hears me speak of the long duration of my life-span and with a deep heart believes and understands it."
"Deep mind" (*gambhīra-citta*) distinguishes it from the preceding moment of faith and understanding (*adhimukti*). △ Second, the perfection of contemplation is most clearly revealed:
"Then one sees the Buddha as always present on Vulture Peak" (up to) "...one should know that this is the mark of deep faith and understanding."
"Seeing the Buddha and so forth" refers to the characteristics of other lands. "Furthermore, seeing and so forth" refers to the characteristics of the Land of Real Reward (*sambhoga-kāya*).

"If there are [beings] below... concludes this profound understanding: one should know that the Tathāgata is always preaching the Dharma on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa, and that the Sahā world has been level from the beginning.
Only those who have opened, shown, awakened to, and entered the Buddha’s knowledge and vision can perceive this realm; all other beings...
[They] are born with deep-seated ignorance and a turbid mind of flattery and crookedness; therefore, they are unable to see [it].
In the past, the Great Master Zhizhe saw this single assembly as a sign of profound faith and understanding. This concludes the present entry into understanding. II.
Clarifying the future entry into understanding, divided into two parts: 1. The five kinds of merit from upholding the sutra. 2. Weighing the merit of sympathetic joy.
The beginning consists of prose and verse. The prose section is divided into five parts. First is the direct expression of sympathetic joy (*anumodanā*).
Furthermore, from "after the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata" up to "one should know that this constitutes the mark of profound faith and understanding."
"Following" means to accord with; "rejoicing" means to feel joy. This refers to the period after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa:
hearing this sublime sūtra from a virtuous friend, one immediately gives rise to a mind of sympathetic joy, without any resistance or opposition, and does not harbor disparagement.

One should know that even a single phrase determines a profound understanding. To say that one hears the sūtra after the parinirvāṇa and gives rise to sympathetic joy is equivalent to hearing it in the present.
Sūtra: “Deep faith and the accomplishment of contemplation. This section merely indicates the characteristics of the person; it is only in the lower grade that the merits are compared.

Furthermore, the preceding section only clarifies the accomplishment of contemplation without any comparison; the lower grade compares the merit of sympathetic joy (*anumodana*), which is also a comparison of the merit of the characteristics of deep faith and understanding.
△ Second, adding one’s own upholding. This is divided into two parts. First, the illustration.
