If this is so for those who merely point to the marks of a person, how much more so for those who read, recite, accept, and uphold it? Such persons shall be considered as bearing the Tathāgata upon their heads.
This is said with sympathetic joy; how much more so for those who go forth to accept and uphold it! To "bear upon the head" means that this sutra is the Tathāgata.
The entire body. If one recites and upholds [this] with single-minded devotion, it carries the meaning of being borne upon the crown of the head. △ Second, the evaluation of its merit:
"Ajita, this good man... (up to)... having made such offerings for thousands of myriads of koṭis of kalpas."

There is no need to affix a label. The reason for this inquiry and explanation is as follows: the sutra is that which expresses, just as a stupa is that which contains; therefore, there is no need to construct a stupa of phenomenal characteristics.
True reality (*dharmatā*) is that which is expressed, which is the *śarīra* of the *dharmakāya*; therefore, there is no need to enshrine the *śarīra* of the physical body.
The text of the sutra can contain the Sangha of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). To recite and uphold it with single-minded devotion is itself an act of making offerings.
[Sangha]. Therefore, there is no need for offerings [to the Sangha] as a separate category. As for what is meant by "following along":
because from the Buddha comes the Dharma, and from the Dharma comes the Sangha, it is thus categorized as "lower.

This clarifies that while building stupas and making offerings to śarīra (relics) is meritorious, simply and exclusively upholding and reciting this sutra constitutes performing various kinds of offerings to śarīra throughout immeasurable kalpas. △ Third, adding others.
Receiving and Upholding. This is divided into two parts. First, the identification of the person:
"Ajita, if after my parinirvāṇa... [up to] ...whether they write it themselves or instruct others to write it."
Previously, he merely recited and upheld [the teachings] himself; now, furthermore, he teaches others to receive, uphold, copy, and transcribe them. △ Second, evaluating the merit:
this constitutes the act of erecting monasteries (up to) and constructing monasteries to make offerings to the assembly of monks.

This constitutes the lower [grade]. To clarify, instructing others to receive, uphold, copy, and transcribe [the scriptures] is equivalent to erecting monasteries and halls, and providing all manner of offerings to me and the Sangha.

Great Nirvāṇa serves as the meditation cave; patience serves as clothing; and the joy of the Dharma serves as food and drink. Therefore, the following section concludes by making this manifest.

How much more so for one who can uphold this sutra—[practicing] patience, diligence, single-mindedness, and wisdom.

Second, the measurement of its merit.
Its virtue is most supreme, immeasurable, and boundless (up to) swiftly reaching all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*).

First, the excellence of the virtue is indicated; next, the analogy; finally, the application. Within the empty space of the ten directions, there are three inconceivable things. The first is... [exceeding].
1. The inconceivability of the beginningless past; 2. The inconceivability of the vast present; 3. The inconceivability of the ultimate future.
"Swiftly reaching a single phrase" clarifies being close to the fruit of Buddhahood. △ Fifth, the complete practice of the six pāramitās, divided into two parts.
First, the presentation of the characteristics of the person.
If a person reads, recites, accepts, and upholds this sutra (up to: possesses keen faculties and wisdom to skillfully answer difficult questions.

Within this context, building stupas and making offerings, as well as preaching the Dharma for others, are the perfection of giving (*dāna-pāramitā*). △ Second, evaluating the merit.
Ajita, after my parinirvāṇa—[up to the point where it says]—all should make offerings to them as if they were the stūpas of a Buddha.
It was beneath a tree that the Tathāgata attained equal and perfect enlightenment; this was the awakening to this wondrous Dharma.

...is below that. Question: The ancients categorized five stages (*pañca-varga*). Why is it not so now? Answer: By practicing the six *pāramitās* concurrently, one swiftly reaches the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*).

If these merits are already attained, I do not yet understand what further practices the three worthies (*traya-ārya*) and ten sages (*daśa-ārya*) must cultivate, what further merits they must acquire, or upon what path they sit.

the intent is for people in the Final Age to propagate the sutra, regardless of whether they are sages or ordinary persons. How could this be restricted only to those of common rank?

The Eighteenth Chapter of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, "Merit of Rejoicing.
The merit of upholding the sūtra, as analyzed previously, is already most excellent, yet its ultimate limit has not been reached.

This chapter, by means of weighing the merit of rejoicing for even a single thought-moment, finally establishes the absolute standard. Furthermore, in the preceding chapters, one directly gives rise to rejoicing...
In the section on "Rejoicing" (*anumodana*), only the physical characteristics of the person were mentioned; it is only here that the merit is clarified.

If the merit of a single moment of rejoicing is already such, how much more so for those who receive, uphold, read, and recite [the sutra]? "Rejoicing" (*anu*) does not mean that the intention was premeditated;

rather, it refers to encountering [the teaching] unexpectedly, according to what one hears. "Rejoicing" (*modana*) does not refer merely to facial expression, but to the mind being delighted and sincerely submissive.
Furthermore, "merit" (gong) refers to the direction toward which practice tends; it is the merit of rejoicing in a single thought-moment.

"Virtue" (de) refers to that to which merit returns; it is the virtue of the karmic reward obtained through the merit of practicing rejoicing. This refers to the period after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa.
Suppose there is a person who happens to attend a Dharma assembly and hears someone preaching the Dharma. Upon entering the faculty of hearing, it meets with no resistance whatsoever;
they do not give rise to disparagement, but instead rejoice in their heart and experience joy. This is called "rejoicing for one's own benefit.
To rejoice according to what was heard and to joyfully explain it to others is called "rejoicing for the benefit of others. Furthermore, as for the eight classes of devas mentioned previously...
Seeing Śāriputra receive his prediction, they gave rise to a mind of sympathetic joy and immediately obtained their own predictions.

When the bodhisattvas emerging from the earth heard of the Tathāgata’s work of delivering sentient beings, they also gave rise to sympathetic joy and immediately received his entrustment; this was due to the Tathāgata’s preaching of the Dharma.
The excellence of form, mind, and action makes it easy to give rise to sympathetic joy (*anumodanā*).

Yet, after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, during the final five hundred years, although there may be those who preach the sūtras, their understanding and practice may not yet be in accord; or their mastery of the scriptures may still lack a foundation in antiquity.
Because people disparage the Dharma, they easily give rise to revilement; thus, sympathetic joy (*anumodanā*) is truly difficult to achieve.
This is why the merit of such sympathetic joy must necessarily be measured and compared. △ Second, the evaluation of the merit of sympathetic joy, divided into two parts. First, Maitreya’s inquiry.
At that time, Maitreya Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva (up to) spoke these verses:
“World-Honored One, after your parinirvāṇa, if there are those who hear this sutra and are able to rejoice in it, how much merit will they obtain?”
Maitreya’s intention was this: those who have previously upheld, recited, and fully practiced the six perfections already possess the aforementioned merits.

If, after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, one hears this sutra and gives rise to joyful faith and acceptance, such that its principles permeate the spirit, a celebration of dancing joy will arise spontaneously.
If even a single thought of sympathetic joy (*anumodanā*) possesses such merit, how much more so? Therefore, it is said: "How much [merit] shall they obtain?"
The Merit [Accrued]. △ Second, the Tathāgata’s response, which consists of both prose and verse. The prose section is divided into two parts:

first, clarifying the merit of one who can preach with sympathetic joy; second, clarifying the merit of listening to the Dharma and exhorting others. The first part is further divided into four sections;
the first is the successive teaching of one another.
At that time, the Buddha addressed Maitreya Bodhisattva... [up to] "...in this manner, passing on successively until the fiftieth person.
First, the fourfold assembly is designated; this internally includes humans and devas of the three vehicles who take refuge in the Triple Gem, as well as other wise ones."

These are people who have not yet taken refuge in the Triple Gem. They may be renowned worthies of the world, recluses of high standing, idle country folk, or followers of heterodox paths; thus they are called those of "residual wisdom.

Whether old or young, male or female, they may come to a Dharma assembly with purpose, or arrive at the lecture hall without intention, perhaps listening to a single chapter, a single section, or even a single phrase.
A single verse: because one directly gives rise to a heart of joyful appreciation, it says, "Having heard the sutra with sympathetic joy (*anumodanā*), they depart from the Dharma assembly.

The mention of encountering others along the way and transmitting [the teaching] according to one's capacity to expound it for others marks a humble and modest state, by which the solemnity and refinement of the Dharma assembly are contrasted.
The listeners being insincere contrasts with the sympathetic joy of profound faith. Regarding the Dharma...

When the assembly gathers, the place of discourse is radiant and solemn; the speaker presides over it with gravity, proclaiming the Dharma with the four analytical knowledges, both detailed and elegant.
The listeners regard it with sincerity, concentrating their single mind in careful examination, reflecting with precision.
Whether the location be as pristine as a secluded monastery or as humble as a village field, [the teaching remains the same].

Whether in capital cities or county towns, in flower-lined streets or willow-lined alleys, in villages or hamlets, or in vulgar and profane places—those who preach may be younger brothers, sons, or nephews, expounding according to their ability;
and those who listen may be parents or kinsmen, amidst the confusion of worldly affairs.
To compare the detailed texts of the Dharma assemblies with such refined contemplation is like the distance between clouds and the earth. These [people]...

"Persons, etc., passing on in turn until the fiftieth person": this indicates the second group who hear the sutra and transmit the teaching until the fiftieth generation, at which point the comparison is made.
"All these persons" refers to the aforementioned parents, kinsmen, and others.
"Having heard it, they rejoice" means that while in monasteries, fields, or other locations, they hear [the teaching] for the first time from...
Those who emerge from the Dharma assembly expound it according to their capacity; having heard it, they also rejoice in their hearts and joyfully explain it to others.
They further proceed to teach a third group of people. Having heard it, these other people also give rise to joy in their hearts and, in turn, teach four or five others.
Thus it is transmitted from one to another until it reaches twelve people.
Tenth: From the first person up to the final fiftieth person, among those who preach and listen— whether they be eminent monks or renowned scholars,
virtuous friends or good companions, or even young children and elderly folk, or ignorant men and women—
the places where this is transmitted may be tea houses or wine shops, inns or pleasure grounds, bean-shed stalls or vegetable gardens, forest paths or fishing boats.

In this manner, as it was transmitted from one to another, gradually spreading further and further until it reached the fiftieth person, the speaker became increasingly base and the setting increasingly vulgar;
the teaching became increasingly deviant and the listeners increasingly indifferent.

Yet even so, they still obtained such merit as described above—how much more so for those who were originally in the assembly of the Dharma, with their sincere and diligent devotion and their firm power of faith! How could the fiftieth person...?

How could ten people be spoken of as being on the same level? That one must take fifty as the standard for discussion is because, through a single thought of sympathetic joy, one’s mind is suddenly enlightened and brought into accord with the true nature (*dharmatā*), thereby severing the fifty kinds of evil within the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*).
△ Second, the citation of the comparative standard. This also has three parts: first, the admonition to listen and the permission for comparison; second, the citation of the recipient of the gift;
third, the citation of the donor. First, the admonition to listen and the permission for comparison.
Ajita, regarding this fiftieth son of good family (up to: I shall now speak of it; you should listen well.

Setting aside for a moment the question of how much merit you would obtain by rejoicing in a single thought, I shall now speak of the merit of the fiftieth person through successive transmission. Know the merit of these fifty persons.
By this virtue, one may know the merit of rejoicing for even a single thought-moment. △ Second, the recipients of the gift:
"If there were as many worlds as four million *asamkhyeya* worlds... [down to] ...those equal in number to all sentient beings."

Regarding the six destinies (*ṣadgati*): they are the paths toward which one proceeds according to the karma one has created. Those born from eggs arise solely through thought; those born from a womb are due to emotional attachment;

those born from moisture are produced by the convergence of conditions; and those born by transformation respond to the separation [of elements]. The *Abhidharmakośa* states: "Humans and animals possess all four modes of birth."

Beings in the hells and the heavens, as well as those in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), are born exclusively by transformation (*upapāduka*). Ghosts (*preta*) may be born either from a womb or by transformation.

[The phrase] "those with form" and so forth indicates the essential nature and the dwelling places of the four modes of birth (*yoni*): "having form" refers to the realms of desire and form; "lacking form" refers to the formless realm.
There is the sphere of infinite consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*), which possesses perception; and the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*), which lacks perception.

That which is neither existent nor non-existent refers to that which is not the existence of perception in the sphere of infinite consciousness, nor the absence of perception in the sphere of nothingness; this is precisely the fourth heaven of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
The *Erya* states: "Those with feet are called insects (*chóng*); those without feet are called *zhài*. [This applies to] those with two feet and those with four feet."
[The section on] "Many-footed" can be understood. △ Third, raising up the person who is able to give:
There is a person seeking merit who, according to their desires... (up to) all attain mastery and are endowed with the eight liberations.
"Someone descends" means that one gives whatever objects are desired by the various sentient beings above. "This is a great descent" refers to the time when one goes forth to practice giving.
"Forms this thought" refers to reflecting upon their old age and infirmity, and instructing them in the Buddha-dharma so that each may attain the fruits of the Path.
The *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra* states: "There are five superior benefits of the gift of Dharma (*dharmadāna*). First, the gift of Dharma..."

It benefits both oneself and others. Material giving is not like this. Second, the gift of Dharma can cause one to transcend the triple world, whereas material giving does not transcend the realm of desire.
Third, the gift of Dharma can purify the Dharma-body, whereas material giving only increases the physical body.

Fourth, the gift of Dharma is inexhaustible, whereas the gift of material wealth is finite. Fifth, the gift of Dharma can sever ignorance, whereas the gift of material wealth merely suppresses craving and attachment.
This concludes the section on the comparison of their fundamental natures. △ Third, the question-and-answer section clarifying their superiority.
What do you think? As for this great donor—let alone causing [beings] to attain the fruit of Arhatship—is that not a great deal?

That is to say, in as many world-systems as there are, with their differing customs and various sentient beings whose likes and dislikes vary, to practice extensive charity and provide relief to the masses is a matter of which even the Sages have found it difficult; this is truly a great [feat].
The donors practiced charity and distributed blessings, providing the necessities for both the physical body and the correct mind.
Their offerings were continuous and uninterrupted, never wearying or indolent even over many years. They ensured that all under heaven could thus achieve their livelihood.
Furthermore, they reflected that material giving benefits life but not death, and provides for the world but not for the Way; therefore, they also instructed them with the Dharma.
May all equally realize the four fruits of the path, so as to avoid the calamity of sinking into the depths of suffering.

If the restoration of human nature throughout the world were to be like this—truly a person who "suffers before the world suffers and rejoices after the world rejoices"—then by inferring the fruit from the cause, what kind of karmic retribution would such merit produce?
Maitreya’s intention was that it would be like [the resonance of] a drum struck by a small stick.
A single contact produces a deep impact and a resonant sound; when the mirror meets the pheasant, the form is exquisite and the image is beautiful.

Because that person’s roots are profound and their fruits are great, the response is like a shadow following a form or an echo following a sound. Their merit is immeasurable and boundless—how could it ever be fathomed?
Yet, even a gift for the mere sustenance of the body makes its virtue difficult to exhaust; how much more so when it benefits the Holy Path! △ Fourth, the formal comparison.
[Regarding] the measure:
The Buddha told Maitreya, "I now speak to you clearly... [up to] 'an *asaṃkhyeya* cannot be compared to it.
As for the phrase 'it is not like these,' this is a comparison based on quantity; it is like comparing a cartload of firewood to a single cun of gold—the difference between their value is vast."
When compared, even a city of jade would not be exchanged for a single cubit of white jade. Such acts of giving as these are not equal to hearing a single verse of this sutra.
They possess merit; I possess wisdom. They possess its outward power; I possess its true substance.

Even if one were to fill four hundred trillion worlds with all manner of rare treasures and bestow them as gifts, such giving remains within the realm of outflows (*āsrava*). Yet, a single moment of thought encompasses it all.
The profound faith and boundless sympathetic joy of the ten directions are limitless. If one examines their teaching, how could the partial fruit rival the perfect cause?
If one examines their practice, how could the provisional *pāramitās* compare to the ultimate *pāramitās*? If one examines their principle, gradual illumination is identical to sudden awakening.
If one examines their people, the coarse person is not as noble as the wondrous person. As for the gift of Dharma, it consists in expounding the twelve divisions of the scriptures.
To recite the sutras is easy; to expound the wondrous Dharma of the One Vehicle is difficult.

When discussing the gates of the Dharma, the Lesser Vehicle and the Great Vehicle are vastly distinct. By such comparison, the merit of that [former] act of giving is narrow and short, whereas the virtue of this rejoicing is vast and long.
How could its merit ever be known through calculation? Thus is the fifth.

If even ten people—let alone those who first rejoiced in the teaching—can obtain such merit when the characters have been transcribed three times over, turning "wu" (烏) into "an" (焉) and "an" into "ma" (馬);
how much more so for fifty people who heard it by the roadside or from hearsay!

Their location was humble, the speakers were lowly, the explanation was erroneous, the listeners were mistaken, their faith was shallow, and their understanding was fallacious; yet they still obtained such merit. How much more so for those at the very first assembly!
If one hears it directly from the midst [of the assembly], their merit is incomparably superior. How much more so for those who receive, uphold, read, and recite it, or explain it for others?
Their merit is even more vast and can never be exhausted. Section 12: Clarifying the Merit of Listening to the Dharma and Encouraging Others to Do So.
Divided into four parts. First: Going in person to listen to the sutras.
Furthermore, Ajita, if a person, for the sake of this sutra, [provides] precious carriages and celestial palaces;

or if, for the sake of this sutra, they go to a monastery and, with a profound and manifest reverence for the Way, sit or stand to listen and receive its teachings—this sincere heart of theirs is made manifest, and thus they shall attain the merit of self-enjoyment in their future births. [This applies even to those who provide] chariots, horses, and attendants.
As for those who ride upon them: there are elephant chariots for those of royal lineage, and celestial palaces for devas and humans.

Yet, because their listening to the sutra for even a brief moment differs—whether with single-minded devotion or a distracted mind—the resulting merit and retribution differ accordingly, manifesting as the distinctions between devas, humans, kings, and commoners. △ Second, sharing one's seat with others.

Furthermore, if there is a person who, at a place where the Dharma is being preached—or even at a place where a Wheel-Turning Sage King sits—urges others to sit and shares their seat with them, they will receive a retribution characterized by the distinction between the heavens and the human realm; this occurs within a single sitting.
The virtue of yielding and bowing in respectful greeting already moves the Heavenly Throne; how much more so the merit of establishing one’s seat and propagating the Sūtras?
△ Third, exhortation to go and listen to the Sūtra:
"Ajita, if there should be another person... [up to] ...who sees the Buddha, hears the Dharma, and faithfully accepts his instructions."

Furthermore, regarding those born in lower realms who receive the retribution of being born in a good place: if they join a companion to go and listen to the Dharma, even if they hear it for only a brief moment, the matter may be extremely subtle, yet its benefit is vast and great.
Their minds will merge in profound harmony with the sages, and their physical forms will dwell together with the Dharmakāya.

When both body and spirit are simultaneously exalted, the fruits of the Path can be known. According to the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra*, a Bodhisattva possessing sharp faculties who dwells in the fifth stage possesses dhāraṇī.
"Lower: Regarding the excellent retribution of the six sense faculties. To have speech that does not form sound and voices that do not emerge from the mouth is called being mute and dumb;
to be neither mute nor dumb means one's voice and sound are clear and penetrating. To be 'not foul-smelling' means one constantly emits fragrance.

To have a tongue 'without disease' means one's speech is agile and swift; it also means it is not crooked. 'Teeth not uneven' means they are white, pure, even, and closely set; they are likewise not uneven."
Firm and well-proportioned; the lips do not hang down, nor are they loose. They are neither retracted nor short. They are not coarse and so forth;
they are red and lustrous, free from disease, and without deficiency. The mouth is not distorted, nor is it crooked.
The nose is not flat, thin, or collapsed; nor is it sunken or crooked. The face is not uneven; the face is like—
This is the "Full Moon. Within this text, the merits of the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍindriya*) are fully present: sharp faculties and wisdom refer to the mental faculty (*manendriya*);

not being mute refers to the tongue faculty (*jihvendriya*); the nose being well-formed, high, and straight refers to the nose faculty (*ghrāṇendriya*); seeing the Buddha refers to the eye faculty (*cakṣurindriya*); hearing the Dharma refers to the ear faculty (*śrotrendriya*);
and all the rest pertain to the body faculty (*kāyendriya*). △ Fourth, possessing the practice of listening.
Ānanda, you should observe this... [down to] ...for the sake of others, distinguishing it and practicing according to what has been taught.
△ Second, the verse summary consists of eighteen lines, divided into two parts. First, nine lines praise the merit of rejoicing in those who can preach.
Second, nine lines praise the merit of listening to the Dharma and exhorting others. Within the first part, there are three sections. First, one and a half lines praise...
They taught it to one another in succession.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"If a person hears this sutra at a Dharma assembly (and so on) until reaching the fiftieth [person]."
△ Two and a half lines [of verse]. This verse presents the standard for comparison;
the merit obtained by the person at the end shall now be analyzed (extending to) the three knowledges and eight liberations.
The two lines concerning "not being firm" are as follows: it is said that this body is impermanent and lacks solidity;

it is a phenomenon that quickly decays. The body is like a mass of foam, which cannot be grasped; the body is like a bubble, which cannot endure for long; the body is like a mirage, born from thirst and craving.
△ Third, these two lines of verse serve as a formal comparison.
Finally, from the fiftieth [verse], "Hearing a Single Stanza with Rejoicing," down to "The First Hearing with Rejoicing.
Part Two: Nine lines. A verse on the merit of listening to the Dharma and exhorting others. Divided into four sections. First, five lines: a verse on exhorting others to go and listen to the sutras.
If there is anyone who exhorts another to lead them to listen to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, [the fragrance] shall constantly issue from their mouth.
Formerly, when King Aśoka invited the saṃgha into his palace for offerings, there was a bhikṣu named Utpala, from whose mouth the fragrance of utpala flowers issued forth.
The king, suspecting that the bhikṣu was young, wondered why he had such fragrance in his mouth. He immediately—
The King ordered him to wash with water. After he had washed, his fragrance was redoubled. The King asked, "How long have you possessed this fragrance? He replied, "No, it is not so.
In the past, during the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, when the human lifespan was twenty thousand years, I was a Dharma Master of the High Seat who praised and extolled the Buddha-dharma.
Consequently, for forty-nine billion years, I was born among humans and devas, and my mouth has emitted this fragrance. Upon hearing this, the King’s reverence increased all the more.
Now, he exhorts others to go and listen, and further praises this sutra as profound and subtle, stating that one obtains such retribution.
How inconceivable is the divine power of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*! △ Second, two lines: a verse on his own practice of listening to the sutra.
If one intentionally goes to a monastic dwelling desiring to hear the Lotus Sūtra—[up to] riding in celestial palaces.
△ Third, the section on sharing seats with others in one verse:

If, at a place where the Dharma is being preached, one exhorts others to sit and listen to the sūtra, by this causal condition of merit, one shall obtain the seat of Śakra, Brahmā, or a Cakravartin King.
△ Four: A single verse encompasses both listening and practice.
How much more so for one who listens with a single mind to the explanation of its meaning and practices according to what was taught; their merit is beyond measure.
The explanation of the merit of realization and understanding in the preceding two chapters is hereby concluded.
*The Lotus Sutra*, Chapter Nineteen: "The Merits of the Dharma-Preacher.
This chapter elucidates the dharma-preachers of the final age who possess the seeds of past causes within and rely upon the external熏習 (xūn xí, perfuming) of the Buddha-dharma.

Constantly persevering and single-mindedly courageous, one receives and upholds this sutra. When the essence of the teachings is realized and worldly attachments are forgotten, both the sense faculties (*indriya*) and their objects (*viṣaya*) are purified.

The wondrous capacity for the six faculties to function interchangeably arises from the storehouse nature (*ālaya-vijñāna-svabhāva*); thus it is said that "by these merits, the six faculties are adorned and all are rendered pure.
*Dharma* refers to the teaching, which carries the meaning of providing a standard and support; *śāstra* refers to a model or paradigm.
It takes the meaning of "molding and casting" as its principle: to govern oneself by the Dharma and Vinaya is to be one's own teacher;

to extend this to instruct others is to be a teacher of men. When these five kinds of merit are complete, it is called "merit. Within these five kinds of merit, when six thousand virtues are perfected, it is called "virtue.
In the preceding "Chapter on the Dharma Master," the perfect prediction was manifested based on the person who upholds the sutra; in this chapter, it is based on the Dharma itself.
This person thereby manifests perfect virtue. Since the names are identical but the meanings differ, the two characters "merit" (gōngdé) are added to distinguish them.
△ Second, explaining the purity of the faculties for one who upholds the sutra. This is divided into two parts. First, a general listing of the purification of the six faculties.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Constantly Diligent (up to the point where it says): "Adorning the six sense organs so that they are all rendered pure.
As for the merit of purifying the six sense organs, unless one possesses a refined mind free from distraction and advances upon the Path without weariness, it is not easily attained.
Therefore, Constantly Diligent is the appropriate recipient for this chapter. To receive and uphold [this teaching] means to maintain it with firm resolve.

[The text] is lost. To read it is to master the phrasing and contemplate its meaning; to recite it is to savor its flavor and nourish the spirit; to explain it is to transcend the literal expression and realize it for oneself;
to transcribe it is to preserve it upon bamboo and silk. These are the practices of the five kinds of Dharma masters. Below this, [the text] clarifies the merits obtained.
If one discusses the merits of the six sense faculties, summarizing them from beginning to end, each of the six faculties possesses its own specific merit.

One thousand two hundred. If one discusses the subtlety of their mutual functioning, then a single faculty can perform the functions of all faculties, and a single consciousness can perceive all objects.
Each of the six faculties is fully endowed with six thousand merits. This calculation is based on the conventional enumeration of the eyes and so forth as worldly phenomena;
therefore, there is an expansion or contraction to one thousand two hundred and eight. This is as when the eye perceives forms.
The rear is dark while the front is bright; the front side is entirely luminous while the rear side is entirely dark. When looking to the left or right, two-thirds of the field is encompassed.
In discussing the meritorious functions performed, three parts are accounted as merit and one part is devoid of virtue.

One should know that the eye possesses only eight hundred merits. As for the ear, it hears all around without omission in the ten directions; whether in motion, it perceives both the near and the far, and when at rest...
It is boundless. You should know that the faculty of the ear is complete with one thousand two hundred merits.

As for the nose smelling odors, it passes through the incoming and outgoing breaths; there is an outflow and an inflow, yet it lacks the middle junction. When verified against the faculty of the nose, it lacks one-third;
you should know that the nose possesses only eight hundred merits. As for the tongue proclaiming all worldly and world-transcending things...

Regarding the intervening wisdom, it is said that there are spatial divisions, yet its principle is inexhaustible. One should know that the tongue faculty is complete with one thousand two hundred merits.
Just as the body perceives touch and consciousness distinguishes between the adverse and the favorable—perceiving when in contact but not knowing when separated—so it is with the tongue.
Free from the duality of unity and combination, when examining the faculty of the body, three parts are missing; it constantly perceives the body as possessing only eight hundred merits.

Yet the faculty of the mind silently accommodates all mundane and supramundane phenomena throughout the ten directions and the three periods of time—whether sacred or profane—encompassing them all to their very limits.
You should know that the faculty of the mind is complete with one thousand two hundred merits.

Regarding the phrase "causing the hundred merits to be entirely pure": because the Dharma Master skillfully upholds this sutra and leads others through its exposition, realization, and penetration, all that is seen, heard, sensed, and known is nothing other than true awakening.
Having realized the various true marks (*dharmatā*), form, fragrance, taste, and touch are nothing other than the true Dharma;
therefore, they are called "pure. Since they are called pure, there is neither increase nor decrease, and the six sense faculties function interchangeably.
One attains great mastery; it is inconceivable. △ Second, the detailed explanation in six chapters. This is divided into six parts.
First, the merit of the eye-faculty. This has two sections. First, the prose exposition.
These good sons and good daughters [know and see] all places where the retribution of their fruits arises.
"Purity" refers to the mastery of mutual functioning. "Fleshly eyes" refers to the physical sense organs (*bu chen gen*): the eyes are like clusters of grapes;
the ears are like newly rolled leaves; the nose is like two hanging claws; the tongue is like a crescent moon just after it has been bent; the body is like...
The frontal part of the waist-drum [is shaped like a drum]. The intention is that it is as if seen in a dark chamber. The *Abhidharmakośa* states:

"The atoms of the eye-faculty (*cakṣur-indriya-paramāṇu*) reside upon the pupil, distributed laterally like crystal (*sphaṭika*). The atoms of the ear-faculty (*śrotrendriya-paramāṇu*) are within the ear-cavity, arranged in a spiral like a rolled birch-bark scroll.
The atoms of the nose-faculty (*ghrāṇendriya-paramāṇu*) are inside the nostrils, with their backs upward and their faces downward, like a pair of..."
The *nakhāgra* (claws) [are present]. The atoms (*paramāṇu*) of the tongue-faculty (*jihvendriya*) are distributed across the surface of the tongue; their shape is like that of a full moon.

The atoms of the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*) are omnipresent throughout the body, corresponding in measure to the dimensions of the physical form. As for the five external objects (*pañca-viṣaya*), they are perceived by the "floating faculties" (*bhautika-indriya*), which assist the pure faculties (*viśuddhendriya*) in illuminating their respective objects.

The self-substance [of the floating faculties] cannot illuminate [the objects] itself, because these floating faculties are coarse, manifest matter (*rūpa*) that serves as the support (*āśraya*) for the pure faculties. This...
The "intermediate purity" is also what is called the *paramārtha-indriya* (ultimate sense-faculty). The "floating dust" mental faculty (*manas*) is the physical heart-mass;
it initially absorbs and adheres to this intermediate state, thereby rushing toward phenomena. "Seeing" refers to the seeing-division (*darśana-bhāga*), such as mountains, rivers, and so forth.

This refers to the perceived objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*). Regarding the "three thousandfold" and so forth: one sun and moon, one Mount Sumeru, the six heavens of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), and the first dhyāna heaven constitute a single world-system.
This is surrounded on the outside by a single iron mountain range.

When such systems are multiplied a thousand times, and above them are covered by the second dhyāna heavens, surrounded on the outside by a smaller iron mountain range, it is called a "small thousandfold" (*sāhasra-cūḍika-lokadhātu*). Increasing this small thousandfold a thousand times [results in a medium thousandfold].
This constitutes a medium chiliocosm, consisting of one million suns and moons and so forth, one thousand second-dhyāna heavens, and one third-dhyāna heaven covering them from above,
all surrounded externally by a ring of iron mountains. One thousand such medium chiliocosms together form a great trichiliocosm,
consisting of ten billion suns and moons and so forth, ten billion second-dhyāna heavens, one thousand third-dhyāna heavens, and one fourth-dhyāna heaven covering them from above, with an external...
A great iron wall encircles it; this is collectively termed the trichiliocosm.
Regarding karmic conditions and retribution—namely, the conditions of good and evil karma and the resulting experiences of favorable or unfavorable rewards—the following verse provides a summary.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"If, in the midst of the great assembly, with a mind free from fear... [the power of the fleshly eye is thus]."
Mount Meru—here translated as "Mountain of Radiance"—is so named because of its golden light; it is the same as the Seven Golden Mountains.
What is seen with the fleshly eye does not extend far, yet the celestial faculty perceives both the interior and exterior of the great trichiliocosm.
Now, by the power of this sutra, there arises the function of superior faculties; that is, the fleshly eye performs the work of the divine eye. Within this text, the five eyes are fully described.
To see the great trichiliocosm is the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*). To see the karmic retributions of sentient beings is the dharma-eye (*dharmacakṣus*).

That these eyes are pure is the wisdom-eye (*prajñācakṣus*). To see all things completely is the buddha-eye (*buddhacakṣus*). Among these, that which is born of one's parents—what each person inherently possesses—is the pure fleshly eye (*māṃsacakṣus*).
That this eye is not obstructed by the various defilements means that right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*) manifests before it. When there is no obstruction, right knowledge is present.
Therefore, all forms and images within and without the great trichiliocosm are fully known and fully seen. That is to say, when it accords with the eye, it is like a thousand suns;
the myriad phenomena cannot escape their shadows and essences. Question: The principle is indeed so. But what of the facts?

Answer: The six sense faculties are profoundly still, perfectly luminous, and constitute one's original merit. Such is the nature of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*); it simply varies according to what has been realized.
Thus, a Lesser Arhat perceives a small chiliocosm; a Great Arhat perceives a great trichiliocosm; a Pratyekabuddha perceives a hundred Buddha-fields; a Bodhisattva perceives a thousand Buddha-fields;
and a Tathāgata perceives as many worlds as there are atoms in a world-system. This is not limited solely to the essence of the fruit of fruition. Nārada [does not perceive it alone].
Having detached from the physical body born of one's parents, one contemplates the great trichiliocosm as if it were a fruit in the palm of one’s hand; then, what within it would not be seen?
For when the dust of delusion is cleared away and awareness is purified, the profound and the distant become one. How could it be that the principle is thus while the phenomenon is otherwise?

Question: What does it mean for the faculty of the nose to be "unimpaired" and "non-erroneous"? Answer: When ordinary people encounter various odors, whether fragrant or foul, that touch the nose, they cannot help but perceive them;
this is the meaning of being "impaired. To be unable to distinguish between fragrance and foulness is the meaning of being "erroneous. In this present practice, however, [it is otherwise].
People from afar can smell the fragrances of the three thousandfold world-system as if they were at the tip of their noses;

yet these do not touch the nose to produce olfactory sensation—this is the meaning of non-destruction. Furthermore, they distinguish between far and near with perfect clarity—this is the meaning of non-error.
Moreover, if one wishes to smell, one smells immediately; if one wishes not to smell, one does not smell immediately. Although the fragrance does not touch the nose, it is nonetheless not obscure.

In the Western Regions, the year is divided into three seasons: the rainy season, the hot season, and the cold season; each consists of four months, which corresponds to the concept of one season here [in China].

This is not restricted; it is discourse that accords with the nature of reality (*dharmatā*). How could it be limited to a single season or a single year?

It is that which, by dissecting a single atom of a scripture, can inscribe the events of three thousandfold world-systems, and by expounding the meaning of a single character, exhausts even the ink of the oceans. It does not deviate from the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).
All are in accord with the True Dharma. The myriad dharmas are but mind; when realized through true wisdom, there is nothing that is not the True Dharma.

his mouth proclaimed the teaching of non-contempt; and people gave him the title "Non-Contemptuous. For these reasons, he is named Ever-Venerable. That is to say:

They all snapped their fingers together;
this was the fourth supernatural power (*ṛddhi*). To snap the fingers signifies rejoicing (*anumodana*). Through this rejoicing, they attained the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*) and realized understanding.

The Bodhisattvas uphold the Great Dharma of True Purity and shall in the future obtain the unsurpassed treasure of the Dharma. This single snap of the fingers penetrates both horizontally and vertically.
"Universally. △ "The fifty directions tremble.
These two sounds reach throughout the Buddha-worlds of the ten directions, and the earth in all of them shakes in six ways.

This is the fifth supernatural power. Regarding the "two sounds," they are the sounds of clearing one's throat and snapping the fingers. Regarding the "six movements," [they are as follows: opening... [text continues]
The assembly represents the sixfold breaking of the delusions of ignorance; now the main body of the teaching has concluded.

Furthermore, "movement" represents the great assembly of the Dharma-assembly, signifying the opening, revealing, awakening, and entering [of the truth], as well as the purification of the six sense faculties. 6. The Universal Vision Great Assembly.
The sentient beings therein—including devas, nāgas, yakṣas, and so forth—were all filled with great joy at having attained what they had never experienced before.
This was the sixth supernatural power. △ Seventh, the exhortation of the various devas.
Immediately, the various devas in the void (up to) shall also pay homage and make offerings to Śākyamuni Buddha.
This is the seventh supernatural power. △ Eighth, the taking refuge of sentient beings.
Those sentient beings, having heard the voice from the midst of space, [proceed] until they cry out, "Namo Śākyamuni Buddha.
This is the eighth supernormal power. △ Ninth: Offering Worship from Afar.
With various flowers, incense, necklaces, banners, and canopies (up to) completely covering all the Buddhas in this realm—this is the ninth supernatural power.
As for the transformation of various objects into canopies that cover the Buddhas: it is because the mind penetrates the transformations of dharmas, uniting all objects to form a single whole.
Question: After sentient beings witness the assembly and the devas proclaim their exhortations, they then take refuge and arouse [the aspiration for enlightenment].
[The assembly] makes offerings. How can these four [phenomena] be considered the supernatural power (*ṛddhi*) of the Tathāgata? Answer:

Were it not for the Tathāgata’s pervasive illumination by light, his shaking of the ten directions, and his stirring of the minds of sentient beings, how could those beings of the ten directions see and hear this assembly, take refuge, and present offerings? △ Ten Worlds Merge into One.
Thereupon, the worlds of the ten directions became unimpeded and pervasive, as if they were a single buddha-land;
this is the tenth supernatural power. To unify them into one means that emotional attachments are dissolved and principle is harmonized, merging all realms into a single whole.
Having reached this point in the assembly, this single scroll of the Great Sutra universally covers the world, penetrating from the highest to the lowest.
There is not even a hair’s breadth of concealment; therefore, the subsequent text earnestly praises it so that one may receive and uphold it with a single mind.
△ Third, the summary and exhortation to uphold, divided into three parts. First, the praise and entrustment.
At that time, the Buddha addressed Superior Conduct (Uttaragati) and the others, saying that even if one were to speak for an eon, the merits of expounding this sutra could not be fully exhausted.
As for his addressing Superior Conduct and the others, they are the great assembly of teachers who emerged from the earth;

each of the eighty thousand and so forth had their own original teacher as a Buddha, and each received the entrustment of their respective original master. Superior Conduct and the others were those who were converted during that original period.
As for the legitimate successor who shall transmit my Way, it must be one of my disciples; for there is no one other than a disciple with whom I can entrust this burden.
Furthermore, as for those such as Shangxing and the others, they are long-established scholars who have resided in this realm since ancient times;

for such supernatural power as that of the Tathāgata requires venerable elders to serve as witnesses. Moreover, when he previously summoned his original disciples, they emerged from the earth and first performed prostrations.
He offered praise to the two World-Honored Ones. Then, with four leaders joining their palms in greeting, he requested that the Original Teacher entrust them with the propagation of this sutra.
At that time, Maitreya led eight thousand bodhisattvas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges to resolve their doubts through inquiry.

Since the Tathāgata had not yet completed the entrustment, he proceeded to reveal his lifespan. Having reached this point, the formal presentation was concluded; furthermore, those who emerged from the earth made their vows.
Therefore, when the Tathāgata wishes to entrust [the teaching], he first addresses those such as Śūraṅgama.
Regarding "by means of this divine power," it encompasses all ten kinds. As for "this most magnificent divine power cannot exhaust the merit of this sutra":
all the profound and wondrous merits of the Tathāgata are fully concentrated in this sutra; therefore, they are inexhaustible. △ Second.
The essential summary and entrustment:
To speak briefly, all that the Tathāgata has [taught] up to this point is proclaimed and revealed within this sutra.
"Essential" refers to the comprehensive intent; while all speech is broad, if one takes the concise and speaks briefly, these four phrases suffice. As for "Dharma," it is...
The provisional and ultimate dharmas attained at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*) are such that the nature of sentient beings is fully endowed with the Tathāgata’s perfection.

Although there is a distinction between being entangled in afflictions and being free from them, the essence of this dharma is fundamentally true and pure; thus, "opening the Buddha’s knowledge and vision" refers to this.

As for "sovereign spiritual power," it is the manifestation in accordance with the nature of reality, establishing transformation through the three wheels and benefiting all things throughout the three periods of time. Emitting...
The manifestation of light as an auspicious omen, which startles and moves the hearts of sentient beings, is what is shown here as the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
As for the "secret and essential treasury," it refers to this very Dharma that cannot be [ordinarily] shown; it is the realm where all Buddhas dwell and the secret treasury of the three virtues.

"Long kept silent and not spoken" refers to this; "awakening to the Buddha’s knowledge and vision" means awakening to this. "The most profound matter" refers to that which is deep, firm, remote, and dark—such that no one can reach it.
"All that is done is always for a single purpose," which is solely the knowledge and vision of the One Buddha.
"To show and awaken sentient beings" and so forth, and "to cause them to enter the Buddha’s knowledge and vision," means to enter this. This is shown in this sutra.

"Speaking" refers to the summary of the merits of this sutra. Though they cannot be fully recounted, their essential pivot is captured in these four words alone, which are then bestowed upon [the recipient].
△ Third, the exhortation to uphold and the entrustment, which has two parts. First, the exhortation to uphold [the sutra] and erect stupas.
Therefore, after the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata, you all should construct stūpas at these sites and make offerings to them. As for "those who should be single-minded":
whether through hearing, reflection, or cultivation, they attain the path of the Buddha's teaching; like one parched with thirst longing for a drink, they have no other thoughts.
Regarding the locations where the sūtra resides, there are seven such places. Although there may be cities, mountains, or forests, [they must be] pure, whether inhabited by monastics or laypeople.
Although the types of impurities differ, the act of erecting a stūpa for offerings is one and the same. △ Second, explaining the intent behind erecting a stūpa:
Why is this so? One should know that this place is where all Buddhas have entered parinirvāṇa.
Stūpas should be erected at four locations. This site of practice (bodhimaṇḍa) is the locus of the Lord of the Dharma-body (dharmakāya).
The other three [locations] are as stated in the text. The merit of this sūtra is difficult to exhaust; its four essentials, summarized in brief, are all revealed within this sūtra.

Wherever this sūtra resides, one should erect a stūpa there. The places where a stūpa is erected are the four locations of the Āgamas; these four locations are precisely what this sūtra proclaims and reveals.

These are the four essential points of the teaching: "Dharmacakra-pravartana" (Turning the Wheel of the Dharma) explains the sovereign spiritual powers; "Parinirvāṇa" explains the secret and essential treasury.
These four essentials encompass the entirety of this sutra. II. The Verse Summary consists of sixteen lines, divided as follows:
Two. The first six lines are a verse summary of the preceding prose. The twenty lines clarify the merit of upholding the sutra. The first section is further divided into two parts.
The first three lines are a verse summary of the Buddha manifesting his supernatural powers.
At that time, the World-Honored One, reiterating this meaning, spoke in verse:
"The Buddhas, the saviors of the world, abide in great supernormal powers; [from] the earth, it shakes in six ways."
In this age of turbidity and evil, sentient beings are heavily defiled. [The Buddha] manifests his descent to maintain the worldly way and turn back the hearts of men;
therefore, he is called the Savior of the World. Regarding the ten kinds of supernatural powers, the latter five are not versified here because the former five are more closely related to the Buddha.
(Verse 23) Two lines verse the summary of the essentials and exhortation to uphold [the teaching].
Because they are able to uphold this sutra after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa... [up to] "its limit cannot be found.
The first two lines praise the upholding of the sutra; the next line reveals the merit of upholding the sutra as being boundless like space.
△ Twenty lines clarify the merit of upholding the sutra, divided into five parts. The first one and a half lines clarify the attainment of vision.
The Three Buddhas.
One who is able to uphold this sutra has already seen me (up to: "and has taught and transformed all bodhisattvas").

To see the Three Buddhas refers to the single assembly on Vulture Peak. Furthermore, "seeing them as equal" refers to [the four stages of] opening, showing, awakening, and entering; it is what the Buddha knows.
The Buddha beheld them and instructed the various bodhisattvas to preach this sutra. △ Second, two lines clarify the joy of all Buddhas:
"Those who are able to uphold this sutra bring joy to me and my emanations (until... and shall likewise cause them to attain joy."
This Way has been transmitted; it accords with the Buddha’s mind, and for this reason all rejoice. △ Third, one practice clarifies that the fruit of Buddhahood is near:
"The secret and essential Dharma attained by all Buddhas when sitting at the site of enlightenment—those who can uphold this sutra shall also attain it before long."
△ Fourth, the four sets of four lines clarify the attainment of great eloquence (*mahā-pratibhāna*).
One who is able to uphold this sutra [attains] the meaning of all dharmas (up to) ultimately abiding in the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*).

The four kinds of unimpeded knowledge (*pratisaṃvid*) are as stated in the text. "Like the wind in space": the wind is a metaphor for the teaching of the Dharma, and space is a metaphor for principle (*tattva*). The wind...
There is sound but no form; emptiness has a name but no characteristics. These are discourses that accord with the nature of reality (*dharmatā*): through words, one transcends words.
Like the wind moving through space, what further obstruction could there be? To manifest the principle through analogy and invocation is called "causes and conditions" (*hetu-pratyaya*).

When the textual threads interpenetrate subtly without losing their proper sequence, it is called "gradual succession" (*anupūrva*). This can shatter the beginningless deluded habits of sentient beings, just as the sun and moon can dispel darkness.
"Profound and dark. A single word entered his ears, and he silently received the prophetic prediction, saying: "In the end, you shall abide in the One Vehicle.
△ Five lines and a half: a summary of what should be upheld.
Therefore, those with wisdom who hear of these merits and benefits (up to) will certainly have no doubts.
△ The praise through supernatural power is concluded.
The Lotus Sutra, Chapter Twenty-two: Entrustment.

Because the Bodhisattvas who emerged from the earth previously made vows to propagate this sutra, and the Tathāgata’s supernatural power had already completed its praise, this chapter now involves the conferring of empowerment by touching their heads as an act of entrustment.
Regarding the term "entrustment" (*zhùlèi*): "entrust" (*zhù*) refers to what the Buddha has committed to them;

"burden" (*lèi*) means to trouble them with the task of proclaiming it. This signifies that he is entrusting this wondrous Dharma to you and burdening you with the duty of disseminating it in the final age.
An ancient virtuous master said: "If you were not such a person, naturally this calamity would not have come to afflict you.

This [term *zhù* (entrustment)] is named after the intent of the Buddha. Furthermore, "to entrust" (*zhù*) means to receive what is entrusted upon one's head; "to burden" (*lèi*) means to accept it with joy rather than weariness.
This is named after the reverent compliance of the Bodhisattvas. Moreover, "to entrust" refers to that which is entrusted by the golden mouth of the Tathāgata; "to burden" [refers to...]
This Bodhisattva accepts this with a willing heart and bears it upon his head. This name is derived from the combined discussion of its transmission and reception.

It is the earnest and ultimate entrustment of the Tathāgata, like a sovereign king’s charge of a minor son. Facing great crises and encountering upheavals, he shall not forget the bequeathed mandate of Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa;
he shall continue the past and open up the future. Whether people believe or do not believe, through skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*), he instructs, benefits, and gladdens them.
Thus the lineage of the Way is transmitted so that this culture shall not perish; even in the final age, there is known to be a place of refuge.

This is a manifestation of the compassion of all Buddhas. Because the patriarchs and ancestors did not fully comprehend it, the consequences reached their descendants, who have passed it down through successive generations;
hence it is called "entrustment. The words of the Sage remain undecaying even through the three calamities, like the *udumbara* flower reflecting the light of the seven suns.

And may [this teaching] ever flourish. I rely upon this entrustment. Question: Why is it that becoming a Buddha is called "receiving a prediction" (vyākaraṇa), while upholding the sutra is called "entrustment" (parindanā)?
Answer: This precisely reveals that while becoming a Buddha is difficult, being a Dharma Master who upholds the sutra is even more so.
Becoming a Buddha is like ascending to the rank of the Nine Palaces; being a Dharma Master is like the time of stabilizing the empire. For indeed...
To clear the land and open up territory requires immeasurable toil and hardship before the great enterprise can be accomplished;
thus we know that it is more difficult to act as a Dharma Master than to become a Buddha. To succeed to the rank of Dharma King is called "bestowing a prediction" (*vyākaraṇa*);

to command one to perform the duties of a Dharma Master is called "entrusting" (*parindanā*). Thus, the Tathāgata first bestowed the rank of Dharma King upon his disciples, and subsequently entrusted them with the office of Dharma Master.
The entrustment to the Bodhisattvas is such that what is expected from the Dharma Master is profound. Does one who occupies the position of a Dharma Master not surely regard themselves with gravity?
II. Entrusting the Transmission. This section is divided into two parts: 1. Entrusting and Transmitting; 2. The Assembly’s Joy.
The first part (Entrusting and Transmitting) is further divided into three: 1. The Tathāgata’s Entrustment; 2. The Bodhisattvas’ Acceptance; 3. The Conclusion and Dispersal.
The first section also has three parts. The first correctly clarifies the entrustment:
"At that time, Śākyamuni Buddha... [omitted] ...causing all sentient beings to hear and know it universally."
Regarding "arising from the Dharma-seat": it means arising from the ultimate emptiness (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*) to manifest the function of boundless great compassion.
Because he simultaneously strokes the crowns of all bodhisattvas with one hand, it is called "great supernormal power.

This stroking of the crowns is like a worldly father entrusting his son; it carries the meaning of patting the back to offer instruction. Thus, the Tathāgata entrusts the propagation of the sutra to the bodhisattvas.
"Entrustment. This means to exhort them to listen attentively so that they shall not forget or lose it; thus, he extends his hand and strokes their crowns.

The "immeasurable bodhisattvas" refers to the bodhisattvas who emerged from the earth in numbers equal to the atoms within a thousand worlds. When the Tathāgata bestows the Way to transform others, it is called the "hand of expedient wisdom" (*upāya-jñāna*);
when the bodhisattvas practice the Way for themselves and receive the Way, it is called the "crown of true wisdom" (*bhūta-jñāna*). By means of expedient...

The hand of wisdom touches the crown of the head of ultimate reality (*paramārtha-satya*), manifesting that the provisional (*upāya*) is identical to the real; thus, the provisional and the real are non-dual.
Furthermore, the "crown" signifies the highest meaning; when Buddhas transmit the Dharma to one another, they always touch the crown of the head in their entrustment.

Now, wishing to entrust the unsurpassed, wondrous Dharma, he touches the most honored crown of the head. As for "difficult to attain," in terms of cultivation, it refers to the practice refined over three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*.
Having disciplined the mind for a hundred kalpas, with respect to severance, the five abodes are thoroughly exhausted and the two deaths forever extinguished.
As for its dissemination and augmentation: by means of this sublime Dharma, it shall circulate in future ages and spread throughout the ten directions;

from now on, expanding from the narrow to the broad, it shall be equal to the dharma-realm without exception, flowing through kalpas as numerous as atoms without obstruction, so that all who see or hear it—
Together they ascend the hall of the elder; equally they obtain the pearl within the topknot. Each and every one is shown, awakened, entered, and realized.
"Samaya" indicates the earnestness and diligence of the entrustment. "Causing all" means that regardless of whether they are noble or lowly, everyone may universally see and hear it.
△ Second, the explanation of the intent of the entrustment.
Why is this? Because the Tathāgata possesses great compassion (up to) do not give rise to stinginess.
Why is it that he causes you all to widely proclaim this sutra so that all may see and hear it? It is because the Tathāgata is the great donor to sentient beings;
he is endowed with the three practices and can bestow the three types of wisdom upon sentient beings. You all should...
One should train accordingly in these three practices: first, the practice of great compassion, because it provides impartial relief and sustenance;

second, the practice of non-avarice, because it exhausts both internal and external wealth; third, the practice of fearlessness, because one does not shrink from toil or difficulty. By means of these three practices, [one should train].
It can bestow upon sentient beings the Buddha-wisdom because it is free from the views of the two vehicles; the Tathāgata-wisdom because it is free from the views of bodhisattvas;

and the spontaneous wisdom (*svayambhū-jñāna*) because it is free from all grasping at realization and is not awakened to through another. These three wisdoms are in fact only the single vehicle’s true wisdom;

they differ slightly only in accordance with their respective qualities and functions. The Buddha’s awakening comprehends all things and is utterly distinct from that of the two vehicles. That is to say:
"Omniscience" (*sarvajñatā*) is the title for the fruit of the Tathāgata; it distinguishes [this state] from the causal stage, namely the "knowledge of the paths" (*mārgajñatā*).
"Spontaneous" means knowing through effortless, natural operation—occurring as it is without contrivance, harmonizing with reality without error, like the moon reflected in a deep pool;
this is the "knowledge of all modes" (*sarvākārajñatā*). Furthermore, the practice of compassion is the "Tathāgata’s chamber"; freedom from stinginess is the "Tathāgata’s robe."
Fearlessness is the seat of the Tathāgata. Within the chamber, one can bestow the three wisdoms; the same applies to the robe and the seat.
Each of the three modes of practice possesses the three wisdoms, capable of bestowing upon sentient beings the function of the three wisdoms of the stage of fruition. Only then is one a great donor.
Since you have vowed to propagate this sutra, you should study the three practices of the Tathāgata. In the dregs of the final age, act accordingly to the present.
Regarding what you have seen and heard, you must propagate and disseminate it without giving rise to even a hair’s breadth of stinginess or parsimony.
△ Third, the exhortation to act as appropriate:
"In future ages, if there are good sons (up to) then one has already repaid the grace of all Buddhas."
If their faculties are deep-rooted and their wisdom sharp, one may speak directly of the Buddha’s wisdom.
However, if their faculties are inferior and they lack right faith, one should keep this wondrous Dharma secret and guide them through skillful means within other teachings.

Although the Buddha-wisdom of the One Vehicle is profound, while the provisional and gradual other teachings are also said to be profound, it is because all these dharmas ultimately constitute the Single Buddha Vehicle.
It may also be said that [the teaching] is profound. To point out what has been received is called "showing" (shì); to instruct and admonish is called "teaching" (jiào).

By causing others to obtain benefit and attain great joy, one should know that the Buddha’s grace is beyond repayment; only by proclaiming the Great Dharma and continuing the Buddha’s life of wisdom can it truly be called repaying the Buddha’s grace.
△ Second, the Bodhisattvas receive [the teaching].
At that time, the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas—[omitted]—replied, “So be it, World-Honored One; we pray you have no further concern.
Having heard the Buddha’s entrustment and attained their aspirations as they had wished, they were all filled with great joy and immeasurable exultation.

With the three karmas of body, speech, and mind in reverent sincerity, they looked up and expressed their gratitude to the Tathāgata. The Tathāgata entrusted them with this Dharma twice and thrice, saying, “Be careful with this Dharma! Thus did the bodhisattvas [respond].
They received and accepted it three times, reverently and respectfully putting it into practice. As for the phrase "may you have no concerns," it means:
"May the Tathāgata not harbor any anxieties regarding the future. Today we have received oral instructions face-to-face; we have personally heard this sutra and personally received its entrustment.
In future ages, we shall act according to the Buddha’s exhortations, teaching and transforming others in accordance with the Dharma, and practicing as it has been taught.
△ When the three matters were concluded, it was announced that the assembly was dismissed.
At that time, the stupa of the Buddha Prabhūtaratna returned to its former state.
Prabhūtaratna had come to bear witness to the entire sutra; he had manifested his divided body to open the jeweled stupa, having previously opened it.
Thereafter, the Tathāgata said: "This sutra has been entrusted to those who shall uphold it.

Now that the task of opening the stupa is complete and the entrustment is finished, I dispatch my emanations to return each to their own lands so that they may abide in peace wherever they go. Thus, the Great Dharma shall be transmitted."
Because the manifested body (*nirmāṇakāya*) ought to remain concealed, the subsequent teaching was not yet complete; it still required full realization.

Therefore, Prabhūtaratna was retained so that the great purport might be provisionally fulfilled, for the profound principle had not yet been exhausted. Furthermore, "as before" means that what was previously opened is now closed.
Hereafter, the Tathāgata emerges from the stupa and, together with the great assembly, returns to Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa to once again preach the latter six chapters of the sūtra. Its...
The actual circulation [of the teaching] is thus established. The first two chapters are now concluded.
The following six chapters do nothing more than exhort those who have newly attained realization in this assembly, so as to strengthen their vows and aspirations. II. The Assembly Rejoices.
When these words were spoken, immeasurable beings throughout the ten directions (up to and including those who heard what the Buddha taught) all rejoiced greatly.
The Buddhas rejoiced because the task of transforming others was accomplished; the Bodhisattvas rejoiced because they attained the Dharma through their own practice;

the Śrāvakas rejoiced because they received the prediction of attaining Buddhahood; and the eight classes of beings rejoiced because they all equally obtained extensive predictions. Thus, [the Buddha] entrusted [the teaching].
The oral transmission has been completed.
This is the twenty-third chapter of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, titled "The Past Deeds of Bhaiṣajyarāja Bodhisattva.

This chapter reveals that one should practice with diligent austerity for the sake of the Dharma, propagating this Way by exhausting all of one's supernatural powers and the entirety of one's physical life.
With profound and sincere devotion, his resolve remained undiminished; thus, he established his name based on the past lives of a Bodhisattva. As the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states:

"Since beginningless kalpas, I have been a skilled physician for the world. With my own mouth, I have tasted the herbs, trees, metals, and stones of this Sahā world, numbering one hundred and eight thousand in all.
In this way, I thoroughly know their bitterness, sourness, saltiness, and sweetness."
Whether tastes are sweet or pungent, cold or hot, poisonous or non-poisonous, he is able to know them all thoroughly.

He understands the nature of taste as being neither empty nor existent, neither identical to the body and mind, nor separate from the body and mind. By discerning the causes of taste, he attains awakening;
the Tathāgata bestows upon him the name Bhaiṣajyarāja. The *Sukhāvatīvyūha-sūtra* states: "Formerly his name was Jyotirasa; from the Venerable Sūrya..."
The Bodhisattva Śāntamati heard of the Buddha’s wisdom and offered medicinal herbs from the Snowy Mountains to the assembly of monks, vowing:
"In the future, may I be able to cure the dual ailments of body and mind for all sentient beings. The entire world rejoiced, and he was named Bhaiṣajyarāja (Medicine King).

Because this bodhisattva thoroughly understands the nature of medicines, he is able to observe the capacities of beings and provide appropriate teachings, administering medicine according to their specific illnesses. [He heals] the bodies of all sentient beings...
The two diseases of the mind are purified and exhausted without remainder. Among all phenomena, one realizes their intrinsic nature and attains great mastery;

therefore, he is named Bhaiṣajyarāja (Medicine King). As for "Bodhisattva," it refers to the simultaneous application of compassion and wisdom, cultivating both self-benefit and the benefit of others.
Regarding "Past Deeds" (*pūrvayoga*), this means events from former times. The following text clarifies how the Bodhisattva Sarvasattvapriyadarśana suddenly renounced [his life].

One body. Furthermore, he burned both arms. He regarded his life lightly and the Dharma as weighty; though his life ended, the Way remained. To illustrate the origin of this event, it is called the "Chapter on Past Deeds.
△ Third, the Austerities of Bhaiṣajyarāja, divided into four parts: First, the Inquiry of Rājanakṣatra; Second, the Response of the Tathāgata;
Third, the Benefits of Hearing This Chapter; Fourth, the Praise of Prabhūtaratna. Regarding the first part, there are further three sections. First, the general [introduction].
Questioning on the Wandering Transformation:
At that time, the Bodhisattva Constellation King Flower (to: how he wanders in the Sahā world).
This chapter clarifies the past ascetic practices of Bhaiṣajyarāja; it does not concern his past mastery. It concerns one who has long practiced the path of causes and conditions.
It cannot be brought forth. Furthermore, as for the previous instance where the Medicine King addressed eighty thousand [bodhisattvas], how could this have occurred without cause?

Therefore, Nakṣatrarājasaṃkusumitābhijña raised the matter and questioned him. Since the bodhisattva already knew the nature of medicines and could universally treat all ailments, [he was thus able to do so].
In all places where there is benefit, how should a bodhisattva travel and transform beings? △ Second, the specific inquiry regarding ascetic practices:
"World-Honored One, this Medicine King Bodhisattva [performed] nayuta difficult ascetic practices."
Although ascetic practices are many, the most difficult to perform is only the relinquishing of the body. △ Third, the request for an answer and the rejoicing:
"Excellent, World-Honored One! We pray that you will briefly explain this" (up to) "...and when the assembly of śrāvakas hears it, they all rejoice."

The ascetic practices of the Bodhisattvas are manifold; I wish to briefly describe one or two matters from among them. The eight classes of beings receive predictions; they vow to propagate the sutra in other lands. The Śrāvakas receive their predictions and give rise to the aspiration for joy; therefore, upon hearing this, all rejoice. It does not mention those who emerge from the earth, for those transformed by the latter part of the teaching are already known and need not be mentioned. As for Avalokiteśvara and Mañjuśrī: I pay homage to the Great Sage of the Lotus Flower, Whose body is like a mountain of gold, Whose countenance is as radiant as the full moon, Whose voice is like the sound of thunder, Whose tongue is broad and long, Whose eyes are like blue lotuses, Whose eyebrows are like a drawn bow, Whose nose is like a hooked jade, Whose ears are like hanging jewels, Whose forehead is like a full moon, Whose head is like a stupa, Whose crown protrusion is like Mount Sumeru, Whose neck is like a conch shell, Whose shoulders are like those of a lion, Whose arms are like
