To dig into the earth and take its soil, or to entomb the entire body in a pit—is this truly tolerable? Both of these methods arise only from necessity.
When a person of great realization contemplates them, they see that both ultimately return to extinction; thus, it is acceptable to bury the remains, or acceptable to leave them exposed.
Whether they are cast away in a ditch or placed within a stone sarcophagus, there is nothing that would not be permissible. Only after the *śarīra* have been collected should a stupa be erected.
“Adorned offerings reaching the height of the three worlds” refers to the trichiliocosm. The small chiliocosm covers the first dhyāna;
the middle chiliocosm covers the second dhyāna; and the great chiliocosm covers the third dhyāna. As for “reaching the height,” it extends to the fourth dhyāna heaven.
△ Second, the offering of burning one’s arm.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Sarvasattvapriyadarśana made offerings for seventy-two thousand years.
To the entire assembly—that is, the assembly entrusted by the Buddha—he said: "You all, in every single word, must be cautioned against distraction."

Regarding the phrase "the arms [endowed with] a hundred blessings," this refers to what is brought forth by various causal practices. As for the "seventy thousand" and so on, these refer to the duration of time during which the arms were burned.
Question: There are eighty-four thousand stupas, and it is certain that they are located in more than one place. How can a single body, by burning its own arms, provide offerings to them all?

Answer: The Bodhisattva has realized the true nature (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena. He makes offerings in accordance with this principle, without destroying the single characteristic (*ekalakṣaṇa*). Thus, he is able to offer universally.
Thus, they were universally offered without exception. Question: Burning the body lasts only for twelve hundred years; why does burning an arm last for seventy-two thousand years? Answer:
The former refers to one's own practice, wherein the body is exhausted and enters extinction; the latter is for the sake of propagating the Dharma.
To cause sentient beings to obtain benefit, the time spent burning the body was short while the time spent burning the arm was long.

Furthermore, the former [act] symbolized the destruction of the two attachments to self and phenomena within the six consciousnesses; the present [act] symbolizes the destruction of the two attachments to self and phenomena within the seventh consciousness.
△ Third, the assembly obtains benefit at that time.
He caused countless seekers of the śrāvaka vehicle (up to all of them) to attain and abide in the Samādhi of Manifesting All Physical Forms.
As for those who had resolved their minds on Bodhicitta, he did not allow this assembly to dwell in the fruits of the Lesser Vehicle.
That they all attained abiding in this samādhi was because he used what he himself had realized to realize it for others. That Buddha then entrusted the great assembly to him.
How could this be in vain? That the Bodhisattva has truly carried on and fulfilled his legacy is indeed beyond doubt. △ Fourth, the restoration of the burnt arm.
At that time, the various bodhisattvas, devas, humans, asuras, and so forth (until) all humans and devas attained what they had never experienced before.
The great assembly was filled with grief and distress, all saying, "The Great Being is the one upon whom the Buddha-dharma relies.

Now that both his arms are gone, his physical form and spirit will soon perish; what can be done? Because of this sorrow, it is because the bodhisattva at the initial stage of practice has not yet forgotten attachment and views.
As for the fact that *Priyadarśana* made a vow and had his arms restored, it is because he realized that objects are nothing but mind and that things revolve according to the mind. However—
The restoration of the arms is brought about by the mind. That one can skillfully subdue and endure insults, and that the entire body is restored—all these are based on this same principle.

Question: When the two arms are restored, do the two attachments arise again? Answer: Previously, the two attachments were destroyed; here, it is manifested that the principle of the two emptinesses has been realized.
"By means of such things" refers to the burning of the body and its subsequent regeneration, as well as the restoration of the arms after they had been severed—remaining in a state of non-abiding.
These causes are in accordance with his nature, being pure and profound; they all arise from the power of his merit, utmost sincerity, and the subtlety of his wisdom and supernatural powers.
This is not for the sake of seeking novelty or deluding the masses today. Having thus concluded the section on manifesting rare wonders, the extensive cultivation of offerings is finished.
△ Third, the conclusion correlating the ancient and the present.
The Buddha told the Bodhisattva宿王華 (Sudāṣa): [This continues] up to "hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas.
This refers to one instance of sacrificing the body among the various ascetic practices mentioned in the preceding summary.

The formal response regarding the ascetic practices has now concluded. △ Second, praising the profound merit of the sutra, divided into three parts. First, explaining the comparison with making offerings.

[This section] has three parts: first, the praise [of the teaching]; second, the praise of the sūtra-dharma that is upheld; and third, the clarification of the merit of upholding the sūtra. The first part [the praise] further has two sections.

First, the manifestation of excellence through offerings to the stūpa: "O Nakṣatrarājasaṃkusumitābhijña, if there should be anyone who resolves their mind... [and] offers all kinds of rare treasures as an offering..."
Now, a finger has three joints; thus, "burning one finger" means burning all three joints. To be able to burn a finger means to burn one joint.
I, the fool, say that whether it be a single finger of the hand or a single toe of the foot, there is nothing that would not be acceptable.
The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* says: "After my parinirvāṇa, if there be bhikṣus who light a single lamp on their bodies, burn a finger joint, or..."

Upon the body, one burns a single incense stick. I say that such a person, having at once repaid their karmic debts from beginningless time, takes a final farewell to the world and is forever liberated from all outflows (*āsrava*). Herein, the fingers and toes are all parts of the body;
they symbolize that the practitioner is unable to sever the two attachments—the mental factors (*caitta*) such as greed and hatred that correspond within the sixth and seventh consciousnesses.
As one abandons each part, one attains a corresponding portion of ultimate truth. One's fingers are the internal body; one's wife and children are the external body;
and kingdoms, cities, and so forth are the remaining possessions external to the body.

Because there is a difference in merit and virtue based on whether something is internal (valued more) or external (valued less), offering one's finger as an act of worship is superior to offering various precious treasures external to the body. 2. Manifesting Superiority by Offering to Persons.
Furthermore, if there were someone who, with the seven treasures—or even as little as a single four-line verse—were to generate the greatest merit;
the offering of the seven treasures throughout the three-thousandfold world system to the four types of noble ones would not equal that of one who upholds a single verse of this sutra.

This is comparing material wealth to the Dharma. For the Dharma is the noble teacher: it can give birth, it can nourish, it can bring fulfillment, and it can bring glory. One should resolve their mind to receive it.

To uphold this sutra is to take the Dharma as one's life; to practice and advance in accordance with the Dharma from beginning to end is its nourishment; to bring it to fulfillment in the ultimate fruit is its completion;

and to be able to respond appropriately to the capacities of all beings is its glory. Although these four aspects differ, they take the Dharma as their water—just as parents must protect their child through these four means.
As for the "four-line verse," the prose version is called the *Sankusumita-gāthā* (Scattered Flower Verse).
Verses consisting of four or five lines and so forth are called *gāthā* (linked verses). As for the phrase "a single four-line [verse]," this refers to using a small number to illustrate a large one.
II. Praising the Dharma that is upheld, divided into two parts: first, praising the essence of the Dharma; second, praising the function of the Dharma.
The first part is further subdivided into eleven sections. The first is the analogy of the depth and shallowness of rivers and oceans.
O Śrīgarbharāja, it is like this: for example, among all flowing streams (up to) the sūtras spoken [in this assembly], this is the most profound and vast.

The four waters—the streams, rivers, and so forth—metaphorically represent the preceding four teachings; the ocean represents the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*. The four waters are narrow and shallow, while the great ocean is vast and expansive.
This metaphor illustrates that the four teachings are not universal, whereas the Great Dharma encompasses all perfectly; therefore, it is the most profound and vast. Thus it is said.
Exhausting the fundamental source constitutes its profundity; encompassing all things constitutes its greatness. If one were to discuss it separately, the river water alone is clear;

drawing from the cold springs of the four valleys, its shallow source quenches thirst. It accomplishes divine merit throughout the six realms of existence. This serves as a metaphor for the partial emptiness of the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna), which clarifies the true principle of the Four Noble Truths.
With inferior aspirations focused on self-benefit, one attains the wondrous application of the Six Supernatural Powers. Thus flows the Water.
Far-reaching, it serves as the essential ford for traversing the ten directions; a conduit for coming and going, it rescues all things from their withered lack.
It is like the Mahāyāna of the Initial Teaching, the primary gateway for practicing the Ten Perfections. Bringing benefit to both self and others, it gathers the adornments of myriad virtues.
Like the waters of the Yangtze River flowing into a lake, it blends the Jing and Wei rivers into a single flavor; like a river current entering a harbor, it ferries people’s boats across.

Reaching the shore is a metaphor for the Final Teaching (Jōgyō) returning to the Middle Way, manifesting the essence and function of the One Mind. The waves of wisdom enter the mundane world, sweeping away the dual emptiness of self and dharmas.
The river’s single current connects with the high-flowing waters at the edge of the heavens; its source flows from ten thousand valleys, traversing the journey between north and south.
This is a metaphor for the Sudden Teaching (Tongyō) of the One Vehicle (Ichijō), which awakens one to the true principle of the Dharmakāya. The mind is empty of the myriad...
The conditions: it liberates one from the delusions of the sense organs and their objects. Like the vast and deep waters of the ocean, which receive the hundred rivers and share a single flavor;

like a source of profound magnitude, which accommodates ten thousand streams as they flow toward the central sea—this serves as a metaphor for the profound *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, which encompasses the four teachings and unifies them within the Perfect.
The wondrous principle is vast and great; it unifies the three vehicles and returns them to the One. Therefore, it is said to be the most profound and great.
△ Second, the analogy of the high and low mountain ranges:
"Furthermore, like the Earth Mountains and the Black Mountains... (up to) it is the most supreme among all sutras."

The "Earth Mountains" (tǔshān) refer to mountains composed of earth and stone. Regarding the "Black Mountains" (hēishān), the *Abhidharmakośa* states that from the center of Jambudvīpa toward the north, there are three successive ranges of Black Mountains.
The "Small Iron Encircling Mountains" (xiǎo tiěwéi) surround the small chiliocosm. As for the "Great Iron Encircling Mountains" (dà tiěwéi):
It encircles the great trichiliocosm. Regarding the ten mountains of jewels, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states:

the Snowy Mountain (*Himavat*), the Fragrant Mountain (*Gandhamādana*), Mount Kailāsa, the Mountain of Seers and Sages (*Ṛṣigiri*), Mount Gandhamādana, Mount Aśvakarṇa, Mount Nimindhara, Mount Cakravāḍa, Mount Pūrva-videha, and Mount Sumeru.
These are the ten jewel mountains, formed by the accumulation of earth and soil; though the Iron Ring Mountains (*Cakravāḍa*) are high, they are not composed of gold.

Mount Sumeru is formed from the four precious substances as its essence; it sits as a guardian over the four continents, its base revolving within the fragrant ocean and its summit providing a dwelling for the various heavens.
It stands preeminent as the king of all mountains. All other teachings are like the surrounding peaks, while the One Vehicle stands towering alongside Mount Sumeru.
△ The Simile of the Moon’s Radiance Among the Stars.
Furthermore, just as among all the stars the Moon Deity (Candradeva) [is supreme]... [it is] the most illuminating among all the dharmas of the various sūtras.
Both the stars and the moon are composed of lunar essence (*soma*) and both appear at night; yet, in the light of a clear night, the stars cannot equal the moon. This is the simile.

The preceding teachings were scriptures that illuminated the world; they were provisional and did not reach the ultimate reality. The two characters "illumination" (*zhào míng*) are employed as a metaphor:
when a great treasure lies in darkness, no lamp can illuminate it unless it is used. The true reality (*dharmatā*) of the One Vehicle is hidden within the *ālayavijñāna*;
without this present sutra to reveal and demonstrate it, sentient beings' Buddha-knowledge and Buddha-vision would remain unclear. Therefore, this sutra is the supreme illumination. △
The metaphor of the four suns dispelling darkness is as follows:
Just as the Sun Deity is able to remove all obscurity, so too can it destroy the darkness of all unwholesome states.
When the sun reaches the meridian, the dark alleys are suddenly illuminated; when this sutra enters the ear, the veils of ignorance are secretly dissolved. By means of this sutra...
It clarifies the true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) of the One Vehicle, for it is able to shatter the darkness of all sentient beings' unwholesome delusions.
△ Fifth, the analogy of the relative rank of royal positions:
Furthermore, just as among all minor kings, the Wheel-Turning Sage King (up to... is the most honored among all [other] kings, so too is this [sūtra] the most honored among all sūtras.
A minor king is honored as the sovereign of a single nation; a Golden Wheel-turning King is the lord who presides over the four continents.

The scriptures of the Three Vehicles each emphasize a particular school, whereas the discourse of the One Vehicle perfectly unifies their essential tenets. Thus, the distinction between the noble and the humble is clearly manifest.
△ Sixth, the Parable of the Superiority and Inferiority of Heavenly Kings.
Furthermore, it is like Śakra, who is the king among the gods of the Thirty-three Heavens (up to) the king among all sūtras.
Śakra is the sovereign of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, while the host of devas serve as his assistants and companions.

This is a metaphor for how the various sūtras constitute the source of the provisional teachings, whereas this scripture embodies the purport of the ultimate teaching. △ Seventh, the analogy of the ordinary and the holy as father.
Furthermore, it is like the Great Brahmā King (up to) being the father of those who have resolved their minds toward Bodhisattvahood.

The Brahmā King presides over the trichiliocosm and serves as the father of the six realms of existence. This sutra elucidates the principle of the One Vehicle and is thus the father of the Three Vehicles.
△ Eighth, the analogy explained by way of the noble ones.
Furthermore, just as [he is] the foremost among all ordinary persons (pṛthagjana) up to the most supreme among all the dharmas of the sūtras;

so too does the Pratyekabuddha transcend the multitude of the seven stages of the virtuous (saptakalyāṇaka), uproot the assembly of the four fruits and four paths, and alone manifests the solitary practice of seclusion of a Pratyekabuddha.
He also attains nirvāṇa and further erodes the residual habitual tendencies (vāsanā); therefore, he is the foremost, and this serves as a metaphor for this.

The Sūtra contains only the Single Buddha Vehicle, which directly transcends and enters [enlightenment] in one leap; it is the scripture for transmitting the Mind, its principle surpassing all other teachings, and is therefore called "the foremost.
△ Ninth: The Parable of the Sublime Dharma and the Honored Person.
Those who are able to receive and uphold this sutra (up to) shall also be the foremost among all sentient beings.
Because the Dharma is sublime, they are foremost; because these people propagate the sublime Dharma, they are foremost among all multitudes.
△ The tenth section: The Analogy of the Great and Small Vehicles.
Among all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas (up to) among all the dharmas of the various sūtras, [the Bodhisattva] is the most supreme.
The śrāvaka is like a small herb; the bodhisattva is like a great tree. The timber of a great tree cannot be compared to medicinal herbs.
△ 11. The Parable of the Buddha’s Sole Uniqueness and Supremacy.
Just as the Buddha is the sovereign king of all dharmas, so too is this sutra the king among all sutras.
The Tathāgata is one who has reached the ultimate fruit; he cannot be compared to those on the path of cause.
Because he has attained great mastery over all dharmas, this sutra stands at the pinnacle of the Three Vehicles and governs the principles of all teachings. There is no cause [that can surpass it].

[The term] "gathers" [means that] there is nothing that does not subsume within its fruit; this is the king among the definitive meanings of all sutras. The above has praised the essence of the Wondrous Dharma;
according to capacities and in whatever place it resides, it is most honored and most supreme. △ Second, praising the function of the Dharma, which is further divided into three parts.
First, praising the function of uprooting suffering.
Śrīgarbharāja, this sutra can save all sentient beings (up to) liberating them from all suffering and affliction.

Because this sutra can cause the sentient beings of the nine realms to leave behind the suffering and affliction of the two kinds of birth-and-death—namely, the fragmented and the transformative—it is said that it "can save all sentient beings. △ Second, praising its function of bestowing bliss.
This sutra is able to bring great benefit to all sentient beings—up to the point where it is "like a merchant obtaining the sea" or "like a torch dispelling darkness.
These two phrases mark the fulfillment of benefits and vows; all subsequent instances of the character *de* (obtain) carry the meaning of being fully satisfied.
The twelve matters, such as "coolness" and so forth, are all functions for bestowing happiness. This sutra is like a pond because it is the supreme flavor of *amṛta* (clarified butter);
it is like fire because it kindles the flames of wisdom; it is like clothing because it is adorned with merit.
Like a sovereign, because one realizes the truth of the Dharma-body; like a mother, because sentient beings rely upon her for protection;
like a ship, because she carries them to the other shore; like a physician, because she cures the maladies of body and mind; like a lamp, because she dispels the darkness of ignorance;
like a treasure, because she can always fulfill wishes as desired; and like a king, because she governs and encompasses all capacities of beings.
"Like the ocean" refers to the ocean of the nature of *nirvāṇa*. "Like a torch" refers to the flame of wisdom that destroys delusions.
△ Third, the summary of the two functions:
This *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* is also like this... [up to] ...it can untie all the bonds of birth and death.
Now, as for the power and efficacy of this sutra: it can uproot the suffering of birth, death, illness, and pain for all sentient beings and bestow upon them the bliss of ultimate nirvana;
it can untie the bonds of delusion and karma for all sentient beings and bestow upon them the bliss of ultimate liberation.
Having finished praising the Dharma of the sutra that is upheld, △ third, the merit of upholding the sutra, divided into two parts.
First, it raises the topic of the merit of hearing the entire sutra:
"If a person should hear this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*... the merit they obtain shall likewise be immeasurable.
From "If a person" below, it clarifies the merit of hearing and copying the sutra. From "If one copies this sutra" below, it clarifies the planting of flowers and incense.
These are the merits of various offerings: *campaka*, the yellow flower; *sumanā*, the flower that well-gathers the mind;
*pāṭala*, the fragrant flower; *bharuṣka*, the summer-blooming flower—also called the "rain-flower" because it grows after rain;
*nava*, the variegated flower; and *mālī*, the garland flower. All these flowers may be used to make oil. Thus it is said.
Offering lamps to the Buddha. △ Second, citing the merit of hearing this chapter. This is divided into two parts: first, the comparative evaluation; second, the entrustment.
The first part is further divided into four sections. First, clarifying the benefit of hearing this chapter.
“Rājanvatsa, if there are those who hear [this]... (until) after the end of this woman’s life, she shall no longer receive [a female body].
First, this generally clarifies the merit of hearing this chapter; next, it clarifies the benefits for women who hear this chapter and uphold it.
For one who upholds the sutra, all obstacles and ugliness are eliminated. “She shall no longer receive [a female body]” means that she transforms from a woman into a man. △ Second, the exhortation.
The Benefit of Practice.

If, during the final five hundred years after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa—up until the time of Buddhas and Tathāgatas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges—one practices according to the sūtras following the Tathāgata’s instructions, one will be reborn in the Pure Land.
According to the *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra*, there are five [types of such practice].
In the first five hundred years, there will be firmness in liberation; in the second, firmness in meditative concentration; in the third, firmness in the observance of precepts;
in the fourth, firmness in extensive learning; and in the fifth, firmness in contention. The latter five hundred years are precisely the time of firmness in contention.
In this age of the final dharma (*mappō*), roots of goodness become increasingly scarce, and the great Dharma becomes obscure and ineffective. Although...
If even women can attain victory, how much more so men? Question: In this context, it is simply stated that practicing according to the teaching is the cause for the Pure Land;
how, then, does one practice? Answer: It consists precisely in upholding, reciting, and deeply believing with understanding.
Question: Amitābha Buddha gathers those who practice mindfulness of him to be reborn in Sukhāvatī. Now, having heard the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, for what reason are they also reborn there?
Answer: It is because they understand the "Peaceful Practices" (*anurakṣaṇācaryā*); because they hear of the Buddha’s lifespan; because this sutra is named "Lotus";
and because they clearly realize that all is but mind (*cittamātra*). Nevertheless, all sutras point toward the pure realm, and every Buddha praises proceeding to the Western Pure Land.
This Dharma gate is the place where sentient beings take refuge. Thus, Mañjuśrī, with his great wisdom, seeks birth [therein], and Samantabhadra, with his myriad practices, vows to go [thither].
Master Huiyuan first founded Donglin, and Master Lian succeeded him at Yunqi. Whether in obscurity or in prominence, [they have all followed this path].
From the sages down to the common folk, from the eminent scholars of the Three Studies to the renowned worthies of the Nine Schools, there are none who do not practice and uphold [this path].
It is like the myriad streams converging upon the ocean, or like the host of stars bowing toward the North Star. The vow-power of Amitābha is vast and profound;

if sentient beings focus their minds on him with single-minded devotion, they will surely go [to his land]. Those who aspire to the Pure Land should exert themselves to the utmost. No longer dwelling below, one clearly leaves behind all worldly defilements and greed.
Hatred and delusion are the root afflictions (*mūlakleśa*); pride and the like are the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*).

Having reached the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (*Sukhāvatī*), that upon which one relies consists of pure karma, and those with whom one associates are virtuous people; therefore, one remains far removed from all defilements.

From the passage "Attaining the stage of a Bodhisattva" onwards, it clarifies that the faculty for realizing the principle is purified and the faculty of mental tranquility is purified; thus, one is able to perceive the various Tathāgatas.
He comes. △ Third, the Buddhas praise from afar:
At that time, all the Buddhas together praised him from afar, saying (up to): "In wisdom and meditative concentration, there is no one who equals you."
Good son, the aforementioned woman practiced and attained rebirth, thereby purifying the faculty of patience (*kṣānti-indriya*).

Those who receive and uphold [this teaching] and explain it to others are those who, having previously heard this sutra, practice according to what was taught. The principle of the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) is not a conditioned merit;
therefore, water and fire cannot burn or drown it. To accord with the principle of the true mark, even the ink of the oceans would not suffice to exhaust its description; thus, the thousand...

The Buddha could not finish describing them all. The various mara-thieves are the afflictions of the five aggregates and so forth; the army of birth and death consists of ignorance, the six consciousnesses, and so forth;
the remaining enemies are the delusions and karmic actions that arise in accordance with one's emotions toward objects. These thieves are capable of inflicting harm.
The army is capable of attack; because you have attained the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*), you are able to crush and extinguish all afflictions and defilements.
There is no one like you. This reveals that all Buddhas protect you, and you walk hand-in-hand with the Tathāgata—how could this be within the reach of gods or humans?
There is none who equals you. Through the wisdom and meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*) of the three vehicles, all are but skillful means (*upāya*).
He also contemplates this sutra as being the ultimate reality. Expedient, gradual teachings cannot equal the perfect reality; how could the three vehicles ever be equated with it?
△ Fourth, the conclusion on the benefits of hearing this chapter.
"O Rājanvatsa, from this bodhisattva [up to] the merit he attains is as described above.
This single phrase summarizes the various merits and wisdom of King of Medicine’s ascetic practices, supernormal powers, samādhis, and so forth. "If there should be...
and so on, clarifies the benefit of rejoicing in and praising this chapter upon hearing it; even a single recitation of the sutra’s title [yields such merit].

The lotus opens its mouth; with a single thought of sympathetic joy (*anumodanā*), the fragrance of the Dharma remains upon one’s person, and the seeds of goodness do not perish. Thus, merit is naturally realized.
The aforementioned merits—namely, those concerning rebirth in the realm of Vimalacitra and the subsequent praises—have now been fully evaluated.
△ Next is the Entrustment (Parindanā).
From "Therefore, O Nakṣatrarājasaṃkusumitābhijña" down to "you should thus give rise to a mind of reverence":
here, first, one chapter is entrusted for circulation among those who are the primary audience (the *dharmabhāṇaka*). From "Nakṣatrarāja" onwards, it next instructs those primary audience members.
The supernatural power protects the entire sutra. To explain the meaning of this protection:
this sutra awakens one to the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, thereby eliminating the conditions for the diseases of delusion and craving; thus it is called "excellent medicine.

When the diseases of delusion and craving are removed, the conditions for birth and death are severed, and one suddenly realizes the true and eternal—how could there be old age and death again? Like the illumination of Prajñā-wisdom, it is able to empty the five [aggregates].
The aggregates (*skandha*). To cross over suffering and distress means to be free from old age and death.

"You see below" clarifies that those who uphold this sutra scatter flowers and form the thought of regarding them as the Buddha. "Taking the grass" refers to when the Buddha attained enlightenment, the householder Śrī gave him soft grass for a seat.
"Blowing the conch and beating the drum" means that once he had become a Buddha, he preached the Dharma to awaken others.
This refers to all living beings. Therefore, the conclusion follows below. The preceding response given by the Tathāgata is now complete. △ Third, the benefits of hearing this chapter:
When this "Chapter on the Past Deeds of Bhaiṣajyarāja Bodhisattva" was being preached—down to the *sarvasattvabhāṣā-dhāraṇī*—[the assembly attained various realizations].
This is the assembly’s gathering to hear the benefits of this chapter. △ Fourth, the praise of Prabhūtaratna:
The Tathāgata Prabhūtaratna, within his jeweled stupa... [benefits] immeasurable all sentient beings.

It is not through the accomplishment of causes and practices from former lives that one attains great mastery; yet, without being able to initiate such benefit, [the Buddha] therefore doubly exclaims, "Excellent, excellent!
This concludes the section on the ascetic practices of the Superior Bhaiṣajyarāja.
The Great Compendium of the Lotus Sutra, Volume Eight;
The Great Compendium of the Lotus Sutra, Volume Nine.
Compiled by the later student Dayi of Jinsui Mountain.
The Lotus Sutra, Chapter Twenty-Four: The Bodhisattva Gadgadasvara.
This chapter elucidates how the Bodhisattva deeply realizes the wondrous Dharma and, by means of his wondrous voice, expounds it according to the capacities of beings to circulate this path.

His eloquence in preaching the Dharma—manifesting through both speech and silence as appropriate for each occasion—is called "Wondrous Sound" (Gadgadasvara). Although his name is Wondrous Sound, in reality...

He manifested wondrous conduct and revealed the two benefits of physical form and voice; his great transformation left no trace, yet such was his virtuous achievement that this chapter was established.
Observing that he formerly served King Cloud-Thunder Sound Buddha with a hundred thousand kinds of arts, he now travels through other lands.
Music followed him of its own accord. Formerly he offered eighty-four thousand precious bowls; now he possesses such a multitude of ritual vessels.
Surrounded by his retinue, he who formerly attained the *dhāraṇī* of the languages of all sentient beings has now attained the *samādhi* of the universal manifestation of physical forms.
With wondrous sounds, he roars throughout the ten directions, widely proclaiming this teaching as an offering of music.

The bowl. [The Buddha] aspired that [Guṇasvara] would preach the Dharma with wondrous sounds and that his sublime conduct (*sucarita*) would accord with the needs of beings; therefore, he was reborn in the land of the Buddha Śakrapuṣpa.

Because he is indeed able to possess such supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*) and desires to cause those who have newly attained the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*) to realize that their essence is sublime conduct and to expound the teaching according to the capacities of various types of beings, the "Chapter on Guṇasvara" is spoken.
△ Fourth, Guṇasvara’s preaching of the Dharma. The text is divided into six sections. First, emitting light.

1. The eastern illumination; 2. Receiving the mandate to come from the West; 3. Propagating the sutra throughout the ten directions; 4. Benefiting both lands; 5. Returning to one's native land; 6. Hearing this chapter and advancing on the Path. First, regarding the emission of light and the eastern illumination: The Buddha emitted a great light from between his eyebrows, which illuminated the eastern direction for a distance of eighty-four thousand *yojanas*. Therein was a world-system named "Flower-Adorned" (*Puṣpavyūha*), where there was a Buddha named "Flower-Light" (*Puṣpaprabhāsa*). At that time, the Buddha Flower-Light addressed the assembly of bodhisattvas, saying: "Good sons, you should know that in the western direction, beyond worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River, there is a world-system called 'Endurance' (*Sahā*). There dwells a Tathāgata named Śākyamuni, who is currently preaching the *Lotus Sutra* of the True Dharma to the fourfold assembly. At that moment, the Buddha Flower-Light extended his tongue, which reached up to the Brahma-heaven, and uttered a lion’s roar, saying: "I entrust this *Lotus Sutra* of the True Dharma to you all. You must protect and uphold it so that no evil demons, heretics, or those of wrong views may obstruct its propagation. Then, from the mouth of the Buddha Flower-Light, there issued forth a hundred thousand *koṭis* of rays of light. From each ray of light emerged a hundred thousand *koṭis* of transformed Buddhas, each holding a lotus flower upon which sat a transformed bodhisattva. These transformed bodhisattvas, with their hands joined in homage, proceeded toward the west. Simultaneously, from the mouths of all the other Buddhas in the eastern direction, there likewise issued forth a hundred thousand *koṭis* of rays of light. From each ray of light emerged a hundred thousand *koṭis* of transformed Buddhas, each holding a lotus flower upon which sat a transformed bodhisattva. These transformed bodhisattvas, with their hands joined in homage, proceeded toward the west. In this manner, the Buddhas of the eastern direction, numbering as many as the sands of the Ganges River, all sent forth transformed bodhisattvas to proceed toward the west. Furthermore, from the mouths of all the Buddhas in the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, and the zenith and nadir, there likewise issued forth a hundred thousand *koṭis* of rays of light. From each ray of light emerged a hundred thousand *koṭis* of transformed Buddhas, each holding a lotus flower upon which sat a transformed bodhisattva. These transformed bodhisattvas, with their hands joined in homage, proceeded toward the west. At that time, the Buddha Flower-Light addressed the assembly of bodhisattvas, saying: "Good sons, you should know that these transformed bodhisattvas have all been dispatched by the Tathāgata Śākyamuni to hear the *Lotus Sutra* of the True Dharma. You should all go together with them to pay homage to the Tathāgata Śākyamuni, and when you see him, you should ask after his health, strength, vigor, and ease, and inquire whether he is free from affliction and dwelling in comfort. Then, the Buddha Flower-Light addressed the transformed bodhisattvas, saying: "Good sons, you should know that the Tathāgata Śākyamuni has long since perfected the path of a Buddha. He manifested the appearance of birth in the palace of King Śuddhodana and displayed the deeds of a bodhisattva for the sake of sentient beings. He has now attained supreme perfect enlightenment and is preaching the *Lotus Sutra* of the True Dharma. You should all go to that place and listen to the Dharma with single-minded devotion. Having spoken thus, the Buddha Flower-Light emitted a great light from his body, illuminating the entire eastern direction. All the worlds therein were clearly visible, like looking at the palm of one's hand. The earth quaked in six ways, and a rain of celestial flowers fell. The transformed bodhisattvas, accompanied by the transformed Buddhas, proceeded through the air, arriving at the Sahā world in an instant. They descended from the sky and paid homage to the feet of the Buddha Śākyamuni. At that time, the Buddha Śākyamuni addressed the assembly of bodhisattvas, saying: "Good sons, these transformed bodhisattvas have come from the Flower-Adorned world in the east, having been dispatched by the Buddha Flower-Light to hear the *Lotus Sutra* of the True Dharma. You should all pay them homage and listen to the Dharma with single-minded devotion. Thus ends the first chapter, "The Eastern Illumination. 2. Receiving the Mandate to Come from the West: At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the venerable Mahākāśyapa and the great disciples, saying: "Kāśyapa, you should know that the Tathāgata has appeared in the world because he wishes to cause sentient beings to attain liberation. For the sake of those who are difficult to transform, he manifests various skillful means. Now, I shall entrust this *Lotus Sutra* of the True Dharma to you all. You must protect and uphold it, ensuring that it is not lost or destroyed. 3. Propagating the Sutra Throughout the Ten Directions: At that time, the Buddha addressed the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, saying: "Good sons, you should know that the Tathāgata possesses immeasurable and boundless wisdom. He preaches the Dharma using various names and forms according to the capacities of sentient beings. However, the ultimate reality is but one vehicle—the Buddha-vehicle. There is no second, nor a third. All the Buddhas of the past, present, and future preach only this one vehicle. Therefore, you should propagate this *Lotus Sutra* throughout the ten directions, ensuring that it reaches even the most remote regions. 4. Benefiting Both Lands: At that time, the Buddha addressed the fourfold assembly, saying: "Good sons, you should know that the Tathāgata has appeared in this Sahā world to benefit two lands: the land of the humans and the land of the heavens. By preaching this *Lotus Sutra*, he causes those in the human realm to abandon their afflictions and attain the path of the Buddha, while causing those in the heavenly realms to transcend their celestial pleasures and seek ultimate liberation. Thus, both lands receive great benefit. 5. Returning to One's Native Land: At that time, the Buddha addressed the transformed bodhisattvas, saying: "Good sons, you should now return to your own lands. When you see the Buddha Flower-Light, you should tell him that I am well and at ease, and that I am preaching the *Lotus Sutra* of the True Dharma. You should also inform him that the sentient beings of this Sahā world have all attained the stage of non-retrogression and are destined for Buddhahood. 6. Hearing This Chapter and Advancing on the Path: At that time, the venerable Mahākāśyapa rose from his seat, adjusted his robes, and, with palms joined, addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, I have now heard this *Lotus Sutra* of the True Dharma. My mind is filled with joy, and I have transcended all doubt. I vow that from this day forward, I shall protect and uphold this sutra, never allowing it to be lost or destroyed. May all who hear it advance swiftly on the path to supreme perfect enlightenment. Thus ends the sixth chapter, "Hearing This Chapter and Advancing on the Path. And so, first, the emission of light and the eastern illumination are concluded.
At that time, Śākyamuni Buddha emitted the light from the ūrṇā-kośa (white tuft of hair between the eyebrows), one of the marks of a Great Man (*mahāpuruṣa-lakṣaṇa*), which shone throughout his land.
These marks of a Great Man constitute an ocean of great characteristics. The merit of all the hairs on his entire body does not equal the merit of even a single secondary mark (*anuvyañjana*).

The merit of all the various secondary marks does not equal the merit of a single primary mark. Among the thirty-two primary marks, each successive one from bottom to top is increasingly superior, yet they do not equal the merit of the white tuft of hair (*ūrṇā*).
The merit of the white tuft of hair does not equal the merit of the cranial protuberance (*uṣṇīṣa*).
Therefore, this is a mark of a Great Man (*mahāpuruṣa*). The Buddha possesses ninety-seven kinds of marks of a Great Man, and the *uṣṇīṣa* (the cranial protuberance) is one of them.

When convening assemblies or summoning his emanations, he merely emits light from the white tuft of hair (*ūrṇā-kośa*). Now, in summoning Gadgadasvara, he simultaneously emits light from the *uṣṇīṣa*.
This is because the *uṣṇīṣa* is the mark of the invisible crown; it is the light of the supreme fruit. Now, as he is about to...

The proclamation of the wondrous sounds and the practices according to the capacities of beings constitute the characteristics of the ultimate fruition. Therefore, it is manifested through the light of that ultimate fruition.

The land is the ancient site of the Wondrous Sound; the Buddha is the Teacher and Master whom he follows. The land represents the principle realized, while the Buddha represents the wisdom that realizes.
Since the essence of original enlightenment inherently possesses virtues and characteristics as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, it is called "Pure."

Radiant Adornment (*Prabhālaṃkāra*). The function of initial awakening (*ādikṣānti*) is able to realize the merit of the fruit; wisdom and practice mutually adorn one another, and cause and effect share a single essence, like a flower and its fruit occurring simultaneously.
Therefore, he is called "Pure Flower Constellation King Wisdom" (*Vimalakusuma-nakṣatra-rāja-jñāna*).

His wondrous voice and wondrous conduct manifest based upon this, and thus light illuminates his land. II. Receiving the Command to Come West. This section has two parts. First, explaining the departure and arrival.

Planting virtue and making offerings to the Buddha, one achieves profound wisdom; thus, both merit and wisdom are fulfilled. The character "attaining" (de) governs the following sixteen phrases, signifying realization.
Because one subdues the heterodox and manifests the orthodox while not dwelling in signs, it is called the "Wondrous Banner.

Therefore, it is called "Pure Virtue. True wisdom realizes the principle, while expedient wisdom illuminates the capacities [of beings]. Through skillful means, it accords with and meets [the needs of others], attaining great mastery;
hence, it is called "Sporting as a Constellation King" (*Nakṣatrarājaviḍūṣita*). Responding without being sought, yet in responding there is no response;

teaching without speaking, yet in teaching there is no teaching; perceiving without conditions, through impartial great compassion; hence, it is called "Conditionless" (*apratyaya*). It is the threefold wisdom within a single mind.

One should not seek to see [Mañjuśrī] through his wondrous voice. If Mañjuśrī’s rank is high, why would Ratnākara suddenly fail to recognize him? The answer is:

Mañjuśrī is a Mahāsattva of the Dharma-body, while Mañjuśrī is one who practices the cause after having attained the fruit; both occupy profound stages. How could there be a distinction of high and low? It was certainly not that he truly did not know.
Rather, because the assembly saw the auspicious omen but failed to understand it, [Ratnākara] manifested this to inspire them and bring about their realization. Therefore, he displayed it.
Questioning the Ear. Furthermore, the Flower Manifestation arises from practice; the Wondrous Sound dispatches the flower, which is thus the realm of wondrous practice.
To accord with this practice, one must rely upon great wisdom; therefore, Mañjuśrī poses the question. △ Third, the Tathāgata answers by means of the Desire to Come.
At that time, Śākyamuni Buddha told Mañjuśrī (up to): “He also wishes to make offerings and listen to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
He desires to come to this land to pay homage to me and to make offerings to this sutra. For these reasons, he has manifested these flowers.
△ Fourth, Mañjuśrī requests to see their appearance.
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying: "Up until [the point where] that bodhisattva comes so that I may see him—what roots of goodness has he planted?
Mañjuśrī surely already knows this; yet, because he wishes for the multitude to know, he asks about his diligent cultivation of practice and so forth.

Mañjuśrī surely has not failed to cultivate it; yet, because he wishes for the multitude to cultivate it, he says, "May I be able to see him. Mañjuśrī surely has not failed to see him; yet, because he wishes for the multitude to see him, he asks.
For this reason, it is so: he desires that the great assembly shall emulate the wondrous voice and profoundly cultivate true wisdom.
△ Fifth, Śākyamuni attributes the merit to Prabhūtaratna.
At that time, Śākyamuni Buddha addressed Mañjuśrī... [omitted] "...he shall manifest his form for you all.
Mañjuśrī then requested, "I pray that the World-Honored One, by means of his supernatural powers, will manifest the Sublime Sound.

As for the World-Honored One's attribution of this merit to Prabhūtaratna, it was because Prabhūtaratna, through the power of his supernatural vows, had witnessed the preaching of the sutra in every place; [Śākyamuni] wished to rely upon his supernatural powers and vows.
It is power. Furthermore, Prabhūtaratna represents the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), while Śākyamuni represents the Reward-body (*saṃbhogakāya*).

As the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* states: "The Reward and Transformation bodies are not the true Buddha, nor are they the speakers of the Dharma. The principle of the true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) must be realized from the standpoint of the Dharma-body;
only then will one be in accord with it. Therefore, Kāśyapa did not summon Prabhūtaratna, yet as soon as he called out once, the latter arrived. 6. Prabhūtaratna.
The Buddha of Precious Life came to this assembly.
At that time, the Buddha Prabhūtaratna addressed those bodhisattvas and noble sons, saying, "He has come because he wishes to see your body.
Although the wondrous voice of Prabhūtaratna was separated by many *koṭis* of lands, it was as if they were face-to-face. This demonstrates that [the manifestation] arises from the Dharma-body.

This is the function of the Response Body (nirmāṇakāya). The section on the conditions for its arrival is concluded. II. Second, the actual simultaneous arrival. This also has six parts. First, the journey with the retinue:
At that time, the Bodhisattva Gadgadasvara vanished from that land... [until] hundreds of thousands of celestial musical instruments resounded spontaneously without being struck.
The eighty-four thousand who came together with him represent the manifestation of the Wondrous Sound (Ghoṣadatta) according to the various types of beings;
these are the eighty-four thousand afflictions (*kleśa*). The lands traversed were as many Buddha-worlds as there are grains of sand in eight hundred and ten million *nayuta* Ganges Rivers.
The rain of lotus flowers everywhere symbolizes the manifestation of wondrous practices according to the various types of beings. Celestial music spontaneously...
"Manifesting" (*míng*) signifies that the wondrous sound is free from volitional mental effort (*manasikāra*). Question:
The distance between Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa and the land of the Buddha Śubhavyūharājasaṃkusumitābhijña consists of hundreds of eight million *koṭi-nayuta* Ganges-sands of worlds.
As for the length of the journey traversed, it is beyond measure. How is it that as soon as Prabhūtaratna gives a single call, Gadgadasvara arrives immediately?
Question: To speak with ultimate precision, Dabao (Prabhūtaratna) is the essence of the true mark (*dharmatā*), while Miaoyin (Ghoṣadatta) is its function.
The jewel-mark is without marks; being without marks, it is not a non-mark. It pervades all places, such that there is nothing that is not the true mark.
When Dabao utters a single call, he simultaneously possesses the great wondrous sound. As previously stated, having entered this samādhi, his body does not move or shake. This...
They pass away in that land and depart together; this is the reality-mark (dharmatā) which is signless.
At the single call of Prabhūtaratna, the reality-mark manifests the function of wondrous sound, and they depart together; wondrous sound returns to the essence of the reality-mark.
△ Second, the description of his ascending the platform.
This Bodhisattva’s eyes were like the petals of a vast blue lotus flower... [omitted] ...to Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa in the Sahā world.
Master Zhaolun said: "In India there is the blue lotus flower; its petals are long and broad, with the blue and white clearly distinguished, possessing the appearance of eyes.
Therefore it is said, 'eyes like those that are vast,' and so forth. 'Harmony' (hehe) refers to an accumulation.

Nārāyaṇa—this is translated here as 'Heavenly Power-Wielder' (Tianlishi)—is so named because he is upright and exceptionally marvelous, and his will and strength are fierce and powerful. △ Third, the inquiry after one's well-being.
The imperial decree was transmitted.
Upon arrival, [the Buddha] descended from the Seven-Jeweled Terrace and asked, "Are you dwelling in peace and security with little affliction, and are you able to endure and remain for a long time?
This inquiry regarding the matter of dwelling in endurance refers to the fact that greed, anger, and so forth are all matters difficult to endure. (5)

"Afflictions" refer to the five desires and also to the five sense organs. The Buddha is free from illness and distress; yet, he dwells among them to teach and transform others, manifesting in accordance with human ways.
Furthermore, this is in accord with worldly conventions and is the natural order of things. △ Fourth: Requesting an Audience with Prabhūtaratna.
“World-Honored One, I now wish to see the body of the Buddha Prabhūtaratna; I only pray that the World-Honored One will show it to me so that I may behold it.
After the emanated bodies have dispersed and the stupa has closed as before, and since Prabhūtaratna remains within the stupa, he thus prays that the Buddha will show him so that he may see him.
Furthermore, because the precious stupa is high and remote, he relies upon the Buddha to seek an audience, thereby expressing his reverence. △ Five. The World-Honored One, for...
[The Buddha] consented. At that time, Śākyamuni Buddha said to the Buddha Prabhūtaratna, "This Bodhisattva Gadgadasvara wishes to meet you.
△ Sixth, the praise within the stupa.
At that time, the Buddha Prabhūtaratna addressed Gadgadasvara, saying: "...and because you shall see Mañjuśrī and the others, you have come here.
Question: Since Gadgadasvara had not yet departed from his own land, how could it be said that he would "see" Mañjuśrī? [The text] states that Mañjuśrī requested him to manifest his form.
Śākyamuni attributed the credit to Prabhūtaratna. Prabhūtaratna then said, "Come, son of good family; Mañjuśrī wishes to see your body.
Once Gadgadasvara had arrived in this land, he inquired after Śākyamuni’s well-being and requested an audience with Prabhūtaratna.
Śākyamuni conveyed the message, saying, "This Bodhisattva Gadgadasvara wishes to meet you. Inside the Prabhūtaratna stupa, it was proclaimed, "Excellent! There is no further text.

In the place where Gadgadasvara beheld [the Buddha], there was likewise no vision of Prabhūtaratna; and in the place where [Prabhūtaratna] beheld Mañjuśrī, there was likewise no vision of Gadgadasvara. Why is this? Answer:
From the perspective of ultimate principle (*tattva*), it is because Gadgadasvara had not yet departed from his own land when he finished meeting Prabhūtaratna and Mañjuśrī;
and Mañjuśrī had not yet questioned Śākyamuni when he finished meeting Gadgadasvara. From the perspective of conventional phenomena (*dharma*), the customs of the two lands differ. People...
The matters are each distinct; therefore, they must be inquired about one by one. The above concludes the account of receiving the command to travel westward.

△ Section Thirty: The Propagation of the Sūtra in All Directions. This is divided into two parts: first, the inquiry and response regarding the power of roots of goodness; second, the inquiry and response regarding which samādhi he dwells in.
The first part is further divided into two: first, the questions of Puṣpadatta.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Flower Virtue addressed the Buddha, saying: "What merit has been cultivated to possess such supernatural power?
Flower Virtue was the final incarnation of King Subhavyūha; he wished to assist and propagate the voice of Wonderful Sound, and to bring forth and manifest the wondrous nature.
Having attained the wondrous fruit, he therefore poses this question. The chariots inquired about are all those previously questioned by Mañjuśrī.
△ Next, the Tathāgata provides the response, which is further divided into two parts. First, the direct answer concerning the merit of the roots of goodness.
The Buddha told Flower Virtue Bodhisattva (up to): "He benefits hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas of buddhas with a single voice, awakening all moving beings;
therefore, he is named Cloud Thunder Sound. He is able to respond appropriately to the root-body and the vessel-world;
therefore, he is named Manifesting All Worlds. Because his benefit and response are joyful, he is named Joyful Vision. (10)

Regarding the ten thousand varieties of musical arts, there is singing and there is dancing. In singing, one relishes the lyrics and expresses them through sound; in dancing, one moves the physical form and follows it with the melody.
These are centered on harmony and proclaim the virtue and achievements of men. The *Erlang* and *Nanshan*, as well as the *Ya* and *Song* odes, all record the deeds of ancient people;
they originate from the heart and relate to the rise and fall of states. [The instruments include] metal and stone...

The lutes and flutes serve to delight the ears of worldly people; yet the exquisite music presented here must surely be the music of the Heavenly Court (*Gūntian*), not of the same class as the *Yā* and *Sòng* odes.
Within it, the songs of "The Spring Sun" and "Snow," and the aesthetic resonance of "High Mountains and Flowing Waters," are fully embodied.
The bowl is said to be "in accordance with measure," for it is a vessel of the Way; the exquisite music presented here is not that of earthenware or iron.
This was accomplished through the merit of offering musical performances to the Buddha, whereby he now obtains celestial music that follows him of its own accord;

and through the merit of the root of goodness from offering the precious bowl to the Buddha, by these causes and conditions, he now obtains this retribution and possesses such supernatural power. Thus it is with the flower.
"Virtue is inferior. This concludes the correlation between the ancient and the present. "This is the Sublime Sound... and below, this concludes the answer regarding the roots of goodness.

△ Second, the extensive explanation of the power of spiritual transformations (*nirmāṇa*). This also has three parts: first, a general summary; second, a detailed explanation; third, a concluding summary. First, the general summary:
"Śubhavyūha, you have merely seen the Bodhisattva Gadgadasvara [up to] preaching this sutra for the sake of all sentient beings.

△ Second, the specific explanation, which has two parts: first, responding to the six classes of ordinary beings; second, responding to the four classes of noble ones. The first part further has six sections. First, responding to the assembly of devas.
He may manifest in the body of Brahmā, or manifest in the body of Śakra (up to) manifesting in the body of Vaiśravaṇa, King of the Heavenly Kings.
Brahmā is the Lord of the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*). Śakra is the Lord of those who dwell on earth.

Īśvara is the summit of the Desire Realm (*kāmadhātu*); in Sanskrit he is called Vaśavartin, which here means "Mastery over Others' Emanations" (*paranirmitavaśavartin*), as he makes use of what others have emanated.
He acts to bring about his own pleasure; he is thus the Māra King. Maheśvara is the summit of the Form Realm (Rūpadhātu);
he is Maheśvara. He is the Great General of the Gods. A major scripture states: "The eight Gaṇadharas are the warriors among the gods.
They are also called Kumāras, which means "Boys. They ride peacocks, carry roosters and bells, and hold red banners. Furthermore...
Vaiśravaṇa (韋紐), here translated as "Pervasive Renown," has four arms, holds a conch and a wheel, and rides upon a garuḍa; he is a great celestial general.
Vaiśravaṇa (毗沙門), here translated as "Much-Hearing," is so called because his fame for merit and virtue resounds in the four directions;
he is the Heavenly King of the North. △ Second, the assembly of responsive beings.
Some manifest as the body of a Wheel-Turning Sage King (up to) some manifest as the bodies of boys or girls.
A *gṛhapati* possesses the virtues of a great man; a *śreṣṭhin* delights in discussing names and principles, dwelling in purity.

An official adjudicates the affairs of the state and assists the king in governance. A *brāhmaṇa*—which here means "one of pure conduct"—is a lineage from the beginning of the eon. [The term for] mountain is *parvata*.

The wildness was naturally at rest; therefore, people called him by the name of "Pure Conduct. "Tongnan" (童男) is a term for a boy who has not yet undergone the capping ceremony; "Tongnu" (童女) is a name for a girl who has not yet married.
△ Third, he should be [honored] by the eight classes of beings.
Or he may manifest the bodies of devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, and so forth, up to humans and non-humans, to preach this sutra.

These three characters "preaching this sutra" encompass all the aforementioned types of manifestations; for whenever he manifests a body, he necessarily preaches the Dharma, and whenever he preaches the Dharma, he necessarily manifests a body.
Wondrous voice and wondrous conduct are always mutually requisite. △ Fourth, responding to the evil realms.
He is able to rescue all those in the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, animals, and other places of great hardship.

While it should be said in all cases that he manifests his body to preach the sutras, the reason he alone does not mention this regarding the evil destinies is that these beings are currently sinking into them.
There was no way for them to hear the sutra; he could only provide salvation through his supernatural powers. △ Fifth, regarding the palace harem:
even within the king’s inner quarters, he transformed himself into a woman and preached this sutra.

The royal palace is a restricted precinct; it is extremely difficult to transform those within it. Yet, by means of his supernatural powers, the Bodhisattva likewise manifested his body there to preach the sutra.
△ Sixth, the conclusion that extensively reveals what precedes.
The Flower Virtue (Puṣpadatta) is like the Wondrous Sound (Ghoṣadatta); it is likewise so throughout worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in the ten directions.

That a bodhisattva manifests various transformations and appears in person to preach the Dharma, yet suffers no diminution in their supernormal powers, transformations, or wisdom, clarifies the actual self-benefiting knowledge realized by the Wondrous Sound; that is to say, having realized this knowledge, one is able to contemplate.
All phenomena ultimately return to True Suchness, their equal intrinsic nature, neither increasing nor decreasing;

for one knows all phenomena exactly as they are, wisdom shines forth clearly. This refers to the skillful means of guidance. That each attains what is known according to their respective capacities refers to understanding according to one's kind.
This is the provisional wisdom of wondrous sound employed for the benefit of others through skillful means. Skillful means opens [the way].
He guides them through causes, conditions, and parables; what is spoken in a single voice is understood according to their respective capacities. △ Second, responding to the four types of noble ones:
if there are those who should be delivered by appearing in the form of a śrāvaka, [the Buddha] manifests up to the point of entering parinirvāṇa.
△ Third, the summary:
From "The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Flower Virtue Wondrous Sound" (to) "the matter was thus. This concludes and clarifies the excellence of Wondrous Sound.
Due to the superior causes of offering music and presenting the alms-bowl in the past, he has now attained supernatural powers and wisdom.
Vast and boundless; such are its matters. The preceding section on the answers regarding the spiritual power of roots of goodness is concluded.
△ Second, the questions and answers concerning which samādhi he dwells in, which has two parts. First, the question:
At that time, the Bodhisattva Flower Virtue addressed the Buddha, saying: [omitted] "...manifesting wherever necessary to deliver sentient beings.

Having received the Buddha’s response, he already knew that the Bodhisattvas’ roots of goodness were profound and far-reaching, and their merit and virtue were vast and great. From "World-Honored One" downwards, he asked:
"In what samādhi do the Bodhisattvas now abide, such that they are able to manifest bodies in the ten realms and preach the Dharma of the One Vehicle? As...
This is the sovereign benefit. △ Next, the answer:
The Buddha told Flower Virtue Bodhisattva (up to) "being able to thus benefit immeasurable sentient beings."
Although this answers Puṇyālaṃkāra, it also answers Mañjuśrī’s question regarding which samādhi he practices and what its name is.
When a bodhisattva dwells in this samādhi, like a pure maṇi gem that manifests colors according to the direction, his wondrous practices are inconceivable.
This is where it all takes root. The extensive exposition of the sutra throughout the ten directions is now complete. △ Fourth, the benefits obtained in both lands:
When this "Chapter on the Bodhisattva Gadgadasvara" was being preached (up to the point where it says), they also attained this samādhi as well as dhāraṇīs.

The bodhisattvas of both lands are all those who possess the physical form yet remain incomplete; therefore, by means of the exposition of this chapter, they are all enabled to manifest their realization.
Samādhi and dhāraṇī are identical in essence but differ in function: quiescence is samādhi, while retention is dhāraṇī.
Furthermore, the manifestation of the form-body is called samādhi, and the eloquent discourse of voice is called dhāraṇī.
Furthermore, the purification of the tongue faculty is called a *dhāraṇī*, while the purification of the remaining faculties is called a *samādhi*;
these are all merely Dharma-gates for the purification of the six sense-faculties. △ Fifth, returning to one's original land.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Gadgadasvara [attained] the Samādhi of Manifesting All Physical Forms.
The lands he passed through on his way there were equal to those he passed through on his return; he demonstrated his coming and going and his walking to and fro, never departing from this path.
Even the Bodhisattva’s every movement could provide incidental benefit to all sentient beings, let alone the radiance emitted by the Buddha.
The light shines upon neighboring lands; how could it not bring benefit? △ Sixth, advancing on the Path by hearing this chapter:
When this "Chapter on the Coming and Going of Bodhisattva Gadgadasvara" was being preached (up to the point where) Bodhisattva Śrīguṇarāja attained the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-samādhi*.
The patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas is the attainment of the essence of the wondrous Dharma; the Samādhi of the Lotus Sūtra is the realization of the function of true reality.
Thus did Gadgadasvara conclude his preaching of the Dharma.
The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, Chapter Twenty-five, "The Universal Gate of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva," states that in the *Brahmāloka* world-system (*Saṃtaraṇa*) of the past,
during the eon known as *Supratiṣṭhita*, there was a Buddha named Ratnagarbha. At that time,
there was a wheel-turning monarch (*cakravartin*) named Amitaviśuddhi, whose eldest crown prince made offerings to the Buddha and observed the fast for three months.

"O Bhikṣu, you have resolved to attain Bodhicitta. If there be any sentient beings who undergo the sufferings of the three miserable realms, and if anyone should call upon me or recite my name, I shall hear and see them with my divine eye and divine ear; if they are not thereby relieved from their suffering, I shall never attain Bodhi.
The Buddha Ratnagarbha said: "You observe all sentient beings and desire to sever their manifold sufferings; therefore, now..."
I shall name you Avalokiteśvara. The Bodhisattva of the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* himself declared:
"Because I made offerings to the Tathāgata Avalokiteśvara, I was granted by that Tathāgata the 'Vajra Samādhi of Illusory Hearing-Perfuming and Hearing-Cultivation.
Through this, I have accomplished the thirty-two manifestations, the fourteen fearlessnesses, and the four inconceivables. That Buddha-Tathāgata praised me."
He has excellently attained the Dharma-gate of Perfect Penetration. Within this great assembly, he conferred upon me the prediction [of Buddhahood] with the name Avalokiteśvara.

Furthermore, the *Mahākaruṇā-sūtra* states: "The inconceivable power of this Bodhisattva’s majestic spiritual authority has already caused him to become a Buddha in the past during immeasurable kalpas, with the title Tathāgata Saddharmaprabhāsa.
By the power of his vow of great compassion, he brings peace and happiness to all beings."
He manifests as a bodhisattva for this reason. The *Biexingxuan* states:

"As for Avalokiteśvara, his correct name in the Western language is Āryāvalokiteśvara, which is translated here as 'Observer of the World’s Sounds. 'Observe' (guān) refers to the wisdom that is capable of observing."

That which is observed by Avalokiteśvara is the realm of observation; as for the observing subject, it is luminous and clear without obscurity, always knowing with perfect clarity, standing out in solitary existence.
Because it reflects back to observe and shines alone, it is called "observation" (guan). That which is observed is the sound of Perfect Enlightenment (Samyak-saṃbodhi).
Because he hears the voices of sentient beings, the voices of the vessel-world (the physical universe), and the voices of various classes of beings, he is called "World-Sound" (Shi-yin).

Because the subject and object are combined in the title and both the objective realm and wisdom are raised together, he is called "Avalokiteśvara" (Guanshiyin). "Pu" (Universal) has the meaning of pervasiveness;

his practice extends throughout the Dharma-realm, benefiting beings according to their minds and encompassing all in accordance with his essential nature; thus he is "Universal. "Men" (Gate) has the meaning of passage; there is no entering or exiting...

"Congestion. Herein, every dharma is fully manifest and every phenomenon is unimpeded; thus it is called a "gate. Through this Bodhisattva’s inconceivable spiritual power, he illuminates the entire Dharma-realm to its furthest limits.
As the myriad forms flow and move, and as diverse sounds and different species arise, he universally manifests his form-body and preaches the Dharma according to the capacities of beings.
His wondrous practices respond perfectly and without obstruction; therefore, he is called the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara of the Universal Gate.
In this chapter, moreover, the Sublime Sound manifests forms and preaches the Dharma to rescue beings from various perils; this is no different from that of Avalokiteśvara.

However, it is merely brief rather than universal, and sublime rather than perfect. While Avalokiteśvara does not depart from these practices, he is able to respond perfectly throughout the great trichiliocosm.

It is devoid of the marks of coming or going; that which is called the karma of sovereign mastery manifests universally through the Universal Gate (*Samantamukha*), thereby advancing toward Wondrous Sound (*Ghoṣadatta*).

In reality, these two sages share a single path, serving as the beginning and end of one another. Thus, while the subsequent verse praises the virtues of Avalokiteśvara, it mentions Ghoṣadatta as well.
From this we know that the single path of these two sages is the practice of Wondrous Sound, which unfolds as the Universal Gate.
[The] Gate. One should know that the "Marks" (Lakṣaṇa) constitute the beginning and end. To embody the preceding Dharma, one must combine both practices;

proceeding from the wondrous to the universal, having a beginning and an end, it is only then that [the teaching] is perfectly complete. Therefore, following the "Wondrous Sound," the "Universal Gate" (Samantamukha) is expounded.

△ Five: The Universal Gate’s Perfect Response. This is divided into two parts: First, questions and answers revealing its virtues; second, the benefits obtained upon hearing this chapter. The first part contains a long [section].
The verse section follows. The prose portion contains two rounds of question and answer. In the first round of question and answer, Avalokiteśvara is the subject.
Furthermore, it begins with Ajita raising a question:
"At that time, the Bodhisattva Ajita rose from his seat... [up to] ...for what reason is he named Avalokiteśvara?"
The reason this chapter is initiated by Akṣayamati (Inexhaustible Intention) is to signify that the universal and perfect practice manifests inexhaustibly.
As the foolish praise me, saying: "The worlds are boundless and turbid with dust; sentient beings are countless and frantic with karma.
The river of craving has no bottom and its waves flow on; therefore, my name is Akṣayamati. The practice of Avalokiteśvara is also like this.

It is so. As for baring the right shoulder: in this region, baring the shoulder is considered an act of arrogance, whereas in foreign lands, baring the shoulder is regarded as an expression of reverence.

Exposing the right side indicates that it is convenient for holding offerings; it represents the ritual of serving one’s teacher and performing laborious tasks, and is thus taken as an act of respect.
As for joining the palms: in this region, folding the hands is considered respectful, while in those countries, joining the palms is regarded as reverent.

I, [Your Name], venture not to speak with arrogance, but rather focus my mind with single-minded devotion. To turn toward the Buddha is to turn toward the fruit of myriad virtues by means of the causes of myriad good deeds.

Regarding the passage "The World-Honored One," it asks about the person who contemplates Avalokiteśvara; the intention is that the name "Avalokiteśvara" looks up to the Honored One within the Dharma-realm.
His influence overcomes the multitude of sages like wind bending grass; the name does not exist of itself, but is manifested through its underlying meaning. This is the locus of Avalokiteśvara’s...
As for why Avalokiteśvara bears this name, it is due to many causes and conditions. To speak briefly, these consist of objective realm and wisdom:
taking the two types of karmic responses—good and evil—of sentient beings as the cause, and the numinous wisdom and compassion of the Bodhisattva as the condition.
The *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* states: "One who possesses the two kinds of adornment is able to question and able to answer.

Now, the Bodhisattva Akṣayamati possesses the two kinds of adornment—concentration and wisdom—and is therefore able to question. The Tathāgata has perfected the two kinds of adornment and is therefore able to answer.
II. The Tathāgata’s Response, divided into three parts: 1. The general response; 2. The detailed response; 3. The response by exhorting the upholding of the name. This...

The three categories are precisely the fourteen merits of fearlessness (*caturdaśa-vaiśāradya-guṇa*) found in the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra*. In that sutra, it is the Bodhisattva who speaks for himself; in this sutra, it is what the Tathāgata has taught.
That sutra describes [the state] from the perspective of the cause; this sutra manifests it from the perspective of the fruit. That sutra clarifies only the capacity to respond;

this sutra clarifies both the receptive capacity (*mārga*) and the response (*prativacana*). Only when these two sutras are discussed together does one come to know that the Great Being’s name accords with its reality. Furthermore...
The first section also has four parts. First, the number of people is indicated:
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Akṣayamati, "Good son, if there are immeasurable hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of sentient beings..."

The capacities of the ten dharma realms are indeed immeasurable; yet, when one speaks of "hundreds, thousands, tens of thousands, millions, and billions," this does not mean that all ten realms collectively possess this number.
Rather, it refers to as many people as there are within a single karma—for instance, in a single hell where beings collectively undergo the same suffering.
By examining their suffering, one knows they share the same karma; by extending this analogy to the other destinies, one sees they are all likewise so. Thus, one should know:
This enumeration indicates the meaning of shared karma. By citing these many objects and sentient beings, it demonstrates that the Bodhisattva’s contemplation is profound and his response is great.
△ Second, a general explanation of encountering suffering.
"They undergo various sufferings and afflictions.

This refers to those currently encountering hardship and calamity. Among them, there are those who alone endure many sufferings, those where many people endure a single suffering, those where one person endures many sufferings, and those where one person endures few sufferings. In the present text, "hundreds, thousands, ten thousands, millions, and billions" refers to many people.
To undergo even a single phrase [of suffering] is to experience much suffering. By mentioning the many, the few are revealed; if even the many can be saved, how much more so the few sufferings?
What was stated above—that hundreds, thousands, ten-thousands, millions, and billions who share the same karma collectively undergo one suffering—is now referred to as "various sufferings."
One suffering is one karma; yet there are hundreds, thousands, ten thousands, millions, and billions of sufferings. The preceding section clarified that the numbers are the same;
this section clarifies the distinctions among karmas. Applying this principle throughout the ten dharma realms, the multitudes of myriad capacities are unspeakable, beyond the reach of calculation.
△ Third, hearing the name and title.
Hearing this, one single-mindedly invokes the name of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva.

Because of past and present evils, one encounters various sufferings; because of past and present virtues, one further hears his name. This constitutes the convergence of conditions through the interplay of good and evil.
"Single-mindedness" involves both the phenomenal and the noumenal: if one applies the mind to maintain mindfulness, it is the phenomenal aspect.
Moment after moment they continue in succession, with no other thoughts intervening; with single-minded reliance, there is no second intention.

This is called "single-mindedness in practice" through the invocation of the Name. If one penetrates this single-mindedness in practice, both self and other are transcended, as neither can be apprehended.
Without mind and without thought, with concentration and wisdom in harmonious accord, both the one who invokes and that which is invoked are unattainable.
This is what is meant by "invoking the Name with the single-mindedness of principle. △ Fourth, one immediately attains liberation.
When Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva immediately observes their voices, all obtain liberation.
Hearing his name above and immediately invoking it is the swiftness of the stimulus; invoking the name and receiving an immediate response is the swiftness of the response.
"All obtain liberation" means they receive the benefit of being met with this response. The word "all" not only manifests the manifold benefits for a multitude of stimuli, but also manifests...

This is the response that is perfectly pervasive. It can be understood that the hidden and manifest responses arise through resonance. Question: Since the capacities of beings within the ten realms are infinite, how can they all attain liberation simultaneously?
Answer: It is like parents who think of their children with deep affection; being possessed of great wisdom and abundant wealth, [they can provide for them all at once].
One who possesses great power can simultaneously rescue all their children when they are in distress. The Bodhisattva is likewise:

his unconditioned compassion is profound, his two wisdoms of skillful means and reality are deep, his noble wealth is immeasurable, and his supernormal powers are vast. Although the ten realms are numerous, he has ample capacity to respond to them all.
Question: Why is it that we see those who have invoked the Name for many years yet fail to receive even a fraction of its efficacy?
Answer: To single-mindedly recite the name involves both the phenomenal (the event) and the noumenal (the principle). If neither of these two paths is grasped, how can one move the Sage?
It is like facing a mirror while looking at one’s back, or standing before a valley with one’s mouth closed; how could one produce reflections or echoes? The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* says:
"First, because I do not observe the sounds themselves, but observe the observer, I cause those suffering sentient beings of the ten directions to observe..."

Upon hearing these sounds, one immediately attains liberation. By contemplating the essence of that which contemplates and the nature of that which hears, one realizes that suffering and pleasure are fundamentally non-existent.
Sentient beings are unable to turn their hearing back toward the source; instead, they follow after sounds and transmigrate, thereby undergoing suffering and affliction.

When Bodhisattvas leave the dust behind and restore their original nature, all delusions are spontaneously liberated. They are thus able to cause sentient beings who suffer and are afflicted to hold the name and receive contemplation, so that they too may attain liberation.
This is indeed due to the empowerment of the power of true, pure compassion and contemplation.

That the Dharma Master Lin was spared from disaster in the Tang dynasty after reciting the name for seven days, and that Sun Jingde remained alive in the Wei dynasty after reciting the sutra a thousand times—these are its proofs.
