Thus, the three were able to manifest their sincerity, and their task was accomplished with perfected merit, bringing benefit to the world for a lifetime.
They underwent immeasurable births. One among them repeatedly entered the human world, frequently encountering sounds and sights.
Once, he happened upon a king going forth, amidst a throng of chariots and horses; his mind was stirred and he conceived a longing for that glory.

Through the cultivation of merit, he received retribution according to that thought, constantly becoming a king among humans and in the heavens. When the three who had attained the Way met together, they discussed it, saying: "I..."
He has escaped the cage; his merit stems from this kingship. Yet he is addicted to karmic retribution, which increases his conditioned existence (*saṃskṛta*).

Once he dies from this state, he will no longer be a king, but will instead sink into a pit of fire, making him truly difficult to save. Fortunately, before he suffers these pains, he is precisely the right time for conversion.
One person said: "This king is attached to desire and furthermore holds wrong views; were it not for the hook of affection, there would be no way [to reach him]."
They may be transformed. First, she became a beautiful wife; second, they became intelligent sons. They must surely obey the words of their mother-in-law.

If one applies skillful means accordingly, they will indeed succeed in reforming their deviance. The wife of former times is now the Bodhisattva Saṃdarśanālakṣaṇa, who is none other than Gadgadasvara.
The two sons of former times are now Bhaiṣajyarāja and Bhaiṣajyasamudgata. The king of former times—
The present Huade is that very person. For this reason, he was summoned from the east by the white tuft of hair between the Buddha’s brows; he ascended the Purple Terrace and was led westward.

Divine mantras protected the sutra so that it might circulate and bring great benefit. Because it recounts the prior conditions of the Four Holy Ones, it is titled "The Chapter on the Past Deeds of King Wonderful Adornment.
It transforms the heterodox and promotes the circulation [of the teaching]. Furthermore, through the merit of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, his various faculties were adorned, and he attained greatness.
Sovereign. This king had a karmic affinity for the Sublime Dharma in the past; his cultivation of the Path has reached maturity, and his faculties are fit to be purified.
As the subsequent text states, he attained the Samādhi Adorned with Pure Merit; for this reason, he is named King Wondrous Adornment. Regarding his "original deeds" (*pūrvayoga*):
these concern the matters of his taking birth, establishing transformations, and turning those who are heterodox toward the orthodox. △ Seven: Wondrous.
The section on "Subduing the Deviant" is divided into six parts: first, a brief explanation of the fundamental matter; second, the designation of the converter and the converted;

third, the skillful means of the converter; fourth, the benefits gained by the converted; fifth, the summary correlating the ancient and the modern; and sixth, advancing on the path upon hearing this chapter.
First, the brief explanation of the fundamental matter:
At that time, the Buddha addressed the great assembly: [omitted] "The land is named Radiant Adornment, and the eon is named Joyful Vision.

Because his causal conduct was sovereign and his resultant wisdom was perfectly luminous, and because he benefits all with a single voice to awaken the various capacities of sentient beings, he is named Cloud-Thunder-Voice-Constellation-King-Flower-Wisdom.
He establishes instruction through the divine way, and all people love to behold him; therefore, the land is named Radiant."
Adorned. The kalpa was named *Priyadarśana*. △ Second, identifying the transformer and the transformed:
Within that Buddha-dharma, there was a king named *Suḍarśana-vyūha* (up to) ... he also fully mastered this samādhi.
One is the object of transformation, while three are the transformers. Below the section on the King, the names of the four noble ones appear.
As for Pure Virtue (Viśuddhaguṇa), although he manifests a defiled body, his virtue is fundamentally pure. As for Pure Treasury (Viśuddhagarbha), he is the repository of the wondrous principle.
As for Pure Eye (Viśuddhanetra), he is that which is revealed by wondrous wisdom. Because they possess this wondrous purity of both principle and wisdom, they are able to transform the heterodox.

This is for the sake of manifesting their virtuous qualities. These two sons are mentioned below to specifically reveal the virtues of each son. The explanation of the six perfections and so forth is seen previously.

Regarding the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*saptatriṃśad-bodhipakṣa-dharmāḥ*): the body, sensations, mind, and phenomena constitute the four foundations of mindfulness (*catvāri smṛtyupasthānāni*). They function to sever evil and give rise to goodness.
These constitute the four right efforts (*samyak-prahāṇa*). Desire, diligence, mind, and investigation constitute the four bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*).

Faith, diligence, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom constitute the five faculties (*indriya*) and also the five powers (*bala*). Mindfulness, discernment, awakening, joy, pliancy, concentration, and equanimity constitute the seven factors of awakening (*bodhyaṅga*).
Right view, intention, speech, action, livelihood, diligence, mindfulness, and concentration constitute the eightfold noble path (*āryāṣṭāṅgamārga*). These are the practices of the Mahāyāna.
Taking the four immeasurable minds as its essence, the six perfections as its function, and the factors of enlightenment as its support, one thereby attains the fruit of Buddhahood.
Both sons have fully realized this; though they will practice it for a long time, how could their merit and wisdom ever be measured?

The seven samādhis receive their names according to their specific functions, yet their underlying principle is no different. Being perfectly free from all defilements is called "purity. True wisdom is like the sun.
Skillful means and wisdom are like stars; they are called the Constellations. Their inherently pure and awakened nature is called Pure Light.
The universal manifestation of the form-body is called Pure Form. That which is illuminated by the great wisdom of primordial purity is called Pure Illumination.
That which is not the mundane Dharma-body is called Long Adornment. Possessing great divine functions, it is called the Treasury of Great Majestic Virtue. These two sons are thus endowed.
This is his virtue; therefore, he is able to manifest his body to transform and deliver others, turning them away from the heterodox and returning them to the orthodox.

△ Third, the skillful means of transformation, divided into eight parts: 1. That Buddha’s preaching of the Dharma; 2. The two sons’ vow to go; 3. The discussion between mother and sons; 4. The two sons’ manifestation of supernatural powers; 5.
The disciple who trusts [the Buddha] subdues the teacher; 6. The son rejoices and reports to his mother; 7. The vow to seek renunciation; 8. [The conclusion].
He exhorted [the king] to personally visit the Buddha.
At that time, when that Buddha first preached the Dharma, he intended to guide King Subhavyūha [to the presence of the Buddha] and spoke this Lotus Sutra.

The time for preaching this sutra has now arrived. That Buddha appeared in the world and constantly proclaimed the True Dharma; however, because the king’s karmic affinity was weak, it was not yet the proper time.
Now that he preaches the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, it is precisely the right occasion. Therefore, it says, "desiring to lead [them]," and so forth.
△ Second, the two sons wish to go.
At that time, the two sons, Viśuddhagarbha and Viśuddhanetra, went to their mother’s place [to hear her preach] the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, which they should have listened to and accepted.
As for why they first addressed their mother: while the father was heterodox and the mother was orthodox, they first addressed the mother so as to devise a means of transformation together.

If one were to rely on their fundamental reality, mother and sons had known [the truth] from the beginning; however, according to the ritual of transformation, when the capacity [of the beings] has matured, the response must arise. Like a mallet striking a sounding block, the vessel is ready.

Only then is it completed; therefore, it is said to be "white. If one were to conform to worldly sentiments, the mother’s compassion would come first, for compassion is the foremost of the roots of benefiting others.
△ Third, the discussion between mother and son.

The mother said to her son: "Your father has placed his faith in non-Buddhist paths (up to the point where he) might permit us to go to the Buddha’s presence to manifest supernatural transformations and so forth, as a means to convert him. Those with false views do not know the True Dharma."

"I will by no means permit you two to approach the Buddha, nor will I allow you to leave the household life. Unless you employ supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*), you will certainly be unable to move his heart and mind.
Only when I see that your minds are pure through supernormal knowledge will I then guide you to hear the Dharma. △ Fourth:
The two sons manifest their supernatural powers.
Thereupon, because the two sons were mindful of their father, they caused the heart of their father, the king, to attain pure faith and understanding.

They manifested transformations corresponding to the eighteen miraculous powers: first, water issued from his right side; second, fire issued from his left side; third, water issued from his left side;
fourth, fire issued from his right side. These four—water and fire issuing from the upper and lower parts of his body—were thus completed.
8. Walking on water as if on land. 9. Walking on land as if on water. 10. Disappearing from the air and reappearing on the ground. 11.
Disappearing from the ground and ascending into the air. The four modes of walking, standing, sitting, and lying within the air constitute four [items].
Together with these, there are sixteen. Manifesting a great body that fills the air constitutes seventeen. That great body again manifesting as small constitutes eighteen. The mind...
As for those with pure faith and understanding, the result was just as their mother had said. △ Fifth, the son who has faith subdues his teacher.
At that time, the father saw that the son’s supernatural power was such as this (up to: "I also wish to see your teachers; let us go together").
Beholding his supernatural transformations, he marveled at their unprecedented nature; out of reverent faith in his son, he inquired after the name of the teacher.
First, the name "Cloud-Thunder" was mentioned to demonstrate that this was not a heterodox sect; next, the title of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* was cited to distinguish it from worldly scriptures.

Upon hearing his father’s words, although his perverse mind had already been stirred by witnessing the traces of the supernatural manifestations, [it was awakened] by hearing the name of the Buddha-dharma through the power of past causes.
Thus, they were moved to action. Therefore, with an open mind, they went to see him—those who are called people of sharp faculties, who turn at a single stroke.
△ Sixth, the two sons joyfully report to their mother.
Thereupon, the two sons descended from mid-air... [until] ...the mind of *samyaksambodhi*.
The *Ratnakūṭa* states: "If a bodhisattva accomplishes three dharmas, they shall attain non-retrogression from bodhi.

First, to cause parents who lack faith to develop faith; second, to cause parents who violate the precepts to abide in the precepts; third, to cause parents who are stingy and greedy to abide in renunciation.
Now, these two sons have been able to cause their parents to give rise to pure faith and to leave the household life to uphold the precepts.
Observing the precepts, renouncing his kingdom, and receiving the prediction [of enlightenment], he may truly be called a great Bodhisattva who has attained non-retrogression.
△ Seventh, the vow to seek renunciation:
"We have already performed the work of a Buddha for our father" (up to the point where), wishing to restate this intention, they addressed their mother in verse.
"Mother, we pray that you allow us to leave the household life and become śramaṇas... (until: ...we pray that you grant us permission to leave the household life.
His mother then replied, "I grant you permission to leave the household life. Why is this? Because a Buddha is difficult to encounter."
To encounter a Buddha is as difficult as encountering the udumbara flower; to leave the household life is the excellent strategy for escaping hardship and the sharp instrument for entering the Way.
Therefore, he said, "I pray that you will listen. His mother then informed him below [of her decision] and granted her permission. △ Eighth, Exhorting Him to Behold the Buddha in Person.
Thereupon the two sons addressed their parents, saying: [up to] "The appearance of the Buddhas is difficult to encounter, and such times are likewise rare to meet, like the *udumbara* flower.
This reiterates from within the verses that the appearance of the Buddhas is difficult to encounter.

Furthermore, the phrase "like the one" reiterates the previous point that escaping from various calamities is also difficult. The *Āgama* states: "Beneath Mount Sumeru, in the midst of the ocean, there is a single eye."
There is a tortoise and a tree with a single hollow. If the tortoise should find the tree's hollow, it may cross over drowning;

yet the tree drifts with the current around Mount Sumeru, and only once every three thousand years do they encounter one another. Moreover, for a single eye to seek out a single hole is an extreme difficulty.
Moments easily pass away, and the human path is hard to encounter. To have the good fortune of seeing a Buddha is even more difficult than for the tortoise and the tree to meet.

How could one fail to draw near to and be intimate with them? This concludes the section on the skillful means of transformation. △ Fourth, the benefits gained by those transformed, divided into eleven sections.
First, an account of the virtues of the palace retinue.
At that time, King Subhavyūha’s harem [became such that they] caused their minds to have faith and understanding, and to delight in the Buddha-dharma.
This describes how those in the palace possessed virtue, making them easy to exhort and transform. The virtue of the harem was such that their fundamental dispositions were pure and sharp.
Therefore, one is able to receive and uphold this sutra. All [teachings] within a single gate are the retinue of Bodhi; they gather together in a circle to discuss non-arising (*anutpāda*).
As for the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-samādhi*, it gathers all dharmas back into the single true mark (*ekalakṣaṇa*). Regarding "leaving the evil realms":

while the three paths are generally considered evil, a comprehensive discussion includes the twenty-five states of existence (*pañcaviṃśati-bhava*), all of which deviate from the truth and give rise to delusion, and are thus entirely evil.
The destinies—now he has departed from them all. This is the King of the Twenty-five [States] who shatters the twenty-five modes of existence (*bhava*).
As for the Buddha’s assembly of *samādhi*, it is the secret treasury of the three virtues (*triguṇa*). Because the Buddha gathers within it, he attains this *samādhi*;
thus one comes to know the secret treasury of all Buddhas. The King and his harem are the primary recipients of the teaching (*yathābhavyatā*), while Jingzang and Jingyan serve as...

He is able to teach. As the faculties [of the disciples] and the teaching strike one another, they are thus easily transformed. This "power of skillful means" refers to the aforementioned manifestation of supernatural powers and transformations.
△ Second, the assembly joins the palace to follow the transformation.
Thereupon, King Subhavyūha [approached] the Buddha, circumambulated him three times, and withdrew to stand to one side.
△ Third, the Buddha preaches the Dharma for him:
At that time, that Buddha preached the Dharma for the king, instructing, exhorting, benefiting, and gladdening him; the king was filled with great joy.

This refers to the preaching of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*. The King advanced with courtesy, and the Buddha responded with the Dharma. As this accorded with his original vow, he attained the characteristics of the Great Dharma;
therefore, he was greatly rejoiced. △ Fourth: Abandoning Attachment and Turning the Mind.
At that time, King Subhavyūha and his consort (up to) scattered [flowers] worth hundreds of thousands over the Buddha.

Having been stained by love and deluded by worldly desires throughout kalpas, they turned their light back in a single thought-moment and thereby attained the cause of the emptiness of the three wheels, perfectly harmonizing with the fruit of unsurpassed Bodhi. △ Five: Manifestation through the Buddha’s Power.
In the void of space, he transformed [the offerings] into a four-pillared precious terrace (up to) sitting cross-legged and emitting great radiance.
The pearl necklaces he offered transformed into the seat of the Dharma-emptiness, the robe of gentle forbearance, and the body of precious awakening;
these were manifestations through the Buddha’s power to inspire right mindfulness. △ Sixth: Evil thoughts were suddenly severed.
At that time, King Subhavyūha had this thought (up to: he accomplished a supreme and most subtle form.
When the king beheld this superior appearance for the first time, he suddenly realized that the illusory and delusive forms of the world were not to be cherished or delighted in;
therefore, he deeply praised the subtle and wondrous form of the Buddha’s body. Thus, his heterodox thoughts were completely severed, and right mindfulness appeared before him. Therefore...
He received the prediction of his future buddhahood. △ Seventh, the Buddhas bestow the prediction.
At that time, from the Buddha Meghadundubhisvararājasaṃkusumitābhijña (up to) "the land is level and upright, and its merits are such as these."
The "Dharmas that assist the Buddha-way" refers to protecting the Buddha-dharma. *Sāla* means "firm and solid.
The name of the Buddha takes its meaning from providing broad shade for all living beings; the name of the land takes its meaning from destroying all false darkness;

and the name of the eon takes its meaning from surpassing all noble heights—all of which accord with his causal practices. Through a single thought of pure faith, he transformed his ministers and subjects by example, causing them all to attain [enlightenment].
The benefit of the Dharma is the practice of providing extensive shade, which destroys heterodox practices. By means of this, one relinquishes the royal throne and attains the state of Buddhahood;
that is, one transcends all noble and high ranks. The phrase "beneath the śāla trees" clarifies the purity of the retinue and the land. △ Eighth, renunciation and cultivation.
The king immediately entrusted the kingdom to his younger brother [and continued] until he attained the Samādhi of Adornments with All Pure Merits.

The Buddha, possessing the discerning faculty that perceives the horizontal alignment of the stars, pointed directly to the wondrous essence of the original state. The king possessed the talent to follow the whip’s stroke with a dance;

thus, with a single word, he emerged like the finest grain from the husk and took up the responsibility. Once a phrase enters the divine, ten thousand conditions are all but a dream; one abandons the myriad...
The nobility of this vehicle lies in donning the robe of the six harmonies; one knows that the Way exists, yet remains unaware of the existence of the world.
For eighty-four thousand years, he practiced the path of the Lotus Sūtra in order to purify the defilements of worldly toil. Following this period—
When the afflictions have been purified, samādhi manifests before one; thus, the defilement of false views is transformed into the pure adornment of merit.
△ Ninth, the expression of admiration for the two sons.
He immediately ascended into the void to a height of seven *tāla* trees... [until] "...he has come to be born into my family for the sake of benefiting me.
The King, together with his two sons, deliberated upon this: "In terms of the state, he is our sovereign; in terms of the household, he is our father.
Now that he addresses us as 'friends' (*jñāti*), this is the etiquette of teacher and friend. We should forget each other in the Way, rather than regarding him merely as a son."
As for his son: he took his son as his teacher, yet did not treat his father as a father; he befriended his son.
Regarding the matter of these four men entering the mountains, they possessed roots of goodness from previous lives. Without conditions, such roots could not have been awakened.

Though they had fallen into deviant paths, their innate nature was capable of rescuing those drowning; thus it is said that [the Buddha] was born into our family. This is what is meant by "not [remaining] in the midst of intoxication."
Awakening: Only after waking does one come to know it. Upon reaching this wondrously adorned state, one finally meets the two sons.
△ Ten Buddhas Describe Their Exalted Practices:
At that time, the Buddha Cloud-Thunder-Sound-Constellation-King-Lotus-Wisdom (until: causing them to abide in right view).
One who is able to perform the work of a Buddha is a spiritual friend of external protection. One who instructs, teaches, benefits, and gladdens is a spiritual friend of instruction.

One who transforms and guides others so that they may see the Buddha is a spiritual friend of shared practice. One who causes others to enter into the reality-mark (bhūtalakṣaṇa) is a spiritual friend of true reality.
"Great King, you see below: the two characters 'bright' (ming) signify the turning away from distant causes of error.
It is said that by serving various Buddhas and taking pity on sentient beings with wrong views, he has not only today turned away from the errors of Subhavyūha. △ Eleven:
Subhavyūha’s Praise and Thanks.
King Subhavyūha immediately descended from mid-air (until) having spoken these words, he prostrated before the Buddha and departed.

"Extremely rare" (downward): he marveled at the merit of his physical marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*). "Merit and wisdom": this refers to the two adornments of *puṇya* and *prajñā*. "Upon the crown of the head" (downward):

this refers to four of the thirty-two major marks (*dvātriṃśan-mahāpuruṣa-lakṣaṇa*) and one of the eighty minor marks (*aśīty-anuvyañjana*). *Bimbi-*... [The text continues with the description of the *bimbi-prabha* mark.]

This is called the *xiāngsī* (myrobalan) fruit; its color is vermilion and lustrous. Regarding the statement that it has never before been seen, and that it praises the transformation of the Dharma through being fully accomplished and so forth:
by hearing the True Dharma once, one is thus able to turn away from evil; by attaining samādhi once, one is thus able to manifest spiritual transformations.
All of this is the Tathāgata’s accomplishment of inconceivable merit. Regarding the two phrases on "instruction" and "admonition":

he joyfully receives the Buddha’s transformation and celebrates what has been accomplished. That he does not follow the movements of his own mind and does not give rise to false views is entirely due to the power of the Dharma-transformation and the instruction and admonition;
therefore, he praises and gives thanks for them. In total, King Subhavyūha initially did not believe in the Buddha.

Subsequently, one sees the Buddha; finally, one comes to love the Buddha, draw near to the Buddha, and praise the Buddha. From this, it is known that all sentient beings originally possess no fixed nature:
if they practice evil, they become evil; if they practice good, they become good; if they enter into the heterodox, they become heterodox; if they turn toward the correct, they become correct.
There is absolutely no fixed characteristic. This is what is meant by: "When the mind is deluded, the Lotus Sūtra is turned [against it]; when the mind awakens, it turns the Lotus Sūtra."
The benefit conferred upon those to be converted is concluded. △ Fifth, the conclusion correlating the past and the present. This also has two parts. First, the correlation:
The Buddha addressed the great assembly, saying, "What do you think? [up to] "...are now the Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja and the Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyasamudgata."
Regarding "the light shining before the Buddha": this refers to the emission of light that shines eastward upon the body of Gadgadasvara.

Regarding "adorned marks": this means that Gadgadasvara’s body is adorned by immeasurable merits; it is as previously stated that he transformed into the body of a woman within the king's inner palace.
△ Second, the concluding praise.
These Bodhisattvas, Bhaiṣajyarāja and Bhaiṣajyasamudgata—[down to] all devas and humans should also pay homage to these ones of great merit.
[The section on] "Gathering the Superior Chapter" and "Guiding and Transforming the Deviant to Make it Right," etc., has already been placed below.
The manifestation of the two Bodhisattvas' names marks their causal stage; they possess the virtues of the Buddha-fruit, with both merit and wisdom flourishing equally. "If there be...
and so forth, exhorts one to offer worship and pay homage. Section Six: Advancing on the Path through Hearing This Chapter.
When the Buddha spoke this chapter on "The Past Deeds of King Subhavyūha," [the assembly] attained the pure Dharma-eye regarding all phenomena.

"Dust" refers to false views; "dirt" refers to false defilements. When one distances oneself from the dust of views externally and leaves behind the defilement of dirt internally, the Dharma-eye becomes perfectly clear and bright, severed from all flaws and obscurations.
Thus ends the account of Subhavyūha’s conversion from error.
The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, Chapter Twenty-Eight: The Encouragement of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva.
In the Sanskrit language, he is called *Bhaiṣajyarāja* (or *Bhaiṣajyasena*), which here is translated as "Samantabhadra" (Universal Worthy). The *Karunāpuṇḍarīka Sūtra* states:

"I vow that within this defiled and evil world, I shall practice the bodhisattva path so as to make it pure and adorned. My conduct must surely surpass that of all other bodhisattvas. [End of] Treasure [Scripture].

The Buddha of the Treasury said: "By these causes and conditions, I now change your name to Samantabhadra. To act throughout the entire Dharma-realm and to possess virtues that are nowhere not pervasive is called 'Universal' (Samanta).
To benefit sentient beings according to their needs and to establish transformation through the power of the times is called 'Worthy' (Bhadra).

This is a title signifying one who assists the Buddha’s transformation from above and benefits the multitude of living beings from below. 'Exhorting and Inspiring' (Kuan-fa) means to encourage and advance; it refers to repeated instruction and admonition to open the way for all things."
This refers to the accomplishment of the task; it is also an expression of longing for the Dharma.

Having heard this sutra in its entirety from beginning to end while remaining far away in that land, and desiring to practice it himself and transform others so that this may continue forever without end, he has come from the East to exhort and inspire us.
Only after exhausting the beginning and end of the wondrous Dharma does he fully manifest the Great Matter, in accord with all Buddhas.
...the practice of wisdom. Thereupon, one beholds the entire body of the Tathāgata. This sutra begins with the dialogue between Mañjuśrī and concludes with the exhortation of Samantabhadra.
Its twenty-eight chapters form a single, coherent system, thereby exhausting the beginning and end and unifying wisdom and practice.
The great causal conditions are here brought to completion; thus, the Dharmakāya of the Tathāgata [is revealed].
It is in its entirety. Wisdom is able to bring about awakening; thus it initiates the beginning. Practice is able to perfect virtue; thus it completes the end.
The phenomena and dharmas in between are none other than wisdom and practice, which mutually assist one another. Therefore, the final chapter is established with Samantabhadra.
△ 8. Samantabhadra’s Exhortation. This section has four parts: first, the narrator’s description of the ritual setting; second, Samantabhadra’s exhortation;
third, the Tathāgata’s account of the arousal [of the mind]; and fourth, the completion of practice through hearing these four chapters. First, the narrator’s description of the ritual setting:
At that time, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva (up to) bowed his head at the feet of Śākyamuni Buddha and circumambulated him seven times to the right.
His unconditioned response to beings pervades the entire Dharma-realm; this is called sovereign supernormal power. His virtue is nowhere not present, and his name is nowhere not heard;
this is called majestic virtue and renown. Together with boundless bodhisattvas who had come, he manifested the perfect inclusion of the myriad practices.
The intention of inexhaustibility: Samantabhadra presides over the phenomena of the *dharmadhātu* and is perfectly endowed with the ten thousand practices; thus, within phenomena, there is reality.

His response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*) is nowhere not present. Furthermore, at the conclusion of the Dharma assembly, he manifests as coming from the East, thereby benefiting sentient beings through effortless action (*anābhoga-caryā*).
II. Samantabhadra’s Exhortation to Practice. This section has two parts. First, the inquiry.
Exhortation. Second, exhortation through the making of vows. The first [section] further has two parts. First is the inquiry:
he addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One... how can one obtain this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*?"
"Ratnatejobhyudgatarāja" (Jewel Splendor Supreme King) is a title for one who possesses mastery over beneficial conduct.
Because Samantabhadra’s mind-hearing can penetrate the ten directions, it is called "hearing from afar. What was asked previously concerned only the practice of cultivation, recitation, and chanting;
this question asks how one can actually attain [this state], desiring that people achieve profound realization through self-attainment. △ Next, the answer follows.
The Buddha told Samantabhadra Bodhisattva (up to): "After the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata, you will certainly obtain this sutra.

This text fully presents the introduction, the explanation, and the conclusion. "Those who are protected by the mindfulness of the Buddha" means their Way accords with the Buddha’s mind. "Those who have planted the roots of all virtues" means they have perfected both merit and wisdom.
"Those who have entered the stage of right determination" means they embody the wondrous essence of the Buddha. "Those who give rise to the aspiration for salvation..."
"Mind" refers to practicing the wondrous conduct of the Buddha. To be able to practice these four matters is to truly obtain this sutra. These four words alone encompass the entire scripture.
That the *Lotus Sutra* was preached again and that [the Buddha] traveled from afar to exhort and inspire us—its meaning is thus. Furthermore:

first, by opening the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, one has already attained the realm of principle (dharmadhātu) and personally inherits the lineage of awakening; thus, one attains mindfulness of the Buddha. Second...

This indicates the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. Having attained the phenomenal dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), he manifests vast and manifold functions; the fifty-two stages are perfectly interfused within a single thought-moment, and for this reason it is called the "Root of Virtue" (*Guṇamūla*).
Third is the awakening to the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, whereby one attains the dharma-realm of both principle and phenomena (*li-shi dharmadhātu*).

Transcending both the ultimate and the conventional, it is the quiescent illumination of suchness (*tathatā*), devoid of the characteristics of entering or emerging; therefore, it is called "Right Concentration" (*samyaksamādhi*).

Fourth is "entering the Buddha’s knowledge and vision": having already attained the dharma-realm of phenomena and events (*dharmadhātu*), one undertakes the activities of Samantabhadra within the equality of true suchness;
therefore, it is called "arousing the mind to rescue all sentient beings. These four dharmas are all the practices of Samantabhadra and encompass them all.
The *Avataṃsaka* contains more than two thousand gates; though their names are many, they do not exceed these four.

II. Encouraging through Vows. This is divided into two parts: first, protecting persons; second, protecting the Dharma. Within the first part, there are six sections. First, warding off external difficulties.
1. To instruct them in the internal Dharma; 2. to shield them with supernormal powers; 3. to demonstrate the superior causes;
4. to demonstrate the proximate fruits; 5. to provide a general conclusion. Regarding the first [point]: to dispel external obstacles.
At that time, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying: [up to] "those who afflict people shall find no opportunity.
*Vetāla*—this is translated as a "ghost of malevolent incantations. The rest is explained as before. △ Second, teaching the internal method. This also has three parts.
First, walking while standing and reciting.
Whether walking or standing, if this person reads and recites this sutra (up to the point mentioned), it is also for the sake of making offerings to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
The six-tusked white elephant symbolizes the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*) and the pure, white Brahma-conduct (*brahmacarya*). △ Second, constant sitting and contemplation.
If this person sits and contemplates this sutra, they will attain such *dhāraṇīs* as these.
By virtue of this sutra, they personally behold the essence of Samantabhadra’s constant practice. Regarding all phenomena, they return to the root and revert to the source;
this is called the *āvartana-dhāraṇī*. Having already turned back from the branches to the root, they then turn back from the essence to the function regarding all things.

Regarding time and place, employing skillful means to benefit sentient beings with mastery over both adverse and favorable conditions—this is called "hundreds, thousands, ten thousands, millions," which is the conduct of Samantabhadra pervading all places.
"The skillful means of the Dharma-sound" refers to preaching the Dharma in accordance with the capacities of those to be converted. △ Third:
Three-Seven Days of Diligence.
"Bhagavān, in a future age, during the final five hundred years... [he] spoke a dhāraṇī before the Buddha, saying:
*Atandati* (1), *Dantapāti* (2)... [up to] *Svābhigītide* (20).
Within the instruction of the internal Dharma, there were three successive teachings. First, he stood up, mounted an elephant, and comforted their minds; next..."

Sitting in contemplation, he taught them the sutras and bestowed upon them samādhi; for these past three weeks, he has single-mindedly applied himself with diligence to instruct, benefit, and gladden them.
Mantras are the secret speech of all Buddhas and efficacious talismans that ward off calamities;

they may be the names of Buddhas, which, when maintained, bring majestic power without anger, or the names of ghost kings, which, when invoked, cause their tribes to revere their lord. Thus it is for those who maintain them.
Not only does it ward off difficulties, but at all times and in all places, it transforms the ominous into the auspicious and turns calamity into blessing.

It fulfills one's wishes according to the mind, even leading to the attainment of sagehood and worthiness; its benefits are great indeed. Having finished teaching the internal methods, △ third, he covers them with his supernatural power.
World-Honored One, if there are bodhisattvas [who... all this is due to the majestic spiritual power of Samantabhadra.
Whether they hear it or uphold it, there is nothing that is not the spiritual power of Samantabhadra. △ Fourth, showing the supreme cause.

If there are those who receive, uphold, read, recite, and correctly bring to mind [this sūtra]—up to being stroked on the head by the hands of all Tathāgatas—they must maintain the essential practice of the sūtra through correct mindfulness (*samyak-smṛti*).
If one’s mindfulness is incorrect, then discursive thoughts will become confused and disordered; if one’s recollection is incorrect, it is not true mindfulness.
Then, as perverse habits will be intermingled and agitated, it will be difficult to achieve profound practice.

Therefore, this section specifically clarifies the practice of right mindfulness, which is mentioned repeatedly in the subsequent text. Once mindfulness is correct, then whatever one practices is nothing other than the right practice of Samantabhadra;
thus, one receives the Tathāgata’s empowerment by touching the crown of the head as a seal of certification. △ Fifth, showing the proximity to the fruit.
If one merely transcribes this, at the end of their life, they will obtain such merits and benefits as these.

The Trāyastriṃśa Heaven is the second heaven, inhabited solely by devas and humans; the Tuṣita Heaven is the fourth heaven, inhabited by Bodhisattvas, and its excellence should be understood as being twofold greater.
"Extending the hand" has the meaning of taking someone by the hand [to welcome them]. The celestial maidens of the inner palace are all emanations.
Because it arises. △ Sixth, the summary:
"Therefore, the wise person should single-mindedly write it themselves... [until] ...right mindfulness and practice according to the teaching.
This concludes the first section on protecting persons. △ Second, protecting the Dharma.
“World-Honored One, by means of my supernatural powers, I shall now cause [this teaching] to be widely circulated so that it shall never be interrupted.
It should be known that the present upholding and so forth are all the supernatural power of Samantabhadra, who constantly protects this sutra so that it may circulate without obstruction.
This concludes the *Samantabhadra-utsāha* (Exhortation of Samantabhadra). Part Three: The Tathāgata’s Account of the Exhortation. This section also has two parts. First, the preliminary...
On the Protection of the Dharma:
At that time, Śākyamuni Buddha [spoke] up to the words, "I shall protect those who are able to receive and uphold the name of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva.
Now, to describe this: you are thus able to provide great benefit externally and accumulate compassion internally. Since the distant past, for many kalpas...

Having made such a protection, I shall, by means of the Buddha’s spiritual power, protect those who uphold your name, causing the practitioner to advance and to propagate [the teaching] with courageous vigor.
II. Describing those whom he protects. This has five parts. First, describing and showing his bodily teachings.

“Samantabhadra, if there are those who receive, uphold, read, and recite [this sutra]—up to being covered by the robe of Śākyamuni Buddha—such people who behold the Buddha will see my fruition-body endowed with ten thousand virtues;
how much more so your causal body as a six-tusked white elephant? They have already heard this sutra directly from the Buddha’s own mouth; how much more so that which you teach?”

Even one who has forgotten the verses and chapters was praised by the Buddha, who stroked their head and covered them with his robe; how much more so for you, who are protected by the *dhāraṇī* of others?
"As heard from the mouth" and so forth refers to correct recollection (*samyak-smṛti*). Thus, by means of this very sutra, one sees the Buddha;

one does not become stuck in names and signs (*nāma-lakṣaṇa*). By means of this very Dharma, one creates the sublime; it is no different from hearing it directly. This is what constitutes making offerings.
"Buddha" means one who is able to perform the Buddha-work. "The Buddha praised him, saying 'Excellent'" means that he deeply accords with the Buddha’s mind.

"Placing his hand upon his head" signifies that there is a set time for attaining the fruit. "Clothing him" signifies the accomplishment of the practice of patience (*kṣānti*). When mindfulness is correct, such is the profound realization.
II. Describing the Superior Causes.
Such a person no longer clings to worldly pleasures (up to) being able to cultivate the conduct of Samantabhadra.

This extensively illustrates that within the causal stage there are no faults or evils; having few desires and being content, one cultivates the conduct of Samantabhadra, thereby describing the superior causes.
Possessing right mindfulness, one naturally fulfills the dharmas of the practice of peaceful dwelling (*sukha-vihāra*), yet [remains free from] the stains of the three poisons and pride.
One cannot cause affliction; this is truly the cultivation of the conduct of Samantabhadra.
One should know that the power of right mindfulness is the dhāraṇī for the four types of conduct and the essential truth of the sublime practices. This is why it is spoken of repeatedly.

The World-Honored One further assists and extols it, intending to let future generations know that the reason for Samantabhadra’s exhortation to initiate and perfect these practices does not lie in mere abundance of words.
The method is simply right mindfulness. △ Third, describing and showing the proximate fruit:
"If Samantabhadra, after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa... (up to) shall also obtain its meritorious retribution in the present life."
Such a person shall proceed to the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa). They will certainly attain the distant fruit; how much more so the proximate fruit?
Furthermore, they shall obtain its proximate fruit even in the present life, not merely rebirth in heaven. △ Fourth, refuting external objections.
If there are those who speak with contempt and slander [them], they will suffer from various grave and evil illnesses, such as dropsy and shortness of breath.

"Liao-li" (繚戾) refers to a state of being twisted and entangled, unable to stretch or extend; "lai-mu" (睞目) refers to looking askance or glancing sideways. Such is the principle of karmic retribution.
It emerges from the subtle depths of nature (*xing*) and destiny (*ming*). For it is from nature that the mind (*xin*) arises, and by destiny that karma (*ye*) is regulated.

The mind perceives internally, while karma invites [retribution] externally; each follows its own kind, without the slightest deviation. Alas! Such is the correspondence between the mind and karma regarding retribution.

It is like the relationship between the myriad forms and their underlying models. Therefore, those who destroy the correct view of upholding the sutras will be without eyes for generation after generation.
By making offerings and offering praise, one obtains immediate results; by exposing its faults and evils, one suffers from malignant diseases;
and by deriding it with laughter, one receives an ugly appearance, such as hands and feet that are twisted and deformed, or eyes that are squinting and askance.
They look upon one another with inverted gazes; all are of hideous appearance. Furthermore, they are afflicted by foul-smelling sores and pus, as well as the grave illness of labored breathing.

These are all the manifestations of their own minds, for they have invited such conditions through their own kindred actions. The hardships, destitution, and grave illnesses encountered in this world are never without causes from past lives.
△ Fifth, an account of the merits of those who possess faith.
Therefore, Samantabhadra, if you see one who receives and upholds this sutra, you should rise to welcome them from afar, just as you would show reverence to the Buddha.
△ Fourth, the accomplishment of practice upon hearing the chapter. This has two parts. First, the benefits of hearing the chapter.
When this "Chapter on Exhortation by Samantabhadra" was being spoken (up to the point where) the bodhisattvas as numerous as atoms had fully realized the path of Samantabhadra.
△ Second, the conclusion of the matter: it is said that [the assembly] dispersed.
When the Buddha spoke this sutra, Samantabhadra and all the other bodhisattvas (up to the point where) they received and upheld the Buddha’s words, paid homage, and departed.
This summarizes the assembly on Vulture Peak, wherein the great multitude heard the sutra and obtained its benefits. Within this entire scripture, there are both teachers and disciples;
however, speaking from the perspective of preeminence, it is called "The Buddha’s Teaching.

The mention of Samantabhadra and others encompasses the bodhisattva assembly within the gathering, while Śāriputra and others encompass the śrāvaka assembly within the gathering. Those who still maintain the seeds of the śrāvaka path are preserved here.
This is merely a provisional designation. In reality, the Mahāyāna śrāvakas cause all beings to hear through the sound of the Buddha-way.
As for the devas and others, they are included among the eight classes of beings within the assembly. They rejoice because they celebrate what they have heard;

having drifted for many kalpas without hearing this Dharma, now that they have heard it, they are filled with such exceeding joy and good fortune, like travelers meeting one another in a foreign land. Thus it is said.

"Joyful hearing" means that because one receives and maintains what has been heard, it is not lost; because one believes it without doubt, as if following the decrees of a sovereign or the commands of a father, one thus "receives and maintains" what was heard.

"Prostrating" means that because one values what has been heard, the heart is moved with deep emotion and the five limbs are applied with diligence, as if having received the ultimate grace, bowing in gratitude without end; thus, one "values" what was heard.
As for those who depart, having heard [the teaching], they retreat to cultivate it. Thus, the ancients advanced to hear the Way from their teachers and retired to cultivate the Way within themselves;
this was not like people of the present day, for whom it merely enters the ears and exits the mouth. The circulation [of the text] is now complete.
